docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
SAP offers RISE with SAP, built on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (marketed as SAP Cloud ERP Private since 2025). It is a managed private-cloud service, not IaaS: SAP Enterprise Cloud Services (SAP ECS), formerly SAP HANA Enterprise Cloud, runs the infrastructure, operating system, database and SAP technical layers of the customer’s SAP systems. These systems usually run on AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud, in accounts that SAP owns and manages, so the customer cannot reach their logs directly.

SAP LogServ, an optional SAP ECS service, collects the logs of those systems and layers (operating system, database, SAP application) and delivers them to cloud object storage with an event notification for each new object: Amazon S3 with an SQS queue, Azure Blob Storage with a Storage Queue, or Google Cloud Storage with Pub/Sub. Your SAP account team or SAP ECS contact provides the full LogServ service description.

Splunk for SAP LogServ ingests those deliveries into Splunk, gives each log type its own sourcetype, and adds the LogServ App: dashboards, an Environment Topology view, a missing-data diagnostic (the LogServ Data Doctor), Enterprise Security content and an optional AI Assistant.

Start here

New to the solution? Follow the Deployment Roadmap. It takes you from the request to SAP to working dashboards in order, with a check at the end of each step.

docs.title: What You Install
docs.text:
Component Splunk Web label App ID Where it goes Data TA Splunk TA for SAP LogServ splunk_ta_sap_logserv Where the data is parsed: each heavy forwarder, or the single instance. A Deployment Server holds it to push it to the heavy forwarders. LogServ App Splunk App for SAP LogServ splunk_app_sap_logserv The search head (or search head cluster), or the single instance. Splunk Add-on for AWS (Splunkbase 1876) Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunk_TA_aws AWS only: each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that runs a LogServ input. Version 8.2.2 or later is recommended (SVD-2026-1005). LogServ Azure add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure Azure only: installed directly on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that may run an Azure input, not through the Deployment Server. LogServ GCP add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp GCP only: installed directly on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that may run a GCP input, not through the Deployment Server.
  • The Data TA collects nothing itself. It parses, routes and filters at index time the data that the Splunk Add-on for AWS or the LogServ Azure / GCP add-on collects. It also holds the Deployment Server automation, the configuration screens, the AWS S3 Direct backfill screen and the definitions of the two indexes.
  • The two indexes, sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit, are created where the data is indexed. On a single instance the Data TA creates them. With a separate indexer tier, or on Splunk Cloud, you create them yourself, with the retention you want, before any data arrives (see Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA).
  • Without a heavy forwarder. The Data TA and the cloud add-ons also work on a search head that runs the inputs itself, Splunk Cloud included. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare the search-head workload, but they have not yet been tested on a Splunk Cloud search head. This is supported and not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended, because ingest then competes with your users’ searches. With Splunk Cloud and no heavy forwarder, they all go on the Splunk Cloud search head (Running the TAs on a search head).
  • On the search head the LogServ App also needs the Splunk Common Information Model add-on and the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (for the Windows panels); the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux adds the CIM fields of linux_secure; the AI Assistant also needs the Splunk MCP Server. See LogServ App Prerequisites.

For every topology, see Where Each Package Goes. Download the four LogServ packages from the release_binaries folder of the public repository, and the Splunk Add-on for AWS from Splunkbase.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• One pipeline for three clouds. Deliveries from AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage become the same sourcetypes, dashboards and Enterprise Security content. Each event can carry an indexed cloud_provider field: the Azure and GCP add-ons stamp it on every event their inputs collect, and for AWS you add it to each input (Choose Cloud Attribution). The LogServ App’s dashboards count events with no stamp as aws; your own searches and tstats see only the stamped value. See Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario and Supported Log Types.
  • Index-time routing and filtering. The Data TA gives each log type its own sourcetype and can leave log types or old events out of the index. Filtered events are never indexed, so they do not count against your license. You configure it in Splunk Web. With a Deployment Server, the Data TA sets up a server class for the heavy forwarders, and once you have assigned them to it, its Deploy to Forwarders button pushes the add-on and your settings to them. See Decide Filtering, Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders and Configuring Filters.
  • Search-time field extractions. The LogServ App extracts the fields of the SAP sourcetypes, of its own Linux sourcetypes (linux:cron, linux:warn, linux:sudolog, linux:slapd, lastlog, who, linux_messages_syslog), and of ISC BIND and Squid, whose parsers it took over from Splunk’s archived add-ons. Windows (XmlWinEventLog) fields come from the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows, and the CIM fields of linux_secure from the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux, both on the search head.
  • Dashboards, Environment Topology and the Data Doctor. An Environment Health landing page and four groups of dashboards: Applications, Integration, Security and Platform. The dashboards read hourly KV Store rollups, so they load fast at any data volume (Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness). Environment Topology draws the SAP systems, their integration partners and endpoints as a graph (Environment Topology). The Data Doctor explains every empty panel and produces a downloadable diagnosis report (Data Doctor).
  • Enterprise Security content. CIM tagging for the Authentication, Change, Network_Sessions, Network_Resolution and Web data models, correlation searches with risk-based alerting, and a feed of SAP systems and user identities into ES asset and identity management. The content ships enabled. On a search head without Enterprise Security, turn it off; 13 of its searches also run AI Assistant prompts, which fail while those searches are disabled, so if you use the prompts, stop only the schedule of those 13 (Disabling or tuning the ES content).
  • AI Assistant (optional). It ships turned off. Once an admin turns it on and the Splunk MCP Server is installed, analysts run a catalog of predefined investigations with no LLM involved. Free-form questions use an LLM provider that an admin configures; raw events never go to the AI vendor, and the privacy tier sets what the vendor does see (OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) Compliance lists the controls). An admin can limit the assistant to predefined prompts with the Templates-only mode setting (Restricting the LLM Path). See Set Up the AI Assistant.
Version 0.1.2 Supported vendor products SAP LogServ for SAP ECS in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Splunk platform versions Splunk Enterprise 9.4.3 and later; Splunk Cloud Platform (tested on the Victoria Experience; see Splunk Cloud Considerations) CIM 5.0.0 and later

docs.title: Audit Log
docs.text:
Every action the AI Assistant takes — predefined-prompt dispatches, free-form vendor calls, security blocks, privacy-tier elevations, legal acknowledgements — produces an audit event in a dedicated logserv_ai_assistant_audit index. The audit trail is the evidence layer for compliance reviews, SOC investigations, and tamper-resistance posture.

Splunk writes those events only for a user whose role holds the edit_tcp or the edit_log_alert_event capability. Of Splunk Enterprise’s default roles, admin holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event and user holds neither. Users without either are not audited, and the AI Assistant panel shows them a warning; see Who Can Write Audit Events.

Which categories fire with no LLM provider configured

With no provider credential, the active provider is the shipped default Mock (development only), which contacts no vendor. In that state:

  • every predefined prompt records local_only, and a failed forward records audit_forwarder_failure;
  • the Settings page records ai_assistant_enable_acceptance and forwarder_disabled_acceptance when an admin answers an acknowledgement, vendor_tier2_elevation when an admin saves Tier 2, and model_discovery when an admin clicks Refresh model list;
  • a question typed to the Mock provider records vendor_tier1 (with provider = mock, zero cost), and can record user_prompt_jailbreak_flag and rate_limited_prompt.

With Templates-only mode on or a compile-time templates-only build installed (Restricting the LLM Path), typed questions are refused before any of those last three. security_blocked_spl, session_tool_cap_hit and daily_spend_cap_hit need a real provider: they follow from tool calls and spend that only a real LLM produces. vendor_tier2 is declared but never emitted (see below).

docs.title: The Thirteen Audit Categories
docs.text:
Category When Key fields local_only Predefined-prompt dispatch (no LLM call). promptId, spl, rowCount, executionMs, ok vendor_tier1 A free-form prompt sent to the vendor completed, at any tier (Tier 1 or Tier 2) — one event per prompt, recorded after its last turn. The event does not carry the tier. provider, model, inputTokens, outputTokens, vendorCostEstimateUsd, outboundBytes, outboundSha256, promptLength, toolDefCount, turnCount, powerMode, tier2RedactionsApplied (the PII redactions Tier 2 applied across the prompt’s tool results; 0 in Tier 1, with redaction off, or when nothing needed redacting) vendor_tier2 Declared, not emitted. Every free-form prompt, at any tier, records vendor_tier1; a non-zero tier2RedactionsApplied on it marks a Tier 2 prompt in which redaction fired. When Tier 2 was switched on is recorded by vendor_tier2_elevation. — vendor_tier2_elevation Admin saves Settings elevating tier to 2 (from Tier 0 or Tier 1). Admin user, previousTier, newTier security_blocked_spl The SPL guard rejected an AI-authored splunk_run_query (its denylist, its command allow-list, or the check against Splunk’s search parser); a splunk_run_saved_search call from the AI named a saved search outside the App’s prompt catalog; or the AI asked for a tool the App does not offer. In each case the call is refused and never dispatched. spl (truncated to 1000 chars): the query for a blocked splunk_run_query, (saved search) <name> for a refused saved search, (tool) <name> for an undeclared tool. operator: for a query the denylist blocks, the forbidden command or word (lower-cased) or one of inline_comment, unbalanced_backtick, unterminated_quote, escaped_quote, external_lookup, fit_into, macro (macro is also the operator for the macro command, an alias of savedsearch; command tells the two apart — the macro’s own name, or macro for the command); for a query the allow-list blocks, one of command_not_allowed (also for union, with command = union), query_start, index_not_allowed, lookup_not_allowed, eval_lookup, subsearch_not_allowed, subsearch_fields, macro_position (also for a macro written against other text), ambiguous_single_quote, unbalanced_bracket, escaped_outside_quotes (a backslash outside double-quoted text); for the search-parser check, parser_mismatch (Splunk’s parser reads the query differently — also when a lookup / inputlookup names, as the parser reports it, a lookup that is not one of the App’s, recorded with command = lookup / inputlookup), parser_rejected (the parser rejected it as invalid SPL) or parser_unavailable (the parser could not be asked, failed or timed out — the query is refused, never run unchecked; a query the user stops while the parser checks it records no event); saved_search_not_in_catalog for a refused saved search; tool_not_declared for an undeclared tool. command (optional): the command, lookup or macro the refusal is about, as the AI wrote it (fit, customer_hr_lookup, customer_hr_macro, index); names that are not made of letters, digits, _ . : - (at most 64 characters) are recorded as (unnamed). The in-app viewers show it next to the operator. rate_limited_prompt Per-user rate limit denied a free-form prompt. threshold, countInWindow, promptLength, secondsUntilNextSlot user_prompt_jailbreak_flag Jailbreak-pattern analyzer flagged a user prompt (flag-and-proceed; the prompt still ran). promptHash, promptLength, matchedGroups, charClassFingerprint session_tool_cap_hit Per-session tool-dispatch cap reached; dispatch refused. cap, attemptedCount, toolName daily_spend_cap_hit Daily USD spend cap reached; vendor call refused. capUsd, spentTodayUsd, promptLength, secondsUntilMidnight audit_forwarder_failure HEC forwarder POST failed (DNS, network, 4xx/5xx response). destinationUrl (sanitized), reason, batchSize forwarder_disabled_acceptance Admin acknowledged the forwarder-disabled legal modal. Admin user, host (Splunk-stamped IP), tcVersion, optInChoice, disclaimerHash ai_assistant_enable_acceptance Admin acknowledged the AI-Assistant-enable legal modal. Same as forwarder acceptance, plus the seven-clause enable-disclaimer hash model_discovery A dynamic model-discovery refresh ran (any trigger, success or failure). provider, trigger (credential_save / settings_refresh / ttl), ok, modelCount, durationMs, error

Every event also carries a small set of common fields:

  • timestamp — ISO-8601 UTC.
  • user — Splunk username (from services/authentication/current-context).
  • sessionId — Per-tab session id baked at AI Assistant init.
  • seq — Monotonic per-session sequence number, useful for ordering events within a session even when timestamps tie.

docs.title: The In-App Audit Log Viewer
docs.text:
The Audit Log tab in Settings → AI Assistant provides a read-only browser of the index. Filters:

Filter Default Notes Time range Last 30 days (the global picker’s default) Reads from the global TimeRange picker; not a separate field. Re-runs on picker change. Category (all 13) Multi-select with colour-coded chips — each category gets a distinct flat accent colour from the app palette; user_prompt_jailbreak_flag is highlighted in red. User contains (empty) Substring filter on the user field. Useful for “what did admin X do?” reviews. Limit 100 One of 50 / 100 / 250 / 500. Larger values slow page rendering.

The table renders 25 rows per page (PAGE_SIZE = 25); footer shows “Page X of Y” + Previous / Next buttons (only when total exceeds 25). Clicking a row’s + button expands to show the full event JSON.

Splunk reserved-field gotcha: the category field on these events is a Splunk reserved name. The viewer’s SPL uses | eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category") after spath to retrieve the audit-event category from the raw JSON, because spath does NOT overwrite reserved fields. It does the same for user (| eval user=json_extract(_raw, "user")): when a search filters on user before spath — as the User contains filter does — Splunk extracts the field to apply the filter and spath adds the same value again, so the field comes back with two values. If you write your own searches against this index, replicate this pattern.

docs.title: Tamper-Resistance Threat Model
docs.text:
Audit events live in a Splunk index on the same host as the LogServ App. A host-root admin can edit the underlying bucket files — they can delete events, rewrite events, replay old events, or delete the entire index. The audit log is NOT tamper-evident on the local instance alone.

Mitigation: forward audit events to a separate Splunk / SIEM / S3-with-Object-Lock destination owned by a different admin team. The HEC forwarder (below) provides this. The threat model assumes a malicious or compromised insider with admin rights to the LogServ Splunk instance but NOT to the destination instance.

Disclaimer text shown at the top of the Audit Log tab:

Audit events live in a Splunk index. A host-root admin can edit the bucket files. Mitigation: forward audit events to a separate Splunk instance / SIEM / S3-with-Object-Lock owned by a different admin team. Configure the HEC forwarder under Settings → General → Audit & Telemetry.

docs.title: HEC Forwarder
docs.text:
Optional admin-configurable forwarding of audit events to a separate Splunk / SIEM via Splunk’s HTTP Event Collector. When enabled:

  • Browser-side dual-write at flush. The AuditWriter.flush() path (and the per-event postOneOff() path) sends to BOTH the local logserv_ai_assistant_audit index (via the standard services/receivers/simple REST endpoint) AND the configured HEC URL. The two writes are independent — local-index failure doesn’t block forwarder write, and vice versa.
  • Failure visibility. When the HEC POST fails (DNS error, network timeout, 4xx/5xx response), an audit_forwarder_failure event is generated locally. So a disabled / down forwarder is visible in the local audit log itself, not silently failing.
  • Auth. The HEC token is sent on every POST as Authorization: Splunk <token> header. Token is stored in Splunk’s encrypted password store at realm logserv_ai_assistant_forwarder name hec_token and never displayed in cleartext.
  • Sanitized URL in failure events. When a forwarder failure event records the destinationUrl, query strings + fragments are stripped to prevent accidental exposure of any auth-bearing URL params.

Who it covers. The forward runs in each user’s browser, which reads the forwarder’s HEC token from Splunk’s password store. By default only admins can read it. For any other user the forward fails (reason no_token) and a local audit_forwarder_failure event is written instead, so the destination receives only the events of users who can read the token.

docs.title: Configuring the forwarder
docs.text:
Before you start, make sure the destination’s HTTP Event Collector accepts cross-origin requests from your Splunk Web address (scheme, host and port, as users open it). The browser sends each copy straight to the destination, so a destination that does not allow your Splunk Web origin refuses every forward. On a Splunk destination, HEC’s list of allowed origins is its crossOriginSharingPolicy setting in inputs.conf; check the setting in the inputs.conf.spec of the destination’s Splunk version.

Store the token first. Each Save Defaults reads the stored token and applies it to your page at once; if forwarding is turned on before the token is stored, your page forwards nothing until it is reloaded, and each event records an audit_forwarder_failure (reason no_token) instead.

  1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → Splunk MCP → Audit Log Forwarder panel.
  2. Paste the HEC token from your destination’s HEC input into the HEC Token field and click Save.
  3. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General and find the Audit & Telemetry section.
  4. Set Forwarder HEC URL to the HEC base URL (e.g., https://siem.example.com:8088 — the App appends /services/collector/event).
  5. Optionally set Forwarder remote index (optional) (recommended: a dedicated index like splunk_audit on the destination).
  6. Optionally set Forwarder source field (defaults to logserv_ai_assistant_remote — deliberately distinct from the local sourcetype logserv:ai_assistant:audit so forwarded copies are distinguishable).
  7. Select Audit log forwarder (it then reads Forwarding) and click Save Defaults. The save applies the stored token to your page at once.
  8. Run a predefined prompt. Its audit event is forwarded.
  9. Check the destination for events arriving at the configured index and source. If none arrive, look for audit_forwarder_failure events in the local index: their reason gives the HTTP status or the failure.

Other pages, yours in other browser tabs and other users’ pages, pick up the forwarder settings and the token at their next page load. If you change only the token later, reload the page so that it uses the new token.

docs.title: When the admin saves with the forwarder OFF
docs.text: A forwarder-disabled-acceptance modal blocks the save until the admin acknowledges the integrity-mitigation responsibility. The acceptance is recorded as a forwarder_disabled_acceptance audit event with admin identity, Splunk-stamped IP, timestamp, and SHA-256 of the disclaimer revision. The event is written as soon as the answer is recorded, with the audit settings in place at that moment, so when the same save turns forwarding off, the acceptance is also sent to that forwarder: an attempt with the forwarder settings the page has applied, and when it fails (no HEC token, no URL, the destination refusing it), a local audit_forwarder_failure record is written instead.

docs.title: Audit Index Provisioning
docs.text:
The logserv_ai_assistant_audit index must exist on the indexer tier before the AI Assistant writes to it: an event sent to an index that does not exist is dropped. The Data TA’s default/indexes.conf defines it, with 90-day retention (frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000):

  • Single instance with the Data TA installed: the index is created; nothing to do.
  • Standalone indexer, indexer cluster or Splunk Cloud Platform: create it yourself, as for the SAP data index: Settings → Indexes, an indexes.conf stanza, an index-only app pushed from the cluster manager with repFactor = auto, or, on Splunk Cloud Platform, Settings → Indexes or ACS. See Create the Indexes.

Who can read it is set per role; see Restricting Who Can Read the Audit Index.

The index name is macro-configurable — see Renaming an index for the procedure (update the sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro macro definition for reads, plus the Audit index name field in Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit & Telemetry for writes).

Retention. The Data TA’s definition keeps events 90 days. For compliance reviews going back further, set a longer retention wherever the index is defined: frozenTimePeriodInSecs in the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf on a single instance, in your own indexes.conf on a standalone indexer, in the index-only app of the cluster manager’s bundle on an indexer cluster, or the Searchable retention under Settings → Indexes on Splunk Cloud Platform. Recommended retention for compliance use cases: 2 years to cover annual audit cycles plus a buffer. For SOX / PCI / HIPAA contexts where regulator records-retention requirements apply, follow the regulator’s spec.

docs.title: Who Can Write Audit Events
docs.text:
The App writes audit events from the browser, as the signed-in user, through Splunk’s services/receivers/simple REST endpoint (by way of Splunk Web’s splunkd proxy). Splunk accepts a write there only from a user whose role holds the edit_tcp or the edit_log_alert_event capability (capability = edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event on [input:simple] in Splunk’s default restmap.conf). Of Splunk Enterprise’s default roles, admin holds both and power holds edit_log_alert_event. With Splunk’s default roles, therefore:

  • Admins and power users are audited.
  • Users whose only role is user are not audited. Splunk refuses each of their writes with HTTP 403 (seen on Splunk Enterprise 9.4.3, where a power user’s write was accepted). The App drops the event and carries on: a refused audit write never blocks the AI Assistant.

When a write fails, the AI Assistant panel shows a warning under the privacy banner, Audit events are not being written, with the HTTP status: for HTTP 403 it names the edit_log_alert_event and edit_tcp capabilities, says Splunk’s default user role has neither, and tells the user to ask their Splunk admin (edit_log_alert_event is the narrower one to grant; see below); for HTTP 401, which usually means the Splunk Web session has ended, it asks for a reload first and names the capabilities as the cause if a reload does not help. The Audit this session list then notes that the events it shows from about that time on may not be in the index. The warning clears as soon as a write succeeds again. Writes can also fail for other reasons, such as an indexer outage; the warning gives the status for those too. A write Splunk accepts but cannot index (for example into an audit_index_name that names no index on the indexers) may raise no warning, so check that the index exists.

The HEC forwarder does not cover these users. It runs in the same browser tab and needs to read the forwarder’s HEC token, which by default only admins can read.

docs.title: Granting a capability: the trade-off
docs.text:
To audit users whose only role is user, give them a role that holds edit_log_alert_event (Settings → Roles → role → Capabilities, or edit_log_alert_event = enabled under [role_<name>] in authorize.conf). It is the narrower of the two capabilities Splunk accepts here. Weigh what each grants first:

  • TCP data inputs (edit_tcp). edit_tcp is the capability that lets a role create and change TCP data inputs on the instance, which is far more than writing audit events; prefer edit_log_alert_event.
  • The Log Event alert action (edit_log_alert_event). It also lets the role use Splunk’s Log Event alert action, which writes events to an index.
  • Any index. receivers/simple takes the destination index from the request, so a holder of either capability can send events to any index, not only the audit index. That includes writing events into the audit index that look like someone else’s activity. With Splunk’s default roles every power user can already do this, and the default user and power roles also hold run_collect, the capability the collect command needs to write search results into an index. The local audit index is therefore not tamper-evident against signed-in users; for tamper-evidence, use the HEC forwarder to a separately-administered destination.
  • The user field comes from the browser. The App stamps the signed-in user’s name on each event in the browser before sending it, and Splunk does not check it. To tie an event to the account that really sent it, find the matching POST /services/receivers/simple request in splunkd’s access log (index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd_access), which Splunk records with the authenticated user.
  • Splunk Cloud. On Splunk Cloud Platform, check under Settings → Roles which of the two capabilities your roles hold or can be given (edit_tcp may not be grantable to customer roles), or ask Splunk Cloud Support. Where neither can be granted, only the roles that already hold one of them are audited.

Grant it narrowly

Grant edit_log_alert_event rather than edit_tcp, in a dedicated role (for example logserv_ai_audit_writer) assigned only to the people whose AI Assistant use must be audited, rather than adding it to user, which most users hold. power already holds it.

docs.title: Restricting Who Can Read the Audit Index
docs.text:
Splunk decides per role which indexes a user can search: the role’s allowed indexes (srchIndexesAllowed in authorize.conf; in Splunk Web, Settings → Roles → role → Indexes). The wildcard * in that list matches every index whose name does not start with _, so it includes logserv_ai_assistant_audit, and Splunk’s default user role allows *. Unless you narrow it, every user can read the audit trail: who used the AI Assistant and when, the SPL each prompt ran, every refused query, and the network address Splunk recorded on each admin acknowledgement.

A role’s allowed indexes are its own list plus those of every role it imports, and a user can search an index if any of their roles allows it. To keep the index to its reviewers:

  1. Narrow the roles that should not read it. In user, and in every other role whose own list contains *, replace * with the indexes the role needs, for example main and sap_logserv_logs (or your renamed SAP data index, so the App’s raw-event panels keep working). Avoid patterns that still match the audit index, such as logserv* or *audit*. A role that imports an unchanged user role can still read every index.
  2. Create a reviewer role, for example logserv_audit_reader, that allows logserv_ai_assistant_audit, and assign it to the people who review the trail.
  3. Keep the index allowed for the admins who use Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log. That tab searches the index as the signed-in user; without access it shows no events, not an error.

The same change in authorize.conf on the search head (on Splunk Cloud, use Settings → Roles):

[role_user]
srchIndexesAllowed = main;sap_logserv_logs

[role_logserv_audit_reader]
importRoles = user
srchIndexesAllowed = logserv_ai_assistant_audit

Verify with two test users. Splunk returns no rows and no error for an index a role cannot search, so a zero count proves nothing on its own:

  1. As a user who holds only the narrowed roles, run `sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-30d | stats count and expect 0.
  2. Run the same search as a member of the reviewer role and expect the events.
  3. As the first user, run one predefined prompt in the AI Assistant, then, as the reviewer, look for its event. Narrowing what a role can read does not change what it can write: writing needs the edit_tcp or the edit_log_alert_event capability (Who Can Write Audit Events). A first user whose only role is user holds neither, so the AI Assistant shows Audit events are not being written and the reviewer finds no event; that comes from the missing capability, not from the narrowing. If a role the first user holds has either capability (power does), the reviewer finds the event:
`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-15m
| spath
| search user="<test user>"

This controls who can read the trail, not who can alter it; for that, see the HEC forwarder.

docs.title: Querying the Audit Index Directly
docs.text:
You can query the audit index from any search bar — the in-app viewer is just a curated UX over the same SPL. The starter searches below use the \sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro`` macro so they continue to work after a rename:

Free-form vendor prompts in the last 7 days, with USD cost and Tier 2 redactions by user (only ever emitted once an LLM provider credential is configured):

`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-7d
| spath
| eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category")
| where category="vendor_tier1"
| eval t2=if(tonumber(tier2RedactionsApplied)>0, 1, 0)
| stats sum(vendorCostEstimateUsd) as total_usd, count as prompts, sum(t2) as tier2_redacted_prompts, sum(tier2RedactionsApplied) as tier2_redactions by user
| sort - total_usd

Every prompt, at any tier, is a vendor_tier1 event, and the event does not say which tier was active. tier2_redacted_prompts counts only the Tier 2 prompts in which PII redaction fired; a Tier 2 prompt with nothing to redact, or one sent with redaction off, records 0 like a Tier 1 prompt. To see when Tier 2 was switched on, read the vendor_tier2_elevation events below; a switch back to Tier 1 is not audited (see Privacy Tiers).

All security blocks in the last 30 days, grouped by user + offending operator:

`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-30d
| spath
| eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category")
| where category="security_blocked_spl"
| stats count by user, operator
| sort - count

Which commands and lookups the AI tried that the allow-list refused (last 30 days):

`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-30d
| spath
| eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category")
| where category="security_blocked_spl" AND isnotnull(command)
| stats count by operator, command
| sort - count

A steady parser_unavailable count (a query the user stopped is not counted) means the App could not reach Splunk’s search parser (search/parser, through Splunk Web’s splunkd proxy, as the signed-in user): every free-form query is refused until it can, by design. Check that the user’s role can run searches and that splunkd answers.

All Tier 2 elevation events ever (compliance review):

`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=0
| spath
| eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category")
| where category="vendor_tier2_elevation"
| table _time, user, previousTier, newTier

Forwarder failures grouped by reason (operational health):

`sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro` earliest=-7d
| spath
| eval category=json_extract(_raw, "category")
| where category="audit_forwarder_failure"
| stats count by reason, destinationUrl

docs.title: Audit Modal in the AI Assistant Panel
docs.text:
The privacy banner at the top of the AI Assistant chat panel includes an Audit this session button. Clicking it opens a per-session audit modal:

The modal shows a chronological list of the audit events recorded by the AI Assistant since this page was loaded (the provider’s in-memory buffer for the current session — it does not query the index, so a page reload starts the list over). Useful for users who want to confirm what their last few prompts triggered without leaving the AI Assistant panel. The modal is the in-pane equivalent of the Settings → Audit Log tab, scoped to the current session.

Because the list is the session’s own record, it shows events whether or not Splunk accepted them. While audit writes are failing (see Who Can Write Audit Events), a note at the top of the list gives the time of the first failed write and the reason, and says that the events listed from about that time on may not be in the index.

docs.title: Drill-down Chips
docs.text:
Drill-down chips are clickable affordances that appear next to AI Assistant tool-result tiles (right pane) and inline citations in the chat narrative (left pane). They connect the AI Assistant’s investigation flow back into the dashboards or Splunk’s universal Search app. A ↗ Run SPL chip opens the search at the dispatch’s exact time range; a dashboard chip opens the dashboard in a new tab at the App’s default time range (Last 30 days), not at the dispatch’s window.

The tile chips and guidance-card chips need no LLM provider: every predefined-prompt tile carries them once the AI Assistant is turned on (Set Up the AI Assistant). The chat-narrative citation chips accompany LLM-written narratives, so they appear only once an LLM provider credential is configured.

docs.title: ↗ Dashboard
docs.text:
Opens the related OOTB dashboard in a new browser tab. Sourced from the per-prompt dashboard mapping in the intent map — single string or array. Roughly half the catalog maps to more than one dashboard (e.g., logserv_hana_failed_auth → HANA Audit + Cross-Stack Authentication) and renders one chip per target.

The link carries no time range: the dashboard opens in a new tab at the App’s default time range (Last 30 days), not at the dispatch’s window and not at the range picked in your current tab. To see the exact window the search ran over, use ↗ Run SPL.

docs.title: ↗ Run SPL
docs.text:
Opens Splunk’s universal Search app in a new browser tab with the dispatched SPL pre-populated and the dispatch’s exact earliest/latest pre-applied. The chip is hidden on synthetic blocked-SPL results so it doesn’t help the user manually run a query that the SPL static-analysis guard just rejected.

For canned-prompt dispatches, the SPL is the prompt’s catalog SPL string. For AI-driven saved-search calls, the SPL is resolved from the same catalog lookup. For AI-driven ad-hoc queries, the SPL is the AI’s own query string.

docs.title: On every tool-result tile in the right pane
docs.text: Chips appear in the tile’s actions slot (in the FramedPanel header), between the tile title and the Clear button. Order: dashboard chip(s) first, then ↗ Run SPL, then Clear.

docs.title: Alongside [→ saved_search] citations in the chat narrative
docs.text:
The AI’s narrative response cites tool dispatches as [→ logserv_xxx]. Each citation in chat becomes a clickable scroll-to-tile span (clicking it scrolls the right pane to the matching tile), with sibling chips auto-appended on the same line: ↗ Dashboard (one per resolvable target) + ↗ Run SPL.

This rendering path requires an AI-generated narrative, so it appears only once an LLM provider credential is configured — until then, and in a compile-time templates-only build, only the tile chips (right pane) and guidance-card links render.

A typical citation in chat reads:

A. [severity:high] Cross-stack auth failures concentrated on Windows. → logserv_cross_stack_auth_failures ↗ Cross-Stack Authentication ↗ Run SPL 7 of the top-10 failing-stack rows are Windows…

Where: - → logserv_cross_stack_auth_failures is the clickable scroll-to-tile span (cyan-light + dotted underline) — the parser drops the brackets when the citation resolves; a citation it cannot resolve renders as muted, non-clickable [→ name] text with no chips - ↗ Cross-Stack Authentication is the dashboard chip (opens that dashboard in a new tab at the App’s default time range, Last 30 days) - ↗ Run SPL is the SPL chip (opens Splunk Search with the dispatched SPL + same time range)

docs.title: Time-Range Preservation
docs.text:
The ↗ Run SPL chip preserves the dispatch’s exact time range — not the user’s current global TimeRange picker. So a -24h verify-query opens the Search app at -24h; a -30d cumulative search opens at -30d. The ↗ Dashboard chip opens the destination dashboard in a new tab at the App’s default time range (Last 30 days), not at the dispatch’s window.

This matters because the user’s TimeRange picker may have changed between when the AI dispatched the search and when the user clicks the drill-down. By embedding the dispatch’s window in the URL, the destination reflects exactly what the AI saw.

docs.title: Security Posture
docs.text:
• target="_blank" + rel="noopener noreferrer" on every chip. The noopener flag breaks the window.opener reference that reverse-tabnabbing relies on.
  • Dashboard row drill-downs quote-escape spliced row values (splQuote()) before URL encoding, so a row value containing a quote or backslash can’t break out of the SPL string context. The AI Assistant’s ↗ Run SPL chip passes the already-composed SPL through unchanged — there is no per-row splicing in that path.
  • No SPL chip on synthetic blocked-SPL results. When the SPL static-analysis guard blocks an AI-authored query, the synthetic error tile is rendered without the ↗ Run SPL chip — the chip would defeat the guard by helping the user manually dispatch the same SPL.
  • No drill-downs from compliance audit-trail tables. Two compliance tables on the Change & Configuration Activity dashboard intentionally have no row drill-downs; see Change & Configuration Activity.

For the orchestrator-layer URL pre-resolution pattern that powers these chips, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Set Up the AI Assistant
docs.text:
The AI Assistant ships turned off: until an admin turns it on, the LogServ App shows no AI Assistant button, panel or route. This page takes you from an installed LogServ App to a working predefined prompt. Use it after the LogServ App is installed and its dashboards show your data (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards).

The predefined prompts need no LLM provider and no vendor credential. Free-form questions, which do use an LLM vendor, are an optional extra at the end.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• The LogServ App is installed on the search head, and the dashboards show data.
  • You hold a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin. Only those three role names open the LogServ App’s Settings page; a delegated-admin role with any other name gets 403 — Admin access required (Application Settings).
  • You can install apps and edit roles on the search head (on Splunk Cloud Platform, as sc_admin or with the help of Splunk Cloud Support).

docs.title: The Steps at a Glance
docs.text:
1. Install the Splunk MCP Server
  2. Grant mcp_tool_execute to the roles that will use the AI Assistant
  3. Decide who is audited and who can read the audit trail
  4. Turn on the AI Assistant and answer both acknowledgements
  5. Optional: turn on Templates-only mode
  6. Backfill the dashboard data
  7. Run a predefined prompt and find its audit event

docs.title: 1. Install the Splunk MCP Server
docs.text:
The AI Assistant runs every search through the Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931), a separate Splunk app. Installing the LogServ App does not bring it in.

  • Version: 1.1.0 or later is required: the predefined prompts use the MCP Server’s Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. 1.2.1 or later is recommended, because it fixes SVD-2026-1004 (server-side request forgery through custom API tools). The App’s own check refuses only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix) and sets no upper limit; the newest version verified with it is 2.0.0.
  • Where: the same search head as the LogServ App. The App calls the MCP Server from the browser through the same Splunk Web session.

Install it the way you install any Splunkbase app: on Splunk Enterprise, Apps → Find More Apps, or download it from Splunkbase and use Apps → Install app from file; on Splunk Cloud Platform, the way your stack installs other Splunkbase apps (Apps → Find More Apps where your stack offers it), or ask Splunk Cloud Support. Restart Splunk if it asks you to. Details and a check that the server answers: Splunk MCP Setup.

Done when: Apps → Manage Apps lists Splunk MCP Server (Splunk_MCP_Server), enabled, at version 1.1.0 or later.

docs.title: 2. Grant mcp_tool_execute to the Roles That Will Use the AI Assistant
docs.text:
The MCP Server checks a capability of its own on every request the AI Assistant sends. Version 1.1.0 defines two, in its default/authorize.conf:

Capability What it allows Granted by default to mcp_tool_execute Connect to the MCP Server and run its tools. Every AI Assistant user needs it. admin, sc_admin mcp_tool_admin Manage the MCP Server’s tools, tokens and rate limits. Not needed to use the AI Assistant. admin, sc_admin

Add mcp_tool_execute to each role whose members will use the AI Assistant: Settings → Roles → role → Capabilities, select mcp_tool_execute, and save (on Splunk Cloud Platform, the same page). In authorize.conf the same grant is mcp_tool_execute = enabled under [role_<name>]. Only admin and sc_admin hold it by default (and roles that import them), so power, user and, unless it imports one of those two, a delegated-admin role such as sc_subadmin need the grant.

A user without it is refused at the MCP Server’s first request (HTTP 403, User lacks required mcp_tool_execute capability), and the AI Assistant panel shows its Setup required card even though the MCP Server is installed.

Done when: every role that will use the AI Assistant holds mcp_tool_execute, directly or through a role it imports.

docs.title: 3. Decide Who Is Audited and Who Can Read the Audit Trail
docs.text:
Every predefined prompt, free-form call, refusal and admin acknowledgement is written to the logserv_ai_assistant_audit index. Settle three things before users start:

  1. The audit index exists on the indexer tier. The Data TA defines it, but outside a single instance you create it yourself, with the retention you need: Create the Indexes. An audit event sent to an index that does not exist is dropped.
  2. Who is audited. Each user’s browser writes that user’s audit events, and Splunk accepts the write only from a role that holds edit_log_alert_event or edit_tcp. Of Splunk’s default roles, admin holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event and user holds neither, so users whose only role is user are not audited (their AI Assistant panel says so). To audit them, give them a role with edit_log_alert_event, the narrower of the two: Who Can Write Audit Events.
  3. Who can read the audit trail. A role whose allowed indexes contain * can search the audit index, and Splunk’s default user role allows *. To keep the trail to its reviewers, narrow those roles: Restricting Who Can Read the Audit Index.

Also decide whether to forward a copy of every audit event to a separately run Splunk instance or SIEM, which is what makes the trail tamper-evident: HEC Forwarder. Two limits apply. The destination’s HTTP Event Collector must accept cross-origin requests from your Splunk Web address, because the browser sends the copy. And the browser must read the forwarder’s HEC token from Splunk’s password store, which by default only admins can do: for other users the copy fails and an audit_forwarder_failure event is written to the local index instead. If you leave forwarding off, step 4 asks you to acknowledge that.

Done when: the audit index exists, and you know which roles are audited and which can read the trail.

docs.title: 4. Turn On the AI Assistant and Answer Both Acknowledgements
docs.text:
1. In the LogServ App, open Settings in the navigation rail (near the bottom, above About). The Application Settings page opens on its AI Assistant tab, General sub-tab.
  2. Under Feature, select Enable AI Assistant. Leave MCP Required on (the default).
  3. Click Save Defaults.
  4. The AI Assistant — Liability terms dialog opens. Read it and click I accept (record Yes and enable).
  5. With audit forwarding off (the default), the Audit log integrity dialog opens next. It explains that without the forwarder the local audit index is the only record, and a host-root admin can edit it. Click I accept (record Yes and save).

The save then completes, and the AI Assistant button appears at the right end of the header’s second row without a page reload. Both answers are recorded with your user name, as ai_assistant_enable_acceptance and forwarder_disabled_acceptance audit events.

  • I do not accept in either dialog stops the save, and the AI Assistant stays off. The answer is recorded too. A No on the Audit log integrity dialog is recorded at its current version, so the next save that turns the AI Assistant on asks only the liability terms again, and then saves with forwarding off; that dialog comes back only when its terms change or a save turns forwarding from on to off.
  • The liability dialog appears every time the AI Assistant is turned on, and again when its terms change. The audit-log integrity dialog appears again when its terms change, and whenever a save turns forwarding off.

Details: Legal Acknowledgement Modals.

Done when: the AI Assistant button shows in the header.

docs.title: 5. Optional: Turn On Templates-only Mode
docs.text: To offer only the predefined prompts and keep the free-form, LLM-driven path off, select Templates-only mode on the same General sub-tab and click Save Defaults. The chat input becomes read-only, the Power Mode toggle and the model picker are hidden, the Provider Credentials sub-tab is hidden, and an info banner explains the mode. Any admin can turn it off again. Where the restriction must not be reversible, see Restricting the LLM Path.

docs.title: 6. Backfill the Dashboard Data
docs.text: About half of the predefined prompts read the same hourly rollups as the dashboards. Until those rollups are backfilled, these prompts return results only for the hours since the App was installed. If you have not run the backfill yet, run it now: Backfilling on first install.

docs.title: 7. Run a Predefined Prompt and Find Its Audit Event
docs.text:
1. Click AI Assistant in the header. The panel opens beside the dashboard.
    • If it shows a Setup required, Security upgrade required or Health check error card instead of the chat, see Health Check and Setup Wizard.
  2. Click Browse prompts below the chat input. Pick a Time range (the default is Last 24 hours) and a tab: Dashboard Focused (prompts for the dashboard you have open), SAP Basis, Security or Operations.
  3. Click a prompt. Its result appears as a tile in the right pane, and a How to read this result card appears in the chat.
  4. Click Audit this session in the banner at the top of the panel. The list shows a local_only event for the prompt you ran.
  5. Open Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log. With a time range that covers the last few minutes, the same local_only event is listed, now read from the index.

Repeat steps 1-5 as a user who holds only an analyst role. That checks the mcp_tool_execute grant of step 2, and whether that role is audited (step 3). If the analyst’s event is missing from the index while the panel shows Audit events are not being written, the role lacks edit_log_alert_event and edit_tcp.

Done when: a predefined prompt returns a tile for an analyst user, and, if that user’s role is audited (step 3), its local_only event is in the audit index.

docs.title: Optional: Free-form Questions with an LLM Provider
docs.text:
If you turned on Templates-only mode in step 5, turn it off first: while it is on, typed questions are refused and the Provider Credentials sub-tab is hidden.

The shipped default provider is Mock (development only): a typed question gets a canned reply, and no vendor is contacted. To answer free-form questions with a real LLM:

  1. Choose a privacy tier first. Tier 1, the default, sends the vendor two numbers per search; Tier 2 also sends aggregated values from your events.
  2. Store the provider’s credential on Settings → AI Assistant → Provider Credentials (Provider Credentials Tab).
  3. Select the provider as Active Provider, pick a Default Model, and click Save Defaults. The liability dialog of step 4 does not appear for this change.

Each user’s browser reads the provider credential from Splunk’s password store when that user sends a question, so a user whose role cannot read stored passwords (Splunk’s list_storage_passwords capability, which admin holds) gets an error instead of an answer. See Free-form Prompts.

docs.title: Turning It Off
docs.text: Clear Enable AI Assistant on the General sub-tab and click Save Defaults. The AI Assistant button disappears from your page at once, and from other users’ pages at their next page load. A page without the button runs no MCP check. The settings you saved are kept for the next time it is turned on.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Predefined Prompts: the prompt catalog and what each tile shows.
  • Audit Log: the categories, the viewer and the searches for reviewing the trail.
  • Application Settings: every setting on the page.
  • Restricting the LLM Path: when the free-form path must stay off.
  • Back to the Deployment Roadmap.

docs.title: Free-form Prompts
docs.text:
Requires a configured LLM provider credential

The released v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build, so the path this page describes is present in it, once the AI Assistant is turned on (Set Up the AI Assistant). It reaches no vendor until an admin selects a provider and configures its LLM provider credential: the shipped default provider is Mock (development only), which answers a typed question with a canned reply. An upgrade creates no credential, so nothing reaches a vendor until someone sets one. An admin can also restrict a deployment to predefined prompts at run time with the Templates-only mode toggle (Settings → AI Assistant → General), and a compile-time templates-only build exists for deployments where that restriction must not be reversible in the field (Restricting the LLM Path).

Free-form prompts are the LLM-driven path through the AI Assistant. The user types a natural-language question; the orchestrator sends a system primer + the question + tool definitions to one of four supported LLM providers; the vendor picks tools, the orchestrator dispatches them via the Splunk MCP Server, and the vendor synthesizes a narrative response from the privacy-tier-bounded summaries. The narrative ends up in the chat panel on the left; the actual data lands in tool-result tiles on the right.

This path requires a configured LLM provider credential, is governed by the active privacy tier, and can be switched off — at run time with the Templates-only mode toggle, or irreversibly in a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path). Each user’s browser reads the provider credential from Splunk’s password store when that user sends a question, so the user’s role must be able to read stored passwords (list_storage_passwords, which admin holds).

docs.title: The Four Supported Providers
docs.text:
Provider API Endpoint Auth Models Anthropic api.anthropic.com (direct) API key Claude Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5 baseline + any model discovered from /v1/models OpenAI api.openai.com (direct) API key GPT-5.1 / GPT-5 / GPT-4o / o3 baseline + discovered chat-capable models Azure OpenAI Customer’s Azure deployment URL Azure auth + URL pattern Per Azure deployment configuration (deployments auto-discovered) AWS Bedrock Bedrock API (Claude on Bedrock) Bedrock API Keys (no SigV4 signing) Claude on Bedrock — baseline + ListFoundationModels discovery

Active provider + default model are admin-configured in Settings → General. Per-user model picker in the chat panel’s privacy banner lets users switch within the active provider’s model list — the curated baseline plus any vendor-discovered models (see How model discovery works).

AWS Bedrock support currently requires Bedrock API Keys. IAM-only credentials (no Bedrock API Key) aren’t supported — the React app can’t sign SigV4 requests from the browser.

docs.title: The Free-form Flow
docs.text:
User types question  -->  Orchestrator builds system primer + tools + history
                                                          |
                                                          v
                                       LLM vendor (streamed response)
                                                          |
                                  AI emits zero or more tool_use blocks
                                                          |
                                                          v
                          For each tool_use, orchestrator dispatches via MCP
                                                          |
                                              MCP returns Hidden<MCPToolResult>
                                                          |
                                  sanitize() chokepoint -> Tier 1 / Tier 2 summary
                                                          |
                                                          v
                                  AI continues, may emit more tool_use blocks
                                                          |
                          (loop until AI emits a final assistant_text response)
                                                          |
                                                          v
                                  Narrative renders in chat; tiles render in right pane

Tool dispatch is parallelized — when the AI emits multiple tool_use blocks in a single turn (e.g., dispatching 5 saved searches at once for a “find the top issues” question), the orchestrator dispatches all of them concurrently via Promise.all. The slowest one bounds the turn latency, not the sum.

Failed tool calls. In every tier, a tool call that fails reaches the AI only as its HTTP status and a fixed error class, for example Tool error (HTTP 400, class=parse_error): Splunk could not parse the query; check the SPL syntax. The error text is shown to the user only. Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error text is never sent, because it repeats the search and can carry event data. The full error stays in the tile in the right pane. A call the App refuses itself (the SPL guard, the saved-search catalog, an undeclared tool, the session tool-call cap) reaches the AI as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>, with the App’s own reason. See Privacy Tiers.

docs.title: The Two MCP Tools the AI Sees
docs.text: The AI’s tool definitions on every free-form request are:

docs.title: splunk_run_saved_search
docs.text:
Dispatch a saved search from the LogServ App’s catalog (one of the catalogued prompts described in Predefined Prompts).

Only the catalog’s names are dispatched. The orchestrator checks the name where every saved-search call is sent to the MCP Server; any other name — a rollup aggregation, retention or backfill, an Enterprise Security feed, or a name the AI made up — is refused with a synthetic error tool_result and a security_blocked_spl audit event, and nothing reaches the MCP Server. The MCP arguments are built from the vetted name, the App (app = splunk_app_sap_logserv) and the time range; other keys the AI supplies are not forwarded. A tool name other than the two on this page is refused the same way.

Arg Type Description name string (required) Saved-search name from the catalog (e.g., logserv_hana_failed_auth) earliest_time string (optional) Splunk earliest token (e.g., -24h, -7d). If omitted, the saved search’s own configured time range applies; the AI’s primer instructs it to pass an explicit window. latest_time string (optional) Splunk latest token (e.g., now). render_hint string (optional) One of table / timechart / kpi / pie. Falls back to the catalog’s per-prompt renderHint. top_n integer (optional, default 10, max 50) Width of categorical aggregates the AI receives in Tier 2 summary. The AI passes this when the user asks for “top 25 X” or similar.

docs.title: splunk_run_query
docs.text:
Dispatch ad-hoc SPL written by the AI. Used when no saved search fits the user’s question.

Arg Type Description query string (required) SPL string. Must start with the LogServ macro \sap_logserv_idx_macro`as its first term — or with| inputlookupof one of the App's lookups,| tstatswith the macro right afterWHEREor| makeresults` — and use only the allowed commands. The App enforces both (below). earliest_time string (optional) Passed to the MCP Server as given. When the AI omits it, the App adds no default: the window is whatever the Splunk MCP Server applies. (The tool description the AI sees says the user’s selected time range is the default; it is not.) latest_time string (optional) Same as above. render_hint string (optional) One of table / timechart / kpi / pie. top_n integer (optional, default 10, max 50) Width of categorical aggregates the AI receives in a Tier 2 summary.

docs.title: The SPL Guard
docs.text:
SPL guard (LLM06 — Excessive Agency): the orchestrator checks every splunk_run_query query three times before dispatch, and a query any check refuses is never sent to Splunk:

  1. The denylist of known risky commands (below), the first fence.
  2. The allow-list. The App reads the query with a strict lexer and refuses it unless every command in it, subsearches included, is on the list, and it reads only what free-form analysis needs (details after the denylist).
  3. Splunk’s own search parser. The App then sends the query to search/parser (parse only, nothing runs; through Splunk Web’s splunkd proxy, as the signed-in user, in this App’s namespace) and refuses it when the parser reads it differently from the App: another list of commands, a command not on the list, a query starting with the data macro whose expansion is not the App’s definition (a macro of the same name the user’s context shadows — where the macro stands after WHERE in tstats or starts a subsearch, only an index term its expansion brings in is caught), an index term other than the LogServ index, or a lookup / inputlookup outside a subsearch whose lookup, as the parser reports it, is not one of the App’s or cannot be read. The parser reports a subsearch as text inside the command that holds it, not as commands of its own, so the commands and lookups inside a subsearch are checked by the App’s lexer only: a command or lookup that a shadowed macro brings into a subsearch is not caught (an index term it brings in is). If the parser cannot be asked — the call fails, times out or returns no command list — the query is refused (parser_unavailable); a query the parser rejects as invalid SPL is refused too (parser_rejected). It fails closed.

The denylist refuses these commands at the start of the query, after a | or after a [, outside quoted strings — also when double or single quotes are written into the command word, as in | "delete" or | de'lete':

  • Write to an index: collect and its aliases stash, summaryindex and sumindex; mcollect; meventcollect.
  • Write lookups, files or other output: outputlookup, outputcsv, outputtext, dump, tscollect, createrss.
  • Delete events: delete.
  • Trigger alerts or email: sendalert, sendemail.
  • Run scripts: script and its alias run; runshellscript.
  • Read REST endpoints: rest — storage/passwords returns stored credentials decrypted.
  • Send data out: outputtelemetry, and the third-party curl, wget and sendresults.
  • Machine Learning Toolkit: ai (it sends the rows to an LLM) and deletemodel.
  • Run other searches: map, and savedsearch’s aliases macro and savedsplunk.

It also refuses savedsearch and savedsplunk as words anywhere in the query, quoted text included (| from savedsearch:X), also when quotes split them (| "saved"search X, | sav"edsearch" X); the external lookup dnslookup anywhere, also split by quotes (| lookup "dns"lookup), because each row becomes a DNS query to an outside name server; a fit command (plain, quoted or split by quotes) followed anywhere later in the query by the word into, because fit ... into saves a model (fit with no into after it, and apply, stay allowed); an SPL inline comment (three backticks); an unmatched backtick; a double quote that is never closed, or a backslash-escaped double quote outside a quoted string; and a macro other than the App’s own (sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro), because a comment, ambiguous quoting or another macro could hide a command. Apart from those words, dnslookup, an into after a fit, and backticks, double-quoted text is read as data, so a bracketed tag inside a quoted string, such as search "[DELETE]", is not mistaken for a command. Where Splunk’s reading of quotes is uncertain, the guard assumes the worst and refuses. That includes a word that forms only once the quotes are removed ("saved""search"), a | or [ inside single quotes (read as a command position), and any into after a fit, even one that belongs to another command or to quoted text (| fit X | stats count by into, | fit X by "a into b").

The allow-list. A query the denylist passes must also pass these rules (operators in brackets, as the audit event records them):

  • Commands (command_not_allowed): only search, where, eval, stats, eventstats, streamstats, tstats, chart, timechart, top, rare, sort, head, tail, dedup, reverse, table, fields, rename, fillnull, filldown, bin, bucket, rex, regex, spath, lookup, inputlookup, makeresults, addinfo, transaction, convert, iplocation, strcat, xyseries, untable, transpose, fieldsummary, addtotals, addcoltotals, makemv, nomv, mvcombine, append, appendcols, join, appendpipe. Everything else is refused, whatever it does and whichever app ships it — custom search commands of other apps, fit and apply, datamodel, metadata, loadjob, inputcsv, foreach, map, mvexpand, fieldformat, rangemap, return, format, multisearch, union. Every allowed command is one the Tier 2 summarizer reads in full. union is refused because Splunk’s search parser rewrites it before it runs (into search … | append [...], or multisearch when every arm streams), so the App cannot check it against the parser’s reading; use append to combine two searches — `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=a | stats count by host | append [search `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=b | stats count by host] — and the refusal of a union tells the model so.
  • Where a query starts (query_start): the query, and every subsearch arm, starts with `sap_logserv_idx_macro` as the first term of its search, or with | inputlookup <one of the App's lookups>, | tstats … WHERE `sap_logserv_idx_macro` or | makeresults; an appendpipe […] group starts with a command (stats, eval, …), never with the macro. Every tstats, anywhere in the query, names the macro right after WHERE.
  • Data scope (index_not_allowed): no index=, index!=, index:: or index IN term anywhere, no audit macro, and no OR or NOT right next to the LogServ macro — Splunk binds OR tighter than the implied AND, so `sap_logserv_idx_macro` OR index=main would leave the index. Put alternatives after the macro, in parentheses: `sap_logserv_idx_macro` (sourcetype=a OR sourcetype=b).
  • Lookups (lookup_not_allowed, eval_lookup): lookup and inputlookup only name the App’s own lookups — its rollups, its threat-intel lookups, its sourcetype metadata and the ISC BIND and Squid lookups. The Data Doctor’s collections, the Enterprise Security asset and identity feeds and the Settings backfill’s scratch collection (logserv_backfill_stage) are excluded, and so is every other app’s lookup and the eval lookup() function (also written lookup ( or across a line break). The lookup’s name must be the one Splunk reads too: an option before it may not have a quoted value (max="5", event_time_field='…'), and nothing may be written against the name (logserv_mc_rollup"_x"). Splunk’s parser must agree: for every lookup and inputlookup outside a subsearch the App reads the lookup again from the parser’s reply (step 3 above) and refuses the query (parser_mismatch) unless it is one of the App’s.
  • Subsearches (subsearch_not_allowed, subsearch_fields): only as a filter in search, ending with | fields or | table naming the fields it returns (no wildcard, not search or query, whose values Splunk would insert as text), or in append, appendcols, join and appendpipe (one group).
  • Macros (macro_position): the LogServ macro only as the first term of a search or right after WHERE in tstats; a macro inside quoted text is refused. A macro must stand apart, with a space, a | or a square bracket on each side: Splunk expands a macro as text, so anything written against it joins its expansion (`sap_logserv_idx_macro`* would become index="sap_logserv_logs"*, where`sap_logserv_idx_macro` would lose the WHERE).
  • Quoting and brackets (ambiguous_single_quote, unbalanced_bracket, escaped_outside_quotes): single quotes only around field names (eval 'User Name'=user) — every ' pairs with the next one, with no |, bracket, double quote, backtick, backslash or line break between them. A search term that contains an apostrophe goes in double quotes: "don't". Square brackets must balance outside quoted text. A backslash may appear only inside double-quoted text (a rex or regex pattern, a quoted value): Splunk reads \| as a pipe character passed to the command rather than the end of a command, so an escaped pipe, bracket or quote outside double quotes would make Splunk and the App see different commands.

The AI’s primer lists the allowed commands exactly, and a refusal names the command, lookup or macro it is about, so the model can rewrite the query. Splunk role permissions remain the authoritative gate. Blocked SPL produces a synthetic error tool_result + a security_blocked_spl audit event (with the operator and, when the refusal is about one, the command). The AI is told Tool call refused by the App before it ran: followed by the guard’s reason, which is text the App wrote, so it can recover by writing a different query.

Limitation: a renamed SAP data index

The parser check compares the expansion of sap_logserv_idx_macro with the definition the App ships, index="sap_logserv_logs", and refuses any other index value. After the macro is changed for a renamed data index (Renaming an index), every free-form query that reads events, starting with the macro or using it in tstats, is refused (parser_mismatch). Predefined prompts are not affected; they are not checked this way. This release has no setting to change it.

docs.title: The System Primer
docs.text:
A system-message prelude is sent on every free-form request. The primer teaches the AI:

  • A data-boundary rule that distinguishes customer data from instructions (mitigates LLM01 / LLM04)
  • The full saved-search catalog, built from the intent map at compile time (so the AI prefers splunk_run_saved_search when a saved search fits)
  • The LogServ data model (sourcetypes + key fields) for ad-hoc SPL
  • The exact list of commands allowed in splunk_run_query, and where a query must start, what it may read and how to quote
  • The time-window reasoning rules that kick in for severity claims
  • Synthesis rules — lettered findings, severity dots, citation format

Two primer variants ship — one for each cloud tier — and the active tier picks which one is sent. For the primer’s full architecture (boundary block, primer constants, per-variant content), see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Citation + Drill-Down Chips in the Narrative
docs.text:
The AI’s narrative response uses a citation format [→ saved_search_name] to attribute each finding to its dispatched tool. Each citation in the chat becomes a clickable scroll-to-tile span (clicking it scrolls the right pane to the matching tile). The parser also auto-appends ↗ Dashboard chips (one per related OOTB dashboard) and a ↗ Run SPL chip on the same line — see Drill-down Chips.

Severity markers ([severity:critical|high|medium|low]) are rendered as glossy colored dots inline next to the finding’s alpha letter. The finding format is enforced by the primer:

A. [severity:high] Cross-stack auth failures concentrated on Windows.
[→ logserv_cross_stack_auth_failures] 7 of the top-10 failing-stack rows are
Windows; one user account hit 4,732 cumulative attempts — verify-query (-24h)
confirmed 412 of those landed today, ~17/hr, an active rate.

docs.title: Per-User Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Free-form prompts are subject to a per-user rolling-1-hour rate limit, configurable in Settings → General (default 30 prompts/hour, 0 = disabled). Canned-prompt dispatches are intentionally NOT rate-limited — they bypass the AI vendor entirely (no token cost) and are bounded by Splunk’s own search-quota controls.

When a user hits the cap, the next prompt:

  1. Renders the user message in chat as usual (preserves history continuity).
  2. Surfaces a system_notice in chat stating the limit was reached, how many free-form prompts were counted against the hourly threshold, roughly how long until the oldest prompt ages out, and which admin setting (rate_limit_per_hour) raises the cap.
  3. Records a rate_limited_prompt audit event with the user’s identity, the cap value, and the timestamp.
  4. Does NOT invoke the LLM vendor.

The cap is per-user, not per-session — opening a new browser tab doesn’t reset it. Enforcement is browser-side (localStorage), so it is per-user per browser: a second browser or device gets its own budget, and clearing site data resets the counter. The rate_limited_prompt / daily_spend_cap_hit audit events still fire on every block, so the SOC record survives either way — treat both caps as defense-in-depth, not a hard quota; vendor-side limits and your billing dashboard remain the enforcement of record. Maps to LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption.

docs.title: Token-Usage Audit + USD Cost Estimate
docs.text:
Every free-form prompt that completes — whichever tier is active — records one vendor_tier1 audit event, after its last turn, with:

  • Provider (anthropic / openai / azure_openai / bedrock, or mock)
  • Model
  • Input tokens and output tokens, summed over the prompt’s turns (for Anthropic also the cached and cache-written input tokens)
  • USD cost estimate (per-vendor pricing table — see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals)
  • Outbound bytes and the SHA-256 of the outbound payload
  • Prompt length (chars) and the number of tool definitions sent
  • Number of AI turns the prompt took
  • tier2RedactionsApplied — number of PII redactions applied across the prompt’s tool results (0 at Tier 1)
  • powerMode — whether the forced-RAG Power Mode was on

The Audit Log tab in Settings lists these events one by one; it has no aggregate views. For totals per user, run the cost search in Audit Log → Querying the Audit Index Directly. The USD cost estimate is a list price (not the customer’s negotiated rate, which the App does not know) and should be treated as an order-of-magnitude indicator.

docs.title: Daily Spend Cap
docs.text:
To prevent runaway vendor spend, the orchestrator enforces a per-user (per browser) daily USD spend cap (Daily spend cap (USD) in Settings, default 50.00; 0 turns it off). Each prompt’s estimated cost is added after it completes, and the check runs before the next prompt, so the prompt that crosses the cap still completes. Once the day’s total has reached the cap, the orchestrator:

  1. Refuses the next prompt before any vendor call.
  2. Records a daily_spend_cap_hit audit event.
  3. Surfaces a system_notice stating the cap was reached, how much of the budget is spent, and that the tally resets at local midnight (the browser’s calendar day).

The cap is cumulative-cost-based, not request-count-based — a single high-token-count free-form turn counts against the budget the same way many cheap turns do. Maps to LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption.

docs.title: Streaming + Abort
docs.text:
The vendor response is streamed token-by-token. The chat-side rendering shows partial responses as they arrive, including partial tool_use blocks. The status indicator switches between three states:

  • streaming — AI is generating text or about to emit a tool_use
  • tool_executing — orchestrator is dispatching a tool the AI requested
  • idle — turn complete

A red Stop button appears in the chat input toolbar during streaming / tool_executing states. Clicking it aborts the in-flight vendor call (closes the SSE stream) and any pending tool dispatches. The conversation history preserves what was emitted up to the abort point so the user can iterate from there.

docs.title: Jailbreak Pattern Detection
docs.text:
Every user prompt is run through a jailbreak-pattern analyzer before dispatch. The analyzer is flag-and-proceed: a match fires a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event but does NOT block the prompt. The defense-in-depth chain (type-system enforcement + Tier 2 sanitizer + tool-result sentinel + primer + vendor-side defenses) already covers the threat; the analyzer adds SOC observability for the user-prompt vector. Each flag captures a hash of the prompt (so SOC can correlate without archiving plain text), which patterns matched, and a character-class fingerprint to surface unusual encodings.

For the analyzer’s pattern groups + audit event schema, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals. Maps to LLM01 — Prompt Injection.

docs.title: Session Tool-Call Cap
docs.text: In addition to the per-user rate limit, every chat session has a per-session tool-dispatch cap to prevent infinite tool loops (a misbehaving model emitting tool_use after tool_use without ever producing a final assistant_text). Counter resets on chat clear. When exceeded, dispatch is refused with a synthetic error tool_result and a session_tool_cap_hit audit event records the hit. Maps to LLM06 — Excessive Agency.

docs.title: Splunk MCP Setup
docs.text:
The AI Assistant runs every search through the Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931), in every build and every configuration: predefined prompts dispatch their saved searches through it, so this page applies to every deployment that uses the AI Assistant. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting LLM applications to external tools and data. The Splunk MCP Server exposes Splunk’s searches and saved searches as MCP tools; the LogServ App is the MCP client. (An LLM vendor also takes part, choosing the tools, only for free-form questions answered by a configured LLM provider; for predefined prompts the App calls the tools itself.)

For the whole turn-on procedure, see Set Up the AI Assistant.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Splunk 9.4.3 or later.
  • Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) 1.1.0 or later is required; 1.2.1 or later is recommended. The predefined prompts run through the MCP Server’s Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. Version 1.2.1 fixes SVD-2026-1004 (server-side request forgery through custom API tools; vendor advisory checked 2026-10-22). The App’s own health check refuses only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix), so 1.0.3 to 1.0.5 pass it but every predefined prompt fails. There is no upper version limit; the newest version verified with the App is 2.0.0.
  • The same search head as the LogServ App. The App calls the MCP Server from the browser through the same Splunk Web session, so both must be on the same Splunk Web host.
  • The mcp_tool_execute capability on every role that will use the AI Assistant (Roles and Capabilities).
  • An admin to install the MCP Server app and grant the capability.

The Splunk MCP Server is the only MCP component the App checks for.

docs.title: Recommended companion: Splunk AI Assistant
docs.text:
Splunk AI Assistant (Splunkbase App 7245) is recommended alongside the Splunk MCP Server. It is not a prerequisite of the LogServ App’s AI Assistant, which uses only the MCP Server’s core splunk_run_saved_search and splunk_run_query tools. However:

  • App 7245 adds saia_*-prefixed MCP tools (for example SPL optimization helpers) that future LogServ releases may use.
  • Installing it alongside the MCP Server follows Splunk’s documented setup pattern.
  • If you are deploying the Splunk MCP Server anyway, adding App 7245 is little extra effort.

docs.title: Install the Splunk MCP Server
docs.text:
Follow the installation guide on Splunkbase App 7931. In short:

  1. Install the app on the search head where the LogServ App runs:
    • Splunk Enterprise: Apps → Find More Apps, or download the package from Splunkbase and use Apps → Install app from file. From the command line: $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk install app /path/to/<package>.tgz.
    • Splunk Cloud Platform: the way your stack installs other Splunkbase apps (Apps → Find More Apps where your stack offers it), or ask Splunk Cloud Support.
  2. Restart Splunk if it asks you to (on Splunk Enterprise: Settings → Server controls → Restart Splunk, or your usual restart method).
  3. Check it is installed: Apps → Manage Apps lists Splunk MCP Server (folder Splunk_MCP_Server), enabled, with its version.
  4. Grant mcp_tool_execute to the roles that will use the AI Assistant (below).

To check that the server answers, run this on a Splunk Enterprise search head (checked against MCP Server 1.1.0, whose ping method needs no capability):

curl -sk -u admin:<password> -X POST https://localhost:8089/services/mcp \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"ping"}'

A working server replies with a JSON-RPC result whose message is pong. The endpoint takes only POST requests, so opening it in a browser or with a plain GET returns HTTP 405 (Method not allowed).

The LogServ App’s AI Assistant runs its own check each time its panel opens (Health Check and Setup Wizard).

docs.title: Roles and Capabilities
docs.text:
The Splunk MCP Server checks a capability of its own on every request the AI Assistant sends. Its default/authorize.conf (version 1.1.0) defines two:

Capability What it allows Granted by default to mcp_tool_execute Connect to the MCP Server and run its tools. Every AI Assistant user needs it. admin, sc_admin mcp_tool_admin Manage the MCP Server’s tools, tokens and rate limits. Not needed to use the AI Assistant. admin, sc_admin
