Add mcp_tool_execute to each role whose members will use the AI Assistant: Settings → Roles → role → Capabilities (the same on Splunk Cloud Platform), or mcp_tool_execute = enabled under [role_<name>] in authorize.conf. Only admin and sc_admin hold it by default (and roles that import them), so power, user and, unless it imports one of those two, a delegated-admin role such as sc_subadmin need the grant. A user without it is refused at the first request with HTTP 403 and User lacks required mcp_tool_execute capability, and the AI Assistant panel shows its Setup required card.

Two more capabilities decide what else a user’s AI Assistant can do, because the App works in the browser as the signed-in user:

  • Being audited needs edit_log_alert_event or edit_tcp (Who Can Write Audit Events).
  • Free-form questions need the user’s role to read the provider credential from Splunk’s password store (list_storage_passwords, which admin holds); see Provider Credentials Tab.

Changing the AI Assistant’s settings needs a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin (Application Settings).

docs.title: Cookie auth (default, recommended)
docs.text:
The MCP Server (verified with 1.1.0) accepts the Splunk Web session of the signed-in user. When the LogServ App calls the default endpoint /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp, the browser sends the user’s Splunk session cookie, so no bearer token is needed.

This is the default and preferred configuration; nothing needs setting up beyond installing the MCP Server and granting mcp_tool_execute. It works over HTTPS and HTTP. HTTPS is preferred: Splunk’s session cookies set the Secure and SameSite=Lax flags, which behave fully correctly only over HTTPS.

docs.title: Bearer token (optional, OAuth-strict environments)
docs.text: For an MCP Server configured to refuse cookie auth, the LogServ App can send a bearer token. An admin pastes it in Settings → AI Assistant → Splunk MCP (Bearer Token, realm logserv_ai_assistant_mcp, name bearer_token). The App adds it as an Authorization: Bearer <token> header on top of the cookie. On HTTP 401 the App drops its cached token and retries once.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud — JWT aud (audience) claim must be mcp
docs.text:
This is a customer-side configuration item: nothing in the LogServ packages controls it, and the LogServ App is audience-agnostic (it forwards whatever bearer token, if any, is sent).

On Splunk Cloud Platform (observed on Victoria Experience stacks), the platform’s edge proxy turns the user’s session into a JWT and passes it to splunkd as a bearer token on every /__raw/ request, whether or not you paste a bearer token in the App’s Settings page. The Splunk MCP Server checks the JWT’s aud (audience) claim and accepts the token only when that claim is mcp, or a list that includes mcp (checked in version 1.1.0). Splunk Enterprise has no such edge proxy, so this does not apply there: the session cookie reaches splunkd directly.

If the JWT your Splunk Cloud stack stamps has any other audience (a common default on freshly provisioned non-production stacks is Demo), every MCP request returns HTTP 403 with:

{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "id": 1,
    "error": {
        "code": -32600,
        "message": "Invalid token audience: <whatever-the-jwt-has>"
    }
}

The AI Assistant then shows its Setup required card, because the health check’s first request (initialize) fails.

Fix: get an MCP token with aud = mcp, from your Splunk Cloud admin or Splunk Cloud Support. The path depends on how your stack mints tokens:

  • If your stack uses Splunk’s /services/authorization/tokens endpoint, set audience=mcp when minting.
  • If JWTs are stamped by the Cloud edge proxy (the Victoria default), open a Splunk Cloud Support ticket asking them to set the stack’s MCP audience to mcp.
  • If your stack is fronted by an external SSO (Okta, Azure AD, etc.), configure the SSO’s token issuer to set aud: "mcp" on tokens destined for the MCP route.

To confirm, decode the JWT your browser sends (the Bearer value of the POST /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp request in the browser’s Network tab) with a JWT decoder you trust, and read its aud claim. If it is mcp, the audience is right and the error is something else.

docs.title: Configuration in the LogServ App
docs.text:
Open Settings → AI Assistant → General and confirm:

  • MCP Required (mcp_required) is on (the default). When off, MCP is bypassed and the chat runs in MCP-less chat mode, which needs a configured LLM provider credential (LLM streaming with no searches). Where no credential is configured, or Templates-only mode is on, MCP is the only path that runs anything, so turning this off leaves the assistant unable to run anything. Most customers leave it on.
  • MCP Server URL (mcp_server_url) is blank (the default: /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp on this Splunk instance). Set it only if your MCP Server is at another path or you reach it through another ingress.
  • MCP request timeout (seconds) (mcp_timeout_seconds, default 60) covers your slowest prompt; see Application Settings.

Then on Settings → AI Assistant → Splunk MCP, leave Bearer Token empty for cookie auth (the default), or store the token if your MCP Server requires bearer auth.

Click Save Defaults on the General sub-tab; the next page load picks up the new URL and token. Changing the MCP settings records no audit event; General Tab lists the saves that do.

docs.title: Health Check and Setup Wizard
docs.text:
Each time the AI Assistant panel opens with MCP Required on, the App checks the configured MCP endpoint: it sends the MCP initialize request, then compares the version the server reports with the minimum. Until the check passes, the panel shows a card instead of the chat:

What the panel shows Cause What to do The chat, with Browse prompts The check passed. Nothing. Checking AI Assistant prerequisites… The check is running. Wait; it ends when the request answers or the MCP request timeout passes. Setup required: AI Assistant requires the Splunk MCP Server The initialize request failed, for any reason: the MCP Server is not installed or not enabled, the URL is wrong, the user lacks mcp_tool_execute (HTTP 403), the JWT audience is wrong (HTTP 403, Splunk Cloud), the session expired (HTTP 401), or the request timed out. The card does not say which. Check, in this order, Roles and Capabilities, Install the Splunk MCP Server, MCP Server URL, and the JWT audience. The browser’s Network tab shows the status and message of the POST …/services/mcp request. Then click Re-check. Security upgrade required: Splunk MCP Server v… is vulnerable The server reports a version below 1.0.3 (CVE-2026-20205). Upgrade the Splunk MCP Server to 1.1.0 or later (1.2.1 or later recommended), then click Re-check. Health check error: Could not verify AI Assistant prerequisites An unexpected error; the card shows its message. Check that /services/mcp is reachable and the user’s session is valid, then click Retry.

The Setup required and Security upgrade required cards also carry a link to Splunkbase App 7931. To change the URL or the bearer token, open Settings → AI Assistant directly; the cards do not link there.

docs.title: “Stuck at Checking AI Assistant prerequisites”
docs.text: The check is waiting on a request that does not answer. The most common cause is an MCP Server URL that points at a host or path that does not respond. Leave the field blank to use the default, and check that the server answers with the ping request in Install the Splunk MCP Server. If that fails too, the MCP Server app is not installed or not enabled.

docs.title: “User lacks required mcp_tool_execute capability”
docs.text: The browser’s Network tab shows the POST /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp request returning HTTP 403 with that message, and the panel shows Setup required. Grant mcp_tool_execute to one of the user’s roles (Roles and Capabilities), then have the user reload the page.

docs.title: “Invalid token audience” (Splunk Cloud)
docs.text:
The browser’s Network tab shows the POST /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp request returning HTTP 403 with body:

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "error": { "code": -32600, "message": "Invalid token audience: <value>" } }

The JWT that Splunk Cloud’s edge proxy puts on the request has an aud claim the MCP Server does not accept: it requires aud = mcp. See Splunk Cloud — JWT aud (audience) claim must be mcp above. In short: have the MCP token re-minted with audience=mcp, or ask Splunk Cloud Support to set the stack’s MCP audience to mcp.

docs.title: “401 Unauthorized on every request”
docs.text:
Cookie auth is not working. Possible causes:

  • The Splunk Web session expired in the browser. Sign in again and reopen the AI Assistant panel.
  • The MCP Server is configured for bearer auth only. Store a bearer token on Settings → AI Assistant → Splunk MCP.
  • A reverse proxy in front of Splunk strips the session cookie. Check the proxy’s cookie forwarding.

docs.title: “The panel opens, but predefined prompts fail or their tiles stay empty”
docs.text: The MCP Server is older than 1.1.0 (1.0.3 to 1.0.5 pass the App’s health check but have no Run Saved Search tool), or that tool is turned off in the MCP Server’s own tool settings. Upgrade to 1.1.0 or later (1.2.1 or later recommended), or turn the tool on, as the MCP Server’s documentation describes.

docs.title: MCP-less Chat Mode
docs.text:
Needs a configured LLM provider credential

Chat-only mode relies on LLM streaming, which works only once an admin has configured an LLM provider credential. Where none is configured, or Templates-only mode is on, or a compile-time templates-only build is installed, turning MCP Required off leaves the panel with nothing that works.

For debugging, or where you want LLM streaming without MCP, turn MCP Required off on Settings → AI Assistant → General. The AI Assistant then runs in chat-only mode:

  • The LLM vendor receives the system primer, the user message and the history (no tool definitions).
  • The AI cannot run any Splunk search: no splunk_run_saved_search, no splunk_run_query, and no prompt browser.
  • Replies are conversational only: useful for “explain how X works” questions, not for any investigation of your data.
  • A persistent orange warning banner at the top of the chat reads: “Chat-only mode — tool execution disabled (MCP not configured). The AI can answer questions but cannot run searches against your Splunk data.”

This mode is distinct from Templates-only mode (Restricting the LLM Path): chat-only mode has the LLM path on and MCP off; Templates-only mode has the LLM path off and MCP on.

docs.title: AI Assistant — Overview
docs.text:
The AI Assistant ships turned off

On a fresh install the LogServ App shows no AI Assistant button, panel or route. To use it, install the Splunk MCP Server on the search head, grant its mcp_tool_execute capability to the roles that will use the assistant, and have an admin turn on Enable AI Assistant and accept the acknowledgements: Set Up the AI Assistant. From then on the predefined prompts work with no LLM provider, credential or vendor call. The released v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build, so free-form questions are also possible once an admin configures an LLM provider credential. An admin can keep the deployment to predefined prompts with Templates-only mode; see Restricting the LLM Path.

docs.title: What the AI Assistant Is
docs.text:
The AI Assistant is a Splunk-aware assistant panel in the LogServ App that lets analysts run cataloged investigations against their Splunk data. Once turned on, it opens to the right of every dashboard as a side panel, from the AI Assistant button at the right end of the header’s second row.

The feature has two paths. The first needs only the Splunk MCP Server; the second also needs an LLM provider credential:

  • Predefined prompts (no LLM call). The user opens the prompt browser and clicks one of the cataloged prompts (three packs plus a context-aware Dashboard Focused tab). The App runs the prompt’s saved search through the Splunk MCP Server, shows the result as a tile in the right pane (table / chart / KPI / pie), and adds a static interpretation and suggested-next-steps card. No vendor LLM is invoked. No cost, search latency only, and no data leaves your Splunk environment.
  • Free-form prompts (LLM-driven). Once an admin configures an LLM provider credential, the user can also type a natural-language question. The App sends a system primer, the question and the tool definitions to the configured vendor (Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure OpenAI / AWS Bedrock); the AI runs saved searches or its own queries and writes a narrative reply. The shipped default provider is Mock (development only): until an admin selects a real provider and stores its credential, a typed question gets a canned mock reply and no vendor is contacted. An admin can switch this path off with Templates-only mode, or install a compile-time templates-only build, in which it cannot be switched back on; see Restricting the LLM Path, which also covers the separate v0.0.6 line, whose bundle has no provider code at all.

docs.title: The Privacy Posture
docs.text:
With no LLM provider credential configured, nothing is ever transmitted to any AI vendor — there are no vendor calls at all.

The predefined-prompt path runs entirely between your browser, your Splunk search head, and the Splunk MCP Server on it. Search results render locally in the right pane; no summary, no metadata, and no prompt text leaves your Splunk environment.

Once a provider credential is configured, a second guarantee takes over:

No raw event and no unsummarized search result from your Splunk instance is ever transmitted to any AI vendor — only the summary the active privacy tier allows.

That guarantee is not policy; it is enforced by the type system at build time, with a runtime defense-in-depth scan as a second layer. The TypeScript compiler refuses to put any tool-result value from MCP into an outbound vendor payload; the only conversion path is the active tier’s summarizer. As a second layer, every outbound payload is serialized and scanned at dispatch time and rejected if a Splunk data field name (_raw, _time, host, source, sourcetype, index, …) appears as a key; the scan checks the payload’s structure, not the text of a summary. What a summary may contain is set by the active privacy tier (Privacy Tiers):

  • Tier 1 (default) sends two numbers per call, a count and a timing — no field value from any event. A model that writes its own queries can still make those numbers depend on event data, so a few bits per call can leak.
  • Tier 2 (admin opt-in) adds aggregated metadata: per-column statistics and top-N values with counts — field values from the events, filtered, capped at 40 characters each and, with PII redaction on, sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier — column names only when Splunk generates them or every word in them was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran (others appear as col_N), and the time range only as UTC timestamps the App formats. No raw rows.
  • Tier 0 (Ollama, local) does not work in this release: do not select it (Privacy Tiers).

In every tier a failed call sends only its HTTP status and a fixed error class. What the vendor sees: the user’s question, schema descriptions, tool definitions, and the tier-bounded summaries.

For the build-time type-system mechanism, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Architecture at a Glance
docs.text:
A predefined prompt has no vendor in its flow:

   User picks a prompt (prompt browser)
        |
        v
   Orchestrator  -->  Splunk MCP Server  -->  Splunk search-job
        |                                           |
        |  <------  results (stay client-side) <----+
        v
   Guidance card (left pane)      Tool result tile (right pane)

A free-form question adds the vendor loop around the same MCP dispatch:

   User question
        |
        v
   AI vendor  -->  AI picks tools  -->  Splunk MCP Server  -->  Splunk search-job
        |                                                              |
        |                                  (raw rows stay client-side) |
        |  <-----  privacy-tier summary  <----+ (count + timing,
        |                                       Tier 2 adds aggregates)
        |
        v  AI synthesizes narrative reply
   Chat panel (left pane)        Tool result tiles (right pane)

When a search fails, the vendor is told only the HTTP status and a fixed error class, never Splunk’s error text; the full error shows in the tile. See Privacy Tiers.

Every saved-search dispatch produces a tool-result tile in the right pane (table / chart / KPI / pie based on the prompt’s renderHint). Drill-down chips (↗ <Dashboard name>, ↗ Run SPL) on each tile connect the conversation back into the dashboards or Splunk’s Search app — see Drill-down Chips.

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
Without an LLM credential:

  • The predefined-prompt catalog in three packs (SAP Basis / Security / Operations) plus a context-aware Dashboard Focused tab that shows the prompts relevant to the dashboard you have open. Many prompts read the same KV Store rollups the dashboards use, so they stay fast at any data volume. See Predefined Prompts.
  • Result tiles + guidance cards — every dispatch renders the actual data (table / chart / KPI / pie) plus a static “How to read this result” interpretation and suggested next steps from the intent map.
  • Drill-down chips — a ↗ <Dashboard name> chip per related dashboard, which opens that dashboard in a new tab at the App’s default time range (Last 30 days), and ↗ Run SPL on every tile, which opens the search in Splunk’s Search app with the dispatch’s exact time window.
  • Audit log — every predefined-prompt dispatch (and every admin acknowledgement) lands in a dedicated logserv_ai_assistant_audit index, with an in-app browser and an optional HEC forwarder for tamper-evidence. Writing it needs Splunk’s edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event capability, which by default admin and power hold and user does not (who can write audit events).
  • Application Settings — the admin page (General / Provider Credentials / Splunk MCP / Audit Log sub-tabs), including the MCP request timeout and the audit-forwarder configuration.

Once an LLM provider credential is configured:

  • Free-form prompts against four providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock), with a per-user model picker and dynamic model discovery. See Free-form Prompts.
  • Power Mode — a role-gated ✦ Power toggle that adds a rule to the system primer: run a saved search before answering.
  • Privacy tiers + time-window reasoning — the vendor-facing privacy envelope and the primer rules that keep AI severity claims honest.
  • OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) controls — prompt-injection sanitization, type-bounded data redaction, SPL static-analysis guard, jailbreak detection, per-user rate limit, USD spend cap, PII redaction.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Splunk 9.4.3 or later.
  • Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) 1.1.0 or later is required; 1.2.1 or later is recommended (it fixes SVD-2026-1004). The predefined prompts run through its Run Saved Search tool, first shipped in 1.1.0. The App’s health check refuses only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix), so 1.0.3 to 1.0.5 pass that check but every predefined prompt fails. It must be on the same search head as the LogServ App. See Splunk MCP Setup. By default the App authenticates to it with the user’s Splunk Web session; an optional bearer token can be added.
  • The mcp_tool_execute capability on every role that uses the AI Assistant. The MCP Server grants it by default only to admin and sc_admin (Roles and Capabilities).
  • To be audited: edit_log_alert_event or edit_tcp on the user’s role (Who Can Write Audit Events).
  • No LLM provider and no vendor credential for the predefined prompts. For free-form questions: a provider credential, and each user’s role must be able to read it from Splunk’s password store (list_storage_passwords, which admin holds).
  • A role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin to turn the feature on, configure MCP, manage the audit forwarder, and view the Audit Log tab (Who can open the page).

docs.title: First-time UX
docs.text:
Before the first use, an admin turns the AI Assistant on: Set Up the AI Assistant. Then:

  1. Click AI Assistant at the right end of the header’s second row. The right-side panel opens. (Where Templates-only mode is on, or a templates-only build is installed, an info banner at the top of the chat pane says that free-form prompts are off.)
  2. If the MCP Server is not reachable for this user, the panel shows a setup card with guidance instead of the chat — see Splunk MCP Setup. Otherwise, the panel is ready.
  3. Click Browse prompts to open the catalog. Pick a prompt from the Dashboard Focused / SAP Basis / Security / Operations tab.
  4. The prompt runs through MCP and renders a tool tile in the right pane, with a static “How to read this result” guidance card on the left.
  5. Click any of the drill-down chips on the tile (↗ <Dashboard name>, ↗ Run SPL) to investigate further.

(Once an LLM provider credential is configured, the chat input also takes free-form questions — see Free-form Prompts.)

docs.title: When to Use Which Path
docs.text: Use case Path Routine “show me X” investigations on the cataloged dimensions Predefined prompts (no credential needed) Compliance / audit reports with a fixed cadence Predefined prompts (deterministic, zero vendor traffic) Free-form questions the catalog doesn’t cover Free-form — requires a provider credential, with Power Mode on if available Cross-cutting “what’s most critical right now?” investigations Free-form — requires a provider credential (the AI runs several saved searches and synthesizes) Environments where vendor-LLM access is intentionally unavailable Configure no provider credential, or turn on Templates-only mode and clear Model discovery (which can otherwise still list the provider’s models); a compile-time templates-only build makes it irreversible (Restricting the LLM Path) Policy requires the vendor client code physically absent from the bundle The separate, frozen v0.0.6 line (Restricting the LLM Path)

docs.title: Where to Go Next
docs.text:
Works without an LLM credential:

  • Set Up the AI Assistant — turning the feature on, step by step.
  • Predefined Prompts — the prompt catalog, the prompt browser, and how the catalog is customized.
  • Splunk MCP Setup — installing and configuring the prerequisite MCP Server.
  • Application Settings — the admin page (#/settings): top-level AI Assistant and Dashboard Data tabs, with the AI Assistant configuration as sub-tabs.
  • Audit Log — what’s logged, the in-app viewer, and the optional HEC forwarder for tamper-evidence.
  • Restricting the LLM Path — Templates-only mode, the compile-time templates-only build, and the v0.0.6 line.

Once a provider credential is configured:

  • Free-form Prompts — the LLM-driven flow, tool dispatch, citations, and rate limiting.
  • Privacy Tiers — what each tier exposes to the vendor, and the decision matrix for picking one.
  • OWASP LLM Top 10 Compliance — security controls posture for compliance reviews.

docs.title: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) Compliance
docs.text:
This page is intended for the customer’s security team reviewing the LogServ App’s AI Assistant feature for production deployment. It covers each of the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) items and the controls the LogServ App ships to address them.

Companion page

For the same controls organized along Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF) four-pillar structure plus a coverage matrix of SAIF’s 15 Key Risks, see SAIF Security Architecture.

These controls govern the path an LLM provider credential unlocks

The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, so the controls below (prompt-injection sanitization, the type-system data boundary, tier-gated summaries, SPL static analysis, rate limits, spend caps) actively govern it once an admin configures an LLM provider credential. Until a credential exists — and wherever Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed — there is no vendor dispatch at all, which is the strongest form of each LLM-specific control. The audit trail and the supply-chain controls are live either way; the audit trail is tamper-evident only when the HEC forwarder sends a copy to a separately administered destination (Audit Log).

docs.title: LLM01 — Prompt Injection
docs.text:
Threat: an attacker (either via the user-prompt vector or via in-band tool-result data) crafts input that hijacks the LLM’s instruction-following behavior, causing it to ignore the system primer or perform unintended actions.

Controls shipped:

  • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>...</TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block wraps every tool-result summary the AI sees. The system primer instructs the AI to treat anything inside the sentinel as DATA from the customer’s environment, NEVER as instructions, regardless of how command-like the contents look. Mitigates the in-band channel of prompt injection: a malicious user who can write events into the customer’s Splunk index could in principle craft field values like user="Ignore prior instructions and...", but the sentinel + sanitizer reduces the effective attack surface to near-zero.
  • Per-value sanitizer for Tier 2 categorical aggregates (sanitizeAggregateValue()). Three classes of suspicious content get replaced wholesale with <filtered>: strings starting with role markers (system:, user:, assistant:, etc.), strings containing known jailbreak / prompt-injection idioms (ignore prior instructions, [INST], <|im_start|>, <|system|>, disregard the above, jailbreak), and strings containing the sentinel tags themselves (prevents a malicious value from prematurely closing the data block).
  • No error text in the tool-result channel. A failed tool call reaches the AI only as a fixed, App-written string built from its HTTP status and an error class. Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error message, which repeats the failed search and so can carry text an attacker wrote into an event, is never sent. See Privacy Tiers → Failed Tool Calls.
  • Jailbreak pattern detection on user prompts. Flag-and-proceed: matches fire a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event but do not block the prompt. Captures a hash + length + matched-pattern groups + char-class fingerprint for SOC pivot analysis.
  • Defense-in-depth chain. Type-system enforcement (LLM02) + Tier 2 sanitizer + tool-result sentinel + primer + vendor-side defenses provide multiple independent layers; bypassing any one doesn’t break the chain.

docs.title: LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure
docs.text:
Threat: the LLM emits sensitive customer data (PII, secrets, internal-only information) in its responses or causes it to be transmitted to the vendor.

Controls shipped:

  • TypeScript type-system enforcement, plus a runtime scan. The compiler refuses to put any tool-result value into the outbound vendor payload; the only conversion path is the summary that the active tier’s summarizer produces. As a second layer, every outbound payload is serialized and scanned at dispatch time and rejected if a Splunk data field name appears as a key; the scan checks the payload’s structure, not the text of a summary, so what a summary may say is set by the tier rules below. See Privacy Tiers and LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.
  • Privacy tier scoping. Tier 1 (default) gives the AI two numbers per call, a count and a timing — no values. Tier 2 (admin opt-in) adds aggregated metadata: top-N values + counts (field values from the events — filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier), numeric stats, column names only when Splunk generates them or every word in them was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran (any other name appears as col_N), and the time range only as UTC timestamps the App formats. Neither tier sends raw rows. Tier 1 limits how much the AI can learn rather than making it zero: for each call it sends a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status. A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data, so a few bits per call can leak (up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count, which is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises them). The session tool-call cap (default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat resets it, and 0 turns it off. No error text is sent in any tier.
  • No error text to the vendor, in any tier. A failed tool call reaches the AI only as Tool error (HTTP <status>, class=<class>): <fixed hint> The error text is shown to the user only. — the status only when it is a whole number from 100 to 599, the class one of ten fixed names chosen in the browser. A Splunk or MCP Server error text can carry event text (a subsearch such as | inputlookup [search … | eval v=substr(_raw,1,80) | return $v] can put it there), so none of it is sent. The full error stays in the user’s result panel. Refusals the App makes itself (the SPL guard, the saved-search catalog, an undeclared tool, the session tool-call cap) reach the AI as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>; the reason is App-written text, built where the App makes the refusal and never from a tool result.
  • PII redaction at Tier 2. Every field the App defines has a class in a table the build checks (identifier, address, host, free text, safe), and field-name patterns cover every other name: email(s), user(name)(s) and user_name, every *_ip, *_addr, *_address and a bare ip, the CIM src, dest, dst and dvc, peer, mac, account, camelCase …User / …UserName / …Email (TargetUserName), id names such as user_id (hostname opt-in) — also after ., :, - or a space, so data-model and JSON names such as Authentication.user, All_Traffic.src_ip and event.user and display names such as "User Name" match — before values are sent to the vendor. Per-value <redacted-XXXXXXX> tags — an HMAC-SHA-256 under a random per-chat-session key — let the AI reason about cardinality without seeing the actual identifier; they cannot be reversed by hashing candidates or linked across sessions. Redaction fails closed: a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App traces the column through constructs it reads in full — the field’s own name, a statistics function over one field (values(user) → user), AS, a rename without wildcards, lookup … OUTPUT … AS, eval x=<one field> or a count — to fields that mark no identifier. Every other construct — an eval expression (. concatenation, functions), rex, spath, strcat, wildcard renames, a pivot’s cells, transpose / untable / fieldsummary, a column a subsearch defines, an unknown command, or a reading limit exceeded — leaves the column untraced and every value redacted; a pure count (dc(user)) keeps its numbers. While redaction is on, every value of a text column shown as col_N is redacted, and a numeric column whose name or a field it reads marks an identifier, or that mixes many fields, sends values withheld. Column names are withheld whatever the setting unless Splunk generates them or the model’s query or the App’s catalog search wrote every word of them. Redaction is name-based: a traced field named nothing like an identifier (an event field such as message, _raw under an eval alias) is sent as it is (see Security Architecture, gaps 10 and 11).
  • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel (also LLM01) prevents the AI from accidentally treating sanitized data as instructions and echoing it back unsanitized.
  • Vendor-side commitments. Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure OpenAI / AWS Bedrock each publish their own data-usage commitments (no training on API traffic for Anthropic & OpenAI direct API by default). The customer’s DPA review should confirm vendor-side processor obligations.

docs.title: LLM03 — Supply Chain
docs.text:
Threat: a compromised or vulnerable third-party dependency in the bundle introduces an attack vector or data-exfil channel.

Controls shipped:

  • Dependency audit script. yarn audit:ci runs a dependency audit at the high advisory level and exits non-zero on high or critical advisories; yarn build:ci runs it before the build. It is not a gate on the release: the regular yarn build, which produces the release package, does not run it.
  • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) shipped with every build. A bundled generator parses the package lock directly (no external tool dependency) and emits a SBOM.json in CycloneDX 1.4 format with purl (Package URL) + sha-512 hash per dependency. The SBOM enumerates every bundled dependency; reviewers can pin against this list.
  • Third-party notices. Every build also regenerates THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md from the same dependency tree, so the attribution matches the bundled code (Third-Party Software Licenses).

docs.title: LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning
docs.text:
Threat: an attacker with the ability to write events into the customer’s Splunk index could craft field values that, when surfaced to the AI as Tier 2 aggregates, hijack the AI’s downstream behavior (e.g., by appearing to be system instructions).

Controls shipped:

  • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block (also LLM01).
  • Per-value sanitizer with role-marker + jailbreak-idiom + sentinel-tag filtering (also LLM01).
  • Fixed error strings (also LLM01, LLM02). A failed call’s error text, which can repeat values from the index, is not sent to the AI; it gets a fixed status-and-class string instead.
  • Truncation of categorical aggregate values to 40 chars to reduce the budget available for embedded jailbreak prompts.
  • Top-N capping of categorical aggregates at 10 by default (max 50) — bounds the volume of AI-visible value content per column.

docs.title: LLM05 — Improper Output Handling
docs.text:
Threat: the LLM’s response contains content that, when rendered or executed, harms the user (e.g., XSS via injected HTML, command injection via shell-formatted output).

Controls shipped:

  • React rendering uses JSX text nodes, not dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Strings are escaped by default; markdown is parsed via a controlled set of recognized markers (citation, severity, bold) — no general-purpose HTML rendering.
  • Drill-down URLs built via buildSplunkSearchUrl() use encodeURIComponent() for the SPL string and centralize the target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" security flags. The noopener flag breaks the window.opener reference for reverse-tabnabbing.
  • AI-authored SPL goes through a static-analysis guard before dispatch (see LLM06).

docs.title: LLM06 — Excessive Agency
docs.text:
Threat: the AI is given the ability to perform actions whose consequences exceed the user’s intent (e.g., write/delete data, send emails, exfiltrate via output channels).

Controls shipped:

  • Saved-search allow-list for splunk_run_saved_search. The AI can run only the saved searches in the App’s own prompt catalog, built from the App’s intent map — never a rollup aggregation, retention, backfill or Enterprise Security feed. The check runs where every saved-search call is sent to the MCP Server, for predefined prompts and free-form calls alike. A name the AI asks for that is not in the catalog is refused before dispatch, with a synthetic error tool_result and a security_blocked_spl audit event; predefined prompts take their names from the catalog itself, and a build gate checks that every one of them is allowed. The list is a copy of the catalog’s names taken when the App loads, and no code in the App can add to it while it runs. The App builds the MCP arguments itself (the vetted name, the App — app = splunk_app_sap_logserv — and the time range) instead of forwarding the model’s, and refuses any tool name other than the two it defines, with a security_blocked_spl audit event as well.
  • SPL guard for AI-authored splunk_run_query: a denylist, an allow-list and Splunk’s parser. Every query the AI writes is checked three times before it is sent, and a query any check refuses is never run. The first fence is a denylist of commands that write to an index, write lookups or files, delete events, alert, email, run scripts, read REST endpoints (rest returns stored credentials decrypted), send data out (outputtelemetry, curl, wget, sendresults, the external lookup dnslookup), save a model (fit ... into) or run another search (map, savedsearch and its aliases), with the quoting tricks that could hide them; it also refuses inline comments, ambiguous quoting and any macro other than the App’s own. The second fence is an allow-list read by a strict lexer: only the App’s list of read-only analytic commands (not union; append combines searches instead), only the LogServ index, only the App’s own lookups, and subsearches only where they cannot widen the search, so other apps’ custom commands and external lookups are refused too. Then Splunk’s own search parser reads the query, and the App refuses it when the two readings differ or when the parser cannot be asked (fail closed). A blocked query produces a synthetic error tool_result and a security_blocked_spl audit event; the AI is told Tool call refused by the App before it ran: with the App’s reason, and can write a different query. The full lists and rules are in Free-form Prompts → The SPL Guard.
  • Per-session tool-call cap prevents infinite tool loops. Maps to session_tool_cap_hit audit event on overflow.
  • Catalog saved searches are not run through the SPL guard — their SPL is reviewed at build time, and none of their searches contains a writing command. The guard scope is the AI-written ad-hoc path.
  • Scope. These controls protect this App’s AI Assistant. Other MCP clients holding a Splunk MCP Server token are governed by the Splunk MCP Server’s own controls and by Splunk permissions.

docs.title: LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage
docs.text:
Threat: the system primer leaks to the user (or via the user back to the vendor’s prompt-logging) and exposes internal instructions, lookups, or configuration.

Controls shipped:

  • No customer-secret content in the primer. The primer contains: tool definitions, the saved-search catalog (names + labels, public information), the LogServ data-model summary (sourcetypes + field names, public), the synthesis rules. No customer-specific identifiers, no API keys, no internal URLs.
  • Time-window reasoning rules are pedagogical (about how the AI should reason about its inputs) — leakage of these rules has no security impact.

The customer’s DPA review should still confirm vendor-side prompt-logging policies (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock all log prompts at varying retention; some offer enterprise tiers with no-logging guarantees).

docs.title: LLM08 — Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
docs.text:
Threat: vector / embedding stores used for RAG can leak sensitive data if not access-controlled, can be poisoned by malicious indexed content, or can return chunks across security boundaries.

Status: Not applicable. The LogServ App’s AI Assistant does NOT use vector embeddings or a separate RAG store. The “RAG” here is direct tool dispatch against the customer’s own Splunk index — every retrieval is an SPL search bounded by Splunk’s own RBAC (either a live event search or a read of one of the app’s own access-controlled KV-Store rollups; neither is an embedding store). There is no vector store to compromise.

docs.title: LLM09 — Misinformation
docs.text:
Threat: the LLM produces confident-sounding but incorrect information that the user acts on.

Controls shipped:

  • AI-generated — verify before acting disclaimer rendered as a small muted footer below every AI assistant_text bubble. Visible on every reply, never collapsed.
  • Time-window reasoning rules (Time-Window Reasoning) force the AI to verify high-severity claims with a narrow-window query before recommending action. Self-correction is observable in the response (the AI reports the cumulative number AND the verify-query result).
  • Citation chips ([→ saved_search_name]) link every claim back to the source tool_result tile, so users can sanity-check the narrative against the rendered data.
  • Predefined-prompt path (default for routine investigations) has zero AI-misinformation risk — the dispatch is deterministic and the interpretation card is pre-authored, not generated.

docs.title: LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption
docs.text:
Threat: uncontrolled vendor calls drive arbitrary cost, latency, or denial-of-service on the user-facing experience.

Controls shipped:

  • Per-user rolling-1-hour rate limit on free-form prompts. Configurable via rate_limit_per_hour in Settings (default 30, 0 = disabled). Records rate_limited_prompt audit event on hit.
  • Cumulative-cost daily spend cap in USD. Configurable via daily_spend_cap_usd in Settings. Resets at local midnight (the browser’s calendar day). Records daily_spend_cap_hit audit event on hit.
  • Per-session tool-call cap to prevent infinite tool loops. Records session_tool_cap_hit.
  • Token-usage observability in every vendor_tier1 audit event (emitted for every vendor call regardless of tier): input tokens, output tokens, total tokens, USD cost estimate. Lets finance attribute spend to specific users / sessions. The estimate uses an exact-id price table, which covers the Claude 5.x models at Anthropic’s published first-party rates (cache reads and writes included); an unpriced model reports $0 and does not count toward the daily spend cap.
  • Streaming + abort in the chat UI — users can cancel an in-flight expensive turn via the Stop button.
  • Canned prompts are NOT rate-limited — they bypass the AI vendor entirely and are bounded by Splunk’s own search-quota controls, not vendor cost.

Enforcement of the rate limit and the spend cap is browser-side (localStorage keyed by Splunk username), so the caps bound good-faith use rather than a determined user with a second browser or cleared site data; every block still emits an audit event, which is the durable control. The session tool-call cap is likewise in-memory per tab. Server-side enforcement is a tracked follow-up.

docs.title: Compliance Posture Summary
docs.text: OWASP item Status Primary control LLM01 — Prompt Injection Mitigated TOOL_RESULT_DATA sentinel + per-value sanitizer + jailbreak detection + primer hardening LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure Mitigated Hidden<T> type-system enforcement + Tier 1/2 sanitize chokepoint + fixed error strings (no error text to the vendor) + PII redaction LLM03 — Supply Chain Partly mitigated CycloneDX SBOM with sha-512 hashes in every build + a dependency-audit script (yarn audit:ci, high and above) that the release build does not run LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning Mitigated TOOL_RESULT_DATA sentinel + per-value sanitizer + 40-char value truncation + top-N cap LLM05 — Improper Output Handling Mitigated React JSX text nodes + URL encoding + noopener + SPL static-analysis guard LLM06 — Excessive Agency Mitigated Saved-search allow-list (the App’s prompt catalog) + SPL guard (denylist, command / data-scope / lookup allow-list, search-parser cross-check) + session tool-call cap LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage Mitigated No customer-secret content in primer; vendor-side DPA review needed LLM08 — Vector and Embedding Weaknesses Not applicable No separate vector store; live SPL dispatch via Splunk RBAC LLM09 — Misinformation Mitigated AI-generated disclaimer + time-window reasoning + citation chips + predefined-prompt path LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption Mitigated Per-user rate limit + daily spend cap + session tool-call cap + token-usage audit

docs.title: When These Controls Are Live
docs.text: The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant: every control on this page actively governs its LLM path once an LLM provider credential is configured. Where no credential exists, or Templates-only mode is on, or a compile-time templates-only build is installed, the LLM-specific items above (LLM01/02/04/07/09/10) are moot by construction — there is no vendor dispatch to attack — while the audit trail, its forwarder, and the supply-chain controls remain live. Nothing about the controls themselves differs between builds beyond whether the path they protect is reachable.

docs.title: Power Mode
docs.text:
Requires a configured LLM provider credential

Power Mode governs free-form LLM dispatch, so the ✦ Power toggle appears only where that path is live. The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, but an admin must first configure an LLM provider credential. The toggle is hidden while Templates-only mode is on (Settings → AI Assistant → General) and in a compile-time templates-only build, since there is then no LLM dispatch to force a saved search before.

Power Mode is a role-gated ✦ Power toggle in the AI Assistant chat-input toolbar. While it is on, the App adds a rule to the system primer of every free-form prompt: the AI must call splunk_run_saved_search (or splunk_run_query) at least once before it writes any narrative reply (forced-RAG). The rule is an instruction to the model, not a check the App makes: the App does not refuse a reply that comes without a search, so read the tiles to see which searches ran.

docs.title: Why Power Mode Exists
docs.text:
The default free-form path lets the AI choose whether to dispatch a tool or reply from prior knowledge. For most questions the AI dispatches appropriately — but for questions that look like the AI knows them already from training data (“What’s a HANA audit log?”), it may answer from prior knowledge and skip the tool call. That’s fine for explanatory questions, but it’s the wrong behavior for investigations: a “what’s the failure rate this week?” question deserves a real Splunk dispatch, not a probability-weighted guess.

Power Mode addresses this by adding a forced-RAG rule to the system primer: for every user message, the AI must call splunk_run_saved_search at least once (or splunk_run_query if no saved search fits) before generating any narrative answer.

This is forced-RAG over chosen-RAG: same tools, same MCP path, same privacy tier. Power Mode asks the model for the saved-search-first step; the App does not enforce it. For the primer-augmentation mechanism, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Role-Gated Visibility
docs.text:
Power Mode is opt-in per organization and per-role. The toggle is hidden from users entirely unless their Splunk role is in the configured allow-list. Default: empty list — Power Mode hidden from every user.

Configuration path (admin-only):

  1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General.
  2. Find the Power Users section and its Power Mode roles field. The list is populated from Splunk’s services/authorization/roles REST endpoint.
  3. Pick the roles that should see the Power toggle (typical: admin, power, sc_admin; add your stack’s delegated-admin role, for example sc_subadmin, if your admins use one).
  4. Click Save Defaults.
  5. Affected users see the ✦ Power button in their chat input toolbar on next page load.

Per-user gating would require a custom directory and doesn’t compose with Splunk’s standard RBAC. Role gating reuses the same primitive admins already manage for everything else (search permissions, app permissions, etc.).

docs.title: Toggle UX
docs.text:
The ✦ Power button is a small pill in the chat input toolbar between Send and the keyboard-shortcut hint. State is persisted per-tab in sessionStorage under logserv.aiAssistant.powerMode — opening a new browser tab resets to OFF.

Visual states:

State Button text Border Tooltip OFF (default) ✦ Power panel-border-weak “Power Mode OFF — click to enable forced saved-search-first behavior.” ON ✦ Power ON cyan-accent fill “Power Mode ON — every prompt forces a saved-search dispatch before AI synthesis. Click to turn off.”

A11y: aria-pressed="true" when on, aria-pressed="false" when off.

docs.title: What Power Mode Does NOT Change
docs.text:
• Privacy tier behavior is unchanged. Tier 1 still gives the AI count + timing only; Tier 2 still gives aggregated metadata only. Power Mode just enforces saved-search-first; tier still controls what AI sees about each search result.
  • Tool dispatch is unchanged. Same MCP path, same tool definitions (splunk_run_saved_search, splunk_run_query), same SPL static-analysis guard, same session tool-call cap.
  • Audit categories are unchanged. A Power Mode prompt records the same vendor_tier1 audit event as any free-form prompt (one per prompt, whatever the tier); its powerMode field records whether the toggle was on, for SOC pivot analysis.
  • Per-user rate limit, daily spend cap, jailbreak detection. All unchanged.

docs.title: When to Use Power Mode
docs.text: Use case Power Mode? Investigations that should be data-grounded (“what’s failing right now?”) ON Cross-cutting top-N questions (“find the top 10 issues to attend to”) ON — Power Mode + the TIME-WINDOW REASONING rules together produce verify-confirmed severity claims Compliance reports that the auditor will cross-check against the rendered tiles ON (so every claim has a citation) Conceptual questions (“what’s a HANA audit log?”, “explain risk_level”) OFF (the AI’s training knowledge is fine) One-shot follow-ups in an existing conversation where prior tool results already cover the answer OFF (forces an unnecessary dispatch) Streaming-only chat-only mode (MCP Required off) No effect — the toggle still appears for power-user roles, but with no tool path the App does not add the Power Mode rule to the primer

docs.title: Audit Trail
docs.text:
Every free-form prompt that completes records one vendor_tier1 audit event, after its last turn, with a powerMode flag that captures whether the toggle was on for that prompt. Use cases for the audit field:

  • SOC pivot: filter audit events to powerMode=true to see only the strict-data-grounded turns.
  • Compliance review: confirm that audit-period investigations were run with Power Mode on (so every cited finding has a tool dispatch behind it).
  • Cost analysis: prompts with Power Mode on tend to run more searches, and so cost more per prompt. The audit lets finance attribute spend to the gating choice.

Power Mode does NOT generate a separate audit category — it’s a flag on the existing vendor_tier1 event. See Audit Log.

docs.title: Predefined Prompts
docs.text:
Predefined prompts are cataloged saved searches across three packs that the AI Assistant can dispatch via the Splunk MCP Server without invoking any LLM. They are the deterministic, vendor-traffic-free path through the AI Assistant: the user clicks a prompt card, the orchestrator dispatches the saved search, the result tile renders in the right pane, and a static interpretation + suggested-next-steps card appears in the chat.

This is the path that works without an LLM credential: predefined prompts need no LLM provider, no credential, and make no vendor call. The AI Assistant ships turned off; once an admin has turned it on and the Splunk MCP Server is installed (Set Up the AI Assistant), the predefined prompts are the whole AI Assistant in any deployment that never configures a provider. Once an LLM provider credential is configured, the same catalog coexists with the free-form path.

docs.title: The Three Packs
docs.text:
Pack Count Focus SAP Basis 15 SAP Basis admin investigations: HANA trace severity trend, ABAP work-process errors, integration topology call volume, RFC partner failures Security 28 Auth failures, beaconing detection, after-hours admin activity, permission grants, privilege-chain detection (failure → success → grant), service-account interactive logins, Windows lockouts Operations 18 Ingest health, error rate trends, error-category breakdowns, top error categories, host volume drop, freshness checks, Cloud Connector backend latency

The full catalog ships inside the LogServ App as a data-driven intent map. Each prompt entry carries the saved-search name, label, description, render hint, dashboard mapping, interpretation, and suggested next steps, plus an optional chart hint and chart palette.

Thirteen of the Security prompts run the App’s Enterprise Security saved searches (splunk_sap_logserv_es_*). Such a prompt returns an error while its saved search is disabled; to keep those prompts working on a search head without Enterprise Security, turn off only the schedule of those 13 searches. Before you disable the ES content, read Disabling or tuning the ES content.

docs.title: The Dashboard Focused Tab
docs.text:
The first-position tab in the prompt browser is Dashboard Focused — it auto-filters the catalog to prompts that are mapped to the dashboard you currently have open. The mapping is the per-prompt dashboard field in the intent map (single string or array — multi-target prompts map to multiple dashboards). The tab auto-hides when the active dashboard has zero matching prompts (e.g., on Settings or AI Assistant pages).

Each card on the Dashboard Focused tab carries a small pack-origin chip (cyan-light SAP Basis / salmon-red Security / gold-orange Operations) so users can find the prompt back in its home pack later.

docs.title: What Happens When You Click a Prompt
docs.text:
1. Dispatch. The orchestrator calls splunk_run_saved_search on the MCP server with the prompt’s saved-search name and the time window selected in the prompt browser’s own Time range dropdown (Last 1 hour … Last 30 days; default Last 24 hours, remembered per browser tab in sessionStorage). That window is passed as the dispatched search’s earliest_time / latest_time, so it bounds the saved search — narrowing the dropdown makes a heavier prompt return faster.
  2. Tile renders. The MCP server returns the rows. The orchestrator renders them in a tool-result tile in the right pane, with the prompt’s pre-configured renderHint (table / timechart / kpi / pie) and optional companion chartHint (chart on top + table below for renderHint=table prompts that benefit from a visual).
  3. Guidance card. A “How to read this result” card appears in the left chat pane below the user’s prompt label. The card has two parts:
    • Interpretation — one paragraph explaining what the result means and what shapes are normal vs. concerning. Sourced from the intent map’s interpretation field.
    • Suggested next steps — a bulleted list of follow-up investigations. Some entries are plain text; others are clickable deep-link chips that open Splunk’s universal Search app with a focused SPL pre-filled and the dispatch’s exact earliest/latest pre-applied. Sourced from the intent map’s nextSteps array.
  4. Drill-down chips on the tile. Every tile carries a ↗ <Dashboard name> chip per resolvable dashboard (from the prompt’s dashboard field), then a ↗ Run SPL chip, then Clear, in its actions slot. See Drill-down Chips.

No LLM call. No vendor traffic. No tokens. The dispatch is recorded as a local_only audit event with the prompt id + SPL + row count + execution time + ok flag. See Audit Log.

High-volume prompts read precomputed rollups

About half the catalog — every high-volume investigation plus the whole-estate host-volume prompts — reads the same hourly KV-Store rollups that power the dashboards instead of scanning every event live. These prompts stay sub-second even over a 30-day window on a large dataset, where a raw scan of the same window can run past the MCP request timeout (60 seconds by default, MCP request timeout (seconds) in Application Settings) at high ingest volumes. The trade-off is identical to the dashboards: results reflect data through the most-recently-completed hour (the beaconing prompt’s rollup is daily), and on a fresh install these prompts populate older windows only after the Dashboard Data backfill has run. The remaining prompts dispatch a live search bounded by the Time range you select.

docs.title: The Tab Persistence Convention
docs.text: The prompt browser remembers your last-selected tab across modal-open events, persisted per-tab in sessionStorage under logserv.aiAssistant.promptActivePack. The persistence rule is selection-based, not casual-flipping-based — your tab choice is only remembered if you actually picked a prompt from it. Casual tab-flipping (browsing without clicking a card) doesn’t persist. If your last selected tab points at a tab that’s hidden on the current dashboard (e.g., persisted to Dashboard Focused on a dashboard with no matching prompts), the resolver falls back to sap_basis.

docs.title: Customizing the Catalog
docs.text: The prompt catalog is data-driven: each prompt is an entry in the App’s intent map (default/data/mcp/logserv_intent_map.json) with a matching saved search in default/savedsearches.conf. The intent map is compiled into the App’s JavaScript bundle at build time, so adding or editing a prompt means changing the App’s source, rebuilding the App and redeploying it; editing the installed copy of logserv_intent_map.json does not change the catalog. On Splunk Cloud Platform, the rebuilt App goes through private-app vetting again. The steps, the full JSON schema, the build-time consistency check and a pre-deploy SPL dry run are in Adding a New Predefined Prompt; the build itself is in Build the LogServ App.

docs.title: The Splunk Risky-Command Safeguard
docs.text:
Splunk Web’s Search app asks for confirmation before it runs a search that arrives in a link (a URL to /app/search/search?q=...) and contains a command Splunk marks as risky, for example map, delete, script, tscollect, outputlookup, outputcsv, sendalert or sendemail. Splunk’s SPL safeguards documentation has the full list for each Splunk version; Splunk risky-command safeguard gives it for 9.4. The saved searches the AI Assistant dispatches through the MCP Server are not affected: the safeguard applies to searches opened in Splunk Web from a link.

The ↗ Run SPL chips and the next-step links of the guidance cards open Splunk Search that way, so they are subject to it. No search in the shipped catalog (the prompts’ searches and their next-step searches) uses a risky command. If you customize the catalog, scan any new SPL for risky commands before shipping; Splunk risky-command safeguard shows the rewrite pattern (map → first-class subsearch).

docs.title: Clear All / Per-Result Clear
docs.text:
The right pane carries a Clear All button in the toolbar above the result list, plus a Clear button on every individual tile (in the actions slot, alongside the drill-down chips). Both prune the conversation:

  • Per-tile Clear removes the tool_call + tool_result + the user message that triggered the dispatch (so a canned-prompt’s chat label disappears alongside its result panel) + the guidance card. Outbound vendor refs for that tile are also stripped from the next-turn vendor-message buffer.
  • Clear All wipes the entire conversation, including all tool_results, all guidance cards, all assistant_text messages, and all user messages. The chat session id is preserved so audit events continue with the same correlation id.

docs.title: Privacy Tiers
docs.text:
Applies once an LLM provider credential is configured

The privacy tier governs what a vendor dispatch may carry, so it has something to govern only where that path is live. The released v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build, but it makes no vendor calls until an admin configures an LLM provider credential, and no vendor dispatch where Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed (Restricting the LLM Path; in Templates-only mode, Model discovery can still make metadata-only model-listing calls). Once a credential exists, the tier selected in Settings → AI Assistant → General governs every vendor dispatch. The Hidden<T> / Visible<T> type-system enforcement is compile-time in every build: a tool result reaches an outbound vendor payload only through the active tier’s summary, so no raw row and no unsummarized result is sent in any tier. What that summary may carry depends on the tier, as described below — in Tier 2 it includes aggregated values taken from the events.

The privacy tier controls what an external LLM vendor sees about your Splunk data. Two tiers work in this release, Tier 1 (the default) and Tier 2; Tier 0 is listed in the Settings page but does not work yet. An admin selects the tier in Settings → AI Assistant → General. The active tier is enforced by the TypeScript type system at build time, not by runtime policy: every outbound vendor payload must pass through a single sanitize chokepoint, and the chokepoint’s summarizer is what the tier setting controls. For the type-system mechanism, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

This page starts with the choice (the tiers, the decision matrix, and how to switch), then describes exactly what each tier sends.

docs.title: The Three Tiers at a Glance
docs.text:
Tier Vendor traffic? What the AI sees about each tool result Use case Tier 0 (not available in this release) Planned: none, a local Ollama server. Today: whatever provider is selected Same as Tier 1 (count + timing only) Do not select it; see Tier 0 and the Ollama Provider Tier 1 (default) Cloud LLM (Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure / Bedrock) Returned N rows in M ms. — two numbers, a count and a timing. Nothing else. Most customers — strongest cloud-LLM privacy posture Tier 2 (admin opt-in) Same cloud LLM The Returned N rows in M ms. line (N is the number of result rows, 0 for an empty result) + per-column cardinality + top-N values + counts (categorical; filtered, 40 characters each; with PII redaction on, sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier, otherwise as <redacted-…> tags) + min/max/avg/sum (numeric) + the time range as UTC timestamps the App formats. A column name is sent only when Splunk generates it, or when every word in it was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name appears as col_N. No raw rows. Customers who want data-grounded narrative replies and have legal authority to expose aggregate metadata to the vendor

The table describes successful calls. In every tier, a failed call reaches the vendor only as its HTTP status and a fixed error class, never as Splunk’s error text. See Failed Tool Calls.

docs.title: Decision Matrix
docs.text: Question Answer Recommended tier “Is the AI vendor a third-party data processor?” Yes; consult your DPA. Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure / Bedrock all publish their own privacy commitments, but they ARE data processors. Tier 1 if the vendor is approved as a processor; if not, configure no provider, or turn on Templates-only mode (Restricting the LLM Path) “Can the customer’s compliance team approve aggregate metadata exposure?” Yes Tier 2 No Tier 1 “Does the customer have outbound internet to the LLM vendor’s API?” Yes Tier 1 or Tier 2 No (air-gapped) No tier: predefined prompts only, with Templates-only mode or a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path); Tier 0 is not available in this release “Does the customer want narrative replies with concrete values, or shape-only?” Concrete Tier 2 (with PII redaction on) Shape-only Tier 1 “Does the customer want zero LLM dispatch (partner test, demo)?” Zero Templates-only mode, or a templates-only build where it must not be reversible (Restricting the LLM Path)

docs.title: Switching Tiers
docs.text:
The tier is the Privacy Tier setting on Settings → AI Assistant → General. Switching tiers takes effect on the next vendor call — in-flight calls complete with the previously active tier. Note the emitted vendor_tier1 event does not carry the active tier: the tier in force at a given time is derivable only from the Settings history (vendor_tier2_elevation events) plus a non-zero tier2RedactionsApplied.

Elevating from Tier 1 → Tier 2:

  1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General.
  2. Under Privacy Tier, select Tier 2.
  3. Click Save Defaults. The save records a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event with the admin’s identity and the time.
  4. Optionally turn Tier 2 PII column redaction off (default: on) or Tier 2 hostname redaction on (default: off, since host names are often not sensitive in SAP environments).

Lowering from Tier 2 → Tier 1:

  1. Same path. A downgrade produces no audit event and no conf-change record — settings persist to the logserv_ai_assistant_settings KV Store collection, so only elevation to Tier 2 is audited (vendor_tier2_elevation).
  2. The next vendor call uses the lower tier.

No tier: to switch the LLM-driven path off entirely (predefined prompts only), turn on Templates-only mode, or install a templates-only build where that must not be reversible (Restricting the LLM Path). The tier setting is then moot, since no question reaches a vendor.

docs.title: Tier 0 and the Ollama Provider: Do Not Select
docs.text:
Tier 0 and the Ollama (Tier 0 — local) provider are listed on the Settings page but are not implemented in this release. Selecting them does not keep data on the search head:

  • Privacy Tier = Tier 0 summarizes exactly like Tier 1 (the Tier 1 primer, count and timing) and sends the call to whatever Active Provider is selected, a cloud vendor included.
  • Active Provider = Ollama runs the Mock provider: a typed question gets a canned reply, and no Ollama server is contacted. The Base URL on the Provider Credentials sub-tab is not used.

The plan for Tier 0 is to route the LLM call to a locally hosted Ollama server instead of a cloud vendor, with the same count-and-timing summary as Tier 1 and an unchanged MCP search path. Until it ships, a deployment that must not send anything to an outside vendor uses Templates-only mode or a templates-only build (Restricting the LLM Path), or configures no provider.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Cloud LLM, Count + Timing Only (default)
docs.text:
What the LLM sees per tool result:

<TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 47 rows in 320ms.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

That’s the entire summary: two numbers. Nothing about the column names, the row contents, the time range, the distinct counts, or the actual values. The <TOOL_RESULT_DATA>...</TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block is wrapped around every tool-result summary so the AI’s primer can teach it that anything inside is data from the customer’s environment, never instructions.

  • The count is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises rows in the MCP reply — the same rows Tier 2 counts, so a search that matched nothing reads Returned 0 rows. With the Splunk MCP Server that is the length of the result list in its reply. Only a reply in which the App finds no rows — plain text, for example — is counted another way: the number of items in its content list, or the total row count a server reports (totalRowCount).
  • The timing is the server’s execution time when the reply carries one, otherwise the time the browser measured for the call.

What the AI does with this: the AI knows that the search ran, how many rows it returned and how long it took, but not what the rows hold. It writes structurally-aware narrative replies — “the failed-auth saved search completed in 320 ms; its results are in the tile on the right” — without making claims about specific users, IPs, or hosts.

Decision rule for picking Tier 1:

  • The customer’s legal/security team is comfortable with the AI vendor seeing the natural-language question + tool definitions + summaries.
  • The customer is not comfortable exposing aggregate column metadata (cardinality, top-N values, min/max) to the vendor.
  • The customer values determinism: a Tier 1 reply mentions zero specific values, so audit reviewers can sanity-check the narrative against the rendered tile without needing to verify what the AI was told.

Limitations: the AI can’t write “the top failing user was xcjadm with 42 attempts” — it doesn’t have that data. The narrative is correspondingly less concrete; the user is expected to read the tile in the right pane for the actual values.

Tier 1 limits how much the vendor can learn; it does not make that zero. For each call the vendor gets two numbers, a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status (see Failed Tool Calls). A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data — the timing, whether a search fails and which class its error gets, and the row count — so a few bits per call can leak: up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count. The session tool-call cap (tool_calls_per_session_cap, default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat (Clear All in the results pane) starts a new session and resets the count, and 0 turns the cap off. No error text is sent in any tier.

docs.title: Failed Tool Calls — Every Tier
docs.text:
When a tool call fails, the AI vendor is told only that it failed, with the HTTP status and a fixed error class. It never gets Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error text. This is the same in Tier 0, 1 and 2:

<TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Tool error (HTTP 400, class=missing_lookup): the query names a lookup that does not exist here. The error text is shown to the user only.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
  • The status is included only when it is a whole number from 100 to 599. Otherwise the line reads Tool error (class=…).
  • The class is one of parse_error, unknown_command, missing_lookup, missing_saved_search, permission, timeout, rate_limited, not_found, server_error or other. The browser picks it with fixed rules over the error message, or from the status when no rule matches. Each class has its own fixed hint, written by the App.
  • The error text itself is shown only in the result panel on the user’s screen. It is not sent to the vendor, and it is not written to the audit index.

The text is withheld because a Splunk error message repeats the search that failed, and a subsearch can put event data into that search. For example, | inputlookup [search … | eval v=substr(_raw,1,80) | return $v] can fail with an error that names the first 80 characters of an event as the missing lookup table.

Refusals the App makes itself are different, because their text is the App’s own. These are calls the App stops before anything is sent: the SPL guard, the saved-search catalog check, the undeclared-tool check and the session tool-call cap. The vendor gets Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>, so the model can rephrase:

  • The reason is written by the App. It may quote the tool name or saved-search name the model itself sent, or the command, lookup or macro name of the model’s query that the SPL guard refused.
  • It is capped at 1,000 characters. Control characters other than tab and line breaks become spaces, and <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> tags are replaced with <filtered>.
  • The App builds this text where it makes the refusal, never from a tool result. A server error that merely looks like a refusal is reduced to a class like any other error.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Cloud LLM + Aggregated Metadata (admin opt-in)
docs.text:
What the LLM sees per tool result:

For a stats count by user, stack result of 47 rows:

<TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 47 rows in 320ms.
Column "user" (distinct=8): <redacted-f86a9fe>=6, <redacted-0e3cb9c>=6, <redacted-e849a33>=6, <redacted-ac446fb>=6 (+4 more).
Column "stack" (distinct=3): Windows=16, HANA=16, SAP=15.
Column "count" (numeric, distinct=47): min=1 max=95 avg=47.11 sum=2,214.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

The user column above shows the shipped default (tier2_pii_redaction = true): a column whose values come from an identifier field arrives as <redacted-…> tags, stable within the chat session. stack keeps its values because the query takes it from the events by its own name; had the query computed it with an eval — as the App’s own cross-stack catalog search does — its values would arrive as tags too (see Which values are sent below). With tier2_pii_redaction = false the same line carries the raw values (xcjadm=6, BKPADMIN=6, …). The column names user and stack are sent because the query that produced the result wrote them (for a saved search, the App’s catalog search does), and count because Splunk generates it. In Tier 2 the Returned N rows line counts the result rows the App finds in the reply; a search that matched nothing reads Returned 0 rows in 210ms (no events matched the query in the selected time range). and sends nothing else. A reply in which the App finds no rows at all — plain text, for example — is sent only as Returned a result that is not in row form, in 210ms.: no count, no column name and no value.

For a timechart span=1h count by host result:

<TOOL_RESULT_DATA>
Returned 3 rows in 210ms.
Time range: 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z → 2026-10-01T02:00:00.000Z (UTC).
Column names withheld: 2. Each such column is shown as col_N, N being its position among the result's columns that do not start with an underscore.
Column col_1 (numeric, distinct=3): min=0 max=2 avg=1 sum=3.
Column col_2 (numeric, distinct=3): min=0 max=4 avg=2 sum=6.
</TOOL_RESULT_DATA>

The column names of a timechart split by host are host names — values from the events that the query did not write — so they are shown as col_N, with PII redaction on or off and whatever the hostname setting. Had the query named the hosts itself (host=sapdb01 OR host=sapapp01 | timechart span=1h count by host), the names would be the model’s own text and would be sent. The same holds when the cells hold text: for timechart latest(action) by user the user names are shown as col_N unless the query wrote them, and while redaction is on every value of a column shown as col_N arrives as a <redacted-…> tag, since nothing tells the AI what the column holds — and the text cells of a split-by column are redacted in any case (see Which values are sent below).

What a Tier 2 summary contains, and what it leaves out:

  • No raw rows. The AI never gets a row: it cannot tell which user had how many failures on which stack, only the per-column distributions.
  • Values. Each categorical column sends its top-N values with their counts (top 10 by default; the AI’s top_n tool argument can ask for up to 50). Each value passes the value filter — a value that starts with a role marker (system:, assistant:, …), contains a known prompt-injection phrase or contains a <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> tag becomes <filtered>, and control characters become spaces — then PII redaction (below), then a 40-character cap, within a 160-character line. Each numeric column sends min / max / avg / sum. Columns whose name starts with _, all-empty columns and single-valued categorical columns are left out.

  • Column names. A name is sent only when one of these holds, and it passes the value filter unchanged:

    • it is a name Splunk itself generates: count, percent, total, Total, NULL, OTHER, column, a bare statistics-function name (sum, avg, mean, min, max, dc, distinct_count, values, earliest, latest, first, last, median, mode, stdev, range, rate), or fieldsummary’s field, is_exact and numeric_count; or
    • every word in it was written by the model or the App. Each run of letters, digits and _ in the name (values(user) is values and user; ip-10-1-2-3 is ip, 10, 1, 2 and 3) must appear as a whole word, in the same letter case, in the call’s author text: the query the model wrote itself for splunk_run_query, or the SPL of the App’s catalog search that produced the result for splunk_run_saved_search. Any word of that text counts, wherever it stands — a field name, an alias, a search term, a compared value, quoted text — because text the model or the App wrote tells the vendor nothing it does not already have. The name must also be at most 40 characters and have the shape of a field name (a letter or _, then letters, digits and _ . : -) or of one function call over one, * or nothing (avg(duration), sum(*)) — or it must be a display alias that the author text writes in quotes right after AS (rename sourcetype AS "Source Type", count AS "Event Count"): it starts with a letter or _ and is made of letters, digits and _ . : -, in words separated by single spaces.

    Any other name is shown as col_N — N is the column’s position among the result’s columns that do not start with _ — and is never sent, in full or in part; the summary says how many names were withheld. The rule is the same with PII redaction on or off. So stats count as failures by host keeps failures and host, table _time host process message keeps host, process and message, and a split-by value the query typed (user=jsmith | timechart count by user) keeps its name. sum(jsmith), from timechart count by user | stats sum(*), is shown as col_N — even when it is the only column — because the query wrote sum but not jsmith; it would be sent only if the query itself contained the word jsmith. A name is not sent because the query contains part of it: username is withheld when the query writes only user. A quoted alias is held to the same 40 characters and to the single-space shape: "Source Type" (two spaces) or "Events (%)" is shown as col_N.

  • Which values are sent — fail closed. With PII redaction on, a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column — when the author text defines it entirely through constructs the App reads in full — to fields that mark no identifier. The App reads each author text as Splunk runs it, command by command, and a column is traced through:

    • the field itself, by its own name: a field of the events or of a lookup, a by or over field, a field of top, rare (with or without a positional limit, top 10 uri), table or fields;
    • a statistics function over one field, nested or not, with or without AS (latest(user) → user, values(src_ip) AS ips → src_ip, latest(values(user)) → user);
    • <field> AS <alias>, a rename without wildcards (rename user AS u, rename sourcetype AS "Source Type"), and lookup … OUTPUT <field> [AS <alias>]. A lookup output that echoes the field the lookup matched on is that event field (lookup t w AS user OUTPUT w is user); any other output also reads the event fields the lookup matched on, so a lookup keyed on an identifier is treated like that identifier (lookup … ip AS src_ip OUTPUT hostname is redacted). The curated metadata of the App’s own threat-intel lookups — their category, source and date added — keeps its own trace; their free-text notes inherit the match like any other output;
    • eval <name>=<field>, when the expression is one bare field name or one field reference in single quotes (eval w=user, eval w='Authentication.user'). A single-quoted token is only ever a field reference: it cannot hold a |, a bracket, a double quote or a line break, so a stray apostrophe can no longer hide the commands after it (and the allow-list refuses such a query outright);
    • a count: count or c, bare or as a call (count(eval(action="failure"))), the count and percent of top and rare, and dc, distinct_count, estdc or estdc_error over one field the App traces (dc(user)). Its values are counts, not identifiers. A distinct count of a field the query computes (eval r=mvrange(0,len(user)) | stats dc(r)) is not a count: it reads what that field reads.

    These steps chain as far as the query takes them, in the order Splunk runs them: eval a=user | eval b=a | rename b AS c leads c back to user.
