Every other construct leaves the column untraced, and with redaction on every value of an untraced text column arrives as a <redacted-…> tag, whatever it holds:

    • any other eval expression — string concatenation with . (eval w=user."@".domain), any function (lower(action), case(…), coalesce(…), substr(_raw,1,200)), even a literal (eval x="a");
    • fieldformat, which only changes how a value is displayed: the column stays untraced and reads both its earlier definition and the format expression;
    • the outputs of rex (named groups written (?<name>…), (?P<name>…) or (?'name'…)), spath, strcat, bin, convert and iplocation, transaction’s duration and the totals of addtotals; and a field makemv cuts into pieces — by a delimiter or a tokenizer pattern, which extracts like rex — reading the field and the words of the delimiter or the pattern;
    • a wildcard rename or AS (rename user* AS w*, stats values(*) AS *_x) and a dynamic eval target (eval {action}=…);
    • the cells of a chart, timechart or xyseries split-by column, and every column of transpose, untable and fieldsummary, which mix the values of many fields;
    • a name defined in two different ways (for example once in the main search and once in a subsearch); a column that an append, appendcols, join, union, multisearch, set or appendpipe subsearch defines — a field it only passes through by its own name stays traced, and a subsearch that only filters (index=x [search … | fields host]) changes nothing; and a column the author text does not output;
    • every column after a command the App does not read in full: lookup without OUTPUT, inputlookup after the first command, a macro used as a command (a macro at the start of the query is read as the search), an eval or rename it cannot split, or — in the App’s own catalog SPL — any command it does not know. The first command inside appendpipe […] is always read as a command, never as a search, so an unknown one there makes the columns untraced too. A free-form query cannot use a command the App does not read: every command on the allow-list (see the Security Architecture) is one the App reads in full.

    The limits on reading fail closed too: a text longer than 20,000 characters, more than 256 commands, subsearches nested more than 8 deep, or more than 12 wildcard definitions (wildcard renames and AS, dynamic eval targets — each one resolves through the ones before it) leave every column untraced. Stacked appendpipe groups are read in time proportional to their number, so they cannot freeze the browser tab either. A column traced to a count that holds text is redacted as well. So stats count by action sends the actions; stats values(target_user) AS new_users and rename user AS u are redacted as user names; and eval stack=case(…), rex "peer=(?<peer>\S+)" and eval w=action."-".status are redacted although they hold no identifier. To keep values readable, aggregate the field by its own name. With PII redaction off, every column’s values are sent, filtered and capped, traced or not.

  • Values of a column shown as col_N. While PII redaction is on, every value of a categorical (text) column whose name is shown as col_N is redacted as an identifier and sent as a <redacted-…> tag, whatever the column holds; the App cannot tell from a placeholder whether its values are user names. A column whose name is sent is redacted unless it is traced to fields that mark no identifier, as above.

  • At most 30 columns are summarized; the rest are reported as R more columns not summarized..
  • Numeric values withheld. With PII redaction on, a numeric column sends values withheld instead of its statistics, at any cardinality, when it is not a count and either its own name or a field its definition may read marks an identifier, or its values mix many fields (transpose, untable, fieldsummary). For a traced column those fields are its source fields; for an untraced one, every field its expression reads (eval n=len(user) | stats avg(n) AS a is withheld) — and after a command the App does not read in full, every word of the author text. A definition that reads more than 64 fields is taken to read every word of the author text, so that limit fails closed as well. The words of a rex pattern, of an spath path and of the quoted strings in an eval count as fields the column reads, so rex "ssn=(?<n>\d{9})" | stats max(n) AS n and spath output=n path=user.id are withheld; and a field set by rex or spath keeps its earlier value on the events where the pattern or the path does not match, so it reads both definitions. Every other numeric column keeps its statistics, untraced ones included (rex "took (?<ms>\d+)" | stats avg(ms) AS a), and so does a count (dc(user) AS users). A field marks an identifier when it matches a PII redaction pattern (below) or names an id: id, uid, gid, guid, uuid, pid, ssn, iban, phone, msisdn, imsi, imei, acct and account / card / employee / personnel numbers — as the whole name or its last part after _, ., : or - (user_id, card_no) — and camelCase names ending in Id, ID, Sid, SID, Guid or GUID (Windows TargetUserSid, LogonGuid). A column with a single distinct value also sends values withheld, whatever the redaction setting, when its name is withheld, or when it is not a count and marks an identifier or mixes many fields. A named single-value column such as total_events — usually the KPI the query asked for — still sends its value.
  • The time range. The Time range: line is sent only when every _time value is a timestamp: an epoch in seconds (a number or a string of digits, from 1970 up to 2100-01-01) or a strict ISO-8601 timestamp with a zone (Z, +hh:mm or +hhmm) on a real calendar date. The App then writes both ends itself, as ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, and the line says so: Time range: 2026-10-01T00:00:00.000Z → 2026-10-01T02:00:00.000Z (UTC). No time zone from the data is sent. If any value is not a timestamp, the line reads Time range: not shown (the _time values are not all timestamps). and no _time text is sent. The range is also sent only when the author text traces _time — every definition of it — to a time source field: _time itself, or the epochs bucket_ts and day_ts of the App’s rollups (timechart, bin _time, tstats … by _time, stats latest(_time) AS _time, eval _time=bucket_ts, rename bucket_ts AS _time, bin bucket_ts span=1d AS _time). A _time the query computes from other fields (eval _time=len(src_ip)*100000000, eval _time=strptime(…), or a bin / bucket of another field into _time: bin n span=1 AS _time) reads Time range: not shown (the query computes _time from other fields). A result without a _time column, such as a stats by … aggregate, has no time-range line.
  • What the AI is told about these shapes. The Tier 2 primer explains col_N and the withheld-names line, <redacted-…> tags, values withheld, Returned a result that is not in row form and Time range: not shown. It says that a tag is stable within the chat session only, and tells the model never to guess, recover or attribute what a placeholder or a tag stands for, to name a user, host, IP address or account only when that exact value appears in clear, and how to get readable values: re-query with stats … by <field>, aggregate a field by its own name rather than computing a new one, or write the values into its own query.

What the naming rule withholds: any name that neither Splunk, the model’s query nor the App’s catalog search wrote, and any name that does not have the shape — a name with spaces that the query does not quote right after AS (eval "Source Type"=…), an unaliased count(eval(…)), a nested call such as upper95(prediction(count)), a name over 40 characters. Besides split-by values, that includes fields a search returns without its text naming them — fields of raw events (host, sourcetype and the like, when the query does not write them), automatically extracted or spath fields, and the columns of an inputlookup that the search does not list. The AI can relate a placeholder to its own query’s columns by position, but the primer tells it never to guess which value — which host, user or series — a col_N column stands for. A catalog trend split by a value is named only where its catalog search writes the value itself: the stacks of the cross-stack authentication-failure trend (HANA, Windows) are named, the host names of the noisy-hosts trend are not. The tiles in the results pane are not affected.

What Tier 2 still sends from the events. Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design: the top-N values of every text column (with redaction on, of every traced column whose name is sent and whose fields mark no identifier), and the statistics of every numeric column that is not withheld — a column shown as col_N or untraced included. Redaction is decided by field names, so a value is sent as it is when its column is traced to a field named nothing like an identifier: an event field such as message, a lookup column that is not keyed on an identifier — or _raw itself, so a model can write eval m=_raw and receive up to 40 characters of an event. A number computed from event text is sent unless a field it reads marks an identifier. A name made only of words the model wrote is sent even if the model copied into its query a value it had seen; that text is the model’s own. PII redaction is name-based hygiene for ordinary queries, not a content filter; where no event value may be sent, use Tier 1.

PII redaction (Tier 2 only, on by default): a field name marks an identifier in two ways.

  • The App’s own fields, one by one. Every field name the App defines — its extractions, aliases and calculated fields, its rollup columns and the columns of its lookups, about 440 names — has a class in a table the build checks: an identifier (user names, statements that name users such as sql_statement and command, the HANA audit target object, identity, info_sid, supplied_by, fetched_by, the topology canonical_value and label, the compliance rollup’s operator and the topology rollup’s error_detail), an address (src, dest, local_ip, peer_ip, icm_peer_ip, ssl_peer_ip, remote_address, the lastlog FROM, fw_dst, the topology rollups’ scope and spl_filter_clauses, the HANA audit client host src_host and its extraction audit_hostname, the SAP Router target saprouter_target_ip, the gateway’s gw_remgw_target and gw_client_ip, the RFC client’s gw_client_hostname, …), a host name (host, Computer, db_hostname, hana_host, … — redacted only with the hostname opt-in), free text, or safe. The client host names audit_hostname and gw_client_hostname are classed as addresses, because a workstation’s name can identify the person who uses it, so they are redacted by default, while a server’s host name such as db_hostname is redacted only with the hostname opt-in. The hostnames column of the topology IP-enrichment lookup, which also holds client workstation names, stays a host name (see Known Limits of Tier 2 below). The build fails if a new App field has no class, so no extraction ships unclassified, and it fails if a rollup column that a free-form query can read with inputlookup is classified weaker than the fields its rollup search writes into it directly; the check looks one step back, so a column filled through an intermediate field, such as hostnames, is not covered. The fields Splunk’s automatic key-value extraction finds in the LogServ Linux events are classified too: pam’s rhost (an address), ruser, logname and euid, and sudo’s PWD and COMMAND.
  • Name patterns, for every name (the App’s and any other) — ignoring letter case, as the whole name or after _, ., :, - or a space: email or emails; user, username, user_name, users or usernames (and "User Name"); src, source, client, remote, dest, destination or dvc followed by ip or addr, with or without _, singular or plural (src_ip, client_ips, remote_addr, dvc_ip); any ip, addr or address — a bare ip and every *_ip, *_addr and *_address (peer_ip, local_ip, "Client IP"); the CIM src, dest, dst and dvc themselves, singular or plural, alone or followed by _host (src, dests, src_host, fw_src, fw_dst) — the App’s own field aliases put client IP addresses and host names into src and dest; peer or peers; mac or mac_addr; account, account_name or "Account Name"; and, with the hostname opt-in, host, hostname, host_name, "Host Name", hosts or hostnames. So src_user, new_users and the dotted data-model and JSON names Authentication.user, All_Traffic.src_ip, All_Traffic.dest and event.user all match. A camelCase name ending in User, UserName or Email, optionally plural, matches too (Windows TargetUserName, SubjectUserName; letter case counts here), and so does one ending in Address, IpAddress, IPAddress or MacAddress (Windows IpAddress) and — with the hostname opt-in — in WorkstationName, HostName, ComputerName or MachineName. The table only ever adds to the patterns.

A text column with such a field — or with an id-named one (above) — sends every value as a <redacted-XXXXXXX> tag, and a numeric one sends values withheld. These are not matched: source, destination, src_port, dest_port, src_category, dvc_type, user_agent and sap_sid; admins with strict postures should verify their own field names against the pattern list. The tag is the first 7 hex digits of a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256) of the value, under a random key the browser makes for each chat session and keeps in memory only; clearing the chat starts a new session with a new key, while closing and reopening the chat panel keeps the session and its key. So the same value gets the same tag within a chat session — the AI can still reason about cardinality and frequency — while tags of different sessions cannot be linked, and nobody without the key can recover a value by hashing candidates (every IPv4 address, short user names, SAP’s standard users). Within a session the model can still compare tags, including tags of values it writes into its own query (see Known Limits of Tier 2 below). While redaction is on it also redacts every value of a text column that is shown as col_N or is not traced to fields that mark no identifier (above). See OWASP LLM Top 10 — LLM02.

What the AI does with this: the AI can write data-grounded narrative replies — “8 distinct users across 3 stacks, with up to 95 failures for one user on one stack and 2,214 in total; the user/stack pairs split 16 Windows, 16 HANA, 15 SAP, so no single stack dominates”. The AI grounds its severity assessments in actual numbers instead of inferring from the shape of the result alone.

Decision rule for picking Tier 2:

  • The customer’s legal/security team has reviewed and approved exposing aggregate metadata (column cardinalities, top-N value distributions) to the AI vendor.
  • The customer wants narrative replies with concrete values, not just shape descriptions.
  • PII concerns are mitigated by the fail-closed, field-name-based redaction (or the customer is comfortable with the redaction’s coverage).

Audit trail: every free-form prompt that completes — whichever tier is active — records one vendor_tier1 audit event (the vendor_tier2 category is declared but never emitted) including: - Token counts (input + output) - USD cost estimate - Number of PII redactions applied (tier2RedactionsApplied): each redacted value (the values of a text column shown as col_N or untraced included) and each numeric column whose values are withheld under redaction — because a field it reads marks an identifier, or because it mixes many fields. A withheld column name is not counted. It is 0 in Tier 1, with redaction off, and in a Tier 2 prompt where nothing needed redacting - The user identity that triggered the call

When elevating to Tier 2 in Settings (from Tier 0 or Tier 1), a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event captures the admin’s identity and timestamp. See Audit Log.

docs.title: Known Limits of Tier 2
docs.text:
Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design, and the App’s reading of a query is name-based hygiene, not a content filter. With PII redaction on, these cases can still carry an identifier or event text to the vendor; where any of them matters, use Tier 1. (The cases earlier builds listed as open are closed; the release notes record each change.)

  • Manufactured counts. A count still carries a few bits that a query computes: stats count by <a multivalue field computed from an identifier> followed by stats count, or the count of rows a filter on an identifier keeps. Counts are not traced to the fields that shaped them. This is documented rather than closed; where it matters, use Tier 1.
  • Fields named nothing like an identifier. A value is sent in clear when its column is traced to a field that neither the App’s table nor the patterns mark — an event field such as message, a field another app extracts, a field Splunk’s automatic key-value extraction finds under a name the App does not know, or _raw (up to 40 characters).
  • Workstation names in the topology IP enrichment. The hostnames column of logserv_topology_ip_enrichment, which a free-form query can read with inputlookup, holds the host names of client workstations (HANA clients and Windows WorkstationName). It is classed as a host name, so Tier 2 redacts it only with the hostname opt-in. Turn the opt-in on, or use Tier 1, where those names must not reach the vendor.
  • Text the model wrote. A column name or a value made only of words the model wrote in its query is sent, even if the model copied a value it had seen into the query.
  • Confirming a guess within a chat session. The model can test identifiers it guesses. A name made of its own words is sent, so a query that filters on guessed user names and splits by user (user="alice" OR user="bob" … | timechart count by user) returns, as column names, exactly the guesses that exist in the data. And a tag is the same for the same value within a chat session, so a column of values the model writes into its own query (eval guess="jsmith") carries the same tags as the real values. The keyed tag stops anyone without the key from reversing tags offline; it does not stop the model from comparing tags online within the session. Where that matters, use Tier 1.

docs.title: How the Privacy Invariant Is Enforced
docs.text:
The privacy invariant — no raw event and no unsummarized tool result leaves the customer’s environment for the AI vendor — is enforced mechanically at build time via TypeScript brand types. Tool-result values from the MCP server carry one type; outbound vendor messages carry a different type; the compiler refuses to assign one to the other. The only conversion path is the active tier’s summarizer: in Tier 1 it produces two numbers, in Tier 2 the aggregated metadata described above, which includes values from the events. The type system guarantees that every result goes through a summarizer; the rules above decide what each summarizer may say. A type cannot tell an error message from data, so the summarizers do not pass error text on at all: a failed call’s summary is one of a fixed set of App-written strings, chosen by its HTTP status and error class (see Failed Tool Calls).

This is the primary defense against LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure. For the brand-type mechanism, summarizer call sites, and the <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel pattern, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Security Architecture — SAIF Alignment
docs.text:
This page is for customer security teams evaluating the LogServ App’s AI Assistant feature against Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF). It complements the OWASP LLM Top 10 Compliance page — same set of controls, organized along SAIF’s four-pillar structure and mapped to SAIF’s 15 Key Risks catalog.

The AI-specific risk surface appears once an LLM provider credential is configured

The published v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build variant, so the architecture described below is the one that governs it — but the vendor-dispatch path that architecture protects is inert until an admin configures an LLM provider credential. Until then, and wherever Templates-only mode is on or a compile-time templates-only build is installed, there is no vendor dispatch and the AI-specific surface does not exist. The audit trail and the type-system data boundary are live in every build.

docs.title: The Privacy Boundary
docs.text:
The LogServ AI Assistant is designed around one flagship security property: no raw event and no unsummarized search result from your Splunk indexes is ever transmitted to any AI vendor; the vendor gets only the summary the active privacy tier allows. This isn’t a policy commitment — it’s enforced by the TypeScript type system at compile time.

  • Tool results returned from Splunk via MCP are typed as Hidden<T>.
  • The compiler refuses to put a Hidden<T> value into an outbound LLM payload.
  • The only conversion path is sanitize(hidden, summarizer) — which forces the caller to supply a summary string; the active tier picks the summarizer.
  • There is no runtime flag, no policy toggle, no override.

What the AI sees:

Privacy Tier What’s sent to the vendor LLM Tier 0 (Ollama, not available in this release) Planned: nothing, fully on-host. Today Tier 0 summarizes like Tier 1 and sends to the selected provider; do not select it (Privacy Tiers) Tier 1 (default) Two numbers per call: a count and a timing. No values. Tier 2 (admin opt-in) Tool result aggregated metadata: cardinality, top-N values + counts (field values from the events — filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only when the App can trace the column to a field that marks no identifier), numeric stats, and the time range as UTC timestamps the App formats. A column name only when Splunk generates it or every word in it was written by the model in its own query or by the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name appears as col_N. No raw rows.

In every tier, a tool call that fails reaches the vendor only as its HTTP status and one of ten fixed error classes, with a hint the App writes (Tool error (HTTP 400, class=missing_lookup): …). Splunk’s or the MCP server’s error text is never sent: a Splunk error repeats the search that failed, and a subsearch can put event data into that search. The full error stays in the result panel on the user’s screen. A call the App refuses itself, before anything is sent, reaches the vendor as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason>, with the App’s own reason.

Detail: Privacy Tiers.

docs.title: SAIF Four-Pillar Mapping
docs.text: Google’s SAIF organizes AI security controls into four pillars. Here’s how the LogServ AI Assistant maps to each.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
SAIF’s Data pillar covers how AI systems handle training data, user data, and the data flowing between system boundaries.

Training data — N/A. The LogServ AI Assistant does not train, fine-tune, or update any model. It uses third-party LLMs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock) through their public APIs. The data-poisoning, unauthorized-training-data, and training-data-sanitization controls in SAIF apply to those vendors, not to LogServ.

User Data Management — fully enforced. The Privacy Boundary (above) is the core control:

  • Hidden<T> type system blocks raw event and unsummarized result egress at compile time.
  • Tier 1 (default) sends only count + timing.
  • Tier 2 sends aggregates only. A column name is sent only when Splunk generates it (count, percent, NULL, OTHER, …) or every word in it appears in the text the model or the App wrote for the call — the model’s own query, or the SPL of the App’s catalog search that ran; any other name, such as a split-by value (timechart … by user) or sum(jsmith) that the query did not type, is replaced with a col_N placeholder, with PII redaction on or off. With redaction on, the values of a text column shown as col_N are all redacted. A result the App finds no rows in is reported only as Returned a result that is not in row form. The _time range is sent only as UTC timestamps the App formats (see Privacy Tiers).
  • A failed tool call, in every tier, sends only its HTTP status and a fixed error class, never the error text (see Failed Tool Calls).
  • Tier 2 PII redaction replaces the values of identifier columns with a per-value pseudonym tag (<redacted-XXXXXXX>: 7 hex digits of an HMAC-SHA-256 under a random key made per chat session and kept in the browser’s memory only). The tag is stable within the chat session, so the LLM can still reason about cardinality, and it cannot be linked across sessions or reversed by hashing candidate values. Every field the App defines is classified one by one (identifier, address, host, free text, safe), checked by the build, and name patterns cover every other field. It fails closed: a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column, through constructs it reads in full, to fields that mark no identifier; any other column is redacted. Hostname redaction is opt-in via Settings. The exact patterns and tracing rules are in Privacy Tiers → Tier 2.
  • Every elevation from Tier 0/1 → Tier 2 is recorded in the audit log with the admin’s user identity, timestamp, and previous tier.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
SAIF’s Model pillar covers model integrity, exfiltration risk, and supply chain.

Model Source Tampering — partial coverage:

  • Our supply chain: a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM.json, CycloneDX 1.4) ships in every release with per-dependency purl + sha-512 hashes; it enumerates every bundled dependency. A dependency-audit script (yarn audit:ci, high and critical advisories) exists, but the build that produces the release package does not run it.
  • Distribution integrity: each release package passes Splunk AppInspect in Splunk Cloud precert mode (--mode precert --included-tags cloud) with 0 errors and 0 failures before it is published; the results are published beside the packages. The packages are not published on Splunkbase. The Splunk Deployment Server delivers the Data TA to heavy forwarders over Splunk’s management port, encrypted with TLS; whether each side also verifies the other’s certificate depends on your Splunk TLS settings.
  • Vendor model weight integrity is the LLM vendor’s responsibility. The customer’s DPA review should confirm vendor-side controls.

Model Exfiltration — N/A. The LogServ App does not host model weights. Cloud LLM models live in vendor infrastructure (Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock). Tier 0 Ollama (not available in this release) would run on the customer’s own host, with model weights under the customer’s existing storage controls.

Model Reverse Engineering — N/A. The LogServ App exposes a known vendor LLM behind a thin wrapper. The system primer is publishable (see the free-form prompts documentation) — there’s no proprietary prompt engineering to reverse-engineer.

docs.title: Application
docs.text:
SAIF’s Application pillar covers input validation, access management, and output handling for the AI-using application.

Input Validation — multi-layered:

  • User-prompt anomaly detection. Five pattern groups (role redefinition, persona shift, system-prompt leak, control tokens, long base64 blobs) run on every user prompt before dispatch; prompt length and a character-class fingerprint are captured as recorded signals alongside the matched groups. Flag-and-proceed semantics: matches fire a user_prompt_jailbreak_flag audit event for SOC review but do not block the prompt — regex-based detection has false positives, and blocking would cripple legitimate investigative queries.
  • SPL static analysis on AI-authored queries. Every splunk_run_query call from the AI runs through two fences and a cross-check before it is sent. The first fence is a denylist of commands that write, delete, alert, email, run scripts, read REST endpoints, send data out or run other searches, plus the quoting tricks, inline comments and foreign macros that could hide one. The second fence is an allow-list read by a strict lexer: only the App’s read-only analytic commands, only the LogServ index, only the App’s own lookups, and subsearches only where they cannot widen the search, so other apps’ custom commands and external lookups are refused even when the denylist does not name them. Then Splunk’s own search parser reads the query (search/parser, parse only), and the App refuses it when the two readings differ or when the parser cannot be asked (fail closed). The AI can rephrase a refused query. Blocked queries surface as a security_blocked_spl audit event with the operator and the command. The full lists and rules: Free-form Prompts → The SPL Guard; the audit fields: Audit Log.
  • Saved-search allow-list. splunk_run_saved_search accepts only the names in the App’s own prompt catalog; any other name is refused before it reaches the MCP Server and recorded as a security_blocked_spl audit event. The list is a copy of the catalog’s names taken when the App loads, and it cannot be changed while the App runs.
  • Tool-result sanitization. AI-authored tool arguments are schema-validated. Tier 2 categorical aggregates pass through a per-value sanitizer that replaces strings matching known jailbreak idioms with <filtered>.
  • <TOOL_RESULT_DATA> sentinel block wraps every tool-result summary the AI sees. The system primer instructs the AI to treat anything inside the sentinel as data from the customer’s environment, never as instructions.

Application Access Management:

  • Per-user prompt rate limit (configurable; default tunable in Settings) bounds free-form prompt volume per hour.
  • Per-user daily spend cap (default 50.00 USD; set to 0 to disable) bounds vendor cost per day. Tally resets at local midnight. Predefined-prompt executions don’t accumulate against the cap.
  • Per-chat-session MCP tool-dispatch cap is defense-in-depth above the per-message limit of at most 8 tool turns. Prevents runaway tool-loops in adversarial automation.
  • Feature toggle. The master enabled switch in Settings gates the entire feature; transitions from OFF to ON require admin acceptance of a liability acknowledgement modal (recorded with the admin’s user identity, timestamp, disclaimer hash, and version per Splunk’s standard opt-in pattern).

Output Validation:

  • The LLM’s output is never executed. Tool calls are schema-validated against a closed catalog of MCP tools; a tool name outside it is refused, and a saved-search name outside the App’s prompt catalog is refused. There is no eval-style path from LLM output to system action.
  • React rendering uses JSX text nodes, not dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Strings are escaped by default. Citation markers, severity badges, and bold markdown are parsed via a controlled set of recognized patterns; no general-purpose HTML rendering.
  • Drill-down URLs are built via a centralized buildSplunkSearchUrl() helper that uses encodeURIComponent() and applies target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" flags to break reverse-tabnabbing attacks.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
SAIF’s Agent pillar — newer in SAIF 2.0 — covers autonomous agent behavior, permissions, user control, and observability.

Agent Permissions — a closed catalog. The AI is offered two MCP tools, and the App refuses any other tool name it emits:

  • splunk_run_query — dispatches an ad-hoc SPL query against the customer’s data, subject to the static-analysis guard (see Input Validation above).
  • splunk_run_saved_search — dispatches a saved search from the App’s own catalog only: the prompt library built from the App’s intent map. The check runs where every saved-search call is sent to the MCP Server, so a name outside the catalog is refused — never a rollup aggregation, retention, backfill or Enterprise Security feed — and recorded as a security_blocked_spl audit event. The App builds the MCP arguments itself (the vetted name, the App — app = splunk_app_sap_logserv — and the time range); other keys the model supplies are not forwarded.

Free-form queries refuse the commands the guard knows to write, delete, alert, run scripts, read REST endpoints, send data out or run other searches — collect, outputlookup, outputcsv, delete, rest, curl, savedsearch, map, mcollect, meventcollect, runshellscript, dump and the rest of the guard’s list (see Input Validation above). Beyond Splunk searches, the AI has no config writes, no user creation, no permission changes, and no outbound network actions of any kind beyond the LLM API call. Within a search, the guard refuses the outbound commands and lookups it names (outputtelemetry, curl, wget, sendresults, dnslookup), and the allow-list refuses every command and lookup that is not on its list, including any another installed app adds.

These controls protect this App’s AI Assistant. Another MCP client holding a Splunk MCP Server token is governed by the Splunk MCP Server’s own controls and by Splunk permissions, not by this App. Running MCP tools needs the MCP Server’s mcp_tool_execute capability, which it grants by default only to admin and sc_admin; every AI Assistant user needs it too (Splunk MCP Setup → Roles and Capabilities).

Agent User Control:

  • Tier selection by an admin in Settings, at any time — Tier 1 (default) or Tier 2; Tier 0 is not available in this release.
  • Master enable toggle — admin-controlled, default OFF.
  • Per-prompt opt-in — every free-form prompt is user-initiated. There is no autonomous loop, no scheduled prompt execution, no background activity.
  • Power Mode is a per-browser-tab toggle, shown only to the roles an admin names. While it is on, the primer asks the model to run a saved search before answering; each prompt’s audit event records whether it was on.
  • Acknowledgement modals at Settings save time — an admin must answer a liability acknowledgement to (a) turn the feature on and (b) save with the audit forwarder off. A tier elevation needs no acknowledgement; it records a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event.

Agent Observability:

  • Sequenced audit log. Every meaningful AI Assistant event (canned prompt execution, free-form vendor call, blocked SPL, rate-limit hit, spend-cap hit, prompt anomaly, tier elevation, legal acknowledgement, model discovery) lands in the logserv_ai_assistant_audit index with a stable per-tab session ID + monotonic per-session sequence number, so gaps and reordering are detectable. The browser writes the events as the signed-in user, which needs Splunk’s edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event capability (by default admin holds both, power holds edit_log_alert_event and user neither); a user without either is not audited, and the chat panel says so (Who can write audit events); tamper-evidence comes from the optional HEC forwarder to a separately-administered destination. The chat panel surfaces “AI is generating response” status; the Audit Log viewer in Settings lets reviewers filter by category, user, and time range.
  • Who can read the audit index follows each role’s allowed indexes; Splunk’s default user role allows every non-internal index, so narrow it (Restricting who can read the audit index).
  • HEC audit forwarder. Admin can configure a Splunk HEC destination (e.g., a separate indexer, a SIEM, S3-with-Object-Lock owned by a different admin team) for tamper-evident off-host audit copies. Forwarder failures themselves are recorded locally so an off-host divergence is detectable.
  • Vendor token-usage audit events capture provider, model, input/output tokens, USD cost estimate (computed locally from list pricing), and turn count — letting SOC teams pivot on cost-anomaly indicators.

docs.title: SAIF 15 Key Risks — Coverage Matrix
docs.text:
The table below maps each SAIF Key Risk to LogServ’s posture. Strong = flagship property of the architecture; Partial = mitigation in place with documented residual surface; N/A = out of scope because LogServ does not train or host models.

# SAIF Risk LogServ Posture Key Controls 1 Data Poisoning (DP) N/A LogServ does not train models. 2 Unauthorized Training Data (UTD) N/A LogServ does not train models. No raw event or unsummarized result leaves the privacy boundary. 3 Model Source Tampering (MST) Partial SBOM in every release; a dependency-audit script the release build does not run. AppInspect (Splunk Cloud precert mode) on every release package. Model weight integrity is vendor responsibility. 4 Excessive Data Handling (EDH) Strong Hidden<T> privacy boundary, Tier 1 default, Tier 2 PII redaction. 5 Model Exfiltration (MXF) N/A LogServ does not host models. 6 Model Deployment Tampering (MDT) Partial AppInspect before release + DS-channel distribution. Tarball GPG signing is a known gap. 7 Denial of ML Service (DMS) Partial Per-user prompt rate limit + per-user daily spend cap + per-session tool dispatch cap (browser-side enforcement — see Known Residual Gaps). 8 Model Reverse Engineering (MRE) N/A Publishable system primer, no proprietary prompt engineering. 9 Insecure Integrated Component (IIC) Strong Closed tool catalog, saved-search allow-list, schema-validated tool calls, SPL static-analysis guard. 10 Prompt Injection (PIJ) Partial Tool-result vector physically blocked by Hidden<T> + sentinel + per-value sanitizer; a failed call’s error text is not sent at all (fixed error classes only). User-prompt vector flagged (five pattern groups), not blocked. 11 Model Evasion (MEV) N/A LogServ has no classifiers to evade; ML-evasion is vendor-side. 12 Sensitive Data Disclosure (SDD) Strong Same controls as EDH (privacy boundary + redaction). 13 Inferred Sensitive Data (ISD) Partial Strong by construction (Tier 1 = no values; Tier 2 = redacted aggregates). Hostname redaction is opt-in — small inference surface for environment topology when off. 14 Insecure Model Output (IMO) Strong LLM output never executed; no dangerouslySetInnerHTML; drill-down URLs encoded + tab-nabbing flags. 15 Rogue Actions (RA) Strong Catalog-only saved searches + write-command guard on free-form SPL, no autonomous loop, sequenced audit log + off-host HEC forwarder.

Summary: 5 Strong, 5 Partial, 5 N/A. Zero “Not covered” — every SAIF risk in scope for LogServ’s architecture has at least partial mitigation.

docs.title: Cross-Reference: SAIF ↔ OWASP LLM Top 10
docs.text:
The OWASP LLM Top 10 Compliance page covers the same controls organized by attack pattern instead of structural pillar. Most LogServ controls map to both frameworks:

SAIF Risk OWASP LLM Item EDH / SDD / ISD LLM02 — Sensitive Information Disclosure MST LLM03 — Supply Chain DP / UTD (N/A here) LLM04 — Data and Model Poisoning IMO LLM05 — Improper Output Handling IIC / RA LLM06 — Excessive Agency PIJ LLM01 — Prompt Injection MRE (N/A here) LLM07 — System Prompt Leakage (related) DMS LLM10 — Unbounded Consumption

docs.title: What’s Out of Scope
docs.text:
Items in SAIF that don’t apply to LogServ’s architecture:

  • Model training, fine-tuning, RAG with embedded sensitive data — the AI Assistant does not train, fine-tune, embed, or persist any customer data into any model.
  • Vendor model integrity and vendor data handling — these are the LLM vendor’s responsibility. Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and AWS Bedrock each publish their own data-usage commitments and security posture; the customer’s DPA review should confirm processor obligations.
  • Customer Splunk infrastructure security — Splunk’s own access controls, role-based ACLs, and indexer encryption apply normally. The AI Assistant inherits the security posture the customer has configured for Splunk Web access.

docs.title: Known Residual Gaps
docs.text:
Honesty matters in a security architecture page. The following gaps are documented:

  1. User-prompt jailbreak detection is flag-and-proceed, not block. Regex pattern matching has false positives. Pattern coverage will grow as new attack patterns surface in the wild. The flag-and-proceed posture lets SOC teams review while preserving legitimate investigative use.
  2. Hostname redaction at Tier 2 is opt-in (default off). Hostname patterns can leak environment topology. Admins can flip the default in Settings if their threat model requires it. (Host names that become column names, as in timechart count by host, are shown as col_N whatever this setting, unless the query itself wrote them.)
  3. Tarball GPG signing is not yet implemented. AppInspect checks before release + DS-channel distribution cover most of the threat model, but a signed tarball would provide an additional integrity proof point. Tracked as a follow-up item.
  4. The rate limit and daily spend cap are enforced browser-side (localStorage keyed by Splunk username). They bound good-faith use; a user with a second browser or cleared storage can exceed them. Every block still writes an audit event, so attempts remain visible. Server-side enforcement is a tracked follow-up.
  5. The saved-search allow-list and the SPL guard protect this App’s assistant only. Other MCP clients holding a Splunk MCP Server token, and users of Splunk’s own search bar, can still run any saved search their Splunk permissions allow, the App’s rollup and retention searches included; Splunk roles and the Splunk MCP Server’s own settings govern them. The SPL guard matches command names in the query text, accepts only the App’s own macros and refuses inline comments; Splunk’s search parser, which expands the macros, cross-checks every free-form query (see gap 8).
  6. The saved-search allow-list matches names, not search text. A build gate proves that the shipped (default/) definitions of the catalog searches are read-only. A local/ edit of a catalog search, or a private saved search of the same name in this App, runs under its allowed name. Keeping such overrides read-only is the Splunk admin’s responsibility; to see which definition is in effect, run splunk btool savedsearches list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --debug.
  7. The SPL guard’s command list is the App’s. Free-form queries may use only the commands and lookups on the App’s allow-list, and Splunk’s search parser cross-checks every query. What remains is what the allowed commands themselves do: they read the LogServ index and the App’s lookups, and a query can still be expensive (a wide transaction, a large join); the rate limit, the session tool-call cap and Splunk’s own search quotas bound that. Splunk role permissions remain the authoritative gate.
  8. Macro definitions are checked through Splunk’s own parser. Splunk expands whichever definition of a macro is in effect for the dispatching user and app: a local/macros.conf override in this App, the user’s own private macro of the same name, or another app’s globally exported macro of the same name can take precedence over the definition the App ships. The App has Splunk’s search parser expand every free-form query in the user’s context and refuses it when the parser finds a command not on the list, a different command list, a query starting with a data macro that does not expand to the App’s definition, an index other than the LogServ index, or a lookup outside a subsearch that is not one of the App’s. What remains: the definition is compared only where the query starts with the macro — where the macro stands after WHERE in tstats or starts a subsearch, a shadowing macro is caught only when its expansion names another index (Splunk’s parser reports a subsearch as text inside the command that holds it, so a command or lookup such a macro brings into a subsearch is not caught); the check relies on the parser being reachable (when it is not, every free-form query is refused, parser_unavailable), and catalog searches are not checked this way — keeping the three macros (sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro) unshadowed stays the Splunk admin’s responsibility. Catalog searches run in the LogServ App’s context; to see the definition a search there gets for a given user, run splunk btool macros list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --user=<user> --debug (without --app and --user, btool shows the global merge, which is not what those searches use), or list every copy with | rest /servicesNS/-/-/configs/conf-macros splunk_server=local | search title=<name> | table eai:acl.app eai:acl.owner eai:acl.sharing definition. Both the LogServ App and the Data TA ship sap_logserv_idx_macro; where both are on the search head, keep the two copies the same (Renaming an index).
  9. Tier 1 limits what the vendor can learn; it does not make it zero. The vendor gets two numbers for each call, a count and a timing, and for a failed call a fixed error class and the HTTP status. A model that writes its own queries can make these depend on event data — the timing, whether a search fails and which class its error gets, and the count, which is the number of result rows whenever the App recognises them — so a few bits per call can leak, up to about log2 of the largest row count the server returns through the count. The session tool-call cap (default 100) limits the calls per chat session; clearing the chat resets it, and 0 turns it off. Error text, which could carry far more, is not sent in any tier (see Failed Tool Calls).
  10. Tier 2 sends aggregated event values by design. Its top-N values are field values from the events (filtered, 40 characters each, and with PII redaction on sent in clear only for columns the App traces to fields that mark no identifier), and a column shown as col_N keeps its numeric statistics. Redaction fails closed for anything the App cannot trace, but it is decided by field names: a value held by a field named nothing like an identifier (an event field such as message, a field another app extracts) is sent as it is, and so is _raw under a plain alias — eval m=_raw sends up to 40 characters of an event. A number computed from event text is sent unless a field it reads marks an identifier. A column name made only of words the model wrote in its own query is its own text and is sent even if it copies a value it has seen, and a count can still carry a few bits a query manufactures (stats count by <a multivalue field computed from an identifier> then stats count). Where no event value may be sent, use Tier 1, which sends no values (subject to gap 9).
  11. Tier 2’s reading of the query. The value rules of gap 10 depend on the App reading the model’s query. The cases earlier builds listed as read wrongly or not at all — a _time the query sets, a stray apostrophe, rex groups written (?'name'…), fieldformat, a lookup that echoes or maps the field it matches on, an unknown first command inside appendpipe, the App’s own identifier fields the patterns missed, rex patterns and spath paths in the numeric rule, and a redaction tag that could be reversed offline — are closed, and free-form queries are limited to commands the App reads in full. What remains is listed in Privacy Tiers — Known Limits of Tier 2: manufactured counts (documented, not traced), fields named nothing like an identifier, and text the model wrote itself.

docs.title: What Customers Can Do
docs.text:
Concrete actions a customer’s security team can take to validate or strengthen the posture:

  • Review the audit log regularly. Open Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log. Filter by category to investigate anomalies. Categories worth scheduled review: user_prompt_jailbreak_flag, security_blocked_spl, rate_limited_prompt, daily_spend_cap_hit, vendor_tier2_elevation.
  • Check what the AI’s searches can reach. Free-form queries read only the LogServ index and the App’s own lookups, with the commands of the App’s allow-list, and Splunk’s search parser cross-checks each one in the user’s context. Review which roles may use the AI Assistant and run searches, and confirm that the App’s three macros are not shadowed for the catalog searches: splunk btool macros list <name> --app=splunk_app_sap_logserv --user=<user> --debug (the user who runs them) for each of sap_logserv_idx_macro, sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro. A steady stream of parser_unavailable refusals in the audit log means the App cannot reach the search parser.
  • Configure the HEC audit forwarder to a separate destination — a different Splunk indexer, a SIEM, an S3 bucket with Object Lock, or any HEC-compatible sink. The acceptance modal recorded when the forwarder is left disabled is a useful compliance artifact.
  • Pick the tier that matches your risk appetite. Tier 1 is the safest default (count + timing only). Tier 2 is more powerful but ships aggregated metadata to the vendor. Tier 0 (Ollama, local) is not available in this release; where nothing may reach a vendor, use Templates-only mode (Restricting the LLM Path).
  • Set the daily spend cap to a number that bounds your monthly liability. The cap can be raised or removed at any time via Settings.
  • Validate the SBOM against your organization’s vulnerability scanning. The SBOM.json ships at the root of the App tarball.

docs.text:

  • Privacy Tiers — the type-system privacy boundary explained

  • Audit Log — viewer + filter conventions + tamper-evidence model

  • Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF) — the external reference framework this page maps against

docs.title: Application Settings
docs.text:
The Application Settings page holds the LogServ App’s admin settings. Open it with Settings in the LogServ App’s navigation rail (near the bottom, above About); its URL is #/settings inside the App, and the old #/settings/ai-assistant URL still opens it. The page has two tabs:

  • AI Assistant: everything that governs the AI Assistant, on four sub-tabs (below). To turn the AI Assistant on for the first time, follow Set Up the AI Assistant.
  • Dashboard Data: the KV Store rollups behind every dashboard and the Environment Topology view: backfill, late-arriving data, retention and clear. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.
Application Settings
+-- AI Assistant              (top-level tab)
|   +-- General               (sub-tab)
|   +-- Provider Credentials  (sub-tab; hidden while Templates-only mode is on)
|   +-- Splunk MCP            (sub-tab)
|   +-- Audit Log             (sub-tab)
+-- Dashboard Data            (top-level tab)

docs.title: The Two Top-Level Tabs
docs.text: Tab Scope AI Assistant Everything specific to the AI Assistant feature, split across four sub-tabs (below). Dashboard Data App-wide admin controls for the KV Store rollup data layer that powers every dashboard and the Environment Topology view: the aggregation master switch, retention, the backfill, per-rollup status and clear (see below).

docs.title: AI Assistant sub-tabs
docs.text:
Sub-tab Scope General Org-wide AI Assistant defaults: on/off, Templates-only mode, provider, model, privacy tier, the MCP gate, server URL and timeout, rate limit, spend cap, Power Mode roles, the audit index and the audit forwarder Provider Credentials LLM provider credentials (Anthropic / OpenAI / Azure OpenAI / AWS Bedrock). Hidden while Templates-only mode is on, and in a compile-time templates-only build Splunk MCP The MCP Server bearer token and the audit forwarder’s HEC token Audit Log Read-only browser of the audit events in the logserv_ai_assistant_audit index

While Templates-only mode is on, an info banner at the top of the AI Assistant tab says that the provider, model, tier and Power Mode fields have no effect.

docs.title: Who Can Open the Page
docs.text: The LogServ App treats a user as an admin only when one of their roles is named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin. Only those users see Settings in the navigation rail. Anyone else who opens #/settings gets 403 — Admin access required, and cannot change the AI Assistant settings or run Dashboard Data Clear and Backfill. A delegated-admin role with any other name, on Splunk Cloud Platform or Splunk Enterprise, is not recognized; give such users one of the three roles itself (whether a role that only imports one of them is enough has not been tested). The page’s own checks are not the security boundary: the KV Store collections and the knowledge objects behind it accept writes only from the same three roles (below).

docs.title: Where the AI Assistant settings are stored
docs.text:
The General sub-tab’s settings and the state of the two legal acknowledgements live in KV Store collections of the LogServ App, not in .conf files:

  • logserv_ai_assistant_settings: one row, keyed defaults, holding every General setting.
  • logserv_ai_assistant_acks: one row per acknowledgement, holding the version last answered, the answer and its time. An acknowledgement is recorded once for the deployment, not per user; the audit event records who answered.
  • logserv_ai_models: the discovered-model cache (How model discovery works).

All three ship with read : [ * ], because every page load reads them, and write : [ admin, sc_admin, sc_subadmin ] in the App’s metadata/default.meta. Writing a KV Store row needs only that collection-level permission, not admin_all_objects, so a delegated admin role without admin_all_objects (common on Splunk Cloud Platform) can still click Save Defaults and answer the acknowledgements. The shipped default/ai_assistant_settings.conf holds the defaults the App uses until the first save. On the first page load by an admin-tier user, the App copies any values left in local/ai_assistant_settings.conf and local/ai_assistant_acks.conf by an older build into these rows.

The dashboard rollup, Environment Topology and platform-snapshot collections take writes from the same three roles, which is why Dashboard Data Clear and Backfill need one of them; the scheduled searches that fill those collections run as Splunk’s system user.

docs.title: General Tab
docs.text:
The General sub-tab is divided into five sections: Feature, Limits & Quotas, Privacy, Power Users and Audit & Telemetry. Each table below lists the settings by their label on screen, then the key they are stored under (the same key as in default/ai_assistant_settings.conf).

On a fresh install, the settings that matter for the predefined prompts are the Enable AI Assistant and Templates-only mode switches, the MCP rows and Audit & Telemetry. The provider, model, tier, Limits & Quotas, Privacy and Power Users settings govern free-form questions only, so they have nothing to govern until an admin selects a provider and stores its credential.

The Save Defaults button, at the bottom, is active once something has changed; Revert discards the unsaved changes. Save Defaults records an audit event in three cases: a save that raises Privacy Tier to 2 (vendor_tier2_elevation; no dialog asks first), and an answer, Yes or No, to either acknowledgement dialog (ai_assistant_enable_acceptance, forwarder_disabled_acceptance). Other saves record none.

docs.title: Feature
docs.text: Setting Key Default What it does Enable AI Assistant enabled Off Master switch. When off, the AI Assistant button is hidden for every user and the MCP check never runs. Every save that turns it on opens the liability acknowledgement first. Templates-only mode templates_only_mode Off (reads Full LLM path) When on, the free-form, LLM-driven path is off at run time: the chat input is read-only, the model picker and the Power Mode toggle are hidden, the Provider Credentials sub-tab is hidden, and an info banner explains the mode. The predefined prompts, the Splunk MCP Server integration and the audit log stay active, and so does Model discovery while it is on (a metadata-only call to the active provider’s model-listing API). Any admin can turn it off again. In a compile-time templates-only build this row is hidden and the mode is always on. Active Provider provider Mock (development only) The LLM vendor every user’s free-form questions go to: Mock (development only), Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock (Claude) or Ollama (Tier 0 — local). Mock contacts no vendor and gives a canned reply. Do not select Ollama in this release: it runs the Mock provider (Privacy Tiers). Default Model default_model mock-fast The model selected when a user opens the AI Assistant. The list is the provider’s curated models plus any discovered ones (How model discovery works); each user’s picker in the chat panel switches within the same list. Model discovery model_discovery_enabled On Lets the model lists refresh from the vendor’s own model-listing API. When off, the App never calls a vendor model-listing endpoint and the pickers offer the curated list only. Hidden in a compile-time templates-only build. Discovered models — — Status row, shown while Model discovery is on: how many models were discovered for the active provider, when the list was last fetched, and the error of the last failed refresh, with a Refresh model list button. Privacy Tier tier Tier 1 What a free-form vendor call may carry about your data: Privacy Tiers. Do not select Tier 0 in this release: it summarizes like Tier 1 and still sends to the selected provider. Raising the tier to 2 records a vendor_tier2_elevation audit event. MCP Required mcp_required On (reads Required) When on, the chat waits for the MCP health check. When off, the AI Assistant runs in MCP-less chat mode: LLM streaming with no searches and no prompt browser (Splunk MCP Setup). MCP Server URL mcp_server_url blank The MCP endpoint. Blank uses /en-US/splunkd/__raw/services/mcp on this Splunk instance. See Splunk MCP Setup. MCP request timeout (seconds) mcp_timeout_seconds 60 How long the browser waits for each MCP request (a search, a saved-search run, the health check) before it aborts it. If a slow prompt shows signal is aborted without reason, raise it. The MCP Server has its own timeout (next row), and the lower of the two applies, so to let a search run past 60 seconds raise both. Range 5–600. MCP server timeout (read-only) — (mcp.conf [server] timeout of the MCP Server app) — Shows the Splunk MCP Server’s own request timeout next to the client timeout, or Not detected when the MCP Server is not installed or reachable. To change it, edit the MCP Server app’s mcp.conf and restart Splunk: that app caches the value in a persistent process, so it cannot be changed from here.

docs.title: Limits & Quotas
docs.text: Setting Key Default What it does Rate limit (free-form prompts/hour) rate_limit_per_hour 30 Per-user limit on free-form prompts in a rolling hour. Predefined prompts never count. 0 turns it off. Maps to LLM10. Session tool-call cap tool_calls_per_session_cap 100 Per-chat-session limit on searches the AI may run (saved searches and ad-hoc queries together), above the per-message limit of 8 tool turns. Clearing the chat starts a new session. 0 turns it off. Maps to LLM06. Daily spend cap (USD) daily_spend_cap_usd 50.00 Per-user daily limit on estimated free-form vendor spend (from token counts). The tally resets at local midnight; the prompt that crosses the cap still completes. 0 turns it off. Maps to LLM10.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: Setting Key Default What it does Tier 2 PII column redaction tier2_pii_redaction On (reads Redact identifiers) In Tier 2, redacts the values of identifier columns before they are sent to the LLM. Every field the App defines is classified one by one (user names, statements that name users, addresses, and host names with the hostname opt-in), and name patterns cover every other field: email, user(name) and user_name and their plurals, every *_ip, *_addr and *_address and a bare ip, the CIM src, dest, dst and dvc, peer, mac, account, camelCase …User / …UserName / …Email, and id names such as user_id, also after ., :, - or a space as in Authentication.user (Privacy Tiers has the exact rules). It fails closed: a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column through the SPL to fields that mark no identifier. values(user) or an alias of user count as user, and a pivot’s text cells or a column computed by an eval expression, rex, spath or any other construct the App does not trace are redacted whatever they hold. Each value becomes a <redacted-XXXXXXX> tag, a keyed hash under a random key per chat session: the same value keeps its tag within a chat session, so cardinality reasoning still works, and tags cannot be linked across sessions or reversed by hashing candidates. While on, it also redacts every value of a text column shown as col_N, and sends values withheld for numeric columns whose name or a field they read marks an identifier, or that mix many fields. Column names are withheld as col_N whatever this setting, unless Splunk generates them or the query wrote every word of them. No effect in Tier 0 or Tier 1. Tier 2 hostname redaction tier2_redact_hostnames Off (reads Send hostnames) Also redacts host-name columns under the Tier 2 rule. Off by default, since host names are often not sensitive in SAP environments. Can be changed only while Tier 2 PII column redaction is on.

docs.title: Power Users
docs.text: Setting Key Default What it does Power Mode roles power_user_roles empty The Splunk roles whose members see the ✦ Power toggle in the chat input (Power Mode). Empty hides the toggle for everyone. The list offers the roles defined on this Splunk instance.

docs.title: Audit & Telemetry
docs.text: Setting Key Default What it does Audit index name audit_index_name logserv_ai_assistant_audit The index that receives audit writes. Rename it together with the sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro macro, which controls reads (Renaming an index). Audit log forwarder audit_forwarder_enabled Off (reads Local-only) When on, every audit event is also sent to the HEC endpoint below, on a separate Splunk instance or SIEM, for tamper-evidence. The destination HEC must allow cross-origin requests from this Splunk Web address. Saving with it off opens the audit-log integrity acknowledgement until that is answered at its current version. See Audit Log → HEC Forwarder. Forwarder HEC URL audit_forwarder_url blank HEC base URL, for example https://siem.example.com:8088; the App appends /services/collector/event. Required when forwarding is on. Forwarder remote index (optional) audit_forwarder_index blank Index on the destination. Blank uses the HEC token’s default index. Forwarder source field audit_forwarder_source logserv_ai_assistant_remote source of every forwarded event, distinct from the local copies (sourcetype logserv:ai_assistant:audit), so the two can be told apart.

docs.title: How Model Discovery Works
docs.text:
Needs a configured provider credential

Model discovery queries the configured provider, so it does nothing useful until a credential is configured. It is inert in a compile-time templates-only build: no vendor model-listing call is ever made there, and its rows are hidden.

The model pickers (the Default Model setting and the chat panel’s per-user picker) offer a merged model list per provider: a curated static baseline plus models discovered live from the configured vendor.

What discovery calls. Discovery is a metadata-only GET against the vendor’s model-listing endpoint, with the same credential and in the same trust envelope as the credential check. No prompt text, no Splunk event data and no aggregates are involved; the request and response carry model metadata only.

Provider Discovery source Anthropic GET /v1/models (paginated; display names and context windows carried through) OpenAI GET /v1/models, filtered to chat-capable families, with dated snapshots collapsed onto their alias Azure OpenAI Three-step deployment discovery: /openai/v1/models → /openai/deployments → the deployment name(s) configured on the Provider Credentials sub-tab AWS Bedrock ListFoundationModels, filtered to Anthropic / on-demand / text / streaming / active Mock A synthetic mock-discovered entry (for testing with no key)

When it refreshes. Three triggers, all governed by Model discovery:

  1. Credential save: saving a provider credential on the Provider Credentials sub-tab refreshes that provider’s list immediately.
  2. Manual: the Refresh model list button on the General sub-tab.
  3. 24-hour TTL: opening the chat panel refreshes the active provider’s list if the cached copy is older than 24 hours (at most once per page load, never for the Mock provider, and never if the panel is not opened).

Where the list lives. Discovered lists are cached in the logserv_ai_models KV Store collection (one row per provider: the sanitized model list, fetch time, fetching user and last error). Model ids and labels are allowlist-sanitized on write and on read, and the static baseline always survives the merge, so a poisoned or malformed cache entry cannot remove the known-good models.

Failure behavior. A failed refresh keeps the row’s last good models and timestamp and only updates the error text (shown on the Discovered models row). The picker never shrinks below the static baseline.

Audit trail. Every refresh, success or failure, from any trigger, writes a model_discovery audit event (provider, trigger, ok, model count, duration, error), browsable on the Audit Log sub-tab.

Cost estimates stay honest. The vendor cost table used for spend tracking is keyed by exact model id. A discovered model with no known price reports $0; the App never guesses a price from an id prefix. The Daily spend cap (USD) therefore only counts models with known pricing. The Claude 5.x models (claude-opus-5-5, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-fable-5-1, claude-fable-5, claude-haiku-5-5) are priced at Anthropic’s published first-party rates, cache reads and writes included, so their turns count toward the cap. claude-haiku-5-5 is priced at its rate for prompts up to 100K tokens; a longer prompt costs more than the estimate. Bedrock prices are set by AWS, so the App’s AWS Bedrock entries are not derived from these rates.

How to turn it off. Clear Model discovery on the General sub-tab and save. From then on the App makes no vendor model-listing calls (all three triggers are gated), and the pickers offer the curated list only. Cached rows in logserv_ai_models are ignored while it is off and overwritten on the next refresh if it is turned on again.

docs.title: Provider Credentials Tab
docs.text:
Hidden while Templates-only mode is on

This sub-tab is hidden while Templates-only mode is on and in a compile-time templates-only build; no LLM provider is used there. Otherwise, storing a credential here is what gives free-form questions a real LLM.

One panel per provider, each with that provider’s credential fields. Credentials are stored in Splunk’s encrypted password store through /servicesNS/nobody/<app>/storage/passwords; the page shows only whether a value is stored, its length and, for some fields, its first characters, never the cleartext.

Panel Fields (realm logserv_ai_assistant_<provider>, name) Anthropic API Key (anthropic, api_key) OpenAI API Key (openai, api_key) Azure OpenAI API Key (azure_openai, api_key), Endpoint URL (endpoint), Deployment Name (deployment) AWS Bedrock API Key (bedrock, api_key), AWS Region (region). Bedrock API keys only; IAM credentials are not supported. Ollama (Tier 0 — air-gapped local) Base URL (ollama, url). Not used in this release: the Ollama provider runs Mock.

Storing a credential:

  1. Find the provider’s panel and type or paste the value into the field.
  2. Click Save (Update when a value is already stored). The value goes to Splunk’s encrypted password store, and the row then reads Stored: length N.

Removing a credential: click Clear next to the field and confirm.

Saving a credential records no audit event itself. When Model discovery is on, saving a field of the Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI or AWS Bedrock panel starts a refresh of that provider’s model list, which records a model_discovery event (trigger credential_save).

If Active Provider names a provider whose credential is not stored, the first free-form question fails with Required credential not set: logserv_ai_assistant_<provider>:<field>.

Each user’s browser reads the provider credential from Splunk’s password store when that user sends a free-form question, so a user whose role cannot read stored passwords (Splunk’s list_storage_passwords capability, which admin holds) gets an error instead of an answer.

docs.title: Splunk MCP Tab
docs.text: Two panels:

docs.title: Splunk MCP Server
docs.text:
Field Realm Name Bearer Token logserv_ai_assistant_mcp bearer_token

An OAuth/JWT token issued for your Splunk MCP Server, pasted by an admin. Optional: by default the App authenticates to the MCP Server with the user’s own Splunk Web session cookie. See Splunk MCP Setup → Authentication.

docs.title: Audit Log Forwarder
docs.text:
Field Realm Name HEC Token logserv_ai_assistant_forwarder hec_token

The HEC token for forwarding audit events to a separate Splunk instance or SIEM. The destination URL and the on/off switch are on the General sub-tab under Audit & Telemetry. The token is sent on every forwarded audit event as Authorization: Splunk <token>. See Audit Log → HEC Forwarder.

docs.title: Audit Log Tab
docs.text:
Read-only browser of every event in the logserv_ai_assistant_audit index. The tab searches the index as the signed-in admin, whose role must allow it (Restricting who can read the audit index). The search window is the global time range in the header: the viewer re-runs on every change, and there is no separate time-range control. Filters: a category multi-select (13 categories: local_only, vendor_tier1, vendor_tier2, security_blocked_spl, rate_limited_prompt, user_prompt_jailbreak_flag, session_tool_cap_hit, daily_spend_cap_hit, audit_forwarder_failure, vendor_tier2_elevation, forwarder_disabled_acceptance, ai_assistant_enable_acceptance, model_discovery), a user-contains text filter, and a result limit (50 / 100 / 250 / 500, default 100).

Clicking a row’s + button shows the full event JSON. The table shows 25 rows per page; a “Showing N-M of T events” line sits above it, and “Page X of Y” with Previous / Next buttons below it when T is over 25.

Tamper-resistance disclaimer at the top of the panel:

Audit events live in a Splunk index. A host-root admin can edit the bucket files. Mitigation: forward audit events to a separate Splunk instance / SIEM / S3-with-Object-Lock owned by a different admin team. Configure the HEC forwarder under Settings → General → Audit & Telemetry.

See Audit Log for the threat model and the forwarder.

docs.title: Dashboard Data Tab
docs.text:
The Dashboard Data top-level tab is the admin control surface for the KV Store rollup layer behind every dashboard and the Environment Topology view: the hourly-aggregation master switch, the 365-day retention, the backfill, the late-arriving data check, a per-rollup status and action table, and a global clear. Its Clear and Backfill need one of the three admin role names (Who can open the page).

It manages the dashboard data layer, not the AI Assistant, so its controls are documented with that layer: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness → The Dashboard Data settings tab. On a fresh install, run its backfill once: Backfilling on first install.

A read-only view of the same rollup health, freshness and 30-day-history completeness, is available to every user on the Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page (Platform → Diagnostics), which points back here for the backfill and clear controls.

docs.title: Legal Acknowledgement Modals
docs.text:
Two legal acknowledgements gate the General sub-tab’s Save Defaults. Both follow Splunk’s splunk_instrumentation optInVersion pattern: each has a version (optInVersion in the App’s default/ai_assistant_acks.conf), the deployment records the version it last answered and the answer (in the logserv_ai_assistant_acks KV Store collection), and raising the version asks again. Both answers, Yes and No, are recorded, and each answer also writes an audit event with the admin’s user name, the network address Splunk records for the request (host), the time, and the SHA-256 of the acknowledgement text.

On a fresh install, the first Save Defaults that turns the AI Assistant on shows both, the liability terms first (Set Up the AI Assistant). If an answer cannot be recorded, or the save after a Yes fails, the dialog closes and the error shows on the page.

docs.title: “AI Assistant — Liability terms” Dialog (orange-bordered)
docs.text:
The AI Assistant — Liability terms dialog opens:

  • on every save that turns Enable AI Assistant on, whatever was answered before; and
  • on a save while the AI Assistant is on, when its terms are at a newer version than the one last answered on this deployment (the current version is 3).

The text has seven clauses: data egress acknowledgement, customer responsibility, AS-IS warranty disclaimer, indemnification, limitation of liability, authority warrant, and record of acknowledgement. Its Active LLM provider line names the provider in effect and, when the same save also changes the provider, the one a Yes saves.

  • I accept (record Yes and enable): the save goes ahead (with the second acknowledgement first, when it is due) and the version is recorded as answered. An ai_assistant_enable_acceptance audit event records the answer.
  • I do not accept: the save stops. An AI Assistant being turned on stays off. One that is already on (asked again after a version change) is turned off: only Enable AI Assistant changes, nothing else in that save, and it is written before the No is recorded, so if turning it off fails, nothing is recorded and the question comes back at the next save. Turning it on again asks every time.

docs.title: “Audit log integrity” Dialog (red-bordered)
docs.text:
The Audit log integrity dialog opens:

  • on every save that turns Audit log forwarder off; and
  • on a save with the forwarder off, when its terms are at a newer version than the one last answered on this deployment (the current version is 2).

The text covers the integrity responsibility: with the forwarder off, the audit events exist only in the local index, which a host-root admin can edit.

  • I accept (record Yes and save): the save goes ahead with forwarding off.
  • I do not accept (record No): the save stops and the forwarder setting stays as it was, but the answer is recorded, so the next save does not ask again unless forwarding is turned from on to off.

Its forwarder_disabled_acceptance audit event is posted as soon as the answer is recorded, for either answer, so a Yes is logged even when the save after it fails. The event goes where the audit settings in place at that moment send it: when the same save turns forwarding off, it is also sent to the forwarder being turned off, and if that send fails, its audit_forwarder_failure record goes to the event’s audit index.

docs.title: Why the hybrid trigger logic
docs.text: Version-only gating (answer once, never asked again until the version changes) is what Splunk’s own telemetry uses. The App also asks on every deliberate turn-on of the AI Assistant and every deliberate turn-off of the forwarder, because each is a change of the legal and security posture that may be made by a different admin, with different context, than the last one.

docs.title: Live UI Refresh on Save
docs.text: When a save changes what users see (Enable AI Assistant, MCP Required, Power Mode roles, Templates-only mode and the like), the App applies the new settings to the running page without a reload: turning the AI Assistant off removes the AI Assistant button, and turning it on shows it. Other users’ open pages pick the change up at their next page load. For the callback wiring, see LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Restricting the LLM Path
docs.text:
The AI Assistant has two paths: predefined prompts, which never call an LLM, and free-form questions, which an LLM vendor answers. This page is for deployments where the free-form path must stay off. There are three ways to keep it off, from the easiest to undo to the hardest; pick the one your policy needs.

Option What it is Who can undo it What you install Templates-only mode A setting on Settings → AI Assistant → General Any LogServ App admin, with a save The released App package (no change) Templates-only build The same App source built with the flag fixed on Nobody, short of installing a different build A package you build from source The v0.0.6 line An older, frozen line whose bundle has no vendor client code Nobody The v0.0.6 App package (not in the v0.1.2 download location)

The released v0.1.2 App package is the full-LLM build: the free-form path is present, and starts working only once an admin selects a provider and stores its credential. Until then a typed question gets a canned reply from the Mock provider and no vendor is contacted.

docs.title: Templates-only Mode (Runtime)
docs.text:
Templates-only mode is a setting (templates_only_mode, default off) in the released package. To turn it on:

  1. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General.
  2. Under Feature, select Templates-only mode (the toggle then reads Templates-only).
  3. Click Save Defaults. The change applies to your page at once and to other users’ pages at their next page load.

While it is on, every source of free-form dispatch is off: the chat input is read-only, Send is disabled, the model picker and the Power Mode toggle are hidden, the Provider Credentials sub-tab is hidden, and the banners described below appear. If any code path still reaches the LLM dispatch entry point, a guard there refuses it with a notice in the chat before any vendor call.

Choose it for demonstration environments, partners, and deployments that do not want the LLM path now but may later. Its limit: any user who can open the Settings page (a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin) can turn it off again with a save. Where that is not acceptable, use a templates-only build.

docs.title: Templates-only Build (Compile-time)
docs.text:
The templates-only build is the LogServ App built from the same source with the free-form path disabled at compile time. No configuration change can restore it: the build flag forces the templates_only_mode setting on where it is read, so every source of that setting (the KV Store settings row, a local/ai_assistant_settings.conf override, or the shipped default) reports templates-only whatever it contains. Changing the setting, by any route including a direct REST write, has no effect, and the Templates-only mode toggle is hidden in this build because it could not change anything. The dispatch guard is tied to the build flag as well as to the setting, so it holds even if the setting never reaches the dispatch layer.

This is a functional disable: the vendor provider code is still in the bundle, but nothing can reach it. It suits demos, partners and most restricted environments. If your policy requires the vendor code to be physically absent, see the v0.0.6 line.

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
No templates-only package is published for v0.1.2: the only App package in the release is the full-LLM build. To get one, build it from the release’s source and package it yourself:

  1. Install the dependencies at the App workspace root (sap_logserv_package/splunk_app_sap_logserv/): yarn install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-engines.
  2. In packages/log-serv-app, run yarn build:templates-only. Like the regular build, it first runs the intent-map and diagnostics checks; it then builds into stage/ and sets templates_only_mode = true in the staged default/ai_assistant_settings.conf, and fails if it cannot.
  3. Package stage/ as splunk_app_sap_logserv: tar -czf splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2-templates-only.tar.gz --transform 's|^stage|splunk_app_sap_logserv|' stage.
  4. Install it like the released package (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards), after checking it with AppInspect if your process requires that.
