docs.text:
The LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) and the LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp) are UCC add-ons with one modular input each and no parsing configuration of their own. Each input fetches the LogServ files its cloud announces and writes their NDJSON lines through the modular-input EventWriter (not HEC), so the events go through the index-time pipeline of the instance that runs the input, where the Data TA routes, filters and stamps them.

LogServ Azure add-on LogServ GCP add-on Input kind and script sap_logserv_azure_queue, bin/sap_logserv_azure_queue.py sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub, bin/sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub.py Helpers (bin/lib/) azure_storage_rest.py, azure_eventgrid.py, azure_checkpoint.py gcp_rest.py, gcp_auth.py, gcp_notifications.py, gcp_checkpoint.py Notification read Event Grid BlobCreated messages on an Azure Storage Queue GCS OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications on a Pub/Sub subscription Credential SAS token Google service-account JSON key (OAuth2 tokens minted with a standard-library RS256 implementation) Batch per request (default) 32 messages (at most 32), visibility timeout 300 s 10 messages When a message is done Each message is deleted on its own, once its blobs are done One acknowledge per pull batch, after every message in it is processed Dedup key Blob URL + ETag bucket/object#generation cloud_provider stamp _meta = cloud_provider::azure on the input-kind stanza _meta = cloud_provider::gcp on the input-kind stanza

The helpers use only the Python standard library (urllib, xml.etree, …), with no Azure or Google SDK, which keeps the add-ons free of compiled wheels that fail AppInspect’s AArch64 check.

docs.title: One Firing
docs.text:
Every interval seconds (60 by default) the input:

  1. Reads its settings and its credential from passwords.conf. UCC stores it under the realm __REST_CREDENTIAL__#<app>#data/inputs/<input kind>.
  2. Drains the queue or subscription within a time budget of 90% of the interval, at most 240 seconds, and at most max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire files (500 by default). Per message:
    • a message delivered more times than the poison threshold (5 by default) is dropped; the Azure input can first copy it to a dead-letter queue, and the GCP input sees the delivery count only when the subscription has a dead-letter policy;
    • the notification is parsed, and the input’s own Include filters / Exclude filters decide which files it keeps;
    • each file that is not in the dedup record is fetched, gunzipped (plain text is accepted too) and split into lines, and every line is written with sourcetype sap_logserv_logs (fixed in the code; the Sourcetype field on the input form is display-only) and the input’s index (sap_logserv_logs by default);
    • the message is deleted (Azure) or acknowledged (GCP) once every file in it is ingested or skipped; a file that no longer exists (HTTP 404) or cannot be decoded is skipped. After a transient or access error the message is left for redelivery.
  3. Writes the dedup record and logs a summary line.

docs.title: Dedup Record and One Input per Queue
docs.text:
Delivery is at-least-once on both clouds, so each input keeps a dedup record: a JSON file named <input name>.dedup.json in the modular input’s checkpoint directory on the instance that runs it. Entries expire after 7 days, and the file keeps at most 50,000. It is written at the end of each firing, so a process killed in the middle of a firing loses that firing’s entries.

Nothing shares the record: not a clone of the input on the same heavy forwarder, not an input with the same name on another one. A single input per queue or subscription is therefore effectively duplicate-free. Every further input on the same queue or subscription is a competing consumer with its own record, and a message that comes back (a lapsed visibility lease or ack deadline, a failed delete or acknowledge, a process that died before it) can be ingested twice. Google also documents that Pub/Sub may redeliver a message even after a successful acknowledge. On GCP the whole pull batch has to finish inside the subscription’s ack deadline, because the input acknowledges once per batch and never extends the deadline.

docs.title: The Input Handler
docs.text: The Inputs page is served by UCC’s generated [admin_external:*] handler, the stock AdminExternalHandler. It runs as the signed-in user, so creating, editing (including replacing the SAS token or key) or deleting an input needs admin_all_objects, on Splunk Cloud and on Splunk Enterprise alike. This is inferred from the identical handler of other UCC add-ons in the project; it has not been retested on these two. The passSystemAuth = true line that each add-on’s additional_packaging.py adds to that stanza has no effect there, and unlike the Data TA’s Configuration tabs the add-ons have no filesystem fallback.

docs.title: Build-Time Patches of the Add-ons
docs.text:
Each add-on’s additional_packaging.py patches the UCC output in five steps:

  1. Adds handlertype, python.version, python.required = 3.13 and passSystemAuth = true to every [admin_external:*] stanza of restmap.conf.
  2. Adds python.version = python3, python.required = 3.13 and the _meta = cloud_provider::<cloud> line to the input-kind stanza of inputs.conf.
  3. Copies the real input script from package/bin/ over the stub UCC generates from globalConfig.json.
  4. Removes gRPC, protobuf and OpenTelemetry packages from lib/ if a dependency brings them in.
  5. Adds sc_subadmin to the global write ACL in metadata/default.meta (see The sc_subadmin Write-ACL Patch).

The build prints an [additional_packaging] ... line for steps 2, 3 and 5.

docs.title: Environment 1: Single Instance (Standalone)
docs.text:
Setup: One Splunk Enterprise instance acting as Search Head, Indexer, and data receiver.

What to test
  • Filter save generates correct local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf
  • Conf reload works without restart
  • Include, exclude, and time filters work correctly in search results
  • Include Sources keeps a file whose folder is not included, and events without folder fields; Exclude Sources drops only the named files while the primary types in the same folder still arrive
  • A long line (4,097 to 99,999 characters, _raw before the metadata keys) is judged like a short one
  • Disabling filtering clears the generated conf files
  • Pattern validation blocks invalid input — the source fields also with filtering disabled
  • No Deployment Server UI elements appear (no banner, no deploy button)

docs.title: Environment 2: Deployment Server + Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
Setup: Three instances minimum: DS (can be combined with SH/Indexer), HF-01 (deployment client), HF-02 (deployment client).

What to test
  • DS detection works (banner and deploy button appear)
  • The first filter save copies the full app to deployment-apps/; a later save with the same version copies only the filter configs
  • Filter configs are mirrored to deployment-apps/local/
  • Server class SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders is auto-created with app mapping
  • Client targeting (IP-based) matches HFs correctly
  • Deploy button triggers reload and HFs receive the TA
  • Filter update round-trip: change on DS → deploy → verify on HFs
  • Time refresh script skips on HFs (deployment client guard)
  • Time refresh script runs correctly on DS and mirrors updated configs, with the source stanzas still present after the refresh

docs.title: Environment 3: Splunk Cloud + On-Premises Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
Setup: Splunk Cloud instance (Search Head / Indexer), separate on-premises DS, on-premises HFs configured as deployment clients.

What to test
  • Same as Environment 2, but additionally verify:
  • The LogServ App is installed on the Splunk Cloud search head for dashboards and search-time knowledge objects. The Data TA is installed on the on-prem DS and HFs. The two indexes are created on the Cloud stack in Settings > Indexes or with ACS, before any data arrives. Filtering is NOT configured on the Cloud side
  • Filter configuration and TA distribution to HFs are managed entirely from the on-premises DS
  • Filtering works at the HF level before data reaches Splunk Cloud
  • No INGEST_EVAL dependency (TRANSFORMS-only filtering)

docs.title: Environment 4: Fresh DS with No Prior Server Classes
docs.text:
Setup: DS with deployment clients connected but no serverclass.conf exists.

What to test
  • DS detection works via the fallback (connected clients check)
  • ensure_serverclass() creates serverclass.conf from scratch
  • The deployment_server role activates after server class creation
  • Full deployment workflow completes successfully

docs.title: Local Imports in Utility Functions
docs.text:
Functions in splunk_ta_sap_logserv_filter_utils.py import splunk.rest locally (inside the function body). splunk.rest exists only in Splunk’s own Python, so a module-level import would fail wherever the module is loaded outside Splunk. Some functions also import standard-library modules (json, configparser, glob) locally; that is style, not necessity.

The critical detail is that local imports are scoped to the function they are declared in. They do NOT carry into sibling functions. Each function that needs splunk.rest or json must import them independently. For example, both get_server_roles() and is_deployment_server() need their own local import splunk.rest as rest and import json statements — the imports inside get_server_roles() are not visible to is_deployment_server() even though one calls the other.

Forgetting a local import inside a function that has a bare except Exception: pass block is particularly dangerous because the resulting NameError is silently swallowed, causing the function to return a default value without any log output.

docs.title: Persistent Handler sys.path
docs.text: Persistent REST handlers (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_rh_deployment_push.py, splunk_ta_sap_logserv_rh_s3_direct_meta.py) do NOT get import_declare_test from UCC. They require explicit sys.path setup at the top of the file to import from the app’s bin/ and lib/ directories. Without this, the handler returns 500 errors from splunkd.

docs.title: web.conf Expose Stanza
docs.text:
Custom persistent endpoints are not accessible through the Splunk Web proxy (port 8000) by default. They require an [expose:] stanza in web.conf. This is injected by additional_packaging.py during the UCC build:

[expose:splunk_ta_sap_logserv_deployment_push]
pattern = splunk_ta_sap_logserv/deployment_push
methods = POST, GET

[expose:splunk_ta_sap_logserv_s3_direct_meta]
pattern = splunk_ta_sap_logserv/s3_direct_meta
methods = POST

docs.title: Server Class REST API Limitations
docs.text:
• The disabled parameter and the app mapping cannot be set through the REST create; see Server Class Creation
  • Splunk may write serverclass.conf to different locations (system/local/ or apps/search/local/). The code searches multiple locations
  • A scoped reload (serverclasses/<name>/reload) must be sent in the namespace of the app that holds the class. Read it from the class’s acl.app (GET /servicesNS/-/-/deployment/server/serverclasses/<name>) rather than relying on /services/..., which resolves in the calling user’s default app — see Daily Time Refresh. Deploy to Forwarders uses the global /services/deployment/server/config/_reload, which has no such dependency but reloads every server class on the DS

docs.title: TRANSFORMS-00-filter Ordering
docs.text:
The 00 prefix sorts the filter class before every other TRANSFORMS-* class of [sap_logserv_logs]. That classes run in ASCII order of their names is not in Splunk’s props.conf specification, which documents only the order inside one class; it is Splunk’s observed behaviour, and the filters working in the lab depend on it. The filters must run before TRANSFORMS-99-set_raw, because they match the NDJSON envelope keys that the unwrap removes. Running first saves no processing: Splunk still applies every later transform to an event the filters dropped.

All queue-setting filter transforms — the source stanzas and every chunk included — MUST stay in that single line: Splunk does not reliably carry DEST_KEY = queue across separate TRANSFORMS-xx directives, and only within one line is “last match wins” guaranteed. Because the filters run before TRANSFORMS-01-metadata, they cannot use SOURCE_KEY = MetaData:Source: at that point it still holds the input’s own source, not the envelope’s source value.

docs.title: Marker Comments
docs.text:
Generated filter content in local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf is wrapped in marker comments:

### BEGIN LOGSERV FILTER CONFIG - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY ###
...
### END LOGSERV FILTER CONFIG ###

The write_local_conf() function replaces content between these markers (or appends them if not present). Manual customizations outside the markers are preserved. The Cloud Provider tab writes its own independent block between ### BEGIN LOGSERV CLOUD_PROVIDER CONFIG - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY ### / ### END LOGSERV CLOUD_PROVIDER CONFIG ### markers (via write_local_conf_section()), so the daily filter time-refresh regenerating the filter block leaves the cloud-provider block untouched. With Not set the block is removed; empty content clears only the block of its own marker pair.

docs.title: Clean Deployment Test (Lab)
docs.text: This is a lab procedure for developers and testers: it installs the Data TA and the LogServ App on a clean test deployment and checks every step from the Deployment Server automation to the dashboards. Run it on test instances only, never on a production Deployment Server, heavy forwarder or search head.

docs.title: What the Test Covers
docs.text:
The test installs two packages:

  • Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv) – installed on the Deployment Server (DS) and pushed to the heavy forwarders (HFs)
  • LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv) – installed on the search head only

It checks the install, the DS automation, the filter configuration, the push to the forwarders, data ingest, filtering and the dashboards. The phases below use the AWS SQS-Based S3 channel. Other Ingest Channels lists what to check when the LogServ Azure add-on, the LogServ GCP add-on or the AWS S3 Direct screen is in scope.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Deployment Server. In a small lab it can also be the search head and indexer.
  • HF-01 and HF-02: heavy forwarders that are already deployment clients of the DS. The Data TA detects a DS by its deployment_server role, which Splunk shows only while at least one server class exists. On a DS that has no server class yet, the Data TA detects the DS only through a connected deployment client, so connect the HFs before Phase 3.
  • On both HFs, the Splunk Add-on for AWS with SQS-Based S3 inputs configured and disabled until Phase 7.
  • The two indexes, sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit, on the indexer. When the indexer is the DS, the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf creates them there.
  • A Data TA .tar.gz and a LogServ App .tar.gz: the release tarballs, or builds made as described in Building the Packages from Source.

docs.title: On the DS
docs.text:
Remove only the LogServ packages and the LogServ server class. Do not delete serverclass.conf files: they hold every other server class on the DS.

  1. Remove the Data TA and its deployment-apps copy:

    sudo su - splunk
rm -rf /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv
rm -rf /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv
exit

  2. In Splunk Web on the DS, open Settings > Forwarder Management (named Agent Management in newer Splunk Enterprise versions) and delete the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class if it exists. This lets the test watch the Data TA create the class again.

  3. If the test also covers the LogServ App, and the App is installed on this instance, remove it:

    sudo su - splunk
rm -rf /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv
exit

    Removing the App’s directory does not remove its KV Store data: the dashboard rollups, the topology data and the AI Assistant settings stay in the KV Store and appear again when the App is reinstalled. If the test needs empty rollups, click Clear all data on the App’s Settings > Dashboard Data tab before you remove the App.

  4. Restart Splunk (on a systemd-managed install: sudo systemctl restart Splunkd).

docs.title: On Each HF (HF-01 and HF-02)
docs.text:
sudo su - splunk
rm -rf /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv
exit
sudo systemctl restart Splunkd

docs.title: Verify the Clean Slate
docs.text:
On the DS:

sudo su - splunk
ls /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv 2>/dev/null
ls /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv 2>/dev/null
find /opt/splunk/etc -name "serverclass.conf" -path "*/local/*" 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -n "SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders" 2>/dev/null

All three should return nothing.

On each HF:

sudo su - splunk
ls /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv 2>/dev/null

This should return nothing.

docs.title: Phase 1: Install the Data TA on the DS
docs.text:
1. Sign in to Splunk Web on the DS.
  2. Go to Apps > Manage Apps > Install app from file.
  3. Upload the Data TA .tar.gz file and install it.
  4. Restart Splunk when prompted.

docs.title: Phase 2: Install the LogServ App on the Search Head
docs.text:
1. Sign in to Splunk Web on the search head (the DS itself in a combined lab topology).
  2. Go to Apps > Manage Apps > Install app from file.
  3. Upload the LogServ App .tar.gz file and install it.
  4. Restart Splunk when prompted.

docs.title: Phase 3: Configure Filters and Trigger the DS Automation
docs.text:
1. On the DS, open the Data TA (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ) > Configuration > Filters.

  2. Turn on Enable Filtering and set rules that exercise every field. For example:

    • Include Filters: linux/* (a list that is not pass-all, so the include gate is on)
    • Exclude Filters: linux/cron
    • Include Sources: /usr/sap/*/HDB*/*/trace/*.trc (keeps HANA trace files although their folder is not included, and HANA trace events that arrive without folder fields)
    • Exclude Sources: one file path you see in the test data under an included folder
    • Days in the Past: 7

    Choose Days in the Past so the test data has events on both sides of the cutoff. The filter drops every event whose embedded _time epoch is older than midnight UTC N days ago, and data copied from an archive bucket keeps its original dates: if all of it is older than the cutoff, every event is dropped and Phase 7 finds no data. In that case set 0 (no time filter), skip step 6 of Phase 7, and test the time filter separately with data newer than the cutoff.

  3. Click Save.

  4. After the page reloads, check that you see:
    • the Deployment Server Detected banner
    • the Server Class Setup Required notice
    • the Deploy to Forwarders button

The Filters tab refuses Include Sources while Include Filters is pass-all (empty, or holding */* or *), because the rule would have no effect. See Configuring Filters for the rule syntax.

docs.title: Phase 3b: Set the Cloud Attribution
docs.text:
1. Leave Configuration > Cloud Provider at Not set (the default).
  2. On each HF, add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to every aws_sqs_based_s3:// input stanza that reads LogServ data, in Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf, and restart the HF. See Choose Cloud Attribution.
  3. In local/transforms.conf of the Data TA on the DS, check that there is no [logserv_set_cloud_provider] stanza: with Not set the Data TA writes none.

To test the dropdown itself, set it to AWS on an AWS-only test fleet, Save, and check that local/transforms.conf now holds the [logserv_set_cloud_provider] stanza between ### BEGIN LOGSERV CLOUD_PROVIDER CONFIG - DO NOT EDIT MANUALLY ### and ### END LOGSERV CLOUD_PROVIDER CONFIG ###. Set it back to Not set and Save before Phase 5, or remove the _meta lines from the HF inputs instead: the dropdown adds its value beside an input’s own _meta without checking it, so using both writes the stamp twice. The dropdown’s value reaches the HFs only with a push: if you have already deployed, Save Not set and click Deploy to Forwarders again.

docs.title: Phase 4: Verify the DS Automation
docs.text:
Confirm the Data TA was copied to deployment-apps:

sudo su - splunk
ls /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/

Confirm the filter configuration was mirrored:

cat /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf
cat /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/props.conf

Confirm the server class was created:

find /opt/splunk/etc -name "serverclass.conf" -path "*/local/*" 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -n -A3 "SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders"

You should see both stanzas:

  • [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders]
  • [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders:app:splunk_ta_sap_logserv] with restartSplunkd = true and stateOnClient = enabled

The full copy to deployment-apps happens only when no copy exists yet, or when the [launcher] version in default/app.conf differs between etc/apps/ and etc/deployment-apps/. A later build with the same version number is not copied; see Data TA Internals.

docs.title: Phase 5: Configure the Server Class and Deploy
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings > Forwarder Management (named Agent Management in newer Splunk Enterprise versions).
  2. Find SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders.
  3. Click the three-dot menu > Edit agent assignment.
  4. Add client targeting that matches the two HFs (for example their IP addresses).
  5. Save the agent assignment. In the lab, saving it also enabled the server class; if the class still shows as disabled, enable it.
  6. Return to the Filters tab and refresh the page: the Server Class Setup Required notice should be gone.
  7. Click Deploy to Forwarders and confirm.

Deploy to Forwarders reloads the whole Deployment Server (/services/deployment/server/config/_reload), not only this server class, so any other server class with pending changes is pushed as well.

docs.title: Phase 6: Verify the HFs Received the Data TA
docs.text:
Each HF downloads the change at its next phone-home (phoneHomeIntervalInSecs, 60 seconds by default) and then restarts, because the app is mapped with restartSplunkd = true. Allow 5 minutes or more, then check:

# On each HF
sudo su - splunk
ls /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/
cat /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf

Confirm both HFs show as clients of the server class in Settings > Forwarder Management.

docs.title: Phase 7: Enable Ingestion and Test Filtering
docs.text:
1. Enable the SQS-Based S3 inputs on both HFs (they belong to the Splunk Add-on for AWS, not the Data TA).
  2. Wait a few minutes for data to flow.

  3. On the search head, search for incoming data:

    `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by host, sourcetype

  4. Check that the included log types are indexed, and that the files kept by Include Sources arrive:

    `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by sourcetype, source

  5. Check that the excluded folder (linux/cron in the example) and the file named in Exclude Sources do not arrive, while the other files of the same folder still do.

  6. Check the time filter. Search for events older than your Days in the Past cutoff that were ingested while the filter was on:

    `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-30d latest=-10d | stats count

    With Days in the Past below 10 this returns 0, apart from events indexed before the filter was deployed. The filter compares the _time epoch inside each event with midnight UTC N days ago, not the S3 object date.

  7. Check the cloud attribution. Every event should carry exactly one value:

    `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | eval n=mvcount(cloud_provider) | stats count by cloud_provider, n

docs.title: Phase 8: Test a Filter Update Round Trip
docs.text:
1. On the DS Filters tab, change a filter setting (for example add an Exclude Filters pattern) and Save.
  2. Click Deploy to Forwarders again.
  3. After the next phone-home and restart, check on both HFs that local/transforms.conf holds the updated filter.
  4. Check that the new filter works in the search results.
  5. Widen the include list before Part 3. With the example filter, Include Filters keeps only linux/*, so DNS, HANA audit and Web Dispatcher events are dropped and their dashboards stay empty. Add dns/*, hana/*, webdispatcher/* to Include Filters (or turn Enable Filtering off), Save, click Deploy to Forwarders, and wait for the next phone-home and for new data to flow. Events dropped earlier are not read again, so these dashboards fill only from files that arrive after the push. Do not set Include Filters back to */* while Include Sources holds a pattern: the Filters tab refuses that combination.

docs.title: Part 3: Dashboard Verification
docs.text:
After data is flowing, check the LogServ App dashboards:

  1. Fill the rollups. The dashboards read hourly KV Store rollups. The hourly searches fill them from the time the App is installed; earlier test data appears only after a backfill. Go to Settings > Dashboard Data and click Run backfill. It covers the last 30 days by default; longer presets up to 365 days and a custom UTC date range are available. Without it, the rolled-up panels fill one hour at a time from the next hourly aggregation.
  2. Open the LogServ App in Splunk Web.
  3. Walk the menus (Applications, Integration, Security, Platform, Topology) and confirm each dashboard renders, starting with Environment Health, the default landing view. A quick sample:
    • Data Pipeline Overview (Platform) – host event counts and sourcetype distribution
    • DNS Analytics (Platform) – DNS query patterns (needs isc:bind:query data)
    • HANA Audit (Applications) – HANA audit events (needs sap:hana:audit data)
    • Web Dispatcher (Integration) – HTTP traffic (needs sap:webdispatcher:access data)
    • Host Details (Platform) – click a host row on Data Pipeline Overview; Host Details opens in a new tab
  4. A panel that has no data for a reason explains itself: click Why is this empty? to open the Data Doctor drawer.

Time range

Pick a range that covers your test data: one of the presets (Last 24h, Last 7d, Last 30d, Last 90d) or a custom range. Rolled-up panels read hourly buckets, so the current hour is not summarised yet; use a window that covers completed hours of test data. Windows under 90 minutes run the exact raw query instead of the rollup.

docs.title: Other Ingest Channels
docs.text:
Run Parts 1-3 with these changes when the channel is in scope.

LogServ Azure add-on or LogServ GCP add-on. Install the add-on directly on each HF that will run an input, never through the DS: a DS push would replace the add-on’s own local/, where its encrypted SAS token or service-account key lives. Create one input per queue or subscription, on one HF only; every input keeps its own dedup record, so a second input on the same queue or subscription can index a redelivered message twice. Use a role with admin_all_objects to create, edit or delete an input: the add-ons’ input handler is expected to refuse other roles, though this has not been tested on these two add-ons (see The Input Handler). Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider at Not set: the add-on stamps cloud_provider itself. Check in Phase 7 that the events carry cloud_provider=azure (or gcp) with one value. See the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide.

AWS S3 Direct. On an HF that has both the Data TA and the Splunk Add-on for AWS, open AWS S3 Direct in the Data TA’s menu, create a backfill for one dashboard row and a short date range, and check that the events arrive with cloud_provider=aws (one value). The screen’s Create button needs admin_all_objects; without it the screen offers the generated configuration for an administrator to apply. See AWS S3 Direct.

docs.title: Asset & Identity Feed for ES Identity Management
docs.text:
The Splunk for SAP LogServ App feeds ES asset and identity management with an SAP system inventory, read from the ABAP gateway, HANA trace, ICM, SAP Router, Cloud Connector and Web Dispatcher logs, and with user identities from the HANA audit, sapstartsrv and sudo logs.

ES correlation searches that return the fields ES’s asset and identity correlation uses (commonly src, dest, dvc, user and src_user), and any app that queries asset_lookup_by_str or identity_lookup_expanded, get this context for SAP systems and accounts. Of the shipped LogServ searches, only the cross-stack authentication-failure search returns one of these fields (user); see Confirm correlation searches enrich notables.

docs.title: What ships
docs.text:
Two scheduled saved searches that emit CSV lookups every 4 hours:

Saved search Cadence Output lookup Schema splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed every 4h (cron 0 */4 * * *) splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets.csv ES Asset (17 std cols + 2 extra) splunk_sap_logserv_es_identity_feed every 4h (cron 1 */4 * * *) splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities.csv ES Identity (16 std cols + 1 extra)

The two feeds are scheduled one minute apart (:00 and :01) so they do not dispatch simultaneously.

Each feed reads all of its sources in one pass — a single search over the last 7 days, with no subsearch that Splunk could stop early — and replaces its CSV with the result:

  • An empty run keeps the last CSV. A run that finds no rows (an ingest outage, for example) writes nothing, so the previous inventory stays in place (outputlookup override_if_empty=false).
  • No row cap. The rows are sorted without a limit (sort 0), so an inventory larger than Splunk’s default sort limit of 10,000 rows is written whole.
  • A short-window run writes nothing. A run whose search window starts later than midnight six days ago (-6d@d) leaves the CSV as it is, so an ad-hoc run over the last hour cannot replace the 7-day inventory with a partial one. This applies to the scheduled runs too: if you override dispatch.earliest_time for either feed (Splunk Web: Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts → Edit → Advanced edit; Splunk Enterprise: local/savedsearches.conf), keep the window starting at or before -6d@d (the default is -7d@d), or every run writes nothing and the CSV stops updating without an error. To make a feed cheaper, run it less often (change its cron) instead.

docs.title: Asset feed
docs.text:
The Asset feed reads 6 inventory sources in one pass and consolidates by IP (when present) or DNS hostname:

  1. sap:abap:gateway events with local_ip=* → IP+host+SID
  2. sap:hana:tracelogs with hana_host=* → hostname+SID (no IP)
  3. sap:abap:icm with icm_local_ip=* → IP+host+SID
  4. sap:saprouter events → host-only, categorized as middleware
  5. sap:scc:audit events → host-only, middleware
  6. sap:webdispatcher:access events → host-only, application

After dedup, SAP-stack heuristics apply:

  • HANA database servers → priority=high, category=Server | Database | SAP HANA
  • Middleware (saprouter, SCC) → priority=high, category=Server | Middleware | SAP
  • NetWeaver application servers → priority=medium, category=Server | Application | SAP NetWeaver

Hardcoded fields (customer overrides via merger): - owner = "SAP-Operations" - bunit = "SAP" - is_expected = 1, should_timesync = 1, should_update = 1, requires_av = 0

Empty-on-emit (out of scope): - mac — log data doesn’t carry MAC addresses - nt_host — Windows hostname not derivable from SAP logs - lat / long / city / country — not in log data - pci_domain — out of scope for SAP-side derivation

Two extra columns for SOC analyst readability. They are not standard ES asset fields, so whether ES keeps them in its merged asset records depends on your ES asset field settings; they are always in the CSV itself: - _sap_sids — comma-joined list of SAP SIDs hosted on this asset - _roles — comma-joined list of roles (e.g., SAP NetWeaver ABAP,SAP NetWeaver ABAP ICM)

docs.title: Identity feed
docs.text:
The Identity feed reads 5 user sources in one pass and consolidates by identity:

  1. sap:hana:audit executing_user → tagged hana_admin
  2. sap:hana:audit target_user → tagged hana_target
  3. sap:sapstartsrv auth_user → tagged sap_host_user
  4. linux:sudolog os_user → tagged sudo_invoker
  5. linux:sudolog target_user → tagged sudo_target

Priority and category are set by two separate rule lists; in each, the first rule that matches wins (matching is case-insensitive).

priority:

Rule priority Identity is SYSTEM or root critical Identity appears in a hana_admin or hana_target source high Identity ends in adm (SAP <sid>adm service accounts) medium Otherwise low

category:

Rule category Identity is SYSTEM or starts with _SYS_ or SAP_ SAP HANA system account Identity ends in adm SAP service account Identity appears in a hana_admin or hana_target source SAP HANA user Identity appears in a sap_host_user source SAP host control user Identity appears in a sudo_invoker or sudo_target source OS user Otherwise SAP user

So an <sid>adm account that also appears in the HANA audit log gets priority high, and a _SYS_ or SAP_ account gets high only when it appears in the HANA audit log (otherwise medium if it ends in adm, else low).

watchlist=1 for critical+high; watchlist=0 for medium+low. ES surfaces watchlisted identities in its identity-risk dashboards.

One extra column: - _source_type_str — comma-joined list of source-type tags this identity appears in

docs.title: Customer wire-up
docs.text:
After the App installs, the lookups don’t exist until the saved searches first run (within 4h of install). The same applies after an App upgrade if your upgrade method does not keep the App’s lookups/ directory: the two CSVs are written there at run time and are not part of the package, so they exist again after the feeds’ next run. To populate immediately:

# Dispatch the asset feed
curl -sk -u admin:<pw> -X POST \
  -d dispatch.earliest_time=-7d@d -d dispatch.latest_time=now \
  https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/saved/searches/splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed/dispatch

# Dispatch the identity feed
curl -sk -u admin:<pw> -X POST \
  -d dispatch.earliest_time=-7d@d -d dispatch.latest_time=now \
  https://<splunk-host>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/saved/searches/splunk_sap_logserv_es_identity_feed/dispatch

The curl calls need the search head’s management port (8089). On Splunk Cloud Platform you may not be able to reach that port from your network. If you cannot reach it, run each feed from Splunk Web instead: Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts, find splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed and splunk_sap_logserv_es_identity_feed, and choose Run for each, signed in as an admin-tier user. Check the time range the run uses: it must start at or before -6d@d (the feed’s saved window starts at -7d@d), or the run writes nothing. Or wait for the feeds’ next scheduled run, which comes within 4 hours.

The explicit dispatch.earliest_time / dispatch.latest_time arguments matter: a REST dispatch does not apply the stanza’s own dispatch window, and each run that finds rows fully overwrites the CSV. The -7d@d window above writes the full inventory; a run whose window starts later than -6d@d writes nothing and leaves the CSV as it was (see What ships). Both feeds set dispatchAs = user: the dispatch runs as the account you call it with, so use an admin-tier account (a non-admin’s run cannot write the CSV), and -7d@d snaps to midnight in that account’s time zone. Wait for both jobs to complete (seconds on a small dataset; longer at customer volume — the feeds read several sourcetypes over 7 days), then verify:

| inputlookup splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets | head 5
| inputlookup splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities | head 5

docs.title: Add to ES Identity Management
docs.text:
In Splunk Web on the ES search head, open Enterprise Security’s asset and identity management settings and add two lookup sources:

  1. An asset source that reads the lookup definition splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets (you can give the source the same name).
  2. An identity source that reads the lookup definition splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities.

The App ships both lookup definitions (in its default/transforms.conf) and shares them with all apps (export = system), so ES can read them. The names of ES’s menus and form fields differ between ES versions; follow the ES documentation for your version on adding an asset or identity lookup. After ES’s next merge of its asset and identity sources, verify by running:

| inputlookup asset_lookup_by_str | search asset="hec53v013858"
| inputlookup identity_lookup_expanded | search identity="xcjadm"

The merged record should now include priority, category, bunit from our feed (alongside any CMDB-sourced fields if present).

docs.title: Confirm correlation searches enrich notables
docs.text: ES enriches a notable from the fields its asset and identity correlation uses, commonly asset fields such as src, dest and dvc, and identity fields such as user and src_user (check the correlation settings of your ES). Of the shipped correlation searches, the cross-stack authentication-failure search returns user, so its notables in Incident Review carry the identity’s priority, category and watchlist flag (for example for user=xcjadm). The other searches name accounts in fields such as executing_user or auth_user and hosts in host, which ES does not correlate on, so their notables are not enriched as shipped. To enrich them, add an eval that copies those fields (for example | eval user=executing_user, dest=host) to the search (Correlation Searches → Customer tuning).

docs.title: Integration with CMDB (additive mode)
docs.text:
If the customer already has a CMDB feeding ES’s Asset framework, our feed is additive:

  • ES merges the records from all of its asset sources
  • Where two sources disagree on a field (e.g., CMDB says owner=John, our feed says owner=SAP-Operations), the precedence you give the sources in ES’s asset and identity management settings decides which value ES keeps; how precedence is set depends on your ES version (see the ES documentation)
  • Our SAP-stack-specific category values (e.g., Server | Database | SAP HANA) fill in gaps where the CMDB doesn’t have SAP-aware data; _sap_sids and _roles do too where your ES asset field settings keep them (see Asset feed)

To make CMDB authoritative for owner/bunit while keeping our SAP categorization:

  1. Give the CMDB source precedence over our feed in ES’s asset and identity management settings
  2. ES applies higher-precedence values for shared fields (owner, bunit)
  3. Our category fills in (CMDB likely doesn’t have it), with _sap_sids and _roles where your ES keeps them

docs.title: Disabling the auto-feed
docs.text:
If a customer doesn’t want our auto-feed (e.g., CMDB is fully authoritative):

  1. Splunk Web → Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts
  2. Filter by splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed and splunk_sap_logserv_es_identity_feed
  3. Edit each → Disable
  4. Save

The lookup CSVs remain on disk (last-known state) but are no longer refreshed. A disabled feed does not re-create its CSV, so an App upgrade that does not keep the App’s lookups/ directory leaves ES without it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• No MAC addresses. SAP application logs don’t expose MAC addresses. Customers needing MAC-based asset resolution must source it elsewhere (DHCP logs, network gear).
  • Short hostnames vs FQDNs. Our dns column is the host field as Splunk indexed it. If Splunk indexed short names but customer DNS uses FQDNs, ES asset lookups by FQDN won’t match these rows. Supply the FQDNs from another asset source (your CMDB, or an override CSV of your own; see the last caveat).
  • No identity start/end dates. Our feed doesn’t track account creation/deactivation. Customers needing startDate/endDate for behavior baselining should layer an HR-system-sourced identity feed alongside ours.
  • A partial run still overwrites. The feeds keep the last CSV only when a run finds nothing. A run that finds part of the estate — one cloud’s ingest stopped for more than 7 days, say — writes the smaller inventory, and the missing assets and identities drop out of ES until their data returns.
  • Static priority/category logic. The heuristics here are SPL case() rules. Customer-specific overrides require a manual override CSV (e.g., my_company_sap_asset_overrides.csv), added as an ES asset source with precedence over our feed.

docs.title: Example output shape (reference environment — your values will differ)
docs.text:
After a first dispatch in a reference environment:

Assets: 22 unique rows - 6 HANA database servers (high priority) - 6 middleware servers (high priority — SCC + saprouter) - 10 NetWeaver application servers (medium priority)

Identities: 31 unique rows - 1 critical OS user (root) - 1 critical HANA system account (SYSTEM) - 1 high HANA system account - 20 high HANA users (DDIC, BKPADMIN, ENCRYPTMON, …) - 4 high SAP service accounts - 2 medium SAP service accounts - 2 low OS users

docs.title: Behavioral & Anomaly Detections
docs.text:
The Splunk for SAP LogServ App ships 4 statistically-baselined anomaly detections that fire when an entity (user, host, edge) deviates from its own historical pattern. They complement the deterministic correlation searches by surfacing threats that don’t match a known threat-pattern signature — credential misuse spikes, latency excursions, integration-volume drift, and after-hours admin activity that’s anomalous for that specific admin.

All 4 use stats-based Z-score detection that runs against built-in Splunk SPL — no Splunk Machine Learning Toolkit (MLTK) dependency. Customers with MLTK installed can swap the stats clauses for fit / apply for sharper baselines.

docs.title: The 4 anomaly searches
docs.text:
Search name What it baselines Z-score threshold Schedule splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume Per-user authentication-event count, hourly buckets Z > 3 + count > 10 daily (02:30) splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_webdisp_response Per-host Web Dispatcher average response time, from the hourly logserv_web_timing_rollup Z > 3 + avg > 200 ms daily (03:30) splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_topology_edge_volume Per-edge call volume from KV Store edge bucket data abs(Z) > 3 + count > 10 daily (04:30) splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin Per-admin off-hours activity, daily buckets Z > 2 + count > 5 daily (05:30)

All four anomaly searches run once daily (scheduler-local early morning): an anomalous hour is reported the following morning, not within the hour.

All 4 emit action.notable=1 (ES Notable Review) and action.risk=1 (RBA — risk score 30-40 / medium).

docs.title: How the stats-based Z-score works
docs.text:
Each search builds the baseline from the same 30-day window of data that’s being scored, using eventstats to compute per-entity mean and standard deviation across the window’s hourly (or daily) buckets. Every bucket of the previous day is then compared (the searches run daily):

| bin _time span=1h
| stats count by entity, _time
| eventstats avg(count) AS avg_count, stdev(count) AS stdev_count by entity
| eval z_score = round((count - avg_count) / stdev_count, 2)
| where _time >= relative_time(now(), "-1d@d") AND z_score > 3 AND count > 10

Combined thresholds (Z + minimum-floor) keep the false-positive rate low:

  • Pure Z-score on a low-volume entity: count=2, avg=0.1, stdev=0.5 → Z = 3.8, but absolute count is meaningless. The count > 10 floor filters this.
  • Pure absolute count: count=15, avg=14, stdev=3 → above floor but Z = 0.33, statistically normal. The Z > 3 requirement filters this.
  • Both pass → genuinely anomalous: count=100, avg=12, stdev=4 → Z = 22, count well above floor.

The thresholds are tunable per search via the where z_score > N clause (see Tuning).

docs.title: 1. Per-User Authentication Volume Z-Score
docs.text:
Compares each user’s authentication-event count in each hourly bucket of the previous day to that user’s own 30-day hourly baseline. Fires when Z > 3 AND count > 10.

Threat model: Brute-force attempts against a previously dormant account, or a misconfigured client polling at high frequency.

FP profile: Low. Healthy environments show 0-2 hits per hour from genuine traffic spikes (batch jobs, planned cutovers). If the traffic of an account is legitimate, exclude the account in the search: add | search NOT auth_user IN ("<account>", ...) after the eval that sets auth_user (see Tuning).

docs.title: 2. Webdispatcher Response-Time Anomaly
docs.text:
Compares each host’s per-hour latency over the previous day to that host’s own 30-day baseline. Fires when Z > 3 AND avg > 200 ms.

Threat model: Backend health degradation, network path issue, or DDoS-style request flood degrading response time.

FP profile: Low for production hosts on consistent workloads; can be moderate on hosts with bursty workloads (overnight batches, end-of-month processing). Disable the search for planned heavy-load windows, or exclude the affected hosts (see Tuning).

docs.title: 3. Topology Edge Call-Volume Anomaly
docs.text:
Reads pre-aggregated edge bucket rows directly from the logserv_topology_edges KV Store collection. Detects edges whose hourly call_count over the previous day is statistically anomalous vs. that edge’s own 30-day baseline. Fires when abs(Z) > 3 AND count > 10.

Threat model: Surge = abnormally high cross-system traffic (DDoS, lateral-movement automation, failed retry storm). Drop = integration outage on either the source or target side.

FP profile: Low. The KV Store’s per-edge time series is much cleaner than raw event data, so the baseline is stable. The bidirectional check (abs(Z) > 3 rather than just Z > 3) catches surges and drops, with one limit: the count > 10 floor applies to drops too, so a drop is flagged only while the edge still has more than 10 calls in the hour. An edge that stops completely writes no bucket row for the hour, so a full outage is not flagged by this search.

Why this search is different: It reads pre-aggregated edge bucket rows from the topology KV Store rather than scanning raw events, so its cost scales with the number of edges rather than event volume.

docs.title: 4. After-Hours Admin Activity Anomaly
docs.text:
Per-admin off-hours activity baseline vs. that admin’s 30-day off-hours pattern, in daily buckets. Off-hours means before 08:00 or from 18:00 on any day, read with strftime(_time, "%H") in the time zone the search runs in (the search head’s default time zone for the scheduled run). Admins are the sap:hana:audit users with is_admin_user="true", the same field as the E3 correlation search; E3. After-Hours Admin Data Access says which accounts it matches and how to change it. Lower Z threshold (Z > 2) than the other 3 searches because admin off-hours activity is naturally rare; a smaller deviation is still significant. Fires when Z > 2 AND count > 5.

Threat model: Admin-account compromise (attacker active outside the admin’s normal window), or insider conducting unauthorized off-hours operations.

FP profile: Low for environments with clear business hours. Higher during planned weekend cutovers — those should map to documented change tickets.

docs.title: MLTK upgrade path (optional)
docs.text:
If you have the Splunk Machine Learning Toolkit (MLTK) installed, you can replace the Z-score steps with an MLTK model trained by fit and applied by apply. For per-entity baselines, MLTK’s DensityFunction algorithm can learn one distribution per value of its by fields and flag outliers. An outline, for example:

Stats-based step MLTK-based replacement (outline) eventstats avg(count) AS avg_count, stdev(count) AS stdev_count by entity and eval z_score = ... A training search over the baseline window that ends in a fit DensityFunction on count, by the entity field, into a model of your own where z_score > 3 In the detection search, apply that model, then keep the rows that the model marks as outliers

Take the exact syntax, the options (distribution type, threshold) and the names of the output fields from the MLTK documentation for your version; the App ships no MLTK search to copy.

MLTK adds:

  • Per-entity model persistence (the baseline is a saved model, not a per-search calculation)
  • Daily and weekly cycles, by adding a time field such as the hour of day or the day of week to the by fields
  • Distributions other than the normal one that the Z-score assumes (DensityFunction), and other outlier algorithms such as OneClassSVM

For most SAP environments the stats-based approach is sufficient. MLTK becomes valuable when you need:

  1. Multi-week seasonal patterns (workload that varies by day-of-week or week-of-month)
  2. Non-Gaussian distributions (network traffic with heavy-tailed shapes)
  3. Per-entity model lifecycle management (training models offline, deploying via export)

To migrate a single search to MLTK without breaking the others, change the search of that one search only (see Tuning).

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Adjust thresholds by editing the search of a given search: in Splunk Web (Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise), Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts → Edit → Advanced edit; on Splunk Enterprise, alternatively, override the search = line in local/savedsearches.conf (never edit default/). An override replaces the whole search, so start from the full shipped line and change only the clause you need. For example, the end of the user-volume search:

[splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume]
search = `sap_logserv_idx_macro` ... | where _time >= relative_time(now(), "-1d@d") AND z_score > 4 AND count > 25 | sort -z_score

General tuning advice:

  • Too many FPs: Raise the Z threshold (3 → 4 → 5) AND/OR raise the absolute-count floor.
  • Missing real attacks: Lower the Z threshold (3 → 2) — but expect more noise; pair with tighter floor.
  • Bursty workloads triggering hits: Add a where NOT (entity IN (<known burst entities>)) exclusion clause, with the search’s own entity field (auth_user, host, or id for the topology edges) in place of entity.
  • Service-account auth volumes drowning out human user signal: split by username pattern — e.g. | eval is_svc=if(match(auth_user, "(?i)(adm$|^sapservice|_svc$|^svc_|_batch$|_daemon$|^sap_)"), 1, 0), the same classification splunk_sap_logserv_es_service_account_interactive applies — into two stanzas: one for service accounts (higher floor), one for humans (lower floor + tighter Z).

docs.title: AI Assistant integration
docs.text:
Each of the 4 anomaly searches has a corresponding entry in the AI Assistant predefined-prompt catalog under the Security pack:

  • security.anomaly_user_auth_volume
  • security.anomaly_webdisp_response
  • security.anomaly_topology_edge_volume
  • security.anomaly_after_hours_admin

Once an admin has turned the AI Assistant on (it ships turned off; see Set Up the AI Assistant), SOC analysts can dispatch them on demand from the AI Assistant’s predefined-prompt browser (Security pack) and read the result table plus its static interpretation guidance. A prompt fails while its saved search is disabled; to keep the prompts but stop the daily runs, turn off only the schedule (Disabling or tuning the ES content). (Asking the assistant in natural language to explain an anomaly requires the free-form path, which activates once an LLM provider credential is configured.)

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Correlation Searches & RBA — Deterministic correlation searches; complement the anomaly detections here
  • Threat Intelligence Integration — Customer-managed CSV lookups for IOC matching
  • Asset & Identity Feed — Identity context that feeds both deterministic + behavioral detections

docs.title: CIM Compliance
docs.text: The Splunk for SAP LogServ App tags the SAP-side sourcetypes that fit a Splunk Common Information Model (CIM) data model (listed below) into those models, so ES correlation searches and RBA risk framework can consume the data through the standard | datamodel <Model> search ... interface.

docs.title: CIM models in scope
docs.text:
The App declares participation in four CIM data models in app.manifest under info.commonInformationModels (Authentication, Change, Network Sessions, Web). It additionally tags events for the Network Resolution (DNS) data model and the Web data model’s Proxy dataset via the absorbed ISC BIND / Squid parsers (tags.conf) without declaring those in the manifest. The data models must search the LogServ index for any of this to show; see the prerequisites.

Model Use case SAP-side sourcetypes Authentication login attempts (success / failure) sap:hana:audit (CONNECT events and the SYSTEM Logins category), sap:sapstartsrv (authentication events), sap:scc:audit (ACCESS_DENIED), linux:sudolog Change account / role / config modifications sap:hana:audit (user, role and privilege DDL events), sap:scc:audit (CONFIGURATION_CHANGED, SERVICE_STARTED, SERVICE_STOPPED) Network_Sessions TCP-level connection tracking sap:abap:gateway (events with a peer IP), sap:saprouter (connection events) Network / Resolution (DNS) DNS query / resolution activity (absorbed ISC BIND parser) isc:bind:query, isc:bind:queryerror Web HTTP request/response sap:webdispatcher:access, sap:scc:http_access, squid:access (absorbed Squid proxy parser)

For sourcetypes that don’t fit any stock CIM model (HANA tracelogs, ABAP application-tier internal logs), the App still extracts rich search-time fields and adds vendor_product = "SAP NetWeaver ABAP" (or similar) for cross-cutting search consistency, but doesn’t tag them into a CIM model.

docs.title: How the tagging works
docs.text: Two configuration files drive CIM tagging:

docs.title: default/eventtypes.conf
docs.text:
Defines 17 eventtypes. Thirteen are CIM-tagged in default/tags.conf — 10 SAP-specific plus isc_bind_query, isc_bind_queryerror, and squid_access; the remaining four (sap_hana_audit_high_risk, sap_abap_audit_event, isc_bind_lameserver, isc_bind_transfer) exist for dashboard/search convenience and are deliberately not tagged into a model. For example:

[sap_hana_authentication]
search = sourcetype="sap:hana:audit" (action_type="CONNECT" OR audit_category="SYSTEM Logins")

[sap_hana_change]
search = sourcetype="sap:hana:audit" (action_type IN ("ALTER USER","CREATE USER","DROP USER","GRANT","REVOKE", ...) OR audit_category IN ("User Administration", ...))

A single sourcetype like sap:hana:audit can route to multiple eventtypes — CONNECT events go to sap_hana_authentication, while DDL events go to sap_hana_change.

docs.title: default/tags.conf
docs.text:
Activates CIM tags on each eventtype:

[eventtype=sap_hana_authentication]
authentication = enabled

[eventtype=sap_hana_change]
change = enabled

[eventtype=sap_abap_gateway_session]
network = enabled
session = enabled

When you query tag=authentication (or use the Authentication data model), Splunk includes events from every eventtype that has authentication = enabled.

docs.title: CIM-required field coverage
docs.text: For each tagged sourcetype, the App’s default/props.conf provides the CIM-required fields via EXTRACT-, EVAL-, and FIELDALIAS- directives.

docs.title: Example: sap:hana:audit
docs.text:
CIM field Source action EVAL — case(action_type=="CONNECT" AND status=="SUCCESSFUL", "success", action_type=="CONNECT" AND status IN ("UNSUCCESSFUL","FAILED"), "failure", match(action_type,"(?i)create"), "created", match(action_type,"(?i)alter|grant|revoke"), "modified", ...) app EVAL literal "sap_hana" vendor_product EVAL literal "SAP HANA" user FIELDALIAS-user = executing_user (the user PERFORMING the action) dest_user FIELDALIAS-dest_user = target_user (the affected user, for Change model) src FIELDALIAS-src = client_ip src_host FIELDALIAS-src_host = audit_hostname (the client’s host name; host stays the HANA host that wrote the record) dest FIELDALIAS-dest = db_hostname change_type EVAL — case(match(action_type,"(?i)(user|role|grant|revoke)"), "account", ...) object FIELDALIAS-object = target_user object_category EVAL — case(match(action_type,"(?i)user"), "user account", ...)

Same pattern applies to other sourcetypes. See default/props.conf in the App package for the full per-sourcetype field-mapping detail.

docs.title: Verifying CIM compliance
docs.text:
Run the following on a Splunk instance with the App installed (and the underlying SAP-side data ingested):

| datamodel Authentication search
| search sourcetype IN ("sap:hana:audit","sap:sapstartsrv","sap:scc:audit","linux:sudolog")
| stats count by sourcetype Authentication.action

You should see results like these (illustrative counts from a reference environment — your values will differ):

sourcetype                  Authentication.action  count
linux:sudolog               success                369
sap:hana:audit              failure                19
sap:hana:audit              success                604
sap:sapstartsrv             failure                566
sap:scc:audit               failure                27

Repeat for the other models:

| datamodel Change search | search sourcetype IN ("sap:hana:audit","sap:scc:audit") | stats count by sourcetype All_Changes.action
| datamodel Web search | search sourcetype IN ("sap:webdispatcher:access","sap:scc:http_access") | stats count by sourcetype Web.action
| datamodel Network_Sessions search | search sourcetype IN ("sap:abap:gateway","sap:saprouter") | stats count by sourcetype

If | datamodel ... returns rows for our sourcetypes, ES can consume them — every standard ES Authentication / Change / Web / Network_Sessions correlation search will include SAP-side events automatically.

docs.title: Sourcetype coverage matrix
docs.text: Sourcetype Tagged into Severity sap:hana:audit Authentication + Change (CONNECT events: high-priority for ES Auth dashboards) sap:webdispatcher:access Web medium sap:scc:http_access Web medium sap:abap:gateway Network_Sessions medium sap:saprouter Network_Sessions medium sap:sapstartsrv Authentication medium sap:scc:audit Authentication (ACCESS_DENIED) + Change (CONFIGURATION_CHANGED, SERVICE_STARTED, SERVICE_STOPPED) medium linux:sudolog Authentication + privileged medium isc:bind:query Network + Resolution (DNS) — absorbed ISC BIND parser medium isc:bind:queryerror Network + Resolution (DNS) — absorbed ISC BIND parser medium squid:access Web + Proxy — absorbed Squid proxy parser medium

docs.title: F5: Web events appear at two tiers
docs.text:
Both sap:webdispatcher:access (front-end TLS-terminating load balancer) and sap:scc:http_access (backend tunnel traversal) capture HTTP events for the same logical request chain. ES’s Web data model surfaces both as distinct events.

This is correct CIM-aligned behavior — each tier records its own view, and ES dashboards can drill into either. But correlation queries that count “unique HTTP requests” should dedupe carefully (e.g., by the request-id field if both tiers carry one, or by _time window + client_ip + uri).

docs.title: F6: Some sourcetypes have no clean CIM fit
docs.text:
ABAP application-tier internal logs (sap:abap:dispatcher, sap:abap:enqueueserver, sap:abap:event, sap:abap:messageserver, sap:abap:sapstartsrv, sap:abap:workprocess) and HANA tracelogs (sap:hana:tracelogs) don’t map cleanly to any stock Splunk CIM model. The App provides rich search-time fields for them but doesn’t force a poor-fit mapping. Our own dashboards consume these directly; ES correlation searches built on these would need to use sourcetype-explicit SPL rather than CIM-data-model search.

The ICM trace (sap:abap:icm) is not tagged either. dev_icm records sessions, connections and the ICM’s own warning and error messages, not HTTP requests with a status, method and URL, so it has no honest Web data model mapping. On ICM connection lines, src and dest follow the connection’s direction (icm_conn_role): the side that opened the connection is src.

Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading.

docs.title: sap:abap:audit currently has minimal extraction
docs.text: The ABAP security audit log (sap:abap:audit) is binary/hex format. The App extracts SID + instance + the audit marker; richer field extraction would require a more accessible source format (e.g. an SM20/SM19 export). As a result, this sourcetype is currently NOT tagged into Authentication or Change — events are in the index but not in CIM dashboards. Expected to land in a future release.

docs.title: Correlation Searches & RBA
docs.text:
The Splunk for SAP LogServ App ships 19 correlation searches in three tiers:

  • 6 base correlation searches — the starter pack, signal-heavy and FP-tuned for the SAP-specific threat patterns SOC analysts encounter most.
  • 6 extended cross-stack correlation searches — added in the extended ES content pack. Detect cross-source chains that customers can’t easily author themselves because they require SAP-specific knowledge of which sourcetype emits the auth event vs. the privilege change vs. the data event.
  • 3 threat-intel correlation searches + 4 behavioral / anomaly searches — see Threat Intelligence Integration and Behavioral & Anomaly Detections for those.

Plus 1 tier-2 Risk Notable that aggregates risk events from all 19 detection searches and fires when accumulated risk on a single object crosses a threshold (Risk-Based Alerting / RBA).

All correlation searches are scheduled saved searches in default/savedsearches.conf. For ES Content Management, the App also ships correlation-search metadata in default/correlationsearches.conf: one stanza for each of the 19 detection searches and the Risk Notable, with rule_name, rule_title, security_domain, severity and nes_fields.

Several searches compare the hour of an event against business hours, 08:00 to 18:00: E3 and E5 below, and the after-hours admin anomaly search (Behavioral & Anomaly Detections). They read the hour with strftime(_time, "%H") and treat an event as outside business hours when it falls before 08:00 or at 18:00 or later, on any day; E5 also counts all of Saturday and Sunday. strftime renders in the time zone of the user the search runs as, so a scheduled run uses the search head’s default time zone. To use other hours, change every oh_hour comparison in the search, so that all of them use the same window: E3 has two (one for the HANA events, one in the subsearch that counts Web Dispatcher requests), E5 has one (next to its day-of-week test), and the after-hours admin anomaly search has one (see Customer tuning).

docs.title: The 6 base correlation searches
docs.text: # Search name What it detects Severity Schedule 1 splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation HANA GRANT WITH ADMIN OPTION or any ALTER USER on the SYSTEM user high hourly 2 splunk_sap_logserv_es_cross_stack_auth_failure Same user fails authentication on 2+ different SAP stacks (HANA, sapstartsrv, SCC, sudo) within the same window high hourly 3 splunk_sap_logserv_es_abap_gateway_anomalous_peer New ABAP gateway peer IP not seen (or seen <5 times) in the prior 30 days medium hourly 4 splunk_sap_logserv_es_scc_access_denied_burst 3+ SCC ACCESS_DENIED events on a single host within 1h medium hourly 5 splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_failed_connect_spike 5+ failed HANA CONNECT attempts by a single user on a single host within 1h medium hourly 6 splunk_sap_logserv_es_oom_kill_burst 3+ Linux OOM-killer (out-of-memory) events on a single host within 1h medium hourly

docs.title: Why “6 starter, well-vetted” instead of 15-20
docs.text:
The starter set is intentionally small + signal-heavy:

  • Each search has been dry-run on live data before shipping
  • Most return 0 rows on healthy-environment data (low FP rate by design — they fire on real attack patterns)
  • Easier to false-positive-tune in customer environments
  • Easier to document for SOC analysts during onboarding

You can add your own correlation searches on top. Use a shipped search as the model, and keep your search under its own name, so an App upgrade does not replace your work. The hourly correlation searches share a pattern you can keep: a 60-minute dispatch window that ends 5 minutes before the run (dispatch.earliest_time = -65m@m, dispatch.latest_time = -5m@m; four set their own earliest / latest in the search instead), the action.notable parameters (severity, rule title, security domain) and an action.risk list of risk objects and scores. The Risk Notable counts only the searches it names in its source IN (...) list, so add a new search’s name there if its risk should count toward the threshold.

There are two ways to make the copy:

  • In ES Content Management, as a new correlation search, with a shipped search’s SPL and actions as the model. ES then manages it as a correlation search.
  • In Splunk Web, with Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts → Edit → Clone. The copy is an ordinary saved search. Before you rely on it, open it with Edit → Advanced edit and check that it kept the shipped search’s action.notable and action.risk settings, which raise its notables and risk events. It has no ES correlation-search metadata: the App’s default/correlationsearches.conf, which holds that metadata (rule_name and the other entries), has one stanza per shipped search name, and none for the copy.

docs.title: 1. HANA Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
`sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype="sap:hana:audit" tag=change
  (action_type=GRANT OR (action_type="ALTER USER" AND target_user="SYSTEM"))
| where (action_type="GRANT" AND match(sql_statement, "(?i)WITH ADMIN OPTION"))
    OR (action_type="ALTER USER" AND target_user="SYSTEM")
| stats count, latest(_time) AS last_seen, values(sql_statement) AS sql_statements
        by executing_user, target_user, host, action_type
| sort -count

match() must not appear in a base-search clause

match() is an eval-only function — in a base-search position it silently matches nothing, so the GRANT disjunct would never fire. That is why the shipped search pre-filters broadly in the base clause and applies the match() predicate in | where. Keep that structure if you copy this search as a template.

Threat model: A SAP HANA admin or compromised account uses GRANT ... WITH ADMIN OPTION (creating a privilege-pivot path) or runs ALTER USER SYSTEM ... (modifying the SYSTEM superuser). Both warrant change-ticket review.

FP profile: Medium. ALTER USER SYSTEM RESET CONNECT ATTEMPTS is operationally common after lockout recovery. SOC needs to correlate with change tickets or whitelist routine maintenance.

docs.title: 2. Cross-Stack Authentication Failure Burst
docs.text:
| datamodel Authentication search
| search Authentication.action="failure" sourcetype IN ("sap:hana:audit","sap:sapstartsrv","sap:scc:audit","linux:sudolog")
| rename Authentication.user AS user
| stats values(sourcetype) AS sourcetypes, dc(sourcetype) AS distinct_sourcetypes,
        count, latest(_time) AS last_seen by user
| where distinct_sourcetypes >= 2
| sort -distinct_sourcetypes -count

Threat model: Credential stuffing or coordinated brute force. The same compromised credential is tried against multiple SAP stacks. A user appearing in failure events across 2+ sourcetypes within the same 60-minute dispatch window is the highest-signal indicator of this attack pattern.

FP profile: Very low. Only fires on actual cross-stack pattern; healthy environments produce 0 rows.

docs.title: 3. ABAP Gateway Anomalous Peer
docs.text:
`sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype="sap:abap:gateway" peer_ip=*
   earliest=-1h@h latest=now
| stats count by peer_ip host
| join type=outer peer_ip [
    search `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype="sap:abap:gateway" peer_ip=*
       earliest=-30d@d latest=-1h@h
    | stats count AS historical_count by peer_ip
  ]
| where isnull(historical_count) OR historical_count < 5
| sort -count

Threat model: A new RFC client appears at the SAP ABAP gateway. Could be a legitimate new integration or an unauthorized scanning attempt. The 30-day baseline + 1-hour detection window catches anything new.

FP profile: Low. Will fire on genuine new peers; SOC reviews → either whitelists or blocks.

docs.title: 4. SCC ACCESS_DENIED Burst
docs.text:
`sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype="sap:scc:audit" scc_audit_type=ACCESS_DENIED
   earliest=-1h@h latest=now
| stats count, latest(_time) AS last_seen, values(scc_account_id) AS account_ids by host
| where count >= 3
| sort -count

Threat model: SAP Cloud Connector logs ACCESS_DENIED when an inbound tunnel request hits a backend that isn’t on the SCC allowlist. 3+ events on a single host in an hour signals either misconfigured allowlist or external probing.

FP profile: Low. ACCESS_DENIED events are sparse under normal operations.

docs.title: 5. HANA Failed CONNECT Spike Per User
docs.text:
`sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype="sap:hana:audit" action_type=CONNECT status=UNSUCCESSFUL
   earliest=-1h@h latest=now
| stats count, latest(_time) AS last_seen, values(client_ip) AS client_ips,
        values(src_host) AS src_hosts by executing_user host
| where count >= 5
| sort -count

Threat model: A user repeatedly failing HANA CONNECT (5+ in an hour) — above the noise floor of routine SCC tunnel-credential failures (~1-2/hr).

FP profile: Low. 5/hr threshold is above routine failure rates.

docs.title: 6. Linux OOM-Killer Burst
docs.text:
Fires when a host logs 3 or more Linux OOM-killer (out-of-memory) events within an hour (sourcetypes linux:warn and syslog). Security domain endpoint.

Threat model: A spike of kernel out-of-memory kills can indicate a memory-exhaustion attack, a runaway/compromised process, or resource-starvation that takes SAP services offline. Clustered OOM kills warrant operational + security review.

FP profile: Low to medium. Legitimately busy hosts under memory pressure can produce bursts; correlate with known workload spikes or capacity events.

docs.title: Extended cross-stack pack (v2)
docs.text:
Six additional correlation searches detect cross-source threat chains that customers can’t easily author themselves. The patterns require SAP-specific knowledge of which sourcetype emits the authentication event vs. the privilege change vs. the data-tier event — knowledge that’s inside the LogServ App rather than in stock Splunk content.

# Search name What it detects Severity Schedule E1 splunk_sap_logserv_es_lateral_movement Same user authenticates successfully into 3+ HANA SIDs within 60s high hourly E2 splunk_sap_logserv_es_privilege_chain Same account on one HANA host: auth failure, auth success and a privilege change in the same hour (in any order) high hourly E3 splunk_sap_logserv_es_after_hours_admin_data_access HANA admin user active in the HANA audit log outside business hours; each result also carries a count of the host’s off-hours Web Dispatcher requests (normally 0 on the scheduled run; see E3) high hourly E4 splunk_sap_logserv_es_service_account_interactive Service account (identified by username pattern) generated interactive HANA CONNECT medium hourly E5 splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_user_creation_off_hours CREATE USER on HANA outside business hours or on weekends medium hourly E6 splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_mass_drop 5+ DROP statements by a single user on a single host within 10 min high hourly

docs.title: E1. Lateral Movement
docs.text:
Same user authenticates successfully into 3+ SAP HANA SIDs within a 60-second window. The cross-SID hop pattern is the canonical lateral-movement signal across the SAP estate.

Threat model: An attacker with valid credentials probing the estate to find which systems the credential is authorized on. Healthy environments show this only for monitoring service accounts that legitimately poll every SID.

FP profile: Low — most environments have monitoring service accounts that legitimately span SIDs. Exclude those accounts in the search: add | search NOT auth_user IN ("<account>", ...) after the eval that sets auth_user (see Customer tuning).

docs.title: E2. Privilege Chain (Credential Stuffing → Escalation)
docs.text:
Same account on a single HANA host has BOTH authentication failures AND a successful authentication AND a privilege-change event (GRANT, ALTER USER, CREATE USER/ROLE) within a 1-hour window. The search counts the three kinds of event; it does not check their order. Highest-priority investigation pattern in the SAP-side ES content.

Threat model: Credential stuffing → established access → escalation chain. The textbook compromise pattern.

FP profile: Very low. Healthy admin operations look like (success + change), not (failure + success + change).

docs.title: E3. After-Hours Admin Data Access
docs.text:
An admin user is active in the HANA audit log outside business hours (before 08:00 or from 18:00). The search groups the off-hours HANA audit events by admin user and HANA host. For each result it adds the number of off-hours Web Dispatcher requests on the same host (host_web_events, read from the App’s hourly rollup; 0 when it finds none), as context: it does not require web traffic, and it does not match the web requests to the user. On the scheduled run this count is normally 0, whatever the web traffic was: the rollup writes an hour’s row only after that hour has ended, and the search’s 60-minute window ends before then. Run on demand over a longer time range, the search shows the off-hours requests.

“Admin user” means is_admin_user="true", a field the App sets on sap:hana:audit events when executing_user contains admin (case-insensitive) or is one of three account names from the App’s reference environment. Apart from those three names, HANA’s SYSTEM user and SAP <sid>adm accounts do not match. If your admin accounts are named differently, change the is_admin_user calculated field for sap:hana:audit, which the App ships as the EVAL-is_admin_user line under [sap:hana:audit] in its default/props.conf (Splunk Web: Settings → Fields → Calculated fields, as an admin-tier user; Splunk Enterprise: the same line in the App’s local/props.conf, never in default/). The same field drives the after-hours admin anomaly search.

Threat model: Admin-account compromise → data exfiltration via authenticated session that spans the database and HTTP tiers. Off-hours timing reduces the likelihood of being noticed in real time.

FP profile: Low for human admin accounts; moderate for service accounts that legitimately do this. Exclude those accounts in the search: add NOT executing_user IN ("<account>", ...) to its base search, before the first | (see Customer tuning).

docs.title: E4. Service-Account Interactive HANA Login
docs.text:
Service accounts generated interactive HANA CONNECT events. Service accounts are identified inside the search itself by username pattern against executing_user (adm$, ^sapservice, _svc$, ^svc_, _batch$, _daemon$, ^sap_). Service accounts should run programmatic workloads, never interactive sessions.

Threat model: Either misuse (admin using a service-account credential because it has higher privileges than their own) or compromise (attacker who obtained a service-account credential and is using it interactively from a workstation).

FP profile: Very low if the username patterns match your naming convention. To change coverage, edit the eval is_svc=... clause in the search (see Customer tuning).

docs.title: E5. HANA User Creation Outside Business Hours
docs.text:
CREATE USER on HANA outside business hours (before 08:00 or from 18:00) or at any time on Saturday or Sunday. Should map to a known change ticket; off-window creation often indicates ad-hoc / unauthorized provisioning.

Threat model: Insider creating a backdoor account when fewer admins are watching. Less aggressive than mass DROP but still a containment-relevant signal.

FP profile: Low for typical environments. Higher during planned cutover weekends — operators expecting weekend CREATE USER activity should pre-disable this search for the maintenance window.

docs.title: E6. HANA Mass DROP
docs.text:
5+ DROP statements (TABLE, SCHEMA, VIEW, PROCEDURE, USER, ROLE, INDEX) by a single user on a single host within one 10-minute bucket. Only these DROP statements count; DELETE statements are not matched. Indicates either large-scale schema cleanup (which should map to a change ticket) or destructive insider activity.

Threat model: Destructive insider, ransomware-style data destruction, or inadvertent operator error during cleanup.

FP profile: Low at this threshold (5 in 10 min is well above routine ad-hoc cleanup activity). Schema migrations for a major release will produce hits — pre-disable the search during planned migration windows or document the mapping in the change ticket.

docs.title: RBA — Risk-Based Alerting
docs.text: Each of the 19 detection searches carries action.risk = 1 annotations, so its results also feed ES’s Risk Framework: each result row of a run adds the listed score to each listed risk object.

docs.title: Per-search risk table
docs.text:
Search risk_object_field risk_object_type risk_score HANA privilege escalation executing_user, target_user, host user, user, system 80, 40, 30 Cross-stack auth failure user user 60 (one result row per user per run, so it accumulates across hourly runs) ABAP gateway anomalous peer peer_ip, host other, system 40, 20 SCC ACCESS_DENIED burst host system 50 HANA failed CONNECT spike executing_user, host user, system 50, 30 Linux OOM-killer burst host system 50 Lateral movement auth_user user 70 Privilege chain auth_user, host user, system 80, 40 After-hours admin data access executing_user, host user, system 70, 30 Service account interactive executing_user user 60 HANA user creation off-hours executing_user user 50 HANA mass DROP executing_user, host user, system 70, 50 TI: DNS to malicious domain src_ips system 80 TI: proxy to malicious IP src_ips system 70 TI: compromised credential use auth_user user 90 Anomaly: user auth volume auth_user user 30 Anomaly: webdispatcher response host system 30 Anomaly: topology edge volume source system 30 Anomaly: after-hours admin auth_user user 40

For the HANA searches, host is the HANA host that wrote the audit record (the client’s host name is src_host), so their system risk lands on the database host. The failed-CONNECT spike and after-hours admin searches list client host names in src_hosts.

docs.title: Multi-object risk per event
docs.text:
Where a result names several objects (operator, target and host for privilege escalation), each object receives its own score from the list, so all three accrue risk at once. Example:

action.risk.param._risk = [
  {"risk_object_field":"executing_user","risk_object_type":"user","risk_score":80},
  {"risk_object_field":"target_user","risk_object_type":"user","risk_score":40},
  {"risk_object_field":"host","risk_object_type":"system","risk_score":30}
]

The tier-2 Risk Notable below sums the scores per risk object (stats sum(All_Risk.risk_score) ... by All_Risk.risk_object), so each of the three objects accumulates its own score.

docs.title: Tier-2 Risk Notable
docs.text:
The App also ships splunk_sap_logserv_es_risk_notable_threshold — a higher-tier correlation search that aggregates risk events from all 19 detection searches and creates a critical-severity Notable when a single risk_object accumulates ≥ 100 risk_score in 24h.

| from datamodel:Risk.All_Risk
| search source IN (
    "splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation",
    "splunk_sap_logserv_es_cross_stack_auth_failure",
    ...                     <- the shipped stanza enumerates all 19 detection
    ...                        searches: base, extended, threat-intel, anomaly
    "splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin")
| stats sum(All_Risk.risk_score) AS total_risk
        values(All_Risk.risk_object_type) AS risk_object_type
        values(source) AS source_searches
        dc(source) AS distinct_searches
