        latest(_time) AS last_event by All_Risk.risk_object
| rename All_Risk.risk_object AS risk_object
| where total_risk >= 100

Why threshold 100? It’s the conservative starter: - Two hourly runs of the cross-stack auth-failure search that flag the same user within 24h (60 + 60 = 120) → fires - One privilege-escalation result gives 80, 40 and 30 to its three objects — none alone reaches 100, but a second result for the same operator compounds (80 + 80 = 160) - The threshold is yours to set: raise it if the Risk Notable fires on activity you accept, lower it if you want notice sooner (see Customer tuning).

ES dependency: the Risk Notable reads from the Risk.All_Risk data model, which ES provides. Without ES there is no Risk data model, so the scheduler skips the search, with the reason “Data model ‘Risk’ was not found”, rather than running it and returning nothing. On a search head without ES, disable it: see Disabling or tuning the ES content.

docs.title: How notables appear in ES Incident Review
docs.text:
When a base correlation search fires:

  1. Notable created with the search’s rule_title template substituted with row field values - Example: “HANA Privilege Escalation: ALTER USER by xcnadm on SYSTEM”
  2. Severity badge matches action.notable.param.severity (high / medium)
  3. Security domain badge from action.notable.param.security_domain: identity, access, network or endpoint for the base searches (E6 and the Risk Notable use threat)
  4. nes_fields: each search names the fields that identify a finding in action.notable.param.nes_fields, for example executing_user,target_user,host (operator, target and host) for privilege escalation. How Incident Review uses these fields depends on your ES version; see the ES documentation.

When the tier-2 Risk Notable fires:

  1. Critical-severity notable with title like “High accumulated risk: xcnadm (160) across 3 SAP correlation searches”
  2. Security domain = threat
  3. One row per risk object: the search returns one result for each risk_object over the threshold (stats ... by All_Risk.risk_object), and names risk_object in nes_fields

docs.title: Customer tuning
docs.text:
Change the severity, schedule, risk scores or SPL of a search in Splunk Web, which works on Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise alike:

  1. Go to Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts, set App to Splunk App for SAP LogServ and find the search.
  2. Choose Edit → Advanced edit and change the attribute: action.notable.param.severity, cron_schedule, action.risk.param._risk or search.
  3. Save.

For example, to raise the Risk Notable threshold to 150, open splunk_sap_logserv_es_risk_notable_threshold and change | where total_risk >= 100 near the end of its search to | where total_risk >= 150, leaving the rest of the search as it is.

On Splunk Enterprise you can instead override the attribute in local/savedsearches.conf (never edit default/). An overridden search replaces the whole shipped search, so copy the full shipped line from default/savedsearches.conf and change only the part you need; then restart Splunk.

docs.title: Disabling individual correlation searches
docs.text: To stop a search without uninstalling the App, disable it in Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts (Edit → Disable), or turn off only its schedule. A disabled search stays in the App and can be enabled again. The extended, threat-intel and anomaly searches also run AI Assistant prompts, which fail while their search is disabled; the steps and the list are in Disabling or tuning the ES content.

  • Asset & Identity Feed — How asset context enriches notable events
  • Threat Intelligence Integration — The 3 customer-managed CSV lookups + 3 TI-driven correlation searches
  • Behavioral & Anomaly Detections — The 4 statistically-baselined anomaly searches with optional MLTK upgrade path

docs.title: Enterprise Security Integration — Overview
docs.text:
The LogServ App ships content for Splunk Enterprise Security (ES), so SOC analysts can investigate SAP-side threats through ES’s Incident Review queue, Risk-Based Alerting (RBA) and CIM-aligned correlation searches. Use this page to check the prerequisites, set the content up in order, and turn it off on search heads that do not run ES.

The ES content ships enabled, with or without ES

All 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* saved searches ship with disabled = 0 and a schedule, so they run on every search head that runs the App. Without ES they do no useful work, and they are not silent: the notable and risk alert actions do not exist there, so Splunk logs errors in _internal (from sendmodalert and SearchScheduler) saying that these alert actions were not found, and, because there is no Risk data model, the scheduler skips the Risk Notable with the reason “Data model ‘Risk’ was not found”. On a search head without ES, we recommend turning the ES content off: see Disabling or tuning the ES content. No dashboard, rollup or AI Assistant prompt reads the results of the scheduled runs.

With ES installed, the 19 detection searches raise notable events in Incident Review and risk events for RBA; one tier-2 Risk Notable fires when accumulated risk on a single object crosses a threshold; and two feeds supply SAP systems and user identities to ES asset and identity management.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Splunk Enterprise Security on the search head that runs the App. Notables, risk events and ES asset and identity management exist only where ES runs, so the App must be installed on the ES search head.
  • If ES runs on a search head of its own. ES can run on a different search head from the one your users open for other apps. On Splunk Cloud Platform in particular, check which search head of your stack runs ES. Install the LogServ App on the ES search head as well, the same way as on the main one (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards); the App’s dashboards and rollup searches then run there too. On a search head that runs the App without ES, turn the ES content off (Disabling or tuning the ES content).
  • The Splunk Common Information Model add-on (Splunk_SA_CIM) 5.0.0 or later. It is the only dependency the App declares in its app.manifest. Check that it is installed on the ES search head; if it is not, install it (where to get it: LogServ App Prerequisites). The App does not declare a dependency on ES (SplunkEnterpriseSecuritySuite), so it installs and works without ES. If you add ES later, turn back on any ES searches you turned off; nothing else in the App changes.
  • The CIM data models must search the LogServ index. On the CIM add-on’s setup page, add sap_logserv_logs (or the index your sap_logserv_idx_macro points at) to the index lists of Authentication, Change, Network_Sessions, Network_Resolution and Web. Add it even where a list is empty: the App does not make sap_logserv_logs an index that any role searches by default, so do not rely on an empty list to include it. The App’s cross-stack authentication-failure search reads the Authentication data model, and ES’s own correlation searches read these data models. Verifying the integration is live shows whether SAP events reach the models.

docs.title: Where the ES content runs
docs.text: The ES content is search-time and scheduled content inside the LogServ App: nothing is installed or changed on the forwarders or indexers for it. Where the App goes in each topology: Where Each Package Goes. In a search head cluster, the App (and with it the ES content) is deployed through the SHC deployer, as usual.

docs.title: Setup checklist
docs.text:
1. Check the prerequisites on the search head that runs ES.
  2. Install the LogServ App there and let SAP data arrive (Install the App and Seed the Dashboards).
  3. Check that SAP events reach the CIM data models: Verifying the integration is live.
  4. Load the asset and identity feeds and add them to ES: Customer wire-up.
  5. Optional: fill the three threat-intel lookups from your own threat-intel feed (Populating the lookups). Until you do, the three threat-intel searches find nothing.
  6. Review the severities, risk scores, schedules and the Risk Notable threshold: Customer-tunable surfaces.
  7. Confirm that notables reach Incident Review: How notables appear in ES Incident Review.
  8. On every other search head that runs the App without ES, turn the ES content off: Disabling or tuning the ES content.

docs.title: Disabling or tuning the ES content
docs.text:
On a search head without ES, the scheduled ES searches use search capacity and add errors to _internal, and nothing reads their results. Turn them off there. On a search head with ES, use the same steps for any single search you do not want.

13 of these searches also run AI Assistant prompts

The AI Assistant’s Security pack runs 13 of these saved searches on demand: the 6 extended cross-stack searches, the 3 threat-intel searches and the 4 behavioral-anomaly searches. A disabled saved search cannot run, so its prompt then returns an error. If you use those prompts, turn off only the schedule of those 13 (option B below) and disable the other 9 (option A).

The 9 searches that no prompt uses are the 6 base correlation searches (splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation, _cross_stack_auth_failure, _abap_gateway_anomalous_peer, _scc_access_denied_burst, _hana_failed_connect_spike, _oom_kill_burst), the Risk Notable (_risk_notable_threshold) and the 2 feeds (_asset_feed, _identity_feed).

Option A: disable a search (Splunk Web; Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise):

  1. Go to Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts.
  2. Set App to Splunk App for SAP LogServ and filter the names on splunk_sap_logserv_es_.
  3. For each search, choose Edit → Disable.

A disabled search stays in the App, and Edit → Enable turns it back on.

Option B: keep a search runnable, but stop its schedule (Splunk Web; Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise):

  1. Go to Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts and find the search as above.
  2. Choose Edit → Advanced edit, set is_scheduled to off, and save.

Splunk Enterprise only: a config override. Instead of the Splunk Web steps, add one stanza per search to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv/local/savedsearches.conf (never edit default/), then restart Splunk:

# Option A: disable the search
[splunk_sap_logserv_es_hana_privilege_escalation]
disabled = 1

# Option B: keep the search runnable on demand, without a schedule
[splunk_sap_logserv_es_lateral_movement]
enableSched = 0
# ... one stanza per splunk_sap_logserv_es_* search

There are 22 ES searches: 19 detections, the Risk Notable and the 2 feeds. To keep some on a search head with ES, but cut the load, start with the anomaly searches below.

The cost of the anomaly searches

Two of the four behavioral-anomaly searches scan 30 days of raw events on each run: splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume (HANA audit and sapstartsrv authentication events) and splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin (HANA audit). They read the index directly, not a data model, so data model acceleration does not make them cheaper; they run once a day for that reason. The other two read the App’s own hourly KV Store rollups (logserv_web_timing_rollup, logserv_topology_edges), so their cost depends on the number of hosts and edges, not on event volume. See Behavioral & Anomaly Detections.

docs.title: The ES schedule (collision-free)
docs.text:
All splunk_sap_logserv_es_* scheduled searches ship enabled on staggered crons, which run in the search head’s local time. They sit in minutes that the App’s other scheduled searches leave free, so no two of the App’s enabled scheduled searches share an (hour, minute). The other bands are the hourly rollup aggregates and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot (:02–:28 every hour), the nightly retention and maintenance (00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36), and the daily late-arrival check at 05:40. The full schedule is in Dashboard Data → Scheduled-search schedule.

  • The hourly searches (the 15 hourly correlation searches and the Risk Notable) run at :29 and the odd minutes :31–:59.
  • 2 Asset/Identity feeds run every 4 hours at :00 / :01.
  • 4 behavioral-anomaly searches run daily at :30 (hours 02–05), so the two heavy 30-day scans run once a day, not every hour. Each daily run evaluates every time bucket since the start of the previous day, so no bucket is skipped.

docs.title: What ships for ES integration
docs.text:
Capability Count / Surface Source CIM data-model tagging Authentication, Change, Network_Sessions, Web, and Network_Resolution for DNS CIM Compliance Base correlation searches 6 (high-confidence SAP threat patterns) Correlation Searches Extended cross-stack correlation searches 6 (lateral movement, privilege chain, after-hours admin activity, service-account interactive, HANA user creation off-hours, HANA mass DROP) Correlation Searches → Extended cross-stack pack Threat-intel correlation searches 3 (DNS to malicious domain, proxy to malicious IP, compromised credential use) — joins against 3 customer-managed CSV lookups (ship empty) Threat Intelligence Integration Behavioral / anomaly detections 4 stats-based Z-score (per-user auth volume, per-host webdispatcher response time, per-edge topology call volume, per-admin off-hours activity); no MLTK dependency Behavioral & Anomaly Detections Tier-2 Risk Notable Critical-severity notable when accumulated risk on a single object ≥ 100 in 24h (aggregates risk from all 19 detection searches — base, extended, threat-intel, and anomaly) Correlation Searches Asset Inventory feed splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets.csv Asset & Identity Feed Identity Inventory feed splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities.csv Asset & Identity Feed

Total: 19 detection correlation searches + 1 Risk Notable + 2 Asset/Identity feeds. The extended cross-stack, threat-intel, and behavioral searches can also be run on demand from the AI Assistant’s predefined-prompt browser (Security pack), once an admin has turned the AI Assistant on (Set Up the AI Assistant); the base correlation searches run on their schedule only.

docs.title: Verifying the integration is live
docs.text:
Once SAP data arrives and the data models cover the LogServ index (see Prerequisites), SAP events appear in the CIM data models without further setup. Verify with:

| datamodel Authentication search
| search sourcetype IN ("sap:hana:audit","sap:sapstartsrv","sap:scc:audit","linux:sudolog")
| stats count by sourcetype Authentication.action

You should see rows for each populated SAP authentication source, with Authentication.action as success / failure.

Same pattern for Change, Web, Network_Sessions — see CIM Compliance for full details.

docs.title: Customer-tunable surfaces
docs.text:
Knob Default Where (Advanced edit attribute) Correlation-search schedules hourly (correlations) / daily (anomalies) / every 4h (feeds) cron_schedule Notable severity per search critical / high / medium action.notable.param.severity Risk scores per result 20–90 (varies per search and per risk object) action.risk.param._risk (JSON) Risk Notable threshold total_risk >= 100 in 24h search of splunk_sap_logserv_es_risk_notable_threshold: the \| where total_risk >= 100 clause Asset/Identity feed cadence every 4h cron_schedule of splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed / _identity_feed

Change these in Splunk Web, which works on Splunk Cloud and Splunk Enterprise alike: Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts, find the search, then Edit → Advanced edit. On Splunk Enterprise you can instead override the same attributes in local/savedsearches.conf; never edit default/. A new cron in a minute another App search already uses gives up the collision-free schedule above.

The time windows of the 15 hourly correlation searches are set for an hourly cron. Eleven use a 60-minute window that ends 5 minutes before the run (dispatch.earliest_time = -65m@m, dispatch.latest_time = -5m@m), so their hourly runs follow on from each other without overlap. Four (the ABAP gateway peer, SCC ACCESS_DENIED, HANA failed-CONNECT and OOM-killer searches) set earliest=-1h@h latest=now in the search text, which takes the place of the dispatch window: each run searches from the start of the previous hour up to the run. If you change the cron of one of these searches, change its window to match: the dispatch.earliest_time / dispatch.latest_time attributes, or the earliest= / latest= in the search text where the search sets them. Run more often with the same window, a search reports the same events again (repeat notables, and risk counted again); run less often, it leaves events between its windows unsearched.

docs.text:

  • Asset & Identity Feed — How the App feeds ES asset and identity management with SAP system inventory + user identities.
  • Threat Intelligence Integration — The 3 customer-managed CSV lookups + the 3 TI-driven correlation searches that join against them. Customer populates the lookups from their own threat-intel feed.
  • Behavioral & Anomaly Detections — The 4 stats-based Z-score anomaly detections that complement the deterministic correlation searches by surfacing entities deviating from their own historical patterns. Optional MLTK upgrade path documented.

docs.title: Threat Intelligence Integration
docs.text:
The Splunk for SAP LogServ App ships 3 customer-managed CSV lookups and 3 correlation searches that join SAP / DNS / proxy events against those lookups to detect known indicators of compromise. Both the lookups and the correlation searches live entirely inside the LogServ App — no separate Splunkbase dependency, no new install step beyond the App itself.

The lookups ship empty (header row only). Customers populate them from their own threat-intel feed; the correlation searches return 0 rows until populated.

docs.title: The 3 lookups
docs.text:
Lookup table CSV columns What it represents logserv_ti_malicious_domains domain,category,source,added_date,notes Domains flagged as C2, phishing, malware-distribution, etc. logserv_ti_malicious_ips ip,category,source,added_date,notes IPs flagged as C2, scanner, exfiltration endpoint, etc. logserv_ti_compromised_credentials username,added_date,notes Usernames known to be compromised (breach lists, internal incident response findings, etc.)

Schema details:

  • domain / ip / username — the indicator itself. Match is case-insensitive (set via case_sensitive_match = false on the transforms.conf stanza). Domain values should NOT have a trailing dot — the search normalizes the DNS query field via rtrim before lookup.
  • category — free-form tag identifying the IOC class (e.g., c2, phishing, malware, exfiltration, scanner). Surfaced in the notable event’s rule_title.
  • source — free-form provenance tag identifying which threat-intel feed the indicator came from (e.g., Mandiant, OpenCTI, internal-IR). Helps tune which feeds produce true positives over time.
  • added_date — ISO 8601 date the indicator was added. Useful for FP analysis (very old indicators are more likely to have been remediated upstream).
  • notes — free-form, optional. Surfaced in the rule_description.

docs.title: The 3 correlation searches
docs.text:
Search name Joins against Severity Schedule splunk_sap_logserv_es_ti_dns_to_malicious_domain isc:bind:query ↔ logserv_ti_malicious_domains high hourly splunk_sap_logserv_es_ti_proxy_to_malicious_ip squid:access ↔ logserv_ti_malicious_ips high hourly splunk_sap_logserv_es_ti_compromised_credential_use sap:hana:audit, sap:abap:audit and sap:sapstartsrv events that carry a user name ↔ logserv_ti_compromised_credentials critical hourly

The compromised-credential search does not limit itself to logins: it takes any event of those three sourcetypes, reads the user from executing_user, user or src_user (the first that is set), lowercases it and looks it up.

All three emit action.notable=1 for ES Notable Review and action.risk=1 for the RBA framework. Risk scores: 80 (DNS hit), 70 (proxy hit), 90 (compromised credential — highest because the action — locking the credential — is unambiguous).

docs.title: Populating the lookups
docs.text: Three workflows, depending on the size and freshness expectations of your TI source:

docs.title: 1. Splunk Web (small, manual, ad-hoc)
docs.text:
For small lists (< 100 indicators) maintained by hand:

  1. Settings → Lookups → Lookup table files
  2. Filter for logserv_ti_*
  3. Click the lookup name → upload a new CSV with the same column structure.

Splunk replaces the file in place. The existing transforms.conf stanza stays unchanged.

docs.title: 2. Customer-authored saved search (recurring, automated)
docs.text:
For TI feeds that update regularly:

  1. Author a saved search that pulls from the TI source (REST API, file ingest, etc.) and emits rows matching the domain,category,source,added_date,notes shape.
  2. End the SPL with | outputlookup override_if_empty=false logserv_ti_malicious_domains to overwrite the file. Without override_if_empty=false, Splunk deletes the file when the search returns no rows — so a run during an outage of your TI connector would empty the list; with it, an empty run leaves the previous list in place.
  3. Schedule the saved search at whatever cadence matches your feed (hourly, daily, etc.).

The customer owns the upstream connector; the LogServ App only reads the lookup.

docs.title: 3. Threat-intel framework (Splunk ES Threat Framework)
docs.text:
If you have ES installed, the ES Threat Framework already maintains its own consolidated threat-intel KV Store collections. Bridge those to the LogServ-side lookups via a saved search of your own. The names of ES’s threat-intel lookups and their fields depend on your ES version and configuration, so look them up first (the ES documentation, or Settings → Lookups → Lookup definitions on the ES search head). In this template, replace each <...> placeholder with the name from your ES:

| inputlookup <ES lookup that holds domain indicators>
| rename <ES domain field> AS domain, <ES description field> AS notes
| eval category="<category>", source="splunk-es-threat-framework", added_date=strftime(now(), "%Y-%m-%d")
| table domain category source added_date notes
| outputlookup override_if_empty=false logserv_ti_malicious_domains

This sets added_date to the day of the copy. If your ES lookup has a time field for each indicator, use it there instead, and add a filter (| where ...) if you want only some of the indicators.

docs.title: Tuning + maintenance
docs.text:
• Stale indicators. Indicators older than ~30 days have a higher false-positive rate (the upstream threat may already be remediated). Periodically prune them with | inputlookup logserv_ti_malicious_domains | where strptime(added_date, "%Y-%m-%d") >= relative_time(now(), "-30d") | outputlookup override_if_empty=false logserv_ti_malicious_domains (and the same for the other two lists) to overwrite each list with a freshness-filtered view. added_date is a date string, so convert it with strptime before comparing it with a time; this form expects YYYY-MM-DD. (With the flag, a prune that would remove every indicator leaves the list as it is; to empty it on purpose, upload a header-only CSV as in workflow 1.)
  • Upgrades. The three lists ship in the App’s lookups/ directory as header-only files, so an upgrade that installs the package may replace rows you added. As a precaution, export a list you maintain by hand (workflow 1, or a one-off outputlookup) before upgrading and re-upload it afterwards; a list written by a recurring saved search (workflow 2 or 3) is refilled on its next run. See Upgrading.
  • Source weighting. If a particular source produces too many FPs, pre-filter at lookup-write time so it never reaches the correlation search. A source that produces TPs reliably can be tagged as such in the notes field for SOC analyst context.
  • Custom domains. The domain column accepts FQDNs. Wildcard domain patterns (e.g., *.evil.com) do not match as shipped, because the lookup definition matches exactly (case-insensitive). For wildcard support, give the lookup definition a wildcard match type (match_type = WILDCARD(domain) on its transforms.conf stanza; in Splunk Web, edit the lookup definition logserv_ti_malicious_domains under Settings → Lookups → Lookup definitions and set the same match type in its advanced options), or write your own detection that uses regex matching against the lookup contents.

docs.title: AI Assistant integration
docs.text:
Each of the 3 TI correlation searches has a corresponding entry in the AI Assistant predefined-prompt catalog:

  • security.ti_dns_to_malicious_domain
  • security.ti_proxy_to_malicious_ip
  • security.ti_compromised_credential_use

Once an admin has turned the AI Assistant on (it ships turned off; see Set Up the AI Assistant), SOC analysts can dispatch them on demand from the AI Assistant’s predefined-prompt browser → Security pack → TI: DNS query to malicious domain (and siblings). A prompt fails while its saved search is disabled. Natural-language routing (“Show me TI hits across DNS in the last hour”) requires the free-form path, which activates once an LLM provider credential is configured; without one, dispatch is via the prompt browser only.

docs.title: Verifying the lookups loaded correctly
docs.text:
After installing or upgrading the LogServ App, verify the 3 TI lookups are queryable:

| inputlookup logserv_ti_malicious_domains | head 5
| inputlookup logserv_ti_malicious_ips | head 5
| inputlookup logserv_ti_compromised_credentials | head 5

Each should return 0 rows (the lookups ship empty). The fact that the queries DISPATCH cleanly without “lookup table not found” errors confirms the transforms.conf wiring is correct.

docs.text:

  • Behavioral & Anomaly Detections — Statistically-baselined detections that complement TI matching
  • Asset & Identity Feed — Customer-managed asset and identity context (similar customer-side population workflow)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page shows how Splunk for SAP LogServ moves SAP LogServ data from your cloud into Splunk, and what each package does on the way. Read it while you plan; which package goes on which Splunk instance is on Where Each Package Goes.

docs.title: The Packages
docs.text:
Splunk for SAP LogServ is four packages of its own, plus the Splunk Add-on for AWS when your SAP ECS data is in AWS:

Package Splunk Web label App ID What it does Data TA Splunk TA for SAP LogServ splunk_ta_sap_logserv Index-time parsing, sourcetype routing and the optional filters for the data your ingest add-on collects. It has no data inputs of its own: its two scripted inputs are maintenance jobs that write to _internal. It also carries the Configuration page (Filters, Cloud Provider), the Deployment Server automation, the AWS S3 Direct backfill screen, and the definitions of the two indexes, sap_logserv_logs (SAP data) and logserv_ai_assistant_audit (AI Assistant audit log). LogServ App Splunk App for SAP LogServ splunk_app_sap_logserv Dashboards, search-time field extractions, macros, the scheduled searches that fill the dashboards’ KV Store rollups, Environment Topology, the Enterprise Security content and the AI Assistant (ships disabled). It contains no Python and no inputs. Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunk_TA_aws (Splunkbase 1876) Collects from AWS S3: its SQS-Based S3 inputs read the notifications of new LogServ objects and download the objects. The AWS S3 Direct screen creates Generic S3 inputs in it for backfill. LogServ Azure add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure Collects from Azure Blob Storage: its sap_logserv_azure_queue input reads the Storage Queue that Event Grid fills with BlobCreated notifications and fetches each blob with a SAS. See the Azure Setup Guide. LogServ GCP add-on Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp Collects from Google Cloud Storage: its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription fed by the bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications and fetches each object with a service-account key. See the GCP Setup Guide.

Each NDJSON line of a LogServ object becomes one event with sourcetype sap_logserv_logs (on AWS you set it on the SQS-Based S3 input, and it must be exactly sap_logserv_logs: the Data TA parses and routes only events that arrive with that sourcetype; the Azure and GCP inputs always use it). The Azure and GCP inputs also stamp cloud_provider on their events. From there the Data TA handles every cloud the same way.

The Data TA works where the data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or on a single instance. A heavy forwarder parses each event before it forwards it, so the indexers receive finished events and the Data TA’s index-time settings do nothing there. The indexers only need the two indexes; in a distributed deployment you create them on the indexer tier. A Deployment Server, if you use one, holds the Data TA to distribute it to the heavy forwarders. The logserv_ai_assistant_audit index is where the AI Assistant writes its audit events; without it they have nowhere to go.

The LogServ App works at search time on the search head (or the single instance). It finds the SAP data through the macro sap_logserv_idx_macro and the audit events through sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro, so a renamed index needs the macros changed rather than the App; see Renaming an index.

Why separate packages?

Index-time work and search-time work run on different Splunk tiers. Keeping them apart means the forwarders carry no dashboards, search-time extractions or AI Assistant code, and the search head carries no ingest logic. On a single instance both packages are installed on the same instance and Splunk merges their configuration.

docs.title: Install Matrix
docs.text: Where you install each package depends on your topology: single instance, Deployment Server with heavy forwarders, Splunk Cloud with or without your own heavy forwarders, search head and indexer clusters. All of them are in one table on Where Each Package Goes.

docs.title: AWS
docs.text:
SAP writes your LogServ objects to an S3 bucket in the SAP ECS account, and the bucket sends a notification for each new object to an SQS queue there. How the notifications reach Splunk depends on the scenario you deploy in your own Secondary AWS account (see Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario):

  SAP ECS account (managed by SAP)
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  SAP LogServ S3 bucket  --(new object)-->  SAP SQS queue    |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------+
          |                       |                       |
       Connect                 Filter                   Copy
          |                       |                       |
          |              Lambda in your account   Lambda in your account
          |              reads SAP's queue and    reads SAP's queue and
          |              forwards the             copies each new object
          |              notifications that       to a bucket in your
          |              pass its filters to a    account; that bucket
          |              queue in your account    notifies a queue in
          |                       |               your account
          |                       |                       |
          v                       v                       v
  Input reads SAP's       Input reads your        Input reads your queue
  queue and downloads     queue and downloads     and downloads from your
  from SAP's bucket       from SAP's bucket       bucket
          |                       |                       |
          +-----------------------+-----------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
            Heavy Forwarder: Splunk Add-on for AWS, SQS-Based S3 input
            (signs in through the IAM role splunk-logserv-ta-role in your
            account; cross-account for Connect and Filter)
  • Connect deploys only an IAM user and a cross-account IAM role in your account.
  • Filter also deploys a Lambda, a queue and a dead-letter queue; the objects are still downloaded from SAP’s bucket.
  • Copy also deploys a Lambda, a bucket, a queue and a dead-letter queue.
  • Filter and Copy need an S3 bucket of your own for the Lambda code.

Backfill and recovery use a fourth channel with no queue: a Generic S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS that reads a bucket prefix directly. The Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen creates these inputs; see AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

docs.title: Azure
docs.text:
SAP LogServ Blob Storage (managed by SAP)
        |
        v  (BlobCreated notifications via Event Grid --> Storage Queue)
  LogServ Azure add-on: sap_logserv_azure_queue input on a Heavy Forwarder
  (add-on installed on each Heavy Forwarder that may run an input)
        |   fetches each blob with a SAS; emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
        v
  Same Data TA filtering + routing --> Indexers --> Search Head

Run one input for each queue. See the Azure Setup Guide.

docs.title: Google Cloud
docs.text:
SAP LogServ GCS bucket (managed by SAP)
        |
        v  (OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications via Pub/Sub topic --> PULL subscription)
  LogServ GCP add-on: sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input on a Heavy Forwarder
  (add-on installed on each Heavy Forwarder that may run an input)
        |   fetches each object with a service-account key; emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
        v
  Same Data TA filtering + routing --> Indexers --> Search Head

The service account is yours: you create it in a GCP account of your own, give its email address to SAP support, and SAP grants it read access to the LogServ subscription and bucket (the GCP counterpart of the AWS cross-account IAM role). Run one input for each subscription. See the GCP Setup Guide.

docs.title: From the Heavy Forwarder to the Dashboards
docs.text:
Whatever the cloud, each event then goes through the same steps:

  Heavy Forwarder (or single instance): the Data TA at index time
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  0. The input reads each object; every NDJSON line becomes   |
  |     one event (sourcetype sap_logserv_logs)                  |
  |  1. Filters, only when Enable Filtering is on (nullQueue)    |
  |  2. Set host, source, clz_dir and clz_subdir                 |
  |  3. Route to the final sourcetype                            |
  |  4. Stamp splunk_solution (and cloud_provider when set)      |
  |  5. Keep only the "_raw" text as the event                   |
  |  6. Forward to the indexers                                  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
        |
        v
  Indexers: sap_logserv_logs
        |
        v
  Search Head: LogServ App (search-time fields, rollups, dashboards)

Steps 1 to 5 are TRANSFORMS- classes of the [sap_logserv_logs] stanza, and Splunk runs them in the order of their names. The filter class, TRANSFORMS-00-filter, is written to the Data TA’s local/props.conf when you save the filters, and sorts before the shipped classes 01 (host, source and folder fields), 02 to 09 (routes), 50 and 51 (stamps) and 99 (unwrap _raw). The filters have to run before step 5, because they match the envelope keys that the unwrap removes. An event the filters drop still passes through the later steps, so filtering saves license and storage, not forwarder CPU (see Capacity Planning and First Start).

docs.title: Index-Time Filtering
docs.text:
The Data TA’s filters decide at index time which LogServ events are indexed. They run on the parsing tier (the heavy forwarders, or the single instance) and send the events they drop to nullQueue, so those events are never indexed and do not count toward ingest-based licensing:

  • Include Filters / Exclude Filters: folder patterns on clz_dir/clz_subdir, for example linux/* or linux/cron.
  • Include Sources / Exclude Sources: patterns on the event’s source (the log file’s path), optionally limited to one folder, for example linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log.
  • Days in the Past: drops events whose own _time (the epoch in the raw NDJSON) is older than midnight UTC N days ago. It keys on the event’s timestamp, not on the storage object’s path date. Default 7.

Enable Filtering is off by default, and none of these settings applies until it is checked. You save the filters on the Data TA’s Configuration page:

  • With a Deployment Server managing your heavy forwarders, save them on the Deployment Server. They reach the forwarders when you click Deploy to Forwarders; with Days in the Past above 0, the daily refresh pushes its new cutoff by itself.
  • Without a Deployment Server, save them on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance); they apply there without a restart.

Filters work at index time: what is indexed before you set them stays indexed. Decide them before the inputs start; see Decide Filtering and, for every setting, Configuring Filters.

docs.title: Sourcetype Routing
docs.text:
During index-time parsing the Data TA reads each event’s envelope (the NDJSON keys around _raw) and assigns its final sourcetype with regex rules in transforms.conf. It keys on one of three things, depending on the log type:

  • The source path: Linux (/var/log/messages, /var/log/cron, …), ISC BIND (/var/lib/named/log/named/...), Squid (/var/log/squid/access.log, …), Windows (WinEventLog:...) and the SAP Web Dispatcher access log (.../log/http_access_log).
  • clz_subdir alone: for example HANA audit (hanaaudit), the ABAP gateway, dispatcher, enqueue server, event, message server and work process logs, the SAP Host Agent and SAP Router.
  • clz_dir and clz_subdir together, where the same folder name exists under more than one clz_dir (for example audit under both abap/ and scc/): ABAP audit, ICM and sapstartsrv, HANA trace, the SAP Cloud Connector logs and sap/sapstartsrv.

HANA trace files delivered without folder fields are routed by their source path instead. The route classes run in order (02 to 09) and a later match replaces an earlier one: /var/log/messages lines in the sap/saprouter folder first match the Linux route, then become sap:saprouter.

For every log type and its sourcetype, see Supported Log Types.

docs.title: The LogServ App and the AI Assistant
docs.text:
The AI Assistant ships disabled. When an admin turns it on, its predefined prompts run the App’s saved searches through the Splunk MCP Server with no LLM involved; for free-form prompts the LLM vendor receives the question and, for each search, a summary whose content the privacy tier sets, never the raw event rows. See Privacy Tiers.

How the LogServ App, the AI Assistant and the Environment Topology view are built is described in LogServ App and AI Assistant Internals.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Supported Log Types: what SAP delivers and how each log type is parsed.
  • Where Each Package Goes: the placement table for every topology.
  • Plan and Prerequisites: what to request from SAP and prepare on each tier.

docs.title: Capacity Planning and First Start
docs.text:
Use this page before you install, to size the instances that parse LogServ data and to plan for the backlog a new input finds in its queue.

The Data TA does its work where LogServ data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders in a distributed deployment, or on the single instance. There every LogServ event passes through the same chain of index-time rules, so the CPU those rules spend per event decides how many events a heavy forwarder can take. This page explains what the Data TA does with each event, what is known of its cost, how to size heavy forwarders from a measurement on your own, what does and does not add capacity, when to give each cloud its own forwarders, and how to handle the first-start backlog.

Upgrading from an earlier build? Update the Data TA to build 1792189743 or later before you size or add hardware; see Upgrading to This Release and Version Check.

docs.title: What the Data TA Does With Each Event
docs.text:
A Splunk instance handles each event in a fixed series of pipelines, linked by queues. Each pipeline runs on one thread. One parsing, merging, typing and index pipeline together form a pipeline set; a heavy forwarder has one pipeline set unless parallelIngestionPipelines says otherwise. The slowest pipeline sets the pace of the whole set: when it cannot keep up, its queue fills and the queues in front of it fill after it.

  LogServ object in S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage
  (gzipped NDJSON, one event per line)
    |
    v
  Input                 Splunk Add-on for AWS (SQS-Based S3), or the LogServ
    |                   Azure / GCP add-on: read the notification, download the
    |                   object, decompress it, hand its lines to Splunk
    v
  [parsingQueue]
    |
    v
  Parsing pipeline      split into lines (LINE_BREAKER), keep lines of up to
    |                   100,000 bytes whole (TRUNCATE)
    v
  [aggQueue]
    |
    v
  Merging pipeline      read the timestamp from the "_time" key
    |
    v
  [typingQueue]
    |
    v
  Typing pipeline       the Data TA's index-time transforms, in order:
    |                   filters (only with Filtering on), host / source /
    |                   folder fields, 34 sourcetype routes, splunk_solution /
    |                   cloud_provider, unwrap "_raw"
    v
  [indexQueue]
    |
    v
  Index pipeline        on a Heavy Forwarder: send the event to the indexers
                        or Splunk Cloud (tcpout); on a single instance: index it

The typing pipeline is where the Data TA’s rules run, in the regexreplacement processor. Splunk tries every rule of the chain on every event, so a route that does not match an event still costs its search:

Step Rules What it does How its cost grows Filters up to 6, only with Filtering on keep or drop the event (Configuring Filters) with the line length Metadata 3 set host and source; write the clz_dir and clz_subdir fields with the line length Sourcetype routes 34 give the event its sourcetype: 26 routes look for one key and value, such as "clz_subdir":"dispatcher" or "source":"/var/log/cron"; 1 checks the source path of events without folder fields; 7 look for two folder keys, such as "clz_dir":"abap" and "clz_subdir":"audit" with the line length Stamps 2 write splunk_solution and cloud_provider small Unwrap 1 keep only the "_raw" text of the envelope with the line length

The routes and the metadata rules read up to 100,000 characters of a line (LOOKAHEAD = 100000), like the filters and the unwrap. A line of up to 4,096 characters costs each rule no more than with a narrower window; a longer line costs each rule a read to its end, in proportion to its length.

The seven two-key routes, for abap/audit, abap/icm, abap/sapstartsrv, hana/tracelogs, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs and sap/sapstartsrv, use the shape of the filter rules, which stays linear in the line length at the 100,000-character window. Older Data TA builds carried six of them in a form whose cost grows with the square of the line length; Version Check shows which form a forwarder runs, and the release notes describe the changes (build 1791935359, build 1792189743).

docs.title: Measured Cost
docs.text: No index-time figure has been measured for the current routing yet. The only index-time figures come from Data TA builds before 1791935359, in which the cost of the two-key routes grows with the square of the line length; they are kept, with a search-time comparison of the route forms, in Reference Measurements at the end of this page. Until a measured figure is published here, size from your own measurement; one busy hour is enough (Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder).

docs.title: Sizing Method
docs.text:
Size from the busiest pipeline’s cost per event and your peak arrival rate. For LogServ data the busiest pipeline is normally the typing pipeline; search 1 shows whether it is on your forwarder.

  1. Peak arrival rate. Take the busiest hour of LogServ events and divide by 3,600 to get events a second (search 5, or search 6 before you have a forwarder).
  2. Cost per event. Measure the busiest pipeline’s CPU per LogServ event at the 90th percentile, in microseconds (search 3).
  3. Ceiling per pipeline set = 1,000,000 / cost per event, in events a second.
  4. Plan rate per pipeline set = half the ceiling. The other half absorbs bursts, because the input fetches objects in batches and the rate within an hour is uneven, and the catch-up after an outage or a delivery delay, when the backlog arrives at once. A first start can bring a backlog of weeks or more; see First Start: The Queue Backlog.
  5. Plan rate per heavy forwarder = plan rate per pipeline set x pipeline sets: one, or two on a forwarder with spare cores (Add a Second Pipeline Set).
  6. Heavy forwarders needed = peak arrival rate / plan rate per heavy forwarder, rounded up. Add one if a forwarder must be able to fail without the others falling behind.

Worked with the lab figures measured before the update (Reference Measurements):

  cost per event (typing pipeline, p90)   2,944 microseconds
  ceiling per pipeline set                1,000,000 / 2,944  =  340 events/s
  plan rate per pipeline set              340 / 2            =  170 events/s  (about 0.6 million an hour)
  plan rate per HF, 1 pipeline set                              170 events/s
  plan rate per HF, 2 pipeline sets                             340 events/s  (about 1.2 million an hour)

At that cost per event, a feed whose busiest hour carries 12 million events (3,333 events a second) would need 10 heavy forwarders with two pipeline sets each. That is why the update comes first.

Data TA Cost per event (90th percentile) Ceiling per pipeline set Plan rate per pipeline set Plan rate per HF, 1 set Plan rate per HF, 2 sets Before build 1791935359, lab feed (short events: 84 bytes of event text) 2.94 ms 340 events/s 170 events/s 170 events/s 340 events/s Before build 1791935359, longer lines higher, with the square of the line length lower lower lower lower Build 1791935359 or later measure (search 3) 1,000,000 / cost half the ceiling plan rate per set 2 x plan rate per set

Your log-type mix and line lengths differ from the lab feed, so measure on your own forwarder, and measure again when the mix changes, for example when log types with long lines are added.

The typing pipeline is not the only limit. The input itself uses CPU outside the pipelines to download and decompress the objects, and the output to the indexers or Splunk Cloud needs network bandwidth. Leave room on the forwarder for the input and the operating system as well.

On a single instance the same chain runs on the instance that also indexes and searches, so the same method applies to its typing pipeline, with less spare CPU around it.

docs.title: Update the Data TA
docs.text:
Install Data TA build 1792189743 or later on every instance that parses LogServ data, then measure again (search 3) before you add hardware:

  • Heavy forwarders managed by a Deployment Server: install it on the Deployment Server, in both etc/apps/ and etc/deployment-apps/, and push it to the forwarders (Upgrading to This Release). Do not also install it directly on those forwarders: the push replaces their copy, local/ included. A Save on the Filters or Cloud Provider tab copies the Data TA into deployment-apps/ only when no copy is there yet or when the copy’s [launcher] version in default/app.conf differs from the one in etc/apps/, so it does not copy a newer build with the same version number, such as a later 0.1.2 build.
  • Heavy forwarders that no Deployment Server manages: install it directly on each one.
  • A single instance: install it directly.
  • A Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs: upload the newer tarball as a private app (Splunk Cloud Considerations).

Version Check shows the build each forwarder runs after the update.

docs.title: Add a Second Pipeline Set
docs.text:
Each input sends its data through one pipeline set, so a second pipeline set gets work only from a second input. Both are needed:

  1. On the heavy forwarder, add to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/server.conf (or a small app of your own) and restart Splunk:

    [general]
parallelIngestionPipelines = 2

  2. Add a second input that reads the same queue:

    • AWS: a second SQS-Based S3 input with the same settings as the first, including the same SQS queue URL and Source Type sap_logserv_logs (step 7 of the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide). The queue hands each message to one input at a time, so the two inputs share the work.
    • Azure and GCP: see Multiple landscapes / fleets in the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide, including the at-least-once trade-off of several inputs on one queue or subscription. Those notes are about how fast the input fetches objects: for typical volumes they find one input enough, and suggest a larger batch_size or max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire, or a shorter interval, before a second input. On a forwarder whose typing pipeline is the limit (search 1) those settings do not help (What Does Not Add Capacity); the second pipeline set gets work only from a second input.

Splunk’s guidance is to add a second pipeline set only on a forwarder that is significantly under-utilized, and not to go beyond two without Splunk Professional Services (Manage pipeline sets). A pipeline set keeps several threads busy, so check the forwarder’s CPU and search 1 first. server.conf is not part of the Data TA, so a Deployment Server push of the Data TA does not change it.

docs.title: Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue
docs.text:
Forwarders that read the same queue share its messages, so adding a forwarder adds a full set of pipelines. The Splunk Add-on for AWS documents scaling SQS-Based S3 inputs this way (SQS-Based S3 input). Give each new forwarder the Data TA (through your Deployment Server’s server class, or installed directly where no Deployment Server manages the forwarders), the ingest add-on, and the same input or inputs as the first.

                              +--> Heavy Forwarder 1
                              |      input A  --> pipeline set 0
                              |      input B  --> pipeline set 1
  one queue  -----------------+
  (SQS queue, Azure Storage   |
   Queue or Pub/Sub           +--> Heavy Forwarder 2
   subscription)                     input A  --> pipeline set 0
                                     input B  --> pipeline set 1

Azure and GCP: more inputs on one queue are at-least-once

Each LogServ Azure or GCP input keeps its own record of the objects it has ingested, in a file on the forwarder that runs it. No other input shares that record: not a second input on the same forwarder, and not an input on another forwarder. The queue or subscription normally hands a message to one input at a time, but when a message comes back (its lease or acknowledgement deadline ran out, a delete or acknowledgement failed, or the process stopped first; Pub/Sub can also, rarely, redeliver a message after it was acknowledged), another input can ingest the same object a second time. So run one input per queue or subscription by default, and add inputs or forwarders on it only for throughput or to catch up a backlog, accepting possible duplicates. See Multiple landscapes / fleets in the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide.

docs.title: What Does Not Add Capacity
docs.text:
• The Data TA’s own filters. The Filters tab saves license and indexing, not forwarder CPU. Its rules run in the typing pipeline as the first steps of the same chain, and the keep-or-drop decision goes to the last filter step that matched, so a dropped event is downloaded, split into lines, timestamped and run through the transforms like any other event before it is discarded. The filters also add rules of their own to the chain (Configuring Filters).
  • More inputs on one pipeline set. They download in parallel, but every event still passes through the same typing pipeline thread.
  • More cores alone. A pipeline is one thread. If the typing pipeline already uses one full core, more cores help only through a second pipeline set or another forwarder.
  • The input’s batch size or interval. They change how fast objects are fetched, not how fast their events are parsed. The Azure and GCP setup guides suggest them before a second input; that advice is for an input that falls behind on fetching, not for a forwarder whose typing pipeline is busy.
  • A smaller LOOKAHEAD on the routing rules. It saves CPU only on lines longer than 4,096 characters, and on AWS those lines would lose their host, source, folder fields and sourcetype.

docs.title: What Reduces the Load
docs.text:
Data that never reaches the forwarder costs nothing to parse:

  • AWS: the Lambda pre-filter. The Lambda drops the notifications of folders you do not want, so the forwarder never downloads those objects and its load falls with the volume. See the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide and Configuring Filters: AWS Lambda-Based Filtering.
  • Azure and GCP: the input’s include_filters / exclude_filters. They match the object path before the download (Azure Setup Guide, GCP Setup Guide).
  • Log types you do not use, left out at the source. Where your SAP LogServ subscription lets you choose the log types delivered, leave out the ones you do not need. Search 7 shows which log types make up your volume.

docs.title: More Than One Cloud
docs.text:
A heavy forwarder can run the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on and the LogServ GCP add-on together. Their inputs are of different kinds (aws_sqs_based_s3, sap_logserv_azure_queue, sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub), each add-on keeps its credentials in its own local/, and the Azure and GCP add-ons call their clouds’ REST APIs without a cloud SDK. Every event goes through the same Data TA chain, so size the forwarder for all its feeds together (Sizing Method). Each input runs through one pipeline set, so with parallelIngestionPipelines = 2 the inputs of two clouds can be spread over the two pipeline sets (Add a Second Pipeline Set).

Give each cloud its own forwarders when:

  • The feeds together are more than one forwarder takes. You need more forwarders anyway: one set per cloud is one way to add them, more forwarders on the same queues is the other (Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue).
  • One cloud must not hold up the other. Inputs on one forwarder share its pipelines, so a backlog, a burst or an outage on one queue delays the other cloud’s data too, and so does a restart to update one add-on. A first start is the common case (First Start: The Queue Backlog).
  • Your security policy wants one cloud per host. A shared forwarder holds the credentials of both clouds, for example an AWS access key and a GCP service-account key, and needs network access to both.

Separate forwarders do not change how events are attributed to their cloud. With a Deployment Server, the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown has one value for every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, including those that read another cloud. Whenever you ingest from more than one cloud, leave it at Not set and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input; the Azure and GCP inputs label their own events (Choose Cloud Attribution).

docs.title: First Start: The Queue Backlog
docs.text:
SAP’s queue receives a notification for every new LogServ object from the day SAP sets it up, which can be well before your input first reads it. The queue keeps each notification until a consumer takes it or it expires, so a new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting, and on Azure even months. The input works through them on top of the live feed, at the pace of the busiest pipeline. Wherever the input runs, on a heavy forwarder, a single instance or a Splunk Cloud search head, that pipeline runs at full load until the backlog is gone and new data can reach Splunk late in the meantime; on an instance that also serves searches, the catch-up competes with them.

How far back the backlog can reach depends on how long the queue keeps a message, which SAP sets:

Cloud Queue How long it keeps a message AWS SQS queue 4 days by default, at most 14 (Amazon SQS message quotas); the queues the Remote S3 Copy and Filter templates create in your Secondary account keep messages 14 days Azure Storage Queue, fed by Event Grid 7 days by default; Event Grid can also send messages that never expire (Event Grid delivery properties) GCP Pub/Sub subscription 7 days by default, at most 31 (Subscription message retention)

A notification that expires before it is read is gone, but the object it names stays in the bucket.

docs.title: Estimate the Catch-Up
docs.text:
The backlog holds about the live rate times the time it covers. It drains at what the forwarders can parse beyond the live feed: the ceiling per pipeline set (search 3) times the pipeline sets, minus the live arrival rate (search 5, or search 6 before you have a forwarder). Worked with the lab figures before the update, for a feed of 0.5 million events an hour, a 14-day backlog and one forwarder with one pipeline set:

  backlog     14 days x 0.5 million events an hour  =  168,000,000 events
  ceiling     one pipeline set, lab cost per event  =  340 events/s
  live feed   0.5 million events an hour            =  139 events/s
  to spare    340 - 139                             =  201 events/s
  catch-up    168,000,000 / 201                     =  835,821 s, about 9.7 days

Forwarders sized by the Sizing Method have at least the peak live rate to spare, so they need at most as long as the backlog covers: up to two weeks for a 14-day backlog, with the busiest pipeline at full load and nothing left for bursts. Before you start the input, ask your SAP representative how long the queue keeps messages and how old its oldest message is.

docs.title: Before You Start the Input
docs.text:
• Ask SAP to purge the older messages. One way to avoid the initial load is to contact your SAP representative and ask them to purge the older messages from the queue before you start the input. A purge removes only the notifications; the objects stay in the bucket. On AWS you can load the days you want afterwards, at a pace you choose, with AWS S3 Direct. On Azure and GCP the add-ons have no backfill: a purged day stays in the bucket, but nothing in this solution will load it (see Historical backfill in the Azure and GCP setup guides). If you will need those days, agree with your Splunk team how to load them before you ask SAP to purge. The purge of an SQS queue or an Azure Storage Queue removes every message in it (PurgeQueue, Clear Messages), so time it shortly before you start the input. A Pub/Sub subscription can instead be moved forward to a point in time, which acknowledges only the messages published before it (Replay and purge messages with seek). Those messages can be replayed later only if SAP’s subscription keeps acknowledged messages or its topic keeps messages; ask SAP before the seek. With the AWS Remote S3 Copy or Filter approach, the Lambda starts taking SAP’s messages as soon as its SQS trigger is active (step 9 of those guides), so ask before that step.
  • AWS Remote S3 Filter: let the Lambda leave the older objects out. The Filter approach’s Lambda passes an object’s notification on only when at least one of the object’s events is newer than DaysInThePast days and in a folder that IncludeFilters includes and ExcludeFilters does not exclude (steps 3.g to 3.i of the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide), so the rest of the backlog never reaches the forwarder. The setting applies to every later object as well.

docs.title: While It Drains
docs.text:
• Add capacity for the catch-up. A second pipeline set with a second input, or another forwarder on the same queue, drains the backlog faster (Adding Capacity). Remove the extra input or forwarder once the backlog is gone. On Azure and GCP, while the extra input runs, a message that comes back to the queue or subscription can be ingested twice, because each input keeps its own record of what it has ingested (Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue).
  • Or slow the input down (Azure and GCP). A lower max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire, or a longer interval, limits how many objects the input takes a minute (Azure, GCP). The catch-up takes longer, but leaves CPU for the rest of the instance: other inputs, and searches on a single instance or a search head. The input’s log line (done: messages=N blobs=N events=N ..., objects=N on GCP) shows how many events an object carries; at 2,000 events an object, 6 objects a firing at the default 60-second interval come to about 200 events a second. Keep that rate above the live rate, or the backlog never shrinks, and the catch-up shorter than the time the oldest notifications have left, or they expire unread.
  • Days in the Past keeps old events out of the index, not off the forwarder. The Data TA’s filter saves license and indexing, but the forwarder downloads and parses each event before it drops it, so the catch-up takes just as long (Days in the Past, What Does Not Add Capacity).

To follow the catch-up: while the backlog lasts, search 1 shows the busiest pipeline near 1.0 and search 2 the queues in front of it full, and the forwarders’ LogServ events an hour stay well above the live level:

index=_internal source=*metrics.log* group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs host IN (<HF1>, <HF2>)
| timechart span=1h sum(ev) as events

On Azure and GCP, a firing that takes the full max_blobs_per_fire / max_objects_per_fire means more may be waiting. Ask SAP how many messages its queue still holds; the depth of the queue in your Secondary account (AWS Remote S3 Copy and Filter) is in its CloudWatch metrics ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible and ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage.

docs.title: Afterwards
docs.text:
• Rebuild the dashboards for the backlog’s days. The LogServ App’s dashboards read hourly rollups, and an event that arrives more than about an hour after its hour is missing from them until its days are rebuilt (Late-arriving data). Settings → Dashboard Data lists such days of the last 30 under Late-arriving data, with a backfill of exactly those days. For older days, or on a new install, run the backfill once the backlog is in, with a window that covers it (Backfilling on first install).
  • Load what never arrived. Notifications that SAP purged, or that expired before they were read, never reach the input. On AWS, load the days you want from the bucket with AWS S3 Direct. On Azure and GCP the shipped add-ons cannot load them (see Ask SAP to purge the older messages above).

docs.title: Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder
docs.text: Run these searches from a search head that sees the forwarder’s _internal data; forwarders send it by default. Replace <HF> with the forwarder’s host name as it appears in _internal, and sap_logserv_logs with your index name if you renamed it. Use a time range with busy LogServ hours: one busy hour for searches 1, 2, 4 and 9, the last 7 days for searches 3 and 5. _internal usually keeps about 30 days. All of them are read-only.

docs.title: 1. Which Pipeline Is Busiest
docs.text:
CPU per pipeline thread, in cores, in 5-minute steps. A pipeline near 1.0 is saturated, however many cores the forwarder has.

index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=pipeline
| eval pipeline=name.":".coalesce(ingest_pipe, "0")
| timechart span=5m per_second(cpu_seconds) by pipeline

The number after the colon is the pipeline set: typing:0, typing:1 and so on.

docs.title: 2. Which Queue Fills
docs.text:
index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=queue
| eval fill_pct=round(100*coalesce(current_size_kb/max_size_kb, current_size/max_size), 1)
| timechart span=5m perc90(fill_pct) by name

The pipeline queues report their size in KB and the output queue in bytes; the coalesce covers both, so the output queue gets a column too.

Events flow parsingqueue, aggqueue, typingqueue, indexqueue, then the output queue (tcpout_*). The bottleneck is the last queue in that order that is full. A full typingqueue with a mostly empty indexqueue points at the index-time transforms; a full indexqueue or output queue points at the output to the indexers or Splunk Cloud.

docs.title: 3. Cost per Event and Capacity per Pipeline Set
docs.text:
The CPU of the typing pipeline (and of its regexreplacement processor, which runs the Data TA’s rules) per LogServ event, over the hours with at least 10,000 LogServ events, and the rates of the Sizing Method from it:

index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log*
    ((group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs) OR (group=pipeline name=typing))
| bin _time span=1h
| eval typing_cpu=if(group="pipeline", cpu_seconds, null()),
       regex_cpu=if(group="pipeline" AND processor="regexreplacement", cpu_seconds, null()),
       logserv_ev=if(group="per_index_thruput", ev, null())
| stats sum(typing_cpu) as typing_cpu_s, sum(regex_cpu) as regex_cpu_s, sum(logserv_ev) as logserv_events by _time
| where logserv_events>=10000
| eval typing_us=typing_cpu_s*1000000/logserv_events, regex_us=regex_cpu_s*1000000/logserv_events
| stats count as busy_hours, sum(logserv_events) as logserv_events,
        median(regex_us) as regex_median_us, perc90(regex_us) as regex_p90_us,
        median(typing_us) as typing_median_us, perc90(typing_us) as typing_p90_us,
        max(typing_cpu_s) as typing_peak_cpu_s_in_an_hour
| eval ceiling_eps_per_set=round(1000000/typing_p90_us, 0), plan_eps_per_set=round(500000/typing_p90_us, 0),
       typing_peak_pct_of_one_core=round(100*typing_peak_cpu_s_in_an_hour/3600, 1)
| foreach *_us [ eval <<FIELD>>=round('<<FIELD>>', 1) ]
  • typing_p90_us is the cost per event of step 2 of the sizing method; ceiling_eps_per_set and plan_eps_per_set are steps 3 and 4.
  • regex_median_us and regex_p90_us are the figures in the lab table under Reference Measurements.
  • On a forwarder that also parses other data, the CPU includes that data, so the cost per LogServ event is an upper bound.
  • Splunk writes per_index_thruput (and per_sourcetype_regex_cpu, search 9) only for the busiest series of each metrics sample: maxseries in the [metrics] stanza of limits.conf, 10 by default. On a forwarder that writes to many indexes, a sample that leaves out sap_logserv_logs makes the search count too few LogServ events, and so overstate the cost per event.
  • With two pipeline sets the search adds up both sets. The cost per event stays right; typing_peak_pct_of_one_core is then for both sets together.
  • If search 1 shows another pipeline as the busiest, replace name=typing with its name.
  • After an update of the Data TA, run it once over hours before the update and once over hours after it, and compare.

docs.title: 4. Where the CPU Goes, by Processor
docs.text:
index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=pipeline
| stats sum(cpu_seconds) as cpu_s by name processor
| addinfo
| eval avg_cores=round(cpu_s/(info_max_time-info_min_time), 3)
| sort - cpu_s
| head 15

Run it over a fixed time range, such as one busy hour. name=typing processor=regexreplacement is the Data TA’s rules; name=merging processor=aggregator is the timestamp; name=parsing processor=linebreaker is the line breaking.

docs.title: 5. Peak Arrival Rate at the Forwarders
docs.text:
index=_internal source=*metrics.log* group=per_index_thruput series=sap_logserv_logs host IN (<HF1>, <HF2>)
| bin _time span=1h
| stats sum(ev) as events by _time
| stats max(events) as peak_events_hour, median(events) as median_events_hour
| eval peak_events_per_s=round(peak_events_hour/3600, 0), median_events_per_s=round(median_events_hour/3600, 0)

List every forwarder that reads LogServ data. The median counts only hours with LogServ data. The same top-series limit as in search 3 applies: on a forwarder with many indexes the counts can come out low.

docs.title: 6. Peak Rate Before You Have a Forwarder
docs.text:
If the data already arrives somewhere, for example on a test forwarder or under another sourcetype, count it by hour in the index instead (replace the macro with index=<your index> if the data is in another index):

| tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-7d@h latest=@h by _time span=1h
| stats max(count) as peak_events_hour, median(count) as median_events_hour
| eval peak_events_per_s=round(peak_events_hour/3600, 0)

This counts by event time, not arrival time, so it smooths out delivery bursts; keep the headroom of step 4.

docs.title: 7. Log-Type Mix
docs.text:
| tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-24h by sourcetype, clz_dir, clz_subdir
| sort - count
| head 20

The folders with the most events are the first to consider for the Lambda pre-filter or for leaving out at the source. The folder fields exist on data the Data TA has parsed; events without them show as (none).

docs.title: 8. Parsing Warnings and Errors
docs.text:
index=_internal host=<HF> sourcetype=splunkd (log_level=WARN OR log_level=ERROR)
    (component=DateParserVerbose OR component=LineBreakingProcessor OR component=AggregatorMiningProcessor OR component=regexExtractionProcessor OR component=Regex)
| timechart span=15m count by component

Each warning is CPU and log volume too. PCRE_ERROR_DEPTHLIMIT errors, or lines truncated at 10,000 bytes, mean a Data TA without the long-line fix of 0.1.2 (release notes).

docs.title: 9. Regex CPU per Sourcetype (Optional)
docs.text:
index=_internal host=<HF> source=*metrics.log* group=per_sourcetype_regex_cpu
| stats sum(cpu) as cpu_ms, sum(ev) as events by series
| eval ms_per_event=round(cpu_ms/events, 2)
| sort - cpu_ms

Splunk reports cpu in milliseconds; across all series it comes to about the regexreplacement CPU of search 4. Events count under the sourcetype they end up with, so add up sap_logserv_logs and the sourcetypes the Data TA routes to. This group, too, lists only the busiest series of each sample (maxseries, 10 by default), so its totals can fall short of search 3: in the lab’s busiest hour its LogServ sourcetypes added up to 394,452 events, against 423,531 in per_index_thruput, about 7% fewer. Splunk reports this group only where regex_cpu_profiling is on; the lab’s Splunk 9.4.3 forwarders report it with nothing set in limits.conf. If it returns nothing, use search 3.

docs.title: Version Check
docs.text:
The current Data TA is version 0.1.2, build 1792598960 (Download the Packages). Every forwarder should show the build you installed on the Deployment Server, or on the forwarder itself where no Deployment Server manages it. The table shows the form of the two-key routes in each build:

Data TA The two-key routes 0.1.2 build 1792189743 and later seven, in the filter generator’s shape with a 100,000-character window: linear, the whole line 0.1.2 build 1791935359 six, anchored with (?s)^: tried once per event, first 4,096 characters 0.1.2 builds before 1791935359, 0.1.1, 0.0.6, 0.0.5.x, 0.0.4.2 unanchored: tried at every character 0.0.4.1 five of them, unanchored 0.0.3.x none

Check on each heavy forwarder, or on the single instance, not only on the Deployment Server: the forwarders are where the rules run.

The installed version and build:

grep -E "^(version|build)" $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/default/app.conf

The routing-cost fix is in place with version = 0.1.2 and build = 1791935359 or higher, the 100,000-character window with build = 1792189743 or higher. In Splunk Web on the forwarder, the same from a search:

| rest /services/apps/local splunk_server=local
| search title=splunk_ta_sap_logserv
| table title version build

The rules in effect, including any local/ override:

$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool transforms list | grep -cF '(?=.*"clz_dir"'
$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool transforms list set_srctype_abap_icm | grep -E '^(REGEX|LOOKAHEAD)'

The first command prints the number of routes still in an older two-key form, (?s)^(?=.*...) or unanchored: 0 after the update to build 1792189743. The second shows the ICM route in the generator’s shape and LOOKAHEAD = 100000.

Remove a local override of the routes before you update

If you added the six anchored routes ((?s)^(?=.*...)(?=.*...)) to the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf as a test, remove them, and restart Splunk, before you install build 1792189743. local/ wins over default/ key by key, so the old REGEX would stay in effect together with the build’s new LOOKAHEAD = 100000, and on lines near 100,000 characters that combination exceeds Splunk’s regex match limit. The first command above prints 0 when no such override is left.

docs.title: Reference Measurements
docs.text:
These measurements predate the current routing. The index-time figures were taken on the lab heavy forwarder with Data TA builds before 1791935359, whose six two-key routes were tried at every character of an event: they show what those builds cost, not a figure for build 1791935359 or later. The Sizing Method and Estimate the Catch-Up use them as worked examples.

Lab heavy forwarder, before build 1791935359 (index time)

These are lab numbers from one heavy forwarder and one feed: Splunk 9.4.3, 2 vCPUs, one pipeline set, real SAP LogServ data delivered through Azure Blob Storage and read by the LogServ Azure add-on’s queue input, and Data TA builds with the six old routes. The cost per event is CPU time from Splunk’s metrics.log divided by the LogServ events the forwarder passed on in the same hour, over every hour with at least 10,000 LogServ events.

Lab heavy forwarder Hours measured 418 hours between 2026-09-14 and 2026-10-01 LogServ events 80.0 million, with 84 bytes of event text on average in Splunk’s throughput metrics; those count after the unwrap, so the lines the routes read were longer (see the note The events were short below) Regex CPU per LogServ event (regexreplacement, the Data TA’s rules) median 2.42 ms, 10th percentile 2.02 ms, 90th percentile 2.93 ms Typing pipeline CPU per LogServ event (all its processors) median 2.44 ms, 90th percentile 2.94 ms Busiest hour by regex CPU 1,298 CPU seconds, 36% of one core, at 118 events a second Busiest hour by events 470,869 events (131 a second), 1,102 CPU seconds Regex CPU in hours without LogServ data 0.37 CPU seconds an hour (median)

Both CPU figures count everything the processor or pipeline did in the hour, divided by the LogServ events. On a forwarder that also parses other data with index-time transforms, they are an upper bound for LogServ.

In the busiest hour the typing pipeline used 1,304 CPU seconds, 1,298 of them in regexreplacement; the merging pipeline used 28, the index pipeline 6 and the parsing pipeline 2. The Data TA’s rules were nearly all of the CPU in the forwarder’s pipelines.

At the typing pipeline’s median of 2.44 ms per event, one pipeline set runs out of time at about 410 events a second (1 second / 2.44 ms), or about 340 at its 90th-percentile cost of 2.94 ms. That ceiling is arithmetic: averaged over an hour, the lab forwarder’s typing pipeline used at most 36% of one core. Over shorter spans it came closer. In the busiest hour it used 0.81 of a core over 5 minutes, and the queues in front of it (typingqueue, aggqueue, parsingqueue) were at times full while the index queue stayed empty (search 1, search 2). The data arrives in bursts, which is why the Sizing Method plans for half the ceiling.

The cost per event depends on the log type. Splunk’s regex CPU per sourcetype (search 9) for the same busiest hour, for the LogServ sourcetypes with more than 1,000 events:

Sourcetype after routing Events Regex CPU per event sap_logserv_logs (no route matched) 334,510 2.4 ms linux_messages_syslog 32,062 6.4 ms isc:bind:query 18,026 5.0 ms sap:sapstartsrv 3,722 3.6 ms linux:cron 2,056 15 ms linux_secure 1,936 21 ms linux:warn 1,378 62 ms

In the same hour the cost per event differed by a factor of about 25 between log types, so the mix matters as much as the volume.

The events were short. The 84 bytes is the event text after the unwrap, which is what Splunk’s throughput metrics count. The routes read the whole NDJSON line, which also carries the envelope keys around "_raw" (_time, host, source, clz_dir, clz_subdir and others); in LogServ sample data they add about 150 characters a line. With the old routes the cost rises steeply with line length. One hour on a second lab heavy forwarder, 845 events with 566 bytes of event text on average, came to about 50 ms per event; that is a single hour, so treat it as an indication only. At search time (Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library), the six old routes alone took 5.8 ms per event on whole lines of about 460 characters and 442 ms on lines of about 4,160. Byte sizes from the throughput metrics do not give the line length the routes read, so measure your forwarder’s cost per event with search 3 or search 9 rather than scaling the lab figure by event size.

docs.title: Build 1791935359 and Later (Index Time)
docs.text:
No index-time figure has been measured for build 1791935359 or later. What is known:

  • Without LogServ data, the lab forwarders’ regex CPU did not change with the update: a median of 0.36 and 0.38 CPU seconds an hour on the two forwarders, against 0.35 and 0.37 before it (measured on build 1791935359).
  • At search time, on the same regex library, the six two-key routes anchored at the start of the line are 179 to 1,778 times faster than the old form (Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library; measured with ^, and the build-1791935359 (?s)^ form measured no slower at about 4,160 characters). Build 1792189743 and later use the filter generator’s form with LOOKAHEAD = 100000 instead, which is not measured here.

How much of the 2.42 ms measured on the older builds the update removes on a forwarder has not been measured.

docs.title: Search Time, Splunk’s Own Regex Library
docs.text:
Splunk 9.4.3 uses the same PCRE2 library (10.40) for index-time transforms and for regex and match() at search time. Measured at search time on generated LogServ events, the six routes cost per event:

Line length (characters) Six old routes Six anchored routes Anchored routes are faster by about 460 5.8 ms 0.032 ms 179 times about 1,160 35 ms 0.073 ms 485 times about 2,660 181 ms 0.162 ms 1,120 times about 4,160 442 ms 0.249 ms 1,778 times

The anchored routes in this table start with ^; the build-1791935359 (?s)^ form measured no slower (0.185 ms per event at about 4,160 characters). Build 1792189743 and later use the filter generator’s form with LOOKAHEAD = 100000, which this table does not measure. Every event got the same result from the old and the anchored routes. Search time is not index time: the table shows the direction and how the cost depends on line length, not what the routes cost on your forwarder.
