docs.title: Where Each Package Goes
docs.text: This page is the one place that says which Splunk instance gets which package, for every supported topology. Use it to plan your install; the install steps are on the pages it links to.

docs.title: Package Matrix
docs.text:
SH = the search tier: the search head, the Splunk Cloud search head, or every member of a search head cluster (through the deployer). IDX = indexers. HFs = heavy forwarders. DS = Deployment Server. On a single instance, install every required package on that instance.

Package Get it from Required? SH IDX HFs DS Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv) GitHub release_binaries required only where the search head runs the inputs — (create the indexes) ✓ (from the DS, or installed directly) ✓ (holds it to distribute it) LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv) GitHub release_binaries required ✓ — — — Splunk Common Information Model (Splunk_SA_CIM) Splunkbase 1621, 5.0.0 or later required (the App’s declared dependency) ✓ — — — Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Splunkbase 742 required for the Windows dashboard ✓ — — — Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux Splunkbase 833 required for CIM / ES coverage of linux_secure ✓ — — — Splunk Add-on for AWS Splunkbase 1876: no minimum enforced; 8.2.2 or later recommended (SVD-2026-1005, third-party package fixes); docs verified on 8.3.1; the AWS S3 Direct screen warns below 8.1.0 required if your SAP ECS data is in AWS only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) — LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) GitHub release_binaries required if your SAP ECS data is in Azure only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) — LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp) GitHub release_binaries required if your SAP ECS data is in Google Cloud only where the search head runs the inputs (see the Splunk Cloud only row) — ✓ (installed directly, not by the DS) — Splunk MCP Server Splunkbase 7931: 1.1.0 or later; 1.2.1 or later recommended (SVD-2026-1004) only for the AI Assistant ✓ — — — Splunk AI Assistant Splunkbase 7245 optional; recommended companion to the MCP Server ✓ — — —

The four LogServ packages are the 0.1.2 tarballs in the release_binaries/ folder of the GitHub repository: splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz, splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz, splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz and splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz, with their AppInspect reports and a README that lists each file’s md5 and size.

docs.title: By Topology
docs.text:
Topology Data TA LogServ App and search-tier add-ons Ingest add-on (AWS, Azure or GCP) The two indexes Single instance The instance The instance The instance Created by the Data TA when it first loads; set the retention of sap_logserv_logs yourself (Splunk’s default applies until you do) DS + HFs + on-prem search head The DS, which pushes it to each HF The search head Each HF, installed directly On the indexer tier: see the indexer rows below DS + HFs + Splunk Cloud The DS, which pushes it to each HF The Splunk Cloud search head Each HF, installed directly On the Splunk Cloud stack: Settings > Indexes or ACS HFs without a DS (Splunk Cloud or on-prem) Each HF, installed directly; save its Configuration tabs on each HF The search head (or the Splunk Cloud search head) Each HF, installed directly On the indexer tier, or on the Splunk Cloud stack Splunk Cloud only, no heavy forwarder: supported (not blocked); a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended The Splunk Cloud search head, which runs the inputs The Splunk Cloud search head The Splunk Cloud search head; the inputs run there (the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have not been installed on a Splunk Cloud search head by the project) On the Splunk Cloud stack: Settings > Indexes or ACS Search head cluster Not on the members (ingest stays on the HFs) Every member, from the deployer Not on the members On the indexer tier Standalone indexer Not needed (allowed: its index definitions then create the indexes; its parsing settings never run there, though its two maintenance scripts still run, every 10 minutes and daily) — — On the indexer: Settings > Indexes, or a small indexes.conf Indexer cluster Not needed on the peers (allowed: its parsing settings never run there, though its two maintenance scripts still run on every peer) — — An index-only app with both index stanzas and repFactor = auto, in the manager node’s manager-apps/, pushed as the configuration bundle

The index settings and the steps for each case are on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The rule behind the table. The Data TA goes where the data is parsed: the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or the single instance. The Deployment Server holds it to distribute it. The indexes are created on the indexer tier: a heavy forwarder parses each event before forwarding it, so the indexers need only the two index definitions.
  • Deployment Server: optional. With one, install the Data TA on the Deployment Server only, never also directly on the heavy forwarders it manages: a push replaces the forwarder’s copy of the app, local/ included. Nothing reaches the forwarders on its own. They must be deployment clients, and the Data TA arrives after its Configuration page is saved on the Deployment Server, the forwarders are added to the server class, and Deploy to Forwarders is clicked; each forwarder restarts when it arrives. See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders. A Splunk Cloud stack is never a Deployment Server: run your own, or install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder.
  • Ingest add-ons are installed directly on each instance that runs an input, never through a Deployment Server. Their credentials and inputs live in their own local/, which a push would replace. When a Deployment Server manages the Splunk Add-on for AWS on an instance, the AWS S3 Direct screen there only generates the configuration for an administrator to apply. Install the Azure or GCP add-on on each heavy forwarder that may run an input, but run one input for each queue or subscription: every input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue can index a redelivered message twice. For Google Cloud, use the LogServ GCP add-on, not the general-purpose Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud Platform (Splunkbase 3088), which cannot decompress the gzipped LogServ objects. One heavy forwarder can run the add-ons of several clouds; see More Than One Cloud.
  • AWS inputs. The SQS-Based S3 inputs read the queue of your scenario (SAP’s queue for Connect, the queue in your Secondary account for Filter or Copy) and download each object from the bucket its notification names (SAP’s bucket for Connect and Filter, your copy bucket for Copy). The index = sap_logserv_logs setting that sends the events to the right index is on these inputs, not in the Data TA.
  • Search heads. We strongly recommend against the Data TA and the ingest add-ons on a search head, Splunk Cloud included: ingest belongs on the heavy forwarders. Nothing blocks it, and a search head that runs the inputs itself (the “Splunk Cloud only” row) needs the Data TA there; see Running the TAs on a search head. On the Splunk Cloud Victoria Experience, installing the Data TA and the LogServ App on the search head and opening the AWS S3 Direct screen there have been checked; creating and running inputs on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested by the project, and the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have not been installed on one. On the Classic Experience, inputs run on an Inputs Data Manager (IDM). The Data TA’s app.manifest does not list the forwarder workload (_forwarders); whether Splunk Cloud installs it on an IDM has not been tested, and neither has this path.
  • Search-tier add-ons go on the search tier only. For LogServ data, CIM (1621), Windows (742) and Unix/Linux (833) provide search-time content only: the Data TA parses every event as sap_logserv_logs and only then routes it to XmlWinEventLog, linux_secure and the other sourcetypes, so these add-ons’ parse-time settings never apply. No LogServ package extracts XmlWinEventLog fields, so without 742 the Windows dashboard’s Event Code, Severity and Service panels stay empty. The App parses its other Linux sourcetypes itself; 833 provides the CIM fields of linux_secure. If you use one of these add-ons’ own inputs for other data, follow that add-on’s placement guidance for them.
  • Enterprise Security. The App’s ES content does its work only where ES runs, so install the LogServ App and its search-tier add-ons on the search head that runs ES too. On Splunk Cloud, ES has its own search head, separate from the one your users open for other apps (Enterprise Security Integration: Prerequisites).
  • No standalone Squid Proxy or ISC BIND add-ons. Their parsing is built into the LogServ App. If either is installed beside it, both parse the same events, and the App’s home view shows a banner recommending you remove the standalone add-on.
  • Splunk Cloud indexes. Create both indexes yourself, in Settings > Indexes or with the Admin Config Service (ACS), with the retention you want, before any data arrives. Do this also when the Data TA is installed on the Cloud stack: Splunk does not document that a private app’s index definitions create the indexes there.
  • The AI Assistant ships disabled. It needs the Splunk MCP Server 1.1.0 or later on the same search head as the LogServ App: the predefined prompts use its Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. The App’s health check blocks only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix) and sets no upper bound; the newest version verified is 2.0.0. See Set Up the AI Assistant.

docs.title: Plan and Prerequisites
docs.text: Use this page before you install anything: it lists what to request from SAP, what each Splunk tier needs, and the access, volume and retention decisions to make first. Which package goes on which instance is on Where Each Package Goes; the order of the whole deployment is on the Deployment Roadmap.

docs.title: Splunk Platform Requirements
docs.text:
• Splunk Enterprise 9.4.3 or later, or Splunk Cloud Platform. 9.4.3 is the minimum supported version: it is the platform this release is tested on. Nothing in the packages enforces it at install, and the LogServ App does not depend on Splunk’s own UI components (it bundles its own React and @splunk UI libraries).
  • Splunk Cloud Platform: checked on Victoria Experience stacks running Splunk Cloud Platform 10.x, most recently 10.5.2605.10 (2026-10-21). No test on the Classic Experience is recorded.
  • Heavy forwarders, not universal forwarders, for the ingest tier: the Data TA does its work while the data is parsed, and the ingest add-ons run as inputs on a full Splunk Enterprise instance.

docs.title: The Packages
docs.text:
A deployment of Splunk for SAP LogServ uses three kinds of package:

  • the Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv): index-time parsing, sourcetype routing and filtering of the data your ingest add-on collects; it has no data inputs of its own;
  • the LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv): dashboards and search-time content on the search head;
  • one ingest add-on for your cloud: the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) or the LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp).

Architecture explains what each does.

docs.title: Request from SAP and Prepare Your Cloud Account
docs.text:
SAP LogServ is an optional SAP ECS service: confirm with SAP that it is enabled for your SAP ECS landscape before you request anything below.

Start these first: they wait on SAP support and on your own cloud administrators, and nothing can be ingested until they are done. Each cloud’s setup guide has the details.

docs.title: SAP ECS on AWS
docs.text:
Choose your AWS scenario first (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario). Connect is the default. Filter is for when the forwarder load or the first-start backlog has to be cut. Copy keeps your own copy of new objects from the time it starts (plus what is still waiting in SAP’s queue); it cannot load older history, and it stores the objects decompressed. History is loaded with AWS S3 Direct in every scenario.

From SAP LogServ support:

  1. The ARNs of the S3 bucket that holds your LogServ data in the SAP ECS account and of the SQS queue that receives its notifications, and their AWS Region.
  2. After you deploy the scenario’s CloudFormation template in your Secondary account: the two access policies, one on SAP’s queue and one on SAP’s bucket, that give your role splunk-logserv-ta-role access. The example policies are in the repository’s aws_assets/sap_ecs_account_policies/ folder.
  3. If you will load history with AWS S3 Direct (in any scenario: data from before your inputs started is only in SAP’s bucket): s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN in SAP’s bucket policy. The example policy includes it, but SQS-based ingest never needs it, so confirm that SAP kept it.

In your own AWS account:

  • A Secondary AWS account, separate from the SAP ECS account, in which you can deploy CloudFormation stacks and create IAM users and roles. Deploy the stack in the Region of SAP’s bucket and queue.
  • Filter and Copy: an S3 bucket for the Lambda code, with a name of your own (bucket names are global), in the stack’s Region.
  • The IAM user’s access key that the setup guides create: plan how you will rotate it (Rotate the Access Key in the Connect, Filter or Copy guide).

docs.title: SAP ECS on Azure
docs.text:
SAP provisions the storage account, the container, the Storage Queue and the Event Grid subscription in the SAP ECS Azure account; you create nothing in Azure. From SAP support:

  1. The storage account name and the Storage Queue name.
  2. An account SAS with ss=bq, srt=o and sp=rp (blob read and queue process), plus a if you will configure a dead-letter queue. See What the SAP-provided SAS must cover.
  3. The SAS expiry date (its se= value) and how SAP renews it. When the SAS expires, the input stops reading until you enter a new one. Put the date in your calendar; see Rotate credentials.

See Parameters to obtain from SAP.

docs.title: SAP ECS on Google Cloud
docs.text:
SAP provisions the bucket, its notification, the Pub/Sub topic and the subscription in the SAP-managed project. The one resource you create is the service account:

  1. In a GCP project of your own, separate from the SAP-managed project, create a service account. It needs no roles in your project.
  2. Enable the Cloud Pub/Sub API and the Cloud Storage API in that project.
  3. Check before install day whether the organization policy iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation applies to the project: it blocks the JSON key the input needs.
  4. Give the service account’s email address to SAP support. SAP grants it roles/pubsub.subscriber on the LogServ subscription and roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket, and returns the project ID and the subscription name for the input. Ask also for the subscription’s acknowledgement deadline.
  5. Plan how you will rotate the service account’s key: it is yours, and nothing renews it for you. See Rotate credentials.

See The onboarding sequence, What SAP must grant your service account and Parameters for the input.

docs.title: Every Cloud: the Queue Backlog
docs.text: Ask SAP how long its queue keeps a message and how old its oldest message is. A new input starts with every notification still waiting, which can be days or weeks of data, and on Azure even months. Decide before the input starts whether SAP purges the older messages or you filter them. On AWS, purged days can be loaded later with AWS S3 Direct; on Azure and Google Cloud, nothing in this solution can load a purged day. See First Start: The Queue Backlog.

docs.title: Deployment Server
docs.text:
A Deployment Server is optional. Use one to manage the Data TA on several heavy forwarders; without one, you install and configure the Data TA on each heavy forwarder.

  • It is a Splunk Enterprise instance you run. A Splunk Cloud stack is never a Deployment Server; your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a license for one you run yourself (request it from Splunk Support).
  • The heavy forwarders must be its deployment clients (deploymentclient.conf) before you distribute the Data TA.
  • Deploy to Forwarders needs the edit_deployment_server capability, which Splunk’s admin role has.
  • Add only the heavy forwarders that collect LogServ data to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, never *: * would push the Data TA, with a restart, to every deployment client, search heads included.
  • Keep the ingest add-ons out of its server classes; see Heavy Forwarders.

See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

docs.title: Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
• Forwarding: each heavy forwarder forwards to your indexers. For Splunk Cloud, install on it the universal forwarder credentials app that your Splunk Cloud stack provides.
  • The Data TA: from your Deployment Server, or installed directly when no Deployment Server manages it.
  • The ingest add-on for your cloud, installed directly on each heavy forwarder that may run an input, never through a Deployment Server. Its credentials and inputs live in its own local/, which a push would replace. A heavy forwarder is strongly recommended over a search head; a search head is not blocked (see Running the TAs on a search head).
    • AWS: the Splunk Add-on for AWS (Splunkbase 1876). No minimum version is enforced; 8.2.2 or later is recommended (Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005, third-party package fixes). These pages were checked with 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen warns about versions below 8.1.0. Install it now and configure it with your AWS setup guide (add-on documentation). Its SQS-Based S3 inputs may share one queue across inputs and forwarders; see Add Heavy Forwarders on the Same Queue.
    • Azure: the LogServ Azure add-on; see Install the Azure add-on. Run one input for each queue: each input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue can index a redelivered message twice.
    • Google Cloud: the LogServ GCP add-on; see the GCP Setup Guide. Run one input for each subscription, for the same reason.
  • Network egress (HTTPS, port 443):
    • AWS: the AWS STS endpoint, and the SQS and S3 endpoints of the Region that holds SAP’s queue and bucket.
    • Azure: <account>.queue.core.windows.net, and the blob endpoint each notification names, normally <account>.blob.core.windows.net.
    • Google Cloud: oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com and storage.googleapis.com.
  • Outbound proxy:
    • The Splunk Add-on for AWS has its own setting, on its Configuration > Proxy tab (checked in version 8.3.1).
    • The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons have no proxy setting. They use Python’s standard HTTP client, which takes its proxy from HTTPS_PROXY in splunkd’s environment. This comes from reading their code and has not been tested in the lab.
    • Whenever splunkd runs with HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY set, also set NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost (plus the host name in mgmtHostPort, if it is not a loopback address). Otherwise calls to splunkd’s own management port, with their session key, go to the proxy.
  • The admin_all_objects capability, on any platform, for creating, editing or deleting an Azure or GCP input, which includes entering a new SAS or key: the add-ons save the input through Splunk’s REST interface as the signed-in user, and Splunk allows that write only with this capability. The Create backfill button of the AWS S3 Direct screen needs it too; without it the screen only generates the configuration for an administrator to apply. Find a role that holds it on each instance where you will do this.
  • Capacity: the Data TA’s work per event decides how many heavy forwarders your volume needs; see Capacity Planning and First Start.

docs.title: Indexers
docs.text:
Create sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit on the indexer tier before any data arrives:

  • Single instance: the Data TA creates both when it first loads.
  • Standalone indexer: Settings > Indexes, or a small indexes.conf.
  • Indexer cluster: an index-only app with both stanzas and repFactor = auto, in the manager node’s manager-apps/, pushed as the configuration bundle. Without repFactor = auto the indexes are not replicated.
  • Splunk Cloud: Settings > Indexes, or the Admin Config Service (ACS).

Separate indexers do not need the Data TA itself. The settings to use are on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA. Both index names can be changed: the LogServ App finds them through the macros sap_logserv_idx_macro and sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro; see Renaming an index.

docs.title: Search Head: the LogServ App and Its Add-ons
docs.text:
On the search tier (the search head, the Splunk Cloud search head, or every member of a search head cluster), install:

  • the LogServ App;
  • Splunk_SA_CIM (Splunkbase 1621) 5.0.0 or later, the App’s declared dependency;
  • the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742), which the Windows dashboard needs;
  • the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (833), for the CIM fields of linux_secure;
  • only for the AI Assistant: the Splunk MCP Server (7931) and, optionally, the Splunk AI Assistant (7245).

These add-ons go on the search tier only, not on the Deployment Server, the heavy forwarders or the indexers. Do not install the standalone Squid Proxy or ISC BIND add-ons: the LogServ App has their parsing built in. KV Store must be enabled on the search head. See LogServ App Prerequisites.

docs.title: Capacity, Volume and Retention
docs.text:
• Daily volume and license. Every event the filters keep is indexed into sap_logserv_logs and counts toward your Splunk license; events the filters drop do not. Measure the log-type mix and the forwarder load with Measure Your Own Heavy Forwarder.
  • Azure Unix command output. On Azure, SAP also delivers Unix command output (ps, top, netstat and others) in a folder named undefined/undefined: on the reference system about 0.7 million events and 125 MB of text a day, which the Data TA indexes unparsed. Decide whether to drop it before the input starts; see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields and Decide Filtering.
  • Retention. The Data TA sets no retention or size limit for sap_logserv_logs, so Splunk’s defaults apply until you set your own; it gives logserv_ai_assistant_audit 90 days (frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000). Where you create the indexes yourself, set both. Make the retention of sap_logserv_logs cover the oldest data you will load: events older than an index’s retention are removed soon after they are indexed.

docs.title: Roles and Access
docs.text:
Check these before users open the dashboards:

  • Every role that uses the dashboards can search sap_logserv_logs. On Splunk Enterprise the default user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so it and the roles that import it (such as power) can already search the index. Add the index to any role with a narrowed list (Settings > Roles > role > Indexes). On Splunk Cloud, check each role’s Indexes tab the same way.
  • The audit index is granted only as Restricting who can read the audit index describes.
  • App admins. The LogServ App treats only roles named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin as admins. Only they can open its Settings page and clear or backfill the dashboard data. Give the people who run the App one of these roles; see LogServ App Prerequisites.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud
docs.text:
• Roles. sc_admin is the customer’s administrator role. Splunk uses the admin role and the system roles to run the stack. sc_subadmin is not a standard role; some stacks create a delegated-admin role with that name.
  • Installs are private-app installs on your stack (on the Victoria Experience: Install app from file, or ACS), which run Splunk’s app vetting.
  • Indexes: create both yourself, as above, with the retention you want.
  • No Deployment Server: the Data TA’s Deploy to Forwarders button never appears on a Splunk Cloud stack. Use a Deployment Server of your own, or install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder.
  • admin_all_objects: the gates above apply on Splunk Cloud too, and whether your admin role holds the capability depends on your stack; check it under Settings > Roles. See Capability-gated REST endpoints.

See Splunk Cloud Considerations.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Splunk Cloud Considerations, if you use Splunk Cloud.
  • Capacity Planning and First Start: how many heavy forwarders, and the first-start backlog.
  • Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

docs.title: Start Here: Deployment Roadmap
docs.text:
This page gives the order in which to set up Splunk for SAP LogServ for the first time, from the request to SAP to working dashboards. Work through the steps in order: each one names the page with the details and ends with a check that tells you the step is done.

Decide before the data flows

The Data TA works at index time. Sourcetype routing, the filters and the cloud_provider stamp are applied when an event is indexed, and the event keeps what it was indexed with. Make the decisions of steps 6 to 8 before you save the Data TA’s Configuration page (step 9), so that a Deployment Server’s first push carries them, and in every case before any input starts (step 10). Whatever SAP’s queue holds when the input starts is indexed with the settings in place at that moment.

docs.title: The Steps at a Glance
docs.text:
The steps are grouped as in the Get Started menu, with three exceptions: step 8 uses a page from 1. Plan (Capacity Planning and First Start), step 12 is on the Configure and Operate tab (AWS S3 Direct), and step 15 is on the AI Assistant and Enterprise Security Integration tabs.

1. Plan

  1. Request from SAP and prepare your cloud
  2. Pick your topology
  3. Prepare the forwarding tier

2. Install the Data TA

  1. Create the indexes and set their retention
  2. Install the Data TA
  3. Choose cloud attribution
  4. Decide filtering
  5. Decide on the first-start queue backlog
  6. Distribute the Data TA (gate: the Data TA is on every heavy forwarder)

3. Connect Your Cloud

  1. Connect your cloud

4. Verify Your Data

  1. Verify your data

Configure and Operate (AWS S3 Direct)

  1. Load history

5. Install the LogServ App

  1. Install the LogServ App and its search-head add-ons
  2. Run Diagnostics, then backfill the dashboards

Optional

  1. The AI Assistant and the Enterprise Security content

docs.title: 1. Request from SAP and Prepare Your Cloud
docs.text:
Start here: SAP does this work on its side, and most later steps need its results. Plan and Prerequisites lists what to ask for, per cloud. SAP’s turnaround can be the longest wait of the whole setup, so send every request to SAP on day one and carry on with steps 2 to 9 while you wait.

  • AWS. Pick your scenario on Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario. AWS Remote S3 Connect is the default; choose AWS Remote S3 Filter now if your forwarders’ load or the first-start backlog (step 8) must be cut, because the scenario decides which template you deploy. Then do the AWS side of your scenario’s guide now, in your own AWS account (the guides’ Secondary account): get the ARNs of the S3 bucket and the SQS queue in your SAP ECS account and their AWS Region, deploy the CloudFormation template, and send SAP LogServ support the request to apply the queue and bucket policies for the role the template creates. In the Connect guide these are steps 1 to 3; in the Filter and Copy guides, steps 1 to 4, which also create the bucket for the Lambda code. If you will load history with AWS S3 Direct (step 12), which reads SAP’s bucket, ask in the same request for s3:ListBucket for that role in SAP’s bucket policy. Nothing reads SAP’s queue yet: the input comes in step 10, and the Filter and Copy templates create no Lambda trigger.
  • Azure. Get the storage account name, the queue name and an account SAS with ss=bq, srt=o and sp=rp (plus a if you configure a dead-letter queue). Ask when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how SAP renews it: the input stops reading when the SAS expires. See Parameters to obtain from SAP and What the SAP-provided SAS must cover.
  • GCP. Create a service account in a GCP project of your own and give its email address to SAP. SAP grants it access to the LogServ subscription and bucket, and gives you the project ID and the subscription name. Check your organization’s policy on service-account keys before install day, and decide how you will rotate the key. See The onboarding sequence, What SAP must grant your service account and Parameters for the input.
  • Every cloud. Ask SAP how long its queue keeps a message and how old the oldest waiting message is. You need both in step 8 (First Start: The Queue Backlog).

Done when: you hold the values your cloud’s guide asks for (AWS: the two ARNs, the Region, a deployed CloudFormation stack, and SAP’s confirmation that both policies are applied; Azure: the account, the queue, the SAS and its expiry; GCP: the project ID, the subscription and SAP’s confirmation of its grants), and you know how long SAP’s queue keeps messages. Steps 2 to 9 can run while you wait for SAP; step 10 cannot start until this step is done.

docs.title: 2. Pick Your Topology
docs.text:
Pick the row that matches your Splunk deployment. The steps below refer to these names. The exact placement of every package is on Where Each Package Goes.

Topology What it means for the steps below Single instance One Splunk Enterprise instance indexes, searches and runs the inputs, and every package goes on it. There is no distribution: in step 9 you save the Data TA’s Configuration page on the instance itself. DS + HFs + on-premises search head Heavy forwarders run the inputs and parse the data, your Deployment Server pushes the Data TA to them, the indexers hold the indexes, and the LogServ App goes on the search head. Every step applies. DS + HFs + Splunk Cloud As above, but the heavy forwarders send to Splunk Cloud, you create the indexes in Splunk Cloud, and the LogServ App goes on the Splunk Cloud search head. The Deployment Server is your own, on premises: Splunk Cloud does not host one. HFs without a DS (Splunk Cloud or on-premises search head) You install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder and save its Configuration page on each one, with the same values: nothing copies them between forwarders. The indexes go on your indexer tier or the Splunk Cloud stack. Splunk Cloud only Supported: not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended. The Data TA, the cloud add-on and the LogServ App go on the Splunk Cloud search head, and the inputs run there, so ingest competes with your users’ searches. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare the search-head workload, but their installation on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested yet.

Clustered tiers: an indexer cluster gets the two indexes from an index-only app on its manager node (step 4); a search head cluster gets the LogServ App and its add-ons from its deployer.

Read Plan and Prerequisites for every topology, Splunk Cloud Considerations if you use Splunk Cloud, and Capacity Planning and First Start to size the heavy forwarders.

Done when: you know which instance gets which package, and how many heavy forwarders you need.

docs.title: 3. Prepare the Forwarding Tier
docs.text:
These items apply to each heavy forwarder, or on a single instance to that instance. With Splunk Cloud only, the add-on and role items apply to the Splunk Cloud search head.

  • Deployment client (topologies with a DS). Point each heavy forwarder at your Deployment Server and check that it phones home.
  • Splunk Cloud (heavy forwarders that send to Splunk Cloud). Install your stack’s universal forwarder credentials app on each heavy forwarder.
  • Network. Allow HTTPS (port 443) from each heavy forwarder to your cloud. AWS: the AWS STS endpoint (the Splunk Add-on for AWS assumes the role splunk-logserv-ta-role through it), and the SQS and S3 endpoints of the Region that holds SAP’s queue and bucket. Azure: <account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net. GCP: oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com and storage.googleapis.com. If the forwarders reach the internet through a proxy, see Plan and Prerequisites → Heavy Forwarders.
  • AWS only: the Splunk Add-on for AWS (Splunkbase 1876) on each heavy forwarder that will run an input. Version 8.2.2 or later is recommended (SVD-2026-1005). Install it directly on the heavy forwarder, not through a Deployment Server: the add-on keeps its accounts and inputs in its local/ folder, which a Deployment Server push replaces, and for an add-on the Deployment Server manages, the AWS S3 Direct screen offers only its Apply this as an administrator view, which generates the configuration but creates nothing.
  • Who does the setup. Creating, editing or deleting an Azure or GCP input, and the Create backfill button on the AWS S3 Direct screen, need a role with the admin_all_objects capability on the instance where you do it, on Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud alike. The LogServ App treats only roles named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin as admins. See Roles and Access, and on Splunk Cloud the role notes on Splunk Cloud Considerations.

Done when: each heavy forwarder is listed in Forwarder Management (Agent Management in Splunk 10.0 and later) on your Deployment Server; with Splunk Cloud, each heavy forwarder’s _internal events can be searched from the Splunk Cloud search head; on AWS, Apps → Manage Apps on each heavy forwarder shows the Splunk Add-on for AWS; and you know which account will create the inputs.

docs.title: 4. Create the Indexes and Set Their Retention
docs.text:
The solution uses two indexes: sap_logserv_logs for the data and logserv_ai_assistant_audit for the AI Assistant’s audit trail. Keep these names unless you have a reason to change them; renaming takes the procedure on Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

  • Single instance. The Data TA creates both indexes when you install it in step 5. Set their retention afterwards.
  • Standalone indexer. Create both under Settings → Indexes, or with a small indexes.conf.
  • Indexer cluster. Put both stanzas in an index-only app under the manager node’s manager-apps/, with repFactor = auto on each, and push it as the configuration bundle. Without repFactor = auto the indexes are not replicated.
  • Splunk Cloud. Create both yourself under Settings → Indexes, or with the Admin Config Service (ACS), before any data arrives.

Retention. The Data TA sets none for sap_logserv_logs, so Splunk’s default applies unless you set one; it keeps the audit index for 90 days. Choose the retention you need when you create the indexes. Events older than an index’s retention can be removed soon after they are indexed, which matters when you load history in step 12.

Who can search the data. Every role that will use the dashboards must be able to search sap_logserv_logs. Roles that may search all non-internal indexes (*, as Splunk’s built-in roles do) already can. Add the index only to roles with a narrowed list (Settings → Roles → role → Indexes, on Splunk Cloud too). Grant the audit index only as Restricting who can read the audit index describes.

See Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA.

Done when: Settings → Indexes on each indexer, or on Splunk Cloud, lists both indexes with the retention you chose (on a single instance, after step 5).

docs.title: 5. Install the Data TA
docs.text:
• Topologies with a DS. Install it on the Deployment Server only. Do not install it on the heavy forwarders by hand: the Deployment Server’s push replaces each forwarder’s copy, local/ included (step 9).
  • HFs without a DS. Install it on each heavy forwarder.
  • Single instance. Install it on the instance.
  • Splunk Cloud only. Install it on the Splunk Cloud search head as a private app. On Splunk Cloud it is needed only where the inputs run on the search head.
  • Indexers and search heads that run no inputs do not need it.

See Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA. Leave its Configuration page unsaved until step 9.

Done when: Apps → Manage Apps shows Splunk TA for SAP LogServ at version 0.1.2, and its Configuration page opens with the Filters and Cloud Provider tabs.

docs.title: 6. Choose Cloud Attribution
docs.text:
Each event can carry an indexed cloud_provider field that says which cloud it came from. The recommended setup is the same for every fleet: leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set (its default). The Azure and GCP inputs stamp their own events, and AWS S3 Direct stamps the inputs it creates. On AWS you add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input as soon as you create it in step 10, following Add the _meta line to an AWS input: create the input, disable it at once, add the line, restart, enable it again. On Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder. Setting the dropdown as well adds a second stamp next to an input’s own. See Choose Cloud Attribution.

Done when: you have written down the dropdown value, and on AWS you have planned the _meta line for each input.

docs.title: 7. Decide Filtering
docs.text:
Filtering is off by default. Decide whether to turn it on and with which values:

  • Folders and sources to include or exclude.
  • Days in the Past (default 7; 0 turns it off). It applies only while filtering is on. It also leaves out of an AWS S3 Direct backfill the days older than its cutoff, so if you will load history (step 12), set it to cover that history.
  • The daily refresh. With filtering on and Days in the Past above 0, a daily job moves the cutoff; on a Deployment Server it also reloads the server class, and each heavy forwarder restarts about once a day to apply it.
  • Azure: the Unix command output. SAP delivers some Azure data in a folder named undefined/undefined: Unix command output, about 0.7 million events and 125 MB a day on the reference system, which stays under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype. Unless you need it, drop it with Exclude Sources ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts. Folder patterns cannot reach it (Data Delivered Without Folder Fields). If you keep it, restrict who can search it: a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with, passwords and tokens included.

See Decide Filtering.

Done when: you have written down Enable Filtering, the include and exclude values and Days in the Past.

docs.title: 8. Decide on the First-Start Queue Backlog
docs.text:
SAP’s queue keeps a notification for each new object until a consumer takes it or it expires, so a new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting, on Azure even months. The input works through them on top of the live feed. Decide now, before the first Save in step 9, how to handle them:

  • Let it drain. Estimate how long the catch-up takes and size the heavy forwarders for it.
  • Ask SAP to purge the older messages, shortly before you start the input in step 10 (in the AWS Filter and Copy scenarios, before you create the Lambda’s trigger). On AWS you can load those days later with AWS S3 Direct (step 12). On Azure and GCP nothing in this solution can load them later.
  • AWS Remote S3 Filter: its Lambda passes on only objects with events newer than its DaysInThePast setting, a parameter of the template you deployed in step 1. To change it, update the stack before you create the Lambda’s trigger.
  • Keep old events out of the index with Days in the Past (step 7). The forwarders still download and parse them, so the catch-up takes as long.

If your choice changes the filter values of step 7, enter the changed values in step 9. See First Start: The Queue Backlog.

Done when: you have chosen how to handle the backlog (if a purge, SAP has agreed to do it shortly before your input starts; otherwise you have accepted the catch-up time), and your filter values reflect that choice.

docs.title: 9. Distribute the Data TA
docs.text:
• Topologies with a DS. On the Deployment Server, open the Data TA’s Configuration page, enter the values from steps 6 to 8 and Save, whether filtering is on or off. The Save stages the Data TA for the heavy forwarders and creates the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, disabled. In Forwarder Management, edit that server class’s agent assignment and name your heavy forwarders by host name or IP address. Never use *: it sends the Data TA, with a restart, to every deployment client, search heads included. Then click Deploy to Forwarders. Each heavy forwarder picks the Data TA up at its next phone-home and restarts; allow 5 minutes or more.
  • HFs without a DS, single instance, Splunk Cloud only. Save the Configuration page with the values from steps 6 to 8 on each instance that holds the Data TA (Without a Deployment Server).

See Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

Gate: the Data TA must be on every heavy forwarder before any input is created

An event that arrives before the Data TA keeps the base sourcetype sap_logserv_logs, its folder fields are never set and its routing never happens, permanently.

Done when: the Version Check on each heavy forwarder shows the Data TA at version 0.1.2 with its build, and, with a Deployment Server, Forwarder Management shows each heavy forwarder as Ok under SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders.

docs.title: 10. Connect Your Cloud
docs.text:
Follow your cloud’s guide, on each heavy forwarder that runs an input (single instance: the instance; Splunk Cloud only: the Splunk Cloud search head): Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario leads to the AWS Remote S3 Connect, Filter or Copy guide, the Azure Setup Guide or the GCP Setup Guide. If you chose a purge in step 8, have SAP do it shortly before you create the input (Filter and Copy: before you create the Lambda’s trigger).

  • AWS. You did the AWS side in step 1, so pick up your guide at its access-key step: step 4 of the Connect guide, step 5 of the Filter and Copy guides. Add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each SQS-Based S3 input as soon as you create it, following Add the _meta line to an AWS input (create, disable at once, add the line, restart, enable); on Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder. In the Filter scenario, create the Lambda’s trigger only once SAP has confirmed both policies: the Lambda discards a notification whose object it cannot read.
  • Azure and GCP. Run one input per queue or subscription, on one heavy forwarder. Each input keeps its own record of what it has read, so a second input on the same queue or subscription can index a message twice (Azure, GCP).
  • Credential renewals. Put the renewal dates in your calendar: the Azure SAS expiry, the GCP service-account key and the AWS access key. Replacing a SAS or key in an Azure or GCP input needs admin_all_objects too. See Rotate credentials in the Azure and GCP guides, and Rotate the Access Key in your AWS guide (Connect, Filter, Copy).

Done when: the input reads without errors (Azure and GCP: its log line done: messages=N ... events=N shows events; AWS: the Splunk Add-on for AWS logs no errors in _internal), and the first events appear in index=sap_logserv_logs.

docs.title: 11. Verify Your Data
docs.text:
Run the searches on Verify Your Data. Use the index name, not the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro: a search head that has neither the Data TA nor the LogServ App does not know the macro yet.

Done when: every event carries splunk_solution=splunk_for_sap_logserv, the sourcetypes match what SAP delivers to you (Supported Log Types), each event indexed since its input got its _meta line has one cloud_provider value (a few AWS events read in the minutes between creating an input and adding the line carry none, which is expected), and no folder that the Data TA routes by folder alone stays under sap_logserv_logs.

docs.title: 12. Load History
docs.text:
The inputs read only what SAP’s queue holds. To load older days:

  • AWS. Use the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen on the heavy forwarder (or Splunk Cloud search head) that has the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Its Create backfill button needs admin_all_objects; without it, the screen shows the configuration for an administrator to apply. The role needs s3:ListBucket on the bucket, and for SAP’s bucket SAP’s bucket policy must also allow it (step 1). With filtering on, Days in the Past must cover the days you load, and the index’s retention must cover them too. See AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.
  • Azure and GCP. The product has no history load. Contact your Splunk team.

Done when: on AWS, the two check searches the AWS S3 Direct screen gives under each backfill show its scan finished and the events of its days in the index.

docs.title: 13. Install the LogServ App and Its Search-Head Add-ons
docs.text:
On the search head (search head cluster: through its deployer; Splunk Cloud: the Splunk Cloud search head; single instance: the instance), install the Splunk Common Information Model add-on (Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunkbase 1621) 5.0.0 or later, the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742) and the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (833), then the LogServ App. Without the Windows add-on, the panels that need Windows event fields stay empty. If you renamed the data index, update the index macro. See LogServ App Prerequisites and Install the App and Seed the Dashboards.

Done when: the LogServ App opens, and the Summary of its Diagnostics page lists Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunk_TA_windows and Splunk_TA_nix as present and names your data index under Index (from the app macro).

docs.title: 14. Run Diagnostics, Then Backfill the Dashboards
docs.text:
The dashboards read hourly rollups, so until you backfill them they show only the hours since the LogServ App was installed.

  1. Open the LogServ App’s Diagnostics page (Data Doctor) and check which sourcetypes it finds.
  2. As an admin (a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin), open Settings → Dashboard Data. Under Backfill window, pick a window that covers the history in your index, including what you loaded in step 12, up to 365 days back: 30 days by default, 60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range of UTC days.
  3. Click Run backfill, and keep the page open until every row has finished: the Environment Topology (graph) row is written only after the page has collected its results.

Start a long backfill so that it does not run during the nightly retention window (00:34 to 02:36 in the search head’s time zone): rows written into a collection while its retention runs can be lost until you run the backfill again.

See Backfilling on first install.

Done when: the Dashboard Data tab reports Backfill complete, and the dashboards show your history.

docs.title: 15. Optional: the AI Assistant and the Enterprise Security Content
docs.text:
• AI Assistant. It ships turned off. To use it, install the Splunk MCP Server on the search head, grant its mcp_tool_execute capability to the roles that will use the AI Assistant (the MCP Server grants it only to admin and sc_admin, so analysts and sc_subadmin need it added: step 2 of Set Up the AI Assistant), decide who is audited (a user’s role needs edit_log_alert_event or edit_tcp), then have an admin turn it on and answer both acknowledgements. See Set Up the AI Assistant.
  • Enterprise Security content. It ships enabled. With ES on its own search head (as on Splunk Cloud), install the LogServ App there as well (Enterprise Security Integration: Prerequisites). On a search head without Enterprise Security, turn it off. The AI Assistant’s Security prompts run 13 of these searches, and a disabled search makes its prompt fail, so if you use those prompts, stop only the schedule of those 13 and disable the rest (Disabling or tuning the ES content).

Done when: the AI Assistant button appears in the LogServ App’s top bar (if you turned it on), and the ES searches run on a schedule only where Enterprise Security does.
