They run on their schedules whether or not Enterprise Security is installed, and their notable and risk actions need it. On a search head without Enterprise Security, disable them (Disabling or Tuning the ES Content). Thirteen of them also run the AI Assistant’s Security-pack prompts: if you use those prompts, read that section before you disable anything.
  9. Check the result. In Settings → Dashboard Data, every row shows its history and none reads failed — re-run or truncated — re-run; the dashboards show data for the ranges you rebuilt.

docs.title: Updating the Data TA
docs.text:
Install the new tarball over the existing one where the Data TA runs: Apps → Manage Apps → Install app from file with Upgrade app selected, or $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk install app <tarball> -update 1, then restart Splunk when asked. An app upgrade keeps local/.

  • Single instance, or heavy forwarders without a Deployment Server: on each instance. Coming from a build before 1791565776 with Filtering on, click Save on Configuration → Filters on each one.
  • Heavy forwarders with a Deployment Server: on the Deployment Server only, then into deployment-apps/ and out to the forwarders, as below. Do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages: the next push replaces that copy, its local/ included.
  • A Splunk Cloud search head that runs LogServ inputs: as a private app (On Splunk Cloud).
  • An indexer: only if you installed the Data TA there. On an indexer only its indexes.conf takes effect. The 0.0.5 builds with the version 0.0.5, and 0.0.6, 0.1.1 and 0.1.2, define the same two indexes, sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit, so such a copy can stay as it is; updating it there as well does no harm. Early 0.0.5 builds (version 0.0.5.0) and 0.0.5.1 define _ai_assistant_audit instead: update that copy, or create logserv_ai_assistant_audit on the indexer tier (Data TA).

With a Deployment Server:

  1. Install the new build over etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ on the Deployment Server.

  2. Replace the copy in etc/deployment-apps/, keeping its local/ folder. A Save on the Configuration page copies the Data TA into deployment-apps/ only when that copy is missing or its version differs, and every 0.1.2 build has the version 0.1.2, so a later 0.1.2 build never gets there by itself (Later Builds With the Same Version). As the user Splunk runs as:

    cd $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/deployment-apps
mv splunk_ta_sap_logserv ~/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.before-upgrade
tar -xzf /path/to/splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz -C .
cp -a ~/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.before-upgrade/local splunk_ta_sap_logserv/
grep -E "^(version|build)" splunk_ta_sap_logserv/default/app.conf

    The last command shows the new build. If the old copy has a metadata/local.meta, copy it into splunk_ta_sap_logserv/metadata/ as well. Keep the moved copy until every forwarder runs the new build. The same steps work coming from 0.0.5, 0.0.6 or 0.1.1. (There a Save would also replace the deployment-apps/ copy, because the version changes, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/, local/ included, which drops anything you added by hand under deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/.)

  3. Coming from a build before 1791565776 with Filtering on: open Configuration → Filters on the Deployment Server and click Save, so the rules are generated in the new form and copied into deployment-apps/.

  4. Click Deploy to Forwarders on the Filters tab. Each forwarder picks the change up at its next phone-home (60 seconds by default) and restarts; allow 5 minutes or more. The button reloads every server class on the Deployment Server (Deploy to Forwarders).
  5. Check the build on each forwarder (Version Check).

docs.title: On Splunk Cloud
docs.text:
Update each package on the Splunk Cloud stack the way you installed it, as a private app: in Splunk Web, open the gear icon next to Apps, then Install app from file and Upload App, sign in with your splunk.com account and upload the tarball. When the Uploaded Apps table shows it as Approved (Splunk Cloud vets the package first), click Install. The Data TA is needed on the stack only where LogServ inputs run on the search head (Splunk Cloud Considerations).

Every 0.1.2 build keeps the version 0.1.2. On a Splunk Cloud 10.5 stack, later 0.1.2 builds of the App and the Data TA installed over earlier ones in this way, without a restart prompt (tested 2026-10-21); other Splunk Cloud versions have not been tested. If your stack does not offer Install because version 0.1.2 is already installed, stop there: do not uninstall the installed app to make room for the new one, because uninstalling removes its local/ configuration. Open a Splunk Cloud support case instead.

Forwarders you run yourself are updated as described above. The narrower repairs below need the search head’s management port, which on Splunk Cloud must first be opened for you. If you cannot reach it, use the Clear and Backfill instead.

docs.title: 4. How to Rebuild a Row
docs.text:
1. Rebuild after the upgrade, on the new build: a Clear done before the upgrade is undone by the old build’s last hourly runs.
  2. Pick a time clear of the nightly retention window, 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time. A retention search rewrites its whole collection and erases rows that a backfill running at the same time has just added.
  3. Open Settings → Dashboard Data (The Dashboard Data Settings Tab). Under Backfill window, choose a window that covers the history you want: the 365-day preset reaches as far back as a rollup keeps rows, and a custom range takes whole UTC days. The default is 30 days. A window longer than 90 days shows a cost warning first; for scale, a 365-day backfill of every row took 195 minutes on the reference system. The two flat Environment Topology collections (the host-to-SID inventory and the IP enrichment) always read the last 30 days.
  4. For each Clear, then Backfill row: note its History, click Clear and confirm, then click the same row’s Backfill. Wait until it has finished before you start the next row.
  5. For each Backfill only row: click its own Backfill, without Clear.
  6. Use each row’s own Backfill, not the button under the window (Run backfill, or Re-run backfill (all)): it backfills only the rows it considers incomplete, or every row when it considers all of them complete. Use it only where this page says so: after Clear all data, coming from build 281 or earlier.
  7. Keep the page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished.
  8. A row that shows failed — re-run or truncated — re-run needs its Backfill again; repeating a backfill is safe.

The Clear removes everything a row holds, including history older than the raw events your index still holds, which no Backfill can bring back. For the two biggest rebuilds a narrower repair keeps that history.

docs.title: Narrower Repair After App Build 378
docs.text:
Use this instead of the Clear and Backfill of Coming From App Build 377 or Earlier to keep history older than your raw events. It deletes only the rows inside the window you will backfill and leaves older rows as they are. It needs the search head’s management port; if you cannot reach it (on Splunk Cloud it must first be opened for you), use the Clear and Backfill instead.

  1. Pick the window. Its first day, W, is the first UTC day whose raw events your index still holds in full, and no earlier than 365 days ago, the furthest a Backfill reaches. This search finds the oldest event over all time (earliest=0; the time picker does not limit it) and returns W as the epoch seconds of that UTC midnight:

    | tstats min(_time) as first where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=0
| eval W = max((floor(first/86400)+1)*86400, floor(relative_time(now(), "-365d")/86400)*86400)

    The day of the oldest event may be held only in part, so W is the UTC midnight after it. Rows older than W keep their old values, and no raw event is left that a later Backfill could count beside them. The custom range of step 3 starts on W’s date in UTC.

  2. Delete the rows from W onward, after the upgrade and clear of the nightly retention window: one REST call per collection in the table, on the search head’s management port, with an admin-tier account. For example:

    curl -k -u admin -G -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/logserv_hana_category_rollup" \
  --data-urlencode 'query={"bucket_ts":{"$gte":<W>}}'

    The same call with -X GET in place of -X DELETE returns rows the query matches (at most 50,000 by default, so it shows what the query matches, not how many): check it first. A DELETE without its query empties the whole collection.

    Row Collections HANA Audit logserv_hana_category_rollup HANA Trace logserv_hana_trace_rollup Environment Health logserv_severity_rollup ABAP Network & Security logserv_abapnet_rollup Host Role Activity (Host Details) logserv_hostrole_rollup Environment Topology (graph) logserv_topology_nodes and logserv_topology_edges; and all of logserv_topology_inventory (the call without query), which has no time field and holds only the current mapping of addresses and hosts to systems: the Backfill rebuilds it from the last 30 days Environment Topology (detail tabs) logserv_topology_detail_rollup Multi-Cloud Overview logserv_mc_rollup Data Pipeline Overview logserv_pipeline_rollup Host Details logserv_hostdetails_rollup Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details / Data Pipeline) logserv_stmap_rollup

  3. Then backfill. Do every delete before any Backfill. Then Backfill each of the eleven rows with its own Backfill over a custom range from W to today, and Backfill Change & Configuration Activity and Cross-Stack Authentication without Clear. Keep the Settings page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished.

docs.title: Narrower Repair After App Build 383
docs.text:
The Clear of Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations also removes the dispatcher, ICM and ABAP Operations panels’ history, although their stored values did not change. To keep the older history, delete only the trace-component rows (metric wp) from W onward, with W chosen as in the build-378 repair above:

curl -k -u admin -G -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/logserv_wp_perf_rollup" \
  --data-urlencode 'query={"metric":"wp","bucket_ts":{"$gte":<W>}}'

Check the query with -X GET first, as above. Then Backfill the row with its own Backfill over a custom range from W to today. The Backfill rewrites the row’s other rows in that range under the keys they already have, so nothing is counted twice; trace-component rows older than W keep their old names. If you cannot reach the management port, use the Clear and Backfill instead.

docs.title: What Is Preserved
docs.text:
• local/ configuration survives an app upgrade: the App’s ai_assistant_settings.conf, any acknowledgement files written by 0.0.5 builds before 192 or 0.1.1 builds before 240 (later builds keep the acknowledgements in the KV Store) and the credentials in its passwords.conf; the Data TA’s filter and Cloud Provider settings; the Azure and GCP inputs and their credentials. On forwarders that a Deployment Server manages, the Data TA’s local/ is the one in the Deployment Server’s deployment-apps/ copy.
  • KV Store data persists: settings, acknowledgements, saved topology layouts, dashboard preferences and the rollup collections. Collections and their data survive an app upgrade; the work list names the rows whose stored values must be rebuilt.
  • Indexed events keep their index, sourcetype and index-time fields. Search-time fields follow the installed App (Search-Time Field Changes).
  • Dashboard URLs are unchanged across recent releases. The Settings page moved from #/settings/ai-assistant to #/settings (the old URL redirects) and is titled Application Settings, with two top-level tabs, AI Assistant and Dashboard Data: update any runbook that names the old page title.

docs.title: Restricted Deployments: Templates-only and v0.0.6
docs.text:
• The published App is the full-LLM build. No templates-only package is published for 0.1.2. After you upgrade a deployment that ran the templates-only build, or the v0.0.6 line, its stored templates_only_mode setting governs, and a deployment with no stored value takes the shipped default, off. Free-form questions are then allowed whenever the AI Assistant is enabled. Nothing goes to an LLM vendor until an admin selects a provider and saves its credential (the shipped provider is a built-in mock), but a provider credential stored before the upgrade is used again. An upgrade creates no credential.
  • To keep the deployment restricted, turn Templates-only mode on under Settings → AI Assistant → General after the upgrade and click Save Defaults, or build the templates-only variant from this release’s source and install that instead (Restricting the LLM Path, Building the Packages from Source).
  • v0.0.6 remains the option where a policy requires the LLM vendor code to be absent from the package. It is frozen at App build 266 and receives no fixes: it lacks every change of 0.1.1 after build 299 and of every 0.1.2 build (Release Notes: 0.1.1, Release Notes: 0.1.2). An upgrade from v0.0.6 to 0.1.2 brings the vendor code back, restricted only by the setting above.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Reinstalling an earlier App tarball restores its default/ content, and your local/ configuration stays. It does not roll back the KV Store data:

  • Collections that only the newer build created stay in place, unused by the older App.
  • If the build you leave changed what a rollup stores (the Clear rows of the work list: builds 282, 356 to 358, 364 to 365, 378 and 383), the restored build’s hourly aggregation rewrites the last hour or two (Beaconing detection: the last two days) under its old keys, beside the rows the newer build wrote, and any Backfill it runs over earlier days does the same. Those hours are then counted twice. After rolling back across such a build, wait until the restored build is running, then Clear and Backfill the rows its work-list entry names (How to Rebuild a Row). A Clear done before the rollback is undone by the newer build’s last runs, and upgrading again later needs the same rebuild again.
  • Rolling back to App build 374 or earlier brings back retention searches that can empty a rollup after a restart.

The Data TA rolls back the same way, and its local/ filter configuration stays. Rolling it back also removes the parsing, routing and filtering changes made since that build (Data TA); events parsed in the meantime keep the sourcetype they got. With a Deployment Server, an earlier build that has the same version goes into deployment-apps/ by hand, as for an upgrade.

docs.title: Removing the Solution
docs.text:
To take Splunk for SAP LogServ out of a deployment, stop the data first, then remove each package from the tier it is on. The indexed data and the App’s KV Store data are handled in their own steps.

  1. Stop the data.
    • AWS: on each heavy forwarder, disable or delete the SQS-Based S3 inputs of the Splunk Add-on for AWS that read SAP’s queue. The backfill inputs that the AWS S3 Direct screen created also live in the Splunk Add-on for AWS: delete them with Delete all on that screen while the Data TA is still installed. In AWS, delete the CloudFormation stack you created from the Connect, Filter or Copy template. With Copy, empty its bucket first: CloudFormation does not delete a bucket that still holds objects. The Lambda code bucket you created for Filter or Copy is not part of the stack.
    • Azure and GCP: delete the inputs on each heavy forwarder or search head that runs them, or remove the add-ons in step 4.
    • Tell SAP that the access it granted for the connection is no longer needed.
  2. Decide what happens to the indexed data, before you remove the Data TA. Removing a package does not delete indexed data: the buckets of sap_logserv_logs and logserv_ai_assistant_audit stay on disk. Where the Data TA’s own indexes.conf defines the two indexes (a single instance, or an indexer you installed it on), removing the Data TA removes their definitions, and the data can no longer be searched. To keep it searchable, define both indexes elsewhere now, for example by copying the two stanzas of the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf into system/local/indexes.conf on that instance. Deleting the data is step 5.

  3. Search head: the LogServ App.

    • If Enterprise Security reads the App’s asset and identity lookups (splunk_for_sap_logserv_assets, splunk_for_sap_logserv_identities), remove them from ES’s Asset and Identity Management first (Add to ES Identity Management): they are removed with the App.

    • Its settings, acknowledgement records, saved layouts and dashboard data are in its KV Store collections, all named logserv_*, not in its directory. Export what you want to keep. If none of it may remain, delete the collections’ contents right before you remove the App, while it is still installed: one REST call per collection, with an admin-tier account, on the management port (on Splunk Cloud it must first be opened for you). The collections are the stanzas of the App’s default/collections.conf, 40 in build 394. This lists their names from the tarball you installed:

      tar -xzOf splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz splunk_app_sap_logserv/default/collections.conf \
  | sed -n 's/^\[\(.*\)\]$/\1/p'

      Then, for each name:

      curl -k -u admin -X DELETE \
  "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/<collection>"

    • Remove the App: on Splunk Enterprise, $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk remove app splunk_app_sap_logserv as the user Splunk runs as, then restart Splunk (or stop Splunk, delete $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv and start Splunk); on a search head cluster, delete splunk_app_sap_logserv from the deployer’s $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/shcluster/apps/ and push the bundle with splunk apply shcluster-bundle, which removes it from the members; on Splunk Cloud, uninstall it as you would any private app. Its own credentials (local/passwords.conf), lookups and configuration go with its directory. Notable and risk events its searches already wrote stay in Enterprise Security’s indexes.

    • The add-ons the App needs on the search head (CIM, the Windows and Unix and Linux add-ons, the Splunk MCP Server) are separate apps: remove them only if nothing else uses them.

  4. Heavy forwarders and the Deployment Server.

    • With a Deployment Server: the Data TA reached the forwarders through the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. In Settings → Forwarder Management (Agent Management in Splunk Enterprise 10.0 and later), take the Data TA out of that class, or delete the class if it holds nothing else (the 0.0.5 Azure setup put the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Cloud Services in it too). In the files, the class is the [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders] stanza and the Data TA’s place in it the [serverClass:SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders:app:splunk_ta_sap_logserv] stanza, in the serverclass.conf that $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk btool serverclass list --debug | grep SAP_LogServ shows. Remove only those stanzas, never the whole file, which holds your other server classes too, then run $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk reload deploy-server. Then check each forwarder, and where $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv is still there, remove it. Last, remove the Data TA from the Deployment Server itself, etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv and etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv together: while it is installed in etc/apps/, its daily filter refresh can copy it back into deployment-apps/.
    • Without a Deployment Server: remove the Data TA from each forwarder ($SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk remove app splunk_ta_sap_logserv, then restart).
    • LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons: remove them from each forwarder or search head that runs them. Each input’s credential is in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf and goes with it.
    • Single instance, an indexer you installed it on, or a Splunk Cloud search head that ran the inputs: remove the Data TA there too, after step 2.

  5. Delete the indexes, if the data is not to be kept. To delete the data, remove the indexes where you created them (Create the Indexes): under Settings → Indexes on a standalone indexer or on Splunk Cloud; on an indexer cluster, with Splunk’s procedure for removing an index from the cluster. Where the Data TA’s own indexes.conf defined them and you removed it in step 4, their buckets are still on disk, in the directories that file gave them: stop Splunk, delete $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs and $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit, and start Splunk again.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text:
• Find your builds (About in the App; Version Check for the Data TA), then apply every work-list row at or above your build.
  • No data re-ingest; local/ and KV Store data are kept. Indexed events keep their sourcetype; some search-time fields change.
  • Rebuild the Dashboard Data rows the work list names, after the upgrade, clear of the nightly retention window, with each row’s own Backfill.
  • With a Deployment Server, a later 0.1.2 Data TA build goes into deployment-apps/ by hand.
  • The published App is the full-LLM build: turn Templates-only mode on to keep a deployment restricted.
  • On a search head without Enterprise Security, disable the App’s ES searches.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify Your Data: check that events arrive with their sourcetypes after the update.
  2. Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness: what each Dashboard Data row holds and how fresh it is.
  3. Release Notes: 0.1.2: what each build changed.

docs.title: Verify Your Data
docs.text:
Run these checks once your first input has read data (step 11 of the Deployment Roadmap, in its 4. Verify Your Data group), before you install the LogServ App. They show whether events arrive, whether the Data TA parsed them, which sourcetypes they got and which cloud they are attributed to.

Use the index name, not the macro

The searches below name the index, index=sap_logserv_logs. The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the Data TA or the LogServ App is installed. A distributed or Splunk Cloud search head usually has neither at this point, so a search that uses the macro fails there. If you renamed the data index, put your index name in place of sap_logserv_logs.

docs.title: Where to Run the Searches
docs.text:
Run them in Search & Reporting on a search head that searches your indexers: the Splunk Cloud search head, your on-premises search head, or the single instance. All of them only read.

They look at the last 24 hours of event time. Events from SAP’s queue backlog keep the time they were logged, so while an input is still working through a backlog, widen earliest= (for example to -14d).

docs.title: 1. Events Arrive and the Data TA Parsed Them
docs.text:
| tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-24h by splunk_solution

The Data TA stamps splunk_solution=splunk_for_sap_logserv on every event it parses. Expect a single row with that value.

  • No rows: nothing has arrived in that time. Check the input on its forwarder (check 5).
  • A (none) row: the Data TA’s rules did not run on those events. Two causes:
    • The Data TA was not on the instance that parsed them. The events keep the base sourcetype sap_logserv_logs, carry no folder fields and keep the whole delivery line as their event text, and they stay that way. Run the Version Check on each heavy forwarder, and distribute the Data TA to any forwarder that lacks it, before more data arrives.
    • On AWS, the SQS-Based S3 input was created with a Source Type other than sap_logserv_logs. The Data TA’s rules run only on that sourcetype, so the events keep the input’s sourcetype, which check 2 shows. Correct the input’s Source Type (step 7 of the Connect guide, step 8 of the Filter and Copy guides); events already indexed stay as they are. The Azure and GCP inputs always send sap_logserv_logs.

docs.title: 2. Sourcetypes and Cloud
docs.text:
| tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-24h by sourcetype, cloud_provider
| sort - count

fillnull_value must come before count. Without it, tstats leaves out every event that carries no cloud_provider at all.

  • sourcetype: compare the list with Supported Log Types. You see only the types SAP delivers for your landscape. sap_logserv_logs holds what the Data TA does not route; check 4 tells whether that is expected.
  • cloud_provider: each row should name your cloud: aws, azure or gcp. Rows for more than one provider are expected only if you ingest from more than one cloud.
  • (none) in cloud_provider: those events carry no stamp. The Azure and GCP inputs always stamp theirs, so on AWS this means the SQS-Based S3 input has no _meta = cloud_provider::aws line, or read these events before the line went in; see Choose Cloud Attribution. The LogServ App’s dashboards count unstamped events as aws, but your own searches and tstats do not, and the stamp cannot be added to events already indexed.

docs.title: 3. One Cloud Value per Event
docs.text:
index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-30d _index_earliest=-15m
| eval cloud_provider_values=mvcount(cloud_provider)
| fillnull value=0 cloud_provider_values
| stats count by cloud_provider_values

_index_earliest=-15m selects the events indexed in the last 15 minutes, whatever their event time, so the check also works while an input drains a backlog. earliest=-30d only limits how far back the search looks; widen it if your backlog is older.

Expect 1, and 0 only for AWS events without a stamp. A 2 means the events carry two stamps: the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown is set while the input stamps its own value. See Troubleshooting.

This check is proven only for two different values (in the lab, an Azure input with the dropdown on AWS gave 2). Whether the same value written twice also shows as 2 (the dropdown on Microsoft Azure for an Azure input, or on AWS for an AWS S3 Direct backfill) has not been tested. A 1 here therefore does not rule it out. Also check that the dropdown is at Not set wherever the Azure or GCP add-on runs or AWS S3 Direct is used (What Gets Stamped).

docs.title: 4. Routing, by Folder
docs.text:
| tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where index=sap_logserv_logs sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-24h by clz_dir, clz_subdir
| sort - count

These events stayed under the base sourcetype. Judge them by their folders, not by how many there are: on Azure, the Unix command output that SAP delivers without folder fields can outnumber all other data, and it stays here by design unless you dropped it (Decide Filtering).

Expected here:

  • (none) / (none): events without folder fields, such as the Azure data under undefined/undefined (Data Delivered Without Folder Fields), and any events that check 1 found without the Data TA.
  • The Secondary log types, which have no routing of their own (Secondary Supported Log Types).
  • Files in folders that the Data TA routes by file path (linux/*, dns/binddns, proxy/squid, windows/*, webdispatcher/accesslog) that are not among the routed files. Add source to the by clause and compare the file paths with Supported Log Types.

Not expected: the folders the Data TA routes by folder alone. A row for any of them means those events were not routed by the Data TA that parsed them; check that each heavy forwarder runs the current build and has no local/ override of the routes (Version Check):

hana/hanaaudit, hana/tracelogs, abap/audit, abap/dispatcher, abap/enqueueserver, abap/event, abap/gateway, abap/icm, abap/messageserver, abap/sapstartsrv, abap/workprocess, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs, sap/sapstartsrv, sap/saphostexec, sap/saprouter.

docs.title: 5. Per-Forwarder Checks
docs.text:
• The Data TA on each heavy forwarder. Run the Version Check on each one: the routing rules run there, not on the Deployment Server.

  • Heavy forwarders that send to Splunk Cloud. From the Splunk Cloud search head, this search must return events for each forwarder; if it returns none, that forwarder is not sending to Splunk Cloud:

    | tstats count where index=_internal host=<HF> earliest=-15m

  • The input’s own log. Forwarders send their _internal data by default, so you can read it from the search head:

    • Azure: index=_internal source=*splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_queue.log* "done:" shows a line Input '<name>' done: messages=N blobs=N events=N ... per firing (Azure Setup Guide → Validation).
    • GCP: index=_internal source=*splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub.log* "done:" shows a line Input '<name>' done: messages=N objects=N events=N ... per firing (GCP Setup Guide → Validation).
    • AWS: index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR, WARNING) earliest=-1h lists the errors and warnings of the Splunk Add-on for AWS.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• If a check fails, find the symptom on Troubleshooting.
  • On AWS, load history with AWS S3 Direct if you need older days.
  • Install the LogServ App and its prerequisites on the search head, then run its Diagnostics page (Data Doctor).

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide
Introduction
docs.text:
This guide connects the Splunk Add-on for AWS directly to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket that SAP LogServ manages for you. It is the default AWS scenario; Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario compares it with the other two.

The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account in the middle of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

No AWS scenario loads history on its own

The input reads only the notifications in SAP’s SQS Queue, which reach back only as far as that queue keeps messages: 4 days by default, at most 14, as SAP sets it. To load older days, use AWS S3 Direct once this setup works. The AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup does not copy history either: choose it only if you want your own copy of new log files.

If you run the Copy scenario today and switch to this one, deactivate the Copy Lambda’s SQS trigger before you enable the input in step 7. Both read SAP’s SQS Queue, and each message goes to only one of them.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

  • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
  1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
  2. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 connect deployment approach in your Secondary account
  3. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
  4. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
  5. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
  6. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
  7. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
  8. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk

docs.title: Where These Steps Run
docs.text:
Steps Where 1 to 4 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 5 to 7 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server 8 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

Several heavy forwarders can read the same SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input. See Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

docs.title: Check These First
docs.text:
Steps 1 to 3 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 4.

  • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check. Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
  • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them.
  • You have planned the first start. The input starts with every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 7, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

docs.title: Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS
docs.text:
Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 5 to 7; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

  • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
  • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 5 to 7.
  • Just install it now; steps 5 to 7 configure it.

docs.title: 1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account
docs.text:
Before you can deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

  • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
  • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the CloudFormation template in the next section must be deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

What does an ARN look like?

AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

  • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
  • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

How to obtain the ARNs:

1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

  • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
  • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location — you will reference them during the next section (Deploy CloudFormation Template) and again when configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input.

docs.title: 2. Deploy CloudFormation Template
docs.text:
Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

What does the CloudFormation template do?

Creates the following resources:

  • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
  • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
  • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
  • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above

It creates no S3 Bucket, no SQS Queue and no access key: the input reads SAP’s resources through the IAM Role, and you create the access key in step 4.

2.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

2.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

Example

2.c Upload the AWS CloudFormation Template file provided for this remote S3 connect deployment approach, then click the Next button

Example

2.d Enter a name for the CloudFormation Stack - splunk-logserv-remote-s3-connect

Example

2.e Enter just the name (not the ARN) of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountS3Bucket parameter - If your ARN looks like this arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd then just use the name like this sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd

Example

2.f Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountSQSQueueArn parameter

Example

2.g Choose and enter a name for the IAM User to be created in your Secondary account in the NewIAMUserName parameter, then click on the Next button

Example

2.h Scroll down to the bottom of the page and check the I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names checkbox, then click on the Next button

Example

2.i Scroll down to the bottom of the page and click on the Submit button

Example

2.j Ensure the deployment of the CloudFormation template completes successfully

Example

docs.title: 3. Contact SAP LogServ Support
docs.text:
Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

  • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
  • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The SQS-Based S3 input does not need it, but AWS S3 Direct, which loads history and recovers outages, does: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the input in step 7. Steps 4 to 6 can be done in the meantime.

docs.title: 4. Create Access Key for IAM User
docs.text:
The CloudFormation template creates the IAM User but no access key for it, so you create one here (AWS: To create an access key for an IAM user).

4.a Navigate to the IAM console in your Secondary account and search for the IAM User name you used when deploying the CloudFormation template. Click on the name of the IAM User to see the user details.

Example

4.b Click on the Security credentials tab in the middle of the screen. Scroll down and click on the Create access key button.

Example

4.c Select the Local code use case, check the Confirmation checkbox and click on the Next button.

Example

4.d Enter a description tag value if desired and click on the Create access key button.

Example

4.e Copy the values for both the Access key and the Secret access key and save them in a secure place as you will need them in the upcoming steps. Now click on the Done button.

Example

docs.title: 5. Configure Secondary Account (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Please ensure the user you log in with in your Splunk instance has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below. Do steps 5 to 7 on each instance that will run the input (Where These Steps Run).

5.a Login to your Splunk console then find and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS App

Example

5.b Click on the Configuration tab, then click on the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

5.c Choose and enter a descriptive name for the account in the Name field. Enter the access key ID you created for the IAM User in the Key ID field and its secret in the Secret Key field. Leave the Region Category set to Global. Click on the Add button.

Example

docs.title: 6. Configure IAM Role (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
6.a Click on the IAM Role tab to the right of the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

6.b Choose and enter a descriptive name for the role in the Name field. Enter the IAM Role ARN in the IAM Role ARN field, then click the Add button. The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

  • arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role
Example

docs.title: 7. Configure SQS-Based S3 Input (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Create the input only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 3 are applied, and after the Data TA is on this instance (Check These First).

Once added, the input starts with every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them), on top of the live feed. Before you add it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

7.a Click on the Inputs tab. Click on the Create New Input button. Select the Custom Data Type option at the bottom of the drop-down, then select the SQS-Based S3 (Recommended) option.

Example

7.b Fill out the first three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Name, AWS Account, Assume Role)

  • Choose and enter a descriptive name for the input
  • Select the AWS Account you configured previously
  • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
Example

7.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

  • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
  • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
  • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
Example

7.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

  • Enter the URL of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account, not the ARN or just the name
    • If the ARN for your SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account looks like this:
      • arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv
    • Then format it as a URL like this:
      • https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/121212121212/sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv
  • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
  • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
Example

7.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

  • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). SAP’s queue receives the S3 notifications directly, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
  • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
  • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
  • Click on the Add button
Example

7.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it, and the input starts reading as soon as you click Add, so:

  • On the Inputs tab, disable the new input straight away.
  • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
_meta = cloud_provider::aws
  • Restart Splunk, then enable the input on the Inputs tab.
  • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

This is the procedure in Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input. It has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. After you enable the input, check the result with the search in Check the Result.

Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.

One SQS-Based S3 input on one heavy forwarder parses its events through one pipeline set, which limits how many events a second it can take. For high LogServ volumes, see Capacity Planning and First Start before you add inputs or forwarders.

docs.title: 8. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested
docs.text:
After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of completing the SQS-Based S3 Input configuration. The input polls the SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

8.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

8.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

8.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes your SAP LogServ subscription delivers, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

8.d If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

  • SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 3) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, your Secondary account cannot receive SQS notifications or read from the S3 Bucket.
  • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 4), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 6), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
  • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 7) is the full URL (https://sqs.<region>.amazonaws.com/<account-id>/<queue-name>), not the ARN or bare queue name.
  • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 2) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 7) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.

docs.title: Rotate the Access Key
docs.text:
The access key from step 4 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users):

  1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 4. Save the new key ID and secret.
  2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 5, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
  3. Check that events still arrive (step 8) and that the _internal search in step 8.d shows no new authentication errors.
  4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify Your Data.
  2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
  3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

docs.title: Legacy: AWS S3 Connect to Filter Migration
docs.text:
Legacy guide

This guide is for an existing AWS Remote S3 Connect deployment that wants to add Lambda-based filtering without recreating its IAM User and IAM Role. Most deployments should use the Data TA’s built-in index-time filtering instead. A new deployment that wants the Lambda filter should follow the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide. The steps below remain valid.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This guide walks you through migrating from an existing splunk-logserv-remote-s3-connect deployment to the splunk-logserv-remote-s3-filter deployment without deleting or recreating your existing IAM User and IAM Role resources.

The migration adds Lambda-based S3 event filtering capabilities to your existing deployment, allowing you to filter S3 event notifications based on time and path patterns before they are processed by Splunk.

Also available: Native TA Index-Time Filtering

The TA also includes built-in index-time filtering that works inside Splunk itself. This can be used alongside or instead of Lambda-based filtering. After completing this migration (or with any deployment scenario), see Configuring Filters or the section at the bottom of this page.

This migration guide assumes you have already completed the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup and have a working deployment in your Secondary account.

docs.title: What the Migration Does
docs.text:
The Python migration script performs the following actions on your existing deployment:

Migration Actions

Updates to Existing Resources:

  • Updates the existing IAM Role trust policy to allow Lambda service
  • Attaches the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy to the existing IAM Role
  • Adds CloudWatch Logs permissions to the existing IAM policy
  • Adds local SQS queue permissions to the existing IAM policy

New Resources Created:

  • An SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue
  • A Dead Letter SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue-dlq
  • A Lambda Function - Default name is splunk-logserv-lambda-filter
  • A CloudWatch LogGroup used by the Lambda Function
  • An Event Source Mapping connecting the Lambda to the cross-account SQS Queue. It is created enabled, so the Lambda starts reading SAP’s queue as soon as the script finishes

docs.title: Architecture After Migration
docs.text:
After migration, the architecture will match the splunk-logserv-remote-s3-filter deployment:

  • S3 event notifications from the SAP ECS account are received by the Lambda function
  • The Lambda function filters events based on time (days in past) and path patterns (include/exclude)
  • Matching events are forwarded to a local SQS queue in your Secondary account
  • Splunk polls the local SQS queue for filtered notifications

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting the migration, ensure you have the following:

Existing Deployment:

  • A working splunk-logserv-remote-s3-connect deployment in your Secondary account
  • The ARN and name of the existing IAM Role (e.g., splunk-logserv-ta-role)
  • The ARN of the existing IAM User (e.g., arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/splunk_logserv_user)
  • The name of the existing IAM policy attached to the role (e.g., splunk-logserv-ta-policy)

Cross-Account Information:

  • The ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
  • The name of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account

Local Environment:

  • Python 3.8 or higher installed
  • boto3 library installed
  • AWS CLI configured with appropriate credentials/profile

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Below are the high level steps for the migration process listed in the order they should be followed.

Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

  1. Install Python and boto3 dependencies (if not already installed)
  2. Create a new S3 Bucket in your Secondary account and upload the Lambda function ZIP file
  3. Download the migration scripts and configuration file
  4. Configure the migration configuration file with your deployment details
  5. Run the migration script in dry-run mode, then execute it to perform the migration
  6. Update the Splunk AWS Add-on SQS-Based S3 Input to use the new local queue
  7. Verify the migration is successful

docs.title: 1. Install Python and boto3
docs.text: The migration scripts require Python 3.8 or higher and the boto3 library.

docs.title: Check Python Version
docs.text:
Open a command prompt or terminal and run the following command to check your Python version:

python --version

If Python is not installed or the version is below 3.8, download and install Python from the official Python website.

On Windows, ensure you check the Add Python to PATH option during installation.

docs.title: Check boto3 Installation
docs.text:
Run the following command to check if boto3 is installed:

pip show boto3

If boto3 is installed, you will see version and location information. If not installed, you will see a warning message.

docs.title: Install boto3
docs.text:
If boto3 is not installed, run the following command to install it:

pip install boto3

docs.title: 2. Create S3 Bucket with Lambda Function ZIP File
docs.text:
2.a Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located.

2.b Log into your AWS Secondary account and change to the region that matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Create the bucket in that Region, the one your deployment runs in: Lambda requires its code bucket in the function’s Region.

2.c Choose a name of your own for the new S3 bucket. S3 bucket names are global: each name can be used by only one AWS account, so pick one no other account is likely to hold, for example splunk-logserv-lambda-code-<your-account-id>-<region>. The splunk-logserv-lambda-binary value in the migration configuration file is only a placeholder: you replace it with your name in step 4.

2.d Navigate to the S3 console and create a general purpose S3 bucket using all the default settings

2.e Upload the splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip file to the root of the S3 bucket

docs.title: 3. Download Migration Scripts
docs.text:
Download the following files from the GitHub repository to a local directory on your machine:

File Description migrate-config.json Configuration file with all migration parameters migrate-to-filter.py Python script that performs the migration migrate-to-filter-rollback.py Python script that rolls back the migration

docs.title: 4. Configure Migration Settings
docs.text: Open the migrate-config.json file in a text editor and update the values to match your deployment.

docs.title: Existing Resources Configuration
docs.text:
Update the existing_resources section with the details from your current splunk-logserv-remote-s3-connect deployment:

"existing_resources": {
    "iam_user_arn": "arn:aws:iam::YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:user/YOUR_IAM_USER_NAME",
    "iam_role_name": "YOUR_IAM_ROLE_NAME",
    "iam_role_arn": "arn:aws:iam::YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID:role/YOUR_IAM_ROLE_NAME",
    "iam_role_policy_name": "YOUR_IAM_POLICY_NAME"
}
Parameter Description Example iam_user_arn ARN of the existing IAM User arn:aws:iam::222222222222:user/splunk_logserv_user iam_role_name Name of the existing IAM Role splunk-logserv-ta-role iam_role_arn ARN of the existing IAM Role arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role iam_role_policy_name Name of the existing inline policy on the IAM Role splunk-logserv-ta-policy

docs.title: Cross-Account Configuration
docs.text:
Update the cross_account section with the details from your SAP ECS account:

"cross_account": {
    "sqs_queue_arn": "arn:aws:sqs:REGION:SAP_ACCOUNT_ID:QUEUE_NAME",
    "s3_bucket_name": "SAP_S3_BUCKET_NAME"
}
Parameter Description Example sqs_queue_arn ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:111111111111:sap-logserv-queue s3_bucket_name Name of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account sap-logserv-bucket

docs.title: Local SQS Configuration
docs.text:
Update the local_sqs section to configure the local SQS queue that will receive filtered notifications:

"local_sqs": {
    "queue_name": "splunk-logserv-local-target-queue",
    "visibility_timeout_seconds": 600,
    "message_retention_seconds": 1209600,
    "dlq_max_receive_count": 3
}
Parameter Description Default queue_name Name for the local SQS queue splunk-logserv-local-target-queue visibility_timeout_seconds Visibility timeout in seconds 600 (10 minutes) message_retention_seconds Message retention period in seconds 1209600 (14 days) dlq_max_receive_count Max receives before sending to DLQ 3

docs.title: Lambda Function Configuration
docs.text:
Update the lambda_function section to configure the Lambda filter function:

"lambda_function": {
    "function_name": "splunk-logserv-lambda-filter",
    "code_s3_bucket": "splunk-logserv-lambda-binary",
    "code_s3_key": "splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip",
    "handler": "log-filterer-lambda.lambda_handler",
    "runtime": "python3.12",
    "timeout_seconds": 300,
    "memory_size_mb": 512
}
Parameter Description Value in the shipped file function_name Name for the Lambda function splunk-logserv-lambda-filter code_s3_bucket S3 bucket containing the Lambda ZIP file. Replace the shipped value with the name of the bucket you created in step 2; the script checks that the ZIP file is there before it changes anything splunk-logserv-lambda-binary (a placeholder) code_s3_key S3 key (path) to the Lambda ZIP file splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip handler Lambda handler function log-filterer-lambda.lambda_handler runtime Lambda runtime python3.12 timeout_seconds Lambda timeout in seconds 300 (5 minutes) memory_size_mb Lambda memory allocation in MB 512

docs.title: Filter Settings Configuration
docs.text:
Update the filter_settings section to configure the S3 event filtering behavior. To start by passing everything, and add exclusions once you know your volumes:

"filter_settings": {
    "days_in_the_past": 7,
    "include_filters": "*/*",
    "exclude_filters": ""
}

Replace the example values in the shipped file

The shipped migrate-config.json holds an example, not a recommended default: its include_filters value linux/*,hana/* passes only the Linux and HANA folders, and its exclude_filters value then drops six of the Linux folders (linux/cron, linux/messages, linux/localmessages, linux/slapd, linux/sudolog, linux/warn). Used as shipped, it leaves out most Linux logs and every other log type. Enter your own values.

Parameter Description Value in the shipped file days_in_the_past The Lambda passes an object on only when at least one of its records has a _time newer than this many days before the moment it processes the notification. Use 1 to 365: the script does not check the value, and 0 would drop almost everything. This is not the Data TA’s Days in the Past, which counts from midnight UTC 7 include_filters Comma-separated fnmatch patterns for paths (clz_dir/clz_subdir) to include. Do not leave it empty: an empty value discards every notification linux/*,hana/* (an example) exclude_filters Comma-separated fnmatch patterns for paths to exclude linux/cron,linux/messages,... (an example)

Use */* for include_filters to include all paths. Leave exclude_filters empty to exclude nothing. The Lambda matches with Python’s fnmatch, so * also matches across the / (linux* matches linux/cron), and a bare * in exclude_filters excludes everything. See AWS Lambda-Based Filtering for how this differs from the Data TA’s filters.

docs.title: Event Source Mapping Configuration
docs.text:
Update the event_source_mapping section to configure the Lambda trigger:

"event_source_mapping": {
    "batch_size": 10,
    "maximum_batching_window_seconds": 5,
    "maximum_concurrency": 10
}
Parameter Description Default batch_size Number of messages per Lambda invocation 10 maximum_batching_window_seconds Max time to wait for a full batch 5 maximum_concurrency Max concurrent Lambda executions 10

docs.title: Command Line Arguments
docs.text:
The migration script supports the following command line arguments:

Argument Short Required Description --config -c Yes Path to the migration configuration JSON file --region -r Yes AWS region (must match your existing deployment region) --profile -p No AWS CLI profile name (uses default credentials if not specified) --dry-run -d No Preview changes without making any modifications

docs.title: Dry Run Mode
docs.text:
Always run the migration script in dry-run mode first to preview the changes that will be made.

Windows Command Prompt:

python migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --dry-run

Windows Command Prompt with AWS Profile:

python migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile --dry-run

Linux/macOS Terminal:

python3 migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --dry-run

Linux/macOS Terminal with AWS Profile:

python3 migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile --dry-run

Review the dry-run output to ensure all steps are correct and the existing resources are found.

docs.title: Execute Migration
docs.text:
Once you have verified the dry-run output, run the migration script without the --dry-run flag:

Windows Command Prompt:

python migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1

Windows Command Prompt with AWS Profile:

python migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile

Linux/macOS Terminal:

python3 migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1

Linux/macOS Terminal with AWS Profile:

python3 migrate-to-filter.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile

The script will display progress for each step and provide a summary upon completion, including the new local SQS queue URL that you will need for the next step.

Do step 6 straight away. From the moment the script finishes, the Lambda and your existing input both read SAP’s SQS queue, and each message goes to only one of them. Objects your existing input takes are indexed without the Lambda’s filter; notifications the Lambda passes on wait in the new local queue until step 6 points the input at it.

docs.title: 6. Update Splunk AWS Add-on Configuration
docs.text:
After the migration completes successfully, you need to update your existing SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS to use the new local SQS queue.

6.a Log into your Splunk instance and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS

6.b Navigate to Inputs and find your existing SQS-Based S3 Input

6.c Click Edit on the input

6.d Update the SQS Queue Name field to use the new local queue URL from the migration output - Example: https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/222222222222/splunk-logserv-local-target-queue

6.e Click Save to apply the changes

The input will restart and begin polling the new local filtered queue.

6.f If you gave the input the line _meta = cloud_provider::aws (Choose Cloud Attribution), check that its stanza in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf still carries it. The form has no field for that line, so make sure the edit in the form did not remove it.

docs.title: 7. Verify Migration
docs.text:
After completing the migration and updating the Splunk configuration:

7.a Check Lambda Logs - Navigate to CloudWatch Logs in the AWS Console and verify the Lambda function is receiving and processing messages

7.b Check Local SQS Queue - Navigate to SQS in the AWS Console and verify messages are appearing in the local queue

7.c Check Splunk - Run a search for recent LogServ logs to confirm data is being ingested: 

index=your_index earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype

docs.title: Rollback Migration
docs.text: If you need to rollback the migration and return to the original splunk-logserv-remote-s3-connect configuration, use the rollback script.

docs.title: Rollback Command Line Arguments
docs.text:
The rollback script supports the same command line arguments as the migration script:

Argument Short Required Description --config -c Yes Path to the migration configuration JSON file --region -r Yes AWS region --profile -p No AWS CLI profile name (uses default credentials if not specified) --dry-run -d No Preview changes without making any modifications

docs.title: Rollback Dry Run
docs.text:
Always run the rollback script in dry-run mode first to preview what will be removed.

Windows Command Prompt:

python migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --dry-run

Windows Command Prompt with AWS Profile:

python migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile --dry-run

Linux/macOS Terminal:

python3 migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --dry-run

Linux/macOS Terminal with AWS Profile:

python3 migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile --dry-run

docs.title: Execute Rollback
docs.text:
Once you have verified the dry-run output, run the rollback script without the --dry-run flag:

Windows Command Prompt:

python migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1

Windows Command Prompt with AWS Profile:

python migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile

Linux/macOS Terminal:

python3 migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1

Linux/macOS Terminal with AWS Profile:

python3 migrate-to-filter-rollback.py --config migrate-config.json --region us-east-1 --profile my-aws-profile
What does the rollback script do?

Removes Created Resources:

  • Deletes the Event Source Mapping
  • Deletes the Lambda function
  • Deletes the CloudWatch Log Group
  • Deletes the local SQS queue and Dead Letter Queue

Reverts IAM Changes:

  • Removes local SQS permissions from the existing IAM policy
  • Removes CloudWatch Logs permissions from the existing IAM policy
  • Detaches the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy
  • Reverts the IAM Role trust policy to remove Lambda service

After rollback, update your Splunk AWS Add-on SQS-Based S3 Input to use the original cross-account SQS queue URL from your SAP ECS account.

docs.title: Lambda Not Receiving Messages
docs.text:
• Verify the Event Source Mapping is enabled in the Lambda console
  • Verify cross-account permissions are correctly configured for your IAM Role
  • Check the IAM Role trust policy includes lambda.amazonaws.com

docs.title: Lambda Errors in CloudWatch
docs.text:
• Check for “Access Denied” errors which indicate IAM permission issues
  • Verify the Lambda code ZIP file was uploaded correctly to S3
  • Check the handler name in the configuration matches the Lambda code

Notifications the Lambda cannot process are lost from this path

The filter Lambda does not retry. When it cannot read an object from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket, or cannot send the notification to the local SQS queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested through this path. An unexpected error while processing a message is handled the same way. Only an invalid configuration of the Lambda itself returns messages to SAP’s queue.

The objects stay in SAP’s S3 Bucket. After you fix the cause, load the days the errors cover with AWS S3 Direct. In the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs, search for Could not retrieve S3 object, discarding message, Failed to forward message to target SQS, discarding and Unexpected error processing message.

docs.title: Messages Not Appearing in Local Queue
docs.text:
• Review the Lambda CloudWatch logs for filtering decisions
  • Verify the include_filters patterns match your expected paths, and that the value is not empty
  • Check that exclude_filters is not a bare *, which excludes everything
  • Check the days_in_the_past setting is not filtering out your messages

docs.title: Splunk Not Ingesting
docs.text:
• Verify the local SQS queue URL is correctly configured in the Splunk input
  • Check the Splunk AWS Add-on internal logs for connection errors
  • Verify messages are present in the local SQS queue

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The Splunk TA for SAP LogServ includes built-in index-time filtering that works inside Splunk itself, independently of the Lambda-based S3 event filtering configured above. You can use both approaches together for defense-in-depth filtering, or use the native TA filtering on its own.

Native TA Filtering vs. Lambda-based Filtering
  • Lambda-based filtering (configured above) filters S3 event notifications before they reach Splunk, reducing the number of SQS messages processed by the Splunk AWS Add-on.
  • Native TA filtering (configured below) filters events inside Splunk at index time via TRANSFORMS-based queue routing. Filtered events never consume Splunk license.

Both match on clz_dir/clz_subdir, but not with the same rules: the Lambda uses Python’s fnmatch on the joined path, where * also crosses the /, while the Data TA accepts only dir/subdir patterns or a bare * and matches each part on its own. Use patterns that are valid on the Filters tab in both places so they select the same folders (AWS Lambda-Based Filtering). Using both together means events are filtered at the AWS level first and then again at the Splunk level, providing a safety net if either filter configuration is incomplete.

docs.title: Open the Filters Tab
docs.text:
1. In Splunk Web, open the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ app
  2. Go to Configuration → Filters

docs.title: Enable Filtering
docs.text: Check the Enable Filtering checkbox to activate index-time filtering.

docs.title: Include Filters
docs.text:
Comma-separated patterns specifying which log types to include. Patterns use the format clz_dir/clz_subdir, where * matches any run of characters within the value and ? one character:

Pattern Meaning */* Include all log types (default) hana/hanaaudit Include only HANA audit logs linux/* Include all Linux log types linux/messages, hana/* Include Linux messages and all HANA logs

This field cannot be empty when filtering is enabled. Use */* to include everything.

docs.title: Exclude Filters
docs.text: Comma-separated patterns for log types to exclude. Events matching any exclude pattern are dropped even if they also match an include pattern. Leave empty to exclude nothing.

docs.title: Include Sources and Exclude Sources
docs.text: These two fields match the event’s whole source value, such as /var/log/zypper.log, rather than its folder. Leave them empty for the migration; see Configuring Filters for what they do.

docs.title: Days in the Past
docs.text: Whole number (0–3650) specifying the maximum age of events to index. Set to 0 to disable time-based filtering. Default: 7.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Click Save. The TA validates your patterns and generates the necessary configuration files.

docs.title: Deployment Server: Deploy to Forwarders
docs.text:
If you are running on a Deployment Server with heavy forwarders, additional steps are required after saving filters.

After saving, the Filters tab will display a “⚠ Deployment Server Detected” banner with a “Deploy to Forwarders” button.

docs.title: Configure the Server Class (First Time Only)
docs.text:
If the Data TA does not yet reach your heavy forwarders through this server class, follow Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders first. In short:

  1. Go to Settings → Forwarder Management
  2. Find the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class
  3. Click the three-dot menu → Edit agent assignment
  4. Add your heavy forwarder IP addresses or hostnames by name. Do not use *: it would send the Data TA to every deployment client, search heads included, and restart each one
  5. Save the agent assignment

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
1. Return to the Filters tab and click “Deploy to Forwarders”
  2. Confirm the deployment
  3. Wait for the HFs to pick up the change at their next phone-home (every 60 seconds by default) and restart; allow 5 minutes or more
  4. Verify deployment status in Settings → Forwarder Management

docs.title: Verify Native Filtering
docs.text:
After deployment, verify that native filtering is operating correctly:

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by clz_dir, clz_subdir

Use your index name if you renamed it.

You should see data only for log types matching your include patterns. See Configuring Filters for the full verification and troubleshooting guide.

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup Guide
Introduction
docs.text:
This guide adds a Lambda function in your AWS account that copies each new LogServ object into a bucket of your own, which Splunk then reads. Use it only if you want your own copy of new log files; otherwise the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup is the default (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario).

The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom left of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

What the copy holds, and what it does not

The Lambda copies the object named in each notification it receives from SAP’s SQS Queue: the notifications still waiting there when you activate its trigger (step 9), then every new object. It never lists SAP’s bucket, so it does not copy history: objects whose notifications are already gone stay only in SAP’s bucket. To load those days, use AWS S3 Direct against SAP’s bucket once this setup works.

The copy is not byte-identical. A gzipped object is stored decompressed, under the same key without .gz (...json.gz becomes ...json), with a content type guessed from its name; only an object that fails to decompress is stored as the original gzip under its original key. The copy therefore takes several times the storage of SAP’s bucket, and each copy’s LastModified time is the time it was copied.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

  • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
  1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
  2. Create a new S3 Bucket, with a name of your own, in the correct AWS Region in your Secondary account and upload the splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip file to the root of the bucket (do not rename the file — the CloudFormation template looks for the object key splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip at the bucket root)
  3. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 copy deployment approach in your Secondary account
  4. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
  5. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
  6. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
  7. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
  8. Configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
  9. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, create the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function the CloudFormation template created (the template does not create the trigger)
  10. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk

docs.title: Where These Steps Run
docs.text:
Steps Where 1 to 5, and 9 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 6 to 8 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server 10 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

Several heavy forwarders can read the same local SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input; see Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

docs.title: Check These First
docs.text:
Steps 1 to 4 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 5.

  • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check.
