Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
  • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them.
  • You have planned the first start. Once its trigger is active, the Lambda copies the object of every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 9, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

docs.title: Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS
docs.text:
Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 6 to 8; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

  • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
  • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 6 to 8.
  • Just install it now; steps 6 to 8 configure it.

docs.title: 1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account
docs.text:
Before you can create the local S3 Bucket and deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

  • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
  • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the S3 Bucket and CloudFormation template in the next two sections must be created and deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

What does an ARN look like?

AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

  • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
  • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

How to obtain the ARNs:

1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

  • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
  • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location – you will reference them when creating the S3 Bucket (next section), deploying the CloudFormation Template, and configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input later in this guide.

docs.title: 2. Create S3 Bucket with Lambda Function ZIP File
docs.text:
This bucket holds the Lambda function’s code. The CloudFormation template does not create it; it creates only the bucket for the copies (step 3.i).

2.a Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located.

2.b Log into your AWS Secondary account and change to the region that matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Create the bucket in that Region, the one you will deploy the stack in: Lambda requires its code bucket in the function’s Region.

2.c Choose a name of your own for the new S3 bucket. S3 bucket names are global: each name can be used by only one AWS account, so pick one no other account is likely to hold, for example splunk-logserv-lambda-code-<your-account-id>-<region>. Write it down; you enter it in step 3.g.

2.d Navigate to the S3 console and create a general purpose S3 bucket using all the default settings

2.e Upload the splunk-logserv-lambda-binary.zip file to the root of the S3 bucket

Example

docs.title: 3. Deploy CloudFormation Template
docs.text:
Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

What does the CloudFormation template do?

Creates the following resources:

  • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
  • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
  • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
  • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above
  • An S3 Bucket with an Event Notification to the SQS Queue below- Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-bucket
  • An SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue
  • A Dead Letter SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue-dlq. It takes the messages of the local SQS Queue that are received three times without being deleted; it does not protect the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
  • A Lambda Function (Python 3.12 runtime) - Default name is splunk-logserv-lambda-logforwarder
  • A LogGroup used by the Lambda Function

It does not create the bucket for the Lambda code (step 2), the access key (step 5) or the Lambda’s SQS trigger (step 9).

A stack created from an earlier copy of this template runs the Lambda on python3.9, which AWS deprecated on 15 December 2025 (AWS: Lambda runtimes). To move it to Python 3.12, update the stack with the current template and keep the existing parameter values. The runtime is the only resource setting the two templates differ in; the function’s code is the same.

3.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

3.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

Example

3.c Upload the AWS CloudFormation Template file provided for this remote S3 copy deployment approach, then click the Next button

Example

3.d Enter a name for the CloudFormation Stack - splunk-logserv-remote-s3-copy

Example

3.e Enter just the name (not the ARN) of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountS3Bucket parameter - If your ARN looks like this arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd then just use the name like this sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd

Example

3.f Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountSQSQueueArn parameter

Example

3.g Enter the exact name of the S3 Bucket you created in step 2 in the LambdaCodeBucket parameter. The parameter has no default; the example image shows an older default name, which you must not use.

Example

3.h Choose and enter a name for the Lambda Function to be created in your Secondary account in the LambdaFunctionName parameter

Example

3.i Choose and enter a name for the S3 Bucket to be created in your Secondary account in the LocalS3BucketName parameter. The template creates this bucket for the copies, and bucket names are global too: replace the default with a name of your own, or the stack fails if another account already holds the name.

Example

3.j Choose and enter a name for the SQS Queue to be created in your Secondary account in the LocalSQSQueueName parameter

Example

3.k Choose and enter a name for the IAM User to be created in your Secondary account in the NewIAMUserName parameter, then click on the Next button

Example

3.l Scroll down to the bottom of the page and check the I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names checkbox, then click on the Next button

Example

3.m Scroll down to the bottom of the page and click on the Submit button

Example

3.n Ensure the deployment of the CloudFormation template completes successfully

Example

docs.title: 4. Contact SAP LogServ Support
docs.text:
Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

  • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
  • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The copy Lambda does not need it, but AWS S3 Direct does when it loads history from SAP’s bucket: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. Steps 5 to 8 can be done in the meantime.

docs.title: 5. Create Access Key for IAM User
docs.text:
The CloudFormation template creates the IAM User but no access key for it, so you create one here (AWS: To create an access key for an IAM user).

5.a Navigate to the IAM console in your Secondary account and search for the IAM User name you used when deploying the CloudFormation template. Click on the name of the IAM User to see the user details.

Example

5.b Click on the Security credentials tab in the middle of the screen. Scroll down and click on the Create access key button.

Example

5.c Select the Local code use case, check the Confirmation checkbox and click on the Next button.

Example

5.d Enter a description tag value if desired and click on the Create access key button.

Example

5.e Copy the values for both the Access key and the Secret access key and save them in a secure place as you will need them in the upcoming steps. Now click on the Done button.

Example

docs.title: 6. Configure Secondary Account (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Please ensure the user you log in with in your Splunk instance has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below. Do steps 6 to 8 on each instance that will run the input (Where These Steps Run).

6.a Login to your Splunk console then find and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS App

Example

6.b Click on the Configuration tab, then click on the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

6.c Choose and enter a descriptive name for the account in the Name field. Enter the access key ID you created for the IAM User in the Key ID field and its secret in the Secret Key field. Leave the Region Category set to Global. Click on the Add button.

Example

docs.title: 7. Configure IAM Role (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
7.a Click on the IAM Role tab to the right of the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

7.b Choose and enter a descriptive name for the role in the Name field. Enter the IAM Role ARN in the IAM Role ARN field, then click the Add button. The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

  • arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role
Example

docs.title: 8. Configure SQS-Based S3 Input (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Create the input only after the Data TA is on this instance (Check These First). It reads the local SQS Queue, which stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active.

8.a Click on the Inputs tab. Click on the Create New Input button. Select the Custom Data Type option at the bottom of the drop-down, then select the SQS-Based S3 (Recommended) option.

Example

8.b Fill out the first three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Name, AWS Account, Assume Role)

  • Choose and enter a descriptive name for the input
  • Select the AWS Account you configured previously
  • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
Example

8.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

  • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
  • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
  • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
Example

8.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

  • Select the SQS Queue Name you entered in step 3.j (LocalSQSQueueName) when previously deploying the CloudFormation template
  • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
  • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
Example

8.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

  • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). The notifications reach the queue directly from S3, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
  • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
  • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
  • Click on the Add button
Example

8.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it. The local SQS Queue stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active, so add the line now, before the input has anything to read:

  • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
_meta = cloud_provider::aws
  • Restart Splunk.
  • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

This follows Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input; the disable and enable steps there are not needed while the local SQS Queue is empty. The sequence has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. Once events arrive (step 10), check the result with the search in Check the Result.

Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.

docs.title: 9. Create the SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
Create the trigger only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 4 are applied, and at least 5 minutes after the stack was created.

Once the trigger is active, the Lambda copies the object of every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them) into the S3 Bucket in your Secondary account, and the forwarder parses them all on top of the live feed. It copies nothing older: objects whose notifications are already gone stay only in SAP’s bucket, and AWS S3 Direct loads them. Before you activate it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

9.a Navigate to the Lambda console in your Secondary account and ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Find the Lambda function that was created by the CloudFormation template and click on its name to view details.

Example

9.b The CloudFormation template does not create this trigger: the Lambda can read SAP’s SQS Queue only after SAP has applied the policies, so the trigger is a manual step. On a new stack, follow the Create SQS Queue Trigger steps below. Use Configure SQS Queue Trigger only if the Function overview diagram already shows an SQS trigger, as in the example image below: for example one you created earlier, or one left from a stack you deleted and created again with the same Lambda function name (AWS does not delete a function’s triggers when it deletes the function).

Example

docs.title: Create SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
1. Click on the Add trigger button on the left side of the Function overview diagram to create a new SQS Queue Trigger
Example
  1. Click on the dropdown and select SQS as the trigger source
Example

  1. Fill out the first three fields in the SQS Trigger (SQS queue ARN, Activate trigger, Enable metrics)

    • Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
    • Check the Activate trigger checkbox
    • Check the Enable metrics checkbox
Example

  1. Fill out the next three fields in the SQS Trigger (Batch size, Batch window, Maximum concurrency)

    • Set the Batch Size to 10
    • Set the Batch window to 5
    • Set the Maximum concurrency to 10, the value in the template’s commented-out trigger. The example image shows 8, an older value: enter 10.
Example

  1. Fill out the last field in the SQS Trigger (Report batch item failures) and save the trigger

    • Check the Report batch item failures checkbox. The copy Lambda returns the ID of each message it could not copy in a batchItemFailures list. With this box checked, Lambda makes only those messages visible again in SAP’s SQS Queue, for another try (AWS: Handling errors for an SQS event source in Lambda). Without it, Lambda deletes the whole batch, those messages included, because the function itself does not fail.
    • Click on the Add button on the bottom right of the screen to save the trigger
Example

docs.title: Configure SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
Use these steps only when a trigger already exists (see 9.b), to check that it has the settings below.

  1. Click on the SQS rectangle on the left side of the Function overview diagram to navigate to the SQS Queue Trigger configuration
Example

  1. Check the checkbox for the SQS trigger and then click on the Edit button
Example

  1. Validate the first three fields in the SQS Trigger (SQS queue ARN, Activate trigger, Enable metrics)

    • Ensure the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account is referenced here
    • Ensure the Activate trigger checkbox is checked
    • Ensure the Enable metrics checkbox is checked
Example

  1. Validate the next three fields in the SQS Trigger (Batch size, Batch window, Maximum concurrency)

    • Ensure the Batch Size is set to 10
    • Ensure the Batch window is set to 5
    • Ensure the Maximum concurrency is set to 10 (the example image shows 8, an older value)
Example

  1. Validate the last field in the SQS Trigger (Report batch item failures) and save the trigger

    • Ensure the Report batch item failures checkbox is checked
    • Click on the Save button on the bottom right of the screen to save the trigger
Example

docs.title: 10. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested
docs.text:
After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of activating the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. The Lambda function copies objects from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket to the local target S3 Bucket in your Secondary account when an SQS notification arrives, then the SQS-Based S3 Input polls the local SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

10.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

10.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

10.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes your SAP LogServ subscription delivers, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

10.d Check that copies arrive: the S3 Bucket in your Secondary account gains new objects under logserv/, without the .gz ending.

10.e If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

  • Lambda function errors – In the AWS Console, open CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function created by the CloudFormation template (Section 3). Check for errors copying objects from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket to your local S3 Bucket. Common causes are missing access policies on the SAP ECS resources (Section 4) or an IAM Role propagation delay (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
  • Local SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 4) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, the Lambda function cannot receive SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account or read from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket. Also verify the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function is active (Section 9).
  • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 5), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 7), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
  • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) points to the local SQS Queue that was created by the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account (not the SAP ECS SQS Queue).
  • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 3) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.

docs.title: Rotate the Access Key
docs.text:
The access key from step 5 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users). The Lambda does not use the key: it runs as the IAM Role.

  1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 5. Save the new key ID and secret.
  2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 6, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
  3. Check that events still arrive (step 10) and that the _internal search in step 10.e shows no new authentication errors.
  4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify Your Data.
  2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
  3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide
Introduction
docs.text:
This guide adds a Lambda function in your AWS account that filters SAP LogServ’s notifications before Splunk sees them, so the forwarder never downloads the objects you do not want. Use it when the forwarders’ load, or the backlog waiting in SAP’s queue at the first start, needs cutting; otherwise the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup is the default (Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario).

The deployment diagram below shows two different AWS accounts. For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom left of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

Your SAP ECS LogServ subscription for AWS (e.g. in your SAP ECS account) should have one S3 Bucket in that account where LogServ will store your LogServ logs. It should also have one SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket in that account.

You will need to obtain the AWS ARN for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket that resides in your SAP ECS account prior to performing the steps in this setup guide.

Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

The Lambda reads SAP’s SQS Queue, downloads each new object from SAP’s S3 Bucket, and checks the _time, clz_dir and clz_subdir fields of its records. When at least one record passes, it sends the original notification on to an SQS Queue in your Secondary account; the Splunk input reads that queue and downloads the whole object from SAP’s S3 Bucket. The Lambda reads every object once, so S3 GET requests rise rather than fall; the saving is on the forwarder. No AWS scenario loads history on its own: to load older days, use AWS S3 Direct once this setup works.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Below are the high level steps for this setup process listed in the order they should be followed.

Please ensure the user you log in with in your AWS Secondary account has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below.

  • Before you begin: check where each step runs, and install the Splunk Add-on for AWS on each instance that will run the input (see Before You Begin)
  1. Obtain the ARNs for the SQS Queue and the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account
  2. Create a new S3 Bucket, with a name of your own, in the correct AWS Region in your Secondary account and upload the splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip file to the root of the bucket (do not rename the file — the CloudFormation template looks for the object key splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip at the bucket root)
  3. Deploy the AWS CloudFormation Template provided for this remote S3 filter deployment approach in your Secondary account
  4. Contact SAP LogServ support and request an update to the access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account, and wait for SAP to confirm that both are applied
  5. Create an Access Key for the new IAM User that was created with the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account
  6. Configure your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS)
  7. Configure the new cross-account IAM Role from your AWS Secondary account in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
  8. Configure a new SQS-Based S3 Input in the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS), and give it the _meta = cloud_provider::aws line.
  9. Once SAP has confirmed both policies, create the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function the CloudFormation template created (the template does not create the trigger)
  10. Confirm that LogServ logs are being ingested into Splunk

docs.title: Where These Steps Run
docs.text:
Steps Where 1 to 5, and 9 The AWS console of your Secondary account, and a request to SAP LogServ Support Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS (below), 6 to 8 Splunk Web on each instance that will run the input: each heavy forwarder (recommended), the single instance, or, with no heavy forwarder, your Splunk Cloud search head. Configure each heavy forwarder directly, not through a Deployment Server 10 A search head that can search the LogServ data index

Several heavy forwarders can read the same local SQS Queue: the queue hands each message to one of them, so they share the work. Give each one the same account, IAM role and input; see Adding Capacity in Capacity Planning and First Start.

docs.title: Check These First
docs.text:
Steps 1 to 4 need nothing in Splunk, so do them on day one (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap). Check the items below before you go on with step 5.

  • The prerequisites are met and the Data TA is on each of those instances (Plan and Prerequisites, Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA). On heavy forwarders, check its build with Version Check. Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, so events indexed before the Data TA arrives keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good.
  • You have decided cloud attribution and filtering. Both apply at index time, to what is indexed after you save them. The Lambda filter in this guide is separate from the Data TA’s filters and behaves differently (AWS Lambda-Based Filtering).
  • You have planned the first start. Once its trigger is active, the Lambda works through every notification already waiting in SAP’s queue. Read First Start: The Queue Backlog before step 9, including whether to ask SAP to purge the older messages.

docs.title: Install the Splunk Add-on for AWS
docs.text:
Install the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services (AWS) (Splunkbase app 1876) on each instance from the table above. It runs the SQS-Based S3 input and holds the AWS account and IAM role you configure in steps 6 to 8; the LogServ dashboards do not need it on the search head. See the add-on’s installation documentation.

  • Version: 8.2.2 or later is recommended. Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1005 (fixes in third-party packages) says to upgrade to 8.2.2 or higher. The solution enforces no minimum version; these guides were checked on 8.3.1, and the AWS S3 Direct screen shows a warning below 8.1.0.
  • Install it directly on each heavy forwarder. Do not add it to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, and do not distribute it with a Deployment Server: a push replaces an app’s local/ folder on the forwarder, which is where Splunk Web saves the account, the IAM role and the input you create in steps 6 to 8.
  • Just install it now; steps 6 to 8 configure it.

docs.title: 1. Obtain ARNs from SAP ECS Account
docs.text:
Before you can create the local S3 Bucket and deploy the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account, you need to obtain the AWS ARN for two resources that reside in your SAP ECS account:

  • The S3 Bucket that stores your LogServ logs
  • The SQS Queue that receives notifications when new logs are added to the S3 Bucket

You will also need to note the AWS Region where these resources are located, because the S3 Bucket and CloudFormation template in the next two sections must be created and deployed into that same region in your Secondary account.

What does an ARN look like?

AWS Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) follow a predictable format. Examples:

  • S3 Bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd
  • SQS Queue ARN: arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:121212121212:sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd-logserv

How to obtain the ARNs:

1.a If you do not have console access to your SAP ECS account, contact SAP LogServ Support to obtain the ARN for the S3 Bucket, the ARN for the SQS Queue, and the AWS Region where these resources reside.

1.b If you do have console access to your SAP ECS account, obtain the ARNs yourself:

  • For the S3 Bucket: navigate to the S3 console, find the bucket used for LogServ logs, click on the bucket name, and copy the ARN from the Properties tab.
  • For the SQS Queue: navigate to the SQS console, find the queue that receives S3 notifications, click on the queue name, and copy the ARN from the Details section.

1.c Save both ARNs and the AWS Region in a secure location – you will reference them when creating the S3 Bucket (next section), deploying the CloudFormation Template, and configuring the SQS-Based S3 Input later in this guide.

docs.title: 2. Create S3 Bucket with Lambda Function ZIP File
docs.text:
This bucket holds the Lambda function’s code. The CloudFormation template does not create it.

2.a Take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located.

2.b Log into your AWS Secondary account and change to the region that matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Create the bucket in that Region, the one you will deploy the stack in: Lambda requires its code bucket in the function’s Region.

2.c Choose a name of your own for the new S3 bucket. S3 bucket names are global: each name can be used by only one AWS account, so pick one no other account is likely to hold, for example splunk-logserv-lambda-code-<your-account-id>-<region>. Write it down; you enter it in step 3.j.

2.d Navigate to the S3 console and create a general purpose S3 bucket using all the default settings

2.e Upload the splunk-logserv-filter-lambda.zip file to the root of the S3 bucket

Example

docs.title: 3. Deploy CloudFormation Template
docs.text:
Before you deploy the CloudFormation template, take note of the AWS Region in your SAP ECS account where the S3 Bucket and SQS Queue are located as you will need to deploy the CloudFormation template provided in that same region in your Secondary account.

What does the CloudFormation template do?

Creates the following resources:

  • An IAM User - Default name is splunk_logserv_user
  • An IAM Policy named splunk-logserv-ta-policy
  • An IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role
  • An Inline IAM Policy on the IAM User to assume the IAM Role created above
  • An SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue
  • A Dead Letter SQS Queue - Default name is splunk-logserv-local-target-queue-dlq. It takes the messages of the local SQS Queue that are received three times without being deleted; it does not protect the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
  • A Lambda Function (Python 3.12 runtime) - Default name is splunk-logserv-lambda-filter
  • A LogGroup used by the Lambda Function

It does not create the bucket for the Lambda code (step 2), the access key (step 5) or the Lambda’s SQS trigger (step 9).

3.a Navigate to the CloudFormation console (ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account)

3.b Click on the Create stack button and select With new resources (standard)

Example

3.c Upload the AWS CloudFormation Template file provided for this remote S3 filter deployment approach, then click the Next button

Example

3.d Enter a name for the CloudFormation Stack - splunk-logserv-remote-s3-filter

Example

3.e Enter just the name (not the ARN) of the S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountS3Bucket parameter - If your ARN looks like this arn:aws:s3:::sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd then just use the name like this sap-hec-clz-ap-south-1-hec53-xsd

Example

3.f Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account in the CrossAccountSQSQueueArn parameter

Example

3.g Enter the number of days in the past to filter messages on, in the DaysInThePast parameter: from 1 to 365, default 7. The Lambda passes an object on only when at least one of its records has a _time newer than this many days before the moment it processes the notification. This is not the Data TA’s Days in the Past, which counts from midnight UTC.

Example

3.h Enter comma-separated patterns for paths to exclude (e.g., ‘linux/cron,*/messages’). Format: <clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>. Leave empty to exclude nothing. The Lambda matches with Python’s fnmatch, so * also matches across the / (linux* matches linux/cron), and a bare * here excludes everything.

Example

3.i Enter comma-separated patterns for paths to include (e.g., ‘hana/hanaaudit,linux/*,webdispatcher/accesslog’). Format: <clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>. Use ‘*/*’ to include all paths. Do not leave it empty: an empty value discards every notification.

Example

3.j Enter the exact name of the S3 Bucket you created in step 2 in the LambdaCodeBucket parameter. The parameter has no default; the example image shows an older default name, which you must not use.

Example

3.k Choose and enter a name for the Lambda Function to be created in your Secondary account in the LambdaFunctionName parameter

Example

3.l Choose and enter a name for the SQS Queue to be created in your Secondary account in the LocalSQSQueueName parameter

Example

3.m Choose and enter a name for the IAM User to be created in your Secondary account in the NewIAMUserName parameter, then click on the Next button

Example

3.n Scroll down to the bottom of the page and check the I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names checkbox, then click on the Next button

Example

3.o Scroll down to the bottom of the page and click on the Submit button

Example

3.p Ensure the deployment of the CloudFormation template completes successfully

Example

docs.title: 4. Contact SAP LogServ Support
docs.text:
Once the deployment of the CloudFormation templates completes successfully, you will need to provide SAP LogServ Support with the ARN of the IAM Role named splunk-logserv-ta-role that was created by the template.

The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role

Example access policies for the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket residing in your SAP ECS account are provided as a reference to provide clarity on the specific permissions that need to be applied by the SAP LogServ Support team.

  • Example SQS Queue Access Policy
  • Example S3 Bucket Access Policy

Ask SAP to keep s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket-name>) in the S3 Bucket policy, as the example does. The Lambda and the SQS-Based S3 input do not need it, but AWS S3 Direct, which loads history and recovers outages, does: for a bucket in SAP’s account, AWS requires both your IAM Role’s policy and SAP’s bucket policy to allow it. The template already grants it on your side.

Wait until SAP LogServ Support confirms that both policies are applied before you create the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. With only the queue policy in place, the Lambda takes SAP’s notifications but cannot read the objects, and those notifications are lost to this path. Steps 5 to 8 can be done in the meantime.

docs.title: 5. Create Access Key for IAM User
docs.text:
The CloudFormation template creates the IAM User but no access key for it, so you create one here (AWS: To create an access key for an IAM user).

5.a Navigate to the IAM console in your Secondary account and search for the IAM User name you used when deploying the CloudFormation template. Click on the name of the IAM User to see the user details.

Example

5.b Click on the Security credentials tab in the middle of the screen. Scroll down and click on the Create access key button.

Example

5.c Select the Local code use case, check the Confirmation checkbox and click on the Next button.

Example

5.d Enter a description tag value if desired and click on the Create access key button.

Example

5.e Copy the values for both the Access key and the Secret access key and save them in a secure place as you will need them in the upcoming steps. Now click on the Done button.

Example

docs.title: 6. Configure Secondary Account (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Please ensure the user you log in with in your Splunk instance has the appropriate permissions to perform all the steps outlined below. Do steps 6 to 8 on each instance that will run the input (Where These Steps Run).

6.a Login to your Splunk console then find and open the Splunk Add-on for AWS App

Example

6.b Click on the Configuration tab, then click on the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

6.c Choose and enter a descriptive name for the account in the Name field. Enter the access key ID you created for the IAM User in the Key ID field and its secret in the Secret Key field. Leave the Region Category set to Global. Click on the Add button.

Example

docs.title: 7. Configure IAM Role (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
7.a Click on the IAM Role tab to the right of the Account tab, then click on the Add button

Example

7.b Choose and enter a descriptive name for the role in the Name field. Enter the IAM Role ARN in the IAM Role ARN field, then click the Add button. The ARN for the IAM Role should look like the one below but with your 12-digit AWS account Id of your Secondary account.

  • arn:aws:iam::secondary-account-id:role/splunk-logserv-ta-role
Example

docs.title: 8. Configure SQS-Based S3 Input (AWS Add-on)
docs.text:
Create the input only after the Data TA is on this instance (Check These First). It reads the local SQS Queue, which stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active.

8.a Click on the Inputs tab. Click on the Create New Input button. Select the Custom Data Type option at the bottom of the drop-down, then select the SQS-Based S3 (Recommended) option.

Example

8.b Fill out the first three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Name, AWS Account, Assume Role)

  • Choose and enter a descriptive name for the input
  • Select the AWS Account you configured previously
  • Select the IAM Role you configured previously
Example

8.c Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Force using DLQ, AWS Region, Use Private Endpoints)

  • Leave the Force using DLQ (Recommended) checkbox checked
  • Select the AWS Region where you deployed the CloudFormation template previously
  • Leave the Use Private Endpoints checkbox unchecked
Example

8.d Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (SQS Queue Name, SQS Batch Size, S3 File Decoder)

  • Select the SQS Queue Name you entered in step 3.l (LocalSQSQueueName) when previously deploying the CloudFormation template
  • Leave the SQS Batch Size set to 10
  • Leave the S3 File Decoder set to Custom Logs
Example

8.e Fill out the next three fields in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Signature Validate All Events, Source Type, Index)

  • Uncheck the Signature Validate All Events checkbox (sqs_sns_validation = 0 in inputs.conf). The notifications reach the queue directly, not through SNS, so they carry no SNS signature; with the box checked, the add-on logs that a message has no valid SNS signature and does not process it.
  • Enter the value of sap_logserv_logs in the Source Type field
  • Enter sap_logserv_logs in the Index field: the LogServ data index, or the name you gave it if you renamed it (Renaming an Index)
  • Click on the Add button
Example

8.f Add the cloud attribution to the input. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set, and give this input its own stamp instead (Choose Cloud Attribution). The form has no field for it. The local SQS Queue stays empty until the trigger in step 9 is active, so add the line now, before the input has anything to read:

  • Add this line to the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf:
_meta = cloud_provider::aws
  • Restart Splunk.
  • After any later edit of this input in the form, check that the line is still there.

This follows Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input; the disable and enable steps there are not needed while the local SQS Queue is empty. The sequence has not yet been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the form keeps the line is not known. Once events arrive (step 10), check the result with the search in Check the Result.

Events the input reads without the line carry no cloud_provider field: the LogServ App’s dashboards count them as AWS, but searches of the raw events do not see it. On Splunk Cloud, where you cannot edit the file, see Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder.

docs.title: 9. Create the SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
Create the trigger only after SAP LogServ Support has confirmed that both policies from step 4 are applied, and at least 5 minutes after the stack was created. The Lambda does not retry: when it cannot read an object from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket, or cannot send the notification to your local SQS Queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested through this path (see the warning in step 10.e).

Once the trigger is active, the Lambda works through every notification already waiting in the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account (up to 14 days of them) and passes on those its DaysInThePast, IncludeFilters and ExcludeFilters settings keep, for the forwarder to parse on top of the live feed. Before you activate it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages.

9.a Navigate to the Lambda console in your Secondary account and ensure the region you are in matches the region in your SAP ECS account. Find the Lambda function that was created by the CloudFormation template and click on its name to view details.

Example

9.b The CloudFormation template does not create this trigger: the Lambda can read SAP’s SQS Queue only after SAP has applied the policies, so the trigger is a manual step. On a new stack, follow the Create SQS Queue Trigger steps below. Use Configure SQS Queue Trigger only if the Function overview diagram already shows an SQS trigger, as in the example image below: for example one you created earlier, or one left from a stack you deleted and created again with the same Lambda function name (AWS does not delete a function’s triggers when it deletes the function).

Example

docs.title: Create SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
1. Click on the Add trigger button on the left side of the Function overview diagram to create a new SQS Queue Trigger
Example
  1. Click on the dropdown and select SQS as the trigger source
Example

  1. Fill out the first three fields in the SQS Trigger (SQS queue ARN, Activate trigger, Enable metrics)

    • Enter the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account
    • Check the Activate trigger checkbox
    • Check the Enable metrics checkbox
Example

  1. Fill out the next three fields in the SQS Trigger (Batch size, Batch window, Maximum concurrency)

    • Set the Batch Size to 10
    • Set the Batch window to 5
    • Set the Maximum concurrency to 10, the value in the template’s commented-out trigger and in the configuration of the automated connect-to-filter migration. The example image shows 8, an older value: enter 10.
Example

  1. Fill out the last field in the SQS Trigger (Report batch item failures) and save the trigger

    • Check the Report batch item failures checkbox. With this Lambda it takes effect only when the Lambda’s own configuration is invalid (a missing or invalid environment variable): the Lambda then returns the whole batch to SAP’s SQS Queue. Every other failure is reported as processed (see step 10.e).
    • Click on the Add button on the bottom right of the screen to save the trigger
Example

docs.title: Configure SQS Queue Trigger
docs.text:
Use these steps only when a trigger already exists (see 9.b), to check that it has the settings below.

  1. Click on the SQS rectangle on the left side of the Function overview diagram to navigate to the SQS Queue Trigger configuration
Example

  1. Check the checkbox for the SQS trigger and then click on the Edit button
Example

  1. Validate the first three fields in the SQS Trigger (SQS queue ARN, Activate trigger, Enable metrics)

    • Ensure the complete ARN of the SQS Queue in your SAP ECS account is referenced here
    • Ensure the Activate trigger checkbox is checked
    • Ensure the Enable metrics checkbox is checked
Example

  1. Validate the next three fields in the SQS Trigger (Batch size, Batch window, Maximum concurrency)

    • Ensure the Batch Size is set to 10
    • Ensure the Batch window is set to 5
    • Ensure the Maximum concurrency is set to 10 (the example image shows 8, an older value)
Example

  1. Validate the last field in the SQS Trigger (Report batch item failures) and save the trigger

    • Ensure the Report batch item failures checkbox is checked (it takes effect only on a configuration error; see the Create steps above)
    • Click on the Save button on the bottom right of the screen to save the trigger
Example

docs.title: 10. Confirm LogServ Logs are Being Ingested
docs.text:
After completing all the previous steps, verify that LogServ logs are successfully being ingested into Splunk.

The first events typically appear within 5-10 minutes of activating the SQS Queue Trigger in step 9. The filter Lambda function receives SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account, drops any that fail your include/exclude/days filters, and re-emits the rest to the local SQS Queue in your Secondary account. The Splunk SQS-Based S3 Input then polls the local SQS Queue at the configured interval (default 300 seconds, under the input’s Advanced Settings), so allow a short lag before the first events arrive.

10.a Log in to Splunk Web on a search head that can search the LogServ data index and open the Search & Reporting app.

10.b Search with the index name itself (sap_logserv_logs, or the name you gave it). The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro is defined only where the LogServ App or the Data TA is installed, which a search head may not have yet.

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype, host

10.c You should see the LogServ sourcetypes of the log types that match your include patterns and are not blocked by your exclude or days filters, from several hosts; Supported Log Types lists them. Log types without a route of their own keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs. Verify Your Data has the full set of checks, including the routing and attribution searches.

10.d Check that the trigger is active: in the Lambda console, open the function’s Monitor tab and choose View CloudWatch logs (AWS: Viewing CloudWatch logs for Lambda functions). The Lambda logs one Processing message line for each notification it takes from SAP’s SQS Queue.

10.e If no events appear after 15-20 minutes, troubleshoot as follows:

  • Filter dropped everything – Review the DaysInThePast, IncludeFilters, and ExcludeFilters parameters you entered in Section 3. An empty IncludeFilters, a bare * in ExcludeFilters, a narrow include pattern, a short DaysInThePast window, or an over-broad exclude pattern can drop every message before it reaches your local SQS Queue. Check the Lambda function’s CloudWatch Logs for filter-decision messages and adjust the CloudFormation stack parameters if needed.
  • Lambda function errors – In the AWS Console, open CloudWatch Logs for the filter Lambda created by the CloudFormation template (Section 3). Look for cross-account access errors reading from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket or pushing to the local SQS Queue. Common causes are missing access policies on the SAP ECS resources (Section 4) or an IAM Role propagation delay (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
  • Local SQS Queue has no messages – Verify the SAP LogServ Support team has applied the updated access policies (from Section 4) to the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account. Without those policies, the filter Lambda cannot receive SQS notifications from the SAP ECS account or read from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket. Also verify the SQS Queue Trigger on the Lambda function is active (Section 9).
  • Authentication or permission errors – In the Splunk Add-on for AWS, check the logs for errors: run index=_internal source=*aws* level IN (ERROR,WARNING) earliest=-1h | head 50. Common causes are a mis-copied Access Key/Secret Key (Section 5), an incorrect IAM Role ARN (Section 7), or the IAM Role not yet propagated through AWS (wait 5 minutes after initial setup).
  • SQS URL format – Double-check the SQS Queue Name field in the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) points to the local SQS Queue that was created by the CloudFormation template in your Secondary account (not the SAP ECS SQS Queue).
  • Wrong AWS Region – The CloudFormation template (Section 3) and the SQS-Based S3 Input (Section 8) must both be in the same AWS Region as the SQS Queue and S3 Bucket in your SAP ECS account.

Notifications the Lambda cannot process are lost from this path

The filter Lambda does not retry. When it cannot read an object from the SAP ECS S3 Bucket, or cannot send the notification to your local SQS Queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested through this path. An unexpected error while processing a message is handled the same way. Only an invalid configuration of the Lambda itself returns messages to SAP’s queue.

The objects stay in SAP’s S3 Bucket. After you fix the cause, load the days the errors cover with AWS S3 Direct. In the Lambda’s CloudWatch Logs, search for these lines:

  • Could not retrieve S3 object, discarding message
  • Failed to forward message to target SQS, discarding
  • Unexpected error processing message

docs.title: Rotate the Access Key
docs.text:
The access key from step 5 does not expire on its own; replace it as your security policy requires. An IAM User can hold two access keys at a time, so you can switch without a gap (AWS: Managing access keys for IAM users). The Lambda does not use the key: it runs as the IAM Role.

  1. In the IAM console of your Secondary account, open the IAM User and create a second access key, as in step 5. Save the new key ID and secret.
  2. On each instance that runs the input, open the Splunk Add-on for AWS, then Configuration → Account, edit the account from step 6, enter the new access key ID in Key ID and the new secret in Secret Key, and save.
  3. Check that events still arrive (step 10) and that the _internal search in step 10.e shows no new authentication errors.
  4. In IAM, make the old key Inactive. Once nothing has failed for a day, delete it.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Verify Your Data.
  2. Load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
  3. Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

docs.title: AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery
docs.text:
Use this page to load LogServ days straight from an S3 bucket: history older than the notifications SAP’s queue still holds, and windows whose notifications expired, were purged or were discarded. It works with every AWS scenario (Connect, Filter and Copy), and none of them loads history on its own.

The three AWS setup guides all use the SQS-Based S3 input: a bucket sends a notification for every new object (SAP’s bucket under Connect and Filter, where the Filter Lambda passes on the notifications it keeps; your copy bucket under Copy), a queue holds it, and the Splunk Add-on for Amazon Web Services fetches exactly that object. That is the steady-state ingest path, and nothing on this page replaces it.

This page covers the Generic S3 input (aws_s3://) that the same add-on also ships. It polls a bucket prefix directly and needs no queue at all. It exists for the cases the notification path cannot serve:

  • Backfilling a date range that predates your input — logs that were already in the bucket before you configured LogServ ingest.
  • Recovering from an outage — if the heavy forwarder is down long enough for queue messages to age out, those notifications are gone permanently, but the objects are still in the bucket. The same holds for notifications SAP purged, and for those the AWS Remote S3 Filter Lambda discarded because it could not read or forward them.
  • A bucket with no notification wiring — for example, a copy of the logs you hold yourself.

The quickest way to run one is the AWS S3 Direct screen in the Data TA (section 2a): you choose dashboards and a range of days, and it builds the inputs. Appendix A explains the input itself, for anyone configuring one by hand.

Note

Direct S3 polling is a secondary channel, intended to be switched on for a specific job and switched off again. Splunk’s own guidance is to use SQS-Based S3 for ongoing ingest; see Scale limits below.

docs.title: 1. Before You Start
docs.text:
Check these before the first backfill. Each one, missed, makes a backfill find nothing, lose its events again soon after, or label them wrongly.

  • Where it runs. Run the screen on the heavy forwarder that will hold the inputs (strongly recommended): a Generic S3 input collects from the instance it is defined on. With no heavy forwarder, the single instance or your Splunk Cloud search head works too. The Splunk Add-on for AWS must be installed there directly, not distributed by a Deployment Server, with the AWS account and IAM role from your setup guide. If a Deployment Server manages the add-on, the screen only shows the configuration to apply there, because the next push would delete inputs created on the forwarder.
  • Your Splunk role holds admin_all_objects. The screen creates inputs only for such an account; without it, it shows the configuration for an administrator to apply (see the note under Creating and managing backfills).
  • The IAM role can list the bucket. It needs s3:ListBucket on the bucket, and for a bucket in SAP’s account SAP’s bucket policy must allow it as well (IAM Permissions).
  • The index keeps old data long enough. Splunk removes data from an index a bucket at a time, once the newest event in the bucket is older than the index’s retention period: the events’ own time counts, not when they were indexed. Check that the retention of sap_logserv_logs (or the name you gave it) reaches back past the oldest day you will load. On Splunk Cloud it is the index’s Searchable retention (days) (Settings → Indexes, then the index’s name). On Splunk Enterprise it is frozenTimePeriodInSecs for the index on the indexers; the Data TA’s index definition sets none, so Splunk’s default of 188697600 seconds (about six years) applies unless you or whoever created the index set another. With a shorter retention, the backfilled events are removed soon after they are indexed, and the dashboard rebuild in section 3 cannot find them. A longer retention uses more storage. The index’s size limit (Max raw data size on Splunk Cloud, maxTotalDataSizeMB on Splunk Enterprise) removes the oldest data the same way once it is reached, so check that the backfill fits too.
  • Days in the Past. With Enable Filtering on, the Data TA drops at index time every event older than its Days in the Past cutoff, backfilled events included; the screen leaves those days out and says so. To load older history, raise Days in the Past on Configuration → Filters first (Decide Filtering, Days in the Past). Where a Deployment Server manages this forwarder’s Data TA, make the change there: Save it, click Deploy to Forwarders, and wait for the forwarders to restart (allow 5 minutes or more) before you create the backfill (Changing Settings Later). The screen on the forwarder still judges by the settings stored there, which the Deployment Server does not keep up to date (What it checks); if it still leaves the older days out, create the inputs for those days by hand (Appendix A).
  • The Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set. The screen stamps each input with _meta = cloud_provider::aws, as the recommended setup does for the SQS-Based S3 inputs (Choose Cloud Attribution). The Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown adds its value next to the input’s, so with the dropdown on AWS the backfilled events can carry aws twice. This follows from how Splunk writes _meta and has not been reproduced in the lab (the dropdown set to AWS).

docs.title: 2. Create the Backfill
docs.text: Create the inputs with the AWS S3 Direct screen (section 2a). You can also create them by hand over REST or inputs.conf (Appendix A), but not with the Splunk Add-on for AWS’s own Generic S3 form, which needs an AWS permission that cannot be scoped to one bucket (A2).

docs.title: 2a. The AWS S3 Direct screen
docs.text:
The Data TA ships a screen for this job: Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct. It is the main way to create these inputs. It creates and manages LogServ-scoped Generic S3 inputs inside the AWS add-on from your browser, as the signed-in user, and adds no capability of its own. Its one server-side part is a small Data TA endpoint, POST /services/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/s3_direct_meta, which writes the _meta = cloud_provider::aws stamp into an input this screen created and restarts that input. It also runs as the signed-in user, so Splunk checks that user’s own permissions.

Run it on the heavy forwarder that will hold the inputs — strongly recommended. A Generic S3 input collects from the instance it is defined on, so creating one on a search head or indexer means that instance starts polling S3, which puts ingest load on the tier your users search on. The screen does not prevent it: on Splunk Cloud, and on an instance with no enabled AWS inputs, it shows a warning that recommends a heavy forwarder, and works as usual. It accepts the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.1.0, the version it was validated against, and any later version without a warning; an older version gets an advisory banner. It reads the add-on’s accounts from its combined account list and, when that cannot be read, from the account endpoint the add-on’s API reference documents. When it cannot read the add-on’s accounts, IAM roles or Generic S3 inputs, it names each request that failed and shows the configuration to apply instead of creating inputs; the account or the IAM role is typed in where its list could not be read. An SQS-Based S3 input list it cannot read is reported too and does not stop a create, but the warning about days those inputs may still be delivering cannot name them, and unless it read an enabled Generic S3 input, the screen cannot tell whether this instance already runs AWS inputs. When it cannot read Splunk’s list of apps, it reads the add-on’s own lists instead: if they answer, it works as usual without the version check; if not, it says it cannot tell whether the add-on is installed. When it cannot read the list of indexes, or the list is empty, it says so, and the Index field takes a typed name, filled in as sap_logserv_logs; a typed name must follow Splunk’s index naming rule (lower-case letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, not starting with an underscore or a hyphen and not containing kvstore).

Example — three rows chosen, and the plan the screen builds from them

docs.title: You choose dashboards and days; the screen builds the keys
docs.text:
• Dashboards — the same rows as the LogServ App’s Settings → Dashboard Data list. Tick one or several. The screen reads every S3 folder (<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>) those rows are built from, and a folder two rows share is read once.
  • Scan from and Scan until — two UTC dates, both included, with no time of day. They select the date in the key, logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/YYYY/MM/DD/, which is the date of the events inside. Scan until can be today at the latest, and a range covers at most 366 days.

From those the screen creates one input per S3 folder and calendar year:

  • its key prefix is the tightest one that holds the chosen days — the day itself, else its month, else its year;
  • a whitelist names the exact days, so an input for 14 to 18 September reads those five day folders and nothing else under …/2026/09/;
  • it is named logserv_backfill_<job>_<folder>_<year>, where <job> is the name you give the backfill (lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, up to 24 characters).
Which S3 folders each dashboard row reads

Derived from the searches that build each rollup, and checked against the LogServ App on every build. The four rows whose searches read the whole index take all 32 folders. Squid appears under both of its real layouts, proxy/squid (the AWS bucket) and linux/proxy (Azure), and the Pacemaker cluster log under linux/pacemaker (GCP); a folder your bucket does not have gives an input that finds nothing.

A row is not always a whole dashboard. Environment Health, DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter also read the Beaconing detection row, the Firewall Drops in Transit count on Network Perimeter reads the Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter row, ABAP Operations is built from the Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations row, and Web Dispatcher reads both Web & API Performance / Web Dispatcher and Web Dispatcher Slowest Traces — tick all the rows a dashboard uses. The Windows event logs are one sourcetype fed by four channel folders, so a row that reads Windows events reads all four.

docs.title: The write-time window is set for you
docs.text: Every input the screen creates selects objects whatever their write time (initial_scan_datetime = 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z) and stops by itself a day after it is created (terminal_scan_datetime = the moment of creation plus 24 hours). The margin is deliberate: the add-on records a scan as finished once a pass that started after the terminal time completes, and a finished input no longer fetches. With no margin, a forwarder restart part-way through the first pass would strand the objects it had found but not yet read. A day out, the next run carries on from the add-on’s own checkpoint. Until then each input re-lists its prefix every 30 minutes, which finds nothing new in a closed day.

docs.title: What it checks before it creates anything
docs.text:
• Days already covered. A folder-day that an earlier backfill from this screen already covers — enabled or disabled — is skipped, and the plan says which backfill covers it. Inputs made another way select by write time, so the screen cannot tell which days they read: where they overlap, it warns but does not skip.
  • The SQS window. A range that reaches today or either of the two days before it (UTC) warns that the SQS-Based S3 input is probably still delivering those days, and objects it has already delivered would be ingested a second time.
  • This forwarder’s own filters. A folder the Configuration → Filters include or exclude patterns drop is left out, and days older than the days_in_past cutoff are left out of the whitelist — their events would be sent to nullQueue on arrival — each with a warning that names the setting to change. If nothing is left, the screen refuses. These checks apply only while Enable Filtering is on.
    • Source rules are notes, not verdicts. Include Sources and Exclude Sources match each event’s source (its file), which the screen cannot see from a folder, so they never change whether a folder is planned. A folder the include filter leaves out is noted some files may be kept by Include Sources and stays left out — add it to Include Filters to backfill it; a planned folder is noted some files may be dropped by Exclude Sources. See Configuring Filters.
    • A refused stored value is reported first. If a stored filter setting holds a value the Data TA refuses (after a hand edit of its settings file, for example), the forwarder keeps the filter it generated before, which the screen cannot see, so the screen says its filter notes may not match that filter until the value is corrected on the Filters tab.
    • On a forwarder a Deployment Server manages, the filter it runs comes from the Deployment Server, which pushes the generated rules but not the settings; the settings stored on the forwarder, which the screen reads, can be older than those rules. Whenever it shows a filter note, the screen says so: check the Filters tab on the Deployment Server before relying on the notes.
  • The basics. A job name not already in use, an AWS account, an IAM role, a region, a valid bucket name and an index.
  • When the Generic S3 input list cannot be read, the screen cannot see which days earlier backfills cover or which job names are taken, so it skips those two checks and says so, in the form and as a comment at the top of the generated stanzas and REST calls.

docs.title: Creating and managing backfills
docs.text:
A plan below the form lists every input to be created with its key prefix and days, and updates as you type. Create backfill (N inputs) re-lists the existing inputs first, and creates nothing if that list cannot be read; then it creates the plan’s inputs one at a time. It stops at the first failure and reports what was and was not created, and it never retries a create. To finish a partial run, create the same selection again under a new job name: the days the created inputs cover are skipped.

Each input is stamped _meta = cloud_provider::aws, the value the recommended setup puts on each SQS-Based S3 input (Choose Cloud Attribution), so the Multi-Cloud dashboard attributes the backfilled events the same way. Leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set: it adds its value next to the input’s, so with it on AWS the backfilled events can carry the value twice (how Splunk writes _meta; not yet reproduced in the lab). The add-on’s create cannot carry that field, so the screen writes it into the new input’s stanza through the Data TA endpoint described above, straight after the create, and restarts the input, before its first scan. If a stamp does not complete, the confirmation names the input and the reason.

After a create, the screen names the next step — rebuild the dashboard rollups in the LogServ App for the same rows and the same dates (section 3).

The list at the top groups backfills by job, with Enable all, Disable all and Delete all. Under each backfill are two searches to copy into Search: whether its inputs finished their scan, and how many events reached the index over its own days. Inputs made another way are listed individually. A backfill cannot be edited: to change one, delete it and create another.

Prefer Disable to Delete once a backfill has finished. The screen knows which days are covered only while the inputs that covered them exist. Deleting a finished backfill makes its days eligible again, and a later backfill of the same rows would read them a second time.

Note

If your Splunk account lacks admin_all_objects the screen cannot write the inputs for you. It does not fail silently: under the heading Apply this as an administrator it renders the exact inputs.conf stanzas and curl commands to hand to an administrator, one per input. The inputs stop by themselves a day after the configuration was generated, so apply it the same day or generate it again. On Splunk Cloud, see Capability-gated REST endpoints.

Everything in the sections below and in Appendix A applies to an input created this way — the screen is a front end to the same aws_s3:// input.

docs.title: 3. Rebuild the Dashboards for the Backfilled Dates
docs.text:
Until you do, the data is searchable but the dashboards will not show it, because every dashboard panel reads an hourly KV Store rollup rather than the index directly, and the hourly aggregation searches only ever process the hour just past. They will never reach back over events that arrived today carrying last year’s timestamps.

In the LogServ App, go to Settings -> Dashboard Data (The Dashboard Data settings tab), choose a Custom range covering the dates you just ingested, and backfill the rows for the dashboards you backfilled.

Match the dates in the key, not a write-time window

The dates to enter are the dates in the keys you read — the YYYY/MM/DD part of logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/YYYY/MM/DD/. If you used the AWS S3 Direct screen, those are its Scan from and Scan until dates: enter the same two, for the same rows. If you created an input by hand, they are not its initial_scan_datetime / terminal_scan_datetime: those bound the S3 object’s upload time, which for a re-staged archive can differ from the event dates by months — see A1. Entering the scan window here rebuilds the wrong months and reports success.

The backfill is idempotent, so re-running it over a range you have already built is safe. Long windows are dispatched a month at a time. Keep the page open until every row has finished, the Environment Topology (graph) row in particular: its rows are written only while the page is open (Backfilling on first install).

Two topology collections always use the last 30 days

The Environment Topology inventory and IP enrichment collections describe current state rather than history — they have no time dimension — so they always refresh over the last 30 days whatever window you choose. The inventory records each IP address or host under its most recent SID (of the SIDs seen in its newest hour of activity, the one with the most events; an exact tie keeps the previous row), so an IP reassigned during the window maps to its new SID once its newest hour names only that one.

docs.title: IAM Permissions
docs.text:
Generic S3 needs one permission more than the SQS-based path:

Action Scopable to one bucket? Needed for Already in the shipped CloudFormation? s3:GetObject ✅ Yes Fetching each object ✅ Yes s3:ListBucket ✅ Yes Discovering keys under the prefix ✅ Yes, on the role. A bucket in SAP’s account also needs it in SAP’s bucket policy s3:ListAllMyBuckets ❌ No — Resource: "*" only The UI dropdown only, never the runtime ❌ No, and not required

s3:ListBucket is the one that catches people out. The SQS-based input never needs it — the queue message supplies the exact object key, so GetObject alone is enough. An environment that was provisioned narrowly for SQS-based ingest will therefore fail at the discovery step with an AccessDenied that mentions the bucket rather than the missing action. The CloudFormation templates shipped with this solution grant it to the role (splunk-logserv-ta-role). For a bucket in your own account, such as the copy bucket of AWS Remote S3 Copy, that is enough (for history under Copy you read SAP’s bucket, so SAP’s bucket policy applies there too). SAP’s bucket belongs to the SAP ECS account, and for such a cross-account request AWS also requires SAP’s bucket policy to allow s3:ListBucket for that role on the bucket ARN (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>, not /*). The example bucket policy shipped with the setup guides includes it, but SQS-based ingest never needed it, so confirm with SAP LogServ Support that it was applied before you run a backfill.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
The input keeps a checkpoint keyed on the highest LastModified it has processed, so a prefix that has already been drained is not re-ingested on the next poll. Re-running the same input is safe.

If you deliberately want to ingest a prefix a second time, create an input under a new name rather than editing the old one — a fresh input starts with a fresh checkpoint. Two inputs over the same keys do not share a checkpoint, so both ingest; that is why the AWS S3 Direct screen skips days an earlier backfill from it already covers.

docs.title: Scale limits
docs.text:
The add-on displays this advisory on the Generic S3 setup page:

Amazon S3 buckets with an excessive number of files or abundant size will result in significant performance degradation and ingestion delays. Configure an SQS-Based S3 input to achieve efficiency.

Take it seriously, and note two things about it:

  • It is unconditional. The equivalent message appears in the input’s own log on every discovery run — it was emitted while scanning a prefix containing five objects. Seeing it in a log is not evidence of a problem with your bucket.
  • The reason behind it is real. Generic S3 has to list the prefix on every polling interval, and listing cost scales with the number of keys underneath it, not with the amount of new data — a whitelist narrows what is fetched, not what is listed.

The practical consequence for LogServ buckets is that prefix scope matters enormously, because LogServ keys are dense:

Prefix Objects logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/ (one type, one day) 39 logserv/proxy/squid/ (one type, all dates) 182,565

Nothing in the input caps the work for you. The input declares max_items = 100000, but the Splunk Add-on for AWS never reads it (checked in 8.1.0 and 8.3.1), so it bounds nothing.

Scope every backfill input to a log type and a date range. The AWS S3 Direct screen already does — one input per folder and year, with the prefix narrowed to the month or the day when the range allows. A range that spans several months lists that folder’s whole year on each pass, so for a very dense folder prefer one backfill per month.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix AccessDenied on the bucket dropdown in the UI The dropdown calls ListBuckets, which needs the unscopable s3:ListAllMyBuckets Use the AWS S3 Direct screen, or create the input over REST or inputs.conf — section 2a and A4 AccessDenied that looks like a bucket or prefix problem aws_iam_role was left empty, so the input authenticated as the bare IAM user Set aws_iam_role on the input (A3) AccessDenied during key discovery while GetObject works s3:ListBucket missing — the SQS-based path never needed it Add s3:ListBucket on the bucket ARN to the role’s policy. For SAP’s bucket, also ask SAP LogServ Support to allow it for your role in the bucket policy (IAM Permissions) The AWS S3 Direct screen shows Apply this as an administrator instead of creating inputs Your account lacks admin_all_objects, a configuration read failed, or a Deployment Server manages the AWS add-on; the reason is shown on the screen Sign in with an account that holds admin_all_objects, or hand the generated configuration to an administrator the same day. On Splunk Cloud, see Capability-gated REST endpoints A hand-made input runs but finds nothing The scan window is bounding LastModified, not event time — and a blank initial_scan_datetime is not “no lower bound”, it is now minus seven days Express the date range in key_name (and a whitelist), and set initial_scan_datetime to an explicit floor such as 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z (not a 1970 date - Splunk’s time parser rejects those, and the input then polls forever without fetching anything). Never leave it blank — A1 The AWS S3 Direct screen offers no Create button Something blocks the plan; the reason is shown above it Fix what the red banners say — often a job name already in use, or every day skipped as covered or filtered The screen skips days you expected it to read An earlier backfill from this screen covers them, or this forwarder’s filters drop them — the plan names which To read covered days again, delete the backfill that covers them first. That ingests its events a second time, so do it only if they never arrived Backfilled events can be searched at first, then disappear The index’s retention is shorter than the age of the days you loaded, or the backfill took the index past its size limit, so Splunk removes them Raise the retention or the size limit before you load (section 1), then load those days again 400 Wrong datetime with format The offset form from the add-on’s spec was used Use the literal Z form, 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z Two inputs ingesting the same prefix name was sent on an update, which forks rather than renames Delete the duplicate; send name only on create Events land under sourcetype sap_logserv_logs rather than a real type The Data TA is not installed on this forwarder, or the object is not a LogServ envelope See installing the Data TA Backfilled events do not appear in the dashboards Dashboard panels read hourly rollups, which summarise only the hour just past Section 3 — rebuild the rollups from Settings → Dashboard Data in the LogServ App, with a Custom range matching the dates in the key (the screen’s Scan from and Scan until)

docs.title: A note on Azure and GCP
docs.text: There is no equivalent to this on the other two clouds. The Azure and GCP add-ons are notification-driven only: if a Storage Queue message or a Pub/Sub notification is purged or expires before it is consumed, the object stays in the bucket but nothing in the shipped add-ons will fetch it. If you need to recover such a window, contact your Splunk team.

docs.title: Appendix A. Generic S3 Inputs by Hand
docs.text: The AWS S3 Direct screen handles everything below for you. Read this appendix to create a Generic S3 input yourself, or to understand what the screen’s inputs do.
