docs.title: A1. The prefix selects the events — the scan window does not
docs.text:
This is the single most important thing to understand before configuring the input by hand, and it is easy to get backwards.

A LogServ object key looks like this:

logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<filename>.json.gz

The date in that path is the event date — the day the logs inside the object were produced.

The input also has two datetime fields, initial_scan_datetime and terminal_scan_datetime. Both bound the object’s S3 LastModified timestamp — the moment the object was written to the bucket. Neither has any relationship to the timestamps of the events inside it. The add-on names the field last_modified internally, and it is last_modified that its resume checkpoint is keyed on.

Those two clocks routinely diverge by a wide margin, because SAP writes objects into event-dated paths some time after the events occur. Objects sampled from a LogServ bucket carried 2025 event dates while every one of them had a LastModified in 2026.

So: to ingest a particular range of log dates, express it in the key — the key_name prefix, and for several days a whitelist (A4). Use the scan-window fields only when you genuinely want to bound by upload time — for example, “only objects written since the outage began”. The AWS S3 Direct screen works this way: its Scan from and Scan until are dates in the key.

A blank scan field does not mean “no bound”

Leaving initial_scan_datetime empty does not mean “from the beginning of the prefix”. The add-on substitutes now minus seven days — aws_s3_conf.py::_get_last_modified_time treats both an empty value and the literal string default that way. A backfill of a historical prefix left blank therefore selects nothing, logs an ordinary keys are scanned line and reports success. Set it to an explicit floor instead - but not a 1970 date. Splunk’s own search/timeparser rejects those (HTTP 400 Invalid time.), and the add-on resolves this field through that parser on every poll while validating only locally on create: the input saves cleanly, reports success and then fetches nothing, permanently. 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z is below anything S3 can hold (S3 launched in 2006) and parses correctly.

Leaving terminal_scan_datetime empty is the opposite problem: the add-on returns an open-ended sentinel and the input keeps polling indefinitely. Set it so a backfill run terminates on its own.

The AWS S3 Direct screen (section 2a) sets both itself and never sends a blank.

How this was established

Objects were copied into a bucket so that their LastModified (2026-09-09) and their envelope event time (2025-06-11) were about fifteen months apart. Three inputs were then created over the identical prefix, differing only in their scan bounds:

test initial_scan_datetime terminal_scan_datetime keys selected events T1 2020-01-01 2026-09-01 (after the events, before the write) 0 0 T2 2020-01-01 2026-12-31 5 5 T3 2026-09-05 (after the events, before the write) — 5 5

Bounding on LastModified predicts 0 and 5; bounding on event time predicts 5 and 0. The measured results match LastModified in both directions.

docs.title: A2. Why the add-on’s own form cannot create this input
docs.text:
The add-on’s S3 Bucket field on the Generic S3 setup page is a dropdown with no free-text entry, and the endpoint that populates it calls the AWS ListBuckets API. That requires the s3:ListAllMyBuckets permission, which cannot be scoped to a single bucket — AWS accepts only Resource: "*" for it.

The consequence is worth stating plainly, because the symptom is confusing:

  • The input works perfectly at runtime on a bucket-scoped policy. Only the form that creates it is blocked.
  • If you try to use the UI you will see AccessDenied on the bucket dropdown, and the form cannot be saved, because there is no way to type the bucket name instead.

Whether granting s3:ListAllMyBuckets is even an option depends on which topology you deployed:

Topology Whose bucket is it? s3:ListAllMyBuckets AWS Remote S3 Connect SAP ECS account Expect SAP to refuse — it would expose their entire bucket inventory AWS Remote S3 Filter SAP ECS account Same AWS Remote S3 Copy Your Secondary account for the copies; the SAP ECS account for history (your copy holds only the files copied since the Lambda’s trigger was activated) Your call for your own bucket, the same as above for SAP’s — and not required either way, since the steps below avoid the form

There are two ways round it, and neither needs s3:ListAllMyBuckets:

  • The AWS S3 Direct screen shipped with the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ (Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct). It types the bucket name rather than listing buckets, so the blocked endpoint is never called. See section 2a.
  • REST or inputs.conf directly, as in A4, which likewise never touches that endpoint.

docs.title: A3. Set aws_iam_role explicitly
docs.text: All three AWS topologies authenticate through a cross-account IAM role, and the Generic S3 input does not infer it. If you set only aws_account and leave aws_iam_role empty, the input authenticates as the bare IAM user — which holds essentially no S3 permissions — and returns an AccessDenied that reads exactly like a bucket or prefix problem. Always set both.

docs.title: A4. Run-once backfill procedure by hand
docs.text:
The pattern is: create the input scoped to the keys you want, let it drain, confirm, then disable it. The AWS S3 Direct screen does steps a and b for you, one input per folder and year; this is the same job by hand. Check section 1 first.

A4.a Work out the prefix. Narrow it as far as you can — ideally to a single log type and a single day, for example logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/. Prefix scope is your main control over how much work the input does; see Scale limits. To read several days in one input, give it the month or year as its prefix and name the days in a whitelist (below).

A4.b Create the input on the heavy forwarder, either by writing a stanza into $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf or over REST. Set both scan bounds explicitly (A1): the floor, and a terminal time a day or so from now so the input stops by itself. The stanza form:

[aws_s3://logserv_backfill_hana_20250611]
aws_account = <your configured AWS account name>
aws_iam_role = <your cross-account IAM role name>
bucket_name = <the LogServ bucket>
key_name = logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/
initial_scan_datetime = 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z
terminal_scan_datetime = <tomorrow, e.g. 2026-09-26T00:00:00Z>
index = sap_logserv_logs
sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
parse_csv_with_delimiter =
polling_interval = 1800
_meta = cloud_provider::aws

The equivalent REST call (curl prompts for the password). It cannot carry _meta — the add-on’s endpoint refuses it with 400 Argument "_meta" is not supported by this handler — so add that line to the stanza afterwards, then disable and enable the input so it starts from the stanza as written:

curl -sk -u '<your-splunk-username>' \
  https://<heavy-forwarder>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/data/inputs/aws_s3 \
  -d name=logserv_backfill_hana_20250611 \
  -d aws_account=<account> \
  -d aws_iam_role=<role> \
  -d bucket_name=<bucket> \
  -d index=sap_logserv_logs \
  -d sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs \
  -d parse_csv_with_delimiter= \
  --data-urlencode initial_scan_datetime=2000-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --data-urlencode terminal_scan_datetime=<tomorrow, e.g. 2026-09-26T00:00:00Z> \
  --data-urlencode key_name=logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/11/
Several days in one input: the whitelist

Give the input the month (or year) as its key_name and a whitelist naming the days — this is what the AWS S3 Direct screen writes:

key_name = logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/06/
whitelist = ^logserv/hana/hanaaudit/2025/(?:06/(?:10|11|12))/.+$

The add-on matches the whitelist against the whole key with Python’s re.search, and appends $ when the pattern does not end with one — so write the pattern to run to the end of the key, as above. A whitelist overrides any blacklist. It filters what the listing returns; the listing itself still covers everything under key_name, so keep the prefix as tight as the days allow.

Note

Creating the input starts it immediately. The add-on rejects disabled on create (400 Argument "disabled" is not supported by this handler); it is accepted only on a later update. If you need to stage a configuration without running it, create it and then disable it as two calls.

A4.c Watch it work. The input logs to $SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunk_ta_aws_aws_s3_<input name>.log. A healthy run logs Start processing last_modified=..., then one line per key, then updates its checkpoint.

A4.d Confirm the data. Search the target index over the event dates you backfilled — not today — and check that the sourcetype resolved to the real LogServ type rather than the fallback:

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-1y | stats count by sourcetype

A4.e Disable the input once the prefix is drained. An input past its terminal time stops fetching, but disabling it says so plainly — and until the terminal time it re-lists the prefix on every polling interval.

curl -sk -u '<your-splunk-username>' -X POST \
  https://<heavy-forwarder>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/data/inputs/aws_s3/logserv_backfill_hana_20250611/disable
Field names and formats that differ from the add-on’s documentation
  • The prefix field is key_name, not key_prefix.
  • An update must echo the full required set — aws_account, bucket_name, index, parse_csv_with_delimiter, sourcetype — or the endpoint returns 400 The following required arguments are missing. Optional fields you omit are preserved.
  • Never send name on an update. It does not rename the input; it creates a second input pointed at the same prefix, and both will ingest. Send name only on create.
  • The datetime fields require a literal trailing Z (2026-09-01T00:00:00Z). The offset example in the add-on’s own inputs.conf.spec (2011-07-06T21:54:23-0700) is rejected by the setup handler.
  • When posting datetimes or a whitelist in a form-encoded body, use --data-urlencode; a plain + in a form body decodes to a space.

A4.f Rebuild the dashboard rollups for the dates you backfilled — section 3.

docs.title: A5. What to expect
docs.text:
Direct polling produces the same events as the SQS-based path — the same envelope handling, the same sourcetype routing, the same index-time filtering. Measured against a LogServ bucket:

Check Result Gzipped .json.gz objects Decompressed natively — no decoder configuration NDJSON splitting 39 objects produced 1,238 events Sourcetype routing sap:hana:audit — the real type, not the sap_logserv_logs fallback _time The embedded envelope epoch (2025-06-11), not the ingest time host / source Taken from the envelope, overriding the S3 key clz_dir / clz_subdir Indexed, as usual _raw Envelope stripped to the inner log line Repeat polls 1,238 → 1,238 across two polling cycles — no duplication

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• After a backfill, rebuild the dashboards for its dates (section 3), then check them with Verify Your Data.
  • New install: Install the LogServ App and seed its dashboards.

docs.title: SAP LogServ on Azure — Setup Guide
docs.text:
This page covers ingesting LogServ data from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage using the standalone LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure) and its sap_logserv_azure_queue modular input — the Azure twin of Splunk_TA_aws’s SQS-Based S3 input. An Azure Event Grid subscription drops a BlobCreated notification onto a Storage Queue; this input consumes the queue, fetches each named blob over a SAS, and emits its NDJSON. This is the model SAP’s LogServ-on-Azure collector uses (Storage Queue notifications). You install this small, first-party add-on on the heavy forwarder that runs the input — the same deployment model as the Splunk Add-on for AWS — and the LogServ Data TA on the same instance provides the downstream sourcetype routing, filtering, and stamping. The downstream pipeline (sourcetype routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) is identical to the AWS S3 path.

The Azure infrastructure is provided by SAP — you only install the add-on and configure the input

In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment the storage account, blob container, Storage Queue, Event Grid subscription, and SAS are all provisioned and managed by SAP in the SAP ECS Azure account. You do not create or configure anything in Azure. Your only tasks are to install the splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure add-on on the heavy forwarder that will run the input and create one Splunk input per Azure queue on it — one per Azure landscape (most deployments have a single landscape, hence one input; you can define several on the same HF if you ingest from more than one — see Multiple landscapes / fleets), using a small set of parameter values that you obtain from your SAP support contact — see Parameters to obtain from SAP.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Follow these steps in order. Each step links to its section below.

  1. Get the parameters from SAP: the storage account name, the queue name and the SAS. Ask also when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how SAP will give you a new one. See Parameters to obtain from SAP.
  2. Decide about the queue backlog with SAP before the input exists. A purged day cannot be loaded later. See First Start: The Queue Backlog and Historical backfill.
  3. Check the Data TA and the indexes. The Data TA must be on the instance that will run the input, and the indexes must exist, before the input reads anything: events indexed without the Data TA keep the base sourcetype for good. See Prerequisites.
  4. Download and install the add-on on that instance, directly (never through the Deployment Server). See Install the Azure add-on.
  5. Before the input starts, check the Data TA’s two index-time settings. Leave Cloud Provider at Not set: the input stamps cloud_provider=azure itself (see cloud_provider attribution and Choose Cloud Attribution). Decide filtering, including whether to drop the Unix command output that arrives under undefined/undefined (see Decide Filtering). Whatever the queue holds when the input starts is indexed with the settings in place at that moment.
  6. Create one input for the queue, with a role that holds admin_all_objects. See Configure the input.
  7. Check that data arrives. See Validation.
  8. Put the SAS expiry in your calendar, and replace the SAS before it. See Rotate credentials.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
SAP LogServ RISE-ECS
  |
  +-> writes NDJSON.gz blobs to Azure Blob Storage under the logserv/ prefix
        |
        +-> Azure Event Grid subscription (Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated)
              |
              +-> Azure Storage Queue (one message per new blob)
                    |
                    +-> [Azure add-on: sap_logserv_azure_queue]  (runs on the Heavy Forwarder)
                          |   reads the queue, fetches each blob over a SAS, gunzips, splits NDJSON
                          |
                          +-> emits via EventWriter, sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, cloud_provider=azure
                                |
                                +-> [LogServ Data TA pipeline]  (same Heavy Forwarder):
                                      sourcetype routing by clz_dir/clz_subdir or source path,
                                      Configuration -> Filters nullQueue, _time drop,
                                      splunk_solution stamping
                                      |
                                      +-> forwarded to the Indexer
                                            |
                                            +-> dashboards + ES integration

Everything from the LogServ blob writer down through the Storage Queue lives in the SAP ECS Azure account and is managed by SAP. The Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input — the only component you install and configure — runs on your heavy forwarder, consumes the queue SAP exposes to you, and hands its events to the LogServ Data TA (also on that HF) for routing/filtering/stamping. This is exactly how Splunk_TA_aws and the Data TA cooperate for the AWS S3 path.

Why EventWriter, not HEC: the input runs on the heavy forwarder and emits through the HF’s native index-time pipeline, so every existing LogServ Data TA feature — sourcetype routing (by the clz_dir / clz_subdir folder fields or by the source path, depending on the log type; see Supported Log Types), the Configuration → Filters nullQueue filtering, the days_in_past / _time drop, and the splunk_solution stamping — applies to Azure events unchanged, exactly as it does to AWS S3 events. The cloud_provider value comes from the add-on itself (see cloud_provider attribution). The input is stdlib-only (Azure Storage REST over urllib — no Azure SDK), so it adds no AArch64 / native-binary burden and is Splunk Cloud-clean.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Provided by SAP (in the SAP ECS Azure account — you obtain the values, you do not build the resources):

  • An Azure Storage Account holding the LogServ container (blobs under the logserv/ prefix — same path convention as AWS S3: <container>/logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<file>.json.gz).
  • A Storage Queue in that account, fed by an Event Grid subscription that routes Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated events to it.
  • A SAS that is both blob-readable and queue-processable (see What the SAP-provided SAS must cover).

Obtain the storage account name, the queue name, and the SAS from your SAP support contact — see Parameters to obtain from SAP.

On your side (the instance that runs the input — a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended):

  • LogServ Data TA 0.1.1+ installed on that instance (it provides the index-time routing/filtering/stamping; see Installing the Data TA). On heavy forwarders the Data TA is normally distributed by the Deployment Server (see Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders). Its build decides the parsing cost on the forwarder: use build 1792189743 or later, and see Version Check to read the build on a forwarder.
  • The indexes (sap_logserv_logs, and the AI Assistant audit index) on your indexer tier, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
  • LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure) 0.1.1+ installed on the same instance (see Install the Azure add-on). It registers the sap_logserv_azure_queue input kind. The input is inert until you create an input instance.
  • A Splunk role that holds the admin_all_objects capability on that instance, to create, edit or delete the input (see Configure the input).
  • Network egress from that instance to <account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net (port 443 / HTTPS). The add-on has no proxy setting of its own; if the instance reaches the internet through a proxy, see Outbound proxy under Heavy Forwarders.

Compact JSON format required

Each blob is gzipped NDJSON (one event per line). The index-time routing transforms assume compact JSON (no whitespace after :). The SAP LogServ collector emits compact JSON natively, so no action is required on your side. (For reference: pretty-printed JSON would bypass the transforms and land as sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, breaking dashboards.)

docs.title: Parameters to obtain from SAP
docs.text:
You do not create any Azure resources. SAP has already provisioned the storage account, container, queue, and Event Grid subscription in the SAP ECS Azure account. Contact your SAP support contact to obtain the following values for your environment, then plug them into the Splunk input (Configure the input):

Parameter Input field Description Storage account name account_name The Azure Storage account holding the LogServ container (^[a-z0-9]{3,24}$). Storage Queue name queue_name The queue receiving the Event Grid BlobCreated notifications. SAS token sas_token An account SAS covering both services (ss=bq, srt=o) with blob read (r) and queue process (p, which covers Get Messages and Delete Message); add a only if you configure a dead_letter_queue. List (l) is not needed, because the input never lists the container. See below. Treat it as a secret.

The blob container name and logserv/ prefix are already covered by the SAS and the queue — they are not separate input fields. The account name also determines the two endpoints your heavy forwarder must reach (<account>.blob.core.windows.net and <account>.queue.core.windows.net).

Ask SAP also when the SAS expires (its se= value) and how they will give you a new one before then. When the SAS expires the input stops (see Rotate credentials).

docs.title: What the SAP-provided SAS must cover
docs.text:
The input fetches blobs and reads/deletes queue messages with the single SAS SAP gives you, so that SAS must cover both services. Confirm with your SAP support contact that the SAS includes:

SAS field Must include For ss (services) b (blob) and q (queue) blob fetch + queue ops srt (resource types) o (object) is what the add-on actually needs; sco is fine if that is what SAP issues account-SAS resource scope sp (permissions) r (blob read) and p (queue process — covers Get + Delete Messages); add a (add) only if you configure a dead_letter_queue (poison messages are written to it) fetch blobs + consume queue se (expiry) a date far enough ahead, and a renewal agreed with SAP the input stops when it passes

l (list) and d (delete) are not needed: the input never lists the container, and in an account SAS p already covers deleting queue messages.

You can decode a SAS string to check its scope and expiry before configuring the input:

echo "$SAS" | tr '&' '\n' | grep -E '^(ss|srt|sp|se)='

If the SAS is queue-only

If ss lacks b, blob fetches fail with HTTP 401/403 and the input logs it explicitly: “blob read forbidden … the SAS likely lacks Blob-read permission or has expired.” The decisive question for your SAP support contact is “is the LogServ SAS Blob-readable, or queue-only?” If it is queue-only, you will need a second, blob-read credential from SAP.

docs.title: Install the Azure add-on
docs.text:
Download splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz from the release_binaries folder of the Splunk for SAP LogServ GitHub repository. Its AppInspect report sits beside it, and the folder’s README.md lists each tarball’s md5. The build and md5 of each package are also listed under Download the Packages.

Install it directly on the instance that runs the input. A heavy forwarder is strongly recommended — it is the tier where Splunk_TA_aws runs for the AWS path. A search head is not blocked (see Running the TAs on a search head). You can install the add-on on every heavy forwarder that may run an input, for example to keep a standby ready; the input for a given queue still runs on one of them (see Configure the input).

  • Splunk Web → Manage Apps → Install app from file → upload the tarball, or
  • /opt/splunk/bin/splunk install app /path/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz, or
  • configuration management (Ansible / Puppet / Chef) drops the app into etc/apps/, then chown -R splunk:splunk and restart.

Do NOT distribute the Azure add-on via the Deployment Server

Install it directly on each instance that runs an input — never as a deployment-app. The input’s SAS is stored, encrypted, in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf; a Deployment Server push replaces the app’s local/ directory, which would wipe the per-HF SAS. (This is the same reason Splunk_TA_aws is configured per-HF rather than DS-distributed.) The Data TA stays DS-managed as before — only the Azure add-on is per-HF.

After installing + restarting, the sap_logserv_azure_queue input kind is registered and the add-on’s Inputs page is available under Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure.

Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Single instance
docs.text: On a single Splunk Enterprise instance (no separate forwarder or indexer), install the Data TA and the Azure add-on on that instance and create the input there, as described below. The Data TA’s bundled indexes.conf creates both indexes on that instance; set the retention of sap_logserv_logs if you want one other than the default (see Create the indexes). There is no Deployment Server step: the Data TA’s settings are saved on the instance itself. The LogServ App goes on the same instance.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud
docs.text:
With Splunk Cloud, run the input on a heavy forwarder you manage:

  1. Create both indexes in your Splunk Cloud stack first (Settings → Indexes, or the Admin Config Service), with the retention you want, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
  2. Set the heavy forwarder up to forward to your stack, with your stack’s universal forwarder credentials app installed on it.
  3. Put the Data TA on the heavy forwarder (through your Deployment Server, or directly if you have none), and install the Azure add-on on it directly, as above.
  4. Create the input on the heavy forwarder (Configure the input).

The LogServ App goes on the Splunk Cloud search head. The Data TA is not needed on the Cloud stack in this layout.

Without a heavy forwarder. The add-on’s app.manifest declares the search-head workload, so a search head is an allowed target for it; installing it on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested. In this layout, install the Data TA and the Azure add-on on the search head as private apps, and create the input there. The Data TA must sit beside the add-on, because it parses the events where the input runs. We strongly recommend against this layout, because the input puts ingest load on the tier your users search on. Creating the input needs a role that holds admin_all_objects there too. See Running the TAs on a search head and Splunk Cloud Considerations.

docs.title: Configure the input
docs.text:
Create one input for each Azure queue, on one instance (normally one heavy forwarder). You can install the add-on on every HF, for example to keep a standby ready, but run the input for a given queue on one HF only. Every other input on the same queue, on the same HF or another one, keeps its own dedup record, so a redelivered message can be indexed twice (see Scaling one queue by cloning below). The SAS is encrypted into the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf and is not Deployment-Server-managed — it survives restarts and Data-TA pushes.

Creating or editing an input needs admin_all_objects

On Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud alike, creating, editing (including replacing the SAS) and deleting an input runs as the signed-in user and needs a role that holds the admin_all_objects capability. Without it, Save fails with HTTP 403, “This operation is forbidden”. The REST call below has the same requirement.

A new input starts with what is already in the queue

The queue may already hold notifications from before your input exists: up to 7 days of them by default, and with no limit if SAP’s Event Grid subscription sets them never to expire. A new input works through all of them on top of the live feed. Before you create it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages. The add-on cannot load purged days later (see Historical backfill).

Decide on the Unix command output before the input starts

SAP files some Azure data under a storage folder named undefined/undefined, without folder fields. Most of it is Unix command output (ps, top, netstat and others, about 0.7 million events a day on the reference system), which stays under the base sourcetype unparsed. Filtering is index time, so decide before the input starts whether to drop it with the Data TA’s Exclude Sources. See Decide Filtering and Data Delivered Without Folder Fields.

docs.title: Via Splunk Web (per Heavy Forwarder)
docs.text: Splunk Web → Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure → Inputs → Create New Input → Azure Storage Queue, and fill in the fields below with the values you obtained from SAP. (For a second landscape on the same HF, use the Inputs table’s Clone action and give it a new name — the SAS is not carried on clone, so re-enter it.)

docs.title: Via REST (scriptable, per Heavy Forwarder)
docs.text:
# Write the SAS to a single-line temp file (no trailing newline), then create the input:
curl -sk -u admin:<pwd> -X POST \
  https://localhost:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_sap_logserv_azure_queue \
  --data-urlencode name=logserv_azure \
  --data-urlencode account_name=<storage-account> \
  --data-urlencode queue_name=logservqueue \
  --data-urlencode index=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode event_sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode interval=60 \
  --data-urlencode sas_token@/tmp/azure_sas.txt
rm -f /tmp/azure_sas.txt

The resulting stanza in the add-on’s local/inputs.conf looks like:

[sap_logserv_azure_queue://logserv_azure]
account_name = <storage-account>
queue_name = logservqueue
sas_token = ******
index = sap_logserv_logs
event_sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
interval = 60
disabled = 0

(Only the masked placeholder sas_token = ****** is written to inputs.conf — the real SAS is stored encrypted in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf.)

Field Default Notes account_name — Storage account name from SAP (^[a-z0-9]{3,24}$). queue_name — The Storage Queue name from SAP (receives Event Grid notifications). sas_token — The SAS from SAP (blob + queue scoped). Encrypted credential: the value lives in the add-on’s local/passwords.conf; inputs.conf carries only the masked ****** placeholder. index sap_logserv_logs Target index. Does not affect parsing — the Data TA’s index-time pipeline keys on the sourcetype, not the index. You may point it at a custom index, but the dashboards query through the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro, so update that macro to match (see caveat below). event_sourcetype (UI label Sourcetype) sap_logserv_logs Fixed at sap_logserv_logs. The add-on hard-codes this sourcetype (it is not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only when editing the input. Leave it at the default. interval 60 Seconds between firings (10–3600). Each firing drains the queue within a per-firing time budget (currently min(240 s, interval × 0.9)). batch_size 32 Queue messages dequeued per request (1–32, the Azure max). visibility_timeout 300 Seconds a dequeued message is hidden while processing (30–604800). max_blobs_per_fire 500 Cap on blobs ingested per firing (1–100000; backlog safety valve). poison_threshold 5 A message redelivered more than this many times (1–100) is dead-lettered / dropped. dead_letter_queue (empty) Optional queue name for poison messages (Storage Queue has no native DLQ). include_filters / exclude_filters (empty) Optional comma-separated, case-insensitive substrings matched against the blob path (the Event Grid subject), applied on top of the built-in logserv requirement. Subjects containing azure-webjobs-hosts are always skipped. verify_ssl 1 TLS verification for Azure REST calls.

Sourcetype is fixed; the Index is yours to change

The Sourcetype is effectively fixed at sap_logserv_logs — the add-on always emits it (the value is hard-coded in the input, not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only (disabled) when editing an existing input. When you create an input the field can still be typed into, but whatever you enter is ignored and the add-on still emits sap_logserv_logs. This is deliberate: the Data TA’s index-time routing, Filters nullQueue, _time drop, and splunk_solution / cloud_provider stamping all key on sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs (props.conf stanzas match on sourcetype, not index), so it must never vary.

The index, by contrast, may be changed safely — parsing is unaffected (events are routed, filtered, and stamped identically no matter which index they land in). You may point it at a custom index (for example a per-customer index such as sap_logserv_logs_con01). The only follow-up is dashboard visibility: the dashboards and rollups search through the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro (default index="sap_logserv_logs"), so override that macro in the App’s local/macros.conf to match your index, or the dashboards won’t find the data.

docs.title: cloud_provider attribution
docs.text:
The input stamps every event it emits with the indexed field cloud_provider=azure (the add-on’s default/inputs.conf sets _meta = cloud_provider::azure for every input of this kind), so search-time queries and the Multi-Cloud Overview dashboard can distinguish Azure-sourced from AWS-sourced data.

When you ingest from AWS as well as Azure

The Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown stamps cloud_provider TA-wide at index time. If it is set to aws on a forwarder that also runs this Azure input, that index-time stamp co-fires with the input’s per-event _meta=azure, leaving cloud_provider multivalued (azure + aws) on the Azure events. For correct per-channel attribution on a mixed forwarder, set the Cloud Provider dropdown to “Not set” and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to the Splunk_TA_aws SQS-S3 input — then each input self-attributes. This applies even when AWS and Azure run on separate forwarders: a Deployment Server pushes the dropdown’s value to every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. Leave the dropdown at Not set on forwarders that run this add-on: its input already stamps cloud_provider, and the dropdown would add the value a second time. A forwarder can run the AWS and Azure add-ons together; see Capacity Planning and First Start → More Than One Cloud for when to separate them. See Choose Cloud Attribution.

docs.title: Multiple landscapes / fleets
docs.text:
• Multiple Azure landscapes on one HF: create one input instance per landscape (different account_name / queue_name), using the Inputs table’s Clone action. The per-instance credential is keyed by the input name; re-enter the SAS on each (clone never carries secrets).
  • A fleet of heavy forwarders: install the add-on on each HF that may run an input (still never through the DS). Create the input for a given queue on one HF. Add it on more HFs only for throughput or to catch up a backlog, accepting at-least-once delivery (see the note below); to fail over, enable the standby HF’s input after you disable the first one. For zero-touch fleets, config management can drop the add-on into etc/apps/ and seed the SAS via the REST call above (it encrypts under each HF’s own splunk.secret). Do not add the add-on to the Deployment Server’s deployment-apps/.

Scaling one queue by cloning — supported (like the AWS add-on), but at-least-once

Separate input instances are normally for different queues (different queue_name). You can also point several identical inputs at the same queue to raise throughput — this is the same competing-consumer pattern Splunk’s AWS add-on uses to scale its SQS-Based S3 input: the queue’s visibility lease hands each message to one consumer at a time, so N inputs fetch and ingest N batches of blobs in parallel (across one HF, since the input is not single-instance, or across several HFs). Understand the trade-off first:

  • A single input is effectively duplicate-free across the queue’s redelivery window — its per-input dedup checkpoint (<input_name>.dedup.json; entries are retained for about 7 days, up to 50,000 blobs) skips an already-ingested blob if a message reappears.
  • Cloned same-queue inputs don’t share that checkpoint, so they fall back to at-least-once (the same guarantee as the AWS SQS-S3 input). If a message is not deleted within its visibility_timeout (default 300 s), the message reappears and another input re-ingests it → duplicate events. The lease starts when a batch of up to batch_size messages is dequeued, and each message is deleted after its own blobs are done, so what must fit is the time from dequeue to delete for the last message of a batch. The guard is identical to the AWS pattern: set visibility_timeout comfortably above that time. (dequeue_count is the queue’s server-side, shared counter, so the poison_threshold decision stays coordinated across the clones — but unlike SQS, Azure Storage Queue has no native dead-letter/redrive, so poison handling is the TA’s client-side poison_threshold + optional dead_letter_queue.)

For typical LogServ volumes a single input already keeps up (it drains up to max_blobs_per_fire blobs per firing). Prefer raising batch_size / max_blobs_per_fire or lowering interval on one input before cloning; clone same-queue inputs only when one input genuinely can’t keep up, and raise visibility_timeout when you do.

docs.title: Reliability behavior
docs.text:
• At-least-once + dedup. A queue message carrying LogServ blobs is deleted only after those blobs ingest successfully (poison messages and irrelevant / unparseable notifications are removed without ingest — see below); each blob is deduplicated by url|etag in a checkpoint sidecar, so a redelivered message re-ingests nothing.
  • Transient failures leave the message. A 5xx / network error on a blob fetch leaves the message on the queue (it redelivers after the visibility timeout); already-ingested blobs in that message are no-ops on retry.
  • Blob-read denied (401/403) leaves the message and logs loudly — this is the queue-only-SAS signal (get a blob-readable credential from SAP, the message reprocesses).
  • Poison messages (redelivered more than poison_threshold times) are moved to dead_letter_queue if configured, else dropped, so one permanently-bad blob can’t loop forever.

docs.title: Historical backfill
docs.text:
Queue-driven ingest is forward-only by nature — Event Grid fires only on new BlobCreated events, so once SAP’s subscription is live the input ingests everything written from that point on (plus the notifications still in the queue when you create the input), but does not replay blobs that already existed. This solution has no historical load for Azure; to load older blobs, agree a method with your Splunk team.

The add-on reads only the blobs that queue messages name and never lists the container. A day whose notifications were purged, or expired before the input read them, stays in SAP’s storage, but nothing in Splunk for SAP LogServ will load it. If you will need such days, agree with your Splunk team how to load them before you ask SAP to purge anything (see First Start: The Queue Backlog).

When filtering is on, the Data TA’s Days in the Past filter applies to everything the input reads, the queue backlog included: events older than its cutoff are dropped before indexing.

docs.title: Rotate credentials
docs.text:
The SAS stops working at its expiry time, the se= value in the SAS string. From then on every queue read fails with HTTP 403 (queue read failed (... 403 ...); aborting firing in the input log), and the input ingests nothing. The notifications wait in the queue only as long as their time-to-live allows (7 days by default); days whose notifications expire before you replace the SAS cannot be loaded later (see Historical backfill).

To replace the SAS:

  1. Ask your SAP support contact for the new SAS before the current one expires. Check its scope and expiry as in What the SAP-provided SAS must cover.
  2. On the instance that runs the input, open Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure → Inputs and choose Edit on the input. The SAS token field shows ******.
  3. Replace ****** with the new SAS and click Update. Saving needs a role that holds admin_all_objects. (If you leave ****** in the field, the stored SAS is kept.)
  4. The input reads the SAS at every firing, so the next firing uses the new one. Check the input log for a done: line and no queue read failed (see Validation).
  5. Repeat on every other instance that has an input using this SAS, such as a standby heavy forwarder. Each instance keeps its own encrypted copy in the add-on’s local/passwords.conf; the Deployment Server does not carry it.

Then put the new se= date in your calendar.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Confirm the input is registered and firing (run on the heavy forwarder):

curl -sk -u admin:<pwd> \
  "https://localhost:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_sap_logserv_azure_queue?output_mode=json"

Watch the input log on the HF:

sudo tail -f /opt/splunk/var/log/splunk/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_queue.log
# look for:  Input 'logserv_azure' done: messages=N blobs=N events=N dups=N deleted=N ...

Search the indexer (events route to per-source sourcetypes just like AWS):

index=sap_logserv_logs cloud_provider=azure _index_earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype

For the full set of checks (sourcetypes, one cloud_provider value per event, routing), see Verify Your Data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom (in the input log unless noted) Cause Fix Splunk Web shows “This operation is forbidden” (HTTP 403) when you save, edit or delete an input The signed-in role lacks the admin_all_objects capability Use a role that holds admin_all_objects on this instance (see Configure the input). SAS token not found in passwords.conf; skipping No credential for this input name on this host Re-enter the SAS on this HF (Inputs tab → Edit, or the REST call above). The SAS lives in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf; it is not affected by Deployment-Server pushes. queue read failed (... 403 ...) The SAS has expired (se= has passed), or it lacks queue process (p), or ss lacks q, or srt lacks o Decode the SAS (see What the SAP-provided SAS must cover). If it has expired, get a new one from SAP and replace it. Otherwise ask SAP for a SAS with ss ⊇ q, srt ⊇ o, sp ⊇ p and a future se=. d is not needed: Delete does not apply to queue messages in an account SAS, and p already covers Delete Message. blob read forbidden (HTTP 401/403) SAS is queue-only (no blob read) or expired Ask SAP for a blob-readable SAS (ss ⊇ b, sp ⊇ r); the message is left for retry. done: messages=0 every firing, but blobs exist The Event Grid subscription (SAP-managed) isn’t enqueuing, or the queue name is wrong Confirm with your SAP support contact that the Event Grid subscription is active and the queue name is correct; verify network egress to <account>.queue.core.windows.net. Input kind sap_logserv_azure_queue not listed / Inputs page missing The Azure add-on isn’t installed (or Splunkd wasn’t restarted) on this HF Install splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure on the HF and restart (see Install the Azure add-on).

For problems that are not specific to the Azure input, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Verify Your Data: check that events arrive with the expected sourcetypes and one cloud_provider value
  • Check the LogServ App prerequisites, then install the LogServ App on your Search Head
  • Review the supported log types reference
  • For Splunk Cloud considerations, see Splunk Cloud Considerations

docs.title: Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario
docs.text:
Use this page to pick the setup guide for the cloud your SAP ECS (RISE) environment runs in and, on AWS, the deployment scenario. You read it twice:

  • While planning (step 1 of the Deployment Roadmap): pick your guide and, on AWS, the scenario, because the scenario decides which template you deploy. Then start the cloud side of the guide, which needs nothing in Splunk.
  • Before you create the inputs (step 10 of the Deployment Roadmap), once:
    • the prerequisites are met;
    • the Data TA is installed (Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA) and has reached the instances that will run your inputs (Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders);
    • you have made the two index-time decisions, cloud attribution and filtering.

Both decisions apply only to what is indexed after you save them, so the first events your inputs deliver get whatever is in place when they start.

Which setup guide?

  1. Choose the cloud first. It is the cloud SAP runs your SAP ECS environment in: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud Platform. Azure and GCP each have one setup guide; AWS has three scenarios.
  2. On AWS, use AWS Remote S3 Connect unless you have a reason not to. It deploys only an IAM user and a role in your own account, and the Splunk Add-on for AWS reads SAP’s queue and bucket directly. The Data TA’s own filters work with it.
  3. Choose AWS Remote S3 Filter when the load on your forwarders, or the backlog of notifications waiting in SAP’s queue at the first start, needs cutting before it reaches Splunk. A Lambda in your account drops the notifications of the objects you do not want, so the forwarder never downloads them.
  4. Choose AWS Remote S3 Copy only if you want your own copy of new log files in a bucket in your account. It copies the objects whose notifications are still waiting in SAP’s queue when you activate its trigger, then every new object, so it cannot load history, and it stores gzipped files decompressed.
  5. History comes from AWS S3 Direct in every case. No AWS scenario loads objects older than the notifications still waiting in SAP’s queue when your input or Lambda first reads it (4 days by default, at most 14; SAP sets the retention). Load older days with AWS S3 Direct once the setup works.

docs.title: Where These Steps Run
docs.text:
Each setup guide has a cloud side, done in your cloud’s console and with SAP, and a Splunk side. The Splunk side runs on the instance that holds the input, because an input collects data on the instance it is defined on:

Your topology Ingest add-on, its account or credential, and its input The Data TA (must be there before the input starts) Single instance The instance The instance Heavy forwarders, with or without a Deployment Server Each heavy forwarder that runs an input, configured directly on it, not through the Deployment Server Each heavy forwarder: pushed by the Deployment Server, or installed directly where there is none Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder The Splunk Cloud search head. Not blocked, but a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended The Splunk Cloud search head
  • The ingest add-on is the Splunk Add-on for AWS, the LogServ Azure add-on or the LogServ GCP add-on. The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare search heads as an allowed target, but neither has been tested on a Splunk Cloud search head.
  • Routing to the LogServ sourcetypes happens at index time, on the instance where the input runs. Events that arrive before the Data TA is there keep the sourcetype sap_logserv_logs for good, so check the Data TA build on each heavy forwarder first (Version Check).
  • Creating an AWS S3 Direct backfill needs the admin_all_objects capability. The Azure and GCP guides say what their inputs need.

docs.title: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
docs.text:
All AWS deployment scenarios ingest the same LogServ logs into Splunk, with some differences in what they deploy and what they add. All of them involve two distinct AWS accounts.

All deployment scenarios for AWS require the use of an AWS Secondary account (a different AWS account than the one SAP ECS is running in) due to the requirement from SAP for a cross-account IAM Role to access the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside. See the diagram below for reference.

For brevity and clarity, the AWS account at the top of the diagram will be referred to as the SAP ECS account and the second AWS account on the bottom of the diagram will be referred to as the Secondary account from this point onward.

The table below lists the AWS Resources required for each deployment scenario:

AWS Resources AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup S3 Bucket (SAP ECS account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required SQS Queue (SAP ECS account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required S3 Bucket for the Lambda code (Secondary account, you create it) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required S3 Bucket for the log copies (Secondary account, the template creates it) ❌ Not Required ❌ Not Required ✅ Required SQS Queue (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required SQS Queue DLQ (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required IAM Policy (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required IAM Role (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required IAM User (Secondary account) ✅ Required ✅ Required ✅ Required Lambda Function (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required Lambda Log Group (Secondary account) ❌ Not Required ✅ Required ✅ Required

Under Connect, the Splunk Add-on for AWS reads SAP’s queue and downloads each object from SAP’s bucket. Under Filter, a Lambda reads SAP’s queue and passes the notifications it keeps to the queue in your account; the add-on reads that queue and still downloads each object from SAP’s bucket. Under Copy, a Lambda copies each new object into the bucket in your account, which notifies the queue in your account; the add-on reads that queue and that bucket. Filter and Copy also need a bucket of your own to hold the Lambda’s code.

If you want your own copy of the LogServ logs, in a bucket in your Secondary account, AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup provides one. Its Lambda copies the object of every notification it receives from SAP’s queue: the notifications still waiting there when you activate the Lambda’s trigger, then every new object. It never lists SAP’s bucket, so objects that were there before are not copied. Gzipped objects are stored decompressed, under the same key without .gz, so the copy takes more storage than SAP’s bucket.

The table below lists the different features supported by each deployment scenario:

Feature AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup Your own copy of the logs ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported, for the notifications in SAP’s queue at trigger activation and every new object after that Loads history from SAP’s bucket ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported ❌ Not Supported Cuts the forwarder’s load before download ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported ❌ Not Supported AWS Lambda-based Filtering ❌ Not Supported ✅ Supported ❌ Not Supported Native TA Index-Time Filtering ✅ Supported ✅ Supported ✅ Supported

To load history in any scenario, use AWS S3 Direct.

Native TA Filtering vs. AWS Lambda-based Filtering

The Data TA’s native index-time filtering works with every scenario and every cloud. It runs inside Splunk, on the heavy forwarders or the single instance, and is configured in Splunk Web. Dropped events cost no license or index storage, but the forwarder still downloads and parses them before it drops them.

The AWS Lambda-based filtering of the S3 Filter Setup runs in your AWS account, before Splunk. The forwarder never downloads the objects it drops. The Lambda itself reads every new object once to decide, so S3 GET requests rise rather than fall, and the Lambda and the queue in your account add AWS cost. It decides per object: when any one record in an object passes, the whole object is passed on. Its patterns and its day cutoff do not behave exactly like the Data TA’s; see AWS Lambda-Based Filtering.

The two can be used together. See Configuring Filters for the native filtering.

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide
docs.text:
Note

This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role to directly access LogServ resources in the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside without the need to copy logs to a secondary S3 bucket. It is the default AWS scenario.

  • No S3 Bucket or SQS Queue in your Secondary account
  • The input reads SAP’s SQS Queue and downloads from SAP’s S3 Bucket
  • CloudFormation Template provided

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide
docs.text:
Note

This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role to directly access LogServ resources in the AWS SAP ECS account where the LogServ logs reside without the need to copy logs to a secondary S3 bucket. A Lambda function filters the notifications by the age and the folder (clz_dir/clz_subdir) of each object’s records, set through parameters on the Lambda function.

  • An S3 Bucket you create for the Lambda code; no bucket for log copies
  • Secondary SQS Queue needed; the input reads it and downloads from SAP’s S3 Bucket
  • Log filtering options supported
  • CloudFormation Template provided

docs.title: AWS Remote S3 Copy Setup Guide
docs.text:
Note

This deployment scenario uses an IAM User with a configured Access Key and a cross-account IAM Role along with a secondary S3 bucket and SQS queue. Use this deployment scenario only if you want your own copy of the new LogServ log files in your own S3 Bucket; it does not copy history.

  • Your own copy of new log files, stored decompressed, under your own retention
  • Requires an S3 Bucket you create for the Lambda code, plus the bucket for the copies that the template creates
  • Requires secondary SQS Queue
  • CloudFormation Template provided

docs.title: AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery
docs.text:
Note

Not a deployment scenario in its own right — a second channel that complements any of the three above. It uses the Splunk Add-on for AWS’s Generic S3 input to read a bucket prefix directly, with no queue in the path.

  • For loading history (days older than the notifications in SAP’s queue), and for recovering a window whose notifications expired, were purged or were discarded
  • Created from the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen (Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct), or by hand over REST or inputs.conf. Not from the add-on’s own Generic S3 form: its bucket list needs an AWS permission that cannot be scoped to one bucket
  • Run it for a specific job, then disable it — SQS-Based S3 remains the steady-state path

docs.title: Microsoft Azure
docs.text:
When your SAP ECS environment runs in Microsoft Azure, LogServ logs land in an Azure Blob Storage container instead of Amazon S3. Ingest is handled by the first-party LogServ Azure add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure), the Azure counterpart to the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Install it directly on the instance that runs its input, not through the Deployment Server, since its SAS credential lives in the add-on’s own local/: a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended, and a search head is not blocked. Its sap_logserv_azure_queue modular input consumes Azure Event Grid → Storage Queue BlobCreated notifications and fetches each blob over a SAS, emitting sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs into the same downstream pipeline (routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) as the AWS path.

In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment, SAP provisions and manages the Azure storage account, Storage Queue, Event Grid subscription, and SAS in the SAP-managed Azure account — you create nothing in Azure; you install the add-on and configure one input with the values SAP provides.

docs.title: Azure Setup Guide
docs.text:
Note

Queue-based Azure Blob ingest — the Azure equivalent of the AWS SQS-Based S3 Connect scenario.

  • Install the LogServ Azure add-on directly on the instance that runs the input, a heavy forwarder where you have one (not via the Deployment Server)
  • Configure one sap_logserv_azure_queue input for the Storage Queue, with the storage account, queue name, and SAS values SAP provides
  • No AWS-style secondary account or cross-account IAM role — SAP provides one account SAS that covers both the Storage Queue and the blobs; the Azure Setup Guide lists the permissions it must include (What the SAP-provided SAS must cover)

docs.title: Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
docs.text:
When your SAP ECS environment runs in Google Cloud Platform, LogServ logs land in a Google Cloud Storage (GCS) bucket instead of Amazon S3. Ingest is handled by the first-party LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP), the GCP counterpart to the Splunk Add-on for AWS. Install it directly on the instance that runs its input, not through the Deployment Server, since its service-account key lives in the add-on’s own local/: a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended, and a search head is not blocked. Its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub modular input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription fed by the bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications and fetches each object with a service-account key, emitting sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs into the same downstream pipeline (routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) as the AWS path.

In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment, SAP provisions and manages the GCS bucket, bucket notification, Pub/Sub topic, and subscription in the SAP-managed GCP project. The one GCP resource you create is the service account: in a GCP account of your own (a secondary account, separate from the RISE project), create a service account, hand its email address to your SAP support contact, and SAP grants it read access to the LogServ subscription + bucket (roles/pubsub.subscriber + roles/storage.objectViewer) — the GCP analogue of the AWS path’s customer-account cross-account IAM role. You then mint the account’s JSON key, install the add-on, and configure one input with the project ID + subscription name SAP provides plus your key.

docs.title: GCP Setup Guide
docs.text:
Note

Notification-driven GCS ingest — the GCP equivalent of the AWS SQS-Based S3 Connect scenario.

  • Create a service account in your own GCP account and hand its email to SAP support, who grant it roles/pubsub.subscriber + roles/storage.objectViewer on the LogServ resources
  • Install the LogServ GCP add-on directly on the instance that runs the input, a heavy forwarder where you have one (not via the Deployment Server)
  • Configure one sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input for the subscription, with the project ID + subscription name SAP provides and your service account’s JSON key
  • Like the AWS Connect scenario’s secondary account, the identity is customer-homed — SAP binds cross-project grants to it; no infrastructure lands in your project

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Follow the setup guide for your cloud and, on AWS, your scenario.
  2. Verify Your Data before you go further.
  3. On AWS, load the history you need with AWS S3 Direct.
  4. Install the LogServ App.

docs.title: Choose Cloud Attribution
docs.text:
This page decides how each LogServ event records the cloud it came from, in the indexed field cloud_provider. Decide before the first Save on the Deployment Server’s Configuration page and before any input first runs: the value is written at index time, and every event keeps the value it was indexed with, the first-start backlog included.

In short: leave the Data TA’s Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set (the default) on every fleet, and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each AWS SQS-Based S3 input. The Azure and GCP inputs, and the AWS S3 Direct backfills, stamp their events themselves.

docs.title: What Gets Stamped
docs.text:
The Data TA’s Configuration page has two tabs: Filters (Configuring Filters) and Cloud Provider. The Data TA stamps two indexed fields at index time on the sap_logserv_logs sourcetype every LogServ event arrives with, with the same WRITE_META mechanism it uses for clz_dir and clz_subdir:

Indexed field Value How it’s set Configurable splunk_solution splunk_for_sap_logserv Always stamped on every event No: ships active, no UI control cloud_provider aws / azure / gcp / (none) By the input’s own _meta line, and by the Cloud Provider dropdown when it is set Yes: per input, and Configuration → Cloud Provider

Both fields are written on the instance that parses the data (the heavy forwarder, or the single instance), so they are available as indexed fields for tstats, accelerated searches and raw-event filtering.

splunk_solution (always on). Every event indexed through the Data TA carries splunk_solution = splunk_for_sap_logserv. There is nothing to configure. It identifies events that flowed through the Splunk for SAP LogServ pipeline, which helps when the same index or Splunk instance also receives data from other solutions.

splunk_solution is distinct from vendor_product

The LogServ App also defines a per-sourcetype vendor_product search-time field (for example SAP HANA, SAP NetWeaver ABAP, SAP Web Dispatcher, ISC:Bind) that dashboards and CIM mapping rely on. That field describes which product produced a given event. splunk_solution is a separate, coarser stamp identifying the solution that ingested it. The two coexist and do not collide.

cloud_provider comes from two places:

  • The input’s _meta line. The LogServ Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input always carries _meta = cloud_provider::azure (the add-on writes it into its input stanza), and the LogServ GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input always carries _meta = cloud_provider::gcp. Every input the AWS S3 Direct screen creates is stamped _meta = cloud_provider::aws straight after it is created. The Splunk Add-on for AWS’s SQS-Based S3 inputs carry no _meta unless you add it; the add-on’s form has no field for it.
  • The Cloud Provider dropdown on the Data TA’s Configuration page:
Selection Effect Not set (default) The Data TA adds no cloud_provider value of its own. AWS Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = aws. Microsoft Azure Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = azure. Not needed with the LogServ Azure add-on, whose input already stamps this value. Google Cloud Platform Every event the Data TA processes on that instance is stamped cloud_provider = gcp. Not needed with the LogServ GCP add-on, whose input already stamps this value.

The dropdown does not replace an input’s _meta; it adds a second value beside it. An Azure event under dropdown = AWS carries both azure and aws (seen in the lab), so mvcount(cloud_provider) is 2 and the event can be counted under both clouds. A repeated value is expected to stay as well, according to Splunk’s description of _meta, so an Azure event under dropdown = Microsoft Azure can carry azure twice; this same-value case has not been reproduced in the lab. That is why the dropdown stays at Not set wherever an input stamps its own events.

docs.title: Recommended: Not Set Plus Per-Input _meta
docs.text:
Use this on every fleet, AWS-only fleets included:

  1. Leave the Cloud Provider dropdown at Not set on every instance that runs the Data TA. With a Deployment Server, that is the value it pushes.
  2. Azure and GCP: nothing to do. Their inputs stamp their own events.
  3. AWS SQS-Based S3 inputs: add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each input’s stanza before the input first runs, as described in Add the _meta line to an AWS input.
  4. AWS S3 Direct backfills: nothing to do. The screen stamps each input it creates.

Adding a second cloud later changes nothing: each input keeps labelling its own events.

docs.title: Add the _meta Line to an AWS Input
docs.text:
On each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that runs an SQS-Based S3 input for LogServ:

  1. Create the SQS-Based S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS, as your AWS setup guide describes.
  2. Right away, set the input to disabled on the add-on’s Inputs page, so that it reads as little as possible before the line is in place.

  3. Open $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf, find the input’s stanza, [aws_sqs_based_s3://<input name>], and add the line:

    _meta = cloud_provider::aws

  4. Restart Splunkd.

  5. Enable the input again on the add-on’s Inputs page.

The line is per instance: the Deployment Server does not manage the Splunk Add-on for AWS, so it neither pushes nor removes it. Events the input read before the line was in place keep no cloud_provider; inside the LogServ App’s dashboards they count as aws anyway (Events without a stamp).

What has been tested

In the lab, adding this line to existing SQS-Based S3 stanzas and restarting Splunkd worked: the events read afterwards carried a single aws. The full create, disable, edit, restart, enable sequence has not been run end to end on Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1, and whether a later edit of the input in the add-on’s form keeps a hand-added _meta line is not known. Check the stanza after any edit of the input, and check the result with the search in Check the Result.

docs.title: Alternative for AWS-Only Fleets: the Dropdown Set to AWS
docs.text:
On a fleet that ingests only from AWS and never uses the AWS S3 Direct screen, you can instead set the dropdown to AWS and leave the SQS-Based S3 inputs without _meta. The Data TA then stamps aws on every event it processes.

Not with AWS S3 Direct, and not with a second cloud

  • AWS S3 Direct stamps every backfill input _meta = cloud_provider::aws, without checking the dropdown, so with the dropdown on AWS a backfilled event gets aws from both, and can carry it twice (mvcount(cloud_provider) = 2), as described in What Gets Stamped; this same-value case has not been reproduced in the lab.
  • Before you add another cloud or load history with AWS S3 Direct, switch to the recommended setup: set the dropdown to Not set and add the _meta line to every SQS-Based S3 input. Events indexed earlier under the dropdown keep their single aws.
  • Never set the dropdown to Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud Platform where the LogServ Azure or GCP add-on runs.

docs.title: With a Deployment Server
docs.text:
The dropdown’s value is written into the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf, which the Deployment Server pushes to every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, so one value applies to all of them. To change it, Save the Cloud Provider tab on the Deployment Server, then click Deploy to Forwarders, as on the Filters tab (Distribute the Data TA). The per-input _meta lines are per heavy forwarder and are not touched by the push.

On a single instance, or a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, the Save takes effect on that instance at once.

More than one cloud

The Cloud Provider dropdown is a Data-TA-wide setting: it stamps the same value on every event that instance’s Data TA processes. If a single heavy forwarder ingests from more than one cloud (any mix of AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage), the dropdown cannot tell the channels apart, and because the sap_logserv_azure_queue and sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub inputs already carry their own _meta values, a dropdown value would tag their events with both values. Leave the dropdown at Not set and attribute per input: set _meta = cloud_provider::aws on the Splunk Add-on for AWS SQS-Based S3 inputs; the Azure and GCP inputs already attribute their own events. With the dropdown at Not set the Data TA adds no cloud_provider value of its own, so each input’s _meta value is the only one written.

This applies when each cloud has its own forwarders too. With a Deployment Server, every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class receives the same dropdown value, so AWS would also be stamped on the events of a forwarder that reads only Azure or GCP. See Capacity Planning → More Than One Cloud for when to give each cloud its own forwarders.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud Without a Heavy Forwarder
docs.text:
When the inputs run on the Splunk Cloud search head, you cannot edit Splunk_TA_aws/local/inputs.conf. The per-input route there is a REST write to the input’s stanza through configs/conf-inputs, the same call the AWS S3 Direct screen makes for its own inputs. It needs a role with the admin_all_objects capability, which splunkd requires for configs/conf-* writes, and REST access to your stack’s search head API on port 8089. Splunk Cloud opens that port only to the subnets on your stack’s search-api IP allow list, which is closed by default; add your address with the Admin Config Service (ACS), for example acs ip-allowlist create search-api --subnets "<your address>/32". Then:

curl -u <admin_user> \
  "https://<your-stack>.splunkcloud.com:8089/servicesNS/nobody/Splunk_TA_aws/configs/conf-inputs/aws_sqs_based_s3%3A%2F%2F<input_name>" \
  -d "_meta=cloud_provider::aws"

Then disable the input and enable it again on the add-on’s Inputs page, so it starts again from the stanza as written. The same configs/conf-inputs write stamps the AWS S3 Direct screen’s Generic S3 inputs, and that has been checked on a heavy forwarder with Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.1; this route for an SQS-Based S3 input, and on Splunk Cloud, has not been tested. Without it, and with the dropdown at Not set, the SQS-Based S3 events carry no cloud_provider: the LogServ App’s dashboards still count them as aws, but your own searches do not (Events without a stamp). See Splunk Cloud Considerations for the capability.

docs.title: Events Without a Stamp
docs.text:
The LogServ App ships a search-time macro, sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro, defined as:

eval cloud_provider=coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws")

The App’s dashboards count events that have no cloud_provider as aws: their rollups apply the same coalesce, and the global Cloud filter treats a missing value as AWS. This covers events indexed before the field existed, and AWS events from inputs without _meta, in dashboards such as Multi-Cloud Overview.

It is not a global default. Outside the App’s dashboards (your own searches, Enterprise Security content, a cloud_provider=aws filter) an unstamped event has no cloud_provider value at all, and tstats ... by cloud_provider leaves such events out unless you give it a fillnull_value (before the count). Stamping at index time, as recommended above, makes the field usable everywhere.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
After the first events arrive, check that every event carries exactly one provider, using the index name (the App’s macros may not exist yet on your search head):

| tstats fillnull_value="(none)" count where index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-24h by cloud_provider, sourcetype

index=sap_logserv_logs earliest=-30d _index_earliest=-15m
| eval cloud_provider_values=mvcount(cloud_provider)
| fillnull value=0 cloud_provider_values
| stats count by cloud_provider_values

(none) in the first search means an input without _meta (and the dropdown at Not set). The second counts the events indexed in the last 15 minutes, whatever their event time, so it also works while an input drains a backlog (Verify Your Data, check 3): 0 is an event without a stamp, and any 2 means the dropdown is set while inputs carry their own _meta: set the dropdown to Not set and deploy. Events already indexed keep their values.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Decide Filtering: the other index-time choice to make before the first Save.
  2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders, if a Deployment Server manages them.

docs.title: Configuring Filters
docs.text: This page is the reference for the Data TA’s filters: what each field does, how the rules combine, how to check and change them, and the AWS Lambda filter. When you set up the Data TA for the first time, decide first with Decide Filtering, and distribute the Data TA with Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Splunk TA for SAP LogServ provides two complementary approaches to filtering LogServ data — you can use either one independently or combine them for defense-in-depth filtering. (A third, lighter layer exists on the Azure and GCP ingest add-ons: their inputs accept optional include_filters / exclude_filters substring patterns applied to the object path before download, a cheap pre-filter — the canonical allow/deny policy still lives on this page’s Filters tab.)

Native TA Index-Time Filtering AWS Lambda-Based Filtering Where it runs Inside Splunk at index time In AWS Lambda, before data reaches Splunk Configured via Splunk Web UI (Configuration → Filters) Lambda environment variables or migration config Works with All deployment scenarios (Connect, Filter, Copy) S3 Filter and Connect-to-Filter migration only What it filters Raw NDJSON events via TRANSFORMS queue routing S3 event notifications: the Lambda downloads each object and forwards its notification only if at least one record passes License impact Filtered events consume zero Splunk license Filtered notifications never reach Splunk Pattern syntax clz_dir/clz_subdir wildcard patterns, plus patterns on the event’s source value (Include Sources / Exclude Sources) fnmatch patterns on clz_dir/clz_subdir, read from each record of the object; no source patterns Time filtering Days in the Past: midnight UTC minus N days (epoch regex, refreshed daily) DAYS_IN_THE_PAST: now minus N days, on each record’s _time AWS resources needed None Lambda function, local SQS queue, DLQ Deployment Server support ✅ Distributed to heavy forwarders with Deploy to Forwarders, after a one-time server-class setup N/A (AWS-side only) Upgrade notifications ✅ Alerts when new log types aren’t covered ❌ Not available

docs.title: Which Approach Should I Use?
docs.text:
Choosing a filtering approach

Use Native TA filtering (recommended for most users) if you want the simplest setup — it works with every deployment scenario, requires no AWS resources beyond what you already have, and is managed entirely from Splunk Web. It also provides upgrade notifications when new log types are added to the TA.

Use Lambda-based filtering if you want to reduce what the heavy forwarder downloads and parses, and the SQS messages it handles. Because the Lambda filters S3 event notifications before they reach Splunk, the heavy forwarder never downloads the unwanted objects, which lowers its download bandwidth, CPU and ingestion overhead in very high-volume environments. The Lambda itself still downloads every object to check its records, so the total number of S3 GET requests does not fall: it rises by one for each object the Lambda keeps. You also pay for the Lambda’s run time and the local SQS queue.

Use both together for defense-in-depth. The Lambda filters at the AWS pipeline level, and the native TA filters catch anything that slips through at the Splunk level. Both match clz_dir/clz_subdir folder patterns, but not in quite the same way (see Lambda Filter Settings): to keep the two aligned, use only patterns the Filters tab accepts. Include Sources and Exclude Sources have no Lambda equivalent: the Lambda reads only _time, clz_dir and clz_subdir from each record, not its source, so file-level rules exist only on the Filters tab.

The remainder of this page covers Native TA Index-Time Filtering in detail. For Lambda-based filtering setup, see the AWS Lambda-Based Filtering section at the bottom of this page or the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
The TA includes built-in index-time filtering configured entirely through the Splunk Web UI — no manual editing of configuration files is required.

How It Works
  • Include Filters — Folder patterns (clz_dir/clz_subdir). Only events matching at least one include pattern — or one Include Sources entry — are eligible for indexing. Everything else is dropped before indexing (zero license cost). An entry of */* or * keeps everything.
  • Exclude Filters — Folder patterns. Events matching any exclude pattern are dropped, even if they also match an include pattern. Excludes override includes.
  • Include Sources — Patterns on the event’s whole source value (the log file’s path, such as /var/log/zypper.log, or a name such as ps). Keeps matching events even when their folder is not in Include Filters — including events that carry no folder fields at all.
  • Exclude Sources — Patterns on the event’s source value. Drops matching events even when their folder is included — for example the zypper and YaST2 logs that share the linux/linux_secure folder with primary log types.
  • Time Filter (Days in the Past) — Events with a _time older than the configured number of days are dropped. This prevents backfill of very old log data during initial setup or recovery scenarios.

All filtering happens at index time via TRANSFORMS-based queue routing, so filtered events never consume Splunk license. How the Rules Combine gives the order in which they are applied.

The Filters tab does not reduce heavy forwarder CPU

The filter rules run on the heavy forwarder in the same chain of index-time transforms as the Data TA’s sourcetype routing, so an event they drop has already been downloaded, split into lines, timestamped and run through that chain. They save license and indexing, not forwarder CPU, and they add rules of their own to the chain. To lower the forwarder’s load, drop data before the forwarder downloads it: with the AWS Lambda pre-filter on AWS, or with the Azure and GCP inputs’ path filters. See Capacity Planning and First Start.

docs.title: Deployment Architectures
docs.text: The filters run on the instance that parses the data. The TA supports three deployment models, and where you save the filters depends on which one you use.

docs.title: Single Instance or Search Head That Runs the Inputs
docs.text: The TA is installed directly on the instance that parses the data: a single instance, or a search head that runs the LogServ inputs itself (Running the TAs on a search head). Filter changes take effect immediately after clicking Save (no restart required).

docs.title: Deployment Server with Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
The TA is installed on the Deployment Server (DS) only. The DS distributes the TA and its filter configurations to the heavy forwarders (HFs) that perform the actual data ingestion. This is the recommended architecture when you run several heavy forwarders.

In this model:

  • You install and configure the TA on the DS only. A push from the DS replaces each HF’s copy of the TA, its local/ folder included, so do not also install it on the HFs.
  • Each Save on the DS stages the generated configurations in deployment-apps/ for distribution.
  • You use the built-in Deploy to Forwarders button to push changes to the HFs.
  • HFs receive the TA and filter configs at their next phone-home, and then restart.

The first distribution takes one-time steps (the HFs as deployment clients, the server class, its agent assignment): see Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

On the DS, the Deploy to Forwarders button, and the check that decides whether to show it, need the edit_deployment_server capability, not admin_all_objects. Splunk Enterprise’s admin role has it; a custom DS operator role needs it added, or the button does not appear.

docs.title: Heavy Forwarder without a Deployment Server
docs.text:
The TA is installed directly on each heavy forwarder that runs a LogServ input, and no Deployment Server manages it. It works like a single instance:

  • Save the Filters (and Cloud Provider) tab on each HF. A Save takes effect on that HF immediately, with no restart, and no Deploy to Forwarders button appears.
  • With several HFs, save the same values on every one: nothing copies them between HFs.
  • The daily Days in the Past refresh rebuilds the rules on the HF itself. If the HF is a deployment client of a DS for other apps, the refresh runs only when the HF’s record of what its DS sent ($SPLUNK_HOME/var/run/serverclass.xml) lists other apps but not this TA; when that record is missing, unreadable or lists no app, the refresh is skipped, the cutoff stops moving, and the filter keeps more older events each day.

Splunk Cloud

Splunk Cloud is never a Deployment Server, so the Deploy to Forwarders button never appears there.
