With Splunk Cloud, a DS is optional: run your own on-premises DS to manage your heavy forwarders centrally (your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a deployment server license, which you request from Splunk Support), or install the TA directly on each heavy forwarder.

docs.title: Open the Configuration > Filters Tab
docs.text:
1. In Splunk Web, open the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ app
  2. Go to Configuration > Filters
Example

On the tab the fields appear in this order: Enable Filtering, Include Filters, Exclude Filters, Include Sources, Exclude Sources, Days in the Past.

docs.title: Enable Filtering
docs.text: Check the Enable Filtering checkbox to activate index-time filtering. Default: unchecked — out of the box no index-time filtering is applied, and the Include Filters, Exclude Filters, Include Sources, Exclude Sources and Days in the Past values below take effect only once this box is checked. When disabled, all events are indexed without any filtering.

docs.title: Include Filters
docs.text:
Comma-separated patterns specifying which log types to include. Patterns use the format clz_dir/clz_subdir with * and ? wildcards:

Pattern Meaning */* Include all log types (default) hana/hanaaudit Include only HANA audit logs linux/* Include all Linux log types linux/messages, hana/* Include Linux messages and all HANA logs dns/* Include all DNS log types

Rules:

  • Each pattern must be in dir/subdir format or a standalone *
  • An entry of */* or a standalone * — anywhere in the list — includes everything: the include gate is left out and the other include entries have no effect (see Include Everything)
  • Valid characters: letters, numbers, *, ?, ., -, :, _
  • * matches any run of characters within its segment and ? exactly one character: linux/* covers every linux subfolder, */cron every cron subfolder. Matching is case-sensitive
  • A folder pattern needs the event’s clz_dir and clz_subdir fields — an event without them matches no folder pattern (see Events Without Folder Fields)
  • This field cannot be empty when filtering is enabled — use */* to include everything
Supported Log Types Reference

See the Supported Log Types section below for a complete list of clz_dir/clz_subdir values you can use in your filter patterns.

docs.title: Exclude Filters
docs.text:
Comma-separated patterns for log types to exclude. Same pattern format as includes. Events matching any exclude pattern are dropped even if they also match an include pattern.

Example: To include all Linux logs except cron and slapd:

  • Include: linux/*
  • Exclude: linux/cron, linux/slapd

Leave this field empty to exclude nothing. A standalone * in Exclude Filters excludes nothing (unlike in Include Filters); */* there drops every event that has folder fields.

docs.title: Include Sources
docs.text:
Comma-separated patterns matched against the event’s whole source value — see Source Pattern Syntax. An event whose source matches an entry is kept even when its folder is not in Include Filters, and even when it carries no folder fields at all. Default: empty (none).

  • Use it beside an Include Filters allow-list, to keep particular files the allow-list would drop — for example the HANA trace files and Unix command output that real Azure deliveries send without folder fields (Recipe 4).
  • It only adds to an allow-list. When Include Filters includes everything (*/* or *), every event is kept already, and with Enable Filtering checked a save that sets Include Sources is refused because its entries would have no effect.
  • Days in the Past and both exclude fields still apply to the events it keeps.

Example: Include Filters hana/hanaaudit, hana/tracelogs, Include Sources /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/* keeps the HANA audit and trace folders, plus HANA trace files that arrive without folder fields.

docs.title: Exclude Sources
docs.text:
Comma-separated patterns matched against the event’s whole source value — see Source Pattern Syntax. An event whose source matches an entry is dropped, even when its folder is included and even when Include Sources matches it: excludes always win. Default: empty (nothing is dropped by source).

  • Use it for log files that share a folder with a primary log type — YaST2 and zypper in linux/linux_secure, corosync in linux/pacemaker. A folder pattern cannot drop them without dropping the primary type too (Recipe 3).
  • Example: /var/log/zypper.log*, /var/log/YaST2/*

A broad source pattern drops primary log types too

Exclude Sources acts on every event whose source matches, whatever its folder. /var/log/* drops /var/log/messages, /var/log/firewall, /var/log/cron and every other file under /var/log. Name the files, or limit an entry to one folder (linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log*). The upgrade notification does not read source rules, so a pattern that drops a primary log type raises no banner.

docs.title: Source Pattern Syntax
docs.text:
Both source fields take a comma-separated list. Each entry is either a source pattern on its own, or a folder and a source pattern joined by =:

Entry Matches /var/log/zypper.log Events whose source is exactly /var/log/zypper.log, in any folder or none /var/log/zypper.log* The same file and its rotated copies, such as /var/log/zypper.log-20260823 /var/log/YaST2/* Every file under /var/log/YaST2/, subfolders included ps Events whose source is ps (Unix command output, which carries no folder fields) /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/* HANA trace files of every SID, instance and host linux/linux_secure=/var/log/YaST2/* YaST2 files, only in the linux/linux_secure folder linux/proxy=/var/log/squid/* Squid files, only in the linux/proxy folder (the Azure layout)

Rules:

  • A pattern must match the whole source value: /var/log/zypper does not match /var/log/zypper.log. The value is the one the indexed event carries in its source field (one exception: see Long Lines). To list the values a folder delivers:

    | tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` by clz_dir, clz_subdir, source

  • * matches any run of characters, including / — unlike a shell glob, /var/log/YaST2/* also covers files in subfolders. ? matches exactly one character

  • Any number of * is fine: a pattern is matched in linear time however many it has, and ** means the same as *
  • Every other character is literal: ., +, - and : have no special meaning
  • A pattern is matched against the source value as it is written in the event’s JSON envelope. Real LogServ source values contain no backslash, quote or non-ASCII character; a value that did would be written escaped there (a backslash as \\, é as \u00e9, a quote as \"), so a ? would not stand for one such character — match a backslash or a non-ASCII character with * instead. A wildcard never crosses a quote; a pattern that ends in * or ? can still match the part of such a value before its first quote
  • Matching is case-sensitive: /var/log/yast2/* does not match /var/log/YaST2/mkinitrd.log
  • A folder entry (dir/subdir=pattern) matches only when the folder part and the source pattern both match. The folder part follows the Include Filters rules, except that a standalone * is not accepted. Events without folder fields never match a folder entry; a plain entry matches them
  • Allowed characters in a source pattern: letters, numbers and / . _ : * ? + @ ~ -. A pattern has at most 512 characters and at least one character that is not *, ? or / — patterns that match everything (*, **, /*, */*) are refused: use the folder filters, or turn filtering off
  • Not allowed: spaces inside an entry, ", \, [, ], a second =, control characters and non-ASCII characters. A comma always separates entries. Spaces around entries are ignored; an empty entry (two commas in a row, or a trailing comma) is refused. The whole field is limited to 4,096 characters
  • A repeated entry is used once

docs.title: Days in the Past
docs.text:
Whole number (0–3650) specifying the maximum age of events to index. Events whose own _time is older than midnight UTC this many days ago are dropped before indexing.

  • Set to 7 to only index events from the last 7 days
  • Set to 0, or leave the field empty, to disable time-based filtering
  • Default: 7
  • It also limits history loads: with filtering on, the AWS S3 Direct screen leaves out every day older than the cutoff, because their events would be dropped on arrival. Raise Days in the Past (or set it to 0) before you load older days.

With a Deployment Server, each heavy forwarder restarts about once a day

While Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0, the daily refresh (below) pushes a new cutoff to the heavy forwarders, and each heavy forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class restarts about once a day to apply it, at a time of day set by when the Deployment Server last started. With filtering disabled, or Days in the Past at 0, the refresh changes nothing and no restart follows. On a single instance, or a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, the refresh reloads the rules in place, without a restart.

How the time filter works

The time filter uses a pre-computed epoch-based regex that is refreshed automatically once per day by a built-in scripted input. If the refresh does not run, the cutoff does not move forward and the filter becomes slightly less restrictive: it keeps up to one extra day of older events for each missed day, until the next refresh or Save. The daily refresh rewrites all the generated filter rules, the source rules included, from the saved settings.

On a Deployment Server the refresh also copies the new rules to deployment-apps/ and reloads the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class (only that class), so the heavy forwarders get the new cutoff at their next phone-home. The cutoff changes every day, and the server class the TA creates maps the TA with restartSplunkd = true, which is why each heavy forwarder restarts to apply it. The refresh runs when splunkd starts and then once a day. After a Data TA version change on the Deployment Server, it first copies the whole new version into deployment-apps/, as a Save would, so the forwarders receive the new version and restart without a Save or Deploy to Forwarders (Later Builds With the Same Version).

docs.title: How the Rules Combine
docs.text:
The Data TA turns the fields into one chain of index-time transforms. Each step that matches an event decides where it goes — kept for indexing or dropped — and the last step that matched wins:

  one NDJSON line (up to 100,000 characters)
    |
    v
  1. Include gate       drop every event                   -+
    |                                                       |  only when Include
    v                                                       |  Filters does not
  2. Include Filters    keep events whose folder matches    |  include everything
    |                                                       |
    v                                                       |
  3. Include Sources    keep events whose source matches   -+
    |
    v
  4. Days in the Past   drop events older than the cutoff
    |
    v
  5. Exclude Filters    drop events whose folder matches
    |
    v
  6. Exclude Sources    drop events whose source matches
    |
    v
  last step that matched: keep -> indexed, drop -> discarded (nullQueue)
  no step matched:        kept

In effect, an event is indexed when all of these hold:

  • Include Filters includes everything, or its folder matches Include Filters, or its source matches Include Sources
  • it is not older than Days in the Past
  • its folder matches no Exclude Filters entry
  • its source matches no Exclude Sources entry

The time filter and both excludes come after the include steps, so they always win. A step whose field is empty is left out of the chain.

docs.title: Include Everything
docs.text:
If any Include Filters entry is */* or a standalone *, there is no include gate: steps 1–3 are left out, every event passes them — events without folder fields included — and the other Include Filters entries have no effect. With Enable Filtering checked, a save that also sets Include Sources is refused; a value that reaches the rules anyway (a hand-edited settings file) is ignored, and the Data TA logs a warning. Days in the Past, Exclude Filters and Exclude Sources still apply.

Upgrading from an earlier build? Some filter behaviour on this page changed between builds; see Upgrading.

docs.title: Events Without Folder Fields
docs.text:
Not every LogServ event carries clz_dir and clz_subdir. SAP files some Azure data in a storage folder named undefined/undefined (<prefix>/undefined/undefined/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/), and its events have neither field. In real Azure deliveries on the reference system that was about 19.9 million events in four weeks, each kind from a single host (Data Delivered Without Folder Fields):

  • the output of Unix commands — about 19.4 million events, with source values such as ps, netstat, iostat, cpu, nfsiostat, top, openPorts, interfaces, df, bandwidth, vmstat and Unix:ListeningPorts. They stay under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype.
  • HANA trace directory files, /usr/sap/<SID>/HDB<nn>/<host>/trace/... (the .trc files and backup.log) — about 566,000 events. The Data TA routes them to sap:hana:tracelogs by their source path (SAP HANA Trace Logs); events indexed by an earlier Data TA build keep sap_logserv_logs.

Routing does not give an event folder fields, so folder patterns cannot see any of these events, the routed HANA trace files included:

  • With Include Filters at */* they are kept.
  • With an allow-list — any Include Filters value that does not include everything — they are all dropped, unless an Include Sources entry keeps them (Recipe 4). Listing hana/tracelogs in Include Filters does not keep the HANA trace files that arrive this way.
  • Exclude Filters never drops them: hana/tracelogs there leaves these HANA trace files in place. Only Exclude Sources can drop them.
  • A folder entry in a source field (dir/subdir=pattern) never matches them; a plain source pattern does.
  • The upgrade notification reasons about folders only, so it does not point to an allow-list that drops these events. The filter verdict of the LogServ App’s Data Doctor for sap:hana:tracelogs does take the HANA trace files that arrive this way into account. Wherever it judges that type, it does not treat their arrival as contradicting an Exclude Filters rule on hana/tracelogs, and it does not call such a rule a full exclusion. On a HANA Trace panel it also names an allow-list that keeps the hana/tracelogs folder but drops these files, as an additional finding listed after the panel’s main verdict (such as Never received or Summary not built), never in its place, because the pasted configuration does not show whether SAP delivers such files to you. A verdict they change is at most possible, because the pasted configuration does not show whether your forwarders route these files by their source path either. The Data Doctor does not judge the Unix command output, which stays under sap_logserv_logs.

Drop the Unix command output if you do not use it. It is almost all of this data — about 0.7 million events and roughly 125 MB of text a day on the reference system, about 80% of it ps — and the LogServ App does not parse it; it only counts it in its volume dashboards. Exclude Sources ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts drops all twelve wherever they arrive. If you keep them, note that a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with — up to 34% of the real ps rows checked on the reference system did — and arguments can contain passwords, keys or tokens.

Before you narrow Include Filters, check what your deliveries carry without folder fields (over a short time range — the search reads raw events):

`sap_logserv_idx_macro` | where isnull(clz_dir) | stats count by source, sourcetype

docs.title: Long Lines
docs.text:
Every rule reads the whole line, up to 100,000 characters — the longest line the Data TA indexes. An index-time transform reads only the first 4,096 characters unless told otherwise, so every filter stanza the Data TA generates sets LOOKAHEAD = 100000. This matters for the AWS envelope, which carries the log text (_raw) before source, clz_dir and clz_subdir: a rule that read only the first 4,096 characters would miss the folder fields of a long line.

The rules expect the envelope’s metadata keys to sit together, all before or all after the _raw value, as in every LogServ delivery seen so far (Azure and GCP put them first, AWS after _raw). An envelope that put _raw between the keys an entry needs would not match that entry: a folder pattern needs clz_dir and clz_subdir, and a dir/subdir= entry also source, on the same side of _raw. A plain source pattern needs only source, so it would still match.

The sourcetype routing and the indexed host, source, clz_dir and clz_subdir fields read the same 100,000 characters as the filters. A line longer than 100,000 characters is cut there (TRUNCATE), so an AWS line that long loses its envelope keys whatever the rules read.

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
Click Save. The TA validates your patterns and generates the necessary configuration files. If there are any validation errors (invalid characters, empty include field, etc.), the save is blocked and an error message is displayed.

Include Sources and Exclude Sources are checked on every save, even with Enable Filtering unchecked, because their values are written to a configuration file either way. For the same reason every field is refused on every save if it contains a line break, a tab or another control character, or ends with a backslash. The folder patterns are checked when Enable Filtering is checked, as before. Validation Error on Save lists the rules.

The rules are generated from the settings as saved. A save through the REST API or the CLI that sends only some of the fields keeps the saved values of the others, so the generated rules always match what the Filters tab shows.

docs.title: Deployment Server: Additional Steps
docs.text: If you are running on a single instance, or on a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, you can skip this section: filter changes take effect immediately after Save. The first-time steps for a Deployment Server are on Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

docs.title: What a Save Does on a Deployment Server
docs.text: A Save does not send anything to the heavy forwarders by itself. A Save on a Deployment Server copies the TA into deployment-apps/ the first time (and again after a version change), stages its generated filter and Cloud Provider rules there on every Save, and creates the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class, disabled, the first time; see Distribute the Data TA → Save the Configuration Page. The daily filter refresh does reload the server class by itself (Days in the Past).

docs.title: Configure the Server Class (First Time Only)
docs.text: The server class needs an agent assignment that names your heavy forwarders (never *); see Distribute the Data TA → Assign the Heavy Forwarders.

docs.title: Deploy to Forwarders
docs.text: The Deploy to Forwarders button pushes the staged configuration; see Distribute the Data TA → Deploy to Forwarders.

docs.title: Updating Filters on a Deployment Server
docs.text:
Whenever you change filter settings:

  1. Make your changes on the Filters tab and click Save.
  2. Click Deploy to Forwarders to distribute the updated configurations. The button reloads every server class on the Deployment Server, not only SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders.
  3. Each heavy forwarder picks up the change at its next phone-home (phoneHomeIntervalInSecs, 60 seconds by default) and then restarts. Allow 5 minutes or more before you check Settings → Forwarder Management.

A change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it. For the first-time setup, see Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.

Note

With a Deployment Server, install the TA on the Deployment Server only. A push replaces each heavy forwarder’s copy of the TA, its local/ folder included, so anything installed or saved directly on a heavy forwarder in the server class is overwritten.

docs.title: Check Included Data Is Arriving
docs.text:
`sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by clz_dir, clz_subdir

You should see data only for log types matching your include patterns.

Index macro

The sap_logserv_idx_macro macro expands to index="sap_logserv_logs" by default. It is defined where the Data TA or the LogServ App is installed; on a search head that has neither yet, use index=sap_logserv_logs instead. If you changed the index name, follow Renaming an index: the macro must be changed in every app on the search head that ships it. Or substitute your index name directly in the search.

docs.title: Check Excluded Data Is Not Present
docs.text:
If you configured exclude patterns, verify those log types are absent from search results.

For source rules, list the source values per folder over a window that starts after the Save (or, on a Deployment Server, after the forwarders received the change) — events indexed earlier stay in the index:

| tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` by clz_dir, clz_subdir, source

The files named in Exclude Sources must be gone, while the other files of the same folder still arrive — for linux/linux_secure, for example, /var/log/firewall, /var/log/kernel, /var/log/sssd/..., lastlog and who. tstats … by clz_dir leaves out events without folder fields; to check those, use the search in Events Without Folder Fields.

docs.title: Check Time Filtering
docs.text:
Search for events older than your configured cutoff:

`sap_logserv_idx_macro` earliest=-30d latest=-10d

If your Days in the Past is less than 10, this search should return no events indexed after the filter took effect.

docs.title: Reading the Active Filter Configuration
docs.text:
Support workflows (and the LogServ App’s Data Doctor) sometimes need the active filter configuration as text. Where to read it:

  • Deployment Server (distributed install), or a single instance: the Data TA’s filter_settings REST endpoint on that instance. It returns filter_enabled, include_filters, exclude_filters, include_sources, exclude_sources and days_in_past as saved.
  • Heavy forwarder that no Deployment Server manages: the same endpoint on that forwarder, whose Filters saves are made on it, or its generated local/transforms.conf.
  • Heavy forwarder that a Deployment Server manages: only its generated $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf.

The exact commands are in Supplying the ingest-filter configuration. The LogServ App’s Platform → Diagnostics page accepts their pasted output and turns the ingest filters into evidence its missing-data diagnosis can reason about.

The HF’s REST endpoint is misleading

On a deployment-server-managed heavy forwarder the filter_settings REST endpoint returns the HF’s copy of local/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_settings.conf on top of the shipped defaults. The Deployment Server copies that file to deployment-apps/ only when it copies the whole TA there: on the first Filters or Cloud Provider save on the Deployment Server, and on the first save or daily filter refresh after a TA version change. Later saves send only local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf. So the endpoint can show an earlier save’s settings, or the shipped defaults, and neither tells you what the HF filters now. The active filter is in the generated local/transforms.conf. Always use the file on an HF that a Deployment Server manages.

Source rules make the Data Doctor’s folder verdicts approximate

A source rule acts on single files, not on whole folders. When a pasted configuration has Include Sources or Exclude Sources in effect, the Data Doctor cannot say for certain whether a folder’s events are kept, and its verdict notes that source rules may drop or keep some files of a folder. Its verdict for sap:hana:tracelogs also accounts for the HANA trace files that arrive without folder fields, which the hana/tracelogs folder rules do not reach: any Include Filters allow-list drops them unless an Include Sources entry without a folder keeps them, and of the exclude rules only Exclude Sources drops them. Where those files change the verdict, it reads Partly excluded? at no more than possible: an Exclude Filters rule on hana/tracelogs leaves them in place wherever the trace type is judged, and on a HANA Trace panel an allow-list that keeps the folder but drops them is listed as an additional finding after the panel’s main verdict, with evidence that explains these files (see Events Without Folder Fields).

The transforms paste also carries the Cloud Provider stamp

A pasted local/transforms.conf includes the generated [logserv_set_cloud_provider] stanza when the Cloud Provider dropdown is set, so the Data Doctor also records the configured stamp and can explain how it interacts with a dashboard’s Cloud filter. A missing stanza is not read as “Not set” — the paste may be truncated; only a settings-conf paste can supply the explicit not_set value.

docs.title: Supported Log Types
docs.text:
The values to use in filter patterns are the clz_dir and clz_subdir values each log type arrives with, and for Include Sources and Exclude Sources its source values. Supported Log Types lists both for every Primary log type (those with dedicated sourcetype routing), and the Secondary log types, which have no dedicated routing but can still be filtered by their own clz_dir/clz_subdir paths, or, where they share a primary type’s folder, by their source values (see Filter Recipes).

Real LogServ deliveries do not all use one folder layout: Azure delivers Squid under linux/proxy (the AWS bucket uses proxy/squid), and GCP delivers pacemaker.log under linux/pacemaker and a proxy VM’s /var/log/messages under linux/proxy. A rule meant to cover a log type on every cloud names all of its paths. SAP discontinued abap/dispatcher, abap/event and abap/workprocess from LogServ delivery in April 2026, so filters on them affect older data only.

Filter pattern examples
  • To include all DNS logs: dns/* or dns/binddns
  • To include all Linux logs except cron: Include linux/*, Exclude linux/cron
  • To exclude Squid on every cloud: Exclude Filters proxy/squid, Exclude Sources linux/proxy=/var/log/squid/*. Excluding the whole linux/proxy folder would also drop the /var/log/messages lines a proxy VM delivers there. Likewise, an Include of linux/* also keeps Azure’s Squid logs
  • To include only HANA audit and web dispatcher logs: hana/hanaaudit, webdispatcher/accesslog
  • To include all Windows event logs: windows/*
  • To include all ABAP application logs: abap/*
  • To include specific ABAP types: abap/icm, abap/gateway
  • To include all SAP Cloud Connector logs: scc/*
  • To include all SAP service logs: sap/*
  • To drop the zypper and YaST2 logs but keep the rest of linux/linux_secure: Exclude Sources /var/log/zypper.log*, /var/log/YaST2/*
  • To drop zypper’s log only where it arrives under linux/linux_secure: Exclude Sources linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log* (Recipe 5)
  • To keep HANA trace files that arrive without folder fields while Include Filters is an allow-list: Include Sources /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/*
  • Do not drop /var/log/messages under sap/saprouter as operating-system syslog: there it carries the SAP Router’s own records (Recipe 5)

docs.title: Filter Recipes
docs.text:
Each recipe below is a Filters-tab setting for one goal; several can be combined. Primary log types are routed to their own sourcetypes; Secondary ones stay under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype (Supported Log Types), so this search lists the unrouted events by folder and file — the ones these recipes are about:

| tstats count where `sap_logserv_idx_macro` sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs by clz_dir, clz_subdir, source

Enable Filtering must be checked for any recipe to take effect. On a Deployment Server, Save and then Deploy to Forwarders; the change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it.

docs.title: Recipe 1: Allow-list of the Primary Log Types
docs.text:
Keep the folders of the Primary log types and drop every other folder.

  • Include Filters: abap/audit, abap/dispatcher, abap/enqueueserver, abap/event, abap/gateway, abap/icm, abap/messageserver, abap/sapstartsrv, abap/workprocess, dns/binddns, hana/hanaaudit, hana/tracelogs, linux/cron, linux/localmessages, linux/messages, linux/linux_secure, linux/pacemaker, linux/proxy, linux/slapd, linux/sudolog, linux/warn, proxy/squid, sap/saphostexec, sap/saprouter, sap/sapstartsrv, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs, webdispatcher/accesslog, windows/*

The ABAP and Web Dispatcher folders are listed one by one because abap/* would also keep the Secondary abap/transport and abap/httpaccess, and webdispatcher/* the Secondary Web Dispatcher traces. abap/dispatcher, abap/event and abap/workprocess stay in the list although SAP discontinued them in April 2026: they keep a backfill of older data, and the Data TA still counts them as supported. Without them, every Save of this list, and every later Data TA upgrade, raises the upgrade notification banner naming the three folders as dropped before indexing; it clears only when they are added.

  • Drops: every folder not named, including the Secondary folders whose names are not known (Network / Flow, WAF / F5, MSSQL) and any folder a future SAP delivery adds. With this list the upgrade notification stays quiet until a Data TA upgrade adds a Primary log type; it then names the folder to add.
  • Also drops: every event without folder fields — Unix command output and HANA trace files on Azure (see Events Without Folder Fields). Add Recipe 4 to keep the ones you want.
  • Still keeps: zypper and YaST2 (they share linux/linux_secure) and corosync (it shares linux/pacemaker). Add Recipe 3.

docs.title: Recipe 2: Deny-list of the Secondary Folders
docs.text:
Keep everything except the Secondary folders that have names of their own.

  • Include Filters: */*
  • Exclude Filters: abap/transport, abap/httpaccess, webdispatcher/process, webdispatcher/icm, webdispatcher/sapstartsrv, webdispatcher/devicm, sybase/*, java/*, bobj_bi/*, bobj_bods/*, bobj_sacagent/*, dpagent/*

The folder names come from the SAP LogServ service description; none of them has appeared in the reference system’s real deliveries. Check the folders your own deliveries use with the search above.

  • Keeps: any folder the list does not name — the Network / Flow, WAF / F5 and MSSQL logs, whose folders are not known, and any folder a future SAP delivery adds. Events without folder fields are kept. With */* the upgrade notification never fires.
  • Still keeps: zypper, YaST2 and corosync. Add Recipe 3.

docs.title: Recipe 3: Drop zypper and YaST2, Keep the Rest of linux/linux_secure
docs.text:
zypper and YaST2 write to linux/linux_secure, the folder of the Primary firewall, kernel, sssd, lastlog and who logs. Exclude them by source:

  • Exclude Sources: /var/log/zypper.log*, /var/log/YaST2/*

/var/log/zypper.log* also covers rotated copies; /var/log/YaST2/* covers every YaST2 file, such as /var/log/YaST2/mkinitrd.log and /var/log/YaST2/config_diff_2026_09_28.log (both seen in real deliveries). To drop them only from that folder, write linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log*, linux/linux_secure=/var/log/YaST2/*.

For corosync in linux/pacemaker, add /var/log/cluster/corosync.log* — that path is the one the SAP LogServ service description names; corosync has not appeared in the reference system’s real deliveries, so check the source value your deliveries carry before relying on it.

Combine with Recipe 1 or Recipe 2. Afterwards, the tstats search in Check Excluded Data Is Not Present must show the other linux/linux_secure files still arriving.

docs.title: Recipe 4: Keep HANA Trace Files with an Allow-list
docs.text:
An Include Filters allow-list drops every event without folder fields, and real Azure deliveries send HANA trace files without them. Keep them by source:

  • Include Filters: your allow-list, for example Recipe 1’s
  • Include Sources: /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/*

The pattern covers /usr/sap/<SID>/HDB<nn>/<host>/trace/ and its subfolders for every SID, instance and host. The Data TA routes the .trc files and backup.log there, and in its DB_<tenant>/ subfolder, to sap:hana:tracelogs; any other file the pattern keeps stays under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype. To keep the Unix command output too, add the source values you want, for example ps, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, top; it stays under sap_logserv_logs. Mind the arguments in ps rows (Events Without Folder Fields).

docs.title: Recipe 5: Limit a Source Rule to One Folder
docs.text:
A plain source pattern acts in every folder, and on events without folder fields. To make it act in one folder only, write the folder and = before it. For example, to drop zypper’s log from linux/linux_secure and nowhere else:

  • Exclude Sources: linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log*

The entry matches only events whose folder is linux/linux_secure and whose source matches /var/log/zypper.log*, so a zypper.log that a delivery files under another folder is kept. A folder entry never matches an event without folder fields.

Under sap/saprouter, /var/log/messages is SAP Router data

On GCP, LogServ files /var/log/messages lines under the sap/saprouter folder, and the Data TA gives them the sap:saprouter sourcetype, so they feed the SAP Router dashboard. On the reference system at least 70% of them, in the one hour measured, were the router’s own connection and trace records, and the rest the router container’s wrapper output and other text; every line had the same tagged syslog form, and the newest lines carry the router container’s tag. An Exclude Sources entry sap/saprouter=/var/log/messages drops router records.

docs.title: How Upgrade Notifications Work
docs.text:
When the TA is upgraded to a new version that supports additional log types, a system message banner appears across all Splunk Web pages if your include filter patterns do not cover the newly supported types. This prevents new log types from being silently dropped.

Example

To resolve the notification:

  1. Open Configuration → Filters in the TA
  2. Review and update your include patterns to cover the new log types (or use */* to include everything)
  3. Save

The banner clears automatically once all supported types are covered.

The same check runs on every Save of the Filters tab with Enable Filtering checked, so an Include Filters list that leaves out a supported folder raises the banner as soon as it is saved, not only after an upgrade.

The check compares the supported folders with Include Filters only. Exclude Filters, Include Sources and Exclude Sources neither raise nor clear the banner, so an exclude that drops a supported log type, or a source rule that drops a primary file, goes unannounced. An Include Filters list with */* or * never raises it. It does not know about events without folder fields either: an allow-list that drops the HANA trace files of Events Without Folder Fields raises no banner, even when it lists hana/tracelogs.

docs.title: Filters Not Taking Effect (Single Instance)
docs.text:
• Verify filtering is enabled: Check the Enable Filtering checkbox
  • Check local/transforms.conf in the app directory for the generated filter stanzas: logserv_filter_include_drop, logserv_filter_include_allow, logserv_filter_include_sources, logserv_filter_time_drop, logserv_filter_exclude and logserv_filter_exclude_sources, each present only when its field is in use, and each ending in LOOKAHEAD = 100000. A long list is split over several stanzas: logserv_filter_exclude, logserv_filter_exclude_2, and so on
  • Check local/props.conf for the TRANSFORMS-00-filter line under [sap_logserv_logs]; it names every generated stanza in the order above
  • A source rule matches the whole source value and is case-sensitive: compare the entry with the values the folder really delivers (see Source Pattern Syntax)
  • Check _internal for errors:
index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=PersistentScript splunk_ta_sap_logserv

docs.title: Daily Refresh Reports an Invalid Setting
docs.text:
The daily refresh regenerates the filter rules from the saved settings (it runs while Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0). If a saved Include Filters, Exclude Filters, Include Sources or Exclude Sources value breaks the rules for that field — for example after a hand edit of local/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_settings.conf — the refresh logs an ERROR and leaves the rules it generated last in place; it never writes a rule built from the invalid value. Find the message with:

index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=ExecProcessor logserv_filter_time_refresh "level=ERROR"

Days in the Past is read the same way the Save reads it, so a value the Save accepted is refreshed: 7.0 counts as 7. A saved value that is not a whole number — such as 7.5, or text from a hand edit — is reported by the same search: an ERROR that names Days in the Past, and the rules generated last stay in place. Until the value is corrected and saved, the time cutoff does not move forward, so the filter keeps more older events each day.

Open Configuration → Filters, correct the field and click Save.

docs.title: Filters Not Reaching Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
• Verify the server class exists and has client targeting configured in Settings → Forwarder Management
  • Verify deployment-apps has the filter configs:
cat /opt/splunk/etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf
  • Click Deploy to Forwarders and wait for the next phone-home (60 seconds by default) and the restart that follows; allow 5 minutes or more
  • If the forwarders still run an older build of the TA, a newer build with the same version number was not copied into deployment-apps/: a Save, or the daily filter refresh, copies the whole TA there only the first time and when the version changes. See Later Builds With the Same Version
  • If only the time cutoff lags behind, check the daily refresh on the Deployment Server: it reloads the server class itself and logs a WARNING when it cannot (the heavy forwarders then keep the previous cutoff until the next Deploy to Forwarders):
index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=ExecProcessor logserv_filter_time_refresh "level=WARNING"
  • Check HF configs:
cat /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/transforms.conf

docs.title: Deployment Server Not Detected
docs.text: The TA recognises a Deployment Server by its server roles (a server class exists) or by deployment clients that phone home to it; until then a Save does no Deployment Server work and no Deploy to Forwarders button appears. Make the heavy forwarders deployment clients first and check that they phone home: see Distribute the Data TA → Make the Heavy Forwarders Deployment Clients. If they do and the button is still missing, check that your role holds edit_deployment_server.

docs.title: Validation Error on Save
docs.text:
• Include patterns must not be empty when filtering is enabled — use */* to include all
  • Patterns must use dir/subdir format with only valid characters (letters, numbers, *, ?, ., -, :, _)
  • Days in the Past must be a whole number between 0 and 3650
  • Include Sources and Exclude Sources (checked on every save, even with filtering disabled):
    • each entry is a source pattern, or dir/subdir= followed by a source pattern
    • a source pattern uses only letters, numbers and / . _ : * ? + @ ~ -, has at most 512 characters, and has at least one character that is not *, ? or / — *, **, /* and */* are refused
    • no spaces inside an entry, no ", \, [, ], control characters or non-ASCII characters, and only one = per entry
    • no empty entries (two commas in a row, or a trailing comma); at most 4,096 characters per field
    • the folder part of a dir/subdir= entry follows the Include Filters rules, without a standalone *
  • With filtering enabled, Include Sources is refused while Include Filters includes everything (*/* or *): its entries would have no effect — see Include Everything
  • A single entry whose generated rule would pass 8,000 characters (a very long pattern with many wildcards) is refused; shorten it
  • On every save, even with filtering disabled, no field may contain a line break, a tab or another control character, or end with a backslash

docs.title: Time Filter Seems Off by a Day
docs.text: The time filter epoch cutoff is refreshed once per day by a scripted input. After changing the Days in the Past value, the cutoff regex is regenerated immediately on Save (on a Deployment Server, the forwarders get it after Deploy to Forwarders). The cutoff is midnight UTC N days ago, so it moves once a day, not continuously. If the daily refresh does not run, or skips because it cannot read the saved settings (see Daily Refresh Reports an Invalid Setting), the cutoff stays where it was and the filter becomes slightly less restrictive: it keeps up to one extra day of older events for each missed day, until the next refresh or Save.

docs.title: Cloud Provider Attribution
docs.text: The Cloud Provider tab of the Configuration page, the always-on splunk_solution stamp and the per-input cloud_provider stamps are described on Choose Cloud Attribution. In short: leave the dropdown at Not set and add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each AWS SQS-Based S3 input; the Azure and GCP inputs and the AWS S3 Direct backfills stamp their own events.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Lambda-based filtering approach filters S3 event notifications in AWS before they reach Splunk. A Lambda function sits between the cross-account SQS queue (in the SAP ECS account) and a local SQS queue (in your Secondary account). For each notification it downloads the object from SAP’s bucket, checks the object’s records against include/exclude folder patterns and a time cutoff, and forwards only the notifications of objects with at least one wanted record to the local queue that Splunk polls. It is a separate filter from the Filters tab, with settings of its own, and it behaves differently in several ways described below.

When to use Lambda-based filtering
  • You want to reduce what the heavy forwarder downloads and parses (the Lambda reads every object first, so the total number of S3 GET requests does not fall)
  • You want to reduce the SQS messages the heavy forwarder processes
  • You want filtering to happen at the AWS pipeline level as an additional layer

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
SAP ECS Account                      Your Secondary Account
+--------------+    +-----------+    +------------+    +-----------+
| S3 Bucket    |--->| SQS Queue |--->|   Lambda   |--->| Local SQS |---> Splunk HF
| (LogServ)    |    | (SAP's)   |    |  (filter)  |    |  Queue    |        |
+--------------+    +-----------+    +------------+    +-----------+        |
    ^    ^                             |    |                               |
    |    |   GetObject: every object   |    | drops a notification when no  |
    |    +-----------------------------+    v record passes, or on an error |
    |                                                                       |
    +------------- GetObject: only the objects the Lambda passed ----------+

For each notification, the Lambda takes its first S3 record, downloads the object from the SAP ECS bucket (decompressing it if it is gzipped) and reads _time, clz_dir and clz_subdir from each NDJSON record. It forwards the notification, unchanged, as soon as one record passes all three checks:

  • the record’s _time is not older than now minus DAYS_IN_THE_PAST days;
  • its clz_dir/clz_subdir matches an INCLUDE_FILTERS pattern;
  • it matches no EXCLUDE_FILTERS pattern.

If no record passes, it drops the notification. An object that passes is ingested whole: Splunk downloads it and indexes all of its records, older or excluded ones included, unless the Filters tab also drops them. That is why using both together is the safe combination.

The Lambda does not retry: a notification it cannot process is lost

When the Lambda cannot read an object from the SAP ECS bucket (for example because SAP’s bucket policy is not in place yet), or cannot send the notification to your local queue, it logs the error and reports the message as processed, so SAP’s notification is deleted and that object is not ingested. Only an invalid Lambda configuration (a missing or invalid environment variable) returns messages to SAP’s queue, even with Report batch item failures turned on, and the dead-letter queue the template creates guards your local queue, not SAP’s.

  • Before you activate the Lambda’s trigger on SAP’s queue, wait until SAP confirms that both access policies (S3 and SQS) are in place, and allow about 5 minutes after the stack is created for IAM changes to apply.
  • To find losses, search the Lambda’s CloudWatch logs for Could not retrieve S3 object, discarding message and Failed to forward message to target SQS, discarding.
  • To recover, fix the cause, then load the days the errors cover from the SAP ECS bucket with AWS S3 Direct; the objects stay in SAP’s bucket.

docs.title: Setup Options
docs.text: There are two ways to deploy Lambda-based filtering:

docs.title: New Deployment (S3 Filter Setup)
docs.text: If you are setting up from scratch, follow the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide. The CloudFormation template creates the Lambda, the local SQS queue, its dead-letter queue and the IAM resources. You create the bucket for the Lambda code first (its name is yours and must be unique, in the stack’s Region) and the access key yourself. You create the Lambda’s SQS trigger only after SAP confirms both access policies. See the guide’s steps 2, 5 and 9.

docs.title: Migration from Existing S3 Connect Deployment
docs.text: If you already have a working S3 Connect deployment and want to add Lambda-based filtering, follow Legacy: AWS S3 Connect to Filter Migration (a legacy guide kept outside the site navigation). The Python migration script adds the Lambda resources to your existing IAM infrastructure without recreating it. For most deployments the native index-time filtering above is the simpler path.

docs.title: Lambda Filter Settings
docs.text:
The Lambda function uses three environment variables for its filter configuration (the Filter template’s parameters DaysInThePast, IncludeFilters and ExcludeFilters):

Variable Description Example DAYS_IN_THE_PAST Forward a notification only if at least one of the object’s records has a _time within this many days: a rolling cutoff, now minus N × 24 hours, recomputed on each run. (The Filters tab uses midnight UTC minus N days, so with the same N the Lambda keeps up to a day less.) 1 to 365 in the CloudFormation template; there is no “0 = off”. 7 INCLUDE_FILTERS Comma-separated fnmatch patterns on clz_dir/clz_subdir; a record must match one of them. An empty value drops every notification: use */* (the template’s default) to include everything. (On the Filters tab an empty Include Filters cannot be saved.) linux/*,hana/* EXCLUDE_FILTERS Comma-separated fnmatch patterns on clz_dir/clz_subdir to exclude. Empty excludes nothing. linux/cron,linux/slapd

If you use both approaches, write the Lambda’s patterns only in the form the Filters tab accepts (dir/subdir or a standalone *, with letters, numbers and * ? . - : _), so both match the same records. The Lambda’s fnmatch accepts more, and differs: [...] character sets work, * also matches across / (linux* matches linux/cron), and a bare * in EXCLUDE_FILTERS drops everything, whereas on the Filters tab it excludes nothing. A record without _time never passes. The Lambda reads only _time, clz_dir and clz_subdir from each record, not its source, so Include Sources and Exclude Sources have no Lambda equivalent: file-level rules apply only on the Filters tab.

docs.title: Comparing the Two Approaches Side by Side
docs.text:
Consider a scenario where you want to ingest only hana/* and linux/messages logs from the last 7 days:

Native TA filtering only (simplest)
  • Setup: Configure the Filters tab with include hana/*, linux/messages and Days in the Past 7
  • What happens: All S3 objects are downloaded by Splunk, but unwanted events are dropped at index time via TRANSFORMS before consuming license
  • Pros: No extra AWS resources, managed from Splunk Web, upgrade notifications, works with any deployment scenario
  • Cons: Splunk still downloads and parses all S3 objects before filtering
Lambda filtering only
  • Setup: Configure Lambda with the same include/exclude/days patterns
  • What happens: The Lambda downloads each object and drops the notifications of objects with no wanted record before Splunk sees them. Splunk downloads only the objects the Lambda passed, and indexes each of them whole
  • Pros: Lower forwarder download, CPU and ingestion overhead
  • Cons: Requires Lambda + local SQS + DLQ in AWS; the Lambda reads every object, so total S3 GETs rise (Lambda + Splunk), plus Lambda and SQS charges; a passed object’s unwanted records are indexed too; a notification the Lambda cannot process is lost; no upgrade notifications; filter changes require updating the Lambda’s environment variables
Both together (defense-in-depth)
  • Setup: Same patterns configured in both Lambda and the Filters tab
  • What happens: Lambda filters at the AWS level first, then native TA filtering drops the unwanted records of the objects the Lambda passed
  • Pros: Maximum coverage, safety net if either filter is misconfigured
  • Cons: Two places to maintain filter configurations

docs.text:
• Setting up for the first time: Decide Filtering, then Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders.
  • Connecting your cloud: Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario.
  • Something not working: Troubleshooting and the Troubleshooting section above.
  • Technical internals: Data TA Internals.

docs.title: Decide Filtering
docs.text:
This page helps you decide whether the Data TA should filter LogServ data, and with which values, before you distribute it. It is a decision page: Configuring Filters is the reference for every field and rule.

Decide before the first Save on the Deployment Server’s Configuration page, and at the latest before any input starts. The Data TA’s filters run at index time, on the heavy forwarders or the single instance: anything indexed before you decide stays as it was indexed. With a Deployment Server, the first push carries your choice to the forwarders, and each forwarder restarts once when the Data TA arrives.

Write your values down as you go (Your Values at the end), then enter them on Configuration → Filters in the next step.

docs.title: 1. Turn Filtering On, or Leave It Off
docs.text:
Enable Filtering is off by default: every LogServ event is indexed, and the other fields on the Filters tab have no effect until you check it.

  • Leave it off if you want all the data SAP delivers, or want to decide later for new data only.
  • Turn it on to drop folders, files or old events before they are indexed. Dropped events use no license and no index space; the forwarder still downloads and parses them (Configuring Filters).

With a Deployment Server, filtering on means a restart a day

While Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily refresh moves the time cutoff, the Deployment Server pushes the new rules, and each heavy forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day to apply them. With Days in the Past at 0 the refresh changes nothing and no daily restart follows, so you can filter by folder or file without it. See Days in the Past.

docs.title: 2. Days in the Past
docs.text:
Days in the Past drops events whose own _time is older than midnight UTC that many days ago. It applies only while Enable Filtering is checked.

  • Default 7. Set 0 (or leave the field empty) to keep events of any age. The range is 0 to 3650.
  • The first-start backlog. A new input can start with days or weeks of notifications waiting in SAP’s queue (First Start: The Queue Backlog). Days in the Past drops the older events of that backlog at index time; the forwarder still downloads and parses them, so it does not make the catch-up shorter.
  • Loading history later. On AWS, history is loaded with AWS S3 Direct. With filtering on, that screen leaves out every day older than the cutoff, because their events would be dropped on arrival. Before a history load, raise Days in the Past to cover the oldest day you will load, or set it to 0.

docs.title: 3. Azure: the Unix Command Output
docs.text:
On Azure, SAP files some data in a storage folder named undefined/undefined, and its events carry no clz_dir or clz_subdir. Almost all of it is the output of Unix commands (source values such as ps, netstat, iostat, top): about 0.7 million events and 125 MB of text a day on the reference system, about 80% of it ps. It stays under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype, and the LogServ App does not parse it; it only counts it in its volume dashboards. See Data Delivered Without Folder Fields.

  • To drop it, which we recommend unless you use it: turn filtering on and set Exclude Sources to ps, top, netstat, iostat, vmstat, df, cpu, interfaces, bandwidth, openPorts, nfsiostat, Unix:ListeningPorts. Folder patterns cannot reach these events, so Exclude Filters cannot drop them. If you turn filtering on only for this, also set Days in the Past to 0: with the default 7, older events are dropped too and, with a Deployment Server, each forwarder restarts about once a day (see 1 and 2).
  • If you keep it, restrict who can search it: a ps row can carry the arguments a process was started with, and arguments can contain passwords, keys or tokens.
  • An Include Filters allow-list drops it too, together with the HANA trace files that arrive in the same folder without folder fields, unless an Include Sources entry keeps them (Events Without Folder Fields).

docs.title: 4. Which Folders and Files to Keep
docs.text: With Include Filters at */* (the default) every folder is kept, and you drop what you do not want with Exclude Filters (folders) and Exclude Sources (files). With an allow-list in Include Filters, only the folders you list are kept. Filter Recipes has ready-made settings for both, and How the Rules Combine gives the order the rules run in.

docs.title: 5. AWS Remote S3 Filter: the Lambda Is a Separate Filter
docs.text: If you use the AWS Remote S3 Filter scenario, its Lambda filters notifications in AWS before the forwarder sees them, with settings of its own that you enter in the CloudFormation template. It is not the Filters tab and behaves differently: it reads every object, its time cutoff is a rolling now minus N days, * in its patterns also matches across /, an empty include list drops everything, and it drops notifications it cannot process. See AWS Lambda-Based Filtering and the AWS Remote S3 Filter Setup Guide.

docs.title: Your Values
docs.text:
Field on Configuration → Filters Default Your value Enable Filtering unchecked Include Filters */* Exclude Filters empty Include Sources empty Exclude Sources empty (on Azure, consider the twelve Unix command names above) Days in the Past 7 (applies only with filtering on)

You can change them later; a change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it (Updating Filters on a Deployment Server).

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. First Start: The Queue Backlog: decide how to handle the notifications already waiting in SAP’s queue. Your choice can change Days in the Past.
  2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders: enter these values there in step 2. On a single instance, or a heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, enter them on Configuration → Filters and click Save.
  3. Then Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario to connect your cloud.

docs.title: Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders
docs.text: When a Deployment Server manages your heavy forwarders, the Data TA reaches them only after the one-time steps on this page: nothing is distributed automatically when you install it. Use this page after you have installed the Data TA on the Deployment Server and made the two index-time decisions. Without a Deployment Server, see Without a Deployment Server at the end.

docs.title: 0. Before the First Save
docs.text:
The first push carries your Configuration values to every forwarder, and each forwarder restarts when the Data TA arrives. Have these ready:

  • The filter values (Decide Filtering), including, for Azure, whether to drop the Unix command output with Exclude Sources.
  • The Cloud Provider value (Choose Cloud Attribution): normally Not set.
  • What to do about the first-start backlog (First Start: The Queue Backlog): ask SAP to purge it (on AWS you can load the purged days later with AWS S3 Direct; on Azure and GCP nothing in this solution can load them), or filter it.

docs.title: 1. Make the Heavy Forwarders Deployment Clients
docs.text:
On each heavy forwarder that will run a LogServ input, point it at the Deployment Server and restart it:

$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk set deploy-poll <deployment-server>:8089
$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk restart

Or put the same in $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/deploymentclient.conf:

[deployment-client]

[target-broker:deploymentServer]
targetUri = <deployment-server>:8089

Then check on the Deployment Server, in Settings → Forwarder Management (named Agent Management in newer Splunk Enterprise versions), that each forwarder is listed. Do this first: the Data TA recognises a Deployment Server by a server class it already has or by forwarders that phone home to it, and a Save on an instance it does not recognise as one does none of the steps below. To check from the Deployment Server’s command line:

curl -sk -u <admin_user> \
  "https://localhost:8089/services/deployment/server/clients?output_mode=json&count=1"

An empty entry list means no forwarder has phoned home yet.

Keep the Splunk Add-on for AWS and the LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons out of the LogServ server class: they are installed on each forwarder directly, and a push replaces an app’s local/ folder, where their credentials and inputs live.

docs.title: 2. Save the Configuration Page on the Deployment Server
docs.text:
On the Deployment Server, open the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ app, go to Configuration, enter your values on the Filters tab (or leave Enable Filtering unchecked) and click Save. Save the Cloud Provider tab too if you set it to anything other than Not set. Save even if you do not want filtering: the first Save is what prepares the distribution.

On a Deployment Server, a Save on either tab:

  1. Copies the whole Data TA from etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ to etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/, its local/ folder included, if that copy does not exist yet or its version ([launcher] version in default/app.conf) differs. Otherwise it copies nothing; see Later Builds With the Same Version.
  2. Creates the server class SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders, if it does not exist: disabled, with no forwarders assigned, and with the Data TA mapped to it with restartSplunkd = true, so each forwarder restarts when it receives the app.
  3. Copies the generated local/transforms.conf and local/props.conf (the filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp) into the deployment-apps copy.

After the Save, the Filters tab shows a Deployment Server Detected banner, a Server Class Setup Required notice while the server class is disabled (or Client Targeting Needed if the class is enabled but has no forwarders assigned) and a Deploy to Forwarders button.

Example

The button, and the check that decides whether to show it, need the edit_deployment_server capability. Splunk Enterprise’s admin role has it; a custom Deployment Server operator role needs it added, or the button does not appear.

docs.title: 3. Assign the Heavy Forwarders to the Server Class
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Forwarder Management (or Agent Management), Groups / Server Classes.
  2. Find the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class.
  3. Click the three-dot menu → Edit agent assignment.
  4. Under Include, enter your heavy forwarders’ IP addresses or host names, separated by commas. Click Preview and check that exactly your LogServ forwarders match.
  5. Click Save.

Never use * here

* assigns the class to every deployment client of this Deployment Server, search heads and unrelated forwarders included. Each of them would receive the Data TA and restart (restartSplunkd = true). Name the heavy forwarders.

Example

Client Targeting

Splunk matches each entry against the forwarder’s IP address, host name, DNS name, client name or GUID (instance ID), not against the Instance Name column. IP addresses are the simplest to get right.

In the lab, saving the assignment also enabled the server class. Return to the Filters tab and refresh the page: the setup notice should be gone. If it still says the class is disabled, enable the class in Forwarder Management. If it shows Client Targeting Needed, the class has no agent assignment yet: repeat this step.

Example

docs.title: 4. Deploy to Forwarders
docs.text:
1. On the Filters tab, click Deploy to Forwarders and confirm. The banner confirms that the deployment reload has started.

    Example

  2. Each forwarder picks up the Data TA at its next phone-home (phoneHomeIntervalInSecs in deploymentclient.conf, 60 seconds by default) and then restarts.

  3. Check Settings → Forwarder Management: the forwarders should show Ok under the server class. Allow 5 minutes or more for the status to change from Pending to Ok.
Example

Deploy to Forwarders reloads the whole Deployment Server

The button reloads every server class on this Deployment Server, not only SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders: if another server class has changes waiting, its clients receive them at their next phone-home too. (Saving an edit in Forwarder Management also reloads the Deployment Server, so the forwarders may start receiving the Data TA as soon as you save the assignment in step 3.) The Data TA’s own daily filter refresh reloads only its own server class.

docs.title: 5. Check the Build on Each Heavy Forwarder
docs.text:
On each heavy forwarder, check that it runs the Data TA build you installed on the Deployment Server: see Version Check. Create no input before every forwarder shows the build. Events a forwarder indexes before it has the Data TA keep the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype and are neither routed nor filtered, permanently.

To see which filter a forwarder applies, read its local/transforms.conf, not its filter_settings REST endpoint, which can show older settings (Reading the Active Filter Configuration).

docs.title: Later Builds With the Same Version
docs.text:
The Save copies the whole Data TA into deployment-apps/ only the first time and when the version changes. Every 0.1.2 build has the version 0.1.2, so a newer 0.1.2 build that you install in etc/apps/ on the Deployment Server is not copied, and the forwarders keep the older build. Install the new build into etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/ as well, keeping its local/ folder, then click Deploy to Forwarders. The commands are in Upgrading to This Release → Updating the Data TA.

While Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily filter refresh makes the same version-change copy (it also runs when splunkd starts) and then reloads the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. After a version upgrade on the Deployment Server, the forwarders can therefore receive the new version and restart without a Save or Deploy to Forwarders. Plan the upgrade for that.

A copy made because the version changed, by a Save or by the daily filter refresh, replaces the whole deployment-apps copy, including anything you added by hand under etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/. Keep hand edits in etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/ too.

docs.title: Changing Settings Later
docs.text:
Change the Filters or Cloud Provider tab on the Deployment Server, click Save, then Deploy to Forwarders: see Updating Filters on a Deployment Server. A change applies to events parsed after the forwarders receive it.

While filtering is on and Days in the Past is above 0, the Data TA’s daily refresh pushes a new time cutoff by itself, and each forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day (Days in the Past).

docs.title: Without a Deployment Server
docs.text:
A Deployment Server is optional, Splunk Cloud included: Splunk Cloud is never a Deployment Server (the Deploy to Forwarders button never appears there), and your Splunk Cloud subscription includes a deployment server license for one you run yourself (you request it from Splunk Support).

Without one:

  1. Install the Data TA directly on each heavy forwarder that runs a LogServ input (Install the Data TA).
  2. On each forwarder, enter your values on Configuration → Filters (and Cloud Provider, if you set it) and click Save. The Save writes the rules on that forwarder and applies them at once, with no restart; no Deploy to Forwarders button appears.
  3. With several forwarders, enter the same values on each one: nothing copies them between forwarders.
  4. Check the build on each forwarder (Version Check).

Do not install the Data TA directly on a forwarder that a Deployment Server also pushes it to: the push replaces the forwarder’s copy, its local/ settings included. A forwarder that a Deployment Server manages for other apps only can hold the Data TA directly; see Heavy Forwarder without a Deployment Server for how its daily refresh behaves.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario, then follow the setup guide for your cloud to create the inputs.
  2. Verify Your Data once events arrive.

docs.title: SAP LogServ on GCP — Setup Guide
docs.text:
This page covers ingesting LogServ data from Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using the standalone LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP) and its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub modular input — the GCP twin of Splunk_TA_aws’s SQS-Based S3 input and of the LogServ Azure add-on’s Storage-Queue input. A GCS bucket notification publishes an OBJECT_FINALIZE message to a Pub/Sub topic; this input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription on that topic, fetches each named object with a Google service-account key, gunzips it, and emits its NDJSON. This is the model SAP’s own LogServ-on-GCP collector uses (Pub/Sub object-creation notifications). You install this small, first-party add-on on the heavy forwarder that runs the input — the same deployment model as the Splunk Add-on for AWS and the LogServ Azure add-on — and the LogServ Data TA on the same instance provides the downstream sourcetype routing, filtering, and stamping. The downstream pipeline (sourcetype routing, filtering, dashboards, ES integration) is identical to the AWS S3 and Azure Blob paths.

SAP provides the GCP infrastructure — you provide the service account that reads it

In a RISE / SAP ECS deployment the GCS bucket, bucket notification, Pub/Sub topic, and Pub/Sub subscription are all provisioned and managed by SAP in the SAP-managed GCP project. You do not build any of that. What you do provide is the identity the Splunk input runs as: a service account you create in a GCP project of your own (any project your organization controls, separate from the SAP-managed RISE project). You hand the service account’s email address to your SAP support contact, SAP grants it read access to the LogServ bucket + Pub/Sub subscription, and you mint its JSON key for the Splunk input — see The onboarding sequence. On the Splunk side your tasks are to install the splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp add-on on the heavy forwarder that will run the input and create one Splunk input per Pub/Sub subscription on it — one per GCP landscape (most deployments have a single landscape, hence one input; you can define several on the same HF if you ingest from more than one — see Multiple landscapes / fleets), using the values from Parameters for the input.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Follow these steps in order. Each step links to its section below.

  1. Create the service account and get SAP’s grants: create it in your own GCP project, give its email to SAP, and get back the project ID and subscription name. Enable the two Google APIs and mint the JSON key (check your organization’s key policy first). See The onboarding sequence.
  2. Decide about the subscription backlog with SAP before the input exists. A purged day cannot be loaded later. See First Start: The Queue Backlog and Historical backfill.
  3. Check the Data TA and the indexes. The Data TA must be on the instance that will run the input, and the indexes must exist, before the input reads anything: events indexed without the Data TA keep the base sourcetype for good. See Prerequisites.
  4. Download and install the add-on on that instance, directly (never through the Deployment Server). See Install the GCP add-on.
  5. Before the input starts, check the Data TA’s two index-time settings. Leave Cloud Provider at Not set: the input stamps cloud_provider=gcp itself (see cloud_provider attribution and Choose Cloud Attribution). Decide filtering (see Decide Filtering). Whatever the subscription holds when the input starts is indexed with the settings in place at that moment.
  6. Create one input for the subscription, with a role that holds admin_all_objects. See Configure the input.
  7. Check that data arrives. See Validation.
  8. Plan the key rotation your security policy requires. See Rotate credentials.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
SAP LogServ RISE-ECS  (SAP-managed GCP project)
  |
  +-> writes NDJSON.gz objects to Google Cloud Storage under the logserv/ prefix
        |
        +-> GCS bucket notification (OBJECT_FINALIZE)
              |
              +-> Pub/Sub topic --> Pub/Sub PULL subscription (one message per new object)
                    |
                    |    [Customer GCP account]  service account created by YOU;
                    |    SAP grants it read access to the LogServ bucket + subscription;
                    |    its JSON key authenticates the Splunk input below
                    |
                    +-> [GCP add-on: sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub]  (runs on the Heavy Forwarder)
                          |   pulls the subscription, fetches each object with the
                          |   service-account credential, gunzips, splits NDJSON
                          |
                          +-> emits via EventWriter, sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, cloud_provider=gcp
                                |
                                +-> [LogServ Data TA pipeline]  (same Heavy Forwarder):
                                      sourcetype routing by clz_dir/clz_subdir or source path,
                                      Configuration -> Filters nullQueue, _time drop,
                                      splunk_solution stamping
                                      |
                                      +-> forwarded to the Indexer
                                            |
                                            +-> dashboards + ES integration

Everything from the LogServ object writer down through the Pub/Sub subscription lives in the SAP-managed GCP project and is managed by SAP. The one piece homed on your side of GCP is the service account: it lives in a GCP project you manage (the Customer GCP account box in the diagram), SAP grants it cross-project read access to the LogServ subscription + bucket, and its JSON key is what the Splunk input authenticates with — the GCP analogue of the AWS path’s customer-account cross-account IAM role. The GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input runs on your heavy forwarder, pulls the subscription SAP exposes to you, and hands its events to the LogServ Data TA (also on that HF) for routing/filtering/stamping. This is exactly how Splunk_TA_aws and the LogServ Azure add-on cooperate with the Data TA on their respective paths.

Why EventWriter, not HEC: the input runs on the heavy forwarder and emits through the HF’s native index-time pipeline, so every existing LogServ Data TA feature — sourcetype routing (by the clz_dir / clz_subdir folder fields or by the source path, depending on the log type; see Supported Log Types), the Configuration → Filters nullQueue filtering, the days_in_past / _time drop, and the splunk_solution stamping — applies to GCP events unchanged, exactly as it does to AWS S3 and Azure Blob events. The cloud_provider value comes from the add-on itself (see cloud_provider attribution). The input is stdlib-only (Pub/Sub + GCS REST over urllib, with a pure-Python OAuth2 service-account token exchange — no Google SDK), so it adds no AArch64 / native-binary burden and is Splunk Cloud-clean.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Provided by SAP (in the SAP-managed GCP project — you obtain the values, you do not build the resources):

  • A GCS bucket holding the LogServ objects (under the logserv/ prefix — same path convention as AWS S3 and Azure Blob: <bucket>/logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/<file>.json.gz).
  • A bucket notification publishing OBJECT_FINALIZE events to a Pub/Sub topic, and a PULL subscription on that topic dedicated to your Splunk consumer (recommended: ack deadline 300 s+ and a dead-letter policy).
  • The cross-project IAM grants on those resources for the service account you provide (see below).

Obtain the GCP project ID and the subscription name from your SAP support contact — see Parameters for the input.

Provided by you in GCP (the service account — see The onboarding sequence):

  • A GCP project of your own: any project your organization controls, separate from the SAP-managed RISE project (the Customer GCP account in the diagram, and the GCP counterpart of the Secondary account in the AWS guides). No infrastructure is deployed in it — it is only the administrative home of the identity.
  • A service account created in that project. You hand its email address to your SAP support contact, and SAP grants it roles/pubsub.subscriber on the LogServ subscription and roles/storage.objectViewer on the LogServ bucket (see What SAP must grant your service account).
  • A JSON key for that service account, minted by your GCP admin (check the org-policy warning in The onboarding sequence before install day).
  • The Cloud Pub/Sub API and Cloud Storage API enabled in the service account’s home project (Google attributes API quota to the credential’s home project, not to the project holding the resources).

On your Splunk side (the instance that runs the input — a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended):

  • LogServ Data TA 0.1.1+ installed on that instance (it provides the index-time routing/filtering/stamping; see Installing the Data TA). On heavy forwarders the Data TA is normally distributed by the Deployment Server (see Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders). Its build decides the parsing cost on the forwarder: use build 1792189743 or later, and see Version Check to read the build on a forwarder.
  • The indexes (sap_logserv_logs, and the AI Assistant audit index) on your indexer tier, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
  • LogServ GCP add-on (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp) 0.1.1+ installed on the same instance (see Install the GCP add-on). It registers the sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input kind. The input is inert until you create an input instance.
  • A Splunk role that holds the admin_all_objects capability on that instance, to create, edit or delete the input (see Configure the input).
  • Network egress from that instance to oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com, and storage.googleapis.com (port 443 / HTTPS). The add-on has no proxy setting of its own; if the instance reaches the internet through a proxy, see Outbound proxy under Heavy Forwarders.

Compact JSON format required

Each object is gzipped NDJSON (one event per line). The index-time routing transforms assume compact JSON (no whitespace after :). The SAP LogServ collector emits compact JSON natively, so no action is required on your side. (For reference: pretty-printed JSON would bypass the transforms and land as sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs, breaking dashboards.)

docs.title: Parameters for the input
docs.text:
SAP has already provisioned the bucket, notification, topic, and subscription in the SAP-managed GCP project — the only GCP resource you create is the service account (The onboarding sequence). Contact your SAP support contact to obtain the two SAP-side values, then plug them — plus your own service-account key — into the Splunk input (Configure the input):

Parameter Input field Provided by Description GCP project ID project_id SAP The GCP project that hosts the LogServ Pub/Sub subscription (SAP’s LogServ project — e.g. the LOGSERV_PROJECT_ID value SAP’s own forwarder documentation references). 6–30 chars: lowercase letters, digits, hyphens; starts with a letter, ends with a letter or digit. Subscription name subscription_name SAP The Pub/Sub PULL subscription receiving the bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications. Must be dedicated to your Splunk consumer (competing consumers split messages). Service-account key service_account_key You The full Google service-account JSON key file contents, minted from the service account you created in your own GCP project (after SAP confirms the grants). Treat it as a secret.

The bucket name and logserv/ prefix are carried inside each notification message — they are not separate input fields. The three Google endpoints your heavy forwarder must reach are fixed (oauth2.googleapis.com, pubsub.googleapis.com, storage.googleapis.com).

Ask SAP also for the subscription’s ack deadline (300 s or more is recommended); the input’s batch_size must fit inside it (see Scaling one subscription across inputs below).

docs.title: The onboarding sequence
docs.text:
The service account is customer-homed: it lives in a GCP project you control (the Customer GCP account in the architecture diagram), and SAP binds cross-project grants on the SAP-managed LogServ resources to it. Nothing is deployed in your project — it is only the administrative home of the identity. The sequence:

  1. Create the service account in a GCP project your organization controls: IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Create service account. A descriptive name such as splunk-logserv-ingest helps everyone’s audit trail. The account needs no roles in your own project.
  2. Hand the service account’s email address (<name>@<your-project-id>.iam.gserviceaccount.com) to your SAP support contact and request LogServ consumer access for it.
  3. SAP grants the account roles/pubsub.subscriber on the LogServ subscription and roles/storage.objectViewer on the LogServ bucket (cross-project IAM bindings on the SAP-managed resources — see What SAP must grant your service account), and returns the project ID and subscription name values for the input.
  4. Enable the Cloud Pub/Sub API and the Cloud Storage API in the service account’s home project (APIs & Services → Enable APIs and services). Google attributes API quota to the credential’s home project, so a missing enablement fails the first connection with 403 SERVICE_DISABLED naming your project (see Troubleshooting).
