  5. Mint the JSON key: IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → (the account) → Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON, and stage the downloaded file for the input configuration. (Read the org-policy warning below first.)
  6. Configure the input on the heavy forwarder that will run it (Configure the input) once SAP confirms the grants are in place.

Organization policy can block key creation entirely

Many enterprises enforce the iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation organization policy as a security guardrail. If it applies to the service account’s home project, minting a JSON key fails regardless of IAM roles — your admin needs roles/iam.serviceAccountKeyAdmin on the account and a policy exemption for it. Check this before install day; it is the most common last-minute blocker.

docs.title: What SAP must grant your service account
docs.text:
The input pulls/acks subscription messages and fetches objects with the single service account you provide, so SAP must bind both grants to its email. Confirm with your SAP support contact that your account holds:

IAM role Scope For roles/pubsub.subscriber the LogServ subscription pull + acknowledge notification messages roles/storage.objectViewer the LogServ bucket fetch the referenced objects

These two roles are the complete runtime set — the input makes exactly four Google API calls (OAuth token mint, subscriptions:pull, subscriptions:acknowledge, and the object download), all covered by the grants above. They are the same two roles SAP documents for its own sap-ecs-gcp-log-forwarder consumer. Unlike the general-purpose Splunk Add-on for GCP, this input needs no extra roles/pubsub.viewer grant (that add-on calls GetSubscription; this input never does) — don’t ask SAP to over-grant.

If the grant is subscription-only

If your service account lacks roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket, object fetches fail with HTTP 403 and the input logs it explicitly: “object read forbidden … the service account likely lacks storage.objectViewer on the bucket; leaving message for retry.” The decisive question for your SAP support contact is “has my service account been granted read on the bucket’s objects, or only the subscription?” If it is subscription-only, ask SAP to add the bucket-read grant (a second credential is not supported — the input uses one account for both).

docs.title: Install the GCP add-on
docs.text:
Download splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz from the release_binaries folder of the Splunk for SAP LogServ GitHub repository. Its AppInspect report sits beside it, and the folder’s README.md lists each tarball’s md5. The build and md5 of each package are also listed under Download the Packages.

Install it directly on the instance that runs the input. A heavy forwarder is strongly recommended — it is the tier where Splunk_TA_aws (AWS) and the LogServ Azure add-on (Azure) run for their paths. A search head is not blocked (see Running the TAs on a search head). You can install the add-on on every heavy forwarder that may run an input, for example to keep a standby ready; the input for a given subscription still runs on one of them (see Configure the input).

  • Splunk Web → Manage Apps → Install app from file → upload the tarball, or
  • /opt/splunk/bin/splunk install app /path/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz, or
  • configuration management (Ansible / Puppet / Chef) drops the app into etc/apps/, then chown -R splunk:splunk and restart.

Do NOT distribute the GCP add-on via the Deployment Server

Install it directly on each instance that runs an input — never as a deployment-app. The input’s service-account key is stored, encrypted, in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf; a Deployment Server push replaces the app’s local/ directory, which would wipe the per-HF credential. (This is the same reason Splunk_TA_aws and the LogServ Azure add-on are configured per-HF rather than DS-distributed.) The Data TA stays DS-managed as before — only the cloud-ingest add-ons are per-HF.

After installing + restarting, the sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input kind is registered and the add-on’s Inputs page is available under Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP.

Upgrading from an earlier build? See Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Single instance
docs.text: On a single Splunk Enterprise instance (no separate forwarder or indexer), install the Data TA and the GCP add-on on that instance and create the input there, as described below. The Data TA’s bundled indexes.conf creates both indexes on that instance; set the retention of sap_logserv_logs if you want one other than the default (see Create the indexes). There is no Deployment Server step: the Data TA’s settings are saved on the instance itself. The LogServ App goes on the same instance.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud
docs.text:
With Splunk Cloud, run the input on a heavy forwarder you manage:

  1. Create both indexes in your Splunk Cloud stack first (Settings → Indexes, or the Admin Config Service), with the retention you want, before any data arrives. See Create the indexes.
  2. Set the heavy forwarder up to forward to your stack, with your stack’s universal forwarder credentials app installed on it.
  3. Put the Data TA on the heavy forwarder (through your Deployment Server, or directly if you have none), and install the GCP add-on on it directly, as above.
  4. Create the input on the heavy forwarder (Configure the input).

The LogServ App goes on the Splunk Cloud search head. The Data TA is not needed on the Cloud stack in this layout.

Without a heavy forwarder. The add-on’s app.manifest declares the search-head workload, so a search head is an allowed target for it; installing it on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested. In this layout, install the Data TA and the GCP add-on on the search head as private apps, and create the input there. The Data TA must sit beside the add-on, because it parses the events where the input runs. We strongly recommend against this layout, because the input puts ingest load on the tier your users search on. Creating the input needs a role that holds admin_all_objects there too. See Running the TAs on a search head and Splunk Cloud Considerations.

docs.title: Configure the input
docs.text:
Create one input for each Pub/Sub subscription, on one instance (normally one heavy forwarder). You can install the add-on on every HF, for example to keep a standby ready, but run the input for a given subscription on one HF only. Every other input on the same subscription, on the same HF or another one, keeps its own dedup record, so a redelivered message can be indexed twice (see Scaling one subscription across inputs below). The service-account key is encrypted into the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf and is not Deployment-Server-managed — it survives restarts and Data-TA pushes.

Creating or editing an input needs admin_all_objects

On Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud alike, creating, editing (including replacing the service-account key) and deleting an input runs as the signed-in user and needs a role that holds the admin_all_objects capability. Without it, Save fails with HTTP 403, “This operation is forbidden”. The REST call below has the same requirement.

A new input starts with what is already in the subscription

The subscription may already hold notifications from before your input exists: up to 7 days of them by default, and up to 31 days if SAP keeps messages longer. A new input works through all of them on top of the live feed. Before you create it, see First Start: The Queue Backlog, which includes asking SAP to purge the older messages. The add-on cannot load purged days later (see Historical backfill).

docs.title: Via Splunk Web (per Heavy Forwarder)
docs.text:
Splunk Web → Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP → Inputs → Create New Input, and fill in the fields below with the project ID + subscription name from SAP — and paste the entire JSON key file of your own service account into the key field. (For a second landscape on the same HF, use the Inputs table’s Clone action and give it a new name — the key is not carried on clone, so re-paste it. On Edit, the key field shows ******; saving without changing it preserves the existing key.)

Paste the whole file — not just the private key

The key field takes the complete downloaded .json file, verbatim — everything from the opening { to the closing } ("type": "service_account", "project_id", "private_key", "client_email", and the rest). Open the file in a text editor, Select All, copy, paste.

  • Keep the -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- and -----END PRIVATE KEY----- lines. They are part of the private_key value inside the JSON — do not remove them, and do not un-escape the \n sequences around them.
  • Do not extract the private key out of the JSON. The add-on parses the pasted text as JSON (it reads client_email, private_key, and token_uri from it); a bare key — with or without the BEGIN/END lines — is not valid JSON and is rejected at the first poll with service-account key unusable.

docs.title: Via REST (scriptable, per Heavy Forwarder)
docs.text:
# Stage the service-account JSON key file, then create the input:
curl -sk -u admin:<pwd> -X POST \
  https://localhost:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub \
  --data-urlencode name=logserv_gcp \
  --data-urlencode project_id=<sap-logserv-project-id> \
  --data-urlencode subscription_name=<subscription-name> \
  --data-urlencode index=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode event_sourcetype=sap_logserv_logs \
  --data-urlencode interval=60 \
  --data-urlencode service_account_key@/tmp/logserv-sa-key.json
rm -f /tmp/logserv-sa-key.json

The resulting stanza in the add-on’s local/inputs.conf looks like:

[sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub://logserv_gcp]
project_id = <sap-logserv-project-id>
subscription_name = <subscription-name>
service_account_key = ******
index = sap_logserv_logs
event_sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs
interval = 60
disabled = 0

(Only the masked placeholder service_account_key = ****** is written to inputs.conf — the real key is stored encrypted in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf.)

Field Default Notes project_id — The SAP LogServ GCP project ID from SAP (6–30 chars: lowercase letters, digits, hyphens; must start with a letter and end with a letter or digit). subscription_name — The Pub/Sub PULL subscription name from SAP (receives the OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications). service_account_key — The complete JSON key file of the service account you created in your own GCP project (The onboarding sequence), pasted verbatim — including the -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- / -----END PRIVATE KEY----- lines inside the private_key value. Encrypted credential: the value lives in the add-on’s local/passwords.conf; inputs.conf carries only the masked ****** placeholder. index sap_logserv_logs Target index. Does not affect parsing — the Data TA’s index-time pipeline keys on the sourcetype, not the index. You may point it at a custom index, but the dashboards query through the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro, so update that macro to match (see caveat below). event_sourcetype (UI label Sourcetype) sap_logserv_logs Fixed at sap_logserv_logs. The add-on hard-codes this sourcetype (it is not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only when editing the input. Leave it at the default. interval 60 Seconds between firings (10–3600). Each firing drains the subscription within a per-firing time budget (currently 90% of interval, capped at 240 s) and the max_objects_per_fire cap. batch_size 10 Pub/Sub messages requested per pull call (maxMessages, 1–1000). The input acknowledges a batch only after processing all of it, so a whole batch must finish within the subscription’s ack deadline. max_objects_per_fire 500 Cap on objects ingested per firing (backlog safety valve). poison_threshold 5 A message redelivered more than this many times (Pub/Sub deliveryAttempt) is acked and dropped. See Reliability behavior. include_filters / exclude_filters (empty) Optional comma-separated substrings applied to the GCS object path as a cheap pre-filter (beyond the built-in logserv match). The canonical allow/deny policy lives in the Data TA’s Filters tab. verify_ssl 1 TLS verification for the Google API endpoints. Leave enabled for production.

Sourcetype is fixed; the Index is yours to change

The Sourcetype is effectively fixed at sap_logserv_logs — the add-on always emits it (the value is hard-coded in the input, not read from the stanza), and the field is shown read-only (disabled) when editing an existing input. When you create an input the field can still be typed into, but whatever you enter is ignored and the add-on still emits sap_logserv_logs. This is deliberate: the Data TA’s index-time routing, Filters nullQueue, _time drop, and splunk_solution / cloud_provider stamping all key on sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs (props.conf stanzas match on sourcetype, not index), so it must never vary.

The index, by contrast, may be changed safely — parsing is unaffected (events are routed, filtered, and stamped identically no matter which index they land in). You may point it at a custom index (for example a per-customer index such as sap_logserv_logs_con01). The only follow-up is dashboard visibility: the dashboards and rollups search through the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro (default index="sap_logserv_logs"), so override that macro in the App’s local/macros.conf to match your index, or the dashboards won’t find the data.

docs.title: cloud_provider attribution
docs.text:
The input stamps every event it emits with the indexed field cloud_provider=gcp (the add-on’s default/inputs.conf sets _meta = cloud_provider::gcp for every input of this kind), so search-time queries and the Multi-Cloud Overview dashboard can distinguish GCP-sourced from AWS- and Azure-sourced data.

When you ingest from more than one cloud

The Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown stamps cloud_provider TA-wide at index time. If it is set to aws (or any provider) on a forwarder that also runs this GCP input, that index-time stamp co-fires with the input’s per-event _meta=gcp, leaving cloud_provider multivalued on the GCP events. For correct per-channel attribution on a mixed forwarder, set the Cloud Provider dropdown to “Not set” and attribute per input: this GCP input and the LogServ Azure add-on’s input already self-attribute via _meta; add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to the Splunk_TA_aws SQS-S3 input. This applies even when each cloud runs on separate forwarders: a Deployment Server pushes the dropdown’s value to every forwarder in the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. Leave the dropdown at Not set on forwarders that run this add-on: its input already stamps cloud_provider, and the dropdown would add the value a second time. A forwarder can run the GCP add-on beside the AWS or Azure add-on; see Capacity Planning and First Start → More Than One Cloud for when to separate them. See Choose Cloud Attribution.

docs.title: Multiple landscapes / fleets
docs.text:
• Multiple GCP landscapes on one HF: create one input instance per landscape (different project_id / subscription_name), using the Inputs table’s Clone action. The per-instance credential is keyed by the input name; re-paste the key on each (clone never carries secrets).
  • A fleet of heavy forwarders: install the add-on on each HF that may run an input (still never through the DS). Create the input for a given subscription on one HF. Add it on more HFs only for throughput or to catch up a backlog, accepting at-least-once delivery (see the note below); to fail over, enable the standby HF’s input after you disable the first one. For zero-touch fleets, config management can drop the add-on into etc/apps/ and seed the key via the REST call above (it encrypts under each HF’s own splunk.secret). Do not add the add-on to the Deployment Server’s deployment-apps/.

Scaling one subscription across inputs — Pub/Sub is natively competing-consumer

Separate input instances are normally for different subscriptions. You can also point several identical inputs at the same subscription to raise throughput — competing consumers are Pub/Sub’s native delivery model: N inputs (across one HF or several) pull and ingest N batches of objects in parallel. Pub/Sub tries not to give a message that is still outstanding to another consumer, but it may rarely redeliver any message, even after it was acknowledged, so several consumers can produce occasional duplicates even within the ack deadline (Google’s subscription overview). Understand the trade-off first:

  • A single input is effectively duplicate-free across the subscription’s redelivery window — its per-input dedup checkpoint (keyed bucket/object#generation; entries are retained for about 7 days, up to 50,000 objects) skips an already-ingested object if a message reappears.
  • Same-subscription inputs don’t share that checkpoint, so they fall back to at-least-once (the same guarantee as the AWS SQS-S3 input). If a message is not acknowledged within the subscription’s ack deadline (SAP-managed; 300 s recommended), the message redelivers and another input may re-ingest it → duplicate events. The guard: the input acknowledges once per pull batch, after processing every message in it, so a whole batch (batch_size objects, default 10) must finish within the ack deadline. Ask SAP what the deadline is (Pub/Sub’s default is 10 s), and lower batch_size if it is short. deliveryAttempt is Pub/Sub’s server-side, shared counter, so the poison_threshold decision stays coordinated across the consumers, and a subscription-level dead-letter policy (SAP-managed) handles poison messages natively.

For typical LogServ volumes a single input already keeps up (it drains up to max_objects_per_fire objects per firing). Prefer raising max_objects_per_fire or lowering interval on one input before adding consumers; raise batch_size only while a whole batch still finishes within the subscription’s ack deadline.

docs.title: Reliability behavior
docs.text:
• At-least-once + dedup. A subscription message carrying a LogServ object is acknowledged only after that object ingests successfully (unparseable / non-OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications and paths your filters reject are acknowledged without ingest and counted as noise= in the done log line; poison messages likewise — see below); each object is deduplicated by bucket/object#generation in a checkpoint sidecar, so a redelivered message re-ingests nothing.
  • Transient failures leave the message. A 5xx / network error on an object fetch leaves the message unacknowledged (it redelivers after the ack deadline); already-ingested objects in that message are no-ops on retry.
  • Object-read denied (HTTP 403) leaves the message and logs loudly — this is the missing-storage.objectViewer signal (get the bucket-read grant from SAP; the message reprocesses).
  • Pull denied (HTTP 403) aborts the firing — the service account lacks roles/pubsub.subscriber (or the project/subscription values are wrong); nothing is consumed until the credential is fixed.
  • Deleted objects (HTTP 404) are acked and skipped — an object that vanished between notification and fetch can’t loop.
  • Poison messages (redelivered more than poison_threshold times, per Pub/Sub’s deliveryAttempt counter) are acked and dropped so one permanently-bad object can’t loop forever. deliveryAttempt is populated only when the subscription has a dead-letter policy — with one attached, Pub/Sub also dead-letters natively (the primary mechanism; the TA’s threshold is a local backstop).

docs.title: Historical backfill
docs.text:
Notification-driven ingest is forward-only by nature — the bucket notification fires only on new OBJECT_FINALIZE events, so once SAP’s notification is live the input ingests everything written from that point on (plus the messages still in the subscription when you create the input), but does not replay objects that already existed. This solution has no historical load for GCP; to load older objects, agree a method with your Splunk team.

The add-on reads only the objects that subscription messages name and never lists the bucket. A day whose messages were purged, or expired before the input read them, stays in SAP’s bucket, but nothing in Splunk for SAP LogServ will load it. If you will need such days, agree with your Splunk team how to load them before you ask SAP to purge anything (see First Start: The Queue Backlog). Moving SAP’s subscription forward in time (a seek) acknowledges the older messages; they can be replayed later only if SAP’s subscription keeps acknowledged messages or its topic keeps messages, so ask SAP before a seek.

When filtering is on, the Data TA’s Days in the Past filter applies to everything the input reads, the subscription backlog included: events older than its cutoff are dropped before indexing.

docs.title: Rotate credentials
docs.text:
A service-account key keeps working until it is disabled or deleted in your GCP project, or until it expires if your organization’s policy gives keys an expiry time (the constraints/iam.serviceAccountKeyExpiryHours organization policy; without it, a key never expires). When the key stops working, token minting fails (token minting failed (...); aborting firing in the input log), and the input ingests nothing. The messages wait in the subscription only as long as its message retention allows (7 days by default); days whose messages are removed before you replace the key cannot be loaded later (see Historical backfill). Rotate the key on the schedule your security policy sets.

To rotate the key:

  1. In your GCP project, add a new JSON key to the service account: IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → (the account) → Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. A service account can hold up to 10 keys, so the old key keeps working meanwhile. The organization-policy warning applies to new keys too.
  2. On the instance that runs the input, open Apps → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP → Inputs and choose Edit on the input. The Service-account key (JSON) field shows ******.
  3. Replace ****** with the whole new JSON key file (see Paste the whole file above) and click Update. Saving needs a role that holds admin_all_objects. (If you leave ****** in the field, the stored key is kept.)
  4. The input reads the key at every firing, so the next firing uses the new one. Check the input log for a done: line and no token minting failed (see Validation).
  5. Repeat on every other instance that has an input using this key, such as a standby heavy forwarder. Each instance keeps its own encrypted copy in the add-on’s local/passwords.conf; the Deployment Server does not carry it.
  6. Then disable or delete the old key in your GCP project (Keys tab of the service account).

SAP’s grants are bound to the service account’s email, not to a key, so a new key needs nothing from SAP.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Confirm the input is registered and firing (run on the heavy forwarder):

curl -sk -u admin:<pwd> \
  "https://localhost:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub?output_mode=json"

Watch the input log on the HF:

sudo tail -f /opt/splunk/var/log/splunk/splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub.log
# look for:  Input 'logserv_gcp' done: messages=N objects=N events=N dups=N acked=N ...

Search the indexer (events route to per-source sourcetypes just like AWS and Azure):

index=sap_logserv_logs cloud_provider=gcp _index_earliest=-1h | stats count by sourcetype

For the full set of checks (sourcetypes, one cloud_provider value per event, routing), see Verify Your Data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom (in the input log unless noted) Cause Fix Splunk Web shows “This operation is forbidden” (HTTP 403) when you save, edit or delete an input The signed-in role lacks the admin_all_objects capability Use a role that holds admin_all_objects on this instance (see Configure the input). service-account key not found in passwords.conf; skipping No credential for this input name on this host Re-enter the key on this HF (Inputs tab → Edit, or the REST call above). The key lives in the add-on’s own local/passwords.conf; it is not affected by Deployment-Server pushes. service-account key unusable (...) The pasted key is not a valid service-account JSON key (truncated paste, wrong file, or only the bare private key was pasted instead of the whole JSON file) Re-paste the entire JSON key file verbatim — the full {...} document, with the -----BEGIN/END PRIVATE KEY----- lines left intact inside the private_key value. token minting failed (...) The key is disabled, deleted or expired, the HF can’t reach oauth2.googleapis.com, or the system clock is skewed (JWTs are time-signed) Verify egress to oauth2.googleapis.com:443 and NTP sync; check in your GCP console whether the key is still active (IAM & Admin → Service Accounts → Keys), and if it is not, mint a new one and replace it. subscription pull failed (... 403 ...) SAP’s roles/pubsub.subscriber grant for your service account is missing or not yet applied, or project_id/subscription_name are wrong Confirm the values with your SAP support contact and that the grant for your service account’s email is in place on this subscription (The onboarding sequence). subscription pull failed (HTTP 403: … SERVICE_DISABLED …) naming the service account’s home project (“…API has not been used in project…”) The service account is homed in your GCP project, a different project from the LogServ resources, and the Pub/Sub or Cloud Storage API isn’t enabled there (Google attributes API quota to the credential’s home project) Enable the Cloud Pub/Sub API and Cloud Storage API in the account’s home project and retry (step 4 of The onboarding sequence). object read forbidden (HTTP 403) The service account lacks roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket Ask SAP to add the bucket-read grant for your service account’s email; the message is left for retry and reprocesses once fixed. done: messages=0 every firing, but objects exist The bucket notification (SAP-managed) isn’t publishing, or the subscription name is wrong Confirm with your SAP support contact that the OBJECT_FINALIZE notification and subscription are active; verify egress to pubsub.googleapis.com. Input kind sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub not listed / Inputs page missing The GCP add-on isn’t installed (or Splunkd wasn’t restarted) on this HF Install splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp on the HF and restart (see Install the GCP add-on).

For problems that are not specific to the GCP input, see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Verify Your Data: check that events arrive with the expected sourcetypes and one cloud_provider value
  • Check the LogServ App prerequisites, then install the LogServ App on your Search Head
  • Review the supported log types reference
  • For Splunk Cloud considerations, see Splunk Cloud Considerations

docs.title: Create the Indexes and Install the Data TA
docs.text: This page creates the two indexes the solution writes to and installs the Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk TA for SAP LogServ). Use it after you have planned your topology (Where Each Package Goes, Plan and Prerequisites) and before you connect your cloud. For the LogServ App, see Installing the LogServ App.

docs.title: High Level Steps
docs.text:
Follow the steps in order:

  1. Decide where the Data TA goes.
  2. Create the two indexes on the indexer tier, with the retention you want, before any data arrives.
  3. Download the packages.
  4. Install the Data TA (Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud).
  5. Before you distribute it: choose cloud attribution and decide filtering.
  6. Distribute the Data TA to the heavy forwarders.
  7. Check the build on each heavy forwarder.

Less common tasks (renaming an index, running the add-ons on a search head, macros on the Deployment Server) are under Advanced at the bottom of this page.

docs.title: 1. Where to Install
docs.text:
The Data TA goes where LogServ data is parsed: on the heavy forwarders that run the ingest inputs, or on the single instance. A Deployment Server holds it in order to distribute it. The indexes are created on the indexer tier (step 2). Which instance gets which package, for every topology, is on Where Each Package Goes (the matrix, and By Topology). For the Data TA, that means one of these:

  • Single instance: that instance.
  • Heavy forwarders managed by a Deployment Server: the Deployment Server only; it pushes the Data TA to the heavy forwarders (Distribute the Data TA). This holds with Splunk Cloud too.
  • Heavy forwarders without a Deployment Server: each heavy forwarder that runs a LogServ input, installed directly.
  • Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder: the Splunk Cloud search head, because the inputs run there. This is not blocked, but we strongly recommend a heavy forwarder; see Running the TAs on a search head.

Indexers and search heads that run no LogServ inputs do not need it: create the two indexes on the indexer tier instead (step 2; installing the Data TA on an indexer is allowed but adds nothing beyond its index definitions), and the LogServ App carries the search-time content.

The Data TA parses every LogServ event on the heavy forwarders (or the single instance), so its cost per event decides how many heavy forwarders your volume needs; see Capacity Planning and First Start.

With a Deployment Server, install the Data TA on the Deployment Server only

When a Deployment Server manages your heavy forwarders, do not also install the Data TA directly on those forwarders. A push from the Deployment Server replaces the forwarder’s copy of the app, its local/ folder included, so local settings on the forwarder are lost. The Data TA does not reach the forwarders by itself either: the forwarders must be deployment clients, you save the Configuration page on the Deployment Server, assign the forwarders to the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class and click Deploy to Forwarders. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders gives the steps.

Why not the Inputs Data Manager (IDM)?

On the Splunk Cloud Classic Experience, inputs run on an Inputs Data Manager (IDM). The Data TA’s app.manifest declares the workloads _search_heads and _indexers only; it does not declare _forwarders. Whether Splunk Cloud installs such an app on an IDM is not documented, and this path has not been tested. Use a heavy forwarder you manage yourself. With no heavy forwarder on the Victoria Experience, the inputs run on the search head, and the Data TA goes there too. (The LogServ Azure and GCP add-ons declare _forwarders, and also _search_heads, so a search head is an allowed target for them too, although a heavy forwarder is strongly recommended; installing them on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested.)

docs.title: 2. Create the Indexes
docs.text:
The solution uses two indexes:

Index Purpose Default name Macro SAP data index Receives every LogServ event (logs ingested from AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage and routed to their sourcetypes) sap_logserv_logs sap_logserv_idx_macro AI Assistant audit index Receives every audit event the AI Assistant writes: predefined-prompt dispatches, free-form vendor calls (when the LLM path is enabled), security blocks, privacy-tier elevations, legal acknowledgements logserv_ai_assistant_audit sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro

Create both on the indexer tier before any data arrives. An event sent to an index that does not exist on the indexers is dropped (unless your indexers set lastChanceIndex), and an index created later does not get those events back.

Retention. The Data TA sets no retention for sap_logserv_logs, so the platform default applies unless you set one. It sets 90 days for the audit index (frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000). Set the retention of sap_logserv_logs to cover the oldest data you will load, including any history you load later with AWS S3 Direct.

How you create them depends on your topology:

  • Single instance — nothing to do. The Data TA ships default/indexes.conf with both indexes, and that one instance is the indexer, so installing the Data TA creates them. To give sap_logserv_logs a retention other than the default, add frozenTimePeriodInSecs = <seconds> under [sap_logserv_logs] in the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf and restart Splunkd.
  • Standalone indexer, indexer cluster or Splunk Cloud — create them yourself, as described in Creating the indexes on a separate indexer tier below.

Why the indexer needs the index definitions

Events are stored on the indexer tier, so both indexes must be defined there. The Data TA does its parsing on the heavy forwarders (or the single instance), and a heavy forwarder parses each event before it forwards it, so on an indexer the only part of the Data TA that would do anything is its indexes.conf. That is why the indexes are created on the indexer tier by the tier’s own method rather than by installing the Data TA there. If you do install the Data TA on a standalone indexer, its default/indexes.conf creates the indexes there, and its two scheduled scripts (the filter upgrade check every 10 minutes and the daily filter refresh) still run on it, doing nothing useful. On the Deployment Server and the heavy forwarders, which store no LogServ events, the index definitions do no harm.

docs.title: Creating the Indexes on a Separate Indexer Tier
docs.text:
Use the same settings the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf uses, so paths and retention match:

[sap_logserv_logs]
homePath   = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/db
coldPath   = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/colddb
thawedPath = $SPLUNK_DB/sap_logserv_logs/thaweddb

[logserv_ai_assistant_audit]
homePath               = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/db
coldPath               = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/colddb
thawedPath             = $SPLUNK_DB/logserv_ai_assistant_audit/thaweddb
frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000

Add frozenTimePeriodInSecs to [sap_logserv_logs] to set its retention. Then pick the method that matches how your indexer tier is managed.

Standalone indexer (Splunk Enterprise). Either:

  • Splunk Web: Settings → Indexes → New Index. Create sap_logserv_logs, then logserv_ai_assistant_audit, leaving the default paths. Then set their retention with frozenTimePeriodInSecs in indexes.conf (Splunk Web writes each new index to the local/indexes.conf of the app chosen in the form’s App field): 7776000 seconds (about 90 days) for the audit index, to match the bundled default, and the value you want for sap_logserv_logs. Restart Splunkd. Or
  • Config file: add the stanzas above to $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/indexes.conf (or to a small index-definition app of your own) on the indexer and restart Splunkd.

Indexer cluster. Put the stanzas in an index-only app under the cluster manager, $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/manager-apps/<your_index_app>/local/indexes.conf, and add repFactor = auto to both stanzas. Without repFactor = auto an index is not replicated across the peers. Then push the configuration bundle from the manager node: splunk apply cluster-bundle on its command line, or the bundle actions on its Settings → Indexer Clustering page in Splunk Web. Every peer receives the index definitions. The peers need nothing else from the Data TA. Putting the whole Data TA in the bundle is allowed but unnecessary; if you do, remove its inputs.conf first, as Splunk recommends for add-ons on indexer clusters.

Splunk Cloud. Create both indexes yourself, with the retention you want, before any data arrives: in the Splunk Cloud console (Settings → Indexes → New Index, where the retention is the Searchable retention) or with the Admin Config Service (ACS). When you install the Data TA on a Victoria Experience stack as a private app, Splunk also installs its indexing-related default/ files, indexes.conf among them, on the Cloud indexers (its local/ files do not go there), but Splunk does not document that this creates the indexes, so do not rely on it.

docs.title: Check Who Can Search the Indexes
docs.text:
Each role that uses the LogServ App’s dashboards must be able to search sap_logserv_logs. On Splunk Enterprise the default user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so roles that keep * (or import such a role) already can. Check your roles in Settings → Roles → role → Indexes, on Splunk Cloud too, and add the index to any role with a narrowed list. Give access to the audit index only as Audit Log → Restricting who can read the audit index describes.

Both index names can be changed; see Renaming an index.

docs.title: 3. Download the Packages
docs.text:
All four packages of this release, their AppInspect reports and a README with the release details are in the release_binaries folder of the GitHub repository:

File Package Version Build md5 splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz Data TA (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ) 0.1.2 1792598960 41a04986683c5d33014d8ab2fdb832f6 splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ App (Splunk App for SAP LogServ) 0.1.2 394 1d82a2ac049391b2d7b2fb347d112649 splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ Azure add-on (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure) 0.1.2 1792558069 5a5b0cfcd5f77dfa1e22dcc3545c8306 splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp-0.1.2.tar.gz LogServ GCP add-on (Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP) 0.1.2 1792558072 42713371e1ba1042b1149065cc1c59a9

This page installs the Data TA. The LogServ App goes on the search tier (Installing the LogServ App); the Azure and GCP add-ons are installed later, per heavy forwarder, in the Azure and GCP setup guides. The Splunk Add-on for AWS comes from Splunkbase (app 1876) and is not part of this release.

To check a download, compare its md5 with the table: md5sum <file> on Linux, md5 <file> on macOS, certutil -hashfile <file> MD5 on Windows.

docs.title: 4. Install the Data TA
docs.text: Install it on each instance that step 1 names: the Deployment Server, each heavy forwarder without a Deployment Server, the single instance, or the Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs.

docs.title: Splunk Enterprise
docs.text:
Your Deployment Server, heavy forwarders and single instance run Splunk Enterprise, also when your search tier is Splunk Cloud.

4.a From the Splunk Web home screen, click the gear icon next to Apps.

4.b Click Install app from file.

4.c Locate the downloaded splunk_ta_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz file and click Upload.

4.d If Splunk Enterprise prompts you to restart, do so.

4.e Verify that the add-on appears in the list of apps and add-ons. You can also find it on the server at $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv.

On a Deployment Server this installs the Data TA in etc/apps/ only. It is copied into etc/deployment-apps/ for the forwarders when you first save its Configuration page there (Distribute the Data TA).

If splunkd runs with a proxy variable, exempt its own management port

The add-on’s configuration pages (and the Azure and GCP add-ons’ inputs) talk to the local splunkd management port, by default 127.0.0.1:8089, through Splunk’s Python HTTP client, which honours the HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY environment variables. If the environment splunkd runs in sets either of them, for example in splunk-launch.conf or the systemd unit, also set NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost (plus the host name in mgmtHostPort, if it is not a loopback address). Otherwise those calls, with their session key, are sent to the proxy instead of to splunkd.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud
docs.text:
Install the Data TA on your Splunk Cloud stack only when the inputs run on the Cloud search head (Splunk Cloud with no heavy forwarder). With your own heavy forwarders, install it there with the Splunk Enterprise steps above instead; the Splunk Cloud stack does not need it (installing it there is allowed).

The app installation workflow depends on your Splunk Cloud Platform Experience, Victoria or Classic. To find yours, in Splunk Web click Support & Services > About.

  • Installation instructions for Victoria Experience
  • Installation instructions for Classic Experience

Create the indexes yourself either way (step 2). For what differs when the inputs run on a search head, see Running the TAs on a search head and Splunk Cloud Considerations.

docs.title: 5. Before You Distribute: Two Index-Time Decisions
docs.text:
The Data TA attributes each event to its cloud and applies your filters at index time, so whatever is indexed before you decide stays as it was indexed. Decide both before the first Save on the Deployment Server, and before any input starts:

  1. Choose Cloud Attribution: the Cloud Provider value (normally Not set) and the per-input _meta line for AWS.
  2. Decide Filtering: whether to turn filtering on, and with which values.

docs.title: 6. Distribute to the Heavy Forwarders
docs.text:
• With a Deployment Server: follow Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders. The forwarders receive the Data TA only after those steps.
  • Without a Deployment Server: the Data TA is already on each heavy forwarder (step 4). Enter the same Configuration values and click Save on each one; see Without a Deployment Server.
  • Single instance, or the Splunk Cloud search head that runs the inputs: nothing to distribute. Enter your Configuration values there and click Save.

docs.title: 7. Check the Build on Each Heavy Forwarder
docs.text: Before you create any input, check on each heavy forwarder (or the single instance) that it runs this Data TA build: see Version Check. The routing runs where the data is parsed, so a forwarder that has not received the Data TA yet indexes every event under the base sap_logserv_logs sourcetype, permanently.

docs.title: Renaming an Index
docs.text:
Both indexes are macro-configurable, so you can use other names (for example, to follow a corporate naming convention) without changing the apps: you create the index, update the macros, and point the writers at the new name.

Note

Both the Data TA and the LogServ App include a macro named sap_logserv_idx_macro that resolves to index="sap_logserv_logs". The LogServ App also includes sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro for the audit index.

docs.title: To Rename the SAP Data Index
docs.text:
A rename touches three places: the indexer tier, every ingest input (normally on the heavy forwarders), and the search head. The Deployment Server is not involved. On a single instance all three are the same instance.

  1. Pick a new name (for example myorg_sap_logs).
  2. Create the index on the indexer tier under that name, with the methods in Creating the indexes on a separate indexer tier (on a single instance: Settings → Indexes → New Index, or a stanza in the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf). On Splunk Cloud, use Settings → Indexes or ACS: a local/indexes.conf does not reach the Cloud indexers. See the Splunk docs for Splunk Cloud or Splunk Enterprise.

  3. Update the macro in every app on the search head that ships it. Open Settings → Advanced search → Search macros, set App to All, and filter on sap_logserv_idx_macro. Edit the row whose app is splunk_app_sap_logserv and change the definition from index="sap_logserv_logs" to index="myorg_sap_logs". Where the Data TA is also installed on this search head (a single instance, or a search head that runs the inputs), edit the row whose app is splunk_ta_sap_logserv too. Each edit is saved in that app’s local/macros.conf. Both are needed: the scheduled rollups and the Settings → Dashboard Data backfill run in the LogServ App and use its copy, while the live dashboard panels run in each user’s default app, where Splunk ranks the Data TA’s copy above the App’s (other apps are ranked in reverse alphabetical order). Check the result:

    | rest /servicesNS/-/-/configs/conf-macros splunk_server=local
| search title=sap_logserv_idx_macro
| table eai:acl.app definition

    Then run `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count in the Search app once data arrives in the new index.

  4. Point every ingest input at the new index. The destination index is set by each input’s index field, in the ingest add-on for your cloud, not in this Data TA: for AWS, each SQS-Based S3 input in the Splunk Add-on for AWS (see the AWS Remote S3 Connect Setup Guide), and the Index field of every later backfill on the AWS S3 Direct screen; for Azure, each sap_logserv_azure_queue input’s index field (Azure Setup Guide); for GCP, each sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input’s index field (GCP Setup Guide). These inputs normally run on the heavy forwarders. The AWS S3 Direct screen offers only the indexes defined on the instance it runs on, so to pick the new name there, define the index on that forwarder too, for example with Settings → Indexes on it. (On a forwarder the Deployment Server manages, do not put it in the Data TA’s local/: the next push replaces that folder.)

The Data TA still ships its own [sap_logserv_logs] stanza in default/indexes.conf, and a local/indexes.conf cannot remove it: Splunk merges the two files setting by setting, so local/ can only override values. An unused, empty sap_logserv_logs index does no harm. If you do not want it, disable it once every ingest input points at the new index: on each instance where the Data TA defines it and events are stored (a single instance, or an indexer you installed the Data TA on), add the following to the Data TA’s local/indexes.conf (or use Settings → Indexes → Disable), then restart Splunkd. Do not edit or delete the Data TA’s default/indexes.conf; an upgrade replaces it and brings the stanza back.

[sap_logserv_logs]
disabled = true

The AI Assistant and a renamed data index

After sap_logserv_idx_macro is changed, the AI Assistant refuses free-form queries that start with the macro: its query guard compares the macro with the shipped definition index="sap_logserv_logs" (The SPL Guard).

docs.title: To Rename the AI Assistant Audit Index
docs.text:
1. Pick a new name. Do not start it with an underscore: _-prefixed index names are reserved for Splunk’s internal indexes, AppInspect rejects them for custom apps, and Splunk Cloud will not accept them (the shipped index was itself renamed off an underscore prefix for these reasons).
  2. Create the index on the indexer tier under that name, with the same methods as above.
  3. Update the macro definition. Open Settings → Advanced search → Search macros, find sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro (only the LogServ App ships it), and change the definition from index="logserv_ai_assistant_audit" to index="<your_new_name>". This controls READS: the in-app Audit Log viewer and any user-written queries resolve the macro to your renamed index.
  4. Update the LogServ App config. Open Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit & Telemetry, set the Audit index name field to your renamed index, and Save Defaults. This controls WRITES: the App posts audit events to the configured index name.

The config field controls writes; the macro controls reads. They MUST point at the same index, but Splunk does not keep them in step for you: keep them aligned whenever you rename.

docs.title: Running the TAs on a search head
docs.text:
We strongly recommend against installing the Data TA, the LogServ Azure add-on or the LogServ GCP add-on on a search head, Splunk Cloud included: ingest belongs on the heavy forwarders, and inputs on a search head put that load on the tier your users search on. Nothing blocks it, though. On a search head that runs the inputs itself (with the Splunk Add-on for AWS, or with the Azure or GCP add-on), the Data TA parses and filters there as it does on a heavy forwarder, and the AWS S3 Direct screen works there too; on Splunk Cloud, and on an instance with no enabled AWS input, it shows a warning that recommends a heavy forwarder. Two things work differently there:

  • Search head clusters. A search head cluster does not replicate inputs, so an input created on a member (on the Azure or GCP add-on’s Inputs page, or on the AWS S3 Direct screen) runs only on that member. An input the deployer pushes to every member runs on every member: a Generic S3 input then reads every object on each member, so each object is indexed once per member; the Azure and GCP add-ons share their queue or subscription between the members, and a message goes to one member, but each member keeps its own dedup record, so a redelivered message can be indexed twice. The filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp that the Data TA’s Configuration page generates are written only on the member where you save them. The saved Filters settings normally reach the other members (not when the save falls back to writing the settings file, as it does for an account without admin_all_objects), and another member rebuilds its rules from them at its own daily filter refresh, but only while Enable Filtering is checked and Days in the Past is greater than 0: turning filtering off, and rules saved with Days in the Past at 0, never reach the other members. Save the Filters and Cloud Provider tabs on every member that runs inputs.
  • Deployment clients. On a search head that is a deployment client for other apps but holds the Data TA directly, the daily filter refresh runs as it does on a single instance. It is skipped only where the Deployment Server delivers the Data TA, or where the instance’s record of what its Deployment Server sent ($SPLUNK_HOME/var/run/serverclass.xml) is missing, unreadable or lists no app. The same rule applies to a heavy forwarder that holds the Data TA directly; see Heavy Forwarder without a Deployment Server.

docs.title: Macros and the Deployment Server
docs.text:
When the Deployment Server pushes the Data TA to the heavy forwarders, its macros.conf travels with it, but heavy forwarders run no user searches, so a macro there has no effect. Macros matter on the search tier. Where the Data TA is also installed on a search head (a single instance, or a search head that runs the inputs), its copy of sap_logserv_idx_macro is the one the live dashboard panels use, ranked above the LogServ App’s copy; see step 3 of To Rename the SAP Data Index.

What this means in practice:

Scenario Where the change happens Deployment Server involved? You rename the data index Indexer tier: create the new index. Ingest inputs (normally on the heavy forwarders): set index to the new name on every SQS-Based S3 input, sap_logserv_azure_queue input and sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input, and on later AWS S3 Direct backfills (WRITE). Search head: override sap_logserv_idx_macro in each app that ships it there (READ). See Renaming an index. No: none of these is pushed by the Deployment Server, and the Data TA routes by sourcetype, not by index You rename the audit index Indexer tier: create the new index. Search head: Settings → AI Assistant → General → Audit index name (WRITE), plus sap_logserv_audit_idx_macro in the LogServ App (READ). See Renaming an index. No You want a custom diagnostic macro on every heavy forwarder Add it to etc/deployment-apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/macros.conf on the Deployment Server, then Deploy to Forwarders; the forwarders pull it at their next phone-home. Operational effect: none, because forwarders do not resolve macros. Keep a copy in etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/local/macros.conf as well: when the Data TA’s version changes, the next Configuration save, or the next daily filter refresh, replaces the whole deployment-apps copy, hand edits included, with a copy of etc/apps/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/. Yes (cosmetic)

What the Deployment Server does push usefully from this Data TA: the filter rules and the Cloud Provider stamp, managed on the Data TA’s Configuration page on the Deployment Server. See Configuring Filters and Choose Cloud Attribution.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose Cloud Attribution, then Decide Filtering: both before the first Save on the Deployment Server.
  2. Distribute the Data TA to Heavy Forwarders, if a Deployment Server manages them.
  3. Choose Your Cloud and AWS Scenario to connect your cloud.

docs.title: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness
docs.text: Most LogServ App dashboard panels read hourly summaries (rollups) kept in KV Store. This page covers the admin tasks on Settings → Dashboard Data: filling the rollups with history after an install, rebuilding days whose data arrived late, and clearing a rollup. It then explains how fresh each panel is, and ends with the reference for the scheduled searches behind the rollups.

docs.title: The Dashboard Data settings tab
docs.text:
The Dashboard Data tab on the Application Settings page (Settings → Dashboard Data) is the single control surface for the KV-Store rollup layer, for every dashboard and the Environment Topology view. It holds the hourly-aggregation master switch, the retention window, the backfill, the late-arriving data check, a per-rollup status and action table, and a global clear.

Who can use it. The Settings page opens only for users who hold a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin, and the rollup collections accept writes only from those roles. A user who holds none of them does not see Settings in the navigation rail and gets “Admin access required” on the page’s URL, so Backfill and Clear need one of those three roles.

The Environment Topology graph and its detail tabs are rows in the same table: their aggregation, backfill, retention and clear work exactly as for every dashboard rollup. The backfill runs each of their searches as its own top-level job, so it does not truncate at high event volume.

Non-admins can SEE this health without Settings access

The Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page (Platform → Diagnostics) shows every rollup collection’s freshness and its 30-day-history completeness — the same completeness convention this tab uses — read-only, to every user. It names this tab as the remedy when a backfill is needed, but the controls themselves stay here.

docs.title: Backfilling on first install
docs.text:
A freshly installed rollup collection is empty until its scheduled aggregation has run, and those runs read only the most recent hours. Any install whose index already holds events (data loaded with AWS S3 Direct, ingest that ran before the App was installed, or a few days of normal arrival) needs a backfill to show that history.

  1. Open Settings → Dashboard Data.
  2. Review the per-rollup status. Rollups with no history show a “Dashboard history backfill needed” banner and a warning row. Rollups whose history could not be measured just now get a banner of their own with Re-check; they are not counted as needing a backfill.
  3. In Backfill window, pick the window (see below).
  4. Click Run backfill (the button targets only the incomplete rollups; once all are complete it becomes Re-run backfill (all)).

By default the backfill seeds 30 days of history into every rollup collection. The Backfill window control above the button also offers 60, 90, 180 and 365 days, or a custom range of whole UTC days, reaching back as far as the 365-day retention (an earlier start is refused rather than silently clamped). A window longer than a month is dispatched in monthly chunks per search, and choosing one longer than 90 days shows a cost warning. The two flat Environment Topology collections (inventory, IP enrichment) always refresh over the last 30 days: they describe current state rather than history — the inventory maps each IP address or host to its most recent SAP system. When backfilling after a historical S3 ingest, match the dates in the S3 keys you ingested — on the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen, its Scan from and Scan until — not a hand-made input’s write-time scan window; see AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

The backfill dispatches each rollup’s component aggregation searches as top-level Splunk jobs — this matters at scale: the bundled *_backfill saved searches use a single \| union that Splunk auto-finalizes at a subsearch wall-clock limit, which silently truncates results at high event volume. The Dashboard Data button avoids that by running each component as its own unrestricted job. It shows a progress bar, is idempotent (re-running upserts the same rows), and is resumable (it detects collections that are already complete and skips them).

After the initial backfill, the hourly aggregation keeps each collection current and the 365-day retention grows the cached history toward a full year (seed-and-grow). You only need to run the backfill again if you reinstall, deliberately clear a collection, an upgrade note asks for one, or you roll the App back to an earlier build across one that changed a rollup key: the restored build writes rows under its old keys beside the newer build’s rows, and those hours are counted twice until you Clear and Backfill the rows that build changed (see Upgrading).

How long it waits. Each search is waited on for as long as Splunk reports it running — there is no fixed time limit, because one month of a large estate can take hours. A rollup is marked failed — re-run only on Splunk’s own verdict: the job failed, its search process died, or the job disappeared. If you cancel, or the panel stops waiting (after 24 hours, or after 15 minutes without being able to reach Splunk), a search that is still running is marked still running on server instead: it finishes on its own and writes its rows. Hover the row for the search IDs to follow them under Activity → Jobs; re-running that rollup before they finish repeats their work.

Environment Topology node counts and inventory. Two of the Environment Topology (graph) collections combine the results of several searches: a node’s event count is the sum over every log source that reports it, and an IP address or host is mapped to its most recent SAP system with its events counted over every source (of the systems seen in its most recent hour, the one with the most events; an exact tie keeps the previous mapping). For those two, each search writes its results into a scratch KV Store collection, logserv_backfill_stage, and once every search of a month (for the inventory, of its 30 days) has finished, one more search adds them up and writes the rows — but only after the page has counted every collected result back from the scratch collection, before and after. Keep the page open until the Environment Topology (graph) row has finished: a month whose searches did not all finish, or whose results did not all read back (KV Store still starting after a restart, for example), is discarded rather than written in part — the row reads failed — re-run, also when the panel stopped waiting for one of those searches — and the next backfill rebuilds it. The scratch rows are deleted once a month is written; rows a closed page or a failed month left behind are deleted by a later backfill after seven days.

Keep long backfills clear of the nightly retention run

Each rollup’s *_retention search rewrites its whole collection once a night (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 in the search head’s time zone). Rows a backfill writes into a collection while that collection’s retention is running can be lost. Start a long backfill so that it does not overlap that window — or re-run it afterwards, which restores anything lost (the backfill is idempotent).

If you skip the backfill

You don’t have to run it. Without a backfill, rolled-up panels simply start populating from the next hourly aggregation onward, filling in one hour at a time. The backfill is purely to make that history available immediately.

docs.title: Late-arriving data
docs.text:
SAP LogServ data reaches Splunk through S3, Azure Blob and GCS notification queues, and some of it arrives after its hour has been aggregated: a log file delivered a few minutes after the hour, a weekly log rotation that delivers a week of lines at once, a queue backlog drained after an outage. Each hourly aggregation re-reads the hour before as well, so an event up to about an hour late is still counted, and an hour whose aggregation was skipped is rebuilt by the next run. Anything later is missing from the rolled-up panels until its hours are rebuilt.

The Late-arriving data row at the top of the Backfill section finds those hours. It compares the index with the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup — which counts every event, per cloud provider, sourcetype and hour — per hour and sourcetype over the last 30 days (UTC), and lists the days on which the index holds events the rollups do not, most recent first:

2026-09-26: 28,193 events in 42 hours (linux_secure, sap_logserv_logs)

It leaves out the last three hours, which the hourly schedule may still rebuild, and anything older than the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup’s oldest hour. It also finds hours whose aggregation was switched off or skipped. Fewer events in the index than in a rollup — deleted or frozen data — is never reported. Backfill N days rebuilds every rollup for exactly those days, one window per run of consecutive days, with the same per-search dispatch as the backfill above, and the check runs again when it finishes; check again re-runs it at any time. A banner at the top of the tab repeats the count while any day is listed.

The check needs the Multi-Cloud Overview aggregation switched on and that rollup’s history measured; otherwise the row says why it did not run.

The same check also runs every day at 05:40 (search-head time) as the saved search logserv_late_arrival_check, over the last 30 days up to three hours ago, and records a triggered alert (Activity → Triggered Alerts, kept 2 days) when it finds a day — so a delivery that arrived days late is reported even if nobody opens this tab. Add an alert action, an email for example, to be told. The daily run never judges an hour older than the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup’s oldest, so a new install that has not run its first backfill raises no alert; it does raise one while hourly aggregation is switched off, because the rollups then fall behind the index. To run it at another time, change its schedule in Settings → Searches, reports, and alerts; keep the window ending at least three hours back, and keep it out of the nightly retention window (00:34–02:36), which rewrites the rollup it compares against.

Why the schedule does not re-read days

Each rollup’s search is one | union of several searches, and Splunk stops a union’s inner searches after about 30 seconds. An hourly run that re-read days would hit that limit on a large estate and overwrite good rows with lower counts. The backfill avoids it by running each inner search on its own — which is why late days are rebuilt from this tab rather than by the schedule.

docs.title: Per-rollup table
docs.text:
One row per logical rollup (each dashboard, plus Environment Topology (graph), Environment Topology (detail tabs), and Beaconing detection). Some rows serve more than one dashboard, and their labels name each one: ABAP Operations is rebuilt with Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations, Web Dispatcher reads Web & API Performance / Web Dispatcher as well as its own Web Dispatcher Slowest Traces, and Network Perimeter reads its Firewall Drops in Transit count from Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter. Rebuild every row a dashboard reads. Columns:

Column Meaning Dashboard The dashboard / view this rollup powers. Schedule The aggregate search’s cron (e.g. 5 * * * *); hover for the next scheduled run. Aggregation Per-rollup enable toggle (acts on that rollup’s aggregate search(es); a multi-collection rollup like the topology graph toggles all of its searches). History How far back the rollup reaches, measured from its oldest bucket — e.g. 106.7d of history (about 30 days or more counts as complete), empty, or live backfilling N/M while a backfill runs, then refreshing… for the moment it takes to re-measure the depth once that row’s searches have finished. After a run it can also read failed — re-run, truncated — re-run, or still running on server (hover for the search IDs). When the panel could not measure the history — Splunk had no free search slot, as is common just after a backfill, or the check search itself failed — the cell reads check failed — re-check: hover for the reason, and re-check measures that row again (checking… meanwhile). The checks run three at a time, and one that Splunk turns away is tried again after 2, 4 and 8 seconds. Actions Backfill (this rollup only, per-arm top-level dispatch) · Clear (delete this rollup’s collection(s), confirm-gated).

docs.title: Aggregation & retention (global controls)
docs.text:
• Hourly aggregation — master switch. Enables/disables the scheduled saved searches that populate every rollup collection. Reads the live state of all aggregate searches and shows Enabled (all), Disabled (all), or Mixed (N/M on). Toggling flips them all (Mixed → enable all). Use the per-rollup toggles in the table to control one at a time.
  • Retention window — 365 days (read-only). Bucket rows older than this are trimmed daily by each rollup’s *_retention saved search. The trim never empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false), so a collection whose rows are all older than 365 days keeps them until new rows arrive. Uniform across all rollups; change default/savedsearches.conf to alter, and keep override_if_empty=false on every outputlookup of a retention search you change.

docs.title: Danger zone
docs.text: Clear all rollups — a confirm-gated button that deletes every row from all rollup collections at once. Use sparingly (e.g. to wipe a contaminated dataset before re-running a backfill against a corrected schema). Every dashboard is empty until the hourly aggregation or a backfill repopulates it.

docs.title: What “data freshness” means per panel
docs.text:
• tstats and raw panels are real-time — they reflect events the instant they are indexed.
  • Rolled-up panels are accurate to the most-recently-completed hour, for time ranges of 90 minutes or wider. The hourly aggregation runs in the first half of each hour (:03–:28, one rollup per minute), so within the current partial hour a rolled-up panel shows data through the last completed hour, not the live partial hour. An event that reaches Splunk more than about an hour after its hour is counted once its days are rebuilt — see Late-arriving data.
  • Sub-hour time ranges are real-time — every rolled-up panel switches to raw events automatically (see below).

docs.title: Sub-hour time ranges (automatic)
docs.text:
The rollups are keyed on whole-hour buckets, so a sub-hour time range — anything narrower than 90 minutes, such as Splunk’s Last 15 minutes or Last 60 minutes — cannot be answered correctly from the hourly cache alone: a window that falls inside a single hour matches no completed bucket (the panel would read empty), and a window that straddles an hour boundary would pull the whole hour (over-counting). To keep short ranges correct, every rolled-up panel automatically routes a sub-hour window to its underlying raw-event query instead of the cache — so a Last 15 minutes range shows accurate, real-time data at minute granularity with no action needed. For a window of 90 minutes or wider, the panel reads the fast hourly cache as usual.

The switch is based purely on the selected range’s span (a 90-minute threshold), is transparent to the user, and applies across every rolled-up dashboard — including the two Sourcetype Mapping link graphs and the Host Details Role Activity tab. At 90 minutes and wider, a rolled-up chart never draws buckets finer than one hour, because the summaries are hourly; at Last 24 hours it draws hourly bars where a chart counted from the index draws 15-minute ones. Every time chart prints its bucket in its subtitle (see Chart Time Buckets). Because the sub-hour path runs the panel’s actual raw query, it is exact — not an approximation of the cache. (The trade-off is only speed, not correctness: a sub-hour raw query is inexpensive because it scans a small window, while a multi-day raw scan is what the hourly cache exists to avoid.)

Investigating live activity

Sub-hour ranges are already real-time (above), so you can simply narrow the time-range picker to see live activity on any rolled-up dashboard. For deeper ad-hoc investigation at any range, a panel’s Open in Search toolbar action jumps into Splunk’s Search app with the panel’s actual query and your selected time range pre-applied — the rollup read for a cached panel at a wide range, the raw query at sub-hour ranges.

docs.title: How the dashboards source their data
docs.text:
Every panel reads from the cheapest correct data source for what it shows. There are two fast tiers plus a small set of panels that stay on raw events.

Tier Used for Freshness Cost tstats on indexed fields Pure counts and averages over indexed dimensions (event volumes, host / sourcetype / cloud-provider breakdowns) Real-time Very low — reads the index’s tsidx, no raw-event scan KV-Store precompute rollups Most charts, tables, and KPIs across the dashboard suite Hourly for wide ranges; real-time for sub-hour ranges (automatic — see above) Near-zero at read time — a scheduled search precomputes the data once per hour Raw events Per-event listings, streamstats periodicity (beaconing), and a few timing traces that cannot be rolled up Real-time Bounded with \| head N where the panel is a time-ordered listing

No CIM data-model acceleration is required

The dashboards do not depend on accelerating the Common Information Model (CIM) Web / Authentication / Network data models. The fast path is the app’s own KV-Store rollups, which work regardless of whether you have accelerated any CIM model. (The app’s CIM tagging for Splunk Enterprise Security correlation is a separate, independent feature — see Enterprise Security → CIM Compliance.)

docs.title: The KV-Store rollup layer
docs.text:
Behind the rolled-up panels is a set of KV-Store rollup collections (logserv_*_rollup, plus the Environment Topology graph collections). For each, a scheduled saved search (one per rollup) aggregates the last two completed hours of raw events into hour-bucketed rows — the previous hour, and the one before it again, so an event that arrives a little late is still counted (see Late-arriving data); the aggregates are staggered one per minute across :03–:28 of every hour. (Three rollups aggregate daily rather than hourly and are day-bucketed: the two beaconing detections and the topology IP-enrichment names.) The dashboard reads the collection back, filtered to the global time-range picker’s window via a bucket_ts range. Because the heavy aggregation happens once per hour in the background, opening a dashboard re-reads precomputed rows in roughly 0.1–0.6 seconds instead of dispatching a full raw scan.

A daily retention search trims each collection to a rolling 365-day window. It never empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false), so a KV Store that is still starting up after a Splunkd restart cannot wipe a rollup.

docs.title: Scheduled-search schedule
docs.text:
The app’s scheduled searches are organized into three non-overlapping bands, plus one daily check, so that no two enabled scheduled searches ever fire in the same minute and the hourly aggregation never contends with the daily retention. This keeps the scheduler from bursting at high event volume.

Band When What runs Hourly aggregates :03–:28 every hour, one per minute The always-on rollup-aggregate searches (logserv_*_aggregate / logserv_topology_aggregate_*), plus the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot at :02 Daily retention + daily aggregates 00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36, two minutes apart Every rollup’s retention trim, the two daily beaconing aggregates, the topology IP-enrichment aggregate, and the Data Doctor report/snapshot trims Enterprise Security :00–:01, :29, odd :31–:59, plus :30 in hours 02–05 (the daily anomaly scans) The splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches (enabled by default) — see note below Late-arriving data check 05:40 daily logserv_late_arrival_check — a read-only tstats comparison of the index with the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup (about 5 s on the reference box); see Late-arriving data

The per-search tables below give each search’s run time as typical / busy — the average and worst single-run duration observed on the validation fleet (~10.7M events/day). Aggregate run times scale with the per-hour event volume; retention run times scale with the collection size. Run times are indicative, measured on a ~10.7M events/day validation instance. Every hourly aggregate completes well within its one-minute slot; the heaviest daily retention trims take about a minute and sit in the two-minutes-apart daily band.

docs.title: Hourly aggregate band (:03–:28)
docs.text:
Each rollup aggregate dispatches the last two completed hours (-2h@h..@h) and rewrites both. The newest bucket is still the just-completed hour, so the firing minute is freshness-neutral — spreading them one-per-minute simply avoids a burst at :05. Peak concurrency is ~1–2 instead of 26. The run times below were measured when each run read one hour; reading two roughly doubles them. Two keep a one-hour window: logserv_topology_aggregate_inventory (keyed by value, not by hour) and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot at :02.

docs.title: Enterprise Security band (enabled by default)
docs.text: The 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches ship enabled (see Enterprise Security → The ES schedule) on crons that sit entirely in the minutes the always-on bands leave free — :00–:01, :29, and the odd minutes :31–:59 — so they are collision-free with both the aggregate band (:02–:28, including the Data Doctor’s :02 platform snapshot) and the daily band (00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36). 16 correlation searches run hourly, the 2 Asset/Identity feeds every 4 hours, and the 4 behavioral-anomaly searches once a day each, at :30 (hours 02–05). Two of them (splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_user_auth_volume and splunk_sap_logserv_es_anomaly_after_hours_admin) scan 30 days of raw events, and the other two read the KV Store rollups.

docs.title: Measured behavior
docs.text:
On the validation fleet (335M events), the hourly aggregates each complete in seconds and the slowest daily retention trim is ~1 minute (see the per-search tables above); the scheduler logs 0 skipped / 0 deferred. The two heaviest ES searches — the 30-day anomaly scans (~150–340 s and ~50–120 s) — run once a day, so they add no hourly load.

The Data Doctor adds two scheduled searches: logserv_diag_platform_aggregate (hourly at :02, a seconds-fast scan of the last hour of index=_internal) and logserv_diag_platform_retention (daily at 01:58, trims the platform snapshot to 30 days). The shipped schedule is verified by a permanent build gate: every enabled scheduled search has a unique (hour, minute) — zero cron collisions.

docs.title: Behavior with multiple search heads
docs.text:
How these scheduled searches behave depends on the search-head topology:

Search Head Cluster (SHC) — the supported multi-SH topology. Works cleanly, with no extra configuration:

  • The SHC captain delegates each scheduled search to a single member per fire, so every aggregate and retention search runs once cluster-wide per interval — not once per member. There is no multiplication of load by the number of search heads.
  • KV Store is automatically replicated across the cluster. Whichever member runs an aggregate writes the rollup to its local KV Store, and Splunk replicates the collection to every member — so all search heads serve the dashboards from the same rolled-up data, regardless of which member computed it. (The rollup design depends on KV Store, which is cluster-replicated by default.)
  • The app’s saved searches and collection definitions deploy to all members via the SHC deployer (splunk apply shcluster-bundle), Splunk’s standard process. The one-click Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill also works cluster-wide — an admin runs it from any member and the results replicate.
  • The one-search-per-minute staggering helps here too: it keeps the per-minute scheduled load at ~1, which the captain can place on any member without bunching.

Independent (non-clustered) search heads. If the app is installed on two or more standalone search heads that are not in a SHC, each one runs its own copy of the schedule against its own KV Store (there is no replication between independent search heads). The aggregates therefore run N times — once per search head — which is redundant indexer load, and each search head maintains its rollups independently (they can drift slightly in timing). It is not broken — each search head’s dashboards work off its own rollups — but it is wasteful. Recommendation: use a SHC for multi-SH deployments. If independent search heads are unavoidable, keep the schedule enabled, and run the backfill, on every one of them: each search head’s dashboards read only the rollups in its own KV Store, so a search head whose aggregates are switched off shows empty rolled-up panels at ranges of 90 minutes or wider.

Single search head (the default — one SH, with or without separate indexers): the search head runs the whole schedule itself, dispatching the raw scans to its indexer peers and writing the rollups to its own KV Store. Nothing special is required.

KV Store must be enabled and healthy

The rollups live in Splunk’s KV Store, so KV Store must be enabled on the search head(s) — it is by default, and is already required for the Environment Topology view and the AI Assistant settings. On a SHC, KV Store replication must be healthy for rollups computed on one member to appear on the others.

docs.title: What to know at a glance
docs.text:
• Most panels are hourly-fresh; counts and per-event listings are real-time. If a rolled-up trend looks an hour behind at a multi-day range, that’s expected.
  • Sub-hour time ranges (under 90 minutes) are real-time automatically — a rolled-up panel routes a Last 15 minutes-style window to its raw query, so short ranges stay minute-accurate with no manual step.
  • Scheduled searches are staggered into collision-free bands — hourly aggregates at :03–:28 (plus the platform snapshot at :02), daily retention + maintenance at 00:30–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:32–02:36, the late-arriving data check at 05:40, and the ES content (enabled by default) in the minutes those bands leave free — :00/:01 for the feeds, :29 and odd :31–:59 for the hourly correlations, and :30 at hours 02–05 for the daily anomaly searches — so no two enabled scheduled searches collide.
  • After installing on an index that already holds history, run Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill once — 30 days by default, or a longer window up to 365 days, or a custom range. It needs a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin.
  • Late-arriving data is listed and rebuilt in Settings → Dashboard Data. The hourly aggregation re-reads the hour before, which catches events up to about an hour late; the days holding anything later are listed under Late-arriving data, with a one-click backfill of exactly those days.
  • No CIM acceleration is needed for dashboard performance.
  • Use a panel’s Open in Search action for ad-hoc raw-event investigation at any range (sub-hour ranges are already real-time on the dashboard itself). The panel toolbar is described in the Dashboards Overview.

docs.title: Install the App and Seed the Dashboards
docs.text:
Use this page to install the LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk App for SAP LogServ) on your search tier, check that it sees your data, and fill the dashboards with the history your index already holds. It covers the last steps of the Deployment Roadmap.

Before you start
