  • Events are arriving in your SAP data index and are routed to their sourcetypes: you have completed Verify Your Data.
  • The search tier meets the LogServ App Prerequisites. KV Store must be enabled; it is by default.
  • You can sign in as a user that holds a role named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin. Only these roles see the App’s Settings page, where step 8 runs.

Upgrading an existing install? Follow Upgrading to This Release instead. It lists the Dashboard Data rows each upgrade must rebuild.

docs.title: About the LogServ App
docs.text:
The LogServ App provides:

  • The dashboards and the Environment Topology view: one Environment Health landing page and four groups (Applications, Integration, Security, Platform). See the Dashboards Overview.
  • The Data Doctor (Platform → Diagnostics), which explains empty panels and checks the health of the whole install. See Data Doctor (Diagnostics).
  • Search-time field extractions (EXTRACT / EVAL / FIELDALIAS) for every SAP-specific sourcetype the Data TA routes, and the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro that points the dashboards at your SAP data index.
  • Enterprise Security content: correlation searches, asset and identity feeds and anomaly searches. See Enterprise Security Integration.
  • An AI Assistant panel, which ships disabled. It is optional; see step 9.

The LogServ App contains no Python code, no REST handlers and no data inputs. The published package is the full-LLM build; to keep the AI Assistant to predefined prompts only, see Restricting the LLM Path.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose where to install
  2. Install the search-tier add-ons
  3. Download the LogServ App
  4. Install the LogServ App
  5. Update the index macro (only if your index is not sap_logserv_logs)
  6. Open the App and check that it sees your data
  7. Run the first health check
  8. Seed the dashboards: the Dashboard Data backfill
  9. Optional: set up the AI Assistant

docs.title: 1. Where to install
docs.text:
Install the LogServ App on the search tier only:

  • Single Splunk instance: on that instance, next to the Data TA. Splunk merges the two apps’ configurations at runtime.
  • Splunk Enterprise with a separate search tier: on the search head, or on every member of a search head cluster through its deployer (step 4).
  • Splunk Cloud Platform: on the Splunk Cloud search head.

Never install the LogServ App on heavy forwarders, indexers or the Deployment Server. For where every package goes, see Where Each Package Goes.

docs.title: 2. Install the search-tier add-ons
docs.text:
Install these Splunkbase add-ons on the same search tier as the App (each search head, the cluster members through the deployer, or the Splunk Cloud search head):

Add-on Why the App needs it Splunk Common Information Model (Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunkbase 1621), version 5.0.0 or later The App declares it as its dependency. The App’s CIM tags and its Enterprise Security content use the CIM data models. Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) It extracts the Windows event fields, such as the event code and severity. No LogServ package extracts them, so without it the Windows panels stay empty. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833) It provides the CIM and Enterprise Security fields of linux_secure, which the App does not extract. The App parses its other Linux sourcetypes itself, and its dashboards read linux_secure from the raw event text, so they work without it.

The Squid Proxy and ISC BIND add-ons are not needed: the App includes their parsing. The Splunk MCP Server is needed only for the AI Assistant (step 9). Details: LogServ App Prerequisites.

docs.title: 3. Download the LogServ App
docs.text: Download splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz from the GitHub repository.

docs.title: 4. Install the LogServ App
docs.text: Use the procedure for your platform.

docs.title: Splunk Cloud Platform
docs.text:
Install the LogServ App as a private app on your Splunk Cloud search head. You do not use a deployer on Splunk Cloud Platform.

Note

The app installation workflow available to you in Splunk Web depends on your Splunk Cloud Platform Experience: Victoria or Classic. To find your Splunk Cloud Platform Experience, in Splunk Web, click Support & Services > About.

  • Installation instructions for Classic Experience
  • Installation instructions for Victoria Experience

For the roles and capabilities a Splunk Cloud admin needs, see Splunk Cloud Considerations.

docs.title: Splunk Enterprise: single instance or standalone search head
docs.text:
1. From the Splunk Web home screen, click the gear icon next to Apps.
  2. Click Install app from file.
  3. Select the downloaded splunk_app_sap_logserv-0.1.2.tar.gz file and click Upload.
  4. If Splunk Enterprise prompts you to restart, do so.
  5. Check that the app appears in the list of apps. On the server it is at $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv.

docs.title: Splunk Enterprise: search head cluster
docs.text:
Distribute the App, and the add-ons of step 2, with the cluster’s deployer. Do not install them on the members one by one.

  1. On the deployer, extract the tarball into $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/shcluster/apps/, so that the App is at $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/shcluster/apps/splunk_app_sap_logserv.

  2. On the deployer, push the bundle to the cluster:

    $SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk apply shcluster-bundle -target https://<any-member>:8089

  3. Wait for the members to finish the restart the push starts, if it needs one.

The cluster’s captain runs each scheduled search on one member, and KV Store replicates the App’s collections to every member, so you run the backfill of step 8 once, from any member. See Behavior with multiple search heads.

docs.title: 5. Update the index macro
docs.text:
Skip this step if your SAP data index is sap_logserv_logs.

The dashboards find your data through the search macro sap_logserv_idx_macro. Both the LogServ App and the Data TA ship this macro. On a search head that has both apps, such as a single instance or a Splunk Cloud stack with the Data TA, change it in both apps: the scheduled rollups and the Dashboard Data backfill use the App’s copy, while the live dashboard panels can use the Data TA’s copy. On a search head without the Data TA, change the App’s copy.

Follow the single procedure in Renaming an Index, then check the result in step 6.

docs.title: 6. Open the App and check that it sees your data
docs.text:
1. In Splunk Web, open Splunk App for SAP LogServ. It opens on Environment Health, with a navigation rail on the left: Environment Health, Topology, Applications, Integration, Security, Platform, and below a divider Settings (admin roles only) and About. The Dashboards Overview describes the rail, the header and the controls every dashboard shares.

  2. In the Search app, run:

    `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by sourcetype

    It must return events from your SAP data index, split across the SAP sourcetypes.

If the search returns nothing:

  • Check that events are arriving: Verify Your Data. The Data TA parses and routes the events where the inputs run (your heavy forwarders, a single instance, or a Splunk Cloud stack that runs the inputs itself); your cloud’s ingest add-on collects them.
  • Check that the macro points at your index (step 5).
  • Check that your role can search the index. On Splunk Enterprise the stock user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so a user who holds that role, or a role that imports it, can already search your SAP data index. A role with a narrowed list of allowed indexes (Settings → Roles → role → Indexes) needs your SAP data index added.

docs.title: 7. Run the first health check
docs.text:
Open Platform → Diagnostics and let its checks finish. Confirm that the summary names your SAP data index and the add-ons of step 2, then click Download report (PDF) and keep the report as the install’s starting point. On a fresh install the History column reads NEVER BUILT, or INCOMPLETE once the first hourly run has written an hour or two; that is expected until step 8.

Details: First health check after install.

docs.title: 8. Seed the dashboards: the Dashboard Data backfill
docs.text:
Most dashboard panels read hourly rollups that start empty. Without a backfill they fill in one hour at a time from the next hourly run, so any install whose index already holds events needs this step: events loaded with AWS S3 Direct, ingest that ran before the App was installed, or a few days of normal arrival.

  1. Sign in as a user with a role named admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin.
  2. Open Settings → Dashboard Data.
  3. In Backfill window, pick a window that covers the history your index holds: 30 days is the default; 60, 90, 180 and 365 days and a Custom range of whole UTC days, back to the 365-day retention, are also offered. After an AWS S3 Direct load, use a custom range that matches the dates you loaded.
  4. Click Run backfill. Start it outside the nightly retention window (00:34-00:58, 01:30-01:58 and 02:34-02:36 in the search head’s time zone), and keep the page open until every row has finished.
  5. Go back to Platform → Diagnostics and click Re-run checks. A row reads COMPLETE once its rollup holds data reaching back at least 29 days, so it needs events of that rollup’s log types at least that old in your index. A row whose log types you do not collect stays NEVER BUILT, and a row with less history in the index reads INCOMPLETE; neither means the backfill failed. If the backfill finishes with issues, Settings → Dashboard Data says so and marks the affected rollups in its table: run the backfill again to retry them.

Details, including the late-arriving data check: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

Enterprise Security content runs by default

The App’s 22 Enterprise Security searches (splunk_sap_logserv_es_*) ship enabled and run on this search head whether or not Enterprise Security is installed. If this search head has no Enterprise Security, consider turning them off: see Disabling or tuning the ES content. The AI Assistant’s Security prompts run 13 of these searches on demand, so if you use those prompts, turn off only the schedules of those 13, as that section describes.

docs.title: 9. Optional: set up the AI Assistant
docs.text:
The AI Assistant ships disabled: no button, panel or route appears until an admin turns it on. To use it:

  • Install the Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) 1.1.0 or later on the same search head as the LogServ App; 1.2.1 or later is recommended, because it fixes SVD-2026-1004. The predefined prompts run through the MCP Server’s Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. The App’s health check only refuses versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix), so 1.0.3 to 1.0.5 pass that check but the predefined prompts fail. There is no upper version limit. Installation and authentication: Splunk MCP Setup.
  • Grant the MCP Server’s mcp_tool_execute capability to every role that will use the AI Assistant. The MCP Server (version 1.1.0) grants it only to admin and sc_admin. See Roles and Capabilities.
  • As an admin, open Settings → AI Assistant → General, turn on Enable AI Assistant and click Save Defaults. Accept the AI Assistant — Liability terms dialog that opens and, while audit forwarding is off (the default), the Audit log integrity dialog after it; nothing is saved until you do. The liability dialog appears every time the AI Assistant is turned on, and again when its terms change. The AI Assistant button then appears at the right end of the header’s second row.

If the panel opens a setup wizard instead of the chat, the MCP Server is missing or older than the App accepts, or your role lacks mcp_tool_execute: see Splunk MCP Setup.

The predefined prompts need no LLM provider credential. The shipped default provider is Mock: until an admin selects a provider and stores its credential, a typed question gets a canned mock reply and no vendor is contacted.

Full procedure: Set Up the AI Assistant.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Explore the dashboards: Dashboards Overview.
  • Keep the dashboards current and rebuild late-arriving days: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.
  • Change what is filtered at ingest: Configuring Filters.
  • Turn on the AI Assistant: Set Up the AI Assistant.
  • Something does not look right: Troubleshooting.

docs.title: LogServ App Prerequisites
docs.text: Use this page before you install the LogServ App (splunk_app_sap_logserv, shown in Splunk Web as Splunk App for SAP LogServ): it lists what the search tier needs beside the App, and who can use and administer it. The ingest tier’s requirements are on Plan and Prerequisites, and the two indexes are created first, on the indexer tier (see Create the indexes).

docs.title: Search-Tier Requirements
docs.text:
Install these on the search tier: the search head, the Splunk Cloud search head, or every member of a search head cluster.

Requirement Version Why Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform Splunk Enterprise 9.4.3 or later. Splunk Cloud Platform: Victoria Experience, checked on 10.x (most recently 10.5.2605.10); see Plan and Prerequisites 9.4.3 is the minimum supported version: the platform this release is tested on. The App bundles its own React, @splunk/react-ui, @splunk/visualizations and @xyflow/react, so the floor is a support baseline, not a component dependency. Splunk Common Information Model (Splunk_SA_CIM, Splunkbase 1621) 5.0.0 or later The only dependency the App’s app.manifest declares. The App’s CIM event tags (Authentication, Change, Network Sessions, Network Resolution, Web) and its Enterprise Security content build on it. Free on Splunkbase, and bundled with Enterprise Security. Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) — (no minimum checked) Required for the Windows panels. No LogServ package extracts fields from XmlWinEventLog, so without it the Windows dashboard’s Event Code, Severity and Service panels stay empty. Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833) — (no minimum checked) The CIM and Enterprise Security fields of linux_secure. The App parses its other Linux sourcetypes itself. KV Store enabled and healthy The dashboards read hourly rollups that scheduled searches write to KV Store; Environment Topology and the App’s settings are stored there too. On a search head cluster, KV Store replication must be healthy. Search head cluster optional Supported. Install the App and the add-ons through the deployer; see Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness for how the scheduled searches behave on a cluster.

These add-ons go on the search tier only, not on the Deployment Server, the heavy forwarders or the indexers: the Data TA parses LogServ events before it gives them these sourcetypes, so the add-ons’ parse-time settings never apply to them.

No standalone Squid Proxy or ISC BIND add-ons

The parsing of the archived Splunk Add-on for Squid Proxy and Splunk Add-on for ISC BIND is built into the LogServ App. Do not install the standalone add-ons. If either is enabled beside the App, both parse the same events, and the App’s home view shows a dismissible banner recommending that you remove it (Settings > Manage Apps).

docs.title: Roles and Access
docs.text:
• Searching the data. Every role that uses the dashboards must be able to search sap_logserv_logs. On Splunk Enterprise the default user role allows *, which matches every index whose name does not start with _, so it and the roles that import it (such as power) can already search the index. Add the index to any role with a narrowed list (Settings > Roles > role > Indexes). On Splunk Cloud, check each role’s Indexes tab the same way.
  • App admins. The App treats only roles named exactly admin, sc_admin or sc_subadmin as admins, and only these roles may write the App’s settings and the dashboards’ KV Store rollups. So only they can open Settings (its AI Assistant and Dashboard Data tabs) and run Clear and Backfill on the dashboard data. A user whose admin role has any other name sees “403 — Admin access required” there. Give the people who run the App one of these three roles; whether a role that imports one of them is enough has not been tested.
  • The audit index. Grant read access to logserv_ai_assistant_audit only as Restricting who can read the audit index describes.

Enterprise Security content ships enabled

The App ships its Enterprise Security searches (the splunk_sap_logserv_es_* saved searches, 22 in this release) scheduled and enabled. On a search head without Enterprise Security, we recommend turning them off; see Disabling or tuning the ES content. If you use the AI Assistant’s Security prompts, do not disable the 13 searches they run (a disabled search makes its prompt fail): turn off only their schedule, and disable the other 9 (see the linked section).

Optional: the AI Assistant

The AI Assistant ships disabled, and nothing in this page’s table needs it. To use it:

  • Install the Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase 7931) 1.1.0 or later on the same search head as the App; 1.2.1 or later is recommended (Splunk advisory SVD-2026-1004). The predefined prompts use its Run Saved Search tool, which first shipped in 1.1.0. The App’s health check blocks only versions below 1.0.3 (the CVE-2026-20205 fix) and sets no upper bound; the newest version verified is 2.0.0.
  • Optionally, install the Splunk AI Assistant (Splunkbase 7245) beside it. The LogServ App does not need it: it uses only the MCP Server’s own splunk_run_saved_search and splunk_run_query tools.
  • An admin turns the AI Assistant on and answers its acknowledgements: the liability terms, asked each time it is turned on, and, while audit forwarding is off (the default), the audit-log integrity terms, asked the first time and again when they change (Set Up the AI Assistant).
  • The predefined prompts need no LLM provider or credential. Free-form questions need a provider and its credential, which an admin configures; the shipped default provider is a mock that contacts no vendor.

The steps are on Set Up the AI Assistant. To turn off or restrict the free-form LLM path, see Restricting the LLM Path.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: • Install the App and Seed the Dashboards

docs.title: Dashboards Overview
docs.text: The LogServ App’s dashboards are organized as in the App itself: one landing page, the Environment Topology view, and four groups (Applications, Integration, Security, Platform). This page lists them and describes the controls every dashboard shares. The App is built on @splunk/react-ui + @splunk/visualizations + @xyflow/react, ships as a single React bundle, and requires Splunk 9.4.3 or later.

docs.title: Navigation rail and header
docs.text:
The navigation rail on the left holds, in this order:

Environment Health (default landing) · Topology · Applications › · Integration › · Security › · Platform › · Settings (admin-tier roles only) · About

Each of the four groups opens a flyout beside the rail that lists its dashboards, with a ✓ on the one you are viewing. The button at the top of the rail collapses it to a 56 px strip of icons; the choice is remembered per user in the browser.

The header’s first row carries the product name, the App version and build pills (on windows wider than 900 px) and the light/dark theme toggle. Its second row carries the global time range (the Last 24h / 7d / 30d / 90d pills and Splunk’s own time-range picker) and, on the right, Actions ▾ · Refresh · AI Assistant (when enabled).

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
Dashboard or group What it covers Environment Health Cross-cutting operations view of errors, security failures and performance across the whole SAP landscape. The default landing page. Reads all sourcetypes. Environment Topology Interactive graph of SAP systems, integration partners and endpoints, built from sap:abap:gateway, sap:abap:icm, sap:saprouter, sap:hana:audit, sap:hana:tracelogs and sap:webdispatcher:access, with IP-node names also from XmlWinEventLog, sap:sapstartsrv, linux_secure and linux_messages_syslog. Refreshed hourly from KV Store (the IP-node names once a day); named layouts saved per user. Applications The SAP application runtime: ABAP Network & Security, ABAP Operations, Work Process Performance, HANA Audit, HANA Trace. Integration How SAP connects to other systems: SAP Services, SAP Router, Cloud Connector, Web Dispatcher, Web and API Performance. Security Cross-source security and compliance views: Network Perimeter, Cross-Stack Authentication, Change & Configuration Activity. Platform The infrastructure and ingest underneath SAP: Data Pipeline Overview, DNS Analytics, Linux, Windows, Proxy, Host Details, Multi-Cloud Overview, and the Data Doctor’s Diagnostics page.

Each group page lists its dashboards with their purpose and key data sources.

docs.title: Time range
docs.text: The selected time range is held app-wide: it follows you when you move between dashboards. Drill-downs carry it to their destination (see Click-Through Drilldowns).

docs.title: Cloud filter
docs.text: Every dashboard except Multi-Cloud Overview, Environment Topology, Diagnostics and Settings carries a Cloud filter (the button reads Cloud: All; options All / aws / azure / gcp) in its title row, to the left of the auto-refresh picker. Choosing a provider filters every panel on the dashboard to that cloud. The choice is global and remembered per user in this browser, so it carries across dashboard navigation and page reloads. Leave it on All to see the whole estate. Events with no cloud attribution are counted as aws, matching the Multi-Cloud Overview convention.

docs.title: Per-dashboard auto-refresh
docs.text: Each dashboard’s title row carries a Refresh picker (Never / 30s / 1m / 5m / 15m / 30m / 1hr), to the right of the Cloud filter. The selection is per user and per dashboard: your choice on Environment Health doesn’t carry over to HANA Audit. It persists across browser sessions in Splunk KV Store. The Diagnostics page has no auto-refresh picker; it re-runs its checks on demand.

docs.title: Refresh the current view on demand
docs.text: The header’s second row carries a Refresh button, between the Actions menu and the AI Assistant button. Clicking it re-runs every panel on the dashboard you’re currently viewing for the selected time range. It is distinct from the per-dashboard auto-refresh picker above (which re-runs on a timer) and from each panel’s own Refresh toolbar action (which re-runs a single panel). Because it lives in the app-wide header, it’s available on every dashboard and on the Environment Topology view. On the Environment Topology view it re-runs the detail searches; the graph itself re-reads only from the view’s own toolbar Refresh button.

docs.title: In-dashboard help: the ? icon
docs.text: Every dashboard’s title row ends with a blue rotating ? help icon. Clicking it opens this online documentation in a new browser tab, at the page for the dashboard you’re looking at. For multi-tab dashboards (Data Pipeline Overview and Host Details) the icon is present on every tab and always links to the same dashboard’s page.

docs.title: Per-panel toolbar
docs.text:
Every chart and table panel header carries a small action toolbar plus a “<1m ago” stamp showing when the panel’s search last ran:

Action What it does Diagnose Runs the Data Doctor’s checks on this panel and opens the diagnosis drawer — explains why the panel is empty or partially blank (Data Doctor). Open in Search Opens Splunk’s Search app in a new tab with the panel’s dispatched query and the current time range pre-applied (the rollup read for a cached panel; the raw query at sub-hour ranges). Download (CSV) Exports the panel’s current result set as CSV. Inspect Opens Splunk’s Job Inspector for the panel’s last search — useful for diagnosing performance or verifying what ran. Refresh Re-runs the panel’s search immediately.

KPI single-value cards show the loading spinner and a corner Diagnose button (revealed on hover or keyboard focus) but no full toolbar — they have no tabular result to export or inspect. While any panel’s search is in flight it renders a dot-ring loading spinner with “Loading data…”.

docs.title: Dashboard Export (Actions Menu)
docs.text: The header’s Actions menu includes Download PNG and Download PDF. Both captures use html2canvas to render the full dashboard DOM (including off-screen content), so the saved output always covers the entire dashboard length — not just what’s visible in the viewport. Useful for sharing in slide decks, embedding in incident reports, or capturing a dashboard’s state at a specific moment for compliance evidence. The same menu carries the two Data Doctor reports — Diagnose dashboard (PDF) and Environment report (PDF).

docs.title: Which build am I running? The About dialog
docs.text: The About item at the bottom of the navigation rail opens a dialog showing the app icon, the product name, and the version, build number and build date (UTC) of the app you are running. Use it to confirm an upgrade landed, or to quote the exact build when reporting an issue. The values are read from the app’s own app.conf at build time (the date is stamped as the bundle is compiled), so they always match the installed bundle. The header’s App and build pills show the same version and build number at a glance.

docs.title: Searching LogServ data
docs.text: All dashboards use the sap_logserv_idx_macro macro to query the LogServ index. You can use this same macro in your own searches: `sap_logserv_idx_macro` | stats count by sourcetype. Some App builds change search-time fields that your own searches may read; when you upgrade, check Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Performance and data freshness
docs.text: The dashboards are tuned to stay fast at high event volume: most panels read from an hourly KV-Store rollup layer rather than scanning raw events on every open. After installing on an index that already holds history, an admin runs a one-time backfill. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness for how each panel sources its data, what “hourly fresh” means, and the backfill step.

docs.title: Visual Style
docs.text:
All dashboards share a consistent framed-card visual language, built on Cisco’s Magnetic design tokens, so that patterns are easy to recognize as you move between views. The app ships light and dark modes — toggled via the sun/moon button at the right end of the header, persisted per user — and every color is a mode-resolved design token rather than a fixed hex:

  • Page background with slightly lighter panel cards outlined by a muted border token — each visualization sits inside its own framed card with consistent spacing
  • KPI typography — large numeric headline with a small muted label; number color carries semantic meaning (white for neutral counts, red for errors/failures/denials, orange for warnings, teal for healthy/positive signals)
  • Standard colors — a single semantic red token is used across all error/failure signals so that “red means something went wrong” is unambiguous in both modes
  • Tables use a fixed header row with alternating row striping; clickable cells are highlighted in the accent color to indicate a drilldown affordance
  • Charts strip non-essential ink (no axis titles, no data labels, no progress bars) so the data shape is what your eye lands on

The implementation uses styled-components on top of @splunk/react-ui primitives.

docs.title: KPI Sparklines
docs.text:
Most KPI panels display a small inline sparkline directly below the headline number. The sparkline visualizes the daily trend across the dashboard’s current time range, so you get both the cumulative total and the shape of how that total accumulated in a single glance. There is no separate “up/down by N” trend value — the sparkline alone carries the trend signal.

Sparklines come in a few flavors depending on what the KPI measures:

  • Count-based KPIs (e.g., Total Events, Auth Failures) — sparkline shows daily event count
  • Distinct-count KPIs (e.g., Active Hosts, Unique Components) — sparkline shows daily distinct count
  • Rate KPIs (e.g., HTTP Error Rate, Web Error Rate %) — sparkline shows daily error percentage
  • Volume KPIs (e.g., Total Volume, Total Bandwidth) — sparkline shows daily MB; headline shows formatted KB/MB/GB
  • No-data rendering — while a KPI’s search runs, the card shows a small spinner; a search that returns no rows renders an em-dash (—) plus a short inline explanation of why (see Data Doctor). KPIs with an empty-safe SPL wrap render 0 instead, with a flat-zero sparkline

Hovering a sparkline shows the value of the nearest day and its date. A sparkline’s days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, and the hover shows the date in that zone. The Beaconing Domains sparklines are the exception: beaconing is detected per UTC day, so each of their points is one UTC day and the hover shows its date labelled (UTC day). A day’s beaconing count is written once that UTC day has ended, so on DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter, whose lines run to the end of the selected range, a UTC day that has not ended yet is drawn at 0 and its hover reads (UTC day, not yet computed). That is today’s UTC day, and west of UTC also the next one, which begins before your local day ends.

docs.title: Chart Time Buckets
docs.text:
Time charts follow the time-range picker: the wider the range, the wider each bar or line point (its bucket), so a chart stays readable from Last 24 hours to Last 90 days. Every time chart prints the bucket it is drawing in its subtitle – for example Proxy request count — span 6h.

Selected range Charts counted from the index Summary-backed charts Under 90 minutes 1 minute 1 minute (they read raw events at this range) 90 minutes to 6 hours 1 minute 1 hour Up to 24 hours (Last 24 hours) 15 minutes 1 hour Up to 7 days (Last 7 days) 1 hour 1 hour Up to 30 days (Last 30 days) 6 hours 6 hours Longer (Last 90 days) 1 day 1 day

Summary-backed charts never draw buckets finer than an hour, because the summaries they read are hourly (see Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness). Day-sized buckets, and the days of the KPI sparklines, follow your Splunk time-zone preference; shorter buckets are aligned to UTC, so a 6-hour bucket starts at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 or 18:00 UTC.

docs.title: Click-Through Drilldowns
docs.text:
Table rows are the main drill-down surface; Environment Health additionally makes its KPI cards and chart panels clickable, and other dashboards wire panel-level drill-downs selectively. A pointer cursor and a hover highlight mark what you can click:

  • Clicking a KPI opens a contextual destination — typically the related drill-down dashboard with the current time range preserved, or Splunk’s Search app with a pre-built SPL query for cross-cutting KPIs (e.g., the Environment Health “Total Errors” KPI runs a cross-cutting OR search spanning every error-bearing sourcetype across the estate).
  • Clicking a table row opens a filtered view — Host Details for host columns, the relevant specialist dashboard for sourcetype columns, or Splunk’s Search app with the row’s context spliced into a SPL filter.
  • Clicking a chart panel — on dashboards that wire a panel-level drill-down, clicking anywhere in the panel (outside its toolbar) opens the related dashboard or search. Individual chart points are not separately clickable.
  • Every drill-down opens in a new browser tab with noopener,noreferrer security flags. Time-range query params (?earliest=...&latest=...) are preserved across the navigation, and the destination sets its time-range picker from them, so it loads at the source dashboard’s window.

The AI Assistant’s result tiles carry their own drill-down chips back into these dashboards; see Drill-down Chips.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text:
The Environment Health dashboard is a single-pane-of-glass operations view that aggregates the most critical signals from across the entire SAP landscape. Instead of switching between individual dashboards to piece together overall health, administrators can use this dashboard to immediately identify active errors, security failures, and performance degradation. Every panel links to the relevant detailed dashboard for investigation, making this the recommended starting point for daily operations monitoring and incident triage.

Environment Health is the default landing page when you open the LogServ App. It is the first entry in the navigation rail, above Topology and the four dashboard groups. Its panels are listed below in screen order: the KPI row, then the charts, then the two tables.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Total Errors – Aggregate count of errors across all monitored sourcetypes. Click to open a detailed search showing errors by category, sourcetype, affected hosts, and last-seen time.
  • HANA Failed Ops – Count of non-successful HANA audit operations (login failures, permission denials, DDL errors). Click to drill down to HANA Audit dashboard.
  • Auth Failures – Combined count of sapstartsrv authentication failures and HANA audit connection failures. Click to drill down to SAP Services dashboard.
  • Firewall Drops at Host – Count of Linux kernel firewall drops of packets addressed to the host itself (IN_DROP, the INPUT chain) across all monitored hosts. Drops of traffic a host was routing on to another system (FWD_DROP, in transit) are not counted as errors here; the Linux and Network Perimeter dashboards show both. Click to drill down to Linux dashboard.
  • Web Error Rate – Percentage of Web Dispatcher requests returning 4xx/5xx status codes. Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
  • Beaconing Domains – Count of DNS domains exhibiting periodic query patterns that may indicate malware or C2 communication. Its sparkline has one point per UTC day (beaconing is detected per UTC day), and hovering a point shows that UTC date. Click to drill down to DNS Analytics dashboard.
  • Data Pipeline – Events/Day (Avg) – Average daily event volume over the selected range (days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, and the current partial day counts as a day), with a daily sparkline, for monitoring pipeline health and detecting ingestion gaps. Click to drill down to the Data Pipeline Overview dashboard.
  • Event Volume Trend – Full-width chart of total events over time across all sourcetypes. Click to drill down to the Data Pipeline Overview dashboard.
  • ABAP Error Trend – Stacked column chart of ABAP errors over time by sub-source (Dispatcher, ICM, Gateway; the ICM series counts dev_icm messages logged as ERROR). Click to drill down to the ABAP Network & Security dashboard.
  • HANA Error Trend – Stacked column chart of HANA errors over time (Audit Failures, Trace Errors). Click to drill down to HANA Audit dashboard.
  • Security Error Trend – Stacked column chart of security errors over time (Auth Failures, Firewall Drops at Host). Click to drill down to SAP Services dashboard.
  • Web/Network Error Trend – Stacked column chart of web/network errors over time (WebDisp 4xx/5xx, Router Errors, Proxy Denied). Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
  • OS/Infra Error Trend – Stacked column chart of Windows events over time by severity (High, Medium). Click to drill down to Windows dashboard.
  • Cloud Connector Error Trend – Stacked column chart of Cloud Connector HTTP errors over time (4xx Client, 5xx Server). Click to drill down to Cloud Connector dashboard.
  • Web Dispatcher Response Time – Column chart of average response time (ms) over time for web dispatcher requests. Click to drill down to Web Dispatcher dashboard.
  • ICM Warnings & Errors – Stacked column chart of ABAP ICM trace messages over time by class (ERROR, WARNING). Click to drill down to the ABAP Network & Security dashboard.
  • Recent Critical Events – Table of the most recent critical signals (up to 200): HANA audit non-successful operations, ABAP dispatcher ERROR/FATAL, HANA trace fatal, sapstartsrv auth failures, and Windows critical-severity events, most-recent first. Click any row to drill down to Host Details for that host.
  • Affected Hosts – Table of hosts ranked by total error count with breakdowns by category (ABAP, HANA, Services, Firewall (at host), Other). Click any host to drill down to Host Details.

docs.title: Drill-Down Behavior
docs.text:
Every KPI card, chart panel, and table row on this dashboard is clickable and opens its drill-down destination in a new browser tab with the source dashboard’s currently-selected time range pre-applied (?earliest=...&latest=...). The destination’s TimeRangeProvider parses the URL and hydrates its initial time-range from those params on mount, so a click from “Last 7 days” lands you in the destination at the same window. Two destination patterns:

  • Cross-dashboard drill-downs — most KPIs and charts navigate to the relevant React dashboard (/applications/hana-audit, /integration/cloud-connector, etc.).
  • Splunk Search drill-downs — the Total Errors KPI runs a cross-cutting OR query spanning every error-bearing sourcetype it counts — a query no single dashboard owns; it opens Splunk’s universal Search app with the SPL pre-filled. Same time-range carry-through.

The dashboard’s title-row toolbar carries a Refresh picker so you can have the page tick continuously (Never / 30s / 1m / 5m / 15m / 30m / 1hr) for use as an operations wallboard.

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
The dashboard reads three kinds of source, chosen per panel for the cheapest path that stays exact:

  • Summary-backed panels — the error/severity KPIs, all six error-trend charts, the web error-rate and response-time panels, the ICM warnings and errors panel, the Auth Failures KPI and the Affected Hosts matrix read the logserv_severity_rollup KV Store collection (metrics toterr, trend, tophost, web, icmsev, authfail — each pre-computes one panel group’s exact classification per hour). Populated at minute :10 of every hour by logserv_severity_aggregate, which classifies events from thirteen sourcetypes across the estate (HANA audit + tracelogs, the ABAP family, Web Dispatcher, SAP Cloud Connector, SAProuter, sapstartsrv, Windows event logs, Linux secure and Squid proxy).
  • The Beaconing Domains KPI reads the daily logserv_beaconing_rollup (populated at 00:30 by a per-UTC-day gap-variance detection over DNS query events — daily cadence because the detection needs at least a day of inter-arrival history).
  • Pure-count pipeline panels run tstats directly against indexed fields — no summary needed, fast at any volume.
  • Recent Critical Events is a live event listing: it dispatches its SPL against the raw events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent matches.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). After install, Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill fills it with the history your index holds: the last 30 days by default, or up to 365 days, or a custom range (see Backfilling on first install). The Cloud filter in the title row filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Rising error trend – An upward slope in any error category chart indicates a worsening condition. Correlate the timing with recent changes, deployments, or infrastructure events. Each chart drills directly to the relevant dashboard for investigation.
  • Auth failure spikes – Sudden increases in the Auth Failures KPI or Security Error Trend may indicate brute-force login attempts, expired credentials, or misconfigured service accounts. Cross-reference with the HANA Audit and SAP Services dashboards.
  • HANA audit failures – Non-zero HANA Failed Ops always warrant investigation. Failed operations may indicate unauthorized access attempts, privilege escalation, or application misconfigurations.
  • Cloud Connector errors – A spike in the Cloud Connector Error Trend (especially 5xx Server errors) may indicate backend system unavailability, network issues between the SCC and SAP BTP, or certificate expiration.
  • Pipeline volume drops – A sudden drop in the Event Volume Trend may indicate an SQS queue backup, S3 input failure, HF outage, or filter misconfiguration. Check the Data Pipeline Overview for per-host visibility.
  • Response time degradation – An increasing trend in Web Dispatcher response time often precedes user-facing performance complaints. Check the ICM Warnings & Errors panel and the Web Dispatcher’s 5xx responses for the same window.
  • Host concentration – If the Affected Hosts table shows errors concentrated on one or two hosts, those systems may have a localized issue (disk full, service crash, misconfiguration) rather than an environment-wide problem.

docs.title: Why This View Matters
docs.text:
The Environment Topology view answers a question every SAP administrator has: “what’s actually talking to what?” Traditional dashboards show events, errors, and aggregates per source — but the shape of how SAP systems integrate with each other (RFC partners, HANA tenant relationships, web traffic boundaries, cross-zone connections) is hidden in those tabular surfaces. This view materializes that shape as an interactive graph drawn from your existing log data — no new ingest, no CMDB integration, no tagging effort required.

Use it to:

  • Validate that your topology matches the as-designed architecture (every system shows up; no rogue partners are talking inbound).
  • Investigate a single SID’s call surface — who calls it, what does it call, where are the errors concentrated?
  • Drill from an edge (a single integration relationship) into the raw events with one click — every edge carries a denormalized SPL filter expression so you can pivot to Splunk’s universal search instantly.
  • Onboard a new analyst by giving them a one-page picture of the SAP landscape before they start digging into individual dashboards.
  • Spot orphaned IPs / hosts that don’t belong to any known SID — these are typically misconfigured load balancers, scanners, or unauthorized integration partners.

This view replaces the manual hand-drawn architecture diagrams that SAP admin teams typically maintain in slides or wikis. Because it’s data-driven, it stays current as systems are added or retired.

docs.title: What’s on Screen
docs.text:
The view is laid out in four regions:

Top toolbar — the layout-mode dropdown (Force / Layered / Tree), Refresh button (re-runs the KV Store fetch while preserving saved positions), Save Layout, Load Layout dropdown with the ⚙ Manage Layouts entry, Snap mode toggle, the saved-layout name chip showing what’s currently loaded, a Saved/Unsaved-changes indicator next to it, and a legend row of colour swatches — one per integration type, matching the edge colours on the canvas.

Left sidebar — two stacked panels. The Systems · Integration panel rolls up the inventory (systems, total calls, partner count) and lists each SAP system with a per-system call-volume bar; High Traffic systems (see below) render highlighted. The Integration types panel is a checkbox list of the nine integration types (RFC sync, iDoc async, qRFC, tRFC, bgRFC, Web service / SOAP, OData / Gateway, BTP iFlow / CPI, SAP Router) — un-ticking a type dims its edges in the canvas without removing them. Three of them carry edges today: RFC (sync) draws RFC connections and HANA tenant traffic, Web service / SOAP draws HTTP and HANA audit edges, and SAP Router draws the connections an SAP Router routed; the other six stay listed so that saved layouts keep their filter state. The Edge Details pane names each edge by what it records (HTTP, RFC, HANA Audit, HANA Tenant, SAP Router).

Center canvas — the interactive graph itself, rendered with @xyflow/react. Nodes:

  • High Traffic SIDs — the five SAP systems with the most total calls touching them (inbound + outbound + bidirectional) in the visible window, ranked at render time. There is no configured focus list — the ranking is purely data-derived, and only SAP systems compete for the five slots (a high-volume client IP cannot occupy one). On an estate with five or fewer systems, every SID is High Traffic.
  • Regular Traffic SIDs — every other internal SAP system. Same large circle and outline as High Traffic; the kinds differ only in the panel’s Kind row and the Systems-panel highlight.
  • Every SAP system circle carries an interior icon: an app-server rack for application systems, a database cylinder for database systems.
  • HANA tenant databases — full-size circles with a combined app-servers + database icon, tagged “APP SERVERS - HANA TENANT” (chip: “HANA TENANT”). A tenant is a logical database inside a HANA system, named after the application SID it backs — its circle deliberately shares that name.
  • DB-tagged partners — circular discs with a cylinder icon when the partner is a database vendor (HANA, Oracle, MSSQL, Postgres, DB2). HANA systems specifically are tagged when their SID appears as a sap_sid clause on a hana_tenant-type edge — distinct from HANA tenants (which are logical databases inside a HANA system, named after the application SID they back).
  • SAP Router hosts — rounded squares with a ⇄ routing glyph, tagged “SAP ROUTER”: the host whose SAP Router log recorded the routed connections. A router is never folded into an SAP system, even when the inventory attributes the same host name to one — a VM that runs both an SAP instance and the router keeps both, the system’s circle and the router’s square.
  • Other partners — rounded squares for non-DB external endpoints (web partners, gateways, generic IPs).

IP-labeled squares can carry name lines. When the logs themselves identify the machine or the people behind an IP endpoint, the square renders up to two extra lines directly under the IP: the hostname, and a user line (the user name when exactly one distinct user was seen; a count like “7 users” otherwise — hover the line for the full list). The evidence comes from four same-event sources, refreshed daily into the logserv_topology_ip_enrichment KV Store collection: HANA audit client registrations (client_ip + client host name + executing_user), Windows successful-logon events (4624 — IpAddress + WorkstationName + TargetUserName), SAP start service authentication lines (auth_user + remote address) and Linux sshd session lines. Two honesty rules govern what renders: a hostname shows only when it is unambiguous — the IP must map to exactly one machine name (a short name and its FQDN count as one), and that name must not be claimed by a crowd of IPs — and nothing is ever guessed (gateway logs, for example, record partner hostnames and peer IPs on different lines, so they are deliberately not correlated). The names are “latest known” rather than time-range-scoped: they do not blink out when you narrow the picker, and the Details panel’s “Names as of” row tells you how fresh the mapping is.

Each SID and DB partner carries a 3-segment health ring painted around its perimeter, showing the proportion of normal (green) / warning (orange) / error (red) calls in the visible time window. Non-DB partners (the rounded squares) carry an equivalent rounded-square perimeter outline. Nodes with no calls or with all calls in a single bucket render as a solid full ring in the dominant color (a healthy node with all-normal calls shows a solid green ring; an idle node still shows green so you can tell the canvas painting succeeded). The classification: edges with errorRate < 10% route their errors to the warning bucket; edges with errorRate ≥ 10% route to the error bucket; everything else is normal. HANA-tagged nodes additionally route WARNING-severity trace events and slow hdbcons commands (hana_op_duration_ms > 1000 — the HANA console commands timed in the tenant’s trace files, each converted to milliseconds from the unit its line records) into the warning bucket as a vendor-specific health signal — these counts are first-class fields on the edge bucket rows, computed at hourly aggregation time from sap:hana:tracelogs.

Edges render as gently bowed curves drawn center-to-center between nodes and clipped at each node’s visible boundary — arrowheads land on the health ring / outline outer edge rather than inside the node. When two systems call each other in both directions, the two edges bow apart so each direction stays separately visible and clickable. Edge labels sit at the curve’s apex.

Right sidebar (selection-driven) — what shows here depends on whether you’ve selected a node or an edge.

When a node is selected, four tabs surface that node’s per-selection context:

  • Overview — a facts table, an hourly chart (Count / hr: the node’s log events per hour), and the partner breakdown. The facts table splits the node’s calls and connections three ways — inbound, outbound and bidirectional — alongside the total, using exact figures so they reconcile against everything below them. On SAP system and tenant nodes it also shows “Hosts (in range)” — the distinct hosts that logged the node’s events in the window, the same figure the Hosts tab’s caption reports (both read the same hourly rollup; on a tenant node the count is scoped by the shared name and the panel says so inline). The same number appears as a Hosts row in the hover tooltip on SAP system circles. On IP-labeled partner squares with name evidence (see IP-labeled squares can carry name lines above), the facts table adds Hostname (with its evidence source), Users (every user seen from that address, grouped by source) and Names as of rows directly under the Tag row. The hourly chart is hardcoded to the last 24 hours regardless of the global time-range picker (its purpose is “what’s happening RIGHT NOW on this node,” not “what happened over the picker’s window”). For HANA-tagged nodes, an additional roll-up section shows tenants list, tenant trace events, p95/max hdbcons command duration, and auth success/fail counts — derived from incident edges in JS, no extra SPL.

    Beneath those sit two partner donuts: partners that call this system, and partners this system calls. Each lists every partner — there is no “other” bucket and the legend is not capped, so a system with a wide fan-out makes the panel taller rather than the list shorter. Edges the data records as bidirectional (HANA Tenant traffic) are counted on their own line instead of being assigned a direction the stored row denies. Each donut’s caption names what it counts - calls, connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections), or calls + connections when that side has both, with “total” under the donut’s centre. Legend rows show the endpoint and its count. (Inventory ownership badges render where ownership can actually vary — the Hosts tab rows and the Edge Details “By app server” table; see Self-Derived IP→SID Inventory.)

    Hover any slice (or its legend row) for that endpoint, its exact count, and its share of the chart’s total. Reach for it whenever a slice is small: a slice too small to survive its own outline is drawn slightly larger so it stays visible, so the angle of the smallest slices is approximate while the number in the tooltip is exact. The panel says so inline whenever that widening has actually been applied.

  • Top Programs — the top ABAP programs seen on this node, from sap:abap:icm’s icm_program field (top 8). RFC remote gateway services and client programs, HANA action types and web URIs are not in this tab — they surface per-edge on the Edge Details Operations tab.

  • Errors — categorized error breakdown for the node (HTTP 4xx/5xx, severity ERROR / CRITICAL / FATAL, gateway gw_error_detail and error_function). Aggregated by sourcetype + error_kind.

  • Hosts — two tables. The first lists the hosts that logged events for this system, with first-seen / last-seen / dc(sourcetype) per host — and, where the events carry them, the SAP instance numbers seen on that host (inst 00, 01) — and — on a SAP system node — an ownership verdict per row. The read returns the 100 busiest hosts; if a system has more, the panel says so rather than presenting the cap as the count.

    The second, Calls by host and edge type, breaks the node’s traffic down per receiving host. A row names a host only where the data supports one: a hostname is only ever the receiving end of a call, so per-host rows are always inbound, and everything else — calls this node makes, and traffic recorded against a system as a whole — appears as an edge-type row. Because every incident edge lands in exactly one row, the column sums to the Total calls + connections figure on the Overview tab, which makes it checkable. Note that its Calls column counts edge calls and connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections) while the Events column in the table above counts log events, from a different rollup — the two are not the same measure.

When an edge is selected, five tabs surface that edge’s per-call context:

  • Overview — endpoint cards (source / direction / target), pre-computed aggregates (call count, error count, error rate, sourcetype), and an inline activity trend chart. The pane names the counts after what the edge records: an RFC edge counts connections — a remote-gateway connection or a client session that closed, plus each distinct broken connection; the gateway trace records connections, not individual RFC calls — and its errors are the broken connections; an SAP Router edge counts routed connections (the router’s CONNECT TO lines) and failed connections (server-side receive failures that name the same target address, counted from their own trace lines, so the failure rate is capped at 100 %). RFC edges add a “By app server” table splitting the edge’s connections and broken connections by the address of the gateway that recorded them — the SAP system’s side of the connection, whichever direction it was made — with inventory owner badges: the app servers as the gateway log names them, not a full instance inventory. Connection records (a remote-gateway connection or a client session that closed) name no local address and are grouped as “(not recorded)”. The rows partition the edge’s connections, so they sum to the count above them.
  • Activity — full-width stacked-area chart of successful calls + errors over the visible time window (for RFC and SAP Router edges: connections + broken or failed connections). Computed in the browser from the same hourly rows that produce the Overview totals, so the two always agree.
  • Operations — donut chart of the top 10 entities for this edge type (HTTP URIs; RFC remote gateway services and client programs; HANA actions; HANA trace components; SAP Router target services such as sapmsXCI, 3300 or sapgw00). Its centre total and hover text count in the edge’s own unit — connections for RFC and SAP Router edges, calls for the others.
  • Performance — for HTTP edges, latency percentiles (P50 / P95 / Max) and bytes-out plus a per-status-class call-count histogram. For HANA Audit, cached auth success / auth fail headline counts plus a dispatched action-status mix. For HANA Tenant, a cached p95 + max hdbcons command duration headline (the HANA console commands timed in the tenant’s trace files, each duration converted to milliseconds from the microsecond, millisecond or second unit its line records; the p95 is a call-weighted blend of the per-hour p95s stored on the edge rows — an approximation), and below it a dispatched avg + max chart: true percentiles cannot be merged across hourly buckets, so the chart reads mean and maximum and says so inline. For RFC, a dispatched connection record mix (remote gateway connection closed / client session closed / broken connection); for SAP Router, a target role mix (message server, gateway, dispatcher, …). Neither has headline cells.
  • Errors — the top 15 failure modes with error_kind, error_detail, count, and last-seen timestamp. For HANA Audit this covers all unsuccessful operations, which is broader than the Overview row (labelled “Auth failures (CONNECT)”) directly above it. For RFC the rows come from the broken-connection lines; for SAP Router they are the failed connections by return code (rc=<code> · server-side connection failed).

Tabs that are legitimately empty

Not every tab has content for every edge type — an empty tab is not necessarily a fault. An RFC edge whose connections were all broken ones has no Operations rows (a broken connection names no remote service or client program), an SAP Router edge with only failed connections in the window has neither Operations nor Performance rows (a failure line names the target address only), and any edge type can have an empty Errors tab simply because nothing failed. The pane distinguishes the two cases: when a tab was queried and came back empty it says so, and when nothing could be queried at all it says that instead.

Selection is mutex — clicking a node clears any selected edge and vice versa, so the right pane never shows mixed context. Clicking empty canvas (the pane) clears both. Each side preserves its own preferred tab independently when you swap between selections. (This inspection selection — the cyan glow plus the Details panel — is separate from group membership below, which uses a dashed outline: a node can be inspected, in a group, both, or neither.)

docs.title: Group select and move
docs.text:
Hold Shift and drag on empty canvas to draw a selection box: every node the box touches joins the group and gains a dashed outline, and a status chip at the canvas top-right shows the count. Then drag any highlighted node to move the whole group rigidly — relative positions are preserved, and the edges follow their nodes (an edge has no position of its own, so moving the nodes is moving the edges; edges are not independently selectable). The gesture set:

  • Shift + drag on empty canvas — draw the selection box (plain drag still pans).
  • Shift / Ctrl / Cmd + click a node — add it to or remove it from the group (these clicks never open the Details panel).
  • Plain click any node — inspect it in the Details panel and release the group.
  • Escape or a click on empty canvas — clear the group.
  • Drag a highlighted node — move the whole group. Dragging a node outside the group releases the group and moves only that node.
  • Arrow keys (with a focused, selected node) — nudge the whole group.

With Snap mode on, releasing a group drag applies one shared grid offset to every member, so the group’s shape is preserved — members are not rounded to the grid independently. Group moves mark the layout Unsaved and are captured by Save Layout exactly like single-node drags. The group survives data refreshes and time-range changes; it clears when the node set itself changes (a layout-mode switch or loading a saved layout).

Bottom panel — Live Activity table showing the eight busiest integration edges (any type) by count (calls, or connections for RFC and SAP Router edges) for the current time range. The panel fills its allotted height exactly — the partners table scrolls internally under a sticky header when it outgrows the panel, so the panel frame always closes cleanly. Drag the divider above the panel to resize it (120–640 px, persisted with saved layouts); expanding the collapsed panel restores at least the 300 px default height. Collapsing or expanding the panel automatically re-fits the graph so it claims (or yields) the freed vertical space.

MiniMap (bottom-right of the canvas) — drag the cursor inside the minimap to pan the main canvas. Direction follows the cursor: dragging right → main canvas shows more right-side content; dragging down → shows more bottom content. Magnitude is proportional to your cursor delta scaled by the minimap’s viewBox-to-pixel ratio. Single-click does nothing — drag-to-pan is the only minimap interaction.

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
The view reads a time-bucketed KV Store that hourly scheduled searches fill, so opening it does not run a search over raw events. The searches, their minutes and their run times are listed in the schedule reference.

The aggregation searches read from these SPL sources:

Source What it contributes sap:abap:gateway RFC connections in the direction they were made: remote-gateway connections that closed (GwDiscRemGw lines — outbound, to the last /H/ hop of the target as a lower-cased short host name, or its address), client sessions that closed (GwDisconnectClient lines — inbound, from the client address), and distinct broken connections from the network-trace lines (P=<peer> / L=<local>; a local port 33NN or 48NN, the gateway’s own listener, means the peer called in). The local IP is canonical for IP→SID inventory because it always belongs to this host’s SID. sap:saprouter SAP Router edges: each CONNECT TO line’s target address (saprouter_target_ip), from the router host that logged it, and server-side receive failures that name a target address (NiBufReceive S… '<IPv4>' failed) as failed connections — client-side failures (NiBufReceive C…) and failures that name a host are not counted. A target named sapms<SID> (that SID’s message server) attributes the target address to the SID in the inventory, so the edge ends on the SID’s circle. Loopback targets (127.0.0.0/8, such as the niping self-test) are excluded. sap:abap:icm ICM local addresses (icm_local_ip): a node for each, and IP→SID inventory entries (except from a Web Dispatcher’s own ICM trace, see below); and the programs on the Top Programs tab (icm_program). sap:hana:tracelogs HANA host + tenant SID extracted from the source path (/usr/sap/<HANA_SID>/HDB<inst>/<host>/trace/DB_<TENANT_SID>/). Yields the rich HANA-side topology including multi-tenant relationships. sap:webdispatcher:access HTTP client IP → web-server host edges (clientip / host / uri / status). The source of every HTTP edge and its status-class distribution. Its events also carry sap_sid / sap_instance from the log’s path, so they count toward the host’s node and the Hosts and Errors tabs of the system the path names, but they never attribute a host to a system in the inventory (see below). sap:hana:audit HANA authentication edges (client_ip → HANA host) with auth success/fail counts; also feeds the IP-node name enrichment (client hostname + executing user). XmlWinEventLog / sap:sapstartsrv / sshd session lines IP-node name enrichment only — the daily pass that puts a hostname / user line under unresolved IP squares. Default Splunk host field (cross-source fallback) Picks up hosts that aren’t surfaced in the above, and attributes a host to the one SAP system its SAP events name (sap_sid) — a Web Dispatcher’s access log and ICM trace excepted (see below).

The node, edge and detail collections are trimmed nightly to 365 days of hourly history, and the IP-name enrichment to the names seen in the last 365 days; none of the trims empties a collection on an empty read (override_if_empty=false). To fill the view with history after an install, use Settings → Dashboard Data and backfill the Environment Topology (graph) and Environment Topology (detail tabs) rows: they take the window you choose (30 days by default, up to 365 days, or a custom range), while the inventory and the IP-name enrichment always refresh over the last 30 days. See Backfilling on first install.

The KV Store collections behind the view, and how the view reads them KV Store collection Schema Populated by logserv_topology_nodes one row per (canonical entity, hourly bucket); 9 fields including event_count, last_seen logserv_topology_aggregate_nodes (hourly) logserv_topology_detail_rollup one row per (metric, scope, hourly bucket); powers the right pane’s per-node and per-edge tabs. Edge metrics (edge_op / edge_perf / edge_err) are keyed by the same stored edge id as logserv_topology_edges.id logserv_topology_detail_aggregate (hourly) logserv_topology_edges one row per (edge, hourly bucket) — RFC edges one row per (edge, app-server local_ip, hourly bucket), so multi-app-server counts stay exact; SAP Router edges one row per (router host, target address, hourly bucket); 20 fields including pre-computed response_time_p50 / _p95 / _max, hana_op_p95_ms / hana_op_max_ms, auth_success_count / auth_fail_count, error_count, warning_count, plus canonical spl_sourcetype + spl_filter_clauses for right-pane drilldowns logserv_topology_aggregate_edges (hourly) logserv_topology_inventory flat (no bucket dimension), keyed by canonical_value; IP / host → SID mapping for retargeting raw IPs to their owning SID node logserv_topology_aggregate_inventory (hourly) logserv_topology_ip_enrichment flat (no bucket dimension), keyed by <ip>:<evidence_source>; hostname + user names behind IP endpoints logserv_topology_enrichment_aggregate (daily)

When you open the view, the React app fetches a time-window slice of these collections via the Splunk Web REST proxy (/en-US/splunkd/__raw/servicesNS/nobody/<APP>/storage/collections/data/<NAME>?query={"bucket_ts":{"$gte":...,"$lte":...}}). The fetch returns in well under a second on production-scale data. Clicking an edge dispatches three small searches against the hourly logserv_topology_detail_rollup — Operations, Performance and Errors — scoped by the stored edge id(s) behind the edge you clicked. Overview and Activity need no search at all: both are derived from the rows already in the browser. Because inventory retargeting can collapse several stored edges into one you see on the canvas, those three reads cover the whole set, and say so if an edge ever spans more than one.

docs.title: Self-Derived IP→SID Inventory
docs.text:
The “which IP belongs to which SID” mapping isn’t read from a CMDB or an admin-maintained lookup — it’s self-derived from the same logs you’re already ingesting. A multi-source union SPL counts, for each IP address and host, how many events each SAP SID logged for it and when it logged the newest one, and the inventory records the endpoint under its most recent SID: of the SIDs whose newest event falls in the endpoint’s most recent hour, the one with the most events (counted over the search window: the last hour for the hourly update, 30 days for a backfill). An address that moves to another system follows it once its most recent hour names only the new SID, and a host that logs a few stray lines under another SID keeps the SID it logs most. A host that really runs two systems at once is shown under the one that logged more. An exact tie writes nothing: the endpoint keeps the row it had, or has no inventory row if it had none.

Coverage depends on what your data exposes — unique hostname/IP appearances across multiple SAP sourcetypes attribute cleanly, while shared NAT IPs and external partners typically have no row at all (their SAP affiliation isn’t observable from logs alone, or they legitimately don’t belong to any single SID).

Reading the ownership badges — and why an address on a system’s panel is never one of its own

An address the inventory has attributed to a system is drawn inside that system’s node: the view folds it in before the graph is laid out. So an address you can still see as a separate endpoint is one no system has claimed — which makes owner not established the expected verdict on the partner donuts, not a data-quality alarm. On the Hosts tab, where hosts are listed by name rather than folded away, both verdicts occur.

“Owner not established” means the inventory has no entry for that host or address. There are several reasons it might not have one: it may emit no system identifier the inventory reads, every update that saw it may have ended in an exact tie between two systems, or it may simply not have been observed since the collection was populated. The panel deliberately does not guess between them.

One scope caveat the panel states inline: ownership is not limited to the selected time range. The inventory accumulates across all observed history, so a badge on a 24-hour view can reflect an attribution learned earlier.

In addition to the inventory, the node-aggregation SPL captures every distinct edge endpoint as a node row in its own right — webdispatcher clientip, ABAP gateway peer_ip, HANA Audit client_ip, SAP Router hosts and their CONNECT TO target addresses (excluding loopback addresses, 127.0.0.0/8). This means external partners that appear only on the receiving side of integration edges still carry real event counts, not zero, even when they don’t have a SID resolution in the inventory.

A Web Dispatcher’s own logs are not an attribution source: neither its access log nor its ICM trace (dev_icm), which LogServ files under webdispatcher/icm and which Data TA builds of 2026-10-13 and earlier typed sap:abap:icm, like an ABAP system’s ICM trace (later builds leave it sap_logserv_logs). Both carry the SID of their log path, but a Web Dispatcher often has its own SID (for example WDP) on a host that also runs another system, and it logs far more often than that system’s own components: counting it would hand the host, or the address its ICM listens on, to the Web Dispatcher’s SID in most hours. The inventory leaves out sap:webdispatcher:access events and, by the LogServ folder the Data TA records with every event (clz_dir = webdispatcher), the ICM trace. So a Web Dispatcher host is attributed only by its other SAP events, and a host that runs nothing but a Web Dispatcher stays a host square until another source names its system.

One attribution source is the SAP Router itself: a CONNECT TO line whose target service is sapms<SID> names the SID whose message server listens at that address, so each such line counts toward that SID, and the address joins the inventory under its most recent SID, as described above. (Targets reached by port or sapgw<NN> name no SID and stay addresses until another source attributes them.)

The inventory itself is extensible per-customer without new ingest: appending another union arm to the inventory aggregation SPL adds a new attribution source. Future arms could include ICM icm_peer_ip, additional CMDB-style lookup tables, or any other field that uniquely associates an IP / host with a SAP SID.

docs.title: Layout Modes
docs.text:
The LAYOUT dropdown switches between three layout algorithms:

  • Force — a d3-force star-system arrangement: every high-traffic hub (focused SIDs, plus any secondary SID with enough leaf partners of its own) gets a proportional horizontal slot, its partners ring around it at a radius scaled to partner count, and smaller secondary systems anchor as satellites fanned around their nearest hub. The layout is deterministic — the same data renders the same picture on every load — and the graph world sizes itself to the canvas aspect ratio. Best for hub-and-spoke SAP landscapes; the default for first-time viewers.
  • Layered — ELK Sugiyama-layered top-to-bottom flow with orthogonal edges and near-zero edge crossings. Best for traffic-flow analysis where you want to see “what flows into what” structurally.
  • Tree — ELK mrtree classic top-down tree with hubs at top and spokes radiating downward. Best when the topology is approximately hub-and-spoke shaped.

Both ELK-based modes (Layered + Tree) share the same lazy-loaded elkjs chunk, fetched only when you first pick a Layered or Tree layout. Force mode remains synchronous (no bundle hit on initial load).

Each layout mode has its own saved-layout slot — saving a layout in Force doesn’t bleed into Layered or Tree. Switching layouts via the LAYOUT dropdown drops the current saved-positions cache so each mode renders fresh from its own algorithm. The Manage Layouts modal (⚙ entry at the top of the Load Layout dropdown) lets you set a per-mode default layout that auto-loads on mount.

docs.title: Saved Layouts
docs.text:
User-arranged graph layouts are persisted in Splunk KV Store collection logserv_topology_layouts. Each saved layout carries:

  • Layout mode — Force / Layered / Tree (so a Force-saved arrangement loads back in Force mode, not Layered)
  • Node positions — where you’ve manually placed each node on the canvas
  • Panel state — sidebar tab + width
  • Viewport — zoom level + pan offset (x, y)
  • Enabled integration types — which checkboxes are ticked on the leftbar. A type added to the view after the layout was saved (SAP Router, for layouts saved before it existed) starts enabled when the layout loads; a type you had switched off stays off
  • Selected node / edge — what was selected when you saved
  • Active right-sidebar tab — Overview / Top Programs / Errors / Hosts (node mode) or Overview / Activity / Operations / Performance / Errors (edge mode)
  • Snap mode — whether new nodes snap to a grid

Layouts are saved per-user-named — you can save your own variants (“focus on XCQ”, “all DBs”, “external partners only”) and switch between them from the Load Layout dropdown.

The Manage Layouts modal (⚙ entry at the top of the Load Layout dropdown) is where two cross-browser preferences live:

  • Per-mode default layout — pick one saved layout per mode (Force / Layered / Tree) to auto-load on mount when you’re using that mode. Each mode section in the modal has its own radio list of mode-matching layouts plus a “(no default)” option.
  • Default layout mode — tick the Open in this mode by default checkbox on one of the three sections to declare which mode the dashboard should open in on next login. The checkbox is mutex across the three sections (or none — “no explicit default” leaves the dashboard opening in Force mode). Ticking the checkbox also switches the active mode immediately so you can see what the default-on-next-login experience will look like.

Both preferences are persisted to Splunk KV Store keyed by Splunk username (collections logserv_topology_layout_defaults and logserv_topology_active_mode). Browser localStorage is used as a fast-mount cache mirror, so on a fresh browser the choices hydrate from KV Store on first paint. If you pick defaults in Chrome and open the topology in Firefox, you’ll see the same defaults the next time you log in to the same Splunk instance. When no defaults are stored, the dashboard opens in Force mode with no auto-loaded layout.

docs.title: Data Refresh Cadence
docs.text:
The topology collections get a new hourly bucket in the first minutes of each hour: four hourly searches run at :05–:08, and the IP-node name enrichment runs once a day at 02:32, recomputing the names over the last 30 days (see the schedule reference). The view re-reads the KV Store:

  • On initial page load
  • On global TimeRange picker change
  • When the user clicks the toolbar’s Refresh button (useful right after a backfill from Settings → Dashboard Data)
  • When the user selects a different node (dispatches on-demand reads against the hourly logserv_topology_detail_rollup KV Store collection — same data layer, dispatched per selection rather than at page load)

The graph itself does not poll. The title row’s Refresh picker and the header’s Refresh button re-run only the searches behind the selected node’s or edge’s detail tabs and the Hosts (in range) count; to re-read the graph, use the toolbar’s Refresh button. The hourly aggregation governs data freshness, and the newest bucket is the last completed hour. Running the aggregates more often would add no newer data, because each run reads whole completed hours.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Health rings with prominent orange or red segments — a SID showing >25% red (error bucket) is a system whose external integrations are systematically failing. Click into the node and the Errors tab to see which specific edges are degraded.
  • Unattributed endpoints with high edge weight — an IP or hostname square carrying hundreds of calls but no inventory owner. Open it and check the Hostname / Users rows: a machine with no SAP identifier and heavy inbound traffic is either a shared NAT / load-balancer address or an integration partner nobody documented. Both warrant investigation.
  • Asymmetric edge counts — RFC edges are drawn in the direction the connection was made, from the calling side to the called side, so two systems joined by edges both ways connect to each other in both directions; a single edge names the caller. The Operations tab shows the remote services and client programs involved.
  • SAP Router failures — an SAP Router edge with failed connections points at a target that refuses or drops routed connections; the SAP Router dashboard’s error tables show the functions and return codes. A router edge that ends on a bare address rather than a system circle is a target the inventory has not attributed — the router’s route table says what it is.
  • Orphan SIDs — a node with no edges is a system that’s running but not integrated with anything else. May be a quiet test system, or a system whose integration partners aren’t monitored.
  • HANA tenants drifting from their HANA system — multi-tenant HANA produces edges from the parent system to each tenant. Missing tenant edges indicate either tenant outage or audit-log gap. The HANA-tagged DB partners specifically use slow hdbcons commands (>1000 ms) in the tenant traces as a warning signal; a tenant lighting up with orange in its ring after a deploy points at slower console commands or new trace warnings — the HANA Trace dashboard shows which.
  • Unexpected external partners — IP-labeled squares with no inventory owner and inbound edges into a production SID are the strongest signal of an undocumented external integration. Use the name lines under the square (hostname / user, where the logs carry them) and the Details panel’s endpoint facts to identify the caller.
  • Edge errors clustered on one sourcetype — clicking an edge and reading the Errors tab can reveal that 90% of failures are 4xx (client-side, not your problem) vs 5xx (server-side, your problem). The status-class breakdown is pre-aggregated hourly into the detail rollup, so clicking through to the Performance tab is a small keyed lookup rather than a scan of raw web-server events.
  • Host counts on the Hosts tab — a SID showing 3 hosts when you expected 2 may indicate a stale forwarder / VM that should have been decommissioned. A row badged with a different system’s name is worth a look on its own: it usually means a shared forwarder, or a management host running commands against this system from elsewhere.
  • A lopsided pair of partner donuts — a system that receives heavily but calls almost nothing (or the reverse) is a useful shape to notice: it separates the integration hubs from the leaf consumers, and a system that has quietly stopped calling out shows up here before it shows up in an error count.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The view’s route is #/topology/integration-topology — the slug stayed integration-topology when the user-visible label changed from “Integration Topology” to “Environment Topology”, so existing bookmarks and saved-layout records remain valid.
  • Layout persistence works across browser tabs and across Splunk Web sessions — your KV Store records survive Splunkd restarts.
  • Layouts are saved per Splunk user — every KV Store record is keyed by <username>::<slug>, so different users have completely separate records and can’t overwrite each other’s layouts.
