Backfill, with the same window, the other rows that read Windows fields: Environment Health, Cross-Stack Authentication, Change & Configuration Activity, Host Role Activity (Host Details), Host Details and Environment Topology (detail tabs). None of them needs a Clear. The first four stored no Windows rows that depend on the add-on. Host Details keys its rows by host and hour, so the Backfill replaces their counts with ones that include the Windows failed logons (EventCode 4625) and critical events; Environment Topology (detail tabs) gains new rows for the Windows events whose add-on severity is critical, which it did not count before. The names that Environment Topology shows for IP addresses take in the Windows logons on their own at the next daily refresh (02:32 search-head time), which reads the last 30 days.

Run the rebuild outside the nightly retention window (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time), when the retention searches rewrite the rollups and can erase rows a backfill is writing; see Backfilling on first install.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Total Events – Aggregate Windows event count
  • Critical / Error – Count of Windows Critical (Level 1) and Error (Level 2) events. In CIM severity vocabulary these are severity="critical" and severity="high" — there is no error severity value
  • Active Hosts – Count of distinct Windows hosts reporting data
  • Event Volume by Log – Trend over time by Windows log source (Application, Security, System, PowerShell)
  • Severity Distribution Over Time – Column chart of events over time, one bar per severity in each time bucket
  • Event Codes – Featured full-width table of the most frequent EventCodes with 7 enriched columns: Event Code, Description (signature), Source log, Severity, Events, Hosts (distinct count), Last Seen. Row drilldown opens the search app filtered by that event code.
  • Service Events – Table of Windows service start/stop activity with latest state
  • PowerShell Activity – Column chart of PowerShell operational event volume over time

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• High-frequency Event Codes – The Event Codes table is the primary starting point. EventCode 7031 / 7034 (service terminated unexpectedly), 1000 (application crash), and 41 (unexpected shutdown) are high-priority. Click through to see every occurrence of a specific code.
  • Service crashes – EventCode 7031 (service terminated unexpectedly) in either the Event Codes table or the Service Events panel indicates a critical service failure. For SAP services (sapstartsrv, SAPService), this requires immediate attention.
  • PowerShell activity spikes – Sudden increases in PowerShell execution may indicate lateral movement by an attacker using PowerShell-based attack tools. Correlate with the Cross-Stack Authentication dashboard to see whether any Windows logons were concurrent.
  • Critical/error severity trends – A rising trend in critical and error events over multiple days indicates accumulating system health issues that need proactive investigation.
  • Event Code hosts expanding – The Hosts column on the Event Codes table makes it obvious when a normally-host-isolated error starts appearing on multiple hosts – a sign the underlying cause is environmental (failed update, domain policy change) rather than local.

docs.title: Related Dashboards
docs.text:
• Cross-Stack Authentication – Windows logon failures beside the SAP and HANA layers.
  • Change & Configuration Activity – Windows account and group changes.
  • Host Details – one host’s event codes beside its other activity.
Where the data comes from

The single source is XmlWinEventLog. Every panel is summary-backed: panels read the logserv_windows_rollup KV Store collection — metric main carries an hourly grain over (event code, severity, source/channel, host) plus per-bucket latest values for the descriptive columns, and metric svc carries the service-event facts. Populated at minute :20 of every hour by logserv_windows_aggregate.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
The Security category contains three cross-source synthesis dashboards designed for security posture analysis and compliance conversations. Each unifies signals that would otherwise live scattered across individual Applications or Platform dashboards, and adds a cross-source correlation panel that surfaces what no single-source dashboard can show.

Dashboard Purpose Key Data Sources Network Perimeter Unified network-boundary view: firewall drops at the host and in transit, proxy outbound traffic, DNS resolution, and cross-source suspicious-activity correlation linux_secure, squid:access, isc:bind:query, isc:bind:queryerror (scoped by tag=dns) Cross-Stack Authentication Unified authentication failure analysis across SAP, HANA, and Windows layers sap:sapstartsrv, sap:hana:audit, XmlWinEventLog Change & Configuration Activity Cross-stack audit trail: HANA user/role/privilege changes, Windows account and group modifications, Linux sudo and user-management activity, with compliance-focused privileged and after-hours views sap:hana:audit, XmlWinEventLog, linux:sudolog, linux_messages_syslog (plus the other linux:* sourcetypes)

Two compliance tables on Change & Configuration Activity, Recent Privileged Changes and Recent After-Hours Changes, deliberately have no row drill-downs; the dashboard’s page explains why.

The controls these dashboards share (time range, Cloud filter, auto-refresh, panel toolbar, drill-downs, export) are described once in the Dashboards Overview.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Compliance conversations (SOX, PCI, internal change management) all require evidence that configuration changes are (1) authorized, (2) attributable to a specific operator, and (3) happening in approved maintenance windows. That evidence lives scattered across three audit trails: HANA audit logs (user/role/privilege/password operations and DDL), Windows Security Event Log (account and group modifications), and Linux syslog (sudo commands plus useradd/usermod/userdel/passwd events). This dashboard unifies the three into a single audit trail with a consistent operator column and category taxonomy, plus two compliance-focused “recent” tables: one filtered to privileged actions, one filtered to after-hours activity.

docs.title: Requires
docs.text:
• Sourcetypes: sap:hana:audit; XmlWinEventLog; and the Linux sourcetypes linux_messages_syslog, linux_secure, linux:sudolog, linux:cron, linux:warn and linux:slapd (plus older data indexed as syslog).
  • Search-head add-ons: the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742), for the Windows rows. See the warning below.
  • Dashboard Data row: Change & Configuration Activity on Settings → Dashboard Data. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the summary-backed panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

The Windows rows need the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows on the Search Head

The LogServ App ships no XmlWinEventLog field extraction of its own. The Windows rows of this dashboard select events by EventCode and name the operator and target from SubjectUserName and TargetUserName; all of these are search-time fields from the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742).

Without add-on 742 on the search tier, the Windows events still index, but they contribute nothing here: the Windows table stays empty, and the KPIs, charts and compliance tables show HANA and Linux changes only.

Tier matters: these are search-time fields, so add-on 742 must be on the Search Head; installing it on a heavy forwarder or indexer does nothing for this dashboard. On Splunk Cloud, install it on the Cloud search head. After installing it, Backfill the Change & Configuration Activity row on Settings → Dashboard Data with a window that covers the history you want, so the summaries pick up the Windows changes. No Clear is needed: without the add-on this row stored no Windows rows. See Where Each Package Goes.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
Leave the Cloud Provider picker on All for compliance reporting

The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker. Any setting other than All silently narrows the audit trail to one ingest channel — for compliance evidence, always leave it on All.

  • Total Change Events – Aggregate count of change events across all three sources
  • User Account Changes – Count of user-management actions (HANA User Management/User Creation/User Deletion; Windows EventCodes 4720/4722/4725/4726/4738/4781; Linux useradd/usermod/userdel)
  • Permission Grants – Count of privilege/group-membership grants (HANA Permission Grant; Windows EventCodes 4728/4732/4756 – “added to group”)
  • Password Events – Count of password changes and resets (HANA Password Management/Password Reset; Windows EventCode 4724; Linux passwd)
  • After-Hours Changes (orange when non-zero) – Count of change events occurring outside business hours (weekday 8am-7pm, i.e. 08:00-18:59) or on weekends, judged in your own time zone (your Splunk time-zone preference). All three sources use the same window, and the KPI, its sparkline and the After-Hours table agree whichever path serves them
  • Unique Operators – Distinct count of source-prefixed operator identities (e.g., HANA:XCPADM, Windows:domain\admin, Linux:ops-user)
  • Change Activity Over Time (by Source) – Column chart over time, its bucket size named in the subtitle (left half of the row, beside the Category donut), one bar per source (HANA / Windows / Linux) in each time bucket. Same-day spikes across two or three series often line up with maintenance windows; isolated spikes in one source worth investigating.
  • Change Events by Category – Donut showing the category mix: Permission Grant, Permission Revoke, User Management, Password Change, Group Membership, Account Status, Sudo Command, DDL / Config, Other.
  • Operators by Change Count (Source-Prefixed) – Full-width table of operator identities across all three stacks ranked by change events (paginated), with source-prefixed identities so operator activity is clearly scoped to each system.
  • HANA Audit – Change Events – Full-width table of the 500 most recent HANA user/role/privilege/password/DDL actions with Operator, Target, Category, Action, Status, HANA Host (the HANA host that wrote the audit record) and Client Host (the host name of the client that ran the action, src_host; empty when the record names none).
  • Windows – Account & Group Modifications – Full-width table of the 500 most recent Windows Security events across all 15 canonical account/group EventCodes, with human-readable Description column derived from EventCode.
  • Linux – Sudo & Command Activity – Full-width table of the 500 most recent sudo commands + useradd/usermod/userdel/groupadd/groupmod/groupdel/passwd activity, with Operator (extracted from sudo prefix or PAM (user) pattern) and Command.
  • Recent Privileged Changes (Compliance Focus) – Table (left half of the bottom row) of the 500 most recent events in the highest-risk subset: HANA Permission Grants + User Creations + Audit Policy changes; Windows account creation/enable/password-reset + local-group additions; Linux useradd / usermod / userdel / visudo activity. This is the “who gave themselves or others more access” report.
  • Recent After-Hours Changes (Outside Business Hours) – Table (right half of the bottom row) of the 500 most recent change events with is_after_hours=1. This is the “who was working outside the change window” report – high compliance value.

Compliance-focused exception: no row drill-downs on the After-Hours and Privileged Changes tables

Two compliance-focused tables on this dashboard intentionally have no row drill-downs — the After-Hours Changes and Recent Privileged Changes tables. Clicking through to raw events from a compliance audit-trail report would pollute the trail with the reviewer’s own search activity in subsequent compliance reports. Per-source operational tables on the same dashboard (HANA Audit, Windows Account & Group Modifications, Linux Sudo & Command Activity) DO get drill-downs.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Rows in the Privileged Changes table with unfamiliar operators – The “headline” compliance question. A permission grant or group-addition you don’t recognize is the first thing to investigate.
  • After-Hours activity on business days – The After-Hours table surfaces all outside-window activity. Weekend entries are often planned maintenance; weekday late-night or early-morning entries warrant a check against your change tickets.
  • Single operator dominating the Operators by Change Count table – One identity generating most changes can be legitimate (an admin performing a large rollout) or concerning (an account being abused). The source prefix tells you which system to look at first.
  • Category-mix drift – If the Change Events by Category donut suddenly shows a large “Permission Grant” slice where it’s historically been minor, someone has been handing out privileges. Check the HANA Audit table for details.
  • Source asymmetry – The Change Activity Over Time chart should show all three sources over time. If one source goes silent, it’s likely a logging-pipeline issue rather than “no changes happened”. Correlate with Data Pipeline Overview. If the Windows series has never appeared, check that add-on 742 is on the search head (see Requires).
  • Linux sudo commands starting with useradd/usermod/visudo/passwd – These are the Linux equivalent of admin changes; they show up in both the Linux table and the Privileged Changes table for visibility.

docs.title: Related Dashboards
docs.text:
• HANA Audit – the full HANA audit trail behind the HANA rows.
  • Windows Events – Windows operational health, on the same add-on 742 fields.
  • Linux System & Security – OS-level activity on the Linux hosts.
  • Cross-Stack Authentication – failed logins across SAP, HANA and Windows.
  • Data Pipeline Overview – whether each source is still arriving.
Where the data comes from

Sources span the three change surfaces: sap:hana:audit (user/role/privilege/DDL changes), XmlWinEventLog (account and group changes) and the Linux family (linux_messages_syslog, linux_secure, linux:sudolog, linux:cron, linux:warn, linux:slapd, plus legacy syslog).

  • Summary-backed panels — the KPIs, sparklines, activity chart, category donut and operator table read the logserv_compliance_rollup KV Store collection: metric main carries an hourly grain over (change source, category, operator), and metrics userchg, permgrant and password pre-compute their KPIs’ exact filters per hour. After-hours is not stored: the After-Hours KPI and sparkline derive it when you view the dashboard, from each hourly bucket, in your time zone — the same rule the raw After-Hours table applies to each event, so the two agree. (In a time zone with a half-hour offset, such as India at UTC+05:30, an hour that straddles 08:00 or 19:00 is judged by its start.) Populated at minute :12 of every hour by logserv_compliance_aggregate.
  • Live panels — the five audit-trail tables (HANA, Windows, Linux, Privileged Changes, After-Hours) are per-event listings dispatched against the raw events at view time (capped at the 500 most recent matches each) — deliberately raw, so the compliance record shows actual events rather than summaries.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Authentication failures are usually investigated one layer at a time – someone looks at HANA audit logs, then switches to Windows Event Log, then opens the SAP services dashboard. An attacker who probes multiple layers at once is therefore hard to spot. Cross-Stack Authentication unifies the failure signal across the three layers that matter in an SAP landscape – SAP sapstartsrv, HANA audit, and Windows Security Event Log – so that one dashboard shows the total, the per-layer split, and the source IPs and users in common across layers. Use it as the first stop when you suspect credential-based attacks or widespread misconfiguration after a password rotation.

docs.title: Requires
docs.text:
• Sourcetypes: sap:sapstartsrv, sap:hana:audit and XmlWinEventLog.
  • Search-head add-ons: the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (742), for the Windows layer. See the warning below.
  • Dashboard Data row: Cross-Stack Authentication on Settings → Dashboard Data. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the summary-backed panels fill one hour at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

The Windows layer needs the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows on the Search Head

The LogServ App ships no XmlWinEventLog field extraction of its own. The Windows layer counts events whose CIM action field is failure, and its table shows the logon type, user and source address; all of these are search-time fields from the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742).

Without add-on 742 on the search tier, the Windows events still index, but the Windows Auth Failures KPI stays at 0, Recent Windows Auth Failures stays empty, and the other panels show the SAP and HANA layers only.

Tier matters: these are search-time fields, so add-on 742 must be on the Search Head; installing it on a heavy forwarder or indexer does nothing for this dashboard. On Splunk Cloud, install it on the Cloud search head. After installing it, Backfill the Cross-Stack Authentication row on Settings → Dashboard Data with a window that covers the history you want, so the summaries pick up the Windows failures. No Clear is needed: without the add-on this row stored no Windows rows. See Where Each Package Goes.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker (All / aws / azure / gcp); any setting other than All scopes every panel below to that ingest channel.

  • Total Auth Failures – Aggregate failed authentication count across all three layers
  • SAP Auth Failures – Count of sapstartsrv authentication failures
  • HANA Auth Failures – Count of HANA audit events where the connection/authentication was rejected
  • Windows Auth Failures – Count of Windows Security-channel events (sourcetype XmlWinEventLog) where the CIM action field is failure (the classification comes from the Splunk Add-on for Windows on the search-head tier)
  • Auth Failures Over Time by Layer – Column chart of failures over time, one bar per layer (SAP / HANA / Windows) in each time bucket, so correlated spikes across layers are visible at a glance
  • Users by Auth Failures – Table of failing usernames ranked by failure count, summed across all three layers (paginated)
  • Auth Failure Source IPs – Table of source IPs ranked by failure count, showing how many layers each IP hit and which ones, plus last-seen time (paginated); row drilldown opens that IP’s full cross-stack auth history in Search
  • HANA Auth Activity by User – Table of HANA users across ALL authentication activity (successes included), showing total events, distinct action types, failure count, risk level, and last-seen time, sorted by failures; row drilldown opens that user’s full HANA auth log
  • Recent Windows Auth Failures – Table of the most recent Windows failure events (up to 200) with user, event signature, source IP, logon type, and host; row drilldown opens Host Details for that host
  • Recent SAP Auth Failures – Table of the most recent sapstartsrv failed-auth events (up to 200) with user, remote IP, source location, and host; row drilldown opens Host Details for that host

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Correlated spikes across layers – If the Auth Failures Over Time by Layer chart shows all three layers rising at the same time, that’s almost always a network-level attack (password spray, credential stuffing) rather than a local misconfiguration. Investigate source IPs immediately.
  • Single source IP across layers – The Auth Failure Source IPs table makes it obvious when one IP is failing against SAP, HANA, AND Windows. That’s the hallmark of a targeted attack rather than an expired-password incident.
  • High user failure count concentrated on service accounts – Service accounts (sapadm, sapservice accounts, DBADMIN-style) with large failure counts suggest either a recently rotated password that wasn’t updated downstream, or an attacker trying to abuse a high-privilege account.
  • Asymmetry between layers – Many HANA failures but zero SAP / Windows failures usually indicates an application-layer issue (bad connection string, expired JDBC cert). Asymmetry the other way (many Windows failures, no HANA failures) often points to a domain-level issue. A Windows layer that is always zero while Windows events are arriving usually means add-on 742 is missing from the search head (see Requires).
  • After a password rotation – Expect a short burst of failures across one or more layers immediately after a change. If the burst persists beyond the rotation window, some downstream system is still using the old credential.

docs.title: Related Dashboards
docs.text:
• Host Details – where the Recent Windows and Recent SAP Auth Failures rows lead.
  • SAP Services – sapstartsrv authentication and TLS failures in detail.
  • HANA Audit – the full HANA audit trail.
  • Windows Events – Windows operational health.
  • Change & Configuration Activity – account and privilege changes that often follow, or explain, a burst of failures.
Where the data comes from
  • Summary-backed panels read the logserv_xstack_auth_rollup KV Store collection — metric fail carries the cross-source authentication-failure grain over (layer, failed user) spanning sap:sapstartsrv, sap:hana:audit and XmlWinEventLog; metric failip the per-source-IP failure facts (layers hit, last seen); metric hanauser the full HANA authentication population (successes included) per user/action/status/risk level. Populated at minute :15 of every hour by logserv_xstack_auth_aggregate.
  • Live panels — the Windows events and SAP authentication tables are per-event listings dispatched against the raw events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent matches each.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Firewall drops, proxy traffic, and DNS queries are three different lenses on the same underlying question: what is crossing the network boundary and should it be there? Each lens lives on its own operational dashboard (Linux, Proxy Analytics, DNS Analytics), but an attacker rarely limits themselves to a single surface – a compromised host often shows up in several of these signals at the same time. Network Perimeter puts the three sources on one dashboard: rejected traffic (firewall drops at the host and in transit), outbound flow (proxy), and resolution activity (DNS), with a dedicated cross-source panel that ranks hosts by combined suspicious-signal score. Use it as the first stop for “is our network perimeter healthy and clean?”

docs.title: Requires
docs.text:
• Sourcetypes: linux_secure (the kernel firewall lines), squid:access (its access.log lines), and isc:bind:query and isc:bind:queryerror (the query events, selected with tag=dns).
  • Search-head add-ons: none beyond the LogServ App. The firewall fields are read from the raw linux_secure lines, and the Squid and BIND parsing is built into the App.
  • Dashboard Data rows on Settings → Dashboard Data: Network Perimeter; Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter (for Firewall Drops in Transit); and Beaconing detection (Environment Health / DNS / Network Perimeter) (for the beaconing panels). Rebuild every row the dashboard reads. On a new install, Run backfill there seeds the last 30 days by default (60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom range, are also offered); without a backfill the summary-backed panels fill one hour (the beaconing panels one day) at a time. See Backfilling on first install.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker (All / aws / azure / gcp). Every panel on this dashboard is scoped by it; leave it on All unless you are deliberately isolating one ingest channel.

  • Firewall Drops at Host – Count of kernel firewall IN_DROP events from linux_secure: packets addressed to the host itself, dropped by its INPUT chain
  • Firewall Drops in Transit – Count of kernel firewall FWD_DROP events: packets a host was routing on to another system, dropped by its FORWARD chain. Only hosts that forward traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways, log these. Read from the Linux dashboard’s summary data, so it shows 0, or undercounts, for any period the Linux rollup has not summarised: its aggregation turned off, or those days not backfilled. The row to rebuild in Settings → Dashboard Data is Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter
  • Proxy Requests – Count of HTTP requests handled by Squid
  • DNS Queries – Count of DNS query events (tag=dns: isc:bind:query and isc:bind:queryerror)
  • Beaconing Domains (red) – Domains exhibiting periodic query patterns (low variance in inter-query interval) – candidate C2 channels. Beaconing is detected per UTC calendar day (a domain’s inter-query gaps are analysed within each UTC day, whatever timezone you view the dashboard in), and the KPI is the sum of each day’s distinct beaconing-domain count over the selected range – a domain beaconing every day for a week counts 7. Its sparkline has one point per UTC day, and hovering a point shows that UTC date; a UTC day that has not ended yet is drawn at 0 and labelled not yet computed. The beaconing panels are refreshed by a daily scheduled search (00:30 search-head local time), so they can lag up to 24 h; the other panels on this dashboard refresh hourly
  • Denied Requests (orange when non-zero) – Count of proxy requests with status=403 or vendor_action="TCP_DENIED"; click to drill down. Proxy Analytics counts denied requests by the App’s action="denied" instead, so the two counts can differ
  • Outbound Bandwidth – sum(bytes_out) across all proxy requests, formatted KB/MB/GB
  • Perimeter Activity Over Time – Full-width column chart of the three sources over time, one bar per source in each time bucket; simultaneous spikes across two or three series are the correlation signal to watch for. Its firewall series is Firewall Drops at Host; drops in transit are not charted here. Its DNS series counts isc:bind:query only, so it can be lower than the DNS Queries KPI.
  • Blocked Source IPs – Every source IP in the firewall log, ranked by Total (paginated) and split into At Host and In Transit / Other, with unique target count and protocols seen; row drilldown to the matching events

  • Blocked Destination Ports – All destination ports targeted by firewall traffic, grouped by port + protocol, ranked by Total (paginated) and split the same way

    Both Blocked tables count every firewall event carrying a source IP / destination port. At Host is the IN_DROP events among them; In Transit / Other is the rest: nearly all FWD_DROP, plus any other firewall line logged with a source or port. ICMP carries no destination port, so ICMP drops appear in Blocked Source IPs but not in Blocked Destination Ports. - Firewall Drops at Host by Protocol – Column chart of IN_DROP events over time (drops at the host, INPUT chain), one bar per protocol in each time bucket: TCP, UDP, ICMP, and any other protocol the drop lines name. Protocol shifts are often the clearest signal (ICMP spikes = ping flood / recon; UDP spikes = DNS amplification / port scan; TCP spikes = SYN-style port scan) - Proxy Denied Traffic Over Time – Column chart of denied proxy requests over time – the outbound complement to the firewall drops - Outbound Domains by Volume & Bytes – All destination domains receiving outbound traffic, ranked by bytes (paginated), with request count and unique client count. Row drilldown opens the events for that domain. - DNS Query Type Distribution – Donut of query-type mix (A / AAAA / PTR / TXT / MX / other). High TXT or MX volume from non-mail hosts is a DNS-tunneling / exfiltration indicator. - Queried Domains – Table (right of the query-type donut) of all queried domains ranked by query count, with unique-client count and per-domain %TXT / %MX ratios for quick anomaly spotting. Row drilldown opens DNS query events for that domain. - Suspicious Activity Indicator – Full-width cross-source table of internal hosts appearing in both beaconing DNS queries and denied proxy requests, ranked by signal score (beacon_domains × 3 + denied_requests). Columns: Host, Beaconing Domains, Beaconing Queries, Denied Proxy Requests, Signal Score. Row drilldown opens the Host Details dashboard for that host (its full cross-sourcetype activity), carrying the current time range.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Correlated spikes across sources – The Perimeter Activity Over Time chart is the quickest read on “is something happening right now?” Watch for days when two or three of the series spike together – that’s usually an active event (port scan, active C2, exfiltration window) rather than baseline drift.
  • Protocol shifts in firewall drops – The protocol chart of drops at the host is more diagnostic than raw drop counts. A normally TCP-heavy mix suddenly showing tall UDP or ICMP bars signals a different attacker technique.
  • Blocked Source IPs concentration – A single source IP generating the overwhelming majority of drops is either a persistent attacker or a misconfigured internal host. Either way, the action is the same: investigate that specific IP.
  • Drops in transit – FWD_DROP comes only from hosts that route traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways. On a gateway it is traffic the forwarding policy does not allow, often a monitoring or discovery job probing the systems behind the gateway, and it can outnumber the drops at the host many times over. Use the In Transit / Other column of Blocked Source IPs to find the source, then allow its traffic or stop the job. Drops in transit on a host that should not route at all mean IP forwarding is switched on there.
  • TXT-heavy queries to a single domain – A domain in Queried Domains with a high %TXT ratio is a DNS-tunneling pattern. Cross-reference the Suspicious Activity Indicator to see which hosts are issuing those queries.
  • Hosts in the Suspicious Activity table – Any non-empty row here is worth investigating. A host showing up in both beaconing DNS and denied proxy is strong evidence of compromise – the DNS lookups suggest malware C2, and the denied proxy requests suggest the same malware trying to reach blocked destinations.
  • Outbound Bandwidth spikes – A sudden rise in the Outbound Bandwidth KPI that isn’t matched by a proportional rise in Proxy Requests means individual transfers are getting larger – often the signature of an exfiltration event.

docs.title: Related Dashboards
docs.text:
• Linux System & Security – the full firewall and kernel view of each Linux host.
  • Proxy Analytics – outbound traffic by domain, client and cache action.
  • DNS Analytics – resolvers, clients and the beaconing tables.
  • Host Details – where the Suspicious Activity Indicator rows lead.
Where the data comes from

This dashboard synthesises three perimeter sources, all summary-backed:

  • logserv_perimeter_rollup (populated at minute :16 of every hour by logserv_perimeter_aggregate) carries seven metrics: fw (firewall actions/sources/ports — the SRC= / DST= / DPT= / PROTO= fields are extracted from the raw linux_secure events at aggregation time), proxy + proxydom (Squid request/denied/bandwidth counts and per-domain traffic), dnscount + dnstype + dnsq (DNS query volume, types, and per-query/source counts over the tag=dns events), and activity (the combined activity chart’s classification).
  • Firewall Drops in Transit reads the Linux dashboard’s logserv_linux_rollup collection (metric kernel, the kernel tag of every linux_secure line per hour), because the perimeter fw metric does not tell a FWD_DROP line from other firewall lines. For any period that rollup has not summarised (its aggregation turned off, or those days not backfilled) it shows 0 or undercounts. The row to rebuild in Settings → Dashboard Data is Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter.
  • The beaconing panels read the daily collections: logserv_beaconing_rollup (00:30) for the KPI and logserv_beaconing_detail_rollup (00:32, metrics qs + denied) for the suspicious activity detail — daily cadence because the gap-variance detection needs a day of inter-arrival history, so these panels update once per day rather than hourly.

The hourly summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time; the beaconing panels always read their daily summaries. Each collection keeps 365 days of history (trimmed by a daily retention search). The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness.

docs.title: Announcing Limited Preview of Splunk for SAP LogServ Integration for SAP RISE/ECS Customers
docs.text:
We are thrilled to announce the limited preview of Splunk for SAP LogServ — a joint step with Splunk by Cisco and SAP Enterprise Cloud Services (ECS) that brings the logs of the world’s most critical business systems into the platform their security teams already trust. For SAP RISE/ECS private cloud edition customers, moving to RISE no longer has to mean a visibility trade-off: the telemetry SAP operates on your behalf now flows into your own Splunk — ready for the dashboards, detections, and AI-assisted investigations your teams run everywhere else.

Splunk and the SAP ECS team have worked side by side to develop this integration and bring it to this point. Thank you to James Schneider (Splunk Senior Partner Solutions Engineer), Hemanth Kusampudi (SAP Chief Security Architect), Mateusz Macalik (Splunk Senior Partner Solutions Engineer), Jim Barton (Splunk Global Strategic Alliances), and Subarno Mukherjee (Splunk WW Leader - Partner Solutions Engineering).

docs.title: SAP LogServ — the centralized log surface for SAP ECS
docs.text:
SAP LogServ is an SAP Enterprise Cloud Services (ECS) service aimed at collection, storage, forwarding and access of logs. LogServ centralizes the logs from all systems, applications, and ECS services used by a registered customer.

Main features include:

  • Near-Realtime Log Collection — with the ability to integrate into customer SIEMs or Log Management systems.
  • Log Retention — a 365-day retention period, adjustable for each data source; logs can be retained indefinitely.
  • Recovery of Logs — ability to recover logs which were retained.

docs.title: Splunk — the data platform behind the world’s most security-conscious SAP customers
docs.text:
Splunk by Cisco is the data platform of choice for security and observability across the world’s largest enterprises. Splunk Enterprise powers the on-premises analytics workload; Splunk Cloud Platform delivers the same capabilities as a managed SaaS service; and Splunk Enterprise Security layers a market-leading SIEM with AI-powered detections, threat-intel correlation, and SOC workflows on top of either deployment.

Together, these products bring the operational depth, scale, and security analytics that SAP customers expect for their mission-critical workloads — from the underlying HANA database through the ABAP application server, Web Dispatcher, Cloud Connector, and beyond.

The Splunk for SAP LogServ integration is the product of that collaboration: SAP operates the log collection and delivery; Splunk turns it into security and operational insight. RISE customers keep the accountability model they signed up for — SAP runs the landscape while the customer’s own security team keeps full-fidelity visibility — and gain an AI-aware investigative experience that extends protection beyond SAP to the whole IT estate.

docs.title: Architecture – Multi-Cloud Support
docs.text:
The Splunk for SAP LogServ integration supports ingest from AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud — the three hyperscalers SAP ECS operates RISE landscapes on. The pattern is the same everywhere: customer SAP systems forward logs into LogServ; LogServ stages the consolidated stream into customer-accessible cloud storage; and Splunk picks up new data automatically the moment it lands, delivering it to the customer’s Splunk environment — on-premises Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud Platform — where the Splunk for SAP LogServ App provides the analyst-facing experience and, optionally, Splunk Enterprise Security provides the SIEM correlation surface. One integration, any hyperscaler: if a landscape moves clouds, the dashboards, detections, and AI Assistant come along unchanged.

Splunk for SAP LogServ — AWS data flow (S3 + SQS notifications)

The same integration runs on Microsoft Azure. For customers whose LogServ delivery targets Azure, the stream lands in Azure Blob Storage and Splunk consumes it through event-driven queue notifications — the Azure twin of the AWS pattern. Everything downstream — the filtering, the dashboards, the AI Assistant, and the Enterprise Security content — is identical to the AWS deployment; only the ingest mechanism differs.

Splunk for SAP LogServ — Azure data flow (Blob Storage + Event Grid queue notifications)

And now: Google Cloud. This preview round extends the same pattern to Google Cloud: for RISE landscapes running on GCP, LogServ delivers to Google Cloud Storage and Splunk consumes it through Pub/Sub notifications — completing coverage of all three hyperscalers SAP ECS operates on.

Splunk for SAP LogServ — Google Cloud data flow (GCS + Pub/Sub notifications)

docs.title: Native index-time filtering
docs.text: Keep only the data you want — before it is indexed. Administrators choose which LogServ log types to keep and how far back in time to accept, from a point-and-click page in Splunk Web — no custom configuration to write or maintain. With a Deployment Server, one click (Deploy to Forwarders) pushes the rules to every forwarder, where unwanted and stale events are dropped before they are ever indexed — controlling ingest and license cost and keeping the environment focused on the data that matters. The same filtering works identically on every cloud ingest path.

docs.title: Log types covered
docs.text:
LogServ complements the existing SAP application layer threat monitoring with the log types owned by SAP ECS as the system provider. This includes logs like:

SAP Security Audit Log, HANA database, ICM, SAP Web Dispatcher, SAP Cloud Connector, OS, SAP Gateway, 3rd-party Database, Network, DNS, Proxy, Firewall… logs

The list is growing as new sources become available and SAP ECS onboards more.

Splunk for SAP LogServ is available as a limited preview today; GA coming soon.

docs.title: What customers see — the Environment Topology view
docs.text:
The LogServ App ships an interactive Environment Topology view that auto-discovers a living map of the customer’s SAP estate directly from the logs — no CMDB integration, no manual diagramming. Teams see at a glance which systems talk to which partners, where errors concentrate, and how the estate is behaving right now — and click any system or connection to drill into the detail behind it.

Environment Topology view in Splunk for SAP LogServ

docs.title: What analysts see — the AI Assistant chat panel
docs.text:
Above any LogServ App dashboard, analysts can open the AI Assistant as a docked side panel. The chat sits next to the data — in the screenshot below, it’s open alongside the Environment Topology dashboard — and the dashboard remains live and interactive while the analyst converses with the assistant.

The assistant offers two paths. Predefined prompts run curated, SAP-aware investigations against the customer’s own data — no AI vendor involved — with results landing inline as charts, KPIs, and tables. Free-form prompts let analysts ask questions in natural language through the customer’s choice of leading AI providers; the assistant plans the investigation, runs it, and writes a narrative answer with citations that link straight back to the underlying data, so an analyst can pivot from summary to source in one click.

Crucially, this is AI on the customer’s terms. A privacy guarantee engineered into the product ensures raw customer events never leave the customer’s Splunk for any AI vendor, and the privacy tier an administrator chooses sets exactly what the vendor does see. Every action the assistant takes for a user whose Splunk role can write audit events is recorded to a dedicated audit trail — with optional tamper-evident forwarding to storage the customer controls — and administrators can switch the AI-vendor path off entirely at any time while keeping the curated investigations. AI-era capability, enterprise-grade governance.

AI Assistant chat panel docked beside the Environment Topology dashboard

docs.title: What ES customers get — out-of-the-box SAP correlation
docs.text:
For SAP RISE customers running Splunk Enterprise Security, the LogServ App includes a complete ES content layer built in — no separate content pack, no extra license SKU. ES features ship enabled and work wherever ES runs once its setup checklist is done; on a search head without ES, an administrator turns them off, so a single App serves every Splunk topology.

SAP events become first-class security citizens. LogServ data is normalized into the same standard data models ES detections, dashboards, and investigations already use — authentication, change, network, and web activity from the SAP stack correlates directly with everything else the SOC monitors, with no per-customer field-mapping work.

Out-of-the-box SAP detections and risk scoring. Curated correlation searches cover the attack patterns that matter most in SAP estates — privilege escalation, cross-stack authentication-failure bursts, anomalous gateway connections, and more — landing directly in ES Incident Review for SOC triage. Each detection also feeds ES’s risk-based alerting, so repeated low-level signals accumulate into high-confidence incidents instead of alert noise.

Asset and identity context, auto-derived. The App builds asset and identity feeds for the SAP estate directly from the logs and keeps them current automatically — no CMDB integration project required to give ES its context.

Dual-mode by design. Customers without ES lose nothing — the dashboards, AI Assistant, and data normalization all work standalone. Install ES later, turn the ES content back on, and the SAP detections light up — nothing else in the App changes.

docs.title: Benefits of Integration
docs.text:
SAP-aware Splunk experience from day one. More than twenty purpose-built dashboards cover the estate end to end — environment health, HANA, ABAP, Web Dispatcher, Cloud Connector, network perimeter, cross-stack authentication, change activity, and more — so teams get value immediately, without writing a single query.

AI-assisted investigations with enterprise governance. Analysts investigate in natural language or through curated SAP prompts, while the product guarantees raw customer events never reach an AI vendor, records every action of users whose role can write audit events to an audit trail that the optional forwarder makes tamper-evident, aligns its safeguards to the OWASP LLM Top 10, and gives administrators a runtime switch to disable the AI-vendor path entirely.

Runs wherever your Splunk — and your SAP — runs. On-premises Splunk Enterprise, Splunk Cloud Platform, and Splunk Enterprise Security are all supported by the same App; on the SAP side, AWS-, Azure-, and Google-Cloud-hosted RISE landscapes are all supported by the same integration. No topology lock-in, no separate editions.

Centralized monitoring across the IT estate. SAP LogServ data sits next to the customer’s existing Splunk-managed infrastructure logs, application logs, network telemetry, and security signals — one platform, one query language, one operations workflow. SOC analysts pivot from a Linux auth-failure to an SAP HANA audit event without leaving the Splunk console.

Auditability and tamper-evidence. Every AI Assistant action of a user whose role can write audit events — every prompt, vendor call, tool dispatch, legal acknowledgement and privacy-tier elevation — is recorded to a dedicated Splunk audit index, with an optional HEC forwarder for tamper-evident dual-write to a customer-controlled remote destination.

docs.title: Splunk Observability Cloud support
docs.text:
For teams that run their operations in Splunk Observability Cloud, RISE takes the SAP core out of reach of the agents they rely on: customers have no operating-system access to the SAP-managed hosts. The Splunk for SAP LogServ add-on for Observability Cloud brings the same LogServ feed into Splunk Observability Cloud — with no agents on SAP systems and no log lines copied.

Live SAP signals as metrics. Every few minutes, the add-on on your Splunk search head counts what arrived from LogServ — event volume and freshness, HANA audit activity, Web Dispatcher traffic and errors, and more — and sends those counts to Observability Cloud as metrics you can filter by SAP system, host and cloud.

The LogServ App’s pages, in Observability Cloud. The SAP-aware views teams know from the Splunk for SAP LogServ App — environment health, HANA audit, Web Dispatcher, the SAP network and more — as Observability Cloud dashboards, next to everything else the team watches.

Logs searched in place. Through Log Observer Connect, analysts search the LogServ data where it already lives in Splunk, with the App’s SAP field extractions; the logs are not copied, and your Splunk permissions apply. Log Observer Connect is included in every Observability Cloud edition at no additional charge.

The SAP landscape on a map. A live map of the SAP landscape in Observability Cloud — application servers, HANA databases, Web Dispatchers and their connections — drawn from the LogServ logs, with calls and errors per connection as charts.

SAP-aware detectors. Ready-made detectors on the SAP health signals, such as a LogServ feed that stops, data that arrives late, or HANA audit failures above their usual level, so problems reach the right team quickly.

One click back to the detail. Links from Observability Cloud into the Splunk for SAP LogServ App, including the interactive Environment Topology view, for when someone needs the story behind a number.

Built for trust. Nothing is sent until an administrator turns it on, and the metrics carry counts only — never user names, IP addresses, URLs or SQL text. The logs themselves stay in Splunk.

Observability Cloud support is designed for Splunk Cloud Platform and Splunk Enterprise and requires Splunk Observability Cloud; LogServ metrics count toward Observability Cloud usage. If your teams also use Splunk Observability Cloud, mention it when you sign up for the preview.

docs.title: What Observability Cloud teams see — the SAP landscape map
docs.text:
The same LogServ logs that draw the Environment Topology view in the Splunk App also draw the SAP landscape where Observability Cloud teams already work. SAP application servers, HANA databases and Web Dispatchers appear as services, with the connections between them drawn from the logs — no agents on SAP systems.

The SAP landscape on a map in Splunk Observability Cloud, drawn from LogServ logs (demo landscape)

docs.title: Release Notes: 0.0.6
docs.text:
This page lists what changed in the 0.0.6 line of Splunk for SAP LogServ. The 0.0.6 line was frozen on 2026-08-07, at App build 266, and receives no further fixes; its work continues in 0.1.2. To upgrade from a 0.0.6 build, follow Upgrading to This Release.

v0.0.6 is primarily a dashboard-performance release

v0.0.6 keeps the entire v0.0.5 feature set unchanged (21 React dashboards + the Environment Topology view, templates-only AI Assistant with 61 canned prompts + audit log, index-time filtering + Deployment Server automation, Cloud Provider attribution, Enterprise Security integration). The headline of this release is a dashboard data-layer rewrite that makes the dashboards fast at high event volume; it also adds Google Cloud Platform as a third ingest channel (a dedicated per-HF add-on, see below) and reworks Azure ingest onto a dedicated per-HF add-on. Search-time field extractions, sourcetype routing, and all dashboard content are unchanged — only how each panel sources its data changed. No data re-ingest is required to upgrade.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Splunk platform versions 9.4.3 and later CIM 5.0.0 and later (per app.manifest) Supported OS for data collection Platform independent Vendor products SAP LogServ for SAP ECS in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) AI Assistant prerequisite Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) v1.1.0 or later, on the search head where the LogServ App is installed Azure ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure), installed per heavy forwarder — ingests Azure Blob via Event Grid → Storage Queue notifications (Azure deployments only; SAP provisions the queue + SAS) GCP ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp), installed per heavy forwarder — ingests Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications (GCP deployments only; SAP provisions the subscription + service-account key)

docs.title: The problem this release solves
docs.text: At a customer’s reported scale (~10.7M events / 24 h, ~321M over 30 days) the 21 non-Topology dashboards took over 10 minutes to populate. Each panel dispatched its own raw, search-time-extraction full-scan with no shared base search, no tstats, and no acceleration. (The Environment Topology view was already fast — it had been moved to a KV-Store-backed data layer in v0.0.5.)

docs.title: New data architecture — two tiers
docs.text:
Every dashboard panel was re-tiered onto the cheapest correct data source and byte-exact-verified against the original raw SPL. The result is a two-tier data layer — no Common Information Model (CIM) acceleration is required.

  1. tstats on indexed dimensions — pure count / average panels (Data Pipeline Overview, Host Details, the Environment Health pipeline panels, Multi-Cloud Overview, and the count KPIs across the suite) read via | tstats over the already-indexed WRITE_META fields. A new default/fields.conf declares INDEXED = true for clz_dir / clz_subdir / splunk_solution / cloud_provider.
  2. KV-Store precompute rollups — every other high-volume panel reads from a set of hourly-aggregated KV-Store rollup collections (logserv_*_rollup; later builds added more — the Settings → Dashboard Data tab lists the current inventory). Scheduled saved searches (logserv_*_aggregate, hourly on staggered per-search minutes — see Scheduled-search schedule) precompute each panel’s data; the dashboards read it back filtered by a bucket_ts range driven by the global time-range picker. Streamstats / per-event-listing panels that cannot be rolled up stay raw (capped with | head N where they are time-ordered listings).

Cached reads are uniformly ~0.1–0.6 s versus 10 s – 19 min raw (speedups of 64× – 5,358×), validated at 335M events on the test fleet. Data freshness on the rolled-up panels is hourly — the same trade-off the Environment Topology view already made. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness for the full picture and the one-time backfill step.

No CIM data-model acceleration needed for dashboards

An interim build had the four HTTP / DNS / proxy dashboards (Proxy, Web Dispatcher, Cloud Connector, DNS Analytics) read from CIM accelerated data models. That approach was removed before this release: when a customer had not accelerated those models (the common case), the queries fell back to a raw full-scan — exactly the slowness this release set out to fix. Those four dashboards now read dedicated KV-Store rollups, so they are fast regardless of the customer’s CIM-acceleration state. The LogServ App’s CIM tagging (eventtypes + tags) for Enterprise Security correlation is unaffected — see Enterprise Security → CIM Compliance.

docs.title: New features
docs.text:
1. “Run backfill” — Dashboard Data settings tab — a new Settings → Dashboard Data tab seeds the rollup collections on first install. It dispatches each rollup’s aggregation searches as top-level jobs (immune to the subsearch wall-clock limits that truncate a bundled backfill at high volume), with a progress bar, completeness banner, and per-rollup status. Idempotent and resumable. An admin clicks this once after installing on a high-volume instance to populate dashboard history immediately; otherwise the hourly aggregation seeds history going forward. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness → Backfilling on first install. Build 245 merged the former Topology settings tab into this tab: the Environment Topology graph became one more rollup in its table, and its backfill moved to the same per-arm top-level dispatch, so it no longer truncates at high event volume.
  2. 365-day cache retention — all rollup-retention searches keep a full year of rolled-up history. The install backfill seeds 30 days; the cache then grows to a year organically via the hourly aggregation (seed-and-grow).
  3. Per-panel action toolbar — every chart and table panel header now carries Open in Search · Download (CSV) · Inspect (Job Inspector) · Refresh plus a “<1m ago” last-run stamp. KPI single-value cards get the loading spinner but no toolbar.
  4. Universal loading spinner — every chart / table renders the orange-dot spinner + “Loading data…” while its search is in flight (KPI cards show a small spinner instead of a dash), replacing the old plain “Loading…” text.

docs.title: Later builds (254–266), backported from v0.1.1
docs.text:
After build 253 the v0.0.6 line shipped builds 254 to 266. Each carries changes first made in the v0.1.1 line, described in Release Notes: 0.1.1 under their v0.1.1 build numbers:

v0.0.6 builds v0.1.1 builds Change 254–255 246–259, 260–277, 278 The Cisco Magnetic re-theme with light and dark mode, the Environment Topology star-system layout and floating edges and the blue-gradient icon set 256–257 279–281 Settings readability, the Live Activity panel and the link-graph restyle 258 282 The global Cloud Provider filter; it changes the rollup key, so its upgrade needs the rollups cleared once and backfilled 259 284 The Linux and Windows chart fixes 260–261 285–286 Predefined prompts on the rollup tier 262–263 287–288 A configurable MCP request timeout, default 30 seconds, and a read-only display of the MCP Server’s own timeout 264–265 289–298 The 60-second MCP timeout default, sub-hour ranges read from raw events, a global Refresh button, and Web Dispatcher follows the Cloud filter 266 299 The after-hours window fix; its upgrade needs the compliance rollup rebuilt

Fixes made after build 266 are in the 0.1.1 and 0.1.2 lines only, for example the nightly retention that cannot empty a rollup (0.1.2 build 375), admin-only write access to the App’s KV Store collections (0.1.2 builds 383–385) and the Data TA’s whole-line routing (Data TA build 1792189743).

docs.title: Role Activity + Sourcetype Mapping performance (build 243)
docs.text:
The last two raw-scan panel groups were moved onto KV-Store rollups so they stay fast at high event volume:

  1. Sourcetype Mapping (Host Details → Sourcetype Mapping tab + Data Pipeline Overview → Linked Graph) now reads a new logserv_stmap_rollup with source normalized (UUIDs, dates, and long digit-runs stripped to collapse per-day / per-tunnel variants into logical sources). This cut the search from ~50 s to ~2 s over a 30-day window and the graph from 4,000+ nodes to a few hundred. User-visible change: the graph now shows normalized logical sources (e.g. one …/audit-log_<id>_<date>.csv node) instead of one node per tunnel-UUID per day.
  2. Role Activity (Host Details → Role Activity tab) — the 7 per-host breakdown panels now read a new logserv_hostrole_rollup (metric discriminator), reproducing the same value / count / percent breakdown byte-exact, ~8× faster. No visible change.

Adds 2 rollup collections (24 → 26 hourly aggregates; 24 → 26 retention searches) — fully within the existing staggered schedule (now :03–:28 aggregates / :30–:58 daily).

docs.title: Scheduling & Enterprise Security (build 242)
docs.text:
1. Enterprise Security content shipped disabled by default. (Superseded by build 249: the ES content now ships enabled by default; see the build-249 entry.) In build 242 all 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* saved searches shipped with disabled = 1. The ES content is dual-mode (it targets the ES Notable / Risk / Asset & Identity frameworks and CIM data models that no-op without ES installed) and no dashboard reads any ES output. See Enterprise Security → The ES schedule.

    Correction (2026-10-23): the ES content is not a no-op without ES. Where its searches run without ES, Splunk logs an error for each notable and risk alert action, which exist only with ES, and the scheduler skips the Risk Notable because the Risk data model is missing. On a search head without ES, turn the ES content off: see Disabling or tuning the ES content.

  2. Scheduled searches re-staggered into three non-overlapping bands — the 24 hourly rollup aggregates spread one-per-minute across :05–:28 (was all at :05), retention + the 2 daily beaconing aggregates moved to an off-peak :30–:58 band, and the (disabled) ES searches re-croned to the back of the hour. No two enabled scheduled searches share an (hour, minute), eliminating the previous :05 burst and two same-minute collisions. Dispatch windows are unchanged, so data freshness is unaffected. See Dashboard Data: Backfill and Freshness → Scheduled-search schedule.

docs.title: Enterprise Security enabled by default + AI Assistant prompt rework (build 249)
docs.text:
1. The 22 splunk_sap_logserv_es_* searches now ship enabled by default, reversing build 242’s disabled-by-default decision. They run on a re-staggered, collision-free schedule (no two enabled scheduled searches share an (hour, minute)): 16 correlation searches hourly in the disjoint minutes :29 / odd :31–:59, the 2 Asset/Identity feeds every 4 hours at :00 / :01, and the 4 behavioral-anomaly searches once daily at :02 (in the 0.1.1 line, build 315 moved them to :30, still in hours 02–05; see builds 315–316). To fit the collision-free schedule, eight correlation searches that ran every 5–15 minutes now run hourly (with matched 65-minute dispatch windows), and the four anomaly searches run daily instead of hourly — a daily run still evaluates every hourly bucket of the prior day, so no detections are missed. The content stays dual-mode (action.notable / action.risk no-op without ES). To disable or re-tune, see Enterprise Security → Disabling or tuning the ES content.

    Correction (2026-10-23): the ES content is not a no-op without ES. On a search head without ES the enabled searches still run: Splunk logs an error for each notable and risk alert action, which exist only with ES, and the scheduler skips the Risk Notable because the Risk data model is missing. On a search head without ES, turn the ES content off: see Disabling or tuning the ES content.

  2. The 13 ES AI Assistant Security-pack prompts were reworked to function as interactive prompts. Dispatched by name, they had been erroring on click ever since build 242 disabled their searches; enabling the searches fixes that, and the SPL was repaired — the anomaly_topology_edge_volume FATAL inputlookup … where error, the dead-constant is_business_hours / is_weekend off-hours fields (replaced with inline _time-based logic), the service_account_interactive field bug, and the structurally-empty after_hours_admin_data_access. The three 30-day anomaly prompts were converted to a daily cadence. Intent map bumped to v0.0.11.

docs.title: Dependency security hygiene — react-router 7.18.1 (build 252)
docs.text: Bumped react-router-dom from 7.14.2 to 7.18.1 (patched line) so dependency / SCA scanners no longer flag the App against GHSA-4hjh-wcwx-xvwj — a __manifest-endpoint DoS in react-router 7.0.0–7.14.x. The App was never exposed to it: it is a client-side single-page app served as static assets by Splunk Web and routed entirely by <HashRouter> (Declarative Mode, which the advisory explicitly exempts), with no React Router / Remix server runtime and therefore no __manifest endpoint. This is a hygiene bump only — no behavior change (routing was re-verified live across the index, settings, dashboard, and topology routes with zero errors).

docs.title: Whole-estate AI Assistant host prompts moved onto a KV-Store rollup (build 251)
docs.text: Four predefined prompts scan the entire estate by host — Top hosts by event volume, Noisiest hosts trend, Distinct hosts seen, and Hosts with the biggest event-volume drop. They were raw | top host / dc(host) / per-host-timechart full-scans, so on a large dataset they exceeded the AI Assistant’s 30-second request timeout at wide windows (e.g. Top hosts at −30 days took > 150 s and aborted with “signal is aborted without reason”). Build 251 rewrites all four to read from the existing logserv_hostdetails_rollup KV-Store rollup (hourly (host, bucket) counts), so each returns sub-second at any window — measured −30 d went from > 150 s (abort) to 0.6 s, and the dropdown window still drives the result. The reads are byte-exact to the original SPL (the rollup uses the same search-time host field, so the displayed hosts and counts are unchanged), and the rollup is the one that already powers the Host Details dashboard (no new collection or scheduled search). On a fresh install the prompts populate older windows once the Dashboard Data backfill has run, the same as every dashboard. See Predefined Prompts.

docs.title: AI Assistant prompt time-range dropdown now bounds the search (build 250)
docs.text: The Time range dropdown in the AI Assistant’s “Browse predefined prompts” window (Last 1h … Last 30d) now actually bounds the dispatched saved search. Previously the selected window was silently dropped, so every predefined prompt ran unbounded over the whole index through the Splunk MCP Server — on a large dataset this took minutes and the prompt timed out client-side with “Error: signal is aborted without reason.” The fix flattens earliest_time / latest_time to the MCP run_saved_search tool’s top-level arguments (where App 7931 expects them) instead of nesting them under an ignored arguments object. No fixed window is baked into the saved searches — the dropdown drives the time range end-to-end, and both the canned-prompt path and the AI-driven path are fixed. See Predefined Prompts.

docs.title: Azure queue-driven ingest (dedicated add-on)
docs.text: Azure ingest is the Azure twin of Splunk_TA_aws’s SQS-Based S3 input, and ships as a dedicated, first-party Heavy-Forwarder add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure), installed per-HF (not via the Deployment Server). Its sap_logserv_azure_queue modular input consumes Azure Event Grid → Storage Queue BlobCreated notifications, fetches each LogServ blob over a SAS, and emits its NDJSON via the native EventWriter, so events flow through the heavy forwarder’s index-time pipeline and reuse the LogServ Data TA’s existing sourcetype routing, Filters nullQueue, _time drop, and cloud_provider / splunk_solution stamping unchanged (it emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs and stamps _meta = cloud_provider::azure). It is stdlib-only (no Azure SDK, Splunk Cloud-clean) and inert until an input instance is configured. This is the model SAP’s LogServ-on-Azure collector uses (Storage Queue notifications), and it replaces the Splunkbase-add-on polling approach the original v0.0.5 Azure support used. Installing the input on the forwarder tier — with the SAS in the add-on’s own local/, never Deployment-Server-managed — makes Azure ingest symmetric with AWS and removes the per-host-secret-inside-a-DS-app fragility of earlier v0.0.6 iterations (the old system/local SAS dance + sas_token = ****** bundle invariant are gone). A per-instance index (default sap_logserv_logs) lets one HF run multiple Azure inputs; the emitted sourcetype is always sap_logserv_logs. Per-HF install + input configuration are documented in SAP LogServ on Azure — Setup Guide. AppInspect Cloud posture: 0 errors / 0 failures / 0 future_failures (the add-on’s stdlib-only modular input adds no gating findings; the input-removed Data TA returns to its 11-warning baseline).

docs.title: Multi-Cloud Overview goes three-way + Data TA gcp dropdown (build 253)
docs.text: Alongside the GCP add-on (below), the Multi-Cloud Overview dashboard was upgraded from a hardcoded two-provider layout to a full AWS / Azure / GCP split: a new GCP Events KPI + sparkline (the KPI row is now Total / AWS / Azure / GCP), a GCP column in the Top Sourcetypes table, and provider-neutral labels. This also fixes a latent bug for third-provider data: the Top Sourcetypes query hardcoded Total = AWS + Azure, which would have silently excluded gcp-attributed counts from the Total (single- and dual-cloud installs were unaffected — verified that a window with zero GCP rows still renders GCP = 0 with a correct Total). The dashboard’s “About the cloud_provider field” reference panel was rewritten (it still described a retired Azure ingest mechanism and linked to a non-existent in-app help URL; it now links to the published Azure/GCP Setup Guides). The Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown gains “Google Cloud Platform” (cloud_provider = gcp) as a fourth choice — see Choose Cloud Attribution.

docs.title: GCP notification-driven ingest (dedicated add-on)
docs.text: Google Cloud Platform joins AWS and Azure as a first-class ingest channel, via a dedicated, first-party Heavy-Forwarder add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp), installed per-HF (not via the Deployment Server). Its sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub modular input pulls a Pub/Sub subscription fed by the LogServ GCS bucket’s OBJECT_FINALIZE notifications, fetches each object with a Google service-account key, gunzips it, and emits its NDJSON via the native EventWriter — so events flow through the heavy forwarder’s index-time pipeline and reuse the LogServ Data TA’s existing sourcetype routing, Filters nullQueue, _time drop, and cloud_provider / splunk_solution stamping unchanged (it emits sourcetype = sap_logserv_logs and stamps _meta = cloud_provider::gcp). This is the same notification-driven model SAP’s own LogServ-on-GCP collector uses, and the same deployment shape as the Azure add-on. It is stdlib-only — Pub/Sub + GCS REST over urllib, with a pure-Python OAuth2 service-account token exchange (no Google SDK, no vendored dependencies) — so it is Splunk Cloud-clean and adds no third-party attributions. The general-purpose Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud Platform (Splunkbase 3088) was evaluated and does not fit: as of v5.0.3 its Pub/Sub-based bucket input cannot decompress the gzipped LogServ objects. The service account needs exactly the two roles SAP documents for its own forwarder (roles/pubsub.subscriber on the subscription + roles/storage.objectViewer on the bucket). Per-HF install + input configuration are documented in SAP LogServ on GCP — Setup Guide. AppInspect Cloud posture: 0 errors / 0 failures / 0 future_failures.

docs.title: Changed (user-visible panel shapes)
docs.text:
A few panels changed shape as a consequence of reading from hourly rollups instead of raw events:

  1. All response-time charts now show Avg + Max by hour instead of p50 / p95 / p99 percentiles. Averages and maxima roll up byte-exact across hourly buckets (Avg = Σsum ÷ Σcount, Max = max-of-per-bucket-max); percentiles cannot be merged across buckets. Affects Web and API Performance (“Response Time (Avg / Max) Over Time”, and the “Slow URIs / Slow Clients” tables now show a Max (ms) column in place of p95) and HANA Trace (“Operation Duration (Avg / Max)”).
  2. HANA Trace “Slowest SQL Operations” is now a top-operations-by-max-duration table (operation, max ms, avg ms, event count) — the per-event _time / host columns cannot survive an aggregate.
  3. Web Dispatcher “URIs by Request Count” dropped its “Unique Clients” column (a 3-dimension grain would explode at scale).
  4. Panels that remain raw (and are therefore unaffected): Network Perimeter “Suspicious Activity Indicator”, the DNS / Network-Perimeter beaconing tables, Web Dispatcher “Slowest Request Traces”, and Cloud Connector “Audit Log” — streamstats / per-event listings that cannot be rolled up byte-exact. (The beaconing and Slowest-Traces panels are now backed by per-day / per-hour rollups so they stay responsive to the time-range picker.)

docs.title: Fixed issues
docs.text:
While re-expressing panels, three pre-existing display bugs (all string-vs-number / match()-in-base-search predicate mistakes that silently returned 0) were found and fixed:

  1. Cloud Connector HTTP Error Rate — the KPI compared a string is_error field against the number 1 and was stuck at 0%; re-expressed as the status >= 400 fraction (now ~7.3% on test data).
  2. Change & Configuration “Password Change” / “User Change” KPIs — a Linux match(_raw, …) clause sat in base-search position where match() (eval-only) silently no-ops; moved to a post-base | where.
  3. icm_is_error predicate — the same string-vs-number trap (icm_is_error = 1 vs the field’s string "true") in the Environment Health severity rollup and the logserv_top_error_categories AI prompt; fixed to = "true".

docs.title: Third-party software attributions
docs.text: THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md was refreshed for v0.0.6 to add elkjs@0.11.1 (EPL-2.0, the Environment Topology layout engine), and builds 237–251 shipped it with 1236 unique top-level npm packages. Known gap: elkjs was never declared as a dependency in this line, so from build 252 the generator no longer found it. The final v0.0.6 build, 266, bundles elkjs unmodified, but its in-app notices list 1235 packages without the elkjs entry. The v0.0.6 source-tree root copy of the notices, and the shipped notices of v0.1.1 build 333 and later, carry the elkjs section with the full EPL-2.0 text. The file is generated from the build’s node_modules/ tree by yarn build and shipped at the root of the installed app directory, alongside the CycloneDX 1.4 SBOM.json. See Third-Party Software Licenses.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
1. The hourly rollup data layer means rolled-up panels are accurate to the most-recently-completed hour; sub-hour time-range selections (e.g. “Last 15 minutes”) read from the hourly buckets and so reflect completed hours rather than the live partial hour. Use the raw Search app (via the per-panel Open in Search toolbar action) for live sub-hour investigation. (Superseded by build 265: ranges under 90 minutes read raw events.)
  2. On a fresh install at high event volume, dashboards show empty until the first hourly aggregation runs or an admin runs the Dashboard Data → Run backfill step.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Before you upgrade, follow Upgrading to This Release.
  • What the current release changes: Release Notes: 0.1.2.

docs.title: Release Notes: 0.1.1
docs.text: This page lists what changed in the 0.1.1 line of Splunk for SAP LogServ, newest first. The 0.1.1 line was frozen on 2026-09-18, at App build 335, and receives no further changes; its work continues in 0.1.2. To upgrade from a 0.1.1 build, follow Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Splunk platform versions 9.4.3 and later CIM 5.0.0 and later (per app.manifest) Supported OS for data collection Platform independent Vendor products SAP LogServ for SAP ECS in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Published App artifact The full-LLM build variant — the free-form LLM path is present but inert until an LLM provider credential is configured; predefined prompts + MCP dispatch work with no credential (see Restricting the LLM Path) AI Assistant prerequisite Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) v1.0.3 or later and below v3.0.0 — the 2.x major is supported as of App build 335; v1.1.0+ recommended — on the search head where the LogServ App is installed Azure ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure), installed per heavy forwarder GCP ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp), installed per heavy forwarder

v0.1.1 = the LLM-capable source line, and the published tarball is the full-LLM build again

v0.1.1 is the LLM-capable source line, at full feature parity with v0.0.6 — the entire dashboard-performance data-layer rewrite (tstats + KV-Store rollups, backfill panel, staggered schedules), the Azure and GCP ingest add-ons, the three-way Multi-Cloud Overview, the Enterprise Security enable + re-stagger, and every AI Assistant fix (prompt repairs, the MCP time-range fix, rollup-backed host prompts). The source additionally carries the full LLM-driven AI Assistant (four vendor providers, free-form chat, Power Mode, privacy tiers, Provider Credentials). As of App build 335 the published v0.1.1 App artifact is the full-LLM build variant (see the build 335 entry), so those features are active once an LLM provider credential is configured; a compile-time templates-only variant of the same source remains available for restricted deployments. Everything in Release Notes: 0.0.6 is included in v0.1.1; that page maps the v0.0.6 builds 254–266 to the v0.1.1 builds they came from.

docs.title: Data TA — the days_in_past guard now fires at the prefix depth the screen recommends (2026-09-18)
docs.text:
The AWS S3 Direct screen blocks a key prefix whose events the forwarder’s own days_in_past filter would discard on arrival — the check that stops you creating an input which ingests nothing and reports success. It reads the date partition out of the prefix, and it required all six path segments (logserv/<clz_dir>/<clz_subdir>/<YYYY>/<MM>/<DD>/), while the screen’s own depth gate admits four and both its message and the field help recommend exactly four. An operator who followed the screen’s advice produced a prefix the guard could never evaluate — and the same blind spot silenced the SQS double-ingest warning for any prefix coarser than a single day.

The check now reads a year, month or day partition, and both callers reason about the newest instant the partition can contain:

  • a <YYYY>/ prefix wholly behind the cutoff now blocks, where it was previously accepted unexamined;
  • a prefix for the year still being written does not block on account of its January — deciding on the oldest instant instead would have produced exactly that false block;
  • a year-wide prefix now raises the SQS overlap warning it could not raise before;
  • a month out of range (2025/13/) and a day that would roll into the next month (2025/06/31/) are refused rather than silently widened to a date you never wrote.

The day-level message is word for word the one that already shipped, so nothing changes for a prefix that already worked. See AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

docs.title: Splunk MCP Server 2.x support, and the published artifact returns to the full-LLM build (build 335)
docs.text:
The AI Assistant refused to operate against Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) v2.0.0: a site that installed the current MCP Server saw an “uncertified version” panel in place of the Assistant. The App carries a deliberate upper bound on the MCP Server version — a supply-chain guard, because a major release is free to rename tools or reshape the request/response envelope, and the bound turns a silent degradation into a clear message. That ceiling moves from 2.0.0 to 3.0.0, so the whole 2.x major is now accepted. Unchanged: the v1.0.3 floor (CVE-2026-20205) and the fail-closed handling of an absent or unparseable version string. 3.x becomes the new ceiling.

What the change rests on is worth stating plainly. The connection handshake is verified against 2.0.0 in the field — the health probe reads the server version only after the connection succeeds, so seeing the “uncertified” panel at all proves that the transport, the authentication and the protocol handshake were accepted. The tool-listing and tool-call shapes have since been verified too, by a manual check against a live 2.0.0 server: the tool names the Assistant dispatches and the result envelope it reads were both unchanged by that major. Two bounds on that — it is a spot-check of 2.0.0, not an automated regression suite, and it says nothing about later 2.x minors. On a 2.x minor you are the first to run, run one predefined prompt and confirm the result tile carries data.

This build is also the point at which the published App artifact returns to the full-LLM build variant — see Restricting the LLM Path and the upgrade note in Upgrading.

docs.title: Data TA — the AWS S3 Direct screen, for backfill and recovery (2026-09-11)
docs.text:
The Data TA gains a screen — Splunk Web → Splunk TA for SAP LogServ → AWS S3 Direct — that creates and manages LogServ-scoped Generic S3 inputs inside the Splunk Add-on for AWS from the browser, as the signed-in user. It adds no Python, no REST handler and no capability of its own.

Generic S3 polls a bucket prefix directly, with no queue. It is a secondary channel — backfill, a bucket with no SQS notifications configured, and recovery after an outage — and SQS-Based S3 remains the steady-state path. The screen exists because the add-on’s own input form is effectively closed to most operators: its bucket dropdown is populated by list_buckets(), which requires the unscopable s3:ListAllMyBuckets.
