Three more forms are refused, because Splunk can read them differently from the App: a backslash outside double quotes (escaped_outside_quotes); the data macro written against other text, such as `sap_logserv_idx_macro`* or where`sap_logserv_idx_macro` (macro_position); and a quoted option value before a lookup name, or a quote glued to the name (lookup_not_allowed). With PII redaction on, Tier 2 now also reads makemv like rex, so the pieces it cuts from an event are redacted; withholds the time range when bin or bucket writes another field AS _time; reads stacked appendpipe groups in linear time, so a long query no longer freezes the tab; redacts the rollup columns operator, scope, error_detail and spl_filter_clauses, which were sent in clear; treats rhost, ruser, logname, euid, PWD, COMMAND, IpAddress, TargetUserSid, WorkstationName, Host Name and Account Name as identifiers; and withholds the numeric statistics of the IpAddress column in the Windows account-lockouts next-step search.
  • Redaction tags can no longer be reversed. A <redacted-…> tag is now a keyed hash (HMAC-SHA-256) under a random key the browser makes for each chat session and keeps in memory only. A value keeps one tag within a chat session, so the model can still count and compare, but tags of different sessions cannot be linked and nobody without the key can recover a value by hashing candidates — IPv4 addresses, short user names or SAP’s standard users. The raw-event samples of a Data Doctor report are redacted the same way, with one key per report. The tags look as before.
  • Claude 5.x models are priced, so their spend counts toward the daily cap. The cost estimate in each vendor_tier1 audit event now covers claude-opus-5-5, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-fable-5-1, claude-fable-5 and claude-haiku-5-5 at Anthropic’s published first-party rates, cache reads and writes included; until now these turns read $0.0000 and did not count toward daily_spend_cap_usd (default 50 USD). An admin whose users run Claude 5.x heavily may now see the cap reached; raise it in Settings if needed. The claude-sonnet-5 price was out of date and is corrected. claude-haiku-5-5 is estimated at its rate for prompts up to 100K tokens. Bedrock prices are unchanged; a model with no listed price still reports $0.
  • HANA trace severity descriptions. The descriptions of the HANA trace event severity trend and HANA trace ERROR events with context prompts now say what each severity means: standard trace lines carry INFO, WARNING or ERROR, and UNKNOWN counts the lines that have no trace level — continuation lines, backup.log entries, hdbcons command timings and the SQL trace, load and availability files — so a failed backup in backup.log is counted under UNKNOWN rather than ERROR (superseded by build 378, in which backup.log lines carry their own level, so a failed backup logged at ERROR counts as ERROR). The searches themselves are unchanged.

Dashboards

  • Environment Health’s Events/Day (Avg) is a per-day average again. Since build 345 the card averaged the chart’s time buckets instead of days: at Last 30 days it showed the average of 6-hour buckets, about a quarter of the true daily figure (a twenty-fourth at Last 7 days). It now counts whole days, as the Data Pipeline Overview card always has; days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, and the current partial day counts as a day. After the upgrade the figure rises accordingly; nothing needs to be rebuilt. The note under Chart buckets follow the time range, and crowded charts stop repeating colours (builds 345, 350–354) says the per-day-average KPI stays daily by design; for Environment Health that was not true until this build.
  • Time charts no longer call themselves daily. Forty chart descriptions on 18 dashboards said “daily” or “per day” while the charts draw 15-minute to 1-day buckets depending on the selected range. They now describe what is counted, two titles change (Event Volume Trend on Environment Health and Event Volume by Cloud Provider on Multi-Cloud Overview), and the Environment Health trend’s series and axis are named Events. Every time chart prints the bucket it actually draws in its subtitle, for example Proxy request count — span 6h. Summary-backed charts never draw buckets finer than an hour, so at Last 24 hours they say span 1h where charts counted from the index say span 15m. The new Chart Time Buckets section lists the bucket for each range.
  • Four DNS Analytics and Web Dispatcher charts draw hourly bars from the hourly summaries. At Last 24 hours, and on custom ranges from 90 minutes to 6 hours, DNS Analytics’ Clients - Request Volume and Requests by Record Type and Web Dispatcher’s Traffic by Status Code and Response Time Trend put each hour’s total into one 15-minute (or 1-minute) bucket and left the others empty: Web Dispatcher drew spikes about four times the real rate with zeros between them, and its average response time fell to 0 in three of every four buckets. They now draw one point per hour, like every other summary-backed chart. Ranges under 90 minutes still read raw events at 1-minute resolution. DNS Analytics’ two charts and the list of its client-IP filter now also follow the Cloud dropdown; they had shown every cloud whatever was selected.
  • Sparkline hover times follow your Splunk time zone. Hovering a KPI sparkline showed the day’s start in the browser’s time zone, while the sparkline’s days follow your Splunk time-zone preference, so a Central-time Splunk user on a browser set to another zone saw the wrong date and hour. The hover now shows the time in your Splunk zone. The Beaconing Domains sparklines on Environment Health, DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter count UTC days, because beaconing is detected per UTC day: each point now carries its UTC date and the hover shows it labelled (UTC day). Before, a user west of UTC saw each day under the previous date, and Environment Health drew up to three points a day when all clouds were selected. A day’s beaconing count is written once that UTC day has ended, so a UTC day that has not ended yet, drawn at 0 at the end of the DNS Analytics and Network Perimeter lines, is labelled (UTC day, not yet computed) instead of reading as a measured zero.
  • HANA Trace counts the components its tables show. Unique Components (the KPI, its sparkline and its raw-event version under 90 minutes) now applies the same filter as the Components table, so the KPI equals the table’s row count; it had also counted fragments of continuation lines such as of, service: and INFO. As in the tables, components of three characters or fewer stay hidden. Slowest SQL Operations is now Slowest hdbcons Commands, with the columns Command and Runs, and Operation Duration (Avg / Max) is hdbcons Command Duration (Avg / Max): the rows are the HANA console (hdbcons) commands the trace times, such as profiler stop or statreg print, not SQL statements.

Environment Topology

  • HANA audit connections from any loopback address (127.0.0.0/8) are now left out of the topology graph and its detail tabs. Before, only 127.0.0.1 was left out, so a client logged as another 127.x.x.x address appeared as a partner node. On the HANA audit data checked for this release every loopback client was 127.0.0.1, so the graph’s counts do not change.
  • The hostname and user lines on IP-labelled partner squares now ignore every loopback address (127.0.0.0/8) in all four kinds of evidence they draw on: HANA audit connections, Windows logons, the SAP start service and ssh logins. Before, only 127.0.0.1 was ignored. A loopback address names no remote machine, so such a line never identified one. Only the HANA audit evidence was checked for other loopback addresses. In the other three, a name line taken from an address such as 127.0.1.1 is no longer refreshed: like any name line whose address has gone quiet, it keeps its last values, shown with their date, until the one-year retention of the name data removes it.
  • HANA tenant edges and the HANA database roll-up in the node panel now label their duration figures as hdbcons command durations instead of SQL durations: they time the HANA console (hdbcons) commands recorded in the tenant’s trace files, the same timings the HANA Trace dashboard’s hdbcons panels show. The roll-up’s event count is now labelled Tenant trace events. The numbers themselves are unchanged.
  • The node and edge rollups no longer declare three fields that no search ever filled: the two ICM task measures on edges and a node health percentage. ICM task load is on the Work Process Performance dashboard, and node health is the three-colour call ring around each node, as before. Nodes look the same: the health-based colouring of the node outline never had a value to show.

Data Doctor

  • HANA trace files delivered without folder fields. SAP delivers some HANA trace files with no folder fields (clz_dir / clz_subdir), and the Data TA can route them to sap:hana:tracelogs by their file path. Folder filters do not reach these files, and the Data Doctor’s ingest-filter verdict now takes that into account. Trace events that keep arriving despite an Exclude Filters rule on hana/tracelogs are no longer reported as an out-of-date filter configuration, and such a rule is no longer reported as excluding all HANA trace data. On a HANA Trace panel, an Include Filters list that keeps the hana/tracelogs folder but drops these files is now named, together with the Include Sources entry that keeps them (/usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/*). The pasted configuration does not show whether SAP delivers such files to you, so this finding is listed after the panel’s main verdict, for example Never received or Summary not built, and never replaces it; panels that also read other log types do not report it. A verdict these files change reads Partly excluded? and is never more certain than possible, because the pasted configuration does not show whether your forwarders route the files this way either. On a HANA Trace panel its evidence explains how each filter treats them. Verdicts that do not involve sap:hana:tracelogs are unchanged.

Who is affected: deployments that use the AI Assistant’s free-form queries, Tier 2 or Claude 5.x models, and every dashboard user (chart descriptions, subtitles and four DNS Analytics and Web Dispatcher charts).

Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild: build 377 changes no rollup key. Check two things after the upgrade: a local/savedsearches.conf override of the search of an Environment Topology aggregation, backfill or IP-enrichment search keeps the old loopback filter, so remove it to take the shipped search; and if your users run Claude 5.x models, check the daily spend cap (daily_spend_cap_usd, Settings → AI Assistant → General), because their turns now count toward it. See Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: The ES feeds keep their inventory, the AI Assistant runs only its own catalog and sends no raw text in Tier 2 column names, and the topology edges are trimmed on their own (build 376)
docs.text:
• Enterprise Security asset and identity feeds. splunk_sap_logserv_es_asset_feed and splunk_sap_logserv_es_identity_feed each read all of their sources in one search instead of a | union of subsearches, which Splunk can stop early. A run that finds no rows no longer deletes its CSV: it writes with override_if_empty=false, and the last inventory stays in place. The rows are sorted without a limit (sort 0); before, an inventory of more than 10,000 rows was cut to 10,000. A run whose search window starts later than midnight six days ago (-6d@d) writes nothing, so an ad-hoc run over a short window cannot replace the 7-day inventory with a partial one; the REST dispatch shown in Asset & Identity Feed passes -7d@d and still writes. The threat-intel examples in Threat Intelligence Integration now write with override_if_empty=false as well.
  • The AI Assistant runs only the saved searches in its catalog. splunk_run_saved_search used to pass any name the model gave it to the Splunk MCP Server, so the model could have run a rollup aggregation, retention, backfill or ES feed — none has been seen in the reference system’s MCP log. The App now dispatches only the saved searches of its prompt library, checked where every saved-search call is sent; it builds the MCP arguments itself — the vetted name, the App and the time range — rather than forwarding what the model passes, and refuses a tool it does not define. Each saved-search call, predefined prompts included, now names this App as app (splunk_app_sap_logserv), so the Splunk MCP Server runs this App’s search and not a same-named one in another app; the argument was checked against Splunk MCP Server 1.1.0’s run_saved_search schema, and 1.1.0 or later is required. Free-form queries are checked against a longer list. The SPL guard is a denylist of known risky commands — every command it does not name passes — and until now refused collect, outputlookup, outputcsv, delete, sendalert, sendemail, script, run and tscollect after a |. It now catches each listed command at the start of the query and after a [ too, and adds collect’s aliases stash, summaryindex and sumindex; mcollect and meventcollect; outputtext, dump and createrss; runshellscript; rest (storage/passwords returns stored credentials decrypted); outputtelemetry and the third-party curl, wget and sendresults; the Machine Learning Toolkit’s ai (it sends the rows to an LLM) and deletemodel; and map and savedsearch’s aliases macro and savedsplunk. It refuses savedsearch and savedsplunk as words anywhere, the external lookup dnslookup (each row is a DNS query to an outside name server), a fit command followed anywhere later in the query by the word into (fit ... into saves a model), an SPL inline comment, an unmatched backtick, a double quote that is never closed, a backslash-escaped double quote outside a quoted string, and any macro other than the App’s own, since a comment, ambiguous quoting or another macro could hide a command. A command written with double or single quotes in it (| "delete", | de'lete') is refused too, and so is a forbidden word, dnslookup or into that quotes split (| "saved"search X, | lookup "dns"lookup, | fit X "in"to m): where Splunk’s reading of quotes is uncertain, the guard assumes the worst and refuses. Otherwise double-quoted text no longer counts as SPL structure: a quoted value that contains a pipe and a command, such as eval x="| collect index=main", was refused before and now passes. Custom commands and external lookups that other installed apps add are not covered unless the guard names them. A refused name or query is recorded as a security_blocked_spl audit event. This protects the App’s own assistant; other MCP clients holding a token are governed by the Splunk MCP Server’s own controls and Splunk permissions. See Security Architecture.
  • Splunk’s error text no longer reaches the AI vendor. When a tool call failed, the AI Assistant used to send the vendor up to 200 characters of the Splunk or MCP Server error message, in every tier. A Splunk error repeats the search that failed, and a subsearch can put event data into that search, so the message could carry event text. A failed call now reaches the model only as its HTTP status and one of ten fixed error classes, with a fixed hint the App writes, for example Tool error (HTTP 400, class=parse_error): Splunk could not parse the query; check the SPL syntax. The error text is shown to the user only. The full error stays in the result panel on the user’s screen. Refusals the App makes itself, before anything is sent, still give the model their reason, as Tool call refused by the App before it ran: <reason> (until now Tool error: <reason>); only instructions of your own that quote the old wording need updating. See Privacy Tiers.
  • Tier 2 column names and time ranges no longer carry raw event text, and with PII redaction on a value is sent in clear only when the App can trace it to a field that is not an identifier. The Tier 2 summary used to send every column name, and the minimum and maximum of _time, exactly as the search returned them. Both can be data: timechart, chart, xyseries and transpose turn the values of a field — user or host names — into column names, eval {f}=… can turn any event text into a column name, timechart count by user | stats sum(*) makes sum(jsmith), and eval can set _time to any text. Now a column name is sent only when Splunk generates it (count, percent, NULL, OTHER, a bare function name such as avg, …) or when every word in it — each run of letters, digits and _, matched whole and in the same letter case — appears in the text the model or the App wrote for that call: the model’s own query (splunk_run_query), or the SPL of the App’s catalog search that ran. Text the model or the App wrote tells the vendor nothing new. Such a name must also be at most 40 characters and shaped like a field name or a single fn(field) call, or be a display alias the text quotes after AS (rename sourcetype AS "Source Type"; words separated by single spaces). Any other name is shown as col_N, with PII redaction on or off, and the summary says how many names were withheld. So stats count as failures by host and table _time host process message keep their names, while split-by values the query did not type — timechart count by host, chart count over host by user, xyseries host user action — and sum(jsmith) are shown as col_N, even as a result’s only column. Values now fail closed. With PII redaction on, a text column’s values are sent in clear only when the App can trace the column through constructs it reads in full — the field by its own name, a statistics function over one field (nested included), field AS alias, a rename without wildcards, lookup … OUTPUT x [AS y], eval y=x with one bare or single-quoted field, or a count — to fields that mark no identifier. Every other column sends every value as a <redacted-…> tag: any other eval expression (. concatenation, any function, a literal), rex, spath, strcat, a wildcard rename or AS, a dynamic eval {f}=… target, the cells of a pivot (timechart values(src_ip) by user), transpose, untable and fieldsummary, a column a subsearch defines, and every column after a command the App does not read in full; a text over 20,000 characters, more than 256 commands or subsearches nested more than 8 deep leave every column untraced. Until build 375 a value was redacted only when its column’s own name matched a pattern, so values(user), rename user AS u or eval w=user."@".domain sent user names in clear. A pure count (count, dc(user), dc(host) AS affected_hosts) keeps its numbers, and a numeric column sends values withheld only when it is not a count and its name or a field it reads marks an identifier, or it mixes many fields. The cost: with redaction on, the computed text columns of some of the App’s own catalog searches now arrive as tags — the error Category, the cross-stack stack, the Cloud Connector uri_prefix, the SAProuter peer, the HANA trace message_preview, the data-freshness last_seen and the threat-intel queries — while their counts are unchanged. The redaction patterns now match after ., : and - as well as _ (Authentication.user, All_Traffic.src_ip, event.user) and treat the CIM src, dest and dvc (plurals, _host, fw_src, dvc_ip) as identifiers, since the App’s own field aliases put client IP addresses and host names there — so dest in the proxy top-denied-URLs search is now redacted. They also cover plurals (users, new_users, emails, src_ips, client_ips, dest_ips), remote_addr-style addresses, camelCase Windows names (TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, …Email) and, with the hostname opt-in, hosts and hostnames. With redaction on, a text column with an id-named source (user_id, employee_id, …) is redacted too, and a numeric one sends values withheld instead of its minimum and maximum. peer_ip, icm_peer_ip, a bare ip and peer are still not matched. The Tier 2 primer now tells the model what col_N, <redacted-…>, values withheld, not in row form and Time range: not shown mean, never to guess what a placeholder or a tag stands for, and to re-query with stats … by <field> when it needs readable values. The time range is sent only when every _time value is a timestamp, written by the App as ISO-8601 UTC and marked (UTC); otherwise it reads not shown. At most 30 columns are summarized. A single-valued numeric column whose name is withheld, or that is not a count and marks an identifier or mixes many fields, sends values withheld whatever the redaction setting. A search that returns no rows now reads Returned 0 rows in both tiers: Tier 1’s count is now the number of result rows, not the number of items in the content list of the MCP reply, so with the Splunk MCP Server it no longer reads Returned 1 rows whatever the search returned. A reply in which the App finds no rows is sent in Tier 2 only as Returned a result that is not in row form, never summarized as a column. A side effect: a column whose name neither Splunk, the catalog search nor the model’s query wrote — a field the search returns without naming it, or a column of an inputlookup the search does not list — appears to the AI as col_N; the AI can relate it to its query by position (the primer tells it never to guess which value a col_N column stands for), and the tiles are unchanged. These pages used to say that no event data reaches the vendor in any tier; Tier 2’s top-N values are field values from the events by design, and Privacy Tiers now says exactly what each tier sends. Tier 1 still sends two numbers per call, a count and a timing; the pages now say how many bits a model that writes its own queries can learn from them.
  • Known gaps in the Tier 2 change. The App’s reading of the model’s query is not yet complete. A few constructs (a _time the query sets, a stray apostrophe, rex groups written (?'name'…), fieldformat, echo lookups, appendpipe) and some of the App’s own identifier fields can still carry a value to the vendor in Tier 2, and a positional top 10 … loses its readable values (write top limit=10 …). Each case is listed in Privacy Tiers; they are to be closed in a later build. Where no event value may reach the vendor, use Tier 1. (Superseded by build 377, which closes these gaps; what remains is listed in Privacy Tiers.)
  • Environment Topology edges retention. The graph’s edges are now trimmed by their own search, logserv_topology_edges_retention, at 02:36 search-head time; logserv_topology_retention keeps 00:34 and trims the nodes only. The edges trim used to run inside a subsearch of the nodes trim, and Splunk limits how long a subsearch may run, so on an estate with many edge rows the trim could have been stopped before it finished. Every retention search now reads and writes one collection in a search of its own, and the nightly retention window ends at 02:36 (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36).

Who is affected: deployments with Enterprise Security or the AI Assistant, and estates with many Environment Topology edge rows.

Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild. If your upgrade method does not keep the App’s lookups/ directory, dispatch the two ES feeds once after upgrading, so ES is not left without their CSVs; remove a local/savedsearches.conf override of the search of logserv_topology_retention; and keep long backfills clear of the nightly retention window, which now ends at 02:36. See Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: A restart just before the nightly retention can no longer empty a rollup (build 375)
docs.text:
Each rollup’s retention search reads its collection once a night, keeps the last 365 days and writes the result back over the whole collection (00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34 in the search head’s local time; superseded by build 376, which ends the window at 02:36). By default Splunk’s outputlookup empties a collection when the result is empty, and right after a Splunkd restart the KV Store can still be starting up and return no rows, so a restart shortly before a retention ran could empty that rollup. Every retention search now writes with override_if_empty=false, and an empty result leaves the collection as it is. Only three had it before — the Data Doctor’s saved-reports and platform-snapshot retentions and the topology IP-enrichment retention; the other 26, which trim the dashboard rollups and the Environment Topology graph and detail collections, did not.

One thing changes: a collection whose rows are all older than 365 days — a rollup whose aggregation has been switched off for more than a year, for example — keeps them until new rows arrive, and the next nightly run then trims them. Meanwhile its History in Settings → Dashboard Data shows more than 365 days; Clear there still empties a collection at any time.

Who is affected: every deployment: a Splunkd restart shortly before the nightly retention could empty a rollup.

Upgrade action: nothing to rebuild. Check Settings → Dashboard Data for a rollup an earlier build emptied this way, and backfill it. A search override for a logserv_*_retention stanza in local/savedsearches.conf takes precedence over the shipped search and keeps the old behaviour: remove it, or add override_if_empty=false to each outputlookup it runs. See Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Firewall drops at the host and in transit (build 374)
docs.text:
The kernel firewall log records two kinds of drop. IN_DROP is a packet addressed to the host itself (the INPUT chain). FWD_DROP is a packet the host was routing on to another system (the FORWARD chain); only hosts that forward traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways, log it. The Firewall Drops KPIs counted only IN_DROP, while the Blocked tables (Blocked Sources on Linux, Blocked Source IPs on Network Perimeter, and Blocked Destination Ports on both) already counted both, so a source could show more drops in a table than the KPI showed in total. On the reference instance FWD_DROP made up 92% of the real firewall drops.

  • Linux and Network Perimeter show Firewall Drops at Host and Firewall Drops in Transit side by side, and their Blocked tables split each row into At Host and In Transit / Other. Network Perimeter reads its in-transit count from the Linux dashboard’s summary data, so it shows 0, or undercounts, for any period the Linux rollup has not summarised: its aggregation turned off, or those days not backfilled.
  • Settings → Dashboard Data labels that rollup’s row Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter, naming both dashboards that read it, as it does the other shared rows; the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen shows the same label (see the Data TA entry of 2026-10-01 below).
  • Linux’s Firewall Drops Over Time charts the two chains. It used to chart every linux_secure line, firewall or not.
  • Environment Health still counts only drops at the host as errors; its KPI, Security Error Trend series and Affected Hosts column now say so.
  • The AI Assistant’s two firewall prompts say which drops they count, and its system prompt names the real kernel tags, IN_DROP and FWD_DROP.

Build 374 was not released; its changes reached customers in build 375.

Who is affected: deployments with Linux firewall logs, above all hosts that forward traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways.

Upgrade action: none: no summary data changes.

docs.title: The late-arriving data check runs every day (build 373)
docs.text:
The Late-arriving data check also runs every day at 05:40 (search-head time) as the saved search logserv_late_arrival_check, and records a triggered alert (Activity → Triggered Alerts) when it finds a day whose events are not all in the rollups — so a late delivery is reported even if nobody opens Settings → Dashboard Data. Add an alert action to be told by email. It never judges an hour older than the Multi-Cloud Overview rollup’s oldest, so a new install raises no alert before its first backfill, and it reads the rollup without a subsearch, so Splunk’s subsearch limits cannot invent late days on a large estate.

Who is affected: every deployment: late deliveries are now reported as triggered alerts.

Upgrade action: none. To be told by email, add an alert action to logserv_late_arrival_check.

docs.title: Late-arriving events reach the dashboards (build 372)
docs.text:
SAP LogServ data reaches Splunk through S3, Azure Blob and GCS queues, and some of it arrives after its hour has been aggregated. Each hourly aggregation used to read its hour once, a few minutes after the hour ended, so an event indexed later was never counted on any rolled-up panel at a range of 90 minutes or more. On the reference instance, 1.4% of the real Azure events arrived after the earliest aggregations had read their hour, and a weekly linux_secure delivery arrived up to a week late, which left the Linux System & Security firewall counts 18% short over 12 days. Every hour-bucketed rollup now re-reads the hour before as well (-2h@h..@h): events up to about an hour late are counted, and an hour whose aggregation was skipped is rebuilt by the next run. Each hourly aggregation reads two hours, so it takes about twice as long. Anything later is listed by Settings → Dashboard Data under Late-arriving data — the days on which the index holds events the rollups do not, over the last 30 days — and Backfill N days rebuilds exactly those days. See Dashboard Data → Late-arriving data.

Build 372 was not released; its changes reached customers in build 373.

Who is affected: every deployment whose LogServ data arrives after its hour has been aggregated.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Time charts fill their panels (build 371)
docs.text:
A row of panels is as tall as its tallest panel, usually a table. A time chart beside one kept its fixed 280 px and left an empty band below it — for example Average Response Time on Cloud Connector, Firewall Drops Over Time on Linux, and Bandwidth Over Time by Domain (Top 5) and Response Time (Avg / Max) on Proxy. Every time chart now grows to the full height of its panel, on every dashboard. A chart is never shorter than before, and a panel that had no empty band looks the same.

Who is affected: every dashboard user.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Dashboard Data measures history a few rollups at a time, and says when it could not (build 370)
docs.text:
The History column of Settings → Dashboard Data comes from one small search per rollup collection. The panel used to send all 27 at once, and every one Splunk did not answer with a result — because its search slots were taken, as they often are just after a backfill — showed the same — as a rollup that had not been measured, which read as missing data. The checks now run three at a time; one that Splunk turns away or does not answer is tried again after 2, 4 and 8 seconds; and a check that still measures nothing reads check failed — re-check, with the reason on hover. A banner offers to re-check all of them, and such a row no longer counts as needing a backfill. A check whose search ran but failed — a missing lookup definition, for example — used to read empty; it reads check failed too.

Who is affected: admins who use Settings → Dashboard Data.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Two Dashboard Data rows name the dashboard that shares them (build 369)
docs.text:
ABAP Operations has no rollup of its own: it reads the one Work Process Performance reads. Web Dispatcher reads the Web & API Performance rollup as well as its own Slowest Traces row. Settings → Dashboard Data now labels those two rows Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations and Web & API Performance / Web Dispatcher, so every dashboard can be found in the list; the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen shows the same labels (see the Data TA entry of 2026-09-28 below). The rollups themselves are unchanged.

Who is affected: admins who use Settings → Dashboard Data.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Downloaded images show the help icon upright (build 368)
docs.text:
Actions → Download PNG and Download PDF copy the page’s styles as they are at that instant, so the help icon’s square at the right of a dashboard’s title row came out at whatever angle it had - tilted whenever the download was clicked while it was turning (4 seconds in every 12). The page’s animations now rest at their start while the copy is taken and carry on where they were afterwards: the square is upright and spinners are still in every download.

Who is affected: users who download dashboards as PNG or PDF.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Pacemaker lines name their own product (build 367)
docs.text:
On the Pacemaker cluster log that the linux:slapd sourcetype also carries, vendor_product and app said OpenLDAP and slapd. They now say Pacemaker and pacemaker; slapd.log lines keep OpenLDAP and slapd (on the reference system 1,932,656 Pacemaker lines and 1,462,405 slapd.log lines). No dashboard or saved search of the App reads the two fields; searches of your own that filter on them see the change.

Who is affected: searches of your own that filter linux:slapd events on vendor_product or app.

Upgrade action: none. Update searches of your own that filter on these two fields.

docs.title: The Data Doctor knows both folder layouts (build 366)
docs.text:
Real LogServ deliveries file some logs under different paths per cloud (see the Data TA entry of 2026-09-25 below). The Data Doctor’s filter diagnosis now maps Squid to proxy/squid and linux/proxy, the Pacemaker cluster log to linux/slapd and linux/pacemaker, and /var/log/messages also to linux/proxy, so a rule that names only one layout is reported as dropping part of the log type, not all of it.

Who is affected: Data Doctor users with Azure or GCP data.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Password statements in any letter case, readable statements, and the right Start Service and cluster fields (build 365)
docs.text:
More differences between real SAP LogServ data and the demo data, measured on the same feeds:

  • HANA Audit’s Password Management recognised password statements in lower case only, so upper-case CREATE USER … PASSWORD *** (480 real events) and ALTER USER … DISABLE PASSWORD LIFETIME (432) counted as Other. They are now Password Change and Disable Lifetime. The HANA Audit rollup keeps the old classes until it is rebuilt; the rebuild Upgrading asks for after build 364 covers it.
  • Statements read as in the database. A statement that quotes identifiers kept real ingest’s JSON escapes (grant \"HEC_HANA_MONITORING\" to NAGIOS); the SQL Statement column and the command field now show grant "HEC_HANA_MONITORING" to NAGIOS.
  • Start Service source location. source_location now reads file names that contain a dot ([nixxi.cpp 464], [CIMPlugin.cpp 999]), which it had missed on most real GCP events, and no longer takes the thread marker [Thr 12] for a location.
  • Pacemaker cluster log. Where the cluster runs, the linux:slapd sourcetype also carries /var/log/pacemaker/pacemaker.log. Its os_user field held a cluster resource or a scheduler function, never a user — and slapd.log lines name no user at all — so the field is gone. Pacemaker lines now carry resource_agent and cluster_resource (SAPHanaController(rsc_SAPHanaController_A44_HDB02)) or pacemaker_daemon and pacemaker_function (pacemaker-schedulerd[…] (determine_op_status)).
  • Squid’s other two files. The App knows the Data TA’s new squid:cache and squid:store sourcetypes (see the Data TA entry below): neither gets automatic key=value fields, as before, and the Data Doctor maps both to the proxy/squid filter path.
  • The upgrading note on Settings → Dashboard Data names the rebuilds that build 364 needs.

Who is affected: deployments with HANA audit, SAP Start Service, Pacemaker or Squid data. Saved searches, alerts and reports of your own that read os_user, command, sql_statement or source_location see the new values.

Upgrade action: coming from build 363 or earlier, the rebuild listed for build 364 covers this; see Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Real SAP LogServ data parses the way the dashboards expect (build 364)
docs.text:
Earlier builds were validated on the generated demo data, which stores log text decoded. Real LogServ ingest keeps the JSON escapes of the source record in the event (\", \n, \t, \\), and some real logs use formats the demo data never produced. Measured on the reference system’s real Azure, GCP and AWS feeds:

  • Proxy Analytics extracted nothing from real data. SAP LogServ proxy logs use Squid’s logformat=splunk_recommended_squid key=value form, which earlier builds did not parse: none of 7,003 real proxy events in 30 days yielded a domain, client, status or byte count, so Proxy Analytics, the Network Perimeter proxy panels and the threat-intel proxy search saw request counts only. The App now parses that form as well as Squid’s native format. The proxy panels also count access-log lines only: Squid’s store.log and cache.log lines share the sourcetype but are not requests (43% of the real feed’s proxy events, 69% of the demo data’s).
  • HANA Audit found a status only for connect-type actions. The action status and target principal are now read by their position in the record, for every action (before: 5.6% of the real feed, which is mostly ALTER FUNCTION). User and privilege statements are recognised in any letter case and when quoted, and audit_datetime parses the Z time zone real records carry (it was empty on every real event).
  • Six more fields. The sudo command keeps the whole command, with sudo’s line wrapping joined and the escapes removed; lastlog reads user names containing - and console logins (4,046 of 115,627 real lines had been missed). Four more were proven on a JSON-escaped copy of the demo data, as real data for them is not on the reference system: the Cloud Connector HTTP version, the ABAP gateway error detail, the Start Service and Host Agent error message, and the HANA Trace slowest-operation name now end where the line does in both forms.

Build 364 was not released; its changes shipped in build 365, which was the current build for under an hour, and in build 366.

Who is affected: every deployment with real SAP LogServ data. Rollups keep the values they stored before, and saved searches, alerts and reports of your own that read these fields see the new values.

Upgrade action: coming from build 363 or earlier, Clear and then Backfill Proxy Analytics, HANA Audit and Cross-Stack Authentication in Settings → Dashboard Data, then Backfill five more rows without Clear; Upgrading to This Release names them.

docs.title: The upgrading note names all three rebuilds, the AI Assistant panel opens below the header, and a narrow window keeps the full width (builds 361–363)
docs.text:
• The upgrading note on Settings → Dashboard Data now names Beaconing detection beside Change & Configuration Activity and Linux System & Security; it had left out the Beaconing rebuild that build 356 requires (build 361).
  • The AI Assistant panel now opens directly below the two-row header and moves up with it as the page scrolls. It had kept a fixed offset sized for Splunk Web’s app bar, which the App hides, so the open panel covered the right end of the header’s second row — including the AI Assistant button that closes it (build 361).
  • The header’s Actions button is the same height as Refresh and AI Assistant beside it; it had been 3 px taller since the header became two rows (build 362).
  • In a narrow window the App no longer shrinks to a strip. Below about 880 px Splunk Web’s own top bar wraps its menus onto a second line, and the App was laid out in the space left beside that line — 118 px wide at a 720 px window; it now starts below the line at full width (build 363).

Build 361 was not released, and build 362 was the current build for about an hour before build 363 replaced it.

Who is affected: admins who use Settings → Dashboard Data, AI Assistant users, and users with narrow browser windows.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Smaller fixes (builds 358–359)
docs.text:
• The rollup retention searches’ descriptions give the right time, stated in the search head’s local time; 23 of 29 had named the wrong one after the schedules were re-staggered (build 358).
  • KPI sparkline tooltips stay inside their card at both ends of the line (build 358).
  • In dark mode the browser draws its own dark scrollbars and form controls (build 359).

Who is affected: every user.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Three rollups count correctly — rebuild each once after upgrading (builds 356–358)
docs.text:
These fixes change what is stored, so rows written by earlier builds stay wrong until the rollup is rebuilt with Clear and then Backfill in Settings → Dashboard Data.

  • Beaconing detection (build 356). Each day was keyed on midnight in the time zone of the search that wrote it — the scheduled job used the search head’s, a Settings backfill the signed-in admin’s. Where the two differed, a day could be stored twice, and the Beaconing Domains KPI summed both: 1,777 against 1,103 over 30 days on the reference system. Days are now UTC calendar days.
  • Change & Configuration Activity (build 357). The after-hours flag was stored in the rollup, classified in the writer’s time zone, which inflated Total Change Events and After-Hours Changes by about 24% over 30 days on the reference system. After-hours is now worked out when you view the dashboard, in your own time zone.
  • Linux System & Security (build 358). Kernel Event Types counted fragments of ordinary words — the first capital of a sentence-case message (“Write cache…” became W) — and tags cut short at a digit (EXT4 became EXT). Only genuine all-caps tags of two or more characters count now.

Who is affected: deployments whose search head does not run in UTC, or where an admin in another time zone ran a backfill from Settings (Beaconing detection, Change & Configuration Activity), and deployments with Linux kernel logs.

Upgrade action: Clear and then Backfill each row once: Beaconing detection coming from build 355 or earlier, Change & Configuration Activity coming from build 356 or earlier, and Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter coming from build 357 or earlier; see Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Dashboard Data backfills a chosen window, and waits as long as a job runs (builds 353–360)
docs.text:
Settings → Dashboard Data could backfill only the last 30 days, although every rollup keeps 365. It now offers 30, 60, 90, 180 or 365 days, or a custom UTC date range. A window longer than 31 days runs in monthly chunks; a start more than 365 days back is refused, because the rollups’ retention would delete what it wrote; and a window over 90 days shows a cost warning first. The two flat Environment Topology collections are always refreshed from the last 30 days, whatever the window.

The panel no longer gives up on a job that is still running: a row is marked failed only when Splunk reports the search failed or gone. When the panel itself stops waiting — Cancel, 15 minutes without contact, or 24 hours — the row reads still running on server, with the search IDs on hover. “Failed” and “truncated” marks survive the refresh after a run, and a finished row shows refreshing… until its new depth appears. The window hint now points at the matching Scan from / Scan until dates on the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen (build 360).

Keep long backfills clear of the rollup retention windows — 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34 in the search head’s local time (superseded by build 376, which ends the window at 02:36) — or re-run the affected rows afterwards: a retention search rewrites its whole collection and erases rows a concurrent backfill has just added. For scale, a 365-day backfill of every row took 195 minutes on the reference system.

Who is affected: admins who backfill Dashboard Data.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Chart buckets follow the time range, and crowded charts stop repeating colours (builds 345, 350–354)
docs.text:
Ninety-five chart time spans across 18 dashboards were fixed at one day. They now scale with the selected range: a Last 24 hours chart draws 12–100 points with time-of-day ticks where it drew two. Sparklines and the per-day-average KPI stay daily by design (build 345). (Correction: on Environment Health the per-day-average KPI averaged the chart’s buckets until build 377; see that entry.)

A chart that draws more series than its palette ramp has colours now switches to the 11-colour categorical palette instead of reusing colours — seven dashboard charts had drawn two different series in the same colour. A chart with more than 11 series still cycles the 11 colours. In the AI Assistant, pies never use severity shades, and a pie whose largest slice is 85% or more of the total, with at least three slices, is drawn as a horizontal bar so the smaller categories stay readable. Windows “critical” no longer shares “high“‘s red, and the HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW risk tiers read red, orange and blue (builds 350–354).

Who is affected: every dashboard user.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Navigation moves to a left rail, with a two-row header and the Cisco Magnetic palette (builds 338–349)
docs.text:
The App takes on the Cisco Magnetic “Workbench scaffold” look: in dark mode a navy page with a blue accent, in light mode higher text contrast, and chart colour ramps that follow the palette (build 338).

The top-bar menus give way to a collapsible left rail, 244 px wide or 56 px with icons only. Each category opens its sub-menu beside its own row, and the sub-menu closes on any navigation, on Escape or on a click outside it. The current dashboard carries a check mark and its category stays lit. The rail’s collapsed or expanded state is remembered per user in the browser; the Environment Topology view opens with it collapsed; and below 860 px the rail floats over the page instead of taking width. Settings (admins only) and About move to the bottom of the rail, below a divider. The header becomes two rows — the brand, the App version and build pills and the light/dark toggle, then the time-range preset pills (Last 24h, 7d, 30d, 90d) beside Splunk’s own time-range picker for any other range, with Actions, Refresh and AI Assistant at the right. Splunk Web’s app bar is hidden (the Splunk bar stays), and a gradient backdrop sits behind the dashboards (builds 339–349).

Panel headers wrap their controls to a second row instead of overflowing the narrower content area, and Splunk tables no longer scroll sideways (build 347).

Who is affected: every user.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Data TA (splunk_ta_sap_logserv)
docs.text: Builds of the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ, which parses, routes and filters LogServ data where it is parsed: on the heavy forwarders or a single instance.

docs.title: Data TA - a newer Splunk Add-on for AWS and a search head are no longer blocked (build 1792598960, 2026-10-21)
docs.text:
• The AWS S3 Direct screen accepts the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.1.0 and any later version. It compared the add-on’s version with a list of validated versions, 8.1.0 alone, and warned about any other, 8.3.0 included. Only a version older than 8.1.0 now gets that advisory.
  • A configuration the screen cannot read is reported, not taken as empty. When the add-on answers a read of its accounts, IAM roles or Generic S3 inputs with an error or without a list (a newer version may serve it at another endpoint), the screen names each request with its HTTP status and what that status most likely means, and shows the configuration to apply instead of creating inputs; the AWS account or the IAM role becomes a typed field where its list could not be read. An unread SQS-Based S3 input list is reported as a warning only. Such a failure used to read as an empty list: No AWS accounts are configured hid the form, and an unread input list let a backfill reuse an existing input name or read days an earlier backfill covers. With the input list unread, the form now says so, and the generated stanzas and REST calls carry the same note. Create backfill re-lists the inputs before it creates anything, and now creates nothing when that list cannot be read; it used to go ahead as if no input existed.
  • No gates on a search head or Splunk Cloud. On Splunk Cloud the screen was read-only, and on an instance with no enabled AWS input it held the form behind a confirmation. Both are warnings now, with a strong recommendation to create the inputs on the heavy forwarder that already collects your LogServ data; nothing is blocked, and the messages for a missing or disabled add-on point to the heavy forwarder first. See Running the TAs on a search head.
  • A list of apps or indexes the screen cannot read no longer stops it. When it could not read Splunk’s list of apps it said The Splunk Add-on for AWS is not installed; it now reads the add-on’s own lists and carries on if they answer, and otherwise says it cannot tell. When it could not read the list of indexes, or the list was empty, it left the Index field empty and stopped at An index is required.; it now says so and lets you type the index, filled in as sap_logserv_logs and checked against Splunk’s index naming rule.
  • The account list has a second source. The screen reads the add-on’s accounts from its combined account list, which the add-on’s current API reference no longer lists, and now falls back to the account endpoint that reference documents; with version 8.1.0 both return the same accounts.
  • The daily filter refresh runs on a deployment client that holds the Data TA directly, such as a search head that gets other apps from a Deployment Server. It used to skip on every deployment client. It now skips only where the Deployment Server delivered the Data TA, or where the instance’s serverclass.xml is missing, unreadable or lists no app; that last skip is logged as a warning.
  • README.txt recommends heavy forwarders strongly and says a search head is not blocked.

transforms.conf and props.conf are unchanged, so parsing, routing and filtering are those of build 1792189743, and nothing has to be saved again after the update.

Who is affected: deployments that use the AWS S3 Direct screen, above all with the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.3.0 or later, on a search head or on Splunk Cloud, and instances that hold the Data TA directly while getting other apps from a Deployment Server.

Upgrade action: update the Data TA where LogServ data is parsed, and on a search head that runs LogServ inputs. With a Deployment Server, install it on the Deployment Server, replace its deployment-apps/ copy and click Deploy to Forwarders; do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages, because the next push replaces that copy. See Updating the Data TA. Nothing has to be saved again.

docs.title: Data TA - every rule reads the whole line, and the ICM route takes only the ABAP folder (build 1792189743, 2026-10-16)
docs.text:
The Data TA’s metadata rules (host, source, clz_dir, clz_subdir) and its 34 sourcetype routes now read up to 100,000 characters of a line (LOOKAHEAD = 100000, as TRUNCATE and the filter rules do); every earlier build read the first 4,096. The AWS envelope puts the log text (_raw) first and the envelope keys after it, so an AWS event longer than about 4 KB kept the input’s own host and source, got no folder fields and stayed sap_logserv_logs: the dashboards, the folder filters and the sourcetype parsing missed it. Azure and GCP envelopes put the keys first and were not affected.

  • The rules stay linear at the new window. The seven routes that check both folder fields (abap/audit, abap/icm, abap/sapstartsrv, hana/tracelogs, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs, sap/sapstartsrv) now use the shape the filter rules already use; the (?s)^(?=.*...)(?=.*...) form of build 1791935359 would exceed Splunk’s regex match limit near 100,000 characters. The HANA trace route for events without folder fields walks the line token by token, with the same matches as before. The four BIND routes keep a path segment inside the source value, so a long line cannot push them past Splunk’s recursion limit, and the Windows and sssd routes keep their channel or file name inside it too ([^"]* where they had .*, which ran on into the log text). Every route and metadata rule was run through Splunk 9.4.3’s own regex library as a search over lines just under 100,000 characters in the AWS, Azure and GCP key orders, with long runs, escaped quotes and decoy keys, runs of slashes and Unicode line separators in the log text: each matched exactly as expected, with no limit message. Lines up to 4,096 characters route as before.
  • The ICM route takes only the ABAP ICM folder (abap/icm). It took every folder named icm, so a Web Dispatcher’s own ICM trace (webdispatcher/icm, a Secondary folder of the LogServ service description, not seen in real deliveries) became sap:abap:icm; it now keeps sap_logserv_logs, like the Web Dispatcher’s other Secondary folders. Events indexed earlier keep their sourcetype.
  • The AWS S3 Direct screen lists sap/saprouter for both Environment Topology rows, which read SAP Router data since App build 378.
  • The two scheduled scripts log by level. The filter upgrade check and the time-filter refresh wrote every line to the error stream, which splunkd records in splunkd.log as an ERROR of component ExecProcessor, INFO lines included. INFO lines now become the scripts’ own events (index=_internal sourcetype=splunk_ta_sap_logserv:filter_check or sourcetype=splunk_ta_sap_logserv:filter_time_refresh); warnings and errors still reach splunkd.log.
  • Third-party notices and exact pins. The add-on ships THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md, naming the nine Python packages in its lib/ folder with their licenses, and lib/requirements.txt pins each one’s exact version and PyPI file hashes, so a rebuild cannot pick up a newer release unseen. The bundled libraries are byte-for-byte those of build 1791935359. README.txt now describes the add-on.

The change takes effect where the Data TA parses LogServ data, on the heavy forwarders or a single instance; events indexed earlier keep their sourcetype and fields, and nothing has to be saved again. If you added the six (?s)^ routes to the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf as a test (Capacity Planning and First Start), remove them before you update: local/ would keep the old REGEX together with the new 100,000-character window, a combination that exceeds the match limit.

Who is affected: AWS deployments with events longer than about 4 KB, deployments with a Web Dispatcher ICM trace, and anyone who reviews the add-on’s third-party content.

Upgrade action: first remove any routes you added to the Data TA’s local/transforms.conf. Then update the Data TA where LogServ data is parsed. With a Deployment Server, install it on the Deployment Server, replace its deployment-apps/ copy and click Deploy to Forwarders; do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages, because the next push replaces that copy. See Updating the Data TA. Nothing has to be saved again.

docs.title: Data TA - six routing rules are tried once per event, not at every character (build 1791935359, 2026-10-13)
docs.text:
Six of the Data TA’s sourcetype routes, for abap/audit, abap/sapstartsrv, hana/tracelogs, scc/audit, scc/tracelogs and sap/sapstartsrv, check two folder keys at once with a pattern such as (?=.*"clz_dir":"abap")(?=.*"clz_subdir":"audit"). Without a ^ at its start, the regex engine tries such a pattern again at every character of an event it does not match, and each try reads to the end of the first 4,096 characters, so the work for one event grows with the square of its length. Each route fails to match nearly every event, so the six ran this way on almost every LogServ event a heavy forwarder parsed. Splunk’s regex match limit counts the work of each start position on its own, so it never stopped these searches and nothing was logged.

The six routes now start with (?s)^, so each is tried once per event. The (?s) keeps the routing as it was: in Splunk’s regular expressions . stops at a carriage return, vertical tab, form feed or a Unicode line or paragraph separator as well as at a line feed, and the forwarder ends an event only at a line feed or carriage return, so with a bare ^ such a character in the log text ahead of the folder keys would have left an event unrouted. With (?s)^ a route matches whenever both folder keys are in the event’s first 4,096 characters: it routes every event it routed before, no event in the real LogServ data checked changes sourcetype, the filter rules are not affected, and nothing has to be saved again after the update. On Splunk 9.4.3’s own regex library, measured at search time on generated LogServ events of 460 to 4,160 characters, anchoring made the six routes 179 to 1,778 times faster, with the same result for every event, and the (?s) costs nothing extra; the gain at index time on a forwarder is still to be measured. Every Data TA version from 0.0.4 on carries these routes. The change takes effect where the Data TA parses LogServ data, on the heavy forwarders or a single instance, once this build is installed there. To size heavy forwarders and measure the cost per event on your own, see Capacity Planning and First Start.

Who is affected: every heavy forwarder or single instance that parses LogServ data.

Upgrade action: update the Data TA where LogServ data is parsed. With a Deployment Server, install it on the Deployment Server, replace its deployment-apps/ copy and click Deploy to Forwarders; do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages, because the next push replaces that copy. See Updating the Data TA. Nothing has to be saved again.

docs.title: Data TA — the Filters tab filters by source file, and its rules read the whole line (build 1791565776, 2026-10-09)
docs.text:
The Configuration → Filters tab gains two fields, Include Sources and Exclude Sources. They match the event’s whole source value — the log file’s path, such as /var/log/zypper.log, or a name such as ps — with * for any run of characters (/ included) and ? for one character, case-sensitive; an entry can be limited to one folder, as in linux/linux_secure=/var/log/zypper.log. Exclude Sources drops log files that share a folder with a Primary log type without dropping the folder: zypper and YaST2 arrive in linux/linux_secure beside the firewall, kernel, sssd, lastlog and who logs (2.1 million /var/log/zypper.log lines in six weeks of real data on the reference system). Include Sources keeps files that an Include Filters allow-list would drop, including events that carry no folder fields at all — Unix command output such as ps and netstat, and HANA trace files, about 19.9 million real Azure events on the reference system. Both fields are empty by default, so nothing changes until you fill them in. Exclude Sources always wins, like Exclude Filters. See Configuring Filters for the order the rules apply in, and Filter Recipes for allow-list, deny-list and shared-folder settings.

The existing filters are fixed in four ways:

  • Wildcards stay inside the value, whatever the Python version. The Data TA built its patterns with Python’s fnmatch, which let a * run past the end of the value into the rest of the line: linux/c*n also matched linux/cache whenever a later value in the line ended in n. The text it generated also differed between Python versions. A * now matches only within the value it stands in, and the generated text is the same on every Python version. Patterns with several * also run in linear time: each * but the last stops at the first place the text after it fits, so the work on a long value no longer multiplies with every *. What a pattern matches does not change.
  • Rules read the whole line. An index-time transform reads only the first 4,096 characters of a line unless told otherwise. In the AWS envelope the log text comes before the source, clz_dir and clz_subdir keys, so on a line whose log text ran past about 4,000 characters the folder keys were out of reach: an Include Filters allow-list dropped the line and an exclude missed it. Every generated filter stanza now sets LOOKAHEAD = 100000, the longest line the Data TA indexes, and the patterns skip over the log text, which keeps them within Splunk’s regex match limit on lines that long — raising LOOKAHEAD alone would have made the old patterns fail there.
  • The AWS S3 Direct screen’s filter preview matches the way the forwarder does. The screen leaves out folders the forwarder’s filters would drop, and it compared pattern text by prefix: with Filtering on and the default Include Filters */* it left out every folder, and a pattern such as */cron matched nothing. It now applies the same wildcard rules and the include-everything rule below, and, because a source rule acts on single files rather than folders, says where source rules may drop or keep some of a folder’s files.
  • */* or * anywhere in Include Filters keeps everything. Only */* or * on its own used to switch the include gate off; mixed with other entries, they did not.

Behaviour change: an Include Filters value that mixes */* or a standalone * with other entries now keeps every event. Before, */*, linux/cron dropped every event without folder fields, and a standalone * beside other entries was ignored, so *, linux/cron kept only linux/cron — although the upgrade notification already treated both lists as covering every log type. To keep an allow-list, remove */* and * from it. With Filtering on, a save that sets Include Sources while Include Filters includes everything is refused, because the entries would have no effect.

The Data TA writes the new rules when the filters are saved, or when the daily refresh rewrites them (with Days in the Past above 0). After updating the Data TA, open Configuration → Filters, click Save, and on a Deployment Server click Deploy to Forwarders, so the forwarders get the regenerated rules. The upgrade notification still reads Include Filters only; source rules neither raise nor clear it.

Smaller changes to how the tab is saved:

  • Days in the Past is read the same way by the Save and by the daily refresh. A value such as 7.0 is refreshed every day like 7. A saved value that is not a whole number is logged by the refresh as an ERROR that names the field, and the rules generated last stay in place.
  • An empty Days in the Past field means no time filter, as the settings file stores it — the same as 0.
  • Every field is checked on every save, also with Filtering off: a value with a line break, a tab or another control character, or one ending in a backslash, is refused.
  • A save through the REST API or the CLI that sends only some fields generates the rules from the saved values of the fields it leaves out, not from their defaults.

The App’s Data Doctor reads the source rules, and the new form of the folder rules, from App build 377 on, which follows this Data TA build. App build 376 and earlier ignore source rules, read a pasted transforms.conf that holds only source rules as filtering with everything included, and report folder patterns with * or ? as only partly read. See Reading the Active Filter Configuration.

The same Data TA build changes two things outside the Filters tab:

  • HANA trace files delivered without folder fields get the sap:hana:tracelogs sourcetype. On the reference system all of the real HANA trace data — about 566,000 events from one Azure HANA system — arrived in a storage folder named undefined/undefined, without clz_dir and clz_subdir, so the route keyed on the hana/tracelogs folder never matched it and it stayed under sap_logserv_logs. A new route takes the .trc files and backup.log of /usr/sap/<SID>/HDB<nn>/<host>/trace/ and of its DB_<tenant>/ subfolder by their source path, and only when the event has no folder fields; an event that has them is routed by its folder as before. The route assumes that these deliveries carry no clz_subdir key at all: an event that carries the key, even empty, keeps the sourcetype it had. That could not yet be checked on a raw delivery, because the reference system’s Azure access has been unavailable since 2026-10-01. Events indexed earlier keep sap_logserv_logs. Routing adds no folder fields, so folder filters still cannot keep or drop these files: Include Filters hana/tracelogs does not keep them — use Include Sources or Exclude Sources /usr/sap/*/HDB??/*/trace/*. About half of these lines — backup.log, the hdbcons timings, the SQL trace and load files and the system_availability file — are not in the trace-line format the App’s HANA Trace extractions read, so the HANA Trace dashboard shows them with severity UNKNOWN. From this build on, the HANA system these files come from also appears in the other places that read sap:hana:tracelogs: the Environment Topology, with an edge to each tenant whose DB_<tenant>/ trace folder is delivered, and the Enterprise Security asset feed. The other data delivered without folder fields, Unix command output such as ps and netstat, stays unrouted; see Data Delivered Without Folder Fields, which also explains why you may want to drop it.
  • The daily time-filter refresh reloads the server class in the app that holds it. On a Deployment Server with Filtering on and Days in the Past above 0, the daily refresh sends the new time cutoff to the heavy forwarders by reloading the SAP_LogServ_HeavyForwarders server class. Until this build it sent that reload without an app namespace, so whether it found the server class depended on the default app of the user the refresh runs as; when it did not, the refresh logged a WARNING and the forwarders kept the previous cutoff — keeping older events, not dropping more — until the next Deploy to Forwarders. The refresh now reads which app holds the server class and reloads it there, falls back to the search app and then to the old form, and logs which one worked. With the reload working, each heavy forwarder in the server class restarts about once a day to apply the new cutoff, because the server class the Data TA creates maps it with restartSplunkd = true. With Filtering off, or Days in the Past at 0, the refresh changes nothing. See Configuring Filters → Days in the Past.

Who is affected: deployments that use the Filters tab, and deployments with HANA trace files delivered without folder fields.

Upgrade action: update the Data TA where LogServ data is parsed, as Updating the Data TA describes; with a Deployment Server, install it on the Deployment Server and replace its deployment-apps/ copy, not the forwarders’ copies. Then, with Filtering on, open Configuration → Filters, click Save (on the Deployment Server, or on each instance without one), and on a Deployment Server click Deploy to Forwarders, so the forwarders get the regenerated rules. An Include Filters value that mixes */* or a standalone * with other entries now keeps every event.

docs.title: Data TA — the AWS S3 Direct Dashboards list names Network Perimeter on the Linux row (build 1790896064, 2026-10-01)
docs.text:
The Dashboards list labels the Linux row Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter, as the App’s Settings → Dashboard Data does: Network Perimeter’s Firewall Drops in Transit count reads that row (see App build 374 above). The row reads the same S3 folders as before.

Who is affected: users of the AWS S3 Direct screen.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Data TA — the AWS S3 Direct job name says what is wrong (build 1790610339, 2026-09-28)
docs.text:
A job name the screen refuses now gets one message per rule it breaks — for example Job name is 35 characters long; the limit is 24. or Job name has an underscore; use a hyphen instead. — where one message used to list every rule. The field’s help no longer shows how the screen names the inputs it creates, which read as a pattern for the job name itself. The Dashboards list shows the App’s labels for the two shared rows (see App build 369 above).

Who is affected: users of the AWS S3 Direct screen.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Data TA — the filter paths real LogServ data uses (build 1790374045, 2026-09-25)
docs.text:
The Data TA declares which folder paths each log type arrives under; the filter’s coverage warning, the App’s Data Doctor and the AWS S3 Direct screen all read that list. Checked against real deliveries, two layouts differ from it: the AWS bucket files Squid under proxy/squid, but Azure delivers it under linux/proxy; and GCP delivers the Pacemaker cluster log under linux/pacemaker and a proxy VM’s /var/log/messages under linux/proxy, where the list named only linux/slapd and linux/messages. The Data TA now declares both layouts — nothing that matched before stops matching, and routing is unchanged. With Filtering on and an include list that names only the older paths, the coverage warning now lists linux/pacemaker and linux/proxy, because events under them are dropped at the forwarder. The AWS S3 Direct screen reads both Squid folders and linux/pacemaker; a folder a bucket does not have gives an input that finds nothing.

Who is affected: Azure and GCP deployments with Filtering on and an explicit include list.

Upgrade action: with Filtering on and an explicit include list, add linux/proxy and linux/pacemaker where those logs should be kept; see Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Data TA — Squid’s cache and store logs get their own sourcetypes (build 1790374045, 2026-09-25)
docs.text:
The Data TA gave all three Squid files the sourcetype squid:access, although only access.log holds requests: cache.log is the daemon’s own log and store.log the object-store journal. On the reference system the two made up 43% of the real feed’s proxy events, counted by any search that takes every squid:access event for a request, and tagged for the CIM Web data model. The Data TA now routes cache.log to squid:cache and store.log to squid:store; access.log stays squid:access. All three keep the proxy/squid filter path, so filter rules need no change and no upgrade warning appears. Events indexed before the update keep squid:access; the App’s proxy dashboards count access.log lines only and are correct either way. Saved searches of your own that read those two files under squid:access need the new names. On the reference system, real cache.log lines from the Azure feed arrive as squid:cache after the update, still carrying the splunk_solution and cloud_provider stamps and no automatic fields, while access.log lines stay squid:access.

Who is affected: deployments with Squid proxy logs, and saved searches of your own that read cache.log or store.log under squid:access.

Upgrade action: update those searches to squid:cache and squid:store; see Upgrading to This Release.

docs.title: Data TA — the S3 Direct scan checks find the add-on’s log (build 1790345882, 2026-09-25)
docs.text:
Each backfill’s Did its inputs finish their scan? search, and the check for all backfills below the list, grouped the Splunk Add-on for AWS’s log lines by log_level. The add-on (8.1.0) writes level=, and stats … by drops every event whose group-by field is empty, so both searches returned no rows even for a backfill that had run. They now group by level, falling back to log_level and then to (none), so a line in any log format is counted. On the first real-data backfill — HANA audit logs for 2026-01-01 and 2026-01-02, 794 events — the old search returned nothing and the new one returns the input’s 187 log lines, all INFO.

The troubleshooting search in the three AWS setup guides had the same flaw: log_level IN (ERROR,WARN) matched nothing, because the add-on writes level and names the warning level WARNING. It now reads level IN (ERROR,WARNING); on the reference system it finds 408 errors and 126 warnings over 30 days, where the old form found none. The step-by-step lists in those guides now render as lists; they had rendered as code blocks, bold markers and all.

Who is affected: users of the AWS S3 Direct screen and of the AWS setup guides’ troubleshooting search.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: Data TA — long NDJSON lines are unwrapped and kept whole (build 1790292318, 2026-09-24)
docs.text:
Each LogServ line arrives wrapped in an NDJSON envelope, and the index-time transform [set_raw_only] keeps only its _raw string. On long lines carrying many escaped characters — from about 1.5 KB, common in some Azure-delivered logs — the transform’s regex exceeded Splunk’s PCRE depth limit, and the event was indexed with its envelope still on (about 400 events an hour on the affected forwarder). Lines longer than 10,000 bytes were also cut by the default TRUNCATE, which took their timestamp with them when _raw came before _time.

[set_raw_only] now uses a possessive pattern that finds the same match at bounded depth; TRUNCATE = 100000 on [sap_logserv_logs] lets lines up to 100,000 bytes through whole; and LOOKAHEAD = 100000 on [set_raw_only] lets the transform reach the end of such a line — an index-time transform searches only the first 4,096 characters by default and misses a longer match silently. Since the fix the heavy forwarders log no regex errors and no truncations, no event arrives wrapped, and the longest line seen (about 52 KB) indexes whole. The fix applies to data parsed after the Data TA is updated on the heavy forwarders; events indexed earlier keep their envelope.

Who is affected: deployments with long NDJSON lines, common in some Azure-delivered logs.

Upgrade action: update the Data TA where LogServ data is parsed. With a Deployment Server, install it on the Deployment Server, replace its deployment-apps/ copy and click Deploy to Forwarders; do not install it directly on a forwarder that the Deployment Server manages, because the next push replaces that copy. See Updating the Data TA. Events indexed earlier keep their envelope.

docs.title: Data TA — AWS S3 Direct backfills by dashboard (build 1790292318, 2026-09-24)
docs.text:
The AWS S3 Direct screen no longer asks for a key prefix. You pick the Dashboard Data rows to backfill — the same 25 rows as the App’s Settings → Dashboard Data — and Scan from / Scan until as UTC dates, inclusive and at most 366 days apart. The dates select the date folders in the S3 key, not the objects’ upload time. The screen creates one Generic S3 input per folder and year, limited to the chosen days and set to stop by itself 24 hours after it is created; it skips days its own earlier backfills already cover, and it leaves out folders or days the TA’s filters would discard on arrival, saying why. The list groups the inputs by backfill job, with Enable all, Disable all and Delete all, and two searches per job: one shows whether its inputs scanned, the other counts the events they indexed. After creating a backfill, backfill the same rows and dates in the App so the dashboards pick the events up. Prefer Disable to Delete: a deleted backfill no longer counts as covering its days.

Inputs created here are stamped cloud_provider = aws through the Data TA’s own endpoint, /services/splunk_ta_sap_logserv/s3_direct_meta — POST only, run as the signed-in user, and limited to the inputs this screen names. Enable and Disable go through the add-on’s own endpoint. The Data TA published on 2026-09-20 made both calls to the add-on’s native data/inputs/aws_s3 endpoint, which Splunk Web does not pass through, so from the browser its Enable/Disable failed and no input was stamped. Tested with the Splunk Add-on for AWS 8.1.0. See AWS S3 Direct: Backfill and Recovery.

Who is affected: users of the AWS S3 Direct screen.

Upgrade action: none.

docs.title: LogServ Azure and GCP Add-ons (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure, splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp)
docs.text: Builds of the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure and on GCP, which run the queue and subscription inputs.

docs.title: Azure and GCP add-ons - a search head is an allowed target (builds 1792558069 and 1792558072, 2026-10-21)
docs.text:
Both add-ons’ app.manifest now declares the search-head workload (_search_heads, and search head clustering) beside the forwarders, so a search head is an allowed target for them. Installing them on a Splunk Cloud search head has not been tested. A heavy forwarder stays strongly recommended: an input puts its ingest load on the instance that runs it. README.txt and the Inputs page say so, and README.txt describes search head clusters, which do not replicate inputs: an input runs only on the member where it was created. Their code is unchanged: every Python file is byte-for-byte that of builds 1792213309 and 1792213464. See Running the TAs on a search head.

Who is affected: deployments that want to run the Azure or GCP input on a search head.

Upgrade action: none on a heavy forwarder that runs builds 1792213309 and 1792213464: the code is unchanged.

docs.title: Azure and GCP add-ons - third-party notices and exact pins (builds 1792213309 and 1792213464, 2026-10-17)
docs.text:
Both ingest add-ons now ship THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md, naming the nine Python packages in their lib/ folder with their licenses, and their lib/requirements.txt pins each package’s exact version and PyPI file hashes, so a rebuild cannot pick up a newer release unseen. Their code is unchanged: every Python file, the add-ons’ own and those of the bundled libraries, is byte-for-byte that of the previous 0.1.2 builds, so a heavy forwarder running those needs no update. README.txt now describes each add-on correctly; the GCP add-on’s described Azure’s resources and input. See Third-Party Software Licenses.

Who is affected: anyone who reviews the add-ons’ third-party content.

Upgrade action: none: the code is unchanged.

docs.title: AWS templates - the Copy Lambda runs on Python 3.12, and the Lambda code bucket has no default (2026-10-23)
docs.text:
• The Copy template’s Lambda runs on Python 3.12. splunk-logserv-remote-s3-copy.yaml created its forwarder function on python3.9, which AWS deprecated on 2025-12-15: AWS no longer applies security patches to it, and blocks creating python3.9 functions from 2027-07-29 and updating them from 2027-08-31. The template now uses python3.12, as the Filter template already did. The function’s code is unchanged.
  • LambdaCodeBucket has no default in the Filter and Copy templates. The default, splunk-logserv-lambda-binary, named a bucket that only one AWS account can own, because S3 bucket names are global. Create a bucket with a name of your own, in the Region of the stack, upload the Lambda ZIP file to it, and enter its name; CloudFormation now asks for it. See the Filter and Copy guides.

Who is affected: customers who deploy the Filter or Copy template, and existing Copy stacks.

Upgrade action: an existing Copy stack keeps python3.9 until you update it: update the stack with the current template and keep the existing parameter values. Against the previous template, the only resource change is the function’s runtime; its code and the bucket it is read from stay the same. Existing Filter and Copy stacks need no change for LambdaCodeBucket: a stack keeps the value it was created with.
